h: Purpose of the Study (why I wrote this book)
t:
This book has two goals. First, it gives a full and fairly easy-to-use description of Shipibo-Konibo. This is a Panoan language spoken by about 30,000 people. They live along the Ucayali River and its main side rivers in the Peruvian Amazon. Part I describes the sounds of the language, how its words are built, how its sentences are put together, and how people use it in longer stretches of speech. It uses fairly standard linguistic ideas and terms. A grammar of Shipibo-Konibo (from now on also called SK) is long overdue. It has many speakers for an Amazonian language. The Panoans of the Ucayali met the Spanish-speaking world early. SK is important for the study of the Panoan languages, and these in turn help us understand the languages and cultural history of native South America. At the same time, Part I gives the reader the background needed for the detailed topics in the second half of this book.
Part II looks closely at a few topics in how SK builds words and sentences. These topics all have to do with one idea: whether a verb has only a doer, or a doer and a receiver. Where I could, I looked at each topic from two sides: what it does and what form it takes. I also compare it with other languages of the world. In some cases I compare it with related languages and suggest how it developed over time.

h: Purpose of the Study (why I wrote this book)
t:
In Panoan languages, one idea matters more than almost anything else: what kind of verb you have. There are intransitive verbs, like ‘sleep’ or ‘fall’, which only need someone doing the action. And there are transitive verbs, like ‘cut’ or ‘hit’, where someone does something to someone else. In SK, almost every bare verb is born as one type or the other. To switch a verb to the other type, you must add a special ending. This difference affects the whole sentence. It decides which people in the sentence get the doer marker and which appear in the plain form. It also decides which “stand-in” verbs you use (like English do in “I did”), which form of certain verbs and endings you pick, and which helper verbs for ‘begin’ or ‘finish’ you use. It also decides the “for someone / against someone” endings that show feelings. Finally, the type of the main verb decides which ending must appear on the other verbs of the sentence. These endings tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. The type of verb also changes the endings on some extra words in the sentence, such as words saying how or where something happened.
Other languages in the world have some of these features too. Some Aboriginal languages of Australia have a doer marker. They also put endings on extra words in the sentence, depending on the type of verb (Austin 1988, Austin 1995, Austin and Bresnan 1996, among others). In Dulong / Rawang (a Tibeto-Burman language), helper verbs must match the type of the main verb (LaPolla 2000). In Tzotzil (a Mayan language), the ending that brings in an extra person only works with verbs of a certain type (Aissen 1983). And Tukanoan languages have different “stand-in” verbs for verbs with one, two or three people

h: Purpose of the Study (why I wrote this book)
t:
(Johnson and Levinsohn 1990). Still, some things may be found only in SK and other Panoan languages. These include the details of these patterns and how they connect to the rest of the language. They include the ways they may have grown over time. They include finding all of them together in one language. And they include how often people use them when they really speak. Look at the two sentences below. In (1), the verb rete-anan- is an intransitive verb: the ending -anan turned ‘kill’ into ‘kill each other’, so there is no receiver left. In (2), rete- ‘kill’ is still a transitive verb. The words in italics show the different endings that each type of verb calls for:
(1) Ja-ska-r[a]-ai-n peo-kot-ax-kaya-ki i-káti-kan-ai | Shipibo-bo betan Kashibo-bo-ki rete-anan-i. | ‘It is said that because of this, the Shipibo and the Kashibo began to fight against each other.’
(2) Ja-ska-r[a]-ai-n peo-xon-kaya-ki a-káti-kan-ai | Shipibo-baon Kashibo-bo-ki rete-kin. | ‘It is said that because of this the Shipibo began to kill the Kashibo.’
I hope that looking closely at these topics will help in several ways. It will help record Shipibo-Konibo and the other Panoan languages. It will also help linguists who build theories about language, who compare languages, and who study how languages change. In some cases, what I describe will support ideas linguists already hold. In others, it will show those ideas are wrong or need changes. For example, without

h: Purpose of the Study (why I wrote this book)
t: this book, someone could claim the following rule. If a language puts matching endings on extra words in a sentence, it also puts matching endings on the words inside a noun group (like matching the, big and dog) (Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann, to appear). As far as I know, this book shows the only known case where that rule does not hold.

h: Organization of the Study (how the book is laid out)
t:
Here is how this book is laid out. In the rest of this first chapter, I give an overview of the Shipibo people and their language. I also introduce the Panoan family of languages. Then I explain the general approach I take, the methods I used, and the data I worked with.
Chapters 2-14 describe SK grammar. Topics that get their own chapters later are dealt with more briefly here. Chapter 2 describes SK using well-known ways of classifying languages. It also previews its main features. Chapter 3 covers the sounds of the language and how sounds change when word pieces meet. It also introduces the spelling used in Chapters 4-19. Chapter 4 explains the ways SK builds words, and Chapter 5 gives an overview of its types of words. Chapters 6 and 7 describe nouns and verbs and the word groups built around them. Chapter 8 describes how simple sentences are built.
Chapters 9 and 10 look at sentences made of several parts, each with its own verb. Chapter 9 covers chains of such parts, and the SK markers that tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. Chapter
10 covers parts of a sentence that are turned into nouns. These include “who/which…” description parts, parts that tell what someone says or wants, and parts that tell when, why or how. Chapter 11 looks at joining sentence parts of equal rank, with meanings like ‘and’, ‘or’ and ‘but’. Chapter 12 brings together patterns from earlier chapters to discuss who does what to whom in a sentence. This part of the book ends with markers that show how the speaker knows something or how sure they are, and with some notes on how longer stretches of speech are organized.

h: Organization of the Study (how the book is laid out)
t: Chapters 15-20 make up the second part of this book, where I look at a few topics in depth. Chapter 15 gives a general picture of intransitive verbs and transitive verbs in SK. Chapters 16 and 17 look at ways to add a person to a verb: the ‘make someone do it’ ending and the endings that bring in an extra person. Chapter 18 looks at ways to take a person away, with endings meaning ‘to yourself’ and ‘to each other’. Chapter 19 describes a special SK feature: endings on extra words that match the people in the sentence. Chapter 20 looks at this feature across the Panoan family. It reconstructs what these endings looked like long ago and outlines how this interesting feature may have developed. Finally, Chapter 21 sums up the main findings of the book.

h: The Shipibo People (who the Shipibo are)
t: Most speakers of Shipibo-Konibo (I explain the origin of the hyphenated name below) see themselves as ethnic Shipibo. This section covers Shipibo territory, way of life, and history.

h: Location (where they live)
t:
The Shipibo, or Jonikon ‘Core People’, are a Panoan ethnic group. They live in the Peruvian Montaña, roughly between six and ten degrees south latitude and seventy-four to seventy-five degrees west longitude. Within Peru’s political divisions, the roughly 130 Shipibo villages are in the Departments of Ucayali (Coronel Portillo Province) and Loreto (Ucayali Province), and a few in the Department of Huánuco (Puerto Inca Province). There is also a small group of Shipibo in the Department of Madre de Dios. They were forced to move there during the “rubber boom” and stayed.
Other Panoan peoples nearby are the Kapanawa and Amawaka to the east of the Shipibo, and the Kashibo-Kakataibo to the west. Non-Panoan neighbors are the Tupian Kokama to the north, and several Arawak groups to the west and south (Amuesha, Asheninka, Ashaninka, Machiguenga, and Piro) (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1986:2). Map 1 shows the general location of Shipibo territory.

h: Demography (how many people there are)
t:
People do not agree on how many Shipibo there are. Recent estimates range from 16,085 (Instituto Nacional de Estadística e Informática 1993) to as many as 40,000 (Tournon and Cauper 1994:30). Indigenous organizations and social researchers say the last Peruvian national census (Instituto Nacional de Estadística e Informática 1993) counted far too few Shipibo. The real number may be close to 30,000.
Even so, the Shipibo are by far the largest Panoan people. They are the third largest people of the Peruvian Amazon, after the Ashaninka (Arawak family) and the Aguaruna (Jivaroan family) (Instituto Nacional de Estadística e Informática 1993).

h: Habitat (the land and rivers they live in)
t:
Unlike other Panoans, the Shipibo are mainly river people. Most of them live along the winding Ucayali River, its main side rivers, and its ox-bow lakes. In fact, the Shipibo see themselves as kikin Paro ibo ‘the very owners of the Ucayali’. The Ucayali is a white-water river 1,900 kilometers (1,200 miles) long. It forms where the Tambo and Urubamba rivers meet; these flow down from the southern Peruvian Andes. Near Iquitos, the Ucayali joins the Marañón River, and together they give birth to
the upper Amazon. Some have claimed that river cultures depended much more on farming the floodplain than cultures living away from the rivers. So river cultures tended to stay in one place, live in larger groups, and build more complex societies (Meggers 1971).
The Ucayali area is a floodplain about 170 meters above sea level on the central Ucayali. “To the east lies the Contamana Range; to the west are the highlands stemming from the peaks of the Azul and Ventanilla mountains and further south are the foothills of the Andes” (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1986:1).
There are two clear seasons. The fairly dry season, or baritia ‘sun season’, runs roughly from April to September. The rainy season, or jenetia ‘flowing water season’, runs from October to March. In late August or early September, only about ten percent of the Shipibo area is under water. At that time, travel by canoe is hard, but fishing is easiest. At the height of the rainy season, as much as ninety-nine percent of Shipibo territory may be under water (Bergman 1974:210, Roe 1982:33-34).

h: Shipibo, Konibo, and Xetebo (the three groups that formed the Shipibo-Konibo)
t:
As I said above, the Shipibo call themselves Jonikon. The word comes from joni ‘people’ and ikon ‘core, true, real’. Other Panoan peoples, such as the Kashinawa and some Yaminawa and Amawaka subgroups, use forms of this word too (Erikson et alia 1994:6). In the past, the Jonikon saw themselves as three different
ethnic groups: Konibo, Eel Ones; Shipibo, Tamarin Monkey Ones; and Xetebo, Rinahuis or Buzzard Ones. Before they merged, the Xetebo lived farthest north on the lower Ucayali, the Konibo farthest south on the upper Ucayali, and the Shipibo in between.¹
According to Trudell (1993:93), the Shipibo have always been the largest and strongest of the three groups. But this does not match what Brinton (1891:289) wrote. He said that near the end of the 19th century the Konibos were the largest Panoan tribe, making up “the greater part of the natives the traveller encounters on the Ucayali.” Shell (1975:26) also says that more people speak Konibo than Shipibo. The Konibo have always been very close to the Shipibo in culture and language. Today the line between the two groups has almost disappeared because so many have married each other (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1986:1). The Xetebo population shrank greatly over the last two centuries because of disease and war. What was left of them joined Shipibo society through conquest and marriage. It has been reported that the Xetebo felt ashamed to be called Xetebo and preferred to be called Shipibo (Shell 1975:26). Today, these three once-separate groups form a single people who call themselves “Shipibo.” The Shipibo and Konibo merged only in the last few decades. It has been reported that as late as the 1960s, the Konibo were offended to be called Shipibo,

Because of this history, written sources up to the first half of the 20th century describe the languages of these groups separately. The joined name Shipibo-Conibo (or Shipibo-Konibo) was made up later. Today, some Native speakers, especially from the Lower and Middle Ucayali, prefer to call their language simply Shipibo.

h: On the Origin of the Name Shipibo (where the name "Shipibo" comes from)
t:
Below is an English version of a story that explains where the name Shipibo comes from.³
Long ago, the people now called Shipibo lived in small settlements of three or four houses, where close relatives lived. Various diseases affected the Native people then, but they had learned how to control them. One day, however, a family group heard someone coming, playing drums. At first they thought it was a group sent by a neighboring family to invite them to an Ani Xeati (a girl’s puberty ceremony). But when they reached the shore to welcome the
During a stay in a village on the upper Ucayali (Nuevo Nazareth del Pozo, also known as Paro Toro Jema) in December 1990, I spoke with a middle-aged man I had taken to be “Shipibo.” He explained to me that he was really a “kikin Konibo,” that is, a ‘true or legitimate Konibo.’
I thank Pesin Rate (Rosa Pinedo) and Yoi Sani (Luis Márquez Pinedo) for sharing this story.
visitors, they could not see anybody. The family soon realized that the newcomers were evil winged spirits with horrible faces and huge ears. They had brought a new and very dangerous disease, later known as the chami disease. Sitting on the roofs of the houses, the evil spirits watched the sick people suffer from vomiting and diarrhea. The people did not know how to fight the chami disease, and many of them died. Then the evil spirits left the settlements, planning to return the next year. Afraid of the chami disease, the people decided to live in larger settlements.

h: On the Origin of the Name Shipibo (where the name "Shipibo" comes from)
t: One day, a great shaman saw in his ayahuasca vision that the chami spirits were coming back, and he hurried to warn the others. He gathered them in a large house and said these words: “The Tamarin people spread themselves over the earth!” With these words the great shaman turned the people into tamarin monkeys (shipi in Shipibo-Konibo), which at once started to climb the trees. Then the great shaman hid himself under a big jar. When the chami spirits arrived, they could not find anybody. They thought no people were left alive in the settlements, so the evil spirits left for good. At that moment the great shaman came out and turned the tamarin monkeys back into people. This is how the Shipibo survived the dangerous chami disease and got their name.

h: Subsistence Activities (how people make a living: farming, fishing, hunting, crafts)
t:
The Shipibo live mainly from slash-and-burn farming, fishing, hunting, gathering, and making pottery and handicrafts. Fish are probably the most plentiful and varied animals with backbones in the region. The Shipibo know a great deal about fishing and hunting in the water (Tournon 1995:27, 37). Hunting and gathering matter more in villages higher up along the smaller rivers that feed the Ucayali.
The main crops grown by the Shipibo are plantain, maize, yuca, beans, squash, peanuts, sugarcane, and rice (usually for selling). They also grow fruit plants, trees and palms, such as pineapple, watermelon, papaya, and lemon. A Shipibo field (chacra) also has plants that are not eaten. These include achiote (Bixa orellana) and huito or jagua (Genipa americana), which give red and black dyes; ishanka (fam. Urticaceae), used to ease pain; and tobacco, which men and women smoke in pipes and also sell at the market (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1980:13-14).
Making pottery and handicrafts is mainly women’s work. These goods are made both for home use and for sale. Sometimes the Shipibo also cut timber, at times working for local patrones (bosses). More on Shipibo ways of life and culture can be found in Bergman (1974), Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra (1980 / 1986), and Tournon (2002), among others.

h: Social Organization and Other Cultural Features (family, community and culture)
t:
The Shipibo are the only people of the Peruvian Amazon whom anthropologists have described as a traditionally matrilocal, matrilineal, and matriarchal society. That is, couples lived with the wife’s family, family line passed through the mother, and women ruled (Chirif, Mora, and Moscoso 1977). These claims are evaluated in Tournon (2002:198-206). Living in large families based around the wife’s side does seem to have been a Shipibo pattern. But the claims about family line passing through the mother need to be revised (Tournon op. cit.; Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1986:27). In fact, there is some evidence of five former clans passed down through the father: Lightning, Jaguar, Macaw, Bird, and Snake (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra op. cit.:35; see also Valenzuela’s ms. study of Shipibo proper names). The claim that women ruled seems unfounded (Tournon op. cit., Illius p.c. 2001). Still, a few traces point to women’s powerful role in traditional society. For example, the word chichi has two meanings, ‘maternal grandmother’ and ‘supreme authority’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:163). Also, a couple of traditional stories show settlements where the highest authority is the oldest woman (Roe 1982).
In the past the basic social unit was the extended family. About forty to sixty people could live in one large house with no walls or inside divisions. Today, houses still have no walls, but they are much smaller and house one or two families of parents and children. Another change is that houses now stand on poles, since half of the

h: Social Organization and Other Cultural Features (family, community and culture)
t:
villages are in areas that flood during the rainy season (Tournon 2002:118). Villages are mostly made up of related families.
According to Tournon (2002:192), there is evidence that people once preferred to marry a cross-cousin. However, it has also been reported that marriage used to be forbidden if the couple turned out to be related by blood within five generations back. A marriage between two people linked in the sixth generation was frowned upon, and the couple probably had to move to another village (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1980:54). Another feature of Shipibo society, still seen today, is sororal polygyny: a man marrying sisters. When a man proves to be a good provider, his parents-in-law may offer him his wife’s younger sister as a wife too.
The Panoan peoples of the rivers used to reshape the heads of babies, especially boys, as a sign of their ethnic identity. Castelnau (1850, cited in Tournon 2002:81), a member of a French-Peruvian expedition to the Amazon, reported this about the Konibo: “Nos decían que teníamos cabezas de monos, mientras las suyas tenían la forma de la luna. [They (i.e. the Konibo) told us that we had monkey heads, while theirs had the shape of the moon.].” Head shaping was seen until the early 1980s (Tournon, p.c. 2002), but it no longer seems to be done. After a child is born, the father must follow set rules: no sex for a time, and avoiding certain foods, animals and trees. Couvade practices during childbirth, where the father also acts out the birth, have also been described.

h: Social Organization and Other Cultural Features (family, community and culture)
t:
There were no puberty ceremonies for boys. But the girls’ ceremony, called Ani Xeati (from ani ‘big’ and xeati ‘drink’), was the most important event in traditional Shipibo society. Families prepared for it for several months. They worked in the fields (chacras), raised wild animals they had caught, stored food and drinks, and made clothes and pottery. An Ani Xeati lasted several days (maybe even weeks). It included strength contests, songs and dances for each main part of the ceremony, and a lot of yuca beer and guarapo (an alcoholic drink made from sugarcane juice). There were also fights between men with the wexati knife, animal sacrifices, cutting the girl’s fringe, and clitoridectomy (female genital cutting). The social and political roles of Ani Xeati have yet to be studied. Traditional Ani Xeati ceremonies were reported as late as 1976 (Heath ms.).
Shipibo shamanism has three levels: meráya, onanya, and raomis. The highest-ranking shaman is the meráya. Through careful use of ayahuasca and the help of friendly spirits, he can heal or harm people and travel to other layers of reality. An onanya also drinks ayahuasca and talks with spirits to heal or harm people, but cannot leave this world. A raomis is simply someone who knows how to use plants to treat people.

h: The Avoidance Relationship of Rayos (the custom of avoiding certain in-laws)
t:
The word rayos means ‘parent-in-law’ and ‘son-in-law,’ but not ‘daughter-in-law.’ In Shipibo society, relatives who are rayos to each other do not speak directly to each
other. Instead, they talk through their daughter or wife. Even young Shipibo men mostly follow this custom, no matter how much contact they have with Spanish-speaking society. Even when a father-in-law and son-in-law travel far away and are alone for some time, they are not supposed to talk to each other directly. They may act as if the daughter or wife were there, pretending to talk through her. Tournon (2002:201:202) recorded the following account from a young Shipibo student:
Some months ago I went fishing for a few days with my father-in-law. We had to stay together away from the village, cook our meals and sleep in a small, uncomfortable hut. My wife, my fishing partner’s daughter, was not with us. Still, my partner and I had to talk to each other during the day to fish, light the fire, cook and eat. How could we do this without speaking directly to each other? We did it ‘as if.’ We acted as if my wife were there with us. I spoke to my absent wife: “Ask your father whether I have to start the fire.” “Tell your husband yes, because we have to cook the meal.” “Ask your father where are the matches.” “Tell your husband they are in the backpack.”

h: The Avoidance Relationship of Rayos (the custom of avoiding certain in-laws)
t:
Tournon (op. cit.) adds that this rayos avoidance also applies to one’s wife’s grandfather. (Tournon does not say whether he means the grandfather on the mother’s side, the father’s side, or both.) According to my own field notes, it also applies between a man
and his wife’s aunt on her mother’s side. One text in Appendix B is about the rayos relationship.

h: Historical Framework (the history of the Shipibo)
t: This section sums up what is known about the history of the Panoan peoples, especially those living on the Ucayali and nearby regions. Sadly, written records show only the outsiders’ point of view. These accounts are often very Eurocentric and even openly racist. Still, they also contain some sharp observations. A few scholars have tried to read the historical records from an Indigenous point of view (e.g., Hvalkof 1998, Tournon 2002). Most of the modern views given here are my own. For a modern Indigenous view, see Valera Rojas and Valenzuela, ms.

h: 1.3.9.1. Panoan Migrations
t:
The most likely idea about where the Panoan peoples came from is that they migrated from the south into the lands where they live now. Evidence from archaeology and from language seems to support this: early Panoan pottery is said to look like Pre-Guarani pottery, and it is widely accepted that Panoan is related
to Takanan, and perhaps to other languages further south.4 According to this idea, the Panoan migration happened on foot around 400-500 A.D. The Panoans first lived in the land between rivers. Later, some groups took control of the valuable varzea, or floodplain, and came to dominate the banks of the Ucayali. They practiced slash-and-burn farming, and their culture relied heavily on yuca (Lathrap 1970, Lathrap, Gebhart-Sayer and Mester 1985, Tournon 1995 and 2002:34; see also Loos 1973).
This idea does not match earlier claims that the Panoans came to their present lands from the north, from an area near the border with Ecuador (Marcoy 1869:642-3, see also de la Grasserie 1890:439, Farabee 1922:79, and Brinton 1891:289). These claims seem to come from the following statement by Marcoy about the Wariapano. (The Wariapano are an ethnic group closely related to the Shipibo; here they are called “Panoans.”)
[Cette nation] était descendue primitivement des contrées de l’Equateur par la rivière Morona, elle s’était fixée d’abord à l’entrée du rio Huallaga, où paraît s’être opérée sa division en tribus. Plus tard, à la suite de démêlés avec les Indiens Xbéros elle avait abandonné ce territoire, erré longtemps à travers les plaines du Sacrement, puis s’était établie dans le voisinage de la rivière Ucayali… (Marcoy 1864:159 in de la Grasserie 1890:439, see also Marcoy 1869:642).

h: 1.3.9.1. Panoan Migrations
t:
Wistrand (1991:275) mentions an unpublished work by Loos (1964) called “Maps of Panoan languages.” It has dialect maps showing Panoan languages moving north from Bolivia into Peru. I haven't been able to see this work.
Finally, following Chirif, Mora, and Moscoso (1977), Trudell describes a Panoan migration from the northeast. She states that “as early as 2000 to 3000 B.C., Arawak and Panoan-speaking peoples were migrating upriver from the lower Amazon basin in present-day Brazil...” (1993:11). No evidence is given for this claim about the Panoans.5
Archaeology also suggests that around 1200 A.D. Tupi-Guarani peoples reached the lower and middle Ucayali. This forced the Panoans there to leave the main river and resettle on the rivers that feed it from the west. The ancestors of the Konibo, however, may have stayed on the upper Ucayali (Lathrap, Gebhart-Sayer and Mester 1985, Tournon 2002:37).

h: 1.3.9.2. Colonial History
t:
The first written (that is, European) account of a Panoan group may date from as early as 1557, by the Spanish explorer Juan Salinas de Loyola. Traveling up the Ucayali River, Salinas met the Kokama (Tupi-Guarani) and the Pariache. Myers (1974) has identified the Pariache as the Konibo, who, as mentioned above, may have stayed on the upper Ucayali. Salinas’s description suggests that the Pariache were organized politically as a chiefdom, a society ruled by a chief (Tournon 1995, 2002:41-42).
But compare Lathrap 1970 on the possible arrival on the Ucayali of an Arawak population from the Central Amazon around 200 A.C.; see also Tournon 2002:33.
The Kokama population probably fell sharply because of diseases brought by the Europeans. This may have led Panoan groups to settle again on the middle and lower Ucayali.
The first attempt to colonize the Ucayali was in 1641. Three Franciscan friars traveled down the Perené and Tambo rivers and so reached the Ucayali. According to missionary sources, the Konibo killed these Franciscans near the mouth of the Aguaytía River. Nobody knows why this clash happened (Hvalkof 1998:138). In 1657, Spanish conquerors and missionaries met the Shipibo, but the Shipibo killed them too. In 1670, a group of Xetebo and Calliseca (probably Shipibo) attacked the mission of Panatahua (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1986:3).
Another missionary attempt came from north to south in 1685-1686. This time, Jesuit priests traveled up the Ucayali River to a fairly large Konibo village on the middle Ucayali. They named it San Miguel de los Cunivos. The Franciscans reached the same village a couple of months later. The two religious orders competed to control the native people and the region. Each order had its own army of Spanish soldiers and its own group of native supporters. In the end, the Franciscans won control of the Ucayali. At that time there was a lot of trade in salt and tools along the river. European goods, especially weapons and iron tools, created or worsened conflicts and raiding among the local native groups. Several times the missionaries themselves stirred up fights between groups. They used old hostilities

h: 1.3.9.2. Colonial History
t:
between groups to weaken the native forces (Hvalkof 1998:138-139). Missionaries also kidnapped Native children. They taught them their religion and Spanish, and later used them to convert their own people to Christianity.
In 1695 there was a major native uprising. The Konibo revolted against the abuse and the epidemics caused by the European invaders. They were partly reacting to being forced to join a Spanish expedition against the Jivaroans. One of the missionaries killed in this uprising was the Jesuit priest Richter, who had played a big part in the missionary work in the region. In 1698, the Shipibo, Konibo, and Xetebo joined forces and drove back a Spanish force sent to punish them (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1986:3). In this way, the native people held off Spanish rule for some time.
About fifty years later, the Franciscan friars set up a new mission on the lower Ucayali. Their spread to the upper Ucayali and the Selva Central was stopped by the most famous native rebellion of the Peruvian Amazon. This uprising was led by Juan Santos Atahualpa in 1742. Several ethnic groups took part, especially the Ashaninka (Arawak).
The Panoans also destroyed the Franciscan missions on the lower Ucayali. The Xetebo, Shipibo and Konibo formed alliances not only with each other but also with the Tupian Kokama. In this way they kept the Spaniards out of their lands until 1790. One of the most important uprisings took place in 1766 and involved the Shipibo, Konibo, and Xetebo. It was led by a Xetebo named Ronkato (Eakin, Lauriault, and Boonstra 1980:5-6). This event is remembered by the

h: 1.3.9.2. Colonial History
t:
Franciscan friar Manuel Navarro in the introduction to his “Vocabulario castellano-quechua-Panoan con sus respectivas gramáticas quechua y pana:”
When the missions of the Ucayali offered a hopeful perspective and an agreeable future... a certain Runcato, a man of fierce instincts, who beneath a false exterior of meekness covered up a vengeful and hypocritical nature, assaulted his countrymen in an unexpected and treacherous manner, victimizing several of them, including the missionary priest and the religious layman who was accompanying him. But that tiger heart was not satisfied with those innocent victims; with his bad example and false reasoning, he induced the Shipibos and the Konibos to perpetrate the atrocious crime of assassinating all of the missionaries among those tribes, and he did not stop until he had satisfied his bloodthirsty and cruel instincts.
[Navarro1927:243].^6
This general rebellion happened in a region that was very hard to reach, so the Spaniards could not put it down. Tournon points out that it may have been the first time the three once-rival groups came together. Today the Shipibo see Ronkato as a hero (Tournon 2002:60).
The river Panoans, especially the people now known as Shipibo, defended their lands so well until the end of the 18th century that this
Phil Young helped me translate this passage. The Spanish original can also be found in Valenzuela (2000:2-3).

h: 1.3.9.2. Colonial History
t:
has earned them the well-deserved name of “regional leaders of resistance to foreign domination” (Trudell 1993:94).
But years later the Franciscans came back, and this time they set up more lasting missions. In 1790-1791 the Franciscans Narciso Girbal and Mariano Márquez founded a new mission in Sarayacu among the Panos (that is, the Wariapanos). Shipibos, Xetebos, and Konibos joined them later (Navarro 1903:171, Tessmann 1999:58). By 1817 the Franciscans had founded nine new missions on the upper Ucayali. Besides teaching their religion and ruling the native people, the colonizers wanted a supply route between the coast and the Amazon. But after Peru’s war of independence in the early 1820s, the Spanish missionaries were thrown out of the country.

h: 1.3.9.3. Republican History
t:
After Peru became independent and the Franciscan friars left, the people of the missions scattered. The Amazon opened up to capitalist trade and suffered a new invasion by would-be landowners and traders. These outsiders made money from the native people by charging too much for goods and paying too little for forced work. The new patrones took advantage of the natives’ inexperience and of the fact that they could not read. To get guns, bullets, cloth, tools, and other goods, the Indians fell into debts they could never pay off. These debts were passed on to their children. The Natives
became practically slaves. Those who tried to escape the system were harshly punished or even killed.
When steamboats arrived in the 1850s, several businesses grew up in the Amazon that took out natural products for North American and European markets. These businesses needed native knowledge of the region and native workers. Important exports were sarsaparilla bark (Smilax sp.), exotic woods, furs, salted fish, and turtle egg oil. Most of this trade went through Brasil. Because the region had become important for politics and the economy, the young Peruvian state grew more and more interested in the Amazon. Its navy began to patrol the Amazon and Ucayali rivers. At the beginning of 1866, two officials landed at a Kashibo (Panoan) village and took bananas from a chacra (a farm plot) without talking to the locals. The owners of the chacra killed them. In revenge, on December the tenth, 1866, the Peruvian navy attacked the Kashibo at Chonas Isla, at the mouth of the Pachitea River. Women and children were captured to be sold as slaves in the city of Iquitos. About 500 Kashibo men were massacred by the warships’ guns when they tried to free the prisoners (Hvalkof 1998:140-141).

h: 1.3.9.3. Republican History
t:
During the “rubber boom”, especially between 1890-1915, outsiders reached deep into the Amazon rainforest. This was when the exploitation of the native people was at its worst. The demand for latex grew after Goodyear discovered vulcanization in 1838 and Dunlop invented the air-filled rubber tire in 1888. Hundreds of thousands of Indians, whole families, were kidnapped,
enslaved and traded to collect latex, the sap of the rubber tree. Whole Native peoples were forced into lands they did not know. They died of European diseases or were worked to death. The rubber patrones ruled the Amazon by terror, and their crimes have not been fully recorded. Among the most famous and cruel patrones of the Ucayali were Carlos Fermín Fitzcarraldo and Carlos Scharff. Scharff was killed by the Panoan Amawaka in 1908. Around 1915 the boom ended. The rubber economy collapsed because prices fell and new plantations started in Malaysia. On the whole, the “rubber boom” did less damage to the Shipibo people and their culture than to other Amazonian peoples, including a few other Panoan groups. Also, the Konibo in particular captured members of groups living away from the rivers and handed them over to the rubber patrones. This may have helped them protect their own people. The “rubber boom” also brought in foreigners and Peruvians from other regions. For example, people from the Department of San Martin settled in Contamana, a place with a SK name (kontá k. palm, manan ‘mountain’) (Hvalkof 1998:135-138, 142-144).

h: 1.3.9.3. Republican History
t:
Other businesses that took out natural products followed, such as lumber, exotic woods, and furs. The most important was probably exotic woods. In many regions lumber is still the most profitable business today. The local patrones fight against native organizations that try to get legal recognition of their ancestral lands and defend their basic democratic rights (Hvalkof ibid.).
Around 1930, Protestant missions settled on the Ucayali. In 1943 the Lima-Pucallpa road, the first road joining the Pacific coast and the Amazon, was
opened. Pucallpa, which the Shipibo call Maioshian⁷, lies in the heart of Shipibo territory. Since the road was built, many settlers have come, and the city has grown enormously, from 4,000 people to 250,000 in only sixty years (Tournon 2002:123). Once again, native peoples’ rights were ignored and their lands invaded.
In 1952 the Peruvian government approved the bilingual education program run by the Summer Institute of Linguistics (SIL). This group of Protestant missionaries, mostly from the United States, set up their national center next to Pucallpa. The Shipibo were among the first groups where SIL built schools, trained bilingual teachers, carried out religious work to win converts, and did linguistic work.
Religious and other institutions also provided medical care. The Shipibo have many births, and since the second half of the 20th century far fewer people have died, thanks to vaccines against infectious diseases and basic medical treatment. According to Tournon, since then the Shipibo population has truly exploded. It has grown from about 3,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 35,000 today (2002:140-144). New villages were formed, and today a village may have from 50 up to 1,000 people.

h: 1.3.9.3. Republican History
t:
In 1974 the Ley de Comunidades Nativas de la Selva y Ceja de Selva made it possible for Amazonian native peoples to get legal titles to their lands (Trudell
Maioshian, ‘the place with red soil,’ is made of these SK word pieces: mai ‘land, soil’ + joshin ‘red,’ + the ending -ya, which means ‘having’. The name Pucallpa is a word-for-word translation of it, made from the Quechua words puka ‘red’ and allpa ‘land, soil.’
1993:17-18). Speaking a Native language was seen as a key sign that a group was an indigenous people. In the late seventies, regional native federations were founded, such as the Shipibo-led FECONAU (Federación de Comunidades Nativas del Ucayali y Afluentes). The Amazonian confederation AIDESEP (Asociación Interétnica de Desarrollo de la Selva Peruana) was created in 1980, and the Shipibo were among its founders. AIDESEP in turn played a major role in creating COICA (Coordinadora Indígena de la Cuenca Amazónica), an organization that brings together several native confederations of Lowland South America.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s the guerrilla groups Shining Path and Movimiento Revolucionario Túpac Amaru were active on the Ucayali and its side rivers. Members of Shining Path entered Shipibo villages to recruit young men, but most people turned them away. These armed groups attacked other Amazonian peoples, especially the Ashaninka, and the mestizo population on the Ucayali. But they did not attack the Shipibo, who managed to stay politically neutral. Still, many people moved into the region from the Andes to escape the war. After about twelve years of political violence, tourism almost disappeared from Peru. This affected the Ucayali region and especially the Shipibo. Shipibo women now travel to Lima and other distant cities to sell their handicrafts. This may affect family life and the status of women (Tournon 2002:133).

h: 1.3.9.4. The Jonikon Today
t:
The Jonikon have kept their own identity, language, and basic way of life, despite long and conflict-filled contact with Spanish and mestizo (Spanish-speaking) society. Of course, these hard conditions have changed the lives of the Shipibo a great deal, and they still do. Even so, most Shipibo still live in their own villages along the Ucayali River, or Paro. They are able to live from farming, hunting, gathering, and above all fishing. Even when they depend on the market for some goods, the Shipibo tend to be self-sufficient and refuse to be ruled by patrones. Many women and men even trade in the market themselves.
A key reason why the Shipibo and Konibo identities have survived is their very high self-esteem and their strong wish to run their own lives. Marcoy (1869:645-646) makes an interesting remark about the Konibo, who “…préférèrent le culte de la liberté et de la barbarie, sous le couvert des bois, aux avantages de la civilisation dans un hameau chrétien…on doit croire que la persistance des Conibos à rester idolâtres en dépit de tout fut cause qu’ils vivent encore…” (that is, they preferred freedom in the forest to the comforts of a Christian village, and their refusal to give up their own religion is probably why they still exist). Brinton (1891:290) made a similar comment: “…none of the Panoans have shown any earnest desire to adopt a civilized life.”

h: 1.3.9.4. The Jonikon Today
t:
Today the Shipibo are very good at adapting to new and often hard situations, and at taking in outside things and making them part of their culture. For example, besides their official nawan join jane ‘names in the outsider’s language,’ each Shipibo has a
‘true / core name’ or janekon, used in the community and when speaking the Native language. Shipibo women buy cooking pots at the mestizo market, but they still make “…what is probably one of the most elaborate and flourishing polychrome pottery traditions in the Amerindian world today…” (Roe 1982:42). Despite the long and aggressive Spanish advance, Shipibo-Konibo is still the main language of the Shipibo people, and for many of them the only one. Children in the villages usually speak only the native language until they go to the bilingual primary schools, which are usually run by Native teachers. Modern native political organizations work at the regional, national, and international levels to defend the rights of the Shipibo. Above all, they work to get official recognition of their ancestral lands, so they can survive as a people. Thanks to this work, most Shipibo villages have legal titles to their lands, and some are even getting more land. But Spanish-speaking mestizos keep invading Shipibo lands, which they see as “empty”, and this causes serious conflicts with the Shipibo villages. A major problem is that the places where the Shipibo fish, hunt, and farm may lie outside the legally recognized areas. For example, Tournon reports that in 1980 the people of Kaimito, a village on Lake Imiria, had planted watermelons on a sandy shore two to three hours away by canoe. They had planted corn on a river terrace one day away by boat. Tournon points out that the people of Kaimito, living on the large Lake Imiria, have plenty of fish, but few farming resources because the soil is acid and poor (2002:165). Another notable point is that Shipibo leaders have recently started taking part in local and national elections. In 1990-1991 I had the

h: 1.3.9.4. The Jonikon Today
t: opportunity to take part in internal meetings on the upper Ucayali. At these meetings the Shipibo planned their first run in the elections for the city hall of the District of Iparía. They took part as one united group and chose a single candidate and his team. The Shipibo won the elections. The first Shipibo mayor in Peruvian history took office in a mestizo town, even though most of the people in the district as a whole had always been Shipibo.

h: Names of the Language (what the language is called)
t:
The Shipibo call their language Non Joi ‘Our Language, Our Word’ or Joikon ‘Core / True Language or Word’. Books about languages usually call it Shipibo-Conibo, Shipibo-Konibo, or just Shipibo. It is hard to find real differences between the way the Shipibo and the Konibo speak. Loriot reports that around the 1960s the difference was about where people lived, not about language or culture (Shell, op.cit.:26).⁸ People who live on the Piski River are called Piskibo. Their way of speaking has a few special features, such as some different words and a different stress on some words. They also still use the form en for ‘my’ (see 2.2.6.5 and 3.3.1.1).
Loriot is also said to have commented that Shipibo might be one language made up of different dialects whose speakers understand each other, while Konibo and Xetebo are two separate languages whose speakers also understand each other. Xetebo might be closer to Konibo than to Shipibo, but speakers of all three can understand each other (Shell op.cit.:26). I have not found any evidence for these claims.

h: State of Endangerment of the Language (is the language in danger of dying out?)
t:
For the Amazon, the Shipibo are quite a large group. As I said above, SK is being passed on to the new generations. Children in the villages usually speak only SK until they start primary school. Most Shipibo learn Spanish, but this has not made them switch to Spanish. Even people who grow up in the city learn SK and speak it fluently.
Outsiders who work with the Shipibo soon notice that they have a strong sense of who they are and a high opinion of themselves. This is especially true in the villages and among more traditional people. In general, people don’t like marrying someone who is not Shipibo, because such partners don’t behave in the right way for the culture and don’t speak SK. You can see this attitude even in villages near the city of Pucallpa, and in the city itself. Shipibo women usually wear traditional clothes even when they travel to towns and cities. When the Shipibo meet in the city, they speak their own language. They switch to Spanish only if someone from outside the group joins them. Even people with more schooling see speaking two languages as an advantage. They point out that they can understand what the mestizos say, but the mestizos can’t understand them.
The native language plays a key part in what it means to be Shipibo. For example, a woman told me why she supported a Shipibo candidate in some local elections. Unlike the mestizo candidates, she said, “jakayara non kaibo

h: State of Endangerment of the Language (is the language in danger of dying out?)
t:
iki, non jimi, non joi”; that is, ‘he is our countryman, our blood, our language’ (Ranin Ama, p.c. 1998).
When people are asked which language is “more beautiful,” SK or Spanish, everyone seems to agree: SK. But when they are asked which of the two is “more important,” the usual answer is: “both are equally important.” Spanish clearly brings advantages: a chance to get ahead socially and economically, access to the market, to schooling, to the media, and so on. But SK is central to the Shipibo way of life. So most Shipibo parents would like their children to become fully at home in both languages, and they support using both languages at school. Especially in the primary school years, many parents prefer Shipibo teachers to mestizo teachers, and they value reading materials written in their own language.
What I have seen matches what Trudell (1993:96-97) says: “The Shipibo appear to maintain strong sentimental and instrumental attachment to their mother tongue, along with an equally strong instrumental attachment to Spanish.” Trudell notes that the Shipibo have a lot of contact with the non-indigenous world. Even so, they generally feel good about their language and culture, and seem to feel little shame about speaking SK in front of others. Valuing Spanish does not make SK less important. According to Trudell (1993:96), the Shipibo are an example of a stable situation in which each of the two languages has its own jobs and settings (linguists call this stable diglossia). “Reasons for the establishment of such stable diglossia, in place of wholesale language shift in favor of Spanish, must lie in the high regard the Shipibo have for their own culture, ethnic

h: State of Endangerment of the Language (is the language in danger of dying out?)
t:
identity, and language.” (1993:97). More people can read and write in Spanish than in Shipibo, but reading and writing in Shipibo is seen as good and something to be proud of. Both older and younger people still use not only the native language but also many traditional customs.
But this situation may change in the near future. We know that in at least one village, Amaquiría, Spanish has replaced SK. Amaquiría might be a special case, because of its particular history (connected with the work of a missionary group, Tournon p.c. 2002). But in large villages like Pao Ian, San Francisco, and Colonia de Caco, Spanish speakers and their language put great pressure on the native people and on SK. Secondary schools bring mestizo teachers and their families to live there for good. On top of that, Spanish speakers keep moving into the large villages on the river route Pucallpa-Contamana-Iquitos. In San Francisco, and probably in other villages near Pucallpa, some children seem to speak more Spanish than SK. Some children have even started to refuse to speak SK (Ranin Ama, p.c. 2000).
Today quite a lot of Shipibo families have moved to the city of Pucallpa and the nearby District of Yarinacocha (Tournon 2002:166 estimates about 5,000 people). The children of these families often look down on village children because they can’t speak Spanish properly. These city children may even prefer to speak Spanish at home with their own families (Yoi Sani, p.c. 2000). City Shipibo

h: State of Endangerment of the Language (is the language in danger of dying out?)
t:
have more access to schooling, to development projects, and to the mestizo world in general. They lead the native political organizations and have their own radio programs, which are heard in very many villages. The SK spoken in the city shows a lot of Spanish influence at different levels, and people often switch and mix the two languages. It is at least possible that village Shipibo may take this fairly powerful city group as a model. They may come to see city SK as a more prestigious way of speaking, and maybe even try to copy it. Children in the city usually grow up speaking both languages, but we don’t know how well they really speak SK. We also still need to find out how much Spanish has crept into the SK spoken by adults and children.
I must also mention that the mestizo population in general looks down strongly on the Shipibo and their language. Tournon reports a visit he made in 1985 to a mestizo settlement on the Ucayali River. When he asked whether the people there spoke SK, the answer was: “No, here they are civilized.”
Many Amazonian languages of Peru survive and stay strong because their speakers live far from the rest of the country. Shipibo villages have no electricity, and most of them can only be reached by river.⁹ Speedboats are few and fast travel is expensive, so a village may be several days away from a town, a shop or a hospital. Big changes in these

h: State of Endangerment of the Language (is the language in danger of dying out?)
t:
In the late 1990s, a road was opened that starts in the District of Yarinacocha and passes through the Shipibo village of San Francisco. It can be used only in the dry season. Also in the late 1990s, some villages were given solar panels and a small black-and-white television set, and two villages got occasional use of community cell phones. In this section I only want to point out how changes like these might affect the way languages are used. I do not mean at all that the Shipibo, or any other people, should stay isolated to keep their languages.
respects may have a huge effect on how the languages are used and on their future. We know, for example, that a community can switch to another language in as little as one generation (Thomason and Kaufman 1991:41).

h: Levels of Spanish Bilingualism (how well people also speak Spanish)
t:
The Shipibo who tend to speak Spanish better are: leaders who are not traditional, people with more schooling, men, young people, people who buy and sell in the market, people in large villages (especially on the river route Pucallpa-Contamana-Iquitos), and men who have served in the army.
The levels of bilingualism below are the ones set by the United States Foreign Service Institute. The information about how well the Shipibo speak Spanish comes from Grimes (1996). Sadly, Grimes doesn’t say where the information came from or in what year it was collected. The percentages seem to refer to people over ten years old.
Level 0. Unable to function in the spoken Spanish language. Oral production in Spanish is limited to occasional isolated words. No communicative ability: 10%
Level 1. Able to use the Spanish language to satisfy minimum courtesy requirements and maintain very simple face-to-face conversations on familiar topics: 20%
Level 2. Able to use the Spanish language to satisfy routine social demands and limited requirements in other domains: 23%
Level 3. Able to speak the Spanish language with sufficient structural accuracy and vocabulary to participate effectively in most formal and informal conversations on practical, social, and occupational topics: 30%
Level 4. Able to use the Spanish language fluently and accurately on all levels normally pertinent to needs. The individual’s language usage and ability to function are fully successful: 15%

h: Levels of Spanish Bilingualism (how well people also speak Spanish)
t: Level 5. Speaking proficiency in Spanish is functionally equivalent to that of a highly articulate formally-educated native speaker and reflects the cultural standards of the country where the language is natively spoken: 2%

h: Previous Literature on Shipibo-Konibo (what others have written about the language)
t:
Missionaries, travellers, officials, and scientists came to the Ucayali region to convert the native people to Christianity, to explore unknown lands, and to use local natural resources. Many of them were also drawn to the rich variety of plants, animals and peoples there. Some missionaries and other scholars described parts of the SK language. They paid special attention to collecting word lists and vocabularies. These first publications on SK include the following vocabularies: Richter 1685, Anonymous 1795?, Marqués 1800 / 1931, Armentia 1898, Carrasco 1901 / 1902, von den Steinen 1904, and Alemany 1906. Notes on some features of the grammar, especially on how words are built, can be found in Castelnau (1851:301-2), Marqués 1800 / 1931:117-130, von den Steinen 1904:31-40, Alemany 1906 / 1927:319-327, Farabee 1922:88-90, and
Tessmann 1929:248-271 (see also Illius 1999:57). No one has yet made a careful study of these early written sources.
James Loriot was a missionary and linguist who worked among the Shipibo for several decades. He probably spoke the language almost like a native speaker. Most of his work has never been published.¹⁰ But two of his articles can be found in well-known journals: “Alternate-Mora Timing in Shipibo” (IJAL 1948) and “Shipibo Paragraph Structure”, written with Hollenbach (Foundations of Language 1970). An important part of Loriot’s legacy is the Shipibo-Spanish Dictionary (see below).

h: Previous Literature on Shipibo-Konibo (what others have written about the language)
t:
In 1973, Norma Faust published “Lecciones para el Aprendizaje del Idioma Shipibo-Conibo.” It is a short and mostly accurate teaching book. It is meant for Spanish speakers who are not linguists and want to learn to hold basic conversations. The lessons are built around dialogues, followed by explanations of the grammar and exercises. Based on Faust’s work, Weisshar and Illius (1990) published a short grammar sketch in German that focuses on how words are built. It includes a text with word-by-word notes.
The Shipibo-Spanish Dictionary by Loriot, Lauriault, and Day (1993) is an important record of the language. Lauriault and Loriot (father and son) started collecting the words for the dictionary in 1959. Loriot carried on with this work until 1979 and gathered about 5,000 entries and sub-entries. The dictionary was finally edited by a third member of the Summer Institute of Linguistics (that is, Day). Among the many Shipibo who helped, we must
This work can be seen on microfiche in the Archives of the Summer Institute of Linguistics in Dallas, Texas. I want to thank the staff in charge of these archives for letting me use their materials in March 2000, and the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology for paying for this visit.
mention Mr. Guillermo Ramírez Guimaraes (Soi Rawa), who comes from the village of Pao Ian. Ramírez worked with Loriot for several years. Thirty years later he helped Day finish the dictionary (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day, op.cit., Prologue). There is a lot of information about the grammar in the short grammar sketch at the start of this dictionary (mostly based on Faust’s work), and in the entries themselves.

h: Previous Literature on Shipibo-Konibo (what others have written about the language)
t: Later studies have looked at the sounds of the language (García 1994; Valenzuela, Márquez, and Maddieson 2001), at how words are built (Valenzuela 1998a), at how words and sentences work together (Valenzuela 1997, 1999, 2000), at meaning (Valenzuela 1998b), and at how people use speech in their culture (Illius 1999). There are also some published texts without any analysis, most of them for use in the bilingual primary schools.

h: 1.4.5.1. Panoan Peoples
t:
According to Wise (1985), at the start of the 20th century about twenty Panoan tribes lived in Peru. Twelve of these groups had no contact with the rest of the country (Amawaka, Kashinawa, Kujareño, Iskobakebo,^11 Mayo, Mayoruna, Moronawa, Nokaman, Yora, Pisabo, Sharanawa-Marinawa, and Yaminawa), two groups
Also known as Iskonawa or Isconahua.
had occasional contact (Kashibo and Sensi), and six had regular contact (Atsawaka, Kapanawa, Panobo, Remo, Xetebo, and Shipibo-Konibo).
Today a few Panoan groups still have no contact with the rest of the country. Examples are the Iskobakebo, the Moronawa, maybe a Kashibo-Kakataibo group in Peru (César Bolívar, p.c. 2000), and other groups in Brazil. Others were contacted quite recently, like the Yora in Peru and the Matis in Brazil, both in the 1980s. Some groups, such as the Atsawaka, the Yamiaka, and possibly the Remo, have simply been wiped out, mainly because of the horrors of the “rubber boom.” (Tournon suggests, though, that the Iskobakebo may be descended from the Remo, p.c. 2002.) Other groups have merged with groups that used to be separate. Examples are the Pakawara, who live among the Chakobo in Bolivia, and a group of Iskobakebo who live among the Shipibo of Callería.
There are thought to be about 40,000 Panoan people: around 30,000 in Peru, 7,700 in Brazil, and 700 in Bolivia (Erikson et alia 1994:4-5).¹²

h: 1.4.5.1. Panoan Peoples
t:
Something interesting about the Panoan peoples is this. Their cultures, lands, and languages are remarkably alike, and yet they stay split into a surprising number of separate, independent groups (Erkison et alia 1994:4). Panoan peoples usually don’t even know that other Panoan groups exist, unless they are neighbors. One big exception is the meetings that happen during training programs and events for bilingual teachers. To a lesser degree they also meet at political meetings of several ethnic groups.
Most Panoan peoples (and languages) have names that end in -bo, an ending that means ‘a group of’ or ‘many’, or in the word nawa, which means ‘people’, ‘outsider’, and maybe also ‘enemy.’
These figures put the Shipibo population at 23,000.
Many of these names were probably given to a group by its neighbors.

h: 1.4.5.2. On the Name “Pano”
t:
The story goes that Franciscan friars from Lima first explored the area of the Huallaga, Marañon, Ucayali and Pachitea Rivers in the second half of the 17th century. There they met several related groups, and the Pano were the most important of them. Pano land included the banks of the Sarayacu River (Marcoy 1869:642-3). Their language was described as the “idioma general de las tribus que habitan en el [río] Ucayali y en el [río] “Madre de Dios”” (Armentia 1898:43, see also Castelnau 1851:292).
In 1888, Raoul de la Grasserie showed that the language of the Pano and of six other related groups all came from one shared ancestor language, separate from other families. He used the name “Pano” for this newly found language family. Pano most likely means ‘giant armadillo’ (Priodontes maximus) (Tessmann 1999:58).

h: The Panoan Language Family (the family of related languages Shipibo belongs to)
t:
Panoan is a well-known language family of the South American lowlands, along with Arawak, Tupian, Ge or Jê, Cariban, Tucanoan, and others. Today about 28
Panoan languages are spoken in western Amazonia, in neighboring areas of today’s Peru (Departments of Loreto, Ucayali, Madre de Dios, and Huánuco), Brazil (States of Acre, Amazonia, and Rondônia), and Bolivia (Departments of Beni and Pando).13 Peru has the most Panoan speakers, and also the greatest variety of Panoan languages.
As I said above, Raoul de la Grasserie was the first to formally propose the Panoan family. He did this in a paper given at the 7th International Congress of Americanists in Berlin in 1888, which was published in 1890. De la Grasserie studied word lists from what he called seven Panoan “languages” (names and spellings are kept as in the original): Pano, Conibo, Pacavara, Caripuna, Culino, Maxuruna, Mayoruna Domestica and Mayoruna Fera. He compared about 90 words for body parts, relatives, animals, plants, nature, numbers, and a few describing words and verbs. With them he tried to find regular patterns in how the sounds match from one language to another. He also included some notes on the grammar of one of the languages, Pano (that is, Wariapano), most likely taken from Castelnau (1851:292-293).
Before de la Grasserie’s work, nobody knew that the Panoan languages belonged together. Some of them had even been wrongly grouped with other languages that are not related to them at all. For example, von Martius (1969 [1867]: 298) said that Wariapano was closely related to Tupi and Movima: “Mit Tupi und Mobima zunächst verwandt.” In a much older classification, Hervas y Panduro (1806:263) lists

h: The Panoan Language Family (the family of related languages Shipibo belongs to)
t:
Wistrand-Robinson (1991:245) says that Panoan languages are spoken by tribes “located in Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, and possibly also previously in Colombia.”

Today Movima (Beni, Bolivia) and Urarina (Loreto, Peru) are seen as “language isolates”, which means they have no known relatives. Shell (1975:16-24) sums up later classifications of Panoan peoples and languages, including Brinton (1891:289-292) and McQuown (1955). But these lists are clearly incomplete. At the same time they split things up too much, because they mistake what were probably clan names and place names for names of peoples and languages.

h: Sub-classification within the Panoan Family (the smaller branches within the family)
t:
To find out which languages in a family are closest relatives, linguists compare words carefully and look for regular sound patterns (they call this the comparative method). Shell’s (1965 / 1975) “Las Lenguas Panoan y su Reconstrucción” is the only study that sorts all the Panoan languages into smaller groups using this method step by step. D’Ans (1973) uses a different method, which counts how many words languages share (lexico-statistics). This method has been strongly criticized, and D’Ans does not show the data behind his numbers. Still, I will show that his groups fit with those of other studies. Loos (1999) offers a tentative grouping. He says it is based on shared sounds, shared ways of building words, and a few shared words. Sadly, he did not publish his data either. Erikson et alia’s (1994) grouping relies mostly on culture rather than on language.
In this section I briefly describe the different proposals for grouping the languages, and then I judge them as a whole. I mention Erikson et alia’s (1994) work where it is useful.

h: 1.5.1.1. Sub-classification Based on the Comparative Method
t:
As I said above, Shell (1975) is the only one who has grouped the Panoan languages using the comparative method and has also published the data. She compared seven Panoan languages: Amawaka, Kapanawa, Kashibo, Kashinawa, Chakobo, Marinawa, and Shipibo-Konibo. She also includes data from several other languages, such as Atsawaka, Kulino, Iskonawa, Karipuna, Mayoruna, Marobo, Nokaman, Pakawara, Poyanawa, Tutxiunawa, Wariapano, Yamiaka, and Yaminawa. Shell finds that many of the sound changes are shared by languages in overlapping ways. So there is no clear proof for splitting the languages into neat subgroups. That is why the history of today’s languages may be better shown as overlapping areas of shared changes (an issoglosic model) than as a family tree. Even so, some of the languages do seem more closely related than others, and this gives some reason to use a family tree after all (p.105).
The oldest sound changes seem to split Kashibo off from the other six languages in the study (Amawaka, Kapanawa, Kashinawa, Chakobo, Marinawa, and Shipibo-Konibo). In the parent language there was a sound written K^{w} (a k said with rounded lips; the star means it is a reconstructed, older sound). Kashibo kept the sound that comes from K^{w}. It also kept groups of consonants that include hissing sounds like s. In the other six languages, the sound that came from K^{w} fused

h: 1.5.1.1. Sub-classification Based on the Comparative Method
t:
with the sound that came from K, and those groups of consonants became simpler. Other changes that happened only in Kashibo support this first split. The vowel pairs /ai/ and /au/ turned into the single vowels /e/ and /ɔ/, and many bare verbs got shorter. Some grammar features also support the idea that the ancestor of Kashibo split off quite early from the ancestor of the other six languages. In fact, Kashibo is the only one of these languages where the marker on a pronoun that is the one person of an intransitive verb has the form -ʂ (see 10.4.3). It is also the only one where ‘me’ and ‘you’ as receivers don’t take the marker -a. Finally, some Kashibo words clearly come from a different source than the matching words in the other six languages (pp.106-108).
Another sound change, involving the sounds that come from β and w, splits Kashinawa, Amawaka, and Marinawa off from the rest.¹⁴ Word meanings also give some reason to group these three languages together. More sound and vocabulary evidence suggests that Kashinawa and Marinawa are even closer to each other. Finally, there is enough evidence to say that Shipibo-Konibo and Kapanawa are closer to each other than either is to Chakobo. Shell suggests that a migration may have taken place at this stage. It is also only at this stage that nouns of three syllables made of one single word piece may have lost their third syllable (see also section 3.2.4). Mayoruna (Matses) has several words that do not come from the same source as

Shell also says something about other Panoan languages that her study only touches on. She notes that the sounds of Wariapano match those of Shipibo-Konibo in form, in where they appear, and in how they developed. Also, several words seem to put Wariapano in one group with Shipibo-Konibo and Kapanawa (p. 110). Nokaman is very close to Kashibo, both in sounds and in words. It is also reasonable to put Pakawara and Karipuna in a group with Chakobo, and to keep all three apart from Atsawaka, Yamiaka, and Arazaire (p.111).
In figure 1.1, I show Shell’s “speculative genealogical tree” (her best-guess family tree). These are the short forms used: RP = Reconstructed Pano, KK = Kashibo-Kakataibo, KP = Kapanawa, SK = Shipibo-Konibo, CH = Chakobo, AM = Amawaka, KN = Kashinawa, MN = Marinawa.

h: 1.5.1.2. Sub-classification Based on Lexico-Statistics
t:
D’Ans (1973) compares ten Panoan languages by counting how many basic words they share (linguists call this lexico-statistics): Kashibo, Panavarro (that is, Wariapano), Shipibo, Kapanawa, Amawaka, Iskonawa, Kashinawa, Yaminawa, Sharanawa, and Chakobo. He compares the words on Swadesh’s short list of 100 basic words, but he does not show his data. D’Ans gives likely dates for when the languages split apart. He points out that his dates are the latest possible ones, because he was very generous in deciding which words come from the same older word (he did it “con la mayor tolerancia”).
D’Ans thinks it is most likely that 2,000 years ago there was no single Proto-Panoan language, that is, no single parent language. Instead there was a group of related languages whose speakers could only partly understand each other, and some of them were more alike than others (p.363). So, he says, it would be “utopic” to try to show his results as one single family tree.
His first conclusion is that Yaminawa and Sharanawa are two dialects of the same language, because they split apart only a short time ago. He calls this language “Pano-Purús”. (But the Yaminawa live on the Upper Yurua, Sepahua, Inomapuya, and Mishagua Rivers, not on the Purús River, Tournon p.c. 2002.) This language would also include Marinawa, Chaninawa, Mastanawa, and probably Yawanawa, as well as other dialects spoken in Brazil (p.355).

h: 1.5.1.2. Sub-classification Based on Lexico-Statistics
t:
D’Ans proposes four groups, named after roughly where they are: Ucayali, Preandine, Beni, and Headwaters.15 Ucayali includes Shipibo, Kapanawa, and Wariapano. These languages may have split from each other less than a thousand years ago. Headwaters includes Amawaka, Iskonawa, Kashinawa, and Yaminawa-Sharanawa. Preandine is Kashibo, and Beni is Chakobo.
Preandine and Beni seem to be closer to the Ucayali group than to the Headwaters group. The Headwaters languages may have split from the Ucayali group about ten to thirteen hundred years ago. But Headwaters is not a real language group, because its languages split from each other ten to fifteen hundred years ago. So

h: 1.5.1.3. Loos’ Tentative Sub-classification
t:
According to Loos (1999:227), the Panoan languages are so much alike that they must have spread out and split apart quite recently: “a fairly shallow time-depth and recent expansion and split”.
Loos sees three possible subgroups, plus some languages that he does not put in any group. As I said above, in this work Loos does not show the data behind his claims. But he says that his conclusions are based on shared sounds and shared ways of building words, and to a lesser degree on shared words. Table 1.2 shows Loos’ tentative grouping.
