h: 1.5.1.4. Balance of the Different Sub-classification Proposals
t:
After looking at the different proposals, and at what I have seen myself in the literature, I conclude that the Panoan family should probably be split into six groups. These names are only provisional. They are based on where one or more of the languages in each group are found: Ucayali, Purus, Southern,
Southwestern, Northern, and Western or Preandine. Table 1.3 below shows how the group names used by D’Ans and Loos match the ones I use here. A few languages still have no reliable place. We still need to find out whether some languages belong to one of the groups above or form groups of their own.
The Ucayali Grouping:
All the proposals put Shipibo-Konibo(-Xetebo) in one group with Kapanawa, and especially with Wariapano. Wariapano seems to be closer to Shipibo-Konibo than to Kapanawa. Besides Shell (op.cit.), others have noticed that Wariapano and SK are built in very similar ways and/or that their speakers can understand each other: Navarro (1903:173), Parker (1994:95), and I myself (Valenzuela 2000b:note 10).
Some other languages, such as Marobo, Remo, Iskonawa, and Kanamari, may also belong in this group, but this still has to be proven. (Note that Loos puts all these languages in his “Kapanawa” group, which is my “Ucayali” group. But D’Ans puts Iskonawa in his “Headwaters” group, which is Loos’ and my “Yaminawa” group.)

h: 1.5.1.4. Balance of the Different Sub-classification Proposals
t:
The Purus Grouping:
D’Ans and Loos agree that Yaminawa, Sharanawa, Marinawa, Chaninawa, Mastanawa, and Yawanawa form one single language unit. Also,
D’Ans concludes that Yaminawa and Sharanawa are versions of the same language. Loos adds Chitonawa, Yoranawa, and Moronawa to this group. Interestingly, Erikson et alia point out that the groups in the Yaminawa cluster were long seen as one single people. In fact, they share one culture but are politically very mixed (1994:6).
Shell’s findings suggest that Kashinawa and Amawaka should also be part of this group. These two languages, along with Marinawa, shared the sound changes involving the sounds that come from β and w. Shell also says that some shared words give a reason to group these three languages together (1975:108). Loos also puts Kashinawa and Amawaka in one group with Yaminawa.
The Southern Grouping:
All the classifications put Chakobo and Pakawara together. Shell also adds Karipuna here, and Erikson et alia add both Karipuna and Kaxarari. I looked at the very little data there is on Kaxarari. I can add that this language keeps a third syllable in a couple of three-syllable nouns that seem to be single word pieces. This sets Chakobo apart from most of the other languages too. So Kaxarari and Chakobo have both kept the same old feature. But that is not enough. To put languages in the same group, we need evidence that they changed in the same new ways, and we don’t have that evidence. Loos adds Katukina to the Southern group, but this claim still needs to be proven.

h: 1.5.1.4. Balance of the Different Sub-classification Proposals
t:
The Southwestern Grouping:
Yamiaka, Atsawaka, and maybe Arazaire are no longer spoken. They may once have formed a separate Southwestern group, different from the Southern Panoan languages.
The Western or Preandine Grouping:
Loos does not put Kashibo and Nokaman in any group. Shell gives evidence that Kashibo may have been the first language to split off from the rest of the family. She also shows that Kashibo and Nokaman went through the same sound changes. So it seems reasonable to treat Kashibo and Nokaman as a small group of their own. A separate Western or Preandine group made up of Kashibo(-Kakataibo) and Nokaman also matches the proposals of d’Ans and Erikson et alia.
The Northern Grouping:
The biggest weakness in Shell’s and D’Ans’ work is probably that they left out all the languages of the Matses / Mayoruna group. But several things point to a separate Northern group: the unusual grammar features you can see in Kneeland’s (1979) description, a few remarks in Shell (1975), and the fact that Loos does not put Matses / Mayoruna
in any of the groups above. According to Erikson et alia, this northern group would also include Matis, Korubo, Maya, Kulina-Panoan, and other groups that have not yet been contacted.
To sum up, a comparison of Panoan languages that fairly represents the whole family should include at least one language from each of these groups: Ucayali, Purus, Southern, Southwestern (if there is data), Western / Preandine, and Northern. It may be a good idea to treat Amawaka apart from the other Purus languages. Of course, each language needs to be studied in depth before anyone can settle on a final grouping. Languages such as Marobo, Katukina, and Iskonawa still have to be placed in one of the groups above.

h: Features of Proto-Pano Grammar (what the shared ancestor language was like)
t:
Shell’s (1975) comparison, which I introduced above, calls the parent language “Reconstructed Pano” (RP) rather than “Proto-Pano” (PP). She does this because her study does not include
all of the languages, and because most of her data comes from Panoan languages of Peru. Still, Proto-Pano and Reconstructed Pano are not expected to be very different (p.11).
Shell rebuilds the older forms of more than 500 sets of related words, most of them bare words (roots). Besides short forms of body-part words, she rebuilds these old grammar word pieces: -aʂï intransitivity agreement, βï ~ βïtã comitative, -βo collective / plural, -kas desiderative, -ki locative, -m[a] causative, -riʔβi repetitive, -ʂõ benefactive, -ʂõ transitivity agreement, -ti nominalizer, -wa factitive, -wï imperative, -ya proprietive / comitative, and [-ya]ma negative. In plain words, these include endings meaning ‘with’, ‘many’, ‘want to’, ‘in / at’, ‘again’, ‘for someone’, ‘having’, and ‘not’; a ‘make someone do it’ ending; an ending that turns a verb into a noun; an ending for orders; and endings that match the kind of verb (intransitive or transitive). The ‘make’ piece (-wa) could also be seen as a separate word meaning ‘make.’ The ‘make someone do it’ ending and the ‘not’ ending seem to show up in several South American languages that are not related (David Payne 1990). Shell notes that the Panoan languages share many related bare words, but their endings are very different in form and in use (op. cit.:11).

h: Features of Proto-Pano Grammar (what the shared ancestor language was like)
t:
Shell rebuilds the sound system of RP with 16 consonants and 8 vowels. The consonants are: p, t, k, kʷ, ʔ, m, n, ts, tʃ, r, β, s, ʃ, ʂ, w, y. The vowels are: i, ï, a, o; and each of the four also had a nasal version (said partly through the nose). She also suggests two tone levels (high and low pitch) that went together with stress. These made a real difference in meaning, but tone and stress seem to have shifted in regular, common patterns. Syllables may have come in pairs that formed a beat. The most common syllables were a vowel alone (V) or a consonant plus a vowel (CV). Also, the hissing sounds made without the voice
and the glottal stop (a catch in the throat) could probably close a syllable. But only vowels, and maybe the glottal stop, seem to have come at the end of a word. There were also some rules about which sounds could come next to each other: i and ĩ cannot occur after y, and o and õ cannot occur after kʷ and w; in addition to this, ï and its nasalized counterpart rarely followed ʃ, and i and ĩ rarely followed ʂ (Shell, op. cit.:53-98 and 192).16 Two vowels can come together inside a word piece. Nasal vowels seem to have been less common in the parent language than in today’s languages (see also Key ms., Inter. Dict:270).

h: Features of Proto-Pano Grammar (what the shared ancestor language was like)
t:
One finding is very important for understanding why endings in Panoan languages change shape. Shell proposes a rule (or set of rules) about RP nouns of three syllables made of one single word piece (and maybe other words too). In most of the languages, these nouns lost their last, unstressed vowel or syllable, so they ended up with only two syllables (pp.55 and 63; see also Loos 1973 and 1978, and Valenzuela 1998a).
Shell does not try to rebuild the old endings for nouns and verbs in a careful, complete way. But she does mention some grammar features. One is how much it matters what kind of verb you have (intransitive or transitive), and the different ways the doer and the receiver are marked (pp. 99-104). Another is how the endings on verbs in a secondary part of the sentence match the kind of verb. She also mentions short forms of words, mostly body-part words, that are joined to bare words, and possible traces of a difference between things that belong to you by nature (like your hand) and things you just happen to own (pp.193-194).
Loos’ (1999:230) list of Proto-Panoan consonants differs from Shell’s RP in two ways. Only Shell has the sound Kʷ while only Loos posits h. The four vowels are the same in both. Loos points out that the daughter languages have kept these vowels very consistently. Matses also has an /e/ vowel. And, as Shell points out (see 1.3.4.1), in Kashibo the vowel pairs /ai/ and /au/ have turned into /e/ and /ɔ/.

h: Features of Proto-Pano Grammar (what the shared ancestor language was like)
t:
Two other works deal with central parts of PP grammar: how the doer of a transitive verb is marked (Loos 1985), and the ‘to yourself’ form (Loos 1978).
Chapter 20 of this book also helps rebuild how Proto-Pano put words and sentences together. In it I suggest that the parent language had verb endings that match the people in the sentence. I also suggest that it marked the doer of a transitive verb, the receiver, and the one person of an intransitive verb in three different ways (linguists call this a tripartite system). Along the way I rebuild a handful of grammar word pieces. Some of them change or take further the ones Shell proposed.

h: More Inclusive Classifications (bigger language groupings)
t:
Most scholars agree that the Panoan and Takanan families are related, coming from one shared ancestor. People were writing about this link as early as the end of the 19th century. Navarro (1903:172) says that Armentia (1887) claimed a family link between Shipibo, Konibo, Xetebo, and Kashibo on one side, and Pakawara and Araona, spoken in the Madre de Dios region, on the other. Pakawara is a Panoan language, but Araona belongs to the Takanan family. Schuller (1930) also suggested that Panoan and Takanan might be related (see Aikenvald and Dixon 1999:365).
Key (1968) rebuilds the sounds of Proto-Takanan, giving around 600 sets of related words. She also includes Panoan words that are, or seem to be, related: “cognates or presumed cognates” (1968:52). Girard (1971) rebuilds 116 words for Proto-Pano-Takanan, with regular sound matches (Aikhenvald and Dixon 1999:365). Key
(ms., Inter. Dict.:270) proposes the following sound matches between Proto-Takanan and the Panoan languages:
Using a method that dates language splits by how many basic words have changed (glottochronology), the Pano-Takanan “stock” is thought to have started splitting at least 47 centuries ago (Swadesh 1959, in Kauffman 1990:51).
Still, some scholars are careful about what kind of link there is between Panoan and Takanan. For example, Fabre (1998:820) does not rule out that the two families simply lived side by side long ago and borrowed from each other. That could explain both the many matching words and some matching word pieces in the two families (see also Loos 1999:227).

h: More Inclusive Classifications (bigger language groupings)
t:
Beyond Pano-Takanan, it is not clear what other languages Panoan is related to. Some scholars have suggested a family link between Panoan and these languages spoken further south: Moseten (Suárez 1969); Chon, Yurakare, Moseten, Ona and Tehuelche (Suárez 1973); Qawasqar, Chon, Yurakare,
Moseten, and Mapudungun (Key and Clairis 1978, Key 1978). But I must point out that none of these studies compares rebuilt Proto-Panoan with other rebuilt parent languages. Instead, they compare chosen words from one or more of today’s languages in each group. Fabre (1998:820) looked at these proposals. He concludes that someone still needs to do a careful comparison of words, sounds, and word pieces before we can test whether Macro Pano-Takanan is really related to languages further south.
Migliazza and Wistrand-Robinson have also put forward ideas. Miggliazza suggested that Pano-Takanan may be related to Yanomamo, spoken on the border between Brazil and Venezuela (see Erikson et alia 1994 and the works listed there). Wistrand-Robinson (1991) raised the idea that Panoan and the Uto-Aztecan languages might be related. Fabre (1998:820) points out several problems with this. One is that Wistrand-Robinson gives a split date of only 1,650 years between Panoan and Uto-Aztecan, which is not acceptable.
McQuown (1965) and Greenberg (1987) put Panoan in one group with Ge and Karib.17 On the other hand, Rodrigues (1985, 2000) has argued that Ge, Karib, and Tupi are more closely related to each other, leaving Panoan out. Clearly, we need more studies of single languages and of language history before we can give an acceptable classification of the Panoan languages that covers everything. That work will also help rebuild the history of the languages and cultures of South America.

h: More Inclusive Classifications (bigger language groupings)
t: Kaufman (1990:65) notes that Greenberg’s evidence for Ge-Panoan-Karib is only 12 word comparisons and 5 grammar comparisons.

h: Notes on Language Contact (how contact with other languages has affected Shipibo)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo and its close sister language Wariapano have borrowed a number of words, and a few grammar features, from Quechua. Missionaries and travellers left us some written records about how Quechua was used in the Catholic missions on the Ucayali. Quechua was promoted as the language for converting people to Christianity. Along with it came other parts of Andean culture (Marcoy 1869, Navarro 1903, Tessmann 1930). Some say that by the early 1900s, Wariapano speakers were switching to Quechua and Spanish, and their own language was suffering for it (Tessmann 1999[1930]:65). Wariapano is now considered extinct.
Quechua words in Shipibo-Konibo include atapa ‘hen, chicken’. It comes from Quechua atawalʸpa or walʸpa. Many Amazonian languages borrowed this word (Campbell 1997:12). The Panoan languages of the Purus branch use the form takara instead. (See also the section on sounds for koríki ‘money’ and kirika ‘book’.) Shipibo-Konibo has also borrowed the Quechua numbers for everything above two. The Purus languages have not (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes).
Shipibo-Konibo has even borrowed some grammar words, not just ordinary words. One is kaman ‘until, up to’, a little word placed after a noun. It comes from the Quechua ending -kama, which means the same thing. The Quechua verb ati- ‘can’ lives on in the Shipibo-Konibo verb atipan-, which also means ‘can’. Quechua words also turn up in the chants of Shipibo healers (shamans), even though they are not Quechua

h: Notes on Language Contact (how contact with other languages has affected Shipibo)
t:
speakers. On top of this, traditional stories describe the Incas as magical figures. They brought tools and skills to the Shipibo, but then left them because the Shipibo disobeyed.
As far as I know, there is no solid proof that Quechua or Aymara speakers were in direct contact with Panoan speakers before the European invasion. (But see Tournon 2002:33, 36, 39, 43, 54, 119-120, and the works he cites, on possible exchanges between the Amazon and the Andes in those times.)
The word /o’tʃiti/ ‘dog’ was most likely borrowed into Shipibo-Konibo from an Arawak language, namely Ashaninka.
Today, most Panoan languages are in heavy contact with Spanish in Peru and Bolivia, and with Portuguese in Brazil. In several places this has been going on for quite a long time. Except for older people who speak only Shipibo-Konibo, speakers now commonly use Spanish sounds and syllable shapes that the language did not have before, especially in place names. At the other end, people who speak both languages fluently often switch back and forth between them in the same conversation. As you would expect, there is much more Spanish where the outside world comes in: at school, at political meetings of indigenous groups, and on radio programs broadcast from the city of Pucallpa.
People who speak languages of the Purus group and live in the Purus area may speak several languages. For example, one Sharanawa speaker told us he speaks Sharanawa with everyone in his family. But when he meets Panoans who are not Sharanawa, they talk in “the language.” He also said that

h: Notes on Language Contact (how contact with other languages has affected Shipibo)
t:
he speaks Spanish with the mestizos and Portuguese with Brazilians.^18 Kensinger made an interesting observation (recorded in Shell 1975:25). When speakers of Kashinawa, Amawaka and Marinawa meet now and then on the rivers, they use a kind of simplified mixed language (a pidgin) to understand each other. They need it because their languages are too different to understand each other directly. This may be “the language” the Sharanawa speaker meant. Loos (1999:228) describes something similar between Kashinawa and Sharanawa speakers. They talk in a kind of “pidgin-Panoan” that drops most word endings, especially the ones the two languages don’t share. Also in this group, Sharanawa, Mastanawa and Chaninawa use the Arawak word shima for ‘fish’ (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes).
A few Panoan words have made it into the Spanish of the Peruvian Amazon. One is the name of the city of Contamana. It comes from kontá (a kind of palm, Attalea tessmanii, Palmae) and manan ‘hill, mountain’. So it means ‘hill or mountain where kontá palm trees’ grow in large numbers. Kashibo seems to have recently borrowed some words from Shipibo. Campbell points out that Amuesha has borrowed many words, not only from Quechua but also from Panoan languages (1997:12). Finally, Pano-Takanan can be compared with the Uru-Chipayan languages spoken around Lake Titicaca and Lake Poopo. The comparison suggests that these two groups once lived next to each other, long ago. Interestingly, Uru-Chipayan shares more similar words with Panoan than with Takanan (Fabre 1991, 1994, to appear). Also, some grammar features

h: Theoretical Framework (the ideas behind how I study language)
t: In this section I first explain the main ideas of what is called the “Functional-Typological Approach” to studying language. It is the general way of thinking about language that I follow in this book. Next, I explain Prototype Theory. Many linguists who follow the Functional-Typological Approach use it, whether they say so openly or not. I also talk about transitivity (how many people a verb involves) and related ideas. Finally, I describe my data and the methods I used.

h: The Functional-Typological Approach (studying grammar by what it does and by comparing languages)
t:
Most people agree that there are two big schools of thought in linguistics today. One is the “formal” approach and the other is the “functionalist” approach (Van Valin and LaPolla 1997:8-15, Croft 1991:chapter 1, Dik 1981:1-5, 1989:81-2, 1997:2-3, Dirven and Fried 1987:x-xi, among others). Some scholars say both schools have existed side by side for most of the twentieth century.¹⁹ The two schools differ in their
According to Halliday (Parret 1974:83), Dirven and Fried (1987:xi) and Dik (1997:2-3), the formal school includes American descriptivism / behaviorism (Bloomfield 1933; and Harris 1951), and
basic idea of what human language is. Because of that, they also disagree on big questions: what linguists should study, what counts as a real explanation, and which methods to use.²⁰ The line between the two schools is not always sharp. One writer may call a theory formalist, while another calls the same theory functionalist. Theories also change over time, and scholars can move from one side toward the other.²¹ So I think it is best to talk about functionalist and formalist “poles”, the way Dirven and Fried (1987) do: two ends of a scale, rather than two separate boxes.
Several linguists, especially in Europe, already thought about language in terms of what it does. But the Prague School was the first to make this idea clear and central, right from the start (Daneš, 1987:3). You could say that the Prague School “…has provided the linguistic world with a functionalist awareness (or at least served as its catalyzer)” (Dirven and Fried 1987:x). Functionalism covers a very wide area. It includes how language is used in context and how the mind handles language, which most functionalists today see as obvious. But it also includes language in society, language and culture, languages in contact, the history of languages, and style.

h: The Functional-Typological Approach (studying grammar by what it does and by comparing languages)
t:
Today, functionalism is not one single theory. It is a family of many different views. Some have names, such as Role and Reference
generativism since Chomsky (1957). Both of these see language as an abstract system, completely cut off from the way people actually use it.
Dik (1981:4-5) has a useful chart that sums up the main ideas of these two schools.
For example, Van Valin and LaPolla (1997:11) list Lexical Functional Grammar as functionalist, but other linguists may see it as formalist. Dirven and Fried 1987:xi-ii mention linguists who used to be generativists and have moved toward the functional side.
Grammar, Cognitive Grammar, or Construction Grammar. There are also important individual linguists who don’t belong to any named theory (see Tomlin 1994:144-145, and the works cited there). And there are linguists best known for comparing many languages, or for writing full descriptions of whole languages.

h: Main Tenets of Functionalism (the main ideas of this approach)
t: The main ideas of functionalism can be summed up in the principles below.

h: 1.8.2.1. Language is an Instrument for Communication
t:
Language is first of all a tool for communicating. It is a way to reach a goal. Being a tool means that language “does not exist in and by itself as an arbitrary structure of some kind,” but “by virtue of being used for certain purposes. These purposes concern the social interaction between human beings” (Dik 1997:5). When speakers talk about an event or situation, they picture it in a certain way and choose a point of view. They talk to listeners on purpose, with a goal in mind. They also make choices based on what they think the listener already knows and believes. So, knowing a language includes knowing how to reach your goals when you talk. It also includes the part language plays in how we think. Both are a key
part of what we know about language (Grimes 1975, Hopper and Thompson 1980, Givón 1983, Schiffrin 1987, DeLancey 1991, among others).

h: 1.8.2.2. Isomorphism of Form and Function, and Arbitrariness
t:
A tool is shaped by the job it does. Grammar is the tool, and communication is the job. So, functionalists believe the link between the shape of language (form) and what it is used for (function) is not random. Instead, the way a sentence is built tends to match what it means. Grammar is limited by what it has to do. Because of this, we can find the same patterns again and again in different languages. And these links between form and job can be explained by more general facts about society and the human mind (Tomlin 1994:152, Croft 2001).
Still, the links between form and job are complicated and indirect. One job does not always match exactly one form. Every language’s grammar has some parts that are simply random. One reason is that different good reasons can pull a language in different directions. How a language settles that tug-of-war is always partly random (Croft 1995:504-509, 2001).

h: 1.8.2.3. Language is not an Autonomous System
t:
Most functionalists share one basic belief. We are born with mental abilities that let us learn and use language. But these abilities are not only for language,
they are shared with other parts of the mind that have nothing to do with language. So we can’t properly describe or explain language and grammar as a system that stands on its own (Givón 1994:xv). The strongest version of this view says that children start with a powerful set of general learning tools. They use these tools to build a grammar out of the rich language they hear around them. Every part of grammar develops fresh from the way people talk to each other. A milder version says some knowledge of language may be there from birth. But the details of each particular language must come from the child’s interaction with the speech around them (Tomlin 1994:148-9). Since grammar is not random, and its shape is guided by what it is used for, languages can be learned.

h: Typological and Descriptive Studies (comparing languages and describing them)
t:
Studies that compare many languages (linguists call this typology) usually start from the job a form does. The forms are different in each language, but the jobs are shared by all. So, to compare grammar in languages that are not related, a good method is to start with a job and see how each language does it.
Such studies first list the possible types for a given feature, and sort languages into those types. But they also look for features that seemed unrelated and yet tend to show up together. They also work out how one structure can change into another over time. In
this way, these studies discover rules that hold for all languages, or rules of the type “if a language has X, it also has Y.” These rules in turn must be explained by what language is used for or by how the mind works.
Studies that compare languages, studies of how languages change, and full descriptions of single languages usually follow what is called “Basic Linguistic Theory” (BLT). BLT is a mixed toolkit that grew slowly over the last hundred years. Its goal is to describe each language on its own terms, in a way that is easy to use. It avoids unnecessary formal machinery taken from theories that might not last. BLT is built on the long experience of describing many particular languages, and it has gained a lot from what we learned by comparing languages (Dixon 1997:128, Dryer http://linguistics.buffalo.edu/people/faculty/dryer/blt December 2002; see also criticisms in Everett 2002).

h: Typological and Descriptive Studies (comparing languages and describing them)
t: BLT has taken over some methods from structuralism, especially for sounds and word pieces. It has also been influenced somewhat by early generative grammar for sentences, and more recently by newer theories of sounds (generative and autosegmental phonology). But unlike structuralism and generativism, BLT also pays attention to meaning, to how language is used in context, and to how it changes over time. That is why BLT fits inside a bigger approach that tries to explain things: the Functional-Typological Approach.

h: Prototype Theory (the idea of "typical" vs. "less typical" examples of a category)
t:
Many functionalist linguists think prototype theory is a way of sorting things into groups that fits the nature of human language. So it also fits the kind of
grammar rules we need to talk about languages. Before looking at how linguists use prototypes, let’s first explain what prototype theory is.
Before prototype theory, the usual way to sort things into groups worked like a checklist. Any feature is either there or not there. Things belong to the same group only if they all share certain features. Those features are both needed and enough to define the group. Under this view, every language category is a single group with sharp edges. All members are equally good examples, and grammar rules should have no exceptions.
Eleanor Rosch was the first to propose that all our thinking is organized around prototypes, that is, typical “best examples”, and around basic-level groups. But the idea goes back to the philosopher Wittgenstein. He talked about groups with fuzzy edges, held together by “family resemblance” (Lakoff 1987). In the prototype view, most members of one group are easy to tell apart from most members of a contrasting group. But at least some groups have members that belong “more” or “less”, instead of having sharp edges. Another idea is that a group is defined by many features, not just one. Some of these features are shared by more members than others. The features don’t come separately; they tend to go together. So in most cases, if something has one feature, it has many of the others too. Each group has a core meaning, and its members fit this core more or less well. Because of this “internal structure,” some members are better examples than others. Think of a robin and a penguin: both are birds, but a robin is a better example. Furthermore, the

h: Prototype Theory (the idea of "typical" vs. "less typical" examples of a category)
t:
features of certain groups come from the nature of the human body and from our experience of living in a physical and social world. Finally, because prototype groups have fuzzy edges, we can stretch them to new uses, as in metaphors (Rosch 1973, 1977, 1978; Givón 1984, 1997; Lakoff 1987). For all these reasons, grammar rules in prototype-based studies don’t have to be free of exceptions.
As I said, several linguists have taken up the prototype view. For example, Keenan (1976) describes roles like “subject” as a bundle of features: some about meaning, some about use in context, and some about grammar. Based on these features, languages build up their roles like subject and object to different degrees. Givón (1995, 1997) has read Keenan’s work as a prototype-based approach. Another example is Hopper and Thompson’s (1980) very influential article on transitivity (how strongly an action passes from a doer to a receiver). They reject the old definition, which used a single feature. Instead they list ten features. With these, any sentence can be placed somewhere on a scale from weak to strong transitivity. Shibatani (1985) openly uses prototype theory for passive sentences (like “the boy was bitten”). He shows that passives and ordinary active sentences form a scale. There is a typical passive. Passives also partly resemble other kinds of sentences: “to yourself” sentences, “to each other” sentences, things that happen by themselves, “can be done” sentences, polite forms, and plural forms. Levin’s (1993) way of sorting verbs is another case that goes against the old checklist idea. Levin says that the way a verb behaves depends mostly on what it means. However, it is unlikely that one piece of meaning alone is enough

h: Prototype Theory (the idea of "typical" vs. "less typical" examples of a category)
t: to define a particular group of verbs. Instead, it is a combination of features that together reflects the meaning the verbs in the group share. Also, many of these pieces of meaning are shared with other groups of verbs. So, what one piece of meaning brings with it will show up in several verb groups (1993:16-7). As I will discuss below, the prototype approach has also been used to study Shipibo-Konibo (Valenzuela 1997).

h: Alignment Typology (ways languages mark the doer and the receiver)
t:
Every language has a way of organizing the main people in a sentence: the doer, the receiver, or the one person a sentence is about. Following Harris and Campbell (1995:240), I call this “alignment.” The good thing about this word is that it doesn’t say how a language shows this organization. It could be endings on nouns, little words before or after nouns, pieces on the verb, word order, the tune of the voice, or a mix of these (Givón 1984:136, 146-7). As is now usual in these studies, I use short labels for the main people in a sentence. S_{a} and S_{o} are for sentences with an intransitive verb. S_{a} is the single person when they actively do something (“she runs”). S_{o} is the single person when something just happens to them (“she falls”). With verbs that need two or more people, the labels depend on the verb’s typical meaning. A is the one most like a doer. O is the one most like a receiver (Dixon 1979, 1994; cf. Harris 1997, Mithun and Chafe 1999).
Linguists widely agree that languages organize these people in at least three basic ways. Lazard (1998:41) says these patterns come from two forces pulling against each other: being clear, and saving effort. The first way is the one English uses. It sets the doer apart from the receiver. S_{a}, S_{o} and A are all treated alike (nominative), while O is treated differently (accusative). Think of English she and her: “she runs”, “she falls” and “she sees him” all use she, but “he sees her” uses her. This pattern highlights the “starting points” of what we say (Mithun and Chafe 1999). The second way is the one Shipibo-Konibo uses. Here S_{a}, S_{o} and O are treated alike, with no marker (absolutive). A, the doer of a transitive verb, is treated differently, with the doer marker (ergative). Some say this pattern shows more clearly who does what to whom in typical actions (Lazard 1998:249). A third way, the active-inactive pattern, separates the single person who acts (S_{a}) from the single person something happens to (S_{o}). S_{a} is then treated like A, and S_{o} like O. This pattern shows the difference between doers and non-doers in meaning. But which verbs count as “active” or “inactive” can differ from language to language.²² From now on, I will call these three basic patterns “accusative,” “ergative” and “active.” Some languages also have a “tripartite” (three-way) pattern, where S (that is, S_{a} and S_{o}), A and O are all treated differently (Dixon 1994:39-41). Others have a “neutral” pattern, where S, A and O are all treated the same.

h: Alignment Typology (ways languages mark the doer and the receiver)
t:
The active-inactive pattern has also been called by other names, such as split-S, active-stative and dual structure; see Mithun 1991, and Lazard 1986.
Most languages with the doer-marker pattern (ergative), and maybe also those with the active pattern, switch to a different pattern in some parts of their grammar. Where the switch happens can depend on several things. It can depend on the kind of noun phrase, or on whether we are dealing with nouns or with person pieces on the verb. It can depend on the tense (past, present, future) or the kind of action. It can depend on what kind of sentence part it is, or on how the sentence fits into the conversation (Dixon 1994, Harris and Campbell 1995, Blake 1977, Blake and Dixon 1979: 6-9, among others). Linguists call this a “split” in the doer-marker pattern: “split-ergativity.”

h: Database and Methodology (where my examples come from and how I gathered them)
t:
I first started working with the Shipibo in early 1990. I was hired as a linguist for a program that trained and certified bilingual teachers. The program was co-directed by the Indigenous Confederation of the Peruvian Amazon (AIDESEP). For about four years I worked closely with Shipibo students in the city of Iquitos. I also worked with them and other Shipibo in several villages on the Ucayali River and the rivers that flow into it. My work then was mostly about teaching, not about recording the language. Still, living in the Shipibo world and the friendships I made gave me priceless experience. They also made it much easier to do my later research on language and culture. I did not focus on describing the language while I lived in the Amazon. But I did learn to speak some Shipibo-Konibo and got a certain feel for the language. However, all the data and all the points in this book are based only
on the speech of native speakers for whom Shipibo-Konibo is their main or even their only language, and / or on what they judged to be correct. During my graduate studies outside Peru, my understanding of Shipibo-Konibo grammar grew a lot, while my ability to speak it dropped sharply.
Most of the data in this book comes from my own work among the Shipibo, mainly recorded stories and conversations. I gathered them mostly during several stays in Shipibo territory and in nearby towns and cities, at different times, especially between 1996 and 2002. Shipibo helpers and I wrote down the recordings and translated them into Spanish. Other texts I used include reading materials written for Shipibo readers. Native speakers checked these texts, and often also translated them into Spanish. I did not use materials first written in another language and then translated into Shipibo-Konibo, such as the New Testament or the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights. Unless I say otherwise, the example sentences in this book come from my own collection. For examples from other sources, I did the analysis, the word-by-word labels, and the English translation myself, except for those from my own earlier publications.

h: Database and Methodology (where my examples come from and how I gathered them)
t:
Besides the texts, I used a lot of material I got by asking speakers directly, plus other field notes. These include things I overheard native speakers say, and their own feelings about whether a sentence sounds right. When asking for sentences, I preferred to set up scenes from Shipibo village life, or sometimes made-up events. I tried to rely as little as possible on asking people to translate single sentences.
I have also asked speakers whether sentences sound right, even though this method has its problems. But I tried to place each sentence in a fitting real-life situation. I want to stress that the Shipibo who worked with me value their identity and language very highly. They also know well that they alone decide what is good Shipibo-Konibo and what is not. I often worked with speakers who had taken basic linguistics classes I taught in the past, or who just naturally enjoyed analyzing language. These helpers knew very well that linguistics is about what native speakers really say and do with their language. It is not about rules of “correct” speech, or about copying sentence patterns from Spanish, the dominant language. As the introduction shows, Shipibo-Konibo is spoken by a small group, but it is very much alive. Besides studying common sentences, my helpers and I often liked to explore the rarer possibilities of the language, and sometimes to test and understand its limits. In several of these talks, my helpers gave me important insights that were the key to the analyses in this book.

h: Database and Methodology (where my examples come from and how I gathered them)
t:
As a rule, I prefer data from natural texts over data I got by asking, especially for describing how sentences are built. I used asked-for material to describe the sounds, to fill in full sets of forms, and to look more closely at things I first noticed in natural speech. I also used it for specific points that natural speech rarely answers. Unless I say otherwise, every example has been checked by at least one more speaker.
My analysis here is mainly about kinds and qualities, not numbers. Still, in a couple of chapters I give some counts of how often a pattern or combination appears in my data. But I don’t claim these numbers are statistically significant.
When I discuss a grammar feature or a type of sentence, I have tried to say both what job it does and what it looks like. I also give a short look at the topic across the world’s languages, to see how Shipibo-Konibo fits in with what we know about other languages. Then I describe Shipibo-Konibo on its own terms, using what is called the Basic Linguistic Theory framework. After that, I compared what I found with specific questions raised by other linguists. But the chapters don’t always follow this order, and different chapters put more weight on different kinds of analysis. For some topics, I also give data from related languages and suggest how things may have changed over time.

h: Database and Methodology (where my examples come from and how I gathered them)
t:
I know very well that this book has many gaps and weak points. But I hope my work captures some of the genius of the Shipibo-Konibo language and encourages more work, especially in Peru.
A GRAMMAR OF SHIPIBO-KONIBO:
TYPOLOGICAL CHARACTERIZATION AND OTHER SALIENT FEATURES:
Before we look at the different layers of the language (its sounds, how its words are built, and how its sentences are put together), I will quickly place SK among a few well-known ways of sorting the world's languages. I will also point out some of its typical features. That way, you can get a feel for what kind of language this is right from the start. I have also added some notes on how the language has changed over time, a short list of things SK does not have, and a summary of points about meaning and culture that some readers may find especially interesting.

h: Typological Characterization of Shipibo-Konibo (what kind of language Shipibo is)
t:
SK builds its words mostly by sticking pieces together, one after another, like beads on a string (linguists call this an agglutinating language). A single word is often made of several word pieces. Usually each piece has one job, and each job has its own piece. In most words it is easy to see where one piece ends and the next begins. Still, many nouns and adjectives appear bare, with nothing added. That is because the plain form (ABS) usually has no ending at all, and the words in a noun phrase don't have to match each other. There are also some strings of word pieces
that run together, so you can't clearly tell where one ends and the next begins. Examples are certain nouns plus the doer marker, or a bare verb plus the ending that takes away the receiver. In addition, a few words change their base form, and a few use a completely different word in some forms (as English ‘go’ becomes ‘went’). Finally, the verb can carry one or more endings that add direction or adverb-like meanings. This is a little like packing a whole sentence into one word (linguists call this a polysynthetic tendency).
SK adds its word pieces at the end of words: it uses endings, not beginning pieces. There is one exception. A small, fixed group of nouns, mostly names of body parts, can appear in a shortened form. These shortened nouns attach to the front of verbs, adjectives and other nouns as beginning pieces. There is also one case where a change in stress (which syllable is said loudest) does the work of an ending. When you call out to someone, nouns that end in an unstressed vowel move the stress to their last syllable. (Linguists call this kind of marking by stress a suprafix, or suprasegmental marking.)

h: Typological Characterization of Shipibo-Konibo (what kind of language Shipibo is)
t: SK also has little relation words that come after a noun, where English puts words like ‘in’ or ‘with’ before it (linguists call these postpositions). It also has several kinds of small pieces that lean on another word (clitics). Some of these can even come before an ending, so they end up inside the word. For that reason they are better called “endoclitics.” The line between the after-words and these small pieces is sometimes blurry. The same is true of the line between two verbs used together (or joined into one) and a verb followed by an ending.

h: Basic Constituent Order (the usual word order in a sentence)
t:
In its basic word order, SK tends to put the main word of each phrase last (linguists call this the head-final type). Some word-order rules are strict. The owner always comes before the thing owned, as in English ‘John's house.’ And, as I said above, SK puts its relation words after the noun, not before it. Still, word order in SK is very flexible. This is true for the main parts of a sentence. The only exception is sentences turned into nouns and sentences that carry a same-person or different-person marker: these always end with the verb. Word order is also flexible inside a noun phrase. For instance, adjectives, some words for amounts, the
numbers ‘one’ and especially ‘two,’ and “who/which…” description parts can come either before or after the noun they describe. This makes no clear difference to the meaning. Also, most helping verbs can come before or after the main verb. The separate word kikin ‘extremely, truly’ always comes before the adjective and the noun it describes. But there are also endings with a similar ‘very’ meaning, namely -yora and -shaman. Words that tell how something is done, and phrases with an after-word, can come before or after the verb. Linking verbs like ‘be’ can come before or after the word they link to. And keen- ‘want’ can come before or after the other part of its sentence. This holds both when it means ‘want someone else to do something’ and when it means ‘want to do something yourself.’

h: Expression of Arguments (how the people in a sentence are shown)
t: In SK, the people and things taking part in an action are named by separate words, nouns or pronouns. These words carry markers that show their role. The verb and the helping verb have no pieces that point back to them. (There is one exception: when there is more than one doer and the noun doesn't show it, the verb must get a plural ending.) So SK is a language where both the doer and the receiver are named by full words (linguists call this a lexical argument language, as defined in Jelinek 1984). When the doer or receiver is simply left out, you understand ‘he,’ ‘she’ or ‘it.’ There is no regular way to tell a direct receiver from an indirect one (like ‘the book’ versus ‘to Mary’ in ‘I gave the book to Mary’). Nor is there a way to tell a main receiver from a second one.

h: Head-Marking versus Dependent-Marking Features (whether markers go on the main word or on the words around it)
t:
Languages differ in where they put their markers. Some put them on the main word of a phrase. Others put them on the words that depend on it. SK mostly marks the dependent words (linguists call this a dependent-marking language). Here are the signs of this. The nouns themselves carry the role markers, and the verb has no pieces pointing to them. Ownership is marked on the owner, not on the thing owned, as with the ‘'s’ on ‘John’ in ‘John's book.’ The noun after a relation word gets a marker too (the plain form or a side marker). And some adverb-like words get an ending that matches the role of the noun they go with. “Who/which…” description parts are also like this. Their verb is not a full verb form, it always comes last, and some of the people involved may be left unsaid. All of these are clear signs of marking the dependent word, and other kinds of sentence parts that hang off a main sentence share them too.
But SK also has some signs of marking the main word. For example, a “who/which…” description part can contain the noun it describes inside itself. Some kinds of ‘not’ also go on the main word instead of on the word that depends on it. When you say ‘nobody’ or ‘nothing,’ or ‘no child came,’ the ‘not’ goes on the verb, not on the noun. And when you say what something is not made of, as in ‘not a wooden house,’ the ‘not’ goes on the noun ‘house,’ not on ‘wooden.’ Finally, the verb can carry adverb-like information. It can show whether an action goes on all night or all day long, is done completely, is done again, is done by two people, is spread out over many things, goes up or down the river, or goes from or towards a certain point in the story, and so on. These last features can be seen as marking the main word. When an adjective describes a noun, neither the noun nor the adjective gets a marker.

h: Case-Marking (the endings that show a noun's role in the sentence)
t:
SK marks the doer in a fairly strict way. The doer of a transitive verb gets the doer marker (ERG). The receiver, and the one person of an intransitive verb, appear in the plain form with no marker (ABS). (Linguists call this an ergative-absolutive system.) The doer marker is -n, a small piece that attaches to the last word of the noun phrase. The plain form is -a for some pronouns and nothing at all everywhere else. Most languages with this kind of system, including most of SK's relatives in the Panoan family, switch to a different system in certain situations. SK has none of the usual switches of this kind. A possible exception is the emphatic pronouns (‘I myself’ and so on). Their markers work more like English ‘I’ and ‘me’: every doer is treated the same, whether the verb has a receiver or not. Also, in ‘want to’ sentences and in sentences that clearly say an action is going on, the doer of a transitive verb can appear either in the plain form or with the doer marker. Which one is used depends on the status of the receiver in the conversation.
The small piece -n has many different forms and many jobs. Besides marking the doer, it also marks the owner (‘of’), the tool or means (‘with’), place and direction (‘in, at, to’), time, and other side roles. So one marker covers several meanings that other languages keep apart (linguists call this case syncretism). The sets of pronouns are uneven: some pronouns have more different forms than other pronouns and than nouns.

h: Participant Agreement (words that "agree" with who is doing the action)
t:
Some adverb-like words, phrases and sentence parts are not core players of the verb, so I call them “adjuncts.” Their meaning is tied to one main person in the sentence, the core participant or
controller. They get an ending that matches the role this person plays in the sentence. These matching endings come in three sets: one for the doer of a transitive verb, one for the one person of an intransitive verb, and one for the receiver (a three-way, or tripartite, pattern). So this feature can be seen as another kind of split in the doer-marking system, one that may be found only in the Panoan family.

h: Clause-Chaining and Switch-Reference System (linking actions in a chain and tracking who does each one)
t:
SK likes to link two or more sentence parts into a chain. Only one of them, the main one, has a full verb form; the others have a shorter verb form (linguists call this a clause-chaining language). The shorter parts carry a marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else (I call this “reference-marking”). Still, SK rarely has the very long chains found in some languages of Papua New Guinea (e.g., Wambon, de Vries ms.; Haruai, Comrie 1998). In SK these marked parts always end with the verb. They usually don't name their doer. They show no obvious sign of being turned into a noun. And they can come before, after, or inside the main sentence. Also, a marked part doesn't have to sit right next to its main sentence, and two or more marked parts can share the same main sentence.
These same-person and different-person markers do more than tell you whether the two actions share a person. They also show the order of the two events in time or in logic. On top of that, the same-person markers can show whether the main verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. That is because most of them look exactly like the matching endings I mentioned above. So their form depends on whether the shared person is the one person of an intransitive verb (S) or the doer of a transitive verb (A) in the main sentence. These same-

h: Clause-Chaining and Switch-Reference System (linking actions in a chain and tracking who does each one)
t: or different-person markers can also be used to show whether a story flows on smoothly or makes a break (discourse continuity or discontinuity).

h: Transitivity Agreement (verb forms that change depending on whether the main verb is transitive or intransitive)
t: SK has other features where things must match the type of verb. Verbs about the stages of an action, like ‘start,’ ‘finish,’ and ‘stop (doing something),’ must match their main verb: intransitive with intransitive, transitive with transitive. The same happens with stand-in verbs or helping verbs, verbs used in a row, certain verb endings, and verbs that have completely different forms for the two types.

h: Split-Ergativity (where the "doer marker" system is used and where it is not)
t: As I said above, SK marks the doer quite consistently with the doer-marker system. The same pattern also shows up in how two kinds of sentences work. In commands, only the one person of an intransitive verb or the receiver may be openly named. In “who/which…” description parts that contain their own noun, only such a person can be understood as the same as someone in the main sentence. On the other hand, some things work the way English does, treating every doer alike, with or without a receiver (linguists call this nominative-accusative). These are the markers on emphatic pronouns, the plural verb ending -kan, and most rules about who is understood to do what across linked sentences. And as I said above, the matching endings on adjuncts follow a three-way pattern. The emphatic pronouns also have different shapes for the one person of an intransitive verb (S), the doer (A), and the receiver (O).

h: Evidentiality (markers that show how the speaker knows something)
t: SK has markers that show how the speaker knows something. They work on two levels. First, they separate what you know firsthand from what you heard from someone else. On top of that, two more markers can be added to show that you are working it out from clues or just guessing. In SK these markers are not verb endings. They are small pieces that usually attach to the first main part of the sentence. But if that first part is a full verb, the markers come before the plural ending and the endings for the stage of the action. In stories, the ‘I saw it’ marker and the ‘they say’ marker don't appear in every sentence. Instead, they mark off certain chunks of the story. SK also lets you pass on someone else's orders or requests with a ‘they say’ command. These markers can also show how sure the speaker is, and surprise at something new.

h: Other Salient Features (other notable features)
t:
The vowel /ɨ/ is one of the four vowels SK has. This sound has been named as one typical feature of Amazonian languages (Aikhenvald and Dixon 1999:8). Probably the most interesting sound is /ɻ/, an r-like sound made with the tongue tip curled back. Its pronunciation varies a lot. Some word pieces have two forms. Which one is used depends on whether the word it attaches to has an even or an odd number of beats (moras). This has been called “alternate mora-timing” (Lauriault 1948). However, the answer to the question of whether
the consonants that close a syllable count as beats in SK, or only the vowels do, is not simple. You can see this from where the stress falls and from how word pieces change their form.
In SK, role markers can be piled on top of each other. A noun can carry up to four markers that we can trace back in history (linguists call this case-stacking). The ‘from’ markers are always built on top of the ‘in/at’ markers.
A few verb endings show specific times, such as different degrees of past (how long ago) and a ‘tomorrow’ future. Other interesting verb endings show direction and adverb-like meanings. SK also has several ways to change how many people a verb involves. There are a few ‘make someone do it’ endings that show different degrees of force. There are three endings that bring in an extra person, and one of them only goes on transitive verbs. There is a ‘middle’ ending that can mean ‘to yourself,’ ‘it happened by itself,’ and sometimes ‘was done.’ And there is a special ending for ‘to each other.’ Verbs can contain body-part beginning pieces. They can also contain sound-imitating words (like English ‘bang’), joined to general verbs meaning ‘do,’ with or without a receiver. Short answers to yes/no questions are interesting. They use these general verbs as stand-in verbs (a bit like English ‘I did’), together with a same-person marker. ‘Let's…’ suggestions that include the listener, and ‘don't…’ commands, are made of two sentence parts. “Who/which…” description parts can come before the noun, after it, around it, or alongside the sentence.

h: Diachronic Observations (how the language has changed over time)
t:
Some verbs have become, or are becoming, pieces that attach to other verbs, while still working as verbs too. For example, the verb yama- ‘not exist’ is also the ‘not’ ending on verbs. The transitive verb pake- ‘cause to fall’ can be
added to another transitive verb to show an action spread over many things. The verbs ‘come’ and ‘go’ seem to have joined with another marker to become endings meaning ‘coming here’ and ‘going away.’ And the verb toshi- ‘pop up, burst’ can be added to another verb to show that something happens suddenly. As I said above, when the sentence's second-position pieces attach to a full verb, they must come before the plural -kan and the endings for the stage of the action. This suggests that the plural and stage endings became endings fairly recently. The endings that bring in an extra person look the same as the same-person markers, and their meanings fit together. This may be because one grew out of the other (Valenzuela 1999). Some pairs of sentence types look the same but behave differently: one is a full sentence, the other is turned into a noun. These are also thought to share a common origin. There are a few verb forms made of several words, such as the “narrative past.” Their structure clearly shows that they come from sentences turned into nouns.

h: Diachronic Observations (how the language has changed over time)
t:
Some after-words grew out of body-part nouns with a place marker added. For example, pekáo ‘behind’ < peká ‘back’ + the ‘around/near’ place marker -o. The ‘with’ after-word betan has also become the word ‘and’ between nouns, while still meaning ‘with.’ A shortened form of this ‘with’ word also combines with the beginning piece ra- ‘body, person’ to form the number rabé ‘two.’ The ‘very’ ending -yora probably comes from yora ‘person, body’ (see also Semantic and Cultural Observations below).
The matching endings on adjuncts show traces of an older three-way marking system. Chapter 20 looks at this unusual feature, both in SK today and compared with related languages. Pointing words (‘this, that’) that carry a same-person or different-person marker have become linking words, joining parts of a sentence or whole sentences. The middle-distance pointing word ja has become
the pronoun ‘he, she, it.’ It can also work like the English article ‘the,’ while the number ‘one’ can be used like ‘a.’

h: Negative Characteristics (things Shipibo does NOT have)
t:
SK has no grammatical gender or noun classes, and no classifier words. It makes no clear difference between things you own that can be given away and things that are always part of you. It has no separate words for ‘we including you’ and ‘we not including you’ (but see the ‘let's’ forms). It has no special form for exactly two (although the verb ending -bekon shows an action done by two people). And it has no polite pronouns. As for verbs, they have no pieces that point to who is doing what to whom.
SK also lacks the usual ways of rearranging a sentence around a different main person. It has no passive with a named doer (like ‘the fish was caught by the man’), and no antipassive (a form that drops the receiver and keeps the doer).

h: Semantic and Cultural Observations (meaning and culture in the language)
t:
Most verbs for seeing, knowing, thinking and saying are used in full transitive sentences. Feelings are usually expressed with intransitive verbs plus an extra phrase. The person who feels is the one person of the verb (S), and the cause of the feeling gets a side marker. Forces, illnesses and other non-living things that affect others act like strong doers in the sentence. For example, the only way to say English ‘drown (intr.)’ (‘he drowned’) is with the verb ‘kill.’ The flowing water is the doer (A), and the person affected is the receiver (O).
In turn, to say English ‘drown (tr.)’ (‘drown someone’) you would need a ‘make someone do it’ sentence. Literally: ‘X caused the flowing water to kill Y’ (see exx. (8)-(9) in Chapter 16). The same goes for ‘to die suffocated’ and ‘to die from vomiting.’ These use the nouns join ‘air’ and kinan ‘vomit,’ respectively. Also, to say that something ‘aches,’ the body part is made the doer of a transitive sentence.
Making compound words is very common. Names of animals and plants at the general level (the genus) tend to be single words. But most names for kinds below that level are compounds. It is common to use the name of a very noticeable animal or plant to describe, as a kind of image, a typical feature of a species. For example, ino-rono ‘jaguar-snake’ is a kind of snake whose head is said to look like a jaguar's (Valenzuela 1998b). Traditional Shipibo personal names are also compounds. As a rule, the first part is shared by women and men, and some of these may be linked to old clan names. The second part is usually specific to each sex. Names of peoples are usually based on animal names; e.g., Kashibo [kaʃi ‘bat’ + -βo collective / plural] ‘Bat People.’

h: Semantic and Cultural Observations (meaning and culture in the language)
t:
Sound-imitating words are a common way to make new words. They are often joined to the general verbs meaning ‘do’ (intransitive or transitive) or to helping verbs. This is used to coin new vocabulary; e.g., to’-a-ti [ONOM-do.T-INF] ‘shotgun’ (lit. ‘sth. to make “to” to so./sth. else’), to' ak- [ONOM-do.T] ‘kill with a shotgun,’ to' ik- [ONOM-do.I] ‘kill oneself with a shotgun.’ In these labels, ONOM is the sound word, do.T is the transitive ‘do,’ do.I is the intransitive ‘do,’ and INF is the basic ‘to do’ form of the verb.
The adverb bakish is best translated as ‘one day from today,’ because it means both ‘yesterday’ and ‘tomorrow.’ There are also two different words for English ‘water.’ Jene is flowing water, and onpax is water in a container. So when you bathe in the river, you must make sure little children do not swallow jene. But you can only drink a glass of onpax. Jene also means ‘sap’ or ‘juice.’ After xoma ‘breast,’ it means ‘milk.’
The word piti is built from the verb pi- ‘eat’ plus the ending -ti, which turns a verb into a noun for something that is going to be done (like English ‘to eat’ used as a thing). So piti literally means ‘food.’ But people mostly understand piti as ‘fish,’ which is the Shipibo food par excellence. Here is a passage from Valenzuela (2000a:4) (see also 1.3.6): “The impressive resources of the major rivers and adjacent ox-bow lakes constitute the principal source of protein for the Shipibo, for whom “a day without fresh fish is a day of starvation” (Lathrap op.cit., p.19)”. There is one more word, yapa, which also means ‘fish.’

h: Semantic and Cultural Observations (meaning and culture in the language)
t:
The color words are joxo ‘white,’ wiso ‘black,’ chexe ‘sharp (color), black,’ yankon ‘blue / green,’ panshin ‘yellow,’ and joshin ‘red’ (also ‘ripe’). Notice that the last two words end the same way, in -shin. One more word, emo, is best translated as ‘faded white, colorless.’ Think of an old piece of cloth that has lost its color. SK is fairly rich in words for smells: about ten different words for kinds of smells have been found (Tournon, p.c.).
Shipibo has only two native number words: westíora ‘one’ and rabé ‘two.’ For higher numbers, people borrowed the Quechua words. Westíora may come from westí ‘few, sparse’ + yora ‘body, person,’ which became an ending that makes things stronger. And, as I mentioned above, rabé comes from ra-
a shortened form of ‘body, person,’ + -bé, a shortened form of beta(n) ‘with,’ which also shows up on pronouns.
The words wetsa and poi both mean ‘brother or sister,’ but they depend on who is speaking. Wetsa is a sibling of the same sex: a man’s brother or a woman’s sister. Poi is a sibling of the opposite sex: a man’s sister or a woman’s brother. The word rayos means a man’s parent-in-law, or a man’s or woman’s son-in-law, but not a daughter-in-law. In Shipibo culture, relatives who are rayos to each other must not speak directly. They talk through their daughter or wife. Because of this custom, people often use the ‘may he do it’ type of sentence. For example, they say ‘May your husband bring firewood’ instead of ‘Bring firewood!’ (linguists call these jussive sentences). The word chichi means both ‘mother’s mother’ and ‘highest authority’ (see 1.3.7).

h: Semantic and Cultural Observations (meaning and culture in the language)
t: PHONOLOGY AND MORPHO-PHONOLOGY:

h: Phonemic Inventory (the list of sounds)
t:
SK has 4 vowels and 15 consonants.¹ The four vowels that make a difference in meaning are shown in Table 3.1:
This section is mainly based on the analysis provided in Valenzuela, Márquez, and Maddieson (2001).
None of the four vowels is said at the very edge of the mouth (fully front, fully back, fully high or fully low). In syllables that end in a consonant, the vowels are often said closer to the middle of the mouth. The SK vowels are the same four that have been proposed for the old parent language of the Pano family, called Reconstructed-Pano (Shell 1975:79-80). Below are pairs of words that differ in only one vowel. Each pair shows that the vowel changes the meaning:
(1) /ˈkini/ | ‘hole’ | /ˈkani-/ | ‘went (remote past)’ | /ˈkoni/ | ‘eel’ | /ˈkɨni/ | ‘whisker, beard’
The vowel /o/ (said with rounded lips, at the back of the mouth) can sound like [o], [U], or [u]. Of these, [o] is probably the most common. The higher sounds [U] and [u] come before /i/, as in [ˈui] ‘rain,’ [ˈhui] ‘word,’ [ˈnui] ‘love,’ and [ˈjui] (a person’s name). The lower sound [o] is often found next to /a/: [ˈʂao] ‘bone,’ [ˈtsoa] ‘who (absolutive, the plain form).’ The vowel /i/ is said as [i] when it is stressed. Otherwise it can also sound like [I] or [e], and speakers switch freely between them. You can hear this in the last vowel of /oˈtʃiti/ ‘dog,’ which comes out as [oˈtʃite] ~ [oˈtʃitI].

h: Phonemic Inventory (the list of sounds)
t:
The vowel /ɨ/ is a high vowel said in the middle of the mouth, with lips spread. After tongue-tip sounds, especially /t, n, s/, it sounds just like that: [ɨ]. After lip sounds and back-of-the-mouth sounds, it moves back and sounds like [ɯ]. That [ɯ] sound is also how people prefer to say the vowel when they say it on its own.²
I could not always hear the difference between /βɨ/ and /wɨ/. But Shipibo speakers who worked with me always kept them apart.
Shipibo has vowels said through the nose, but in this book I treat them as a vowel + /n/ (written /Vn/).³ Some words have vowels that sound long, like [na:] ‘nest,’ [βo:] ‘hair,’ [tɨ:] ‘work,’ [mi:n-] ‘bury,’ and [kɨ:n-] ‘want.’ But vowel length never changes the meaning of a word, so long and short vowels are not really different sounds in the language (see 3.1.5).
SK has fifteen consonant sounds, as shown in Table 3.2.
There are three ‘stop’ sounds (sounds where the air is blocked and then let go, like English p, t, k). None of them uses the voice, and none has a puff of air after it. They are made at the lips, at the teeth, and at the back of the mouth. There is also a glottal stop, the little catch in the throat you hear in the middle of English ‘uh-oh.’ Where it shows up seems to be predictable: before a vowel that starts what you say, after a stressed vowel that ends what you say, and at certain places where word pieces join, such as between one-syllable

h: Phonemic Inventory (the list of sounds)
t:
This way of analyzing them also fits other facts about the sounds of the language and how word pieces change when they join (see 3.1.3.1 and 3.1.6.2).
sound-imitating words and the helper verbs that go with them.⁴ Shipibo is different from the old parent language, Reconstructed-Pano, in three ways: it has no /ʔ/ as a real sound, no /kʷ/ (a ‘k’ said with rounded lips), and it does have /h/ (Shell 1975:53-78).
The sounds /ts/ and /tʃ/ (like the ‘ts’ in ‘cats’ and the ‘ch’ in ‘church’) are each treated as one single sound, not two. The reason is that no word in the language starts with two consonants in a row. Below are pairs of words that show these sounds change the meaning:
(2) /mɨˈtʃa/ | ‘wet’ | /mɨˈtsa/ | ‘beautiful’ | /tʃaˈma/ | ‘enemy (vocative)’ | /tsaˈma-/ | ‘get together’
There are five ‘hissing or breathy’ sounds (sounds made by pushing air through a narrow gap). Three are ‘s’-like sounds made with the front of the tongue: /s, ʃ, ʂ/. Then there is /h/, made in the throat, and /β/, made with both lips and the voice on. The words below show that the three ‘s’-like sounds change the meaning of a word (from Dávila, Lauriault, and Loriot 1976):
(3) /ˈhanʃo/ | ‘scurvy’. | /ˈhanso/ | ‘liar’ | /ˈhanʂo/ | ‘(something) stinky (e.g., blood; noun and modifier)’

h: Phonemic Inventory (the list of sounds)
t:
Both /ʃ/ and /ʂ/ are said just behind the ridge above the top teeth. The difference is the shape of the tongue. For /ʃ/ the tongue is flatter and uses its front surface. For /ʂ/ the tongue makes a groove and uses its tip. So linguists can call them laminal (blade of the tongue) and
We still need more research to know all the places where [ʔ] appears. Interestingly, long ago there seems to have been a glottal stop between the two vowels of words like /βai/ ‘road.’ I base this on Armentia (1898), who writes an <h> in this spot, fairly consistently.
apical (tip of the tongue). The sound /β/ changes a lot. It can sound like a [b], like a [b] sliding into [β], like a [β], or like a very soft [β̞]. Most often it is a [β]: air is pushed between the two lips, with the lips spread, and they touch only at the left and right corners. The [b] sound tends to come at the start of a stressed first syllable, and after a nasal sound. The very soft sound is found at the start of a syllable that is not first in the word and not stressed.
The pairs below show that /h/ at the start of a word changes the meaning. Compare words with /h/ to words with no consonant at all, and to words with the other ‘hissing’ sounds:

h: Phonemic Inventory (the list of sounds)
t:
(4) /ˈhono/ ‘collared-peccary’ | /ˈono/ ‘over there’ | /ˈhoni/ ‘person, man’ | /ˈoni/ ‘ayahuasca’⁵ | /ˈhono/ ‘collared-peccary’ | /ˈʂono/ k. tree (‘lupuna⁶’) | /hiˈnan/ ‘with the tail’ | /ʃiˈnan/ ‘thought, thinking, mind’ | /ˈhoi/ ‘word, language’ | /ˈsoi/ ‘nice, pretty’ | /ˈhana/ ‘tongue’ | /ˈβana-/ ‘sow’
The sound /ɻ/ also changes a lot. In this book I treat it as a retroflex consonant, made with the tip of the tongue curled back, something like an American English ‘r.’ But it can also sound like a quick tap, a hissing sound, or a ‘dzh’-like sound. When it starts a stressed syllable, /ɻ/ may sound like the ‘dzh’-like sound or like the soft ‘r’ (for more details on how this sound is said, see Valenzuela,
Banisteriopsis, Malpighiaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
Ceiba pentandra, Bombacaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
Márquez, and Maddieson 2001). The pair of words below shows that the language’s two curled-tongue consonants change the meaning:
(5) /ˈʂono/ | k. tree (‘lupuna’) | /ˈɻono/ | ‘snake’ | /ˈʂao/ | ‘bone’ | /ˈɻao/ | ‘(vegetal) medicine’
The sound /w/ changes with the vowel after it. Before /i/ it is said with lips slightly rounded and the tongue toward the front. Before /a/ it is said with rounded lips and the tongue toward the back. Before /ɨ/ it is said with the tongue at the back but without rounding the lips (see footnote 2).

h: Phonemic Inventory (the list of sounds)
t: No sound in the language has an extra feature added on top, such as rounded lips on a ‘k’ (linguists call these secondary articulations).

h: Phonotactics (which sounds can go next to each other)
t:
Some combinations of sounds never happen in Shipibo: /ʂi/, /wo/, and /ji/ (the star means ‘not found’). Also, the sound /h/ can only appear in one place: at the start of a word.⁷
Every consonant except /h/ can start a syllable, both at the start of a word and inside it. Four consonants, /n, s, ʃ, ʂ/, can also end a syllable. A syllable that ends in a consonant is ‘heavy,’ and heavy syllables pull the stress onto themselves (see 3.1.6.2). As I said before, a vowel + /n/ is said as a vowel through the nose. Sometimes you can hear a short [n] or [m] between that nose vowel and a following consonant like /p/ or /t/. This is a good reason to treat it as a vowel + /n/.
Table 3.3 shows that each consonant makes a difference in meaning. Each of the fifteen consonants appears at the start of a word before each of the four vowels, and also between two vowels. Where possible, the consonant starts the second syllable, between two of the same vowel.
One exception to these rules is the sound-imitating verb /ʂonˈʂin iti/ ‘to whistle’.
One speaker gave me the verb form /mɨ-haˈma-kɨ/ [HAND-kick-CMPL] ‘kicked after pulling,’ with a body-part beginning piece. But a second speaker rejected it.

h: 3.1.3.1. Nasalization Spread
t:
When a nasal consonant like /n/ ends a syllable, it makes the vowel before it sound ‘through the nose’ too. This nose sound spreads backwards. It stops when it meets any consonant except /w/ or /j/. Compare the pairs below:
(6) /βaˈwan/ ‘parrot (ergative) → [βãˈw̃ã], but | /βaˈβan/ ‘child (ergative) → [βaˈβã]
The nose sound also spreads forward from a syllable-final /n/ onto the vowels that come after it, and it can pass through /w/ and /j/:
(7) /iˈkon akɨ/ [true-do.T-CMPL] → [iˈkõãɣɯ] | /kiˈkin aˈkin [extremely do.T-SSSA]→ [kiˈkĩãɣĩ] | /βɨˈkanwɨ/ ‘come (plural)’ → [βɨˈkãw̃ɨ̃]
When /j/ gets this nose sound, it may come out as a palatal nasal, a sound like the ‘ñ’ in Spanish señor:
(8) /ˈwan.jo/ ‘diseased’ → [ˈwãɲo] | /paˈjon/ ‘kerchief’ → [pãˈɲõ]

h: 3.1.3.2. Voicing and Weakening
t:
The sound /k/ often gets softer between two vowels. It can turn into a buzzy, voiced sound, or even something close to a glide. This happens mostly with word pieces that people use all the time. These are the ending /-kɨ/ that marks a finished action, the short ending /-ki/ that means ‘I heard that…’, and the helper verb /iki/ used with intransitive verbs. Below you can see the helper verb together with the verb ‘say:’
(9) /ˈjoija iki/ ‘said’ → [ˈjuija iɣi]

h: 3.1.3.3. Deletion of Word Initial /h/
t:
The sound /h/ (like English ‘h’) may be dropped at the start of a word when the next vowel is /a/:
(10) /ˈhakɨ/ → [ˈaɣɨ] | /haˈkonʃaman/ → [aˈkõʃamã] | /haˈwɨn/ → [awɨ̃]

h: 3.1.3.4. Vowel Devoicing and Deletion
t:
A vowel that is not stressed may be whispered, or dropped completely, when it sits between two consonants that don’t use the voice (like /p, t, k, s/):
(11) /kiˈkin/ ‘extremely’ → [ki̥ˈkin] ~ [kˈkin]

h: 3.1.3.5. Loss of Syllabicity
t:
In normal fast speech, there is another change. Two vowels side by side can blend into one syllable. When that happens, one of the vowels stops being a full vowel and becomes a glide, like the ‘y’ in ‘yes’ or the ‘w’ in ‘wet’:
(12) /ˈnokoanani/ ‘met each other’ → [ˈnoko̯anani] | /piˈa/ ‘nephew’ → [pja]

h: Syllable Structure (how syllables are built)
t:
A Shipibo syllable is built like this: an optional consonant, then a vowel, then an optional consonant. Linguists write this as (C)V(C). So all four types are possible: V, CV, VC, and CVC. Any of them can be stressed or unstressed. Here are examples of each kind (I mark the stress just to show it):
(13) V: /ˈa.no/ ‘k. agouti,’ /ˈi.no/ ‘jaguar,’ /ˈo.kɨ/ ‘on the other side,’ /ˈpi.a/ ‘arrow’ | CV: /ˈko.ka/ ‘maternal uncle,’ /ˈma.nɨ/ male proper name, /ˈβi.na/ ‘wasp’ | CVC: /kan.ˈkan/ ‘pineapple,’ /sin.ˈto.{?:t-esh-or-similar}a/ ‘belt’,/ˈnon.ti/ ‘canoe,’ /piʃ.ˈto.kɨ/ k. bird, /ja.ˈwiʃ/ ‘armadillo,’ /min.ˈtsis/ ‘nail,’ /nɨʂ.ˈnɨʂ/ k. bird, /βa.ˈkoʂ/ ‘foam’. | VC: /on.ˈpaʂ/ ‘contained water,’ /ˈiʃ.to/ ‘fast,’ /ˈis.ko/ k. bird, /ˈaʂ.pa/ ‘crossed legs,’ /ɨn/ ‘I (A form)’
Only vowels can be the center of a syllable. As I said above, every consonant can start a syllable at the beginning of a word. Every consonant except /h/ can start a syllable inside a word. But only the ‘s’-like sounds and /n/ can really end a syllable. When two consonants come together inside a word, they always belong to different syllables: one ends the first syllable, the other starts the next.9
When native speakers say a word slowly, two vowels side by side in the same word piece are heard as two separate syllables (see footnote 4):
(14) /ˈpi.a/ | ‘arrow’ | /pi.ˈa/ | man’s nephew, niece | /ˈpɨ.o-/ | ‘start’

h: Syllable Structure (how syllables are built)
t: Sadly, I have not been able to find any sound rule that works on the syllable as a whole.

h: Minimal Word Condition (the shortest a word can be)
t:
In SK, every word must be at least ‘two beats’ long (linguists call these beats moras). A short vowel counts as one beat, and a long vowel counts as two. So one-syllable words with a short vowel get their vowel stretched out. Examples are /βi/ ‘night mosquito,’ /ɻo/ ‘howler monkey,’ and /ni/ ‘forest.’ In one way of drawing sound structure (called autosegmental phonology), the vowel of these words is one sound linked to two time slots (but see also Group 4 in 3.2.2):
(15)

h: 3.1.6.1. Contrasting Pairs
t:
In SK, you cannot always guess which syllable is stressed. Look at the pairs below: the words differ only in where the stress falls (the glottal stops below are predictable, see 3.1.1):
(16) [ˈʔi.sa] | ‘porcupine’ | [i. ˈsaʔ] | ‘bird’ | [ˈma.po] | ‘head’ | [ma.ˈpoʔ] | ‘mud’ | [ˈpi.a] | ‘arrow’ | [pi.ˈaʔ] | ‘crossed nephew, niece’ | [ˈmɯtʃa] | ‘good fisher/hunter’ | [mɯ.ˈtʃaʔ] | ‘wet’ | [ˈpo.po] | ‘owl’ | [po.ˈpoʔ] | k. fruit (‘cocona’) | [ˈti.ta] | ‘mother’ | [ti.ˈtaʔ] | ‘mother (vocative)’ | [ˈpa.ɻo] | ‘river’ | [pa.ˈɻoʔ] | ‘square’ | [ˈpo.to] | ‘dust, powder’ | [po.ˈtoʔ] | ‘full, satisfied’ | [ˈpa.no] | ‘giant armadillo’ | [pa.ˈnoʔ] | k. aquatic frog | [ˈpaʂ.na] | ‘weak, exhausted’ | [paʂ.ˈnaʔ] | ‘light (color)’ | [ˈhĩⁿ.to] | ‘without tail’ | [hĩⁿ.ˈtoʔ] | ‘designs on the tail of fish’ | [ˈʂa.na] | ‘hot’ | [ʂa.ˈnaʔ] | k. tree (‘tamamuri’) | [ˈsɨ.ɻɨ] | k. súngaro fish | [sɨ.ˈɻɨʔ] | ‘striped’

h: 3.1.6.2. Stress Rule
t:
Still, many words do follow a pattern you can predict. The stress falls in the first part of the word. Normally that means the first syllable gets the stress, like English ‘TA-ble.’ But if the second syllable is ‘heavy’ (ends in a consonant), it takes the stress instead.
When that happens, the stress falls on the second syllable, even if the first syllable is heavy too (see the examples in 18):
(17) /ˈa.tsa/ | ‘yuca’ | /ˈβa.wa/ | ‘parrot’ | /ˈɻo.no/ | ‘snake’ | /ˈnon.ti/ | ‘canoe’ | /ˈβɨ.nɨ/ | ‘husband’ | /ˈmaʂ.ko/ | ‘small’ | /ˈjo.pa/ | ‘bad fisher/hunter’ | /ˈo.ʃi/ | ‘skinny’ | /ˈʂa.na/ | ‘hot’ | /ˈpi.kɨ/ | ‘ate’
(18) /βa.ˈwan/ | ‘parrot (ergative)’ | /ho.ˈpoʂ/ | ‘chigger’ | /wa.ˈɻan/ | ‘squash’ | /ho.ˈʃin/ | ‘red’ | /ha.ˈkon/ | ‘good’ | /kɨ.ˈɻas/ | ‘dirty’ | /pi.ˈkas/ | ‘one who likes to eat’
(19) /kan.ˈkan/ | ‘pineapple’ | /man.ˈʂan/ | ‘heron’ | /mɨn.ˈtsis/ | ‘nail’ | /pon.ˈsɨn/ | ‘sloth’ | /nɨʂ.ˈnɨʂ/ | k. bird (‘shansho’) | /bin.ˈpiʃ/ | ‘guayaba’¹⁰ | /ɻas.ˈton/ | ‘thick’ | /pan.ˈʃin/ | ‘yellow’
Psidium guayava, Myrtaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
Linguists who study stress have special tools for describing it.
