In the theory of Hayes (1995), the pattern so far can be described as ‘moraic trochees with end-rule right.’ In plain words: the word is split into chunks of two beats. In each chunk the first beat is the strong one. And the chunks are counted from the end of the word towards the start.

h: 3.1.6.3. Codas as Moraic
t:
But there is a group of words that breaks the rule above. In these words, the second syllable is ‘light’ (it ends in a vowel), and yet it gets the stress (some of these examples already appeared in (17); the glottal stop at the end is predictable):
(20) [i.ˈsaʔ] | ‘bird’ | [ɻa.ˈwiʔ] | ‘enemy’ | [pɯ.ˈkaʔ] | ‘back’ | [ka.ˈpɯʔ] | ‘alligator’ | [ma.ˈʂoʔ] | ‘opossum’ | [tɨ.ˈtɨʔ] | ‘hawk’ | [pan.ˈtʃaʔ] | ‘flat’ | [nɨn.ˈkɨʔ] | ‘long’ | [kɨ.ˈjaʔ] | ‘high, steep’ | [mɯ.ˈtʃaʔ] | ‘good fisher/hunter’ | [kɨs.ˈkaʔ] | ‘like, such as’
One way to explain these odd words is this. Maybe each of them really has a hidden consonant at the end. That consonant makes the second syllable heavy, so it gets the stress. Then, after the stress is placed, the consonant is dropped. In terms of
autosegmental phonology, the final consonant would have a time slot, but no actual sound would fill that slot.
(21) 
This idea may look like a trick made up just to fix the rule. But there is evidence for it. Look at the doer marker, the ending -n (ergative). When it is added to these words, an extra syllable appears before it, starting with a stop sound like [k]. The stress also moves, just as the stress rule predicts. So [iˈsaʔ] ‘bird’ becomes [ˈʔisakã], and [maˈʂoʔ] ‘opossum’ becomes [ˈmaʂokã], and so on. The same extra syllable shows up in some forms used to call someone. For example, [pjaʔ] ‘crossed nephew or niece’ becomes [pjaˈkaʔ]. So the hidden consonant is really there. On its own, at the end of the word, it would make a syllable that the language doesn’t allow, so it is dropped or left silent (see also 3.2.4).

h: 3.1.6.3. Codas as Moraic
t: If we accept this explanation, these words also follow the same rule: two-beat chunks, strong beat first, counted from the end of the word (moraic trochees with end-rule right). However, I will show below that words of four syllables need the chunks counted from the start instead (end-rule left). Words of three syllables need some extra explanation, as we will see below.

h: 3.1.6.4. Trisyllabic Words
t:
Some three-syllable words, however, break the stress rule (“stress the first syllable unless the second one is heavy”). The words in (22) follow the rule, but those in (23) do not:
(22) /ˈa.ta.pa/ | ‘hen, chicken’ | /ˈki.ɻi.ka/ | ‘paper, book’ | /ˈʂon.ta.ko/ | ‘young unmarried girl’ | /pa.ˈɻan.ta/ | ‘banana’
(23) /o.ˈtʃi.ti/ | ‘dog’ | /piʃ.ˈto.kɨ/ | k. bird | /ma.ˈtʃi.to/ | ‘machete’ | /ko.ˈɻi.ki/ | ‘silver, money’ | /sin.ˈto.ɻa/ | ‘belt’ | /pa.ˈja.ɻi/ | kind of fish (‘arahuana’)
Why don't three-syllable words follow the rule consistently? Because the vocabulary has layers: words borrowed from other languages are treated differently from native words. In fact, let's compare some of the nouns in (22) and (23) with the matching words in unrelated Amazonian languages of Peru. We find the following (from Valenzuela 1998a):
(24) 
/ˈatapa/ and /koˈɻiki/, for example, come from Quechua. As Campbell (1997:12-3) points out, words derived from the Quechua atawalʸpa and meaning ‘hen’ and ‘chicken’ are found in several languages of the South American Lowlands. These include Paez, Zaparo, Kayapa, Esmeralda, Mapudungun, Moseten and Yurakare, as well as the Witoto, Jivaro, Takana and Kampa languages (see more on /koˈɻiki/ below). /paˈɻanta/, /maˈtʃito/ and /sinˈtoɻa/ were borrowed from Spanish. They most probably come from planta (or plátano), machete and cintura, respectively. Some words may have been borrowed from other native languages; for example, /o.ˈtʃi.ti/ ‘dog’ may come from an Arawak language. So it makes sense that borrowed words tend to keep their original stress, instead of changing it to fit the native pattern (see also 3.1.7).

h: 3.1.6.4. Trisyllabic Words
t:
There are also native three-syllable words, but most of them are clearly made of two word pieces. For example, the following words combine a verb with /-ti/, an ending that turns a verb into a noun. Their stress is predictable: /ˈmiʃkiti/ ‘hook,’ /βoˈnanti/ ‘piece of luggage,’ /ˈtɨoti/ ‘necklace,’ /jaˈkati/ ‘seat,’ etc. The word /jaˈkati/ has the stress on the second syllable because the bare verb actually ends in a consonant: /jakat-/ ‘to sit.’ This is a general stress rule
(see 4.3 and 18.1). There is at least one three-syllable noun that comes from the old Panoan parent language and that the rule given here cannot explain: /paˈβiki/ ‘ear.’ Interestingly, this word has been reconstructed as paβiki (Shell 1975:162). In other words, it once had a heavy second syllable.

h: 3.1.6.5. Tetrasyllabic Words
t:
Probably all four-syllable words are made of two or more word pieces. Their stress follows the rule given above:
(25) /ˈtitaʃoko/ | ‘grandmother’ | /maˈnanʂawɨ/ | ‘tortoise’ | /ʂaˈwanwaɻan/ | k. large fish (‘pejetorre’) | /ˈapaʃiɻo/ | ‘chameleon’

h: 3.1.6.6. Remaining Questions
t:
Some verb forms have stress that can't be predicted. Some of these are one-syllable verbs combined with certain small add-on pieces. One of these is -ra, the marker showing that the speaker knows something firsthand, which pulls the stress onto itself (see also ex. (55) in Chapter 6):
(26) /pi-ˈɻa-kɨ/ | ‘(s/he, it) ate (direct evidence)’
The command ending also pulls the stress in an unpredictable way when added to one-syllable verbs. You can't explain this by saying that commands always stress the last syllable. Commands built on two-syllable verbs do follow the normal stress rule:
(27) /pi-ˈwɨ/ | ‘eat!’ | /ˈmɨni-wɨ/ | ‘give!’ | /yaˈtan-wɨ/ | ‘catch!’

h: 3.1.6.7. Dialectal Variation
t:
Finally, I must point out that differences between dialects can affect stress. Speakers from the Piski River may stress the ending that means the action is finished, instead of the bare verb, in verb forms like the ones below (see ex. (124) in Chapter 10):
(28) /ˈpikɨ/ ~ [piˈkɨʔ] | ‘ate’ | /ˈkakɨ/ ~ [kaˈkɨʔ] | ‘went’ | /ˈβikɨ/ ~ [βiˈkɨʔ] | ‘got’

h: Adaptation of Loanwords (how borrowed words are changed to fit)
t:
When borrowed words contain sounds and syllable shapes that SK doesn't allow, they usually change in ways that are common in many languages. For example, a sound that doesn't
exist in SK is replaced by a native sound that is close enough. Groups of consonants are simplified, an extra vowel is added, or the syllables are split up differently. In this way the borrowed word fits the syllable patterns of SK. The stress stays where it was in the original word, as long as it falls on the first foot (the first stress group of the word) (see rokotoro ‘doctor’). Here are some examples:
(29) /ˈplato/ > /ˈɻato/ | ‘dish’ | /guaˈrapo/ > /waˈɻapo/ | sugarcane alcoholic drink | /ˈgringo/ > /kiˈɻinko/ | ‘gringo’ | /solˈdado/ > /sonˈtaɻo/ | ‘soldier’ | /aˈsukar/ > /aˈsokaɻo/ | ‘sugar’ | /dokˈtor/ > /ˈɻokotoɻo/ | ‘doctor’
The Spanish word for ‘soldier’ has two /d/ sounds. SK replaced the first /d/ with /t/, but the second with /ɻ/. Why the difference? In Spanish, /d/ is a full stop sound after another consonant. Between two vowels, however, it becomes soft, with air still flowing through. So SK replaced the stop /d/ with another stop sound, and the soft /d/ with a sound that is not a stop.
Sometimes a stressed syllable has a shape SK doesn't allow, so it gets split into two simpler syllables. Then either of the two new syllables may end up with the stress. In the two Quechua borrowings below, the first stressed syllable ends in a palatal ‘l’ sound (close to the ‘lli’ in ‘million’). SK doesn't have this sound, so it is replaced by /ɻ/. But

h: Adaptation of Loanwords (how borrowed words are changed to fit)
t:
only s-like sounds and /n/ can end a syllable in SK. So /ɻ/ moves to the start of a new syllable, and an /i/ is added. In /ˈkiɻika/ the stress ended up on the first syllable, but in /koˈɻiki/ it is the second syllable that has the stress:
(30) /ˈkiʎ.ka/ > /ˈki.ɻi.ka/ ‘book, letter’ | /ˈkuʎ.ki/ > /ko. ˈɻi.ki/ ‘money’
In short, the stress rule applies to native words but not to words borrowed from another language; borrowed words tend to keep their original stress.

h: Simplification Processes: Deletion and Merging (sounds that drop out or merge)
t:
Many verbs are made of a two-syllable bare verb plus the middle ending /-t/. When the next word piece starts with a consonant, /-t/ closes the second syllable and so pulls the stress onto it. But in SK a syllable can only end in /n, s, ʃ, ʂ/. So another rule then deletes the /t/, but the stress stays where it was. To show this, I use the intransitive verbs /jaka-t-/ ‘sit’ and /noko-t-/ ‘arrive’ (their transitive partners are /jasa-n-/ ‘seat’ and /noko-/ ‘meet,’ respectively). These are followed by the ‘not finished’ ending
/-ai/ (for contrast), the ‘finished’ ending /-kɨ/, the plural /-kan/, and the ‘not’ ending /-jama/. Stress is marked:
(31) ‘sit’ /jaˈkat-/ /ˈjakat-ai/ /jaˈka-kɨ/ /jaˈka-kan-/ /jaˈka-jama-/ | ‘arrive’ /noˈkot-/ /ˈnokotai/ /noˈko-kɨ/ /noˈko-kan-/ /noˈko-jama-/
Adding the middle ending brings other changes too (see 18.1).
Other sounds get dropped when two identical or very similar sounds meet where two word pieces join: /a/ + /a/, and /i/ + /j/. In these cases, the second sound is dropped:
(32) /ka-/ ‘go’ + -ai INC → /ˈkai/ | /ˈmɨɻa-/ ‘meet’ + -ai INC → /ˈmɨɻai/
(33) /βi-/ ‘get’ + /-jama/ NEG → /ˈβiama/ | /pi-/ ‘eat’ + /-jama/ NEG → /ˈpiama/ | /ˈmɨni-/ ‘give’ + /-jama/ NEG → /ˈmɨniama/
When a bare verb ending in an s-like sound is joined to the ‘not’ ending /-jama/, the two sounds merge. Together they become the first sound of the ‘not’ ending, said as a ‘sh’-like sound. The verb keeps its original stress:

h: Simplification Processes: Deletion and Merging (sounds that drop out or merge)
t:
(34) /piˈkas-jama-/ (eat-DES-NEG) → /piˈkaʃama/ | /naˈtɨʂ-jama-/ (bite-NEG) → /naˈtɨʃama/
When the ‘I know it firsthand’ marker /-ɻa/ attaches to a word ending in an s-like sound, it often loses its first sound:
(35) /hainoaʂ-ɻa/ (then:S-EV) → /hainoaʂa/ | /moa-ɻɨs-ɻa/ (already-just-EV) → /moaɻɨsa/
Before the linking verb /iki/ ‘be,’ the marker /-ɻa/ shrinks to /ɻ-/ and attaches to the front of it, forming the word /ɻiki/.

h: The {-n} Morpheme (the -n ending and its forms)
t:
Apart from the ‘my’ and ‘his/her’ forms used before nouns, nouns and pronouns have one and the same form for ‘of’ (the owner), ‘with’ (the tool) and other side roles. I will call these forms “-n forms.” {-n} is not a true ending. It attaches to the last word of the whole noun phrase, so it should be seen as a clitic, a phrase ending.
The {-n} piece has these different forms:¹¹ /-n; -an, -ɨn, -in; -kan, -tɨn, -tan; -man; -nin; -ton, -tonin/. Also, nouns with the plural / group ending {-βo} may have a -n form ending in /-βaon/, /-βoan/, or even /-βoon/, depending on the speaker. Most of these different forms can be explained by the number of
In these forms I include the final nasal (n-like) sound of nouns in Group 3, and also the final [-continuant] consonant that I proposed for nouns in Group 4.
beats (moras) the noun has (Faust 1973:32-36, Valenzuela 1998a). In the examples below, I always mark the stress to make things clear.

Two-syllable nouns ending in a vowel make their -n form by adding /-n/. Following the stress rule, the stress moves to the second syllable, which has now become heavy. Probably most SK nouns belong to this group. Here are some examples:
(36) /ˈβakɨ/ /βaˈkɨn/ ‘child’ | /ˈino/ /iˈnon/ ‘jaguar’ | /ˈtʃai/ /tʃaˈin/ ‘man’s brother-in-law’ | /ˈwastɨ/ /wasˈtɨn/ ‘piripiri’¹²

Two-syllable nouns ending in an s-like sound need an extra vowel before /-n/ is added, so they become three syllables long. The stress moves to the first syllable, as expected. The extra vowel varies a lot. The same speaker may accept /-ɨ/ and /-a/ for most nouns; /i/ is only possible
Cyperus spp., Cyperaceae, Eleutherine sp., Iridaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
when the basic form of the noun ends in /iS/ (S = an s-like sound). So the extra vowel matches the vowel before it (linguists call this vowel harmony).
(37) /kaˈmoʂ/ /ˈkamoʂɨn/ ~ /ˈkamoʂan/ k. snake (‘shushupe’) | /tʃaˈɻaʂ/ /ˈtʂaɻaʂɨn/ ~ /ˈtʃaɻaʂan/ k. bird | /maˈwis/ /ˈmawisɨn/ ~ /ˈmawisan/ ~ /ˈmawisin/ k. ant | /jaˈwiʃ/ /ˈjawiʃɨn/ ~ /ˈjawiʂan/ ~ /ˈjawiʃin/ ‘armadillo’

This group contains two-syllable nouns ending in /n/. To make the -n form, the last /n/ changes to /m/, an /a/ is added, -n is added, and the stress rule applies:
(38) /aˈmɨn/ /ˈamɨman/ ‘capybara’ | /noˈnon/ /ˈnonoman/ ‘duck’ | /haˈsin/ /ˈhasiman/ k. bird (‘paujil’)
In an earlier work (Valenzuela 1998a:footnote 7) I pointed out that nouns in this group come from older three-syllable nouns whose last syllable started with /m/ or /n/. When the last vowel of these nouns was lost, the nasal sound moved over to close the second syllable (where it is heard as nasal quality on the vowel before it). At that point, the difference between the two nasal sounds, m and n, disappeared.

Group 4 is for nouns that end in a stressed vowel. Remember from 3.1.6.3 (Codas as Moraic): I think these words have a hidden consonant at the end. You can't hear it, because the rules about how syllables are built don't let it be said there. (These hidden consonants are not hissing sounds like /s/ and not /n/.) When you say such a word on its own, it ends with a little catch in the throat (a glottal stop). To make the -n form, the hidden consonant comes out as /k/. Then an /a/ is slipped in, /-n/ is added, and the usual stress rule applies. So /iˈsa/ ‘bird’ becomes /ˈisakan/.
(39) /iˈsa/ /ˈisakan/ ‘bird’ | /{?:retroflex-r-like-glyph}aˈwi/ /ˈ{?:retroflex-r-like-glyph}awikan/ ‘enemy’ | /piˈa/ /ˈpiakan/ ‘man’s crossed nephew, niece’
Sometimes the word already has a /k/ somewhere else in it. Then the hidden consonant may come out as /t/ instead, so the word doesn't get two /k/ sounds. The slipped-in vowel is then /a/ or /ɨ/. (Linguists call this kind of avoiding two of the same sound dissimilation.) Speakers vary a lot here. Even one person may treat each word differently. In (40), ‘alligator’, ‘back’ and ‘bark’ each have three possible forms.
(40) /kaˈpɨ/ /ˈkapɨkan/ ~ /ˈkapɨtan/ ~ /ˈkapɨtɨn/ ‘alligator’ | /pɨˈka/ /ˈpɨkakan/ ~ /ˈpɨkatan/ ~ /ˈpɨkatɨn/ ‘back’ | /ʂaˈka/ /ˈʂakakan/ ~ /ˈʂakatan/ ~ /ˈʂakatɨn/ ‘bark’

As I said earlier, a word has at least two beats (moras). So a one-syllable word ending in a vowel must count as two beats. These words belong to Group 4 too:
(41) /ɻoo/ /ˈɻookan/ | ‘howler monkey’ | /βii/ /ˈβiikan/ | ‘(night) mosquito’
Even a noun made of a single vowel counts as two beats, so it goes in this group as well. The next example comes from a reading class:
(42) /ˈipo ˈiikan ˈpɨotai/ | {ipo i-n pɨo-t-ai} | ‘The (word) “ipo” starts with “i”.’ (ipo ‘carachama’ fish)
The noun /ˈnai/ ‘sky’ breaks the rule. Judging by its sounds, it should be in Group 1, like /ˈtʃai/ ‘man’s brother-in-law,’ and /ˈwai/ ‘garden.’ Then its form would be the wrong form /ˈnai-n/. Instead, /ˈnai/ takes the -n form /ˈnaikan/, like the nouns in Group 4.

Nouns with three syllables make their -n form by adding /-nin/. You can think of this as /-ni/ + /-n/. The stress stays where it was. As I discuss in 3.2.4, probably most nouns in
this group are either borrowed from other languages or made of more than one word piece. Why are there almost no plain, native three-syllable nouns here? Long ago, a sound change cut off the last syllable or vowel of three-syllable words, as these languages developed into what they are today. So native three-syllable nouns mostly disappeared. The extra /-ni/ may be connected to this old change. Perhaps it was a way to avoid a word shape that was no longer allowed.¹³
(43) /oˈtʃiti/ /oˈtʃitinin/ | ‘dog’ | /paˈβiki/ /paˈβikinin/ | ‘ear’ | /ˈtsontsoɻo/ /ˈtsontsoɻonin/ | k. fish | /piʃˈtokɨ/ /piʃˈtokɨnin/ | k. bird | /maˈɻia/ /maˈɻianin/ | female proper name (Spanish loan)
The noun /awin/ ‘wife, female’ usually takes /-ni-n/. Going by its shape, it should act like Group 3 and have the -n form /ˈawiman/. You do sometimes hear that form. But normally people say /ˈawinin/ instead.
Interestingly, Quechua has an empty piece -ni that is put between two word pieces so that two consonants don't meet. For example, yawar ‘blood’ + -nchis ‘our (inclusive)’ -> yawar-ni-nchis ‘our blood’ (not \yawar-nchis). Wariapano, a very close relative of Shipibo, seems to be the only other Panoan language with the form -nin. This supports the idea that -nin came from Quechua. The Panoan peoples on the Ucayali river, like today's Shipibo and especially the Wariapano, had the most contact with missionaries, and so also with Quechua.

Nouns with four syllables are made of two word pieces. They make their -n form in one of two ways. Either they use the rules for Groups 1-4, applied to the last piece of the word. Or they just add /-ni-n/, like the nouns in Group 5. Look at (44): each word has both possible forms.
(44) /ˈtitaʃoko/ /ˈtitaʃokon/ ~ /ˈtitaʃokonin/ | ‘grandmother’ | /maˈnanʂawɨ/ /maˈnanʂawɨn/ ~ /maˈnanʂawɨnin/ | ‘tortoise’ | /ʂaˈwanwaɻan/ /ʂaˈwanwaɻaman/ ~ /ʂaˈwanwaɻanin/ | k. fish

This group is for nouns that carry the ending {-βo}, which means more than one, or a kind of thing in general. In the -n form, this ending becomes /-βaon/ or /-βoan/. Some speakers also say /-βoon/:
(45) /ˈkoʃiβo/ /ˈkoʃiβaon/ ~ /ˈkoʃiβoan/ ~ /ˈkoʃiβoon/ | ‘chiefs’ | /oˈtʃitiβo/ /oˈtʃitiβaon/ ~ /oˈtʃitiβoan/ ~ /oˈtʃitiβoon/ | ‘dogs’
The noun /ainβo/ ‘woman’ comes from /awin/ ‘wife, female’ + the ending /-βo/. /ainβo/ has two possible -n forms. It can act like the three-syllable
nouns of Group 5, giving /ainβonin/. Or it can act like the nouns ending in /-βo/, giving /ainβaon/, and so on.

h: 3.2.2.8. Group 8: Derived Nominals
t:
Nouns that were made from other words have their own -n forms: /-ton/ or /-tonin/. We still need more research to know when each one is used. Look at these examples:
Before leaving the -n forms, let's look at one more question: which vowel gets slipped in? Remember that sometimes an extra vowel is added before the ending. There are signs of an old rule about which vowel this was. The vowel seemed to copy something from the sound just before it. After /k/ and /m/, the added vowel was /a/. After /t/, it was /ɨ/. After a hissing sound like /s/ or /ʃ/, it depended on the vowel before that. If that vowel was /i/, the added vowel was also /i/. Otherwise it was /ɨ/. This last pattern is like a sound "leaking" across the consonant, so the vowels match. It was not always applied, though. Linguists call this kind of matching vowel harmony. Today the old rule seems to be fading. Speakers are spreading /a/ to more and more words. They are also using /ɨ/ more after sounds like /t/ (see Loriot’s observation in Shell 1975:103, also Valenzuela 1998a).

h: Alternate Mora Timing (the rhythm of light and heavy beats)
t: Some endings in Shipibo change form depending on the length of the word they attach to. To decide, you count the beats in the base word (linguists call these beats moras). An even number of beats gets one form of the ending. An odd number gets the other form. This is called "alternate mora timing." James Lauriault (1948) was the first to notice it. He saw it in the "again" ending, which has two forms, /-ɻiβa/ and /-ɻiβi/. The same idea also explains several other endings. First, I will look at the endings meaning "in / at / to a place." After that, I will look at endings on verbs that change form in this way.

h: 3.2.3.1. Locative-Allative
t:
Shipibo has more than one ending meaning ‘in / at / to a place’. Which one you use depends on the word it attaches to. To explain this, I will use the same groups as for the {-n} ending. Only Groups 6 and 7 are different here.
Nouns from Groups 1 and 6 take /-nko/. Nouns from Groups 2-5 take /-ain/. Put simply: nouns with an even number of beats take /-nko/, and nouns with an odd number of beats take /-ain/. Remember how we count beats here. A consonant at the end of a syllable counts as a beat. And a word ending in a stressed vowel has a hidden consonant at the end, which counts too. Now let's look at a few examples (see also 6.5.5). Notice that borrowed words like /ˈɻima/ ‘Lima’ follow the same pattern.
(48) 
Nouns in Group 1 can also use their -n form to mean ‘in / at / to’: /ʂoˈβon/, /kaˈkon/, /waˈin/, and /ɻiˈman/.
(49) /iˈpaɻia/ /iˈpaɻianko/ | /ɻoˈaβoja/ /ɻoˈaβojanko/ | /ˈoɻopanpa/ /ˈoɻopanpanko/
The place name Oropampa in this group seems to break the rule. It has five beats, not four. But Oropampa is a borrowed word (see also Pokalpa in (53)).
Groups 2-5:
Nouns in these groups come in two kinds. The first kind are the nouns from Groups 2-4. They have two syllables, and the second one ends in a consonant, like (C)V.(C)VC. The second kind have three syllables. The key point is that all of them have three beats. So they all take the ending /-ain/.

h: 3.2.3.1. Locative-Allative
t:
I couldn't find real place names from Groups 2 and 4. So to test the "alternate mora timing" idea, I made up place names. I gave them to native speakers and asked them to make sentences using these names with the ‘in / at / to’ ending.¹⁴
Typical Shipibo-Konibo place names are two nouns put together (for example /tʃaˈɻaʂ-maˈnan/ ‘Charash (Bird) Mountain’ and /ˈpao-iˈan/ ‘Shell Lake’). Or they are simple nouns with the ending /-ja/ ‘with’ added (for example /ˈɻono-ja/ ‘With Snakes’ and /ˈtama-ja ‘With Peanut’). Because of how they are built, native names like these could not

The place names in this group are real Shipibo villages. Most of these names, however, are borrowed (from the Bible). Notice that in /eˈden/ the Spanish sounds /e/ and /d/ have not been changed into Shipibo sounds. The only native word here is /ian/ ‘lake.’
(51) /eˈden/ /edenain/ [ɛˈdɛ̃ãĩ] | /kaˈnan/ /kananain/ [kaˈnããĩ] | /iˈan/ /iˈain/ [ĩˈãĩ]

(52) /tɨˈtɨ/ /tɨˈtɨain/ | /kaˈpɨ/ /kaˈpɨain/ | /ɻoo/ /ɻooain/
belong to Groups 2-4. Ordinary nouns from Groups 2-4 that can be used to mean ‘in / at / to’

These names are real places. The names /maˈkaja/, /ɻoˈnoja/, and /ˈɻooja/ come from Shipibo-Konibo. The others are borrowed, probably all from Spanish. Most speakers have taken over the Spanish sound /l/ in /poˈkalpa/.

Group 7 has nouns with more than four beats. They take the ‘in / at / to’ ending /-ain/:
such as /wɨan/ ‘small river’ or /ian/ ‘lake,’ tend to take {-n} instead, giving /ˈwɨaman/ and /ˈiaman/.

h: 3.2.3.2. Ablative
t:
Now a few words about the endings meaning ‘from a place’ (linguists call this the ablative). They are built on top of the ‘in / at / to’ forms. If the ‘in / at / to’ form ends in /-nko/, you add /-ni-a/. If it ends in /n/, you drop the /n/ and add /-mɨa/. (/-mɨa/ is also added to certain pronoun forms that end in a nasal sound; see 19.2.2.3.) If it ends in a vowel or /ʂ/, you add /-kɨa/. If it ends in /-ain/, you add /-oa/. There are two exceptions. /mɨran/ ‘inside’ can also take /-oa/. And /manaon/ takes /-kɨa/, even though it ends in /n/ (Faust 1973:59-61). /katʃio/ ‘in/to the forest’ is an adverb (see also 6.5.6):
(55) 
Where do these pieces come from? /-ni-a/ is probably two pieces: the linking piece /-ni/ plus the real ‘from’ ending /-a/. /-kɨ-a/ and its nasal form /-mɨ-a/ are probably the place ending /-kɨ/ plus the ‘from’ ending. You can see /-kɨ/ in /o-kɨ/ [DIST-on the side] ‘on the other side’ and /nɨ-kɨ/ [PROX-on the side] ‘on this side’. The ending /-ainoa/ may have come from /-ain/ plus a second place ending /-no/ plus the ‘from’ ending /-a/.

h: 3.2.3.3. The Repetitive /-ɻiβa/ ~ /-ɻiβi/
t:
As I said already, the idea of "alternate mora timing" first came up with the "again" ending. Lauriault (1948) noticed that verbs with an odd number of beats take /-ɻiβa/, and verbs with an even number of beats take /-ɻiβi/. This may have to do with the rhythm and stress of the word. (A sister language, Kapanawa, has a similar pair, /-riβi/ and /-riʔβi/; Loos and Loos 1998:21.) But there is a twist. Up to now, we counted a consonant at the end of a syllable as a beat. Lauriault said that here only vowels count, and consonants don't matter at all. He was right. For the "again" ending (and the other verb endings below), you must count only vowels. If you counted consonants too, verbs like ‘dance,’ ‘want,’ ‘finish,’ ‘see,’ ‘ask,’ and ‘go (tomorrow)’ could not belong to the two-beat group.
Monomoraic Stems:
Notice that the "again" ending /-ɻiβa/ pulls the stress onto itself. You can't predict this from the Stress Rule in 3.1.6.2.

I have met speakers who don't follow this rule for verbs longer than two beats. They are starting to use /-ɻiβi/ everywhere.

h: Towards a Single Notion of Mora (one idea of the "beat" (mora) for the whole language)
t:
So what counts as a beat? Some languages count consonants at the end of a syllable, and some count only vowels. Each language decides for itself (Hayes 1989:255). But I have shown that Shipibo-Konibo needs both ways of counting. Three things only work if we count end-consonants as beats: where the stress falls, the -n forms, and the ‘in / at / to’ forms. But five endings only work if we count vowels alone: the "again" ending, the "to each other" ending, the associative, the malefactive, and the "long ago" past. In general, it seems that endings on non-verbs
count end-consonants as beats, while endings on verbs count only vowels.¹⁶
This looks like a contradiction, but history explains it. Most Panoan languages went through a change that affected three-syllable words. They lost their last unstressed vowel or syllable (Shell 1975, Valenzuela 1998a; see also Features of Proto-Pano Grammar in section 1.5.2). We can compare related languages and older forms. This evidence shows that the nouns in Groups 2-4 once had an extra vowel. These are the two-syllable nouns ending in a consonant, heard or hidden. So they used to have three syllables. Look at these examples of reconstructed old Pano words, taken from Shell (1975):
In short, there is evidence that long ago only vowels counted as beats. And probably the stress, at least on nouns, always fell on the second-to-last syllable (Valenzuela 1998a).

h: Practical Transcription (the spelling used in this book)
t:
From Chapter 4 to Chapter 19, the examples are written in a practical spelling. With a few changes, it is the spelling used in Shipibo-Konibo school books (especially those published by the Programa de Formación de Maestros Bilingües de la Amazonía Peruana). The letters are the same as the sound symbols I have used so far, except for these changes:
‘broken’ plurals, but another way for where the stress falls (Derry Malsch, p.c.)
Some words don't follow the stress rule given in this chapter. In those words, the stressed syllable gets an acute accent (á). The same goes for words with a hidden final consonant. In all other words, the stress is not written.
In Chapter 20 I keep the sound-by-sound spelling. That chapter compares Shipibo-Konibo with its sister languages, and their sound systems can be quite different.
MORPHOLOGICAL AND RELATED PROCESSES:
As I said in 2.1., Shipibo-Konibo mostly builds words by sticking pieces together, one after another. A word is often made of several pieces. Each piece usually has one meaning. And you can usually see clearly where one piece ends and the next begins. (Linguists call this kind of language agglutinative.) But there are exceptions. Many nouns and describing words appear bare, with no ending at all. Some combinations of pieces blend together, so the borders aren't clear. And a few words change their base or use a totally different base. Also, verbs can take a number of pieces that show movement, direction or manner. This leans a little toward languages that pack a whole sentence into one long word (linguists call those polysynthetic).

h: Practical Transcription (the spelling used in this book)
t: In this chapter I give an overview of the ways Shipibo-Konibo builds and changes words. These include adding pieces and changing the base word. I also cover other ways that do similar jobs: repeating a whole word, using a completely different word, small words that lean on other words (clitics), and switching between helper verbs.

h: Affixation (adding pieces to words)
t: Shipibo-Konibo uses many endings. It also has a small, fixed set of beginning pieces that come from body parts. It has one marker that works by shifting the stress rather than adding sounds. And it has no pieces that go in the middle of a word.

h: Suffixation (adding endings)
t:
The verb below starts with the bare verb oro- ‘clear (a chacra),’ (a chacra is a farm plot). After it come several endings, always in the same order:
(1) Oro-kin-yama-wan-kan-ke. | ‘(They) did not help (her / him) clear the chacra earlier today.’
The endings shown above go only on verbs (or on words acting as verbs). Some pieces look like endings at first. But below I will show that they are better seen as clitics: small pieces that lean on a word but behave more freely.

h: Prefixation (adding beginning pieces)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has a small, fixed set of beginning pieces that come from body parts. They can go on verbs, nouns, and describing words. Adding one does not change the type of word: a verb stays a verb. On a verb, the body-part piece does not add a new person to the sentence. Usually it just tells you where the action happens, on which part of the body. In (2) below, the beginning pieces wi- ‘on the leg’ (from witax ‘leg’) and be-
‘on the face / forehead’ (from bemanan ‘face’) come before the noun kené ‘design’. (Only nouns can take the ending -ya ‘having’. A sentence with ‘be’ and a -ya noun means the same as English ‘have’.)
(2) Ja-tian ja bake xontako iki moa wi-kené-ya, | kori-ya, be-kené-ya, jonxe-ya, jatíbi-ya; | moa kikin-i raot-a. | ‘Then the young girl already has designs on her legs, a lip ornament, designs on her face, wrist ornaments, everything; she (is) very well adorned.’
In (3), the beginning piece no- (from noi ‘abdomen’) comes before the verb xate- ‘cut.’ Notice that xate- also gets shortened:
(3) Ja-tian jawéki ak-ai ainbaon no-xte-xon | pano-a-i ka-[a]i. | ‘Then, the woman in charge, after cutting (the baby girl) on the abdomen (i.e., the umbilical cord) is going to make her her granddaughter.’
Here are some describing words with a body-part beginning piece: be-wis [FACE-‘black’] ‘black on the face / forehead,’ be-keras (FACE-dirty) ‘dirty on the face / forehead,’ be-pancha [FACE-flat] ‘flat on the forehead,’ ke-bá [MOUTH-sweet] ‘with sweet taste.’ Notice that wiso ‘black’ and bata ‘sweet’ appear in a shortened form.

h: Suprafixation (changing a word by its stress or pitch)
t: Many nouns have a special form for calling someone ("Hey, Mom!"). Linguists call this the vocative. To make it, you just move the stress to the last syllable. This happens especially with nouns ending in an unstressed vowel:

h: Cliticization (small pieces that attach to whole phrases)
t: Clitics are small pieces that lean on other words. They come in three types: phrase endings, second-place clitics, and "less-fixed" clitics.

h: Phrasal Suffixes (endings that go on a whole phrase)
t:
Endings like the doer marker go on the last word of the whole noun phrase, not on the main noun. (A noun phrase is a noun with all its describing words.) They come before the markers that show how the speaker knows something. So they always have a fixed place, and they only attach to noun phrases. In (5) below, the doer of the main sentence is a long phrase: ‘the woman who arrived from Caco yesterday’. That whole phrase gets the doer marker (ERG). Notice that the marker is not on the noun ‘woman’ itself. It is at the very end:
(5) [Ainbo [Kako-nko-ni-a-x nokó-ibat-a]]-tonin-ra | rao kobin ak-ai. | ‘The woman who arrived from Caco yesterday is boiling the medicine.’
Example (6) has two nouns that each come with a describing word. Again, the marker goes at the end of the whole noun phrase:
(6) Ka-xon oin-a-ki ik-á iki [[maxko-shoko [joni]], [[montária] | anita-ma-shoko]-tonin-ki.... | ‘Once getting there, he saw a little person in a small canoe....’
The ending -bo, meaning ‘more than one’ or ‘a group’, usually works the same way. It attaches to the last word of the noun phrase (see 6.6).

h: Second Position Clitics (pieces that always come second in the sentence)
t:
Second-place clitics always come right after the first part of the sentence. So their place is fixed. But unlike the markers above, they don't care much what kind of word they attach to. The first part of the sentence can be the doer, the receiver, a place or time phrase, a linking word like ‘then’, a verb, a whole smaller sentence, or anything else. The second-place clitics are the direct evidential -ra (‘I saw it myself’), the reportative -ronki (‘I heard it’), the question marker -ki,
and the guessing marker -mein (though -mein can be followed by -ra, -ronki, or the question marker -ki). Examples (7)-(9) below, among many others, show the only place in the sentence these clitics can go. Put them anywhere else and the sentence is wrong. In all three, the clitic comes right after the long first part in brackets, ‘the man whom they invited to drink guarapo’:
(7) [Warápo xea-ma-iba-kan-a joni]-ra neno oxa-ke. | ‘The man whom they invited to drink guarapo¹ yesterday slept here’
(8) [Warápo xea-ma-iba-kan-a joni]-ronki neno oxa-ke. | ‘I heard that the man whom they invited to drink guarapo yesterday slept here.’
(9) [Warápo xea-ma-iba-kan-a joni]-ki neno oxa-a? | ‘Did the man whom they invite to drink guarapo yesterday sleep here?
But when these clitics go on a finished verb form, they end up inside the word. They come before the endings for ‘more than one doer’ and for how the action unfolds (see where the evidentials go in Chapter 13, and the question marker in 8.4).

h: “Less-fixed” Clitics (pieces that can move around)
t:
"Less-fixed" clitics attach to whatever thing they are describing. So they can go on many kinds of words, and they have no fixed place in the sentence. What they attach to may be a noun phrase, a verb part, or a phrase about time, place or manner. These clitics seem to share
An alcoholic drink made from sugar-cane juice.
meanings like those of adverbs (words such as ‘only’, ‘again’, ‘very’). They are: -bira ‘probably / about / must be’; -shoko, which makes things small or dear; -pari ‘yet, first;’ the emphasis marker -bi; -bicho ‘only;’ -bires ‘purely;’ -shaman ‘very, nicely;’ -pacho ‘always,’ -ribi ~ -riba ‘again, also;’ and -tani ‘a bit,’ which softens things. The examples below show that -shoko attaches to different kinds of noun phrases and phrases about time, place or manner:
The piece -shoko also attaches to verbs. Example (11) is about someone important who gives up during a competition. Here -shoko adds a feeling to the words. Notice one difference from (10): on a verb, -shoko goes inside the word:
(11) Jain-xon Biri yoi-shoko-a iki: “E-n-ra moa | atipan-yama-ke, rama mi-n tana-shoko-t-a” a-kin. | ‘Then he told Biri: ‘I can’t anymore, now you try!’
Also, shoko can be a word on its own, meaning ‘a little bit:’
(12) Shoko-res oxa-[a]i / pi-ai. | ‘I’m gonna sleep / eat just a little bit.’

h: “Less-fixed” Clitics (pieces that can move around)
t:
-ribi ‘again, also’ is different from shoko: it can't be a word on its own. In example (13), -ribi attaches to a noun phrase and to a side part of the sentence done by the same person. In (14), -ribi attaches to a finished verb, inside the word, before the endings for ‘more than one doer’ and for how the action unfolds.
(13) E-a ka-[a]i-tian resto no-n kaibo-baon-ribi e-a | chiban-a iki, onan-kas-kin-ribi. | ‘When I was going (to the Salt Mountain), the rest of my fellow Shipibo followed me, wanting to know (the way) too.’
(14) Moa icha baritia pekáo, Shipibo joni-bo moa | kai-ribi-kan-a iki ja kimisha joni-nko-ni-a-x. | ‘After many years, the Shipibo reproduced again from these three people.’
Sentences (15)-(20) show that -bicho, -tani, and -(bi)res can also attach to very different parts of the sentence:
(15) E-a-tani wetsa meni-kan-we! | ‘Give another one to me (please).’
(16) E-a-bicho-ra ka-[a]i. | ‘Only I am going.’ (Faust 1973:24)
When they go on a finished verb, -tani, -(bi)res, and -bicho go inside the word:
(17) E-a-ra keen-tani-ke. | ‘I liked it a bit.’ (Faust 1973:24)
(18) Bake-ra ka-res-ai. | ‘The child keeps on going / The child just goes.’ (Faust 1973:24)
(19) Nato bake-ra axe-bicho-ai. | ‘This child just learns / studies (i.e., he doesn’t do anything else)’ (Faust 1973:24)

h: “Less-fixed” Clitics (pieces that can move around)
t:
-Bires (from the emphasis marker -bi plus -res ‘just’) and -tani ‘a bit’ can swap places with no clear change in meaning (Faust 1973:24):
(20) Jakon-tani-biressiki e-a. | jakon-tani-bires-r-iki | ‘I am just a bit fine.’ (Faust 1973:24) | Jakon-bires-tani r-iki e-a. | ‘I am just a bit fine.’ (Faust 1973:24)
Table 4.1 sums up the main features of Shipibo-Konibo clitics.
You can find more examples of "less-fixed" clitics in 7.9.

h: Alternate Derivation (making new words with different helper verbs)
t:
Some bare verbs describe body positions or moving into a position (like sitting down or lying down). On their own, they are neither intransitive verbs nor transitive verbs. They need an ending. Add -t and you get an intransitive verb (‘sit down’). Add -n and you get a transitive verb (‘sit someone down’):
I call this "alternate derivation". It means neither form of these verbs is the basic one. Both need an ending, so they are equal.

h: Stem Modification (changing the inside of a word)
t:
The verbs for sitting do one more thing. Besides taking -t or -n like the verbs in (21), they also change the second consonant of the bare verb:
The base also changes in the endings that mean ‘going’ and ‘coming’ while doing something. These endings come from the verbs ‘come’ and ‘go’ (see also 4.5 and 4.9):

h: Suppletion (completely different forms of the same word (like go/went))
t: Sometimes a language uses a completely different word for one form of the same word, like English go and went. Linguists call this suppletion. In Shipibo-Konibo it happens with ‘I/me/my’. The possessive nokon ‘my’ comes from a different base than the other forms: e-a (plain form), e-n (doer form), e-on, e-ki, and others (see section 6.1 on Pronouns). It also happens with the very common verbs ‘come’ and ‘go:’

h: Reduplication (repeating part of a word)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo can repeat a word to change its meaning. This happens with verbs, describing words, phrases about time, place or manner, and nouns. As a rule, the whole word is repeated. But with verbs made of two parts, or sound-imitating verbs, only one part is repeated, as I show below. Sometimes a clitic comes between the two copies (see ex. (27)). Repeating can mean an action happens again and again or keeps going. It can also make something stronger, add emphasis, show more than one, or show things spread out one to each. Look at the following examples:
Emphasis:
(25) Kikin wiso wiso-bires r-iki nokon bachi. | ‘My mosquito net is very very dirty.’
(26) Nato no-n kené-bo-ra kirikain-bo wisha wisha-kan-a | yama-ke, no-n mapo-nko-bicho. | ‘These designs of ours are not written in any book, (they exist) only in our mind.’
Intensification:
(27) E-a-ra moa jawe keskat-a-x-bi ka-yama-[a]i, | e-a-ra kikin-i notsi-bi notsi-a iki. | ‘There is no way that I will go (back); I feel extremely, totally hurt.’
Look at (27). The word piece -bi, which adds emphasis, sits right between the two copies of the same base word.
Continuity, intensification:
(28) Jaino-a-x-ki bewa bewa-kain-i ka-a iki, | onis onis-kain-i ja joni-n bi-[y]ama. | ‘Then she left singing and singing, feeling sad, very sad, the one the man didn’t take as wife.’

h: Reduplication (repeating part of a word)
t:
Continuity:
(29) ...jawen poi-n, bachi benxo benxo a-kin-bi-ronki... | ‘..while his sister was tidying up his mosquito net...’
Look at (29). The verb benxo ak- ‘tidy up’ is made of two parts, but only the first part is repeated. Something similar happens in (30) with biski ik- ‘shake oneself,’ a verb built from a sound word:
(30) Ochíti jene-nko pota-kan-a mapet-ax-a | biski biski ik-ai. | ‘The dog that was thrown into the water climbed up (to the shore) and is shaking.’
Iterativity:
In (31) the verb starts with a beginning piece that names a body part. Here the whole verb, body-part piece included, is repeated:
(31) Ka-kin no-n na-tsá’ na-tsá-bain-a iki, | na-tsá’ na-tsá-bain-a iki. | ‘While going (up the river) we kept on spearing (arrows) into the water.’
Plurality:
(32) Joni-n-ronki oin-a iki xobo xobo mestá-shoko. | ‘(It is said that) the man saw very nice houses.’
Distribution:
In the example below, the last repeated word has a “one each / here and there” meaning. It spreads the action out over several people or places:
(33) Ja chosko bake piko-t-a-ki i-káti-ai, | xoxo bake a-kan-ai, kikin yoitima yoitima-bo; | ja-ska-ra ik-ax-ki westíora westíora i-káti-ai. | ‘Those four children were born and people called them illegitimate / orphan children, they were extremely disobedient; since they were illegitimate / orphan children they lived (going) from house to house.’

h: Reduplication (repeating part of a word)
t:
(34) Westíora westíora-bo, maan-i keyó-kan-a iki. | ‘One by one, they finished coming down.’
Shipibo-Konibo also has a separate verb piece for this “one by one” meaning, pake-. It only goes on transitive verbs (see 4.9 and 7.5).
In the next example, a word that points to a place (like ‘there’) is repeated:
(35) Ne-ská-bi ne-ská-bi-ra mato ja-nonx iki. | ‘Just like this you will live (from now on).’
Finally, the next example shows a two-part verb, masá-shinan-, where only the second part is repeated:
(36) Ja-tian chaxo masá-shinan shinan-bain-i ka-a iki, | piti bena-i. | ‘So the deer went to look for meat, feeling very, very sad and scared.’

h: Alternate Auxiliarization (using different helper verbs)
t:
Some base words can work in two ways. It depends on which helper verb comes after them. With the helper ak-, the verb has a receiver: someone does something to something. With the helper ik-, there is only one person or thing involved. So kobin plus ak- means ‘boil (tr.),’ as in “I boil the water.” The same kobin plus ik- means ‘boil (intr.),’ as in “the water boils.” We already saw part of another case in (30): biski ak- ‘to shake something’ versus biski ik- ‘to shake oneself.’ The same is true of words that clearly imitate sounds, such as she, jojó, and to:’
Most verbs about body position (sitting, lying) or getting into a position work the same way. Neither form is the “basic” one with the other built from it. The transitive form and the intransitive form are equally simple: each just takes its own helper verb.

h: Compounding (joining two words into one)
t: Nouns and verbs can be joined together into compounds, like English toothbrush. When you say them, and when you add endings, such compounds behave like single words. Still, we write their parts as separate words. I do this on purpose. In some sentences, verb compounds act as if their parts were separate (see 4.6. and 16.2.5).

h: Compound Nouns (nouns made of two words)
t:
In compound nouns, the describing word comes first and the main word comes second, as in English apple tree:
Describing words also come before the main word. For example, joxo shino [‘white’ ‘monkey’] is a kind of monkey (Cebus albifrons). There is one exception, though: iso koro ‘Humboldt’s woolly monkey’ (Lagothrix cana). It is made of iso ‘spidermonkey’ and koro ‘gray,’ so here the describing word comes second.
In some compound nouns, the first part carries the ending -n. This is most likely the “of” ending, like English ’s in tapir’s. The next example is especially interesting. The -n form of awá ‘tapir’ is awaran. We would expect awakan instead (3.2.2):
Shell (1975:116) pointed out where this comes from. awaran is most likely the old -n form of \ʔawara ‘tapir.’ Long ago the word for tapir had three syllables. Later a sound rule dropped the last vowel of such nouns, and \ʔawara became awá. The compound kept the older form (see 1.5.2 and 3.1.6).
Many compound nouns are names of animals and plants. This is especially true for the names of very specific kinds, below the level of the genus (Valenzuela 2000a, 1998b).

h: Compound Verbs (verbs made of two words)
t:
The helper verb ak- means ‘do (tr.), make.’ It often joins with a noun or a describing word to make a loose compound verb. The meaning is “make something be X” or “turn something into X.” Look at the following examples:
Sometimes the two base words in these compounds are pronounced as one word. Even then, some parts of the grammar treat them as two separate pieces. Two examples are repeating a word and joining words with ‘and’ (see sections 4.6 above and 16.2.5).
Some compounds are made of a verb turned into a noun plus another verb. One example is shinan-benot- ‘slip the mind, forget,’ shown in ex. (42). It comes from shinan ‘mind, thinking’ plus benot- ‘get lost.’ The word shinan is itself the noun form of the verb shinan- ‘think, plan, remember.’ So ‘forget’ is literally ‘the thinking gets lost.’ Another example is masá-tene- ‘suffer from sth.’ It comes from masá plus tene- ‘stand sth.’ Here masá is the noun form of masá- ‘be responsible, break (intr.), have bad luck.’ See also masá-shinan- in ex. (36).

h: From Verb Serialization to Derivation (how strings of verbs turned into endings)
t:
Sometimes two verbs are put side by side. Over time, the second verb can slowly turn into an ending. Different verbs have changed to different degrees. I looked at one case in an earlier study (Valenzuela 1997). The word yama- can still occur on its own as a verb meaning ‘there is none.’ You can see this in (41). But it can also combine with other verbs in order to make them negative, like English not. You can see this in (42):
(41) Ja-tian motóro yama-katit-ai. | ‘In those times there were no motorboats.’
(42) E-n oin-a iki ja-ska-ra; icha baritia iki ja, | ikaxbi e-a shinan-beno[t]-yama-[a]i. | ‘That is what I saw; this happened a long time ago, but I don’t forget it.’
The last word in the example above is a full verb built from three base words joined together. They are shinan- ‘mind, thinking’ and benot- ‘get lost,’ which together mean ‘forget.’ Then comes yama- ‘not / no.’ So the word means ‘not forget.’
Other verbs work the same way. inat- means ‘go up the river.’ pake- means ‘cause to fall,’ and its “to yourself” form pake-t means ‘fall, go down.’ Each can stand on its own as a verb. Each can also be stuck onto another verb as an ending. Then they mean ‘moving upward,’ ‘one by one,’ and ‘moving downward.’ Look at the following examples with pake-:

h: From Verb Serialization to Derivation (how strings of verbs turned into endings)
t:
pake- ‘cause to fall’
(43) E-n-ra bake pake-ke weyóti-aino-a. | ‘I caused the child to fall from the hammock.’
-pake distributive ‘one by one’
(44) …Bai Shita-n-ki jato yatan-xon jene | rete-ma-pake-a iki. | ‘…the Bai Shita held them and drowned them one by one (lit. held them and caused the flowing water to kill (them) one by one).’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)
(45) Ja-skat-ai-tian-ronki ak-á iki, ja joni-n-ki | jiwi bi-xon ma-rishki-pake-kin keyo-kin. | ‘Then the man got a pole and killed the monkeys hitting them on the head one by one.’
Things are a bit different with the “going” and “coming” endings. These endings show that the action happens while going away or while coming toward here. They come historically from the present-day verbs ‘go’ and
‘come.’ In their form, these endings are less independent than -yama and -pake. That is because they no longer look like the verbs they came from:²
In their meaning, though, the “going” and “coming” endings are closer to real verbs than -yama and -pake are. They don’t just add a little detail to the main verb. They can describe a separate action that happens next, as in “eat and then go.” The next examples use the “going” endings:
(47) E-a-ra bewa-kain-ke. | ‘I sang while going.’/ ‘I sang and left.’
(48) E-n-ra bake-bo kena-bain-ke. | ‘I called the children while going.’/ ‘I called the children and left.’

h: From Verb Serialization to Derivation (how strings of verbs turned into endings)
t:
A “going” ending can even appear together with the verb ‘go’ in the same sentence:
(49) Ja-ska-rain-ronki i-ni-ke, ja chaikoni ainbo | notsi-kain-i ka-[a]i. | ‘And so it happened, the chaikoni³ woman got angry and left / left angrily.’
The “going” endings -kain and -bain have been explained as ka- / bo- ‘go’ plus the ending -ain that means ‘in / at’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:132).
To sum up, in all the verb + verb combinations in this section, both verbs belong to the same sentence. No other word can come between them. The second verb may still look like a present-day verb on its own (e.g., pake- and yama-), or it may not (e.g., the “going” and “coming” endings). Its meaning may be easy to guess, or it may have faded into something new (e.g., inat- ‘going up (the river)’ vs. pake- ‘one by one’). Also, the second verb may still be able to describe a separate action.
The chaikoni or ‘hidden people’ live in a different layer of reality, or in the higher world. Today the Shipibo can reach them only through the great shamans. But in very old times, the Shipibo had direct contact with the chaikoni.
OVERVIEW OF WORD CLASSES:
In this chapter I try for the first time to sort the words of Shipibo-Konibo into groups, like noun and verb. I mostly use clues from the grammar: what endings a word takes and where it can go in a sentence. Some groups seem real and are useful, but they need more work before I can give clear tests for them. Pronouns, nouns, verbs, and time-place-manner words get their own chapters later. Other groups, such as joining words (‘and,’ ‘but’) and exclamations, are covered only here.

h: From Verb Serialization to Derivation (how strings of verbs turned into endings)
t:
For now, I divide Shipibo-Konibo words into these groups: noun, verb, describing word (adjective), amount word, time-place-manner word, postposition (a word like ‘under’ or ‘with’ that comes after a noun), pronoun, joining word, exclamation, and sound word (see also Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:38-9). Roughly speaking, nouns name things. Describing words tell you what a thing is like. Amount words tell you how many or how much. Verbs tell you about actions or events.¹
In Shipibo-Konibo some words can do more than one job without any change in form. But when they switch jobs, their meaning also shifts, often in a regular way. The meaning moves toward what that job usually expresses. For example, the noun oxe ‘moon’ can be used as a verb just by adding verb endings to it. But then oxe- no longer means ‘moon.’ It means a change: ‘become moon.’ Many languages do the same thing (Croft 2000).
I make a difference between two kinds of possessive words. Words like English ‘mine’ and ‘yours’ stand on their own, like nouns. Words like ‘my’ and ‘your’ go in front of a noun. Words like ‘this’ and ‘that’ can do both jobs: they can stand alone or point out a noun. The verb group also includes several kinds of helper verbs. Time-place-manner words, as we will see, are not all alike. Only some of them can take endings that agree with a person in the sentence.

h: Nouns vs. Adjectives (telling nouns and adjectives apart)
t:
In this section I give some tests for telling nouns and describing words apart. Nouns and describing words come back in Ch. 6, where I describe in more detail how they behave in the grammar.
A noun is the main word of a noun group, like dog in the big dog. You can swap a noun for a pronoun (‘he,’ ‘it’). You can even leave it out completely, if everyone already knows who you mean. Sentence (1a) could be the start of a story. Compare (1a) with (1b) and (1c). At the start of a story, nobody knows yet who you are talking about, so a real noun is needed:
(1) Moa-tian-ronki ik-á iki westíora ainbo (siná). | ‘A long time ago, there was a (brave) woman.’ | Moa-tian-ronki ik-á iki westíora siná. | ‘A long time ago, there was a fierce (one).’
(None) Moa-tian-ronki ik-á iki westíora. | ‘A long time ago, there was a / one.’
As in Spanish, a describing word can sometimes be used as a noun without any added ending. When this happens, its meaning changes. Instead of a quality, it now names someone who has that quality, for example from ‘brave’ to ‘brave one.’ A few base words belong to both groups, nouns and describing words. Examples are ani ‘big / forefather / parent,’ yosi ‘old / old one / ancestor,’ koshi ‘strong / chief.’

h: Nouns vs. Adjectives (telling nouns and adjectives apart)
t:
Nouns can take the ending -ya ‘having’ or the ending -oma ‘without.’ This turns them into describing words, like English -ful and -less. Describing words cannot take these endings (see also ex. 2 in Chapter 4):
koshi, yosi, and ani can take the ‘having’ and ‘without’ endings directly. That shows they really are nouns too. They are not just describing words standing in for a missing noun.
Nouns and describing words also behave differently when you join them with ‘and.’ Betan can join two nouns, but not two describing words:
(3) papa betan tita | ‘father and mother’ | \wiso betan siná | ‘black and fierce’ | wiso itan siná | ‘black and fierce’
A noun can be described by another noun or by a describing word. But there is a difference in where they go. A describing word can come before or after the main noun. A noun that describes another noun must come before it. This is true both for the “of” form and for two nouns stuck together into a compound:
Describing words and amount words can take the ending -cha ‘a bit more’ and the strengthening ending -yora ‘very.’ Nouns cannot.² For example, ani-cha means ‘a bit big(ger),’ and jakon-yora means ‘very good.’ But these endings don’t go only on describing words: -cha also attaches
The ending -yora ‘very’ may have come from the noun yora ‘body.’ In other related Panoan languages, yora also means ‘person.’

h: Nouns vs. Adjectives (telling nouns and adjectives apart)
t: to time-place-manner words, as in ori-cha ‘a bit more over there’ or ochó-cha ‘a bit further.’ And -yora also goes on verbs, as in keen-yora- [want-INTENS] ‘to want sth. very much.’ There is also a separate word kikin³ that strengthens describing words: kikin jakon ‘extremely good,’ kikin siná ‘extremely brave,’ etc. However, kikin is also used before a noun, meaning ‘elegant, legitimate,’ as in kikin xobo ‘luxurious house.’ And it can mean ‘extremely.’

h: Adjectives and Quantifiers (describing words and amount words)
t: As I said earlier, describing words tell you what a thing is like, while amount words tell you how many or how much. In both groups, some words can come before the noun and some after it.

h: Adjectives (describing words)
t:
Describing words (adjectives) include: toró ‘round;’ panchá ‘flat;’ ani ‘large;’ maxko ‘small;’ nenké ‘long;’ kextó ‘thick;’ wacho ‘soft, fluffy;’ raston ‘broad, wide;’ nemí ‘deep;’ keyá ‘steep;’ xoa ‘fat;’ oshi ‘skinny;’ yosi ‘old (person);’ payo ‘old;’ bená ‘new;’ koshi ‘strong;’ ishto ‘rapid;’ menin ‘skillful;’ siná ‘brave, fierce, angry;’ mecha ‘good fisher / hunter;’ yoashi ‘stingy;’ jakon ‘good;’ metsá ‘beautiful;’ joshin ‘red;’ panshin
Kikin is borrowed from Quechua. It is made of two Quechua word pieces: kiki ‘same’ + -n, the ‘his/her’ ending, because in Quechua kiki takes possessive endings. The ending -cha ‘a little (more)’ was most likely borrowed too, from the Quechua ending of the same form that means ‘little.’ In Shipibo-Konibo you can even add the native ‘little’ ending -shoko after -cha, as in ani-cha-shoko ‘the little oldest one.’
‘yellow;’ yankon ‘green / blue;’ wiso ‘black;’ joxo ‘white;’ chexe ‘sharp (color);’ inin ‘perfumed;’ pisi ‘stinky;’ moka ‘sour;’ etc.
To get the opposite of a describing word, you can add the ending -ma ‘not,’ like English un- in unhappy. Or you can use a completely different word, like English good and bad:

h: Derived Adjectives (describing words made from other words)
t:
You can make describing words by adding -ya ‘having’ or -oma ‘without’ to a noun. We saw this in (2) above. There is another way, too. Transitive verbs, plus a few intransitive verbs like jo- ‘come,’ ka- ‘go,’ wini- ‘cry,’ and siná- ‘get angry,’ can become describing words or nouns. To do this, they take one of three endings. -mis means ‘one who always Vs.’ Its opposite, -(y)osma ~ -isma, means ‘one who never Vs.’ And -kas means ‘one who likes to V.’ Compare English -er in a crier:
Which form of the ‘never’ ending you use depends on how the verb ends. -yosma comes after a verb that ends in an unstressed vowel, except /i/. (Recall from 3.2.1: when two identical or very similar sounds meet where two word pieces join, the second one drops out.) -isma comes after verbs ending in a stressed vowel. In my data, -yosma never comes after a consonant:
(10) Jatíribi-baon kapé pi-kan-ai, ikaxbi e-n kapé | pi-osma iki. | ‘Some (people) eat alligator, but I never eat it.’
The ending -kas shown above is most likely the same ending that means ‘want to’ on ordinary verbs (see Desiderative Clauses in section 8.2.8).
There is a second ‘without’ ending, -nto. It goes on short forms of body-part words to make describing words. For example, cha-nto [BOTH.LEGS-PRIV] means ‘without the normal use of both legs’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:159), and ji-nto [TAIL-PRIV] means ‘without tail.’ The full body-part words are chapata ‘bifurcation, confluence, two legs’ and jina ‘tail, penis.’

h: Derived Adjectives (describing words made from other words)
t: Finally, you can make a describing word by adding a special ending to a verb, much like English tire > tired. For example, paxkin- ‘get tired’ > paxkin-a [get.tired-PP2] ‘tired.’

h: Quantifiers (amount words (many, all, few))
t:
Amount words come in two kinds: numbers and other amount words. Only two numbers are originally Shipibo-Konibo or Panoan. They are westíora ‘one’ [from westí ‘sparse, few’ + -yora ‘body, person’ > intensifier] and rabé ‘two’ [from ra- ‘body, person’ + -bé ‘with’]. All numbers higher than ‘two’ were borrowed from Quechua. The other amount words are jatíbi(ri) ‘all,’ jatíribi ‘some,’ and icha ‘many.’ Reken ‘first’ and chiní ‘last, youngest’ tell you the position of something in a row. They contain the body-part beginning pieces re- ‘nose’ and chi- ‘buttocks.’
One more word that describes nouns is meskó keská ‘different kinds of.’ It is made of meskó ‘different, distinct’ and keská ‘like.’

h: Pronominal and Demonstrative Modifiers (words like "my", "this", "that" before a noun)
t:
Possessive words and pointing words (‘this,’ ‘that’) can also go with a noun to describe it. The possessive words are nokon ‘my,’ min ‘your (sing.),’ jawen ‘his, her, its,’ non ‘our,’ maton ‘your (pl.),’ and jaton ~ jabon ~ jabaon ~ jaboon ‘their.’ Except for ‘my’ and ‘his/her/its,’ each possessive word looks exactly the same
as the -n form of the matching pronoun. The pointing words are nato ‘this’ (near me), ja ‘that’ (a bit farther), and oa ‘yonder’ (far away). See also 6.1.

h: Time-Location-Manner Words (words for when, where and how)
t:
Time-place-manner words are different from all the other word groups. They are never the doer or the receiver of the verb. They just add extra information about when, where, or how. They fit into sentence frames like the one in (12) without any added ending. I call them “time-place-manner words” instead of using the usual term “adverb.” Here is why. In English, an adverb like quickly describes the action. In Shipibo-Konibo, these words often describe one of the main people in the sentence instead of the action.
Time-place-manner words in Shipibo-Konibo tell you about distance, time, how long, place, and how much. They include: ochó ‘far,’ bakish ‘one day from today (i.e., ‘yesterday’ or ‘tomorrow’),’ rama ‘now,’ yantan ‘in the afternoon,’ yamé ‘at night,’ yamékiri ‘in the morning,’ kachio ‘in / to the forest or center (i.e., far from the river),’ moa ‘already,’ kikin ‘extremely,’ yanka ‘in vain,’ shokores ‘a little,’ neno ‘here,’ jain ‘there,’ ono ‘further over there,’ basi ‘some time / long ago.’
(12) E-a-ra ka-[a]i bakish /ochó / moa /kachio | ‘I am going tomorrow / far away / already / to the forest.’ | E-a-ra ka-[a]i \siná / \ainbo / \ja | ‘I am going \angry / \woman / \that.’
As I said in 5.1, time-place-manner words can take the ending -cha ‘a little more.’ So can describing words and amount words. Examples are ochó-cha ‘a little further’ and basi-cha ‘some little time long / ago.’

h: Time-Location-Manner Words (words for when, where and how)
t:
A few words for parts of the day work both as time words and as nouns, with no change in form: yantan ‘in the afternoon / afternoon,’ yamé ‘at night / night, darkness,’ yamékiri ‘in the morning / morning.’ This is like English tonight, which can be a time word or a noun. Other words, like ochó ‘far (away),’ jakon ‘good, well’ and moatian ‘long ago, old,’ work both as time-place-manner words and as describing words.
(13) Westíora yamé | ‘one night’
(14) Kako r-iki ochó jema. | ‘Kako is a far away village.’ (cf. (12) above)
(15) Isá Bea-ra jakon joni iki. | ‘Isá Bea is an extremely good person.’
(16) Jakon r-iki e-a. | ‘I am very well.’

h: Derived Time-Location-Manner Words (when/where/how words made from other words)
t:
Some manner words are made by adding -n to a describing word, like English -ly: koshi ‘strong’ > koshi-n ‘strongly,’ ishto ‘rapid’ > ishto-n ‘rapidly.’ Some nouns become time words by adding the time ending -tian ‘when, during’: bari ‘sun’ > bari-tian ‘during the dry season,’ jene ‘flowing water’ > jene-tian ‘during the rainy season,’ bake ‘child’ > bake-tian ‘when being a child,’⁴ wetsa ‘same-sex sibling, other’ > wetsa-tian ‘sometimes.’ The amount word jatíbi ‘all’ can also take -tian, giving jatíbi-tian ‘always.’ A few time words take -tian to make new time words: moa ‘already’ > moa-tian ‘long time ago,’ rama ‘now’ > rama-tian ‘in those times.’ And some place words are made from a noun plus -ki ‘at’: chipon ‘broadest extreme of sth.’ > chipon-ki ‘down the river,’ rebo ‘extreme, endpoint’ > rebo-ki ‘up the river.’
As we will see in 9.2, the time ending -tian has turned into a marker that tells you the next action is done by someone else. When it is added to the pointing word ‘that,’ it forms the joining word ja-tian. There, -tian signals a break or change in the story in a broad sense. But when it is added to a noun like bake, the resulting word bake-tian may or may not be about the doer of the sentence:
(i) E-n-ra onan-ke Sanken Bari bake-tian-bi. | ‘I know Sanken Bari since I was a child / since he was a child.’

h: Derived Time-Location-Manner Words (when/where/how words made from other words)
t:
In the longer sentence below, on the other hand, -tian does a different job. It tells you the action is done by someone else:
(ii) Bake i-ke-tian-bi-ra Sanken Bari e-n onan-a iki. | ‘I know Sanken Bari, since he was a child.’
(iii) Bake i-xon-bi-ra e-n Sanken Bari onan-a iki. | ‘I know Sanken Bari since I was a child.’

h: Participant Agreement (words that "agree" with who is doing the action)
t:
Some of these words always look the same. Examples are time words like bakish ‘one day from today’ and manner words made by adding -n to a describing word. But certain place, manner, amount and other words describe one of the people in the sentence. These words take a special ending that matches that person’s role: whether that person is the doer, the receiver, and so on. Compare the examples below:
(17) Bakisha paké-ke / pi-ke. | ‘(S)he fell / ate yesterday.’
(18) Neno-ra paké-ke. / \neno-xon | ‘(S)he fell here.’ | Neno-xon pi-ke. / \neno | ‘(S)he ate here.’
The word kikin can be a manner word (‘how’), a strengthening word (‘very’), or a describing word. But it takes this matching ending only when it works as a manner word:
(20) Kikin-i paké-ke. | ‘(S)he fell and hurt herself hard.’
(None) Kikin-xon pi-ke. | ‘(S)he ate in an elegant mestizo style (i.e., at a table, on a chair, with tablecloth, silverware, etc.)’
(None) kikin-ax yakat-a | ‘sitting like posing (e.g., crossing the legs)’
I will say more about these matching endings in Chapter 19.

h: Postpositions (words like "in", "on", "with" that come after the noun)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has about twenty postpositions. These are words like English ‘in,’ ‘behind,’ or ‘with,’ but they come after the noun instead of before it. The noun usually has no marker, the plain form. Some postpositions come from words for body parts: napo ‘in the middle of’ < napo ‘interior’ + -n ‘in,’ kexá ‘at the edge of’ < kexá ‘mouth,’ pekáo ‘after, behind’ < peká ‘back’ + -o ‘at.’ English does the same with in front of and at the foot of. The postpositions chichó ‘inside’ and bochiki ‘above’ most likely contain the body-part beginning piece chi- ‘buttocks, behind.’ The first syllable of bebon ‘in front of’ must be be- ‘face, forehead.’ The following passage has four postpositions, each after a different kind of noun group. (Strictly speaking, moa miina pekáo is a whole “after…” part of the sentence; see 10.5.)
(21) Moa miin-a pekáo yamékiri-tiibi, chii keté-a-kan-ai | ja mawá manaon, xobo chichó xana a-kin. Ja-tian
(None) pantion-'ain-bi bo-yama-kan-ai, jato patax-bi ja mawá. | ‘Every morning after burying the corpse they lit a fire above the grave in order to heat the house.⁵ The dead person remained close to them, (s)he was never taken to a cemetery.’

h: Time-Location-Manner Words and Postpositions (how these two kinds of words differ)
t:
Some words can be used both as time-place-manner words and as postpositions. English has the same thing: “he went inside” and “inside the house.” These words are: bebí ‘on the surface (of),’ bochiki ‘above,’ bebon ‘in (the) front (of),’ chichó ‘inside,’ manaon ‘on top (of) / above,’ naman ‘under,’ napon ‘in the middle (of),’ kexá ‘at the edge (of),’ meran ‘inside.’ Look at example (22) with kexá, from kexá ‘mouth:’
(22) Ja-ská-a-kin yoi-kan-a jo-ax-ki | yaka-t-ai bachi kexá. | ‘Once being called, he would come and sit at the edge of the mosquito net.’
(23) Ja-ská-a-kin yoi-kan-a jo-ax-ki | yaka-t-ai kexá. | ‘Once being called, he would come and sit at the edge.’
Sometimes the same word can work as a time-place-manner word or as a postposition after a small change. For example, senen ‘exactly’ and
In the old days, the remains of a dead relative were put in a big jar and buried under the house.
senen-ainko [senen + LOC:LOC] ‘at the end of’ need a noun with them, while senen-bires [senen + ‘purely’] ‘the same’ does not.
Some words are only ever postpositions and always need a noun with them. These are: patax ‘beside / next to,’ pekáo ‘behind / after,’ betan ‘with,’ kopí ‘because of,’ kaman ‘until / up to,’ keská ‘like,’ xaran ‘between / among,’ and paranan, which gives a (negative) reason. The following example shows pekáo. It comes from peká ‘back’ + -o, a kind of ‘at’ ending. (We saw this sentence in Chapter 4 as (14).)

h: Time-Location-Manner Words and Postpositions (how these two kinds of words differ)
t:
(24) Moa icha baritia pekáo, Shipibo joni-bo moa | kai-ribi-kan-a iki ja kimisha joni-nko-ni-a-x. | ‘After many years, the Shipibo reproduced again from these three people.’
The ‘because’ word kopí can be used without a noun, as in example (b) below. But then its meaning changes:
(25) Ja r-iki Rama kopí. | ‘That / it is because of Rama.’ | Ja r-iki kopí. | ‘That / it has to be paid for (i.e., is not for free).’
Some speakers accept the sentence below, where xaran has no noun with it:
(26) Ja r-iki xaran. | ‘It / that is between (two other things).’
The examples below show xaran with a noun:
(27) Tsoma betan Wesna xaran-ra e-a yaká-ke. | ‘I am seated between Tsoma and Wesna.’
(28) Koshi-bo xaran-ra e-a yaká-ke. | ‘I am seated among the authorities.’
Usually the noun that goes with a postposition is in the plain form, with no marker (5.3.4).
There is one exception: paranan, which gives a (negative) reason. The noun before it must be in a special form, the -on form (see 6.1). Compare the nouns used with kopí and with paranan below:
kopí reason
(29) Ja i-káti-ai yanka-ma, e-a kopí. | ‘That was not unmotivated, (that was) because of me.’
paranan (negative) reason
(30) Ainbo-ra e-on paranan bachin-anan-ke. | ‘The women pulled each other by the hair because of me.’

h: Time-Location-Manner Words and Postpositions (how these two kinds of words differ)
t:
Also, some postpositions attach to the bare base of a pronoun instead of to the full plain-form pronoun. In the next example, naman is added to the base e- ‘I/me,’ not to the full pronoun e-a:
(31) E-namamea-x-ra ashá keo keo-wan-ke yamé. | ‘The ashá toads sang and sang under me (i.e., under my house) last night.’
Look at the underlined ending -x in the example above. It shows that place groups built with postpositions can also take the ending that matches a person in the sentence.

h: Verbs (action words)
t:
Verbs tell you about actions, processes, and states. Some endings go only on verbs, or on words used as verbs. These include endings that add or remove a person from the sentence, some endings that act a bit like adverbs, and endings for time (see sections 7.4-7.8). Two more endings go only on verbs: the plural -kan and the ‘not’ ending -yama. Other words use a different plural, -bo, and a different ‘not,’ -ma. The following examples show plural and ‘not,’ first on non-verbs and then on verbs:
Verbs usually need an extra ending before they can be used like nouns. For example, xea- ‘drink (verb)’ > xea-ti ‘drink (noun),’ xea-[a]i ‘the one drinking,’ etc. A few verbs, though, can be used as nouns or describing words directly, with no change at all: keen ‘to want / desire,’ onan ‘to know / knowledgeable,’ shinan ‘think / mind.’ (The noun mawá in (21) might be mawa(t)- ‘die’ plus the ending -a, which makes a describing word from a verb.)
Most verbs can be replaced by two all-purpose verbs, much like English do in “Yes, I do.” They are ak- ‘do (tr.), make, tell’ and ik- ‘do (intr.), be, say.’ You can see this, for example, in short answers to yes/no questions (section 8.5).

h: Predicative Function (verbs as the main part of a sentence)
t:
The word groups are not equal in how easily they change jobs. Most verbs need a special ending before they can work as another kind of word. But nouns, describing words, and even some time-place-manner words and postpositions can take verb endings directly. With no change in form, they become the verb of the sentence (Valenzuela 1997:84-9). When this happens, their meaning shifts. A noun comes to mean ‘become that thing.’ A describing word comes to mean ‘become like that.’ A place postposition used as a verb usually means ‘get to that place.’ These new verbs almost always have just one person in them. In the following examples, the base word kapé- ‘alligator’ takes noun endings or verb endings directly:
(34) Ja-ská-ke-tian-ronki, kapetan kishi tseka-nan-a iki. | ‘Then, it is said that the alligator bit off his leg (to his detriment).’
(35) Yoashi-kon⁶ Inka-n shinan-ke-tian-ronki rabé joni | kapé-ni-ke. | ‘It is said that when the Stingy Inka concentrated on it, the two men turned into alligators.’ (Valenzuela 1997:85)
The next examples show the same thing with the describing word ani ‘big’ and the postposition napon ‘in the middle of.’ When ani becomes a verb (37), it works like kapé in (35). It means a change that simply happens to someone, who does nothing to cause it (‘become big’). The verb made from napon (39) is different. It needs someone who acts on purpose, like ‘go into the middle.’

h: Predicative Function (verbs as the main part of a sentence)
t:
(36) ...ani nonti-n westíora atsa xeati chomo | na-yása-n-kan-a iki. | ‘...they placed a jar of yuca beer inside the big canoe.’
(37) Ja-n yapa beshé-shoko tsak[a]-a-ronki kikin-i | ani-a iki. | ‘It is said that the tiny fish he had driven with his arrow grew tremendously.’
(38) Aniwapóro-ra paro napon reo-koo-ke.... | ‘A ship sank in the middle of the river.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Another name for this Inka is Yoashiko Inka ‘Stingy Inka.’ The ending -ko looks just like the ‘little’ ending used with names in the local Spanish. For example, Ishaco /iˈʃako/ < Isaías.
(39) E-a-ra napon-ke. | ‘I reached the center (of the river or lake).’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Here are more examples of postpositions that take verb endings directly:
(40) xobo meran | ‘inside the house’ | E-a-ra meran-kain-ke. | ‘I fell asleep.’
(41) xobo naman | ‘under the house’ | Moa-ra naman-ke. | ‘It came down (e.g., a hammock, the price)
(42) xobo bebon | ‘in front of the house’ | Moa-ra bebon-ke | ‘(S)he cut in the line.’
Surprisingly, two postpositions become transitive verbs: patax ‘next to’ means ‘approach sb.,’ and betan ‘with’ means ‘pass next to sb.’ Look at the next example with patax-:
(43) xobo patax | ‘next to the house’ | Ja-n-ra moa patax-ke. | ‘(S)he already approached (her / him).’

h: Conjunctions (linking words (and, but, or))
t:
SK has only a handful of conjunctions (joining words like ‘and’, ‘then’, ‘or’). Many of them are built from the middle pointing word ja ‘that’, or from its place form jain ‘there’. Conjunctions often carry the marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. Because of this, their ending can change to match the person they refer to. Here are some: ja-tian [that-TEMP/DD] ‘then,’ ja-skat-ai [that-SIML-INC] ‘so / in this way,’ ja-ská-ke-tian [that-SIML-P-DD] ‘so / in this way,’ jain-xon [there-A] ‘and / then’ (matching the doer of a transitive verb, A), jainoa-x [there:LOC:ABL-S] ‘and / then’ (matching the doer of an intransitive verb, S), jainoa [there:LOC:ABL] ‘and / then,’ and others. Other conjunctions are betan ‘and,’ itan ‘and / or,’ iamax ‘or’ (matching S), and iamaxon ‘or’ (matching A). Conjunctions can be quite long and complicated:
(44) ja-ska-r[a]-aino-a-x-kaya-ki | ‘but instead it is said that (+ intransitive clause).’
The -ra in this example is a frozen piece, left over from an older stage of the language. It is not the same as today’s -ra, the marker that shows the speaker knows something firsthand. In fact, in this example the speaker is passing on what others said, as the hearsay marker -ki shows. So I simply gloss this frozen piece as -ra. You can find more about conjunctions in 19.2.2.11.

h: Interjections (exclamations (oh!, wow!))
t:
Interjections are little words that show a feeling, like English “wow!” or “ouch!”. In SK they include jeje ‘yes (man speaking),’ jojo ‘yes (woman speaking),’ eeri surprise, arí pain, ayáoo pain, shii ~ jii disgust, jass admiration, choon ‘really?,’ ojojói ‘how huge!,’ atashái self-encouragement. Shii and jass appear in the examples below. They are about two traditional customs: decorating the forehead with designs, and reshaping the head of newborn babies, mostly boys (cranial deformation):
(45) Jass! Ja joni r-iki metsá-shoko, | oa be-kenet-a metsá... | ‘Jass! That man is very handsome, his forehead is beautifully designed.’
(46) Shii! Ja mapo tonko tonko-isi metsá-tani-ma-isi. | ‘Shii! That one with the head all rounded (i.e., not deformed) looks very ugly.’
A few Spanish interjections have also entered SK. Two examples are chuu, from the everyday Peruvian Spanish chucha ‘vagina,’ and pucha, from Spanish pucha, a variation of pues (see ex. (96) in Chapter 7).

h: Onomatopoeic Words (sound words (like "splash"))
t:
Onomatopoeic words are words that imitate a sound, like English “splash” or “bang.” In SK they can be used alone. They can also join with two all-purpose verbs to make new verbs: ik-, a general intransitive verb, and ak-, a general transitive verb. You can find sentences where a sound word is the main part of the verb in 4.7 and 8.2.7.
THE NOUN AND THE NOUN PHRASE:
A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun, like “my big new canoe.” The main word can be a simple noun, a verb turned into a noun, another noun phrase, or a pronoun. Around it there can be one or more describing words, usually right next to it. These include adjectives, number and amount words, pointing words (‘this’, ‘that’), owner words (‘my’, ‘your’), another noun (simple or compound), a ‘who/which…’ description part, and so on. As I said in 5.1, the describing words can even appear without the main word. This happens when the speaker thinks the listener can guess it from the situation.
In this chapter we look at pronouns first, then at nouns and noun phrases. In many languages, things like plural or the markers that show who does what to whom are endings on each single noun. In SK, these markers actually attach to the whole noun phrase.

h: Pronouns
t:
Pronouns in SK fall into three main groups: personal pronouns (‘I’, ‘you’, ‘she’…), question pronouns (‘who?’, ‘what?’), and pointing words (‘this’, ‘that’). What about ‘my’, ‘your’ and so on? It is best to treat them as a special owner form of the personal pronouns, not as a separate group of their own.
Real possessive pronouns (‘mine’, ‘yours’) are made by adding the ending -a to ‘my’, ‘your’ and so on. This ending turns a word into a noun. Question pronouns are used in questions, and also to mean ‘someone’ or ‘something’. Pointing words can stand alone as pronouns or describe a noun.

h: Personal Pronouns (I, you, he, she, we, they)
t:
There are six basic pronouns. They cover three persons (1, 2, 3: ‘I’, ‘you’, ‘he / she’) and two numbers (one, or more than one). SK pronouns do not show male or female. There is no separate ‘we’ for “we including you” versus “we without you.” And there are no special polite pronouns either.
In the Panoan languages, third person pronouns (‘he, she, they’) come from pointing words (‘that’). In SK, only the middle pointing word ja ‘that’ became a pronoun this way. Today, the two forms for ‘they’, jato and jabo, can be swapped freely in most situations.¹
‘I’, ‘you’ (one person) and ‘we’ show a visible ending, -a, in the plain form (ABS, the plain form). All other pronouns, and all nouns, have no ending at all in the plain form. The plain form of ‘he / she’ is sometimes said with a long vowel: jaa. This long vowel is just a matter of pronunciation. It also happens with the pointing word ja ‘that’. So jaa should not be read as ja ‘he / she’ plus the ending -a.
The doer form of a pronoun and its ‘my / your’ form look the same, except for ‘I’ and ‘he / she’. But in some traditional kinds of speech, ‘my’ is en instead of nokon. The next piece comes from a song. A group of women sing it to a dead white-lipped peccary (a wild pig) during the Yoina Reteti ‘Animal Sacrifice’ ceremony. This ceremony was part of the rites for girls coming of age, or Ani Xeati:

h: Personal Pronouns (I, you, he, she, we, they)
t:
(1) Mi-n ibo-n kaya, kaya bo-yama-tan-we, | kokoxtobi-kain-i, Bari naman ka-tan-we,
In the related language Kashinawa, habu means a mixed plural (a group of different things), while hatu means a plural of the same kind (Camargo 1996:4). Also for Kashinawa, Cromack (p.c., 1998) says -bu means a group taken together and -tu means individuals taken one by one. I have not been able to find this difference consistently in SK (/haβo/ in SK is clearly used as a same-kind plural). Still, in some situations speakers may prefer one form over the other in a way that fits the Kashinawa rule.
