Also, when listing different things, /haβo/ is used at the end of the list to sum them all up (as in ex. (15) in Ch. 19). There, the other form /hato/ is not acceptable.
(1) ka-tan-we, ka-tan-we, e-n-ria bake…. | ‘Your owner’s soul, don’t take your owner’s soul. Turning into kokoshtobi hawk fly away, go where the Sun sets. Go, go, my son….’ (Soi Rawa 1995:28)
Also, in the Piski dialect speakers may say en instead of nokon for ‘my’: ‘my child’ is en bake in Piski but nokon bake in Ucayali.²
The following examples show the ‘my’ words and the ‘mine’ words in use:
(2) Nato r-iki nokon nonti. | ‘This is my canoe.’ | Nato nonti r-iki nokon-a. | ‘This canoe is mine.’

h: Personal Pronouns (I, you, he, she, we, they)
t:
(3) No-n atapa-baon-ra rete-anan-ai. Nokon-a-ton-ra | mi-n-a jamat-ai; mi-n-a-tonin-kaya-ra | nokon-a kresta-n pi-ai. | ‘Our chickens are fighting. Mine is kicking yours, and yours is biting mine on the crest.’
In several other Panoan languages, the word for ‘my’ is based on the root e(e)-. These include Kashibo-Kakataibo (Western), Kapanawa (Ucayali), and Kashinawa, Yaminawa, Marinawa and Sharanawa (Purus). On the other hand, Wariapano (Ucayali), Chakobo (Southern), and probably Matses (through the form kon) use forms related to nokon. This form nokon is most likely related to no-, the root for ‘we’. As for jawen ‘his / her’: a relative of its ending -wen shows up in other languages. In Yaminawa it marks an owner (e.g., e-fe ‘my’ and a-fe ‘his, her;’ Eakin 1991:30). In Kashinawa it means ‘with / by means of’ (e.g., tsisuda-ven ‘with scissors,’ xaxu-ven ‘by canoe;’ Montag 1981:593).
Some intransitive verbs need an extra person: the one the feeling is about, “the person or thing in whom one is interested” (Faust 1973:81, translation mine). Think of English “angry at you” or “in love with you.” On most pronouns, this extra person gets a special ending, -on. I call it “interessive” in the glosses (INTRSS, the ‘about whom’ ending). ‘You all’, ‘they’, and all nouns don’t take -on. Instead they use the -n form. That is the same ending used for the doer, the tool, the owner, and some other roles. The rules from section 3.2.2 about the different forms of -n apply here too. Look at the examples below:

h: Personal Pronouns (I, you, he, she, we, they)
t:
(4) E-a-ra mi-on / ja-on / no-on sinat-ai. | ‘I am angry (at sb. else) on your / his / our account.’
(5) Ja joni-ra mi-on keen-ai / yoben-'iba-ke. | ‘That man loves you / has asked for you in matrimony.’

h: Emphatic Pronouns (strong forms like "I myself")
t:
Emphatic pronouns are like English “myself” in “I did it myself.” They stress that the doer did the action on her own. They can also set the doer apart from the receiver, for contrast. Earlier writers called them “reflexive pronouns” (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:67), because they can appear in “to yourself” sentences. Those sentences are built with the “to yourself” ending (linguists call it the middle ending). But these pronouns are (usually) not needed to make a “to yourself” sentence correct; the middle ending alone is enough. Also, there are sentences
that contain an emphatic pronoun even though the verb does not have the middle ending that gives the “to yourself” meaning.
How are emphatic pronouns built when they refer to the doer? You start with the pronoun in its -n form. Then you add -bi for emphasis. Last comes a matching ending: -x if the verb is an intransitive verb (S), and nothing (-0) if it is a transitive verb (A). Here I treat the fixed -n on the pronoun as a marker for the doer of any kind of verb (linguists call this nominative case). The table below shows the emphatic pronouns used with intransitive verbs, so they all end in -x. Some speakers use the longer ending -bi-ni-x [-EM-LIG-S] with ‘you all’ and ‘they’. The stress always falls on the second syllable:

h: Emphatic Pronouns (strong forms like "I myself")
t:
The following examples, taken from Valenzuela (1997), show that you don’t need the emphatic pronoun, or any other pronoun, to get the “to yourself” meaning:
Transitive
(6) Tsoma-n-ra Wexá Betsa chachi-ke. | ‘Tsoma pinched Wexá Betsa (with an arrow, a knife, something pointed).’
(None) Tsoma-ra (ja-n-bi-x) chachí-ke. | ‘Tsoma (himself) pinched himself.’
The next example has an emphatic pronoun with the verb beno- ‘to get a husband, to marry a man.’ This verb is an intransitive verb by nature. So the middle ending plays no part here, and yet the emphatic form enbix still appears. Notice also that enbix gets a second emphatic -bi on top:
(7) E-a-ra e-n-bi-x-bi-shaman beno-ama[-a] iki. | ‘I didn’t get married on my own will.’
The next example has a verb with the “each other” ending. Like the “to yourself” ending, it takes away the separate receiver, but the meaning is not “to yourself”:
(8) No-n-bi-x-ra no-a rao-n-anan-kan-ai. | ‘We ourselves treat each other with (plant) medicine.’
The next example shows that when an emphatic pronoun is the doer of a transitive verb (A), it has no matching ending at all:
(9) Wesna-n-ra ja-n-bi rao xea-ke. | ‘Wesna herself drank the medicine.’
When an emphatic pronoun is the receiver, it has no role marker and no matching ending:
(10) Nato r-iki e-n piti be-á; | ja-bi moa bo-tan-we. | ‘This is the fish I have caught; you better take THIS home already (rather than continue waiting for your father who also went fishing).’

h: Emphatic Pronouns (strong forms like "I myself")
t: So emphatic pronouns come in three forms: janbix for the doer of an intransitive verb (S), janbi for the doer of a transitive verb (A), and ja(a)bi for the receiver (O). You can read more about emphatic pronouns in 8.1.

h: Doubled Pronouns (pronouns said twice in one sentence)
t:
You can say a pronoun twice for emphasis, either twice in its doer form or twice in its plain form. Mixing the two (one doer form plus one plain form) is judged wrong by speakers:
(11) E-n e-n a-res-ke. | ‘I defeated him / her (on my own).’
(12) E-a e-a a-res-ai. | ‘(S)he is defeating me.’
(13) E-a e-a ka-ke.³ | ‘I myself left.’
Not all the speakers I asked accept this sentence.

h: Other Personal Pronominal Forms (other forms of the personal pronouns)
t:
Three more endings can be added to pronoun roots. The dative -ki means ‘to / at someone’. The chezative -iba works like French chez: ‘at someone’s place’. The comitative -bé means ‘with’ (it is a shortened form of betan). They attach to these pronoun roots: e-, mi-, ja-, no-, mato-, no-, and jato- / jabo-. These forms are shown in Table 6.3.
Here are examples using the forms in the table above:
(14) ...mi-ki ainbo sinat-ai-tian.... | ‘...if a woman gets angry at you....’
(15) E-a-ra mi-bé jato-iba ka-kas-ai. | ‘I want to go with you to where they are / live.’
Pronoun roots can also join with place words that come after a word, like English ‘under’ or ‘behind’ but placed at the end (linguists call them postpositions). Here they are attached right onto the pronoun when you say them: -bebon ‘in front of,’ -kaman ‘up to,’ -manaon ‘high up with respect to,’ -napon ‘in the middle of,’ -meran ‘among,’ -patax ‘next to,’ -pekáo ‘behind,’ -naman ‘under.’ Look at the examples below. In (17), bebon is part of a comparison (‘more than me’):
(16) Ochíti-ra e-bebon ka-[a]i. | ‘The dog goes in front of me.’ (Faust 1973:56)
(17) Ja-ke nokon bake e-bebon onan... | ‘I have a daughter who knows more than me....’
(18) Ponsen-ra no-kaman jo-ke. | ‘The sloth came up to us (i.e., up to where we are / were).’ (Faust 1973:56)

h: Other Personal Pronominal Forms (other forms of the personal pronouns)
t:
(19) Bake-ra e-manaon iki jiwi-n yaka-t-a. | ‘The boy is above me, on the tree.’ (Faust 1973:56)
(20) Ja-ra no-meran yaka-t-ai. | ‘He sits among us.’ (Faust 1973:57)
(21) Yawisha no-napon iki. | ‘The armadillo is in the middle of us.’ (Faust 1973:57)
(22) Tso-a-rin mi-pekáo? | ‘Who is behind you?’ (Faust 1973:57)
(23) no-patax ik-á jema-bo | ‘our neighboring villages’
Other forms like the ones below are also found:

h: Interrogative Pronouns (question words (who? what?))
t:
Question pronouns are built on two basic roots: jawe ‘what’ and tso- ‘who.’ You can see them in the question words below. (See section 8.4 on questions for when to use -rin and when to use -ki, and for other related topics.)
tso-a ‘who (absolutive)’
(25) Tso-a-rin oa joni? | ‘Who is that man over there?’
tso-n ‘who (-n form)’
Ergative
(26) Tso-n-ki mi-a karo be-xon-a? | ‘Who brought you firewood?’
Genitive
(27) [Tso-n nonti-rin] nato? | ‘Whose canoe is this?’
Notice that in (27) tso-n comes with a noun (‘whose canoe’). In (28), tso-n-a stands alone and takes the noun’s place:
(28) Tso-n-a-rin nato nonon? | ‘Whose duck is this? / For whom is this duck?’
jawe ‘what (absolutive)’
(29) Jawe-rin nato? | ‘What is this?
jawen ‘what (-n form)’
Instrumental:
(30) Jawe-n-ki mi-n wame rete-a? | ‘With what did you kill the paiche (fish)?’
jaweti ‘how much, how many’
(31) Jaweti bake-ya-rin mi-a? | ‘How many children do you have?’
jawerato ‘which’
(32) Jawerato yoina-nin-ki xae jawen bichi
(32) yometso-a-ni? | ‘Which animal stole the skin from the ant-eater?’
jawerano ~ jaweno ‘where (intransitive)’
(33) Jawerano-ki mi-a ka-[a]i? | ‘Where are you going?’
(34) Jawerano-ki Inka-bo ja-a? | ‘Where did the Inkas live?
jaweranoxon ‘where (A agreement)’
(35) Jawerano-xon-ki epa-n pi-ai? | ‘Where is paternal uncle eating?’
jaweranoa ‘from where (O agreement)’

h: Interrogative Pronouns (question words (who? what?))
t:
(36) Jawerano-a-ki mi-n paranta be-a? | ‘From where did you bring banana?’
jaweranoax ‘from where’ (S agreement)
(37) Jawerano-a-x-ki mi-a jo-a? | ‘From where did you come?’
jawetian ‘when’
(38) Jawe-tian-ki mi-a noko-t-a? | ‘When did you arrive?’
jawe kopí ‘why?’
(39) Jawe kopí-ki mi-a ransa-kashama-[a]i? | ‘Why don’t you want to dance?’
jawe keská ‘how (copular construction), what kind of’
(40) Jawe keská-rin mi-a? | ‘How are you?’
(41) Jawe keská rono-rin ja? | ‘What kind of snake is that?’
jawe keskatax ‘how (S agreement)’
(42) Jawe keskat-ax-ki mi-a jo-a? | ‘How did you come?’
jawe keskáxon ‘how (A agreement)’
(43) Jawe keská-xon-ki yapa-n join-ai? | ‘How do fish breathe? (‘breathe’ is transitive in SK)’
Question pronouns can also take the endings -bé ‘with’, -iba ‘at the place of’, and -ki ‘to’. They can also combine with different place words:
(44) Tso-bé-shaman-ki mi-a ka-ti iki Kontámanain? | ‘With whom are you going to Contamana?’
(45) Tso-a patax-ki Wesna yaka-t-ai? | ‘Next to whom is Wesna sitting?’
Question words also work as ‘someone / something / nobody / nothing’ words (linguists call these indefinites). The examples below show this. (These kinds of sentences are covered in 8.2.9.)
(46) Tso-a-ra sai i-bira-i. | ‘Somebody is crying out for help.’
(47) Ja no-n joné merati-bo tso-n onan-yama-[a]i. | ‘Nobody knows (about) our secret lovers.’

h: Interrogative Pronouns (question words (who? what?))
t:
(48) Jawen ani-baon jawe-bi a-xon-yama-ke. | ‘Her parents did not do anything (prohibited) to her benefit.’
The example above is about the rules that parents of a newborn must follow, so they don’t cause their baby any harm. Notice what the ‘not’ ending -yama applies to. It denies the main verb ‘do’ (‘did not do anything’). It does not deny -xon, the ending that brings in the extra person (‘to her benefit’).

h: Demonstrative Pronouns (pointing words (this, that))
t:
Pointing words (‘this’, ‘that’) can describe a noun or stand alone as pronouns, with no change in form. They show three distances: nato ‘this’ (near and visible), ja ‘that’ (middle distance, visible or not), and oa ‘that over there’ (far, visible or not). In the sentences below, each of the three pointing words stands alone as one of the main people or things in the sentence:
(49) Nato-n-ra bakish paranta bo-ai. | ‘This one will carry plantain with her / him tomorrow.’
(50) Moa westíora oxe r -iki ja ik -á. | ‘It’s been already a month since that happened.’
(51) Oa-bo-ra e-n onan-a-bo iki. | ‘Those are my acquaintances.’
In (49)-(51), the pointing words in italics could be replaced by these full phrases, in order: nato jonin [this man-ERG] ‘this man,’ ja jawéki [that thing:ABS] ‘that event,’ and oa jonibo [DIST person-PL:ABS] ‘those people (further away).’

h: Time-Location-Manner Demonstratives (pointing words for time, place and manner (here, then, like this))
t:
You can build words for time, place, and manner (how) from the pointing words ne- ~ nato ‘this’ (near), ja- ‘that’ (middle), and o(a)- ‘that over there’ (far). As Table 6.4 shows, some of these sets have gaps: not every form exists. Look at the following examples with these time-place-manner words:
(52) Oa-tian-ronki sapen icha ja-káti-ai, Paro-n. | ‘In those times, it is said that there were a lot of manatees in the Ucayali River.’
(53) Nato-tian-kaya-ra sapen yama-ke moa. | ‘But in these times there are no manatees anymore.’
(54) Tashi-nko-ronki metsá iki, ja kopí-ra e-a onan-kas-ai. | ‘I heard it is beautiful in the Salt (Mountain), therefore I want to know it.’

h: Nouns
t:
In Ch. 5 the goal was to tell nouns apart from other kinds of words. This section looks instead at how nouns themselves behave: the endings they take and the place they have in the sentence.
In SK, nouns are an open group: new ones can always be added. A noun can appear bare, with nothing added to it. Or it can combine with various describing words. SK does not sort nouns into classes (like the masculine and feminine nouns of Spanish). It also has no clear split between things you can’t help owning, like body parts or relatives, and things you just happen to own. Words for relatives and body parts behave like any other noun (but see the body-part beginning pieces below).
A noun can be replaced by a pronoun, or simply left out. Speakers do this when they judge that the listener can tell from the situation who or what is meant:
(55) Ja-rá-ke ranó-ya joni, ja-ríba-ke ainbo | ranó-ya, ja-ríba-ke ranó-oma-bo. | ‘There are jealous men and jealous women, there are also those (men and women) who are not jealous.’
For example, the next piece comes from a story about a great shaman. He goes to the upper world to put an end to an eclipse of the sun, which was making the Shipibo suffer greatly. After he succeeds, the great shaman comes back to this world and finds the people already doing well. Notice that ‘the people’ are never named in the example below. In the first sentence, the describing word nekea ‘from this side’ acts as a noun and takes the plural ending -bo. In the second sentence, the people are not mentioned in any way at all. Meanwhile, the same-doer marker -xon keeps track of the doer (A), the great shaman:

h: Nouns
t:
(56) Jo-xon jis-á-ki ik-á iki moa
(None) ne-ke-a-bo-ki jakon-i.... | ‘Coming back, he saw that the people from this world were well already....’
(57) Jain-xon-ki yoiy-a iki:.... | ‘Then, (the shaman) told (them)...’
Unless the situation shows otherwise, when a person who should be in the sentence is left out, you normally understand it as ‘he’, ‘she’ or ‘it’ (see 8.2.3 on Transitive Clauses).

h: Female vs. Male Distinction (words for female vs. male)
t:
SK has no grammatical gender. To show whether a person is male or female, you can add the nouns ainbo ‘woman’ or benbo ‘man’ as describing words. Ainbo comes from awin-bo [‘wife’ + plural] and benbo from bene-bo [‘husband’ + plural]. Look at the following examples:
For animals, unlike people, you use awin for female and bene for male:
According to some native speakers, animal names such as ‘capybara’ and ‘manatee’ cannot take awin or bene. Also, some speakers think that fish, snakes, rats, and herons are always female. Awin and bene also go with a couple of plants:

h: Number (one vs. many)
t:
SK tells apart one (singular) and more than one (plural). (Verbs can also take the ending -bekon, which means two people did the action.) Singular has no marker. Plural can be shown on the noun side, with a plural pronoun or with -bo after a noun. Or it can be shown on the verb, with the verb plural ending -kan. The next example is about one single bird flying, since nothing shows there is more than one:
(61) Isá-ra noya-[a]i. | ‘The / a bird is flying.’
To show that two or more birds are flying, you can add the plural ending -bo:
Hura crepitans, Euphorbiaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
(None) Isá-bo-ra noya-[a]i. | ‘(The) birds are flying.’
Other possibilities are:
(None) Isá-ra noya-kan-ai. | ‘The birds are flying.’
(None) Isá-bo-ra noya-kan-ai. | ‘The birds are flying.’

h: Non-Count Nouns (things you can't count (water, sand))
t:
Some nouns can’t be counted. They don’t combine with numbers and can’t take the plural -bo. This group includes things in nature and weather, such as tashi ‘salt,’ jene ‘flowing water,’ onpax ‘contained water,’ oi ‘rain,’ wakanawa ‘school of fish,’ koin ‘cloud(s),’ niwe ‘wind,’ bechon ‘wave,’ mashi ‘sand,’ mai ‘land,’ mano ‘mud,’ nai ‘sky,’ manish ‘weed.’ It also includes foods and drinks like aros ‘rice,’ atsa poto ‘yuca flour,’ bata ‘sugar,’ bexnan ‘sugarcane liquor.’ Body parts that can’t be counted are: rani ‘body hair,’ bero karani ‘eyebrow,’ bero kexni ‘eyelash,’ keni ‘beard, moustache,’ boo ‘hair.’ There are also non-count nouns for cultural items, such as mei ‘apacharama’ (a powder made from the dried and charred bark of the apacharama⁵ tree, which is mixed with clay
Licania spp., Chrysobalanaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
to make pottery).⁶ When oi ‘rain,’ wakanawa ‘school of fish,’ koin ‘cloud(s),’ niwe ‘wind,’ and bechon ‘wave’ are the doer, the verbs ‘come’ and ‘go’ must use their special forms for more than one (see meteorological-nature verbs, the verbs about weather and nature).

h: Count Nouns (things you can count)
t: Count nouns can be combined with numbers and can take the plural -bo. Here are some examples: joni ‘person / man,’ nonti ‘canoe,’ makan ‘stone,’ yapa ‘fish,’ ison xoma ‘zapote⁷ (tree or its fruit),’ wishtin ‘star,’ jiwi ‘tree,’ xobo ‘house,’ xawi ‘sugar cane,’ jina ‘tail,’ mapo ‘head,’ chopa ‘piece of clothes,’ kebí ‘lip,’ rekin ‘nose,’ rekin kini ‘nostril,’ paro ‘river,’ wean ‘creek,’ ian ‘lake,’ bata ‘candy,’ xaté ‘wound from a cutting,’ isin ‘pain (from illness),’ chexá ‘pain,’ mei ‘apacharama tree,’ boo ‘hair,’ etc.

h: Proper Nouns (names)
t:
This group includes the names of people, places, and ethnic groups or clans. A Shipibo can have three different kinds of personal names: ikon jane ~ janekon ‘true or core name,’ nawan jane ~ nawan join jane ‘Spanish name, name in the outsider’s language,’ and shiro jane ‘joke name.’ Janekon are made of two parts. While the first part
One person I consulted treated these as count nouns: wakanawa ‘school of fish,’ koin ‘cloud,’ bechon ‘wave,’ manish ‘weed,’ rani ‘body hair,’ bero karani ‘eyebrow,’ bero kexni ‘eyelash,’ and keni ‘beard, moustache.’ Note that boo ‘hair’ appears in both groups, non-count and count nouns.
Matisia cordata, Bombacaceae (Tournon 1995:Appendix 1).
of the compound is usually used by both men and women. The second part is, in most cases, only for men or only for women. Nawan jane are the same names that Spanish-speaking people use. Many Shipibo carry the last names of former patrones. Shiro jane are given by friends or relatives, based on a funny story about the person.
Place names can also be made of two words joined together. For example, kontá manan is a kind of palm tree plus ‘hills.’ It literally means ‘hills where there are konta palm trees.’ Another way to make a place name is to take an animal or plant name and add the ending -ya. This ending means ‘having’ or ‘full of’ (in glosses: PROP). For example, amakiri-ya is a kind of fish plus PROP (the "having" ending). It literally means ‘place where gamitana⁸ fish abound.’

h: Proper Nouns (names)
t: Names of peoples end in -bo. This ending marks more than one, or a group. In the Panoan language family, many people-names are an animal name plus -bo. For example, Shipi-bo is ‘tamarin monkey’ + -bo, so ‘the Tamarin Monkey People.’ Koni-bo is ‘eel’ + -bo, so ‘the Eel People.’ Other Panoan people-names join an animal name with nawa. This word means ‘outsider, other people, enemy.’ Examples are Kashi-nawa (‘bat’ + nawa) and Kapa-nawa (‘squirrel’ + nawa). Names with nawa may have been made up by neighboring groups, not by the people themselves.

h: Nouns Denoting Parts of the Body (body-part words)
t:
A small, fixed group of nouns can be shortened into little word pieces. Almost all of these nouns are body parts. One exception is jene ‘flowing water.’ The short piece is usually the same as the first syllable of the full noun. But there are a few that don’t follow this pattern, like ra- ‘body’ and ne- ‘flowing water.’ These short word pieces are
Colossoma macropomum, Colossoma oculus, Characidae, Characiforme (Tournon 1995, Appendix 4).
added to the front of other nouns, adjectives, and especially verbs. They add a meaning like an adverb, usually telling where (on which part of the body) something happens. So instead of naming the body part as a separate word with its owner, you put the body-part piece onto the main word (linguists could call this a required kind of “possessor raising”). Sometimes the word they attach to also appears in a shortened form. Adding a body-part beginning piece does not change the kind of word: a verb stays a verb, and a noun stays a noun. Table 6.5 lists the body-part beginning pieces and the nouns they come from.
In be-wis above, the describing root wiso appears in a shortened form.
When I talked about adjectives made from other words in 5.2.2, I also mentioned something else. These short body-part pieces can act as base words and take the ‘without’ ending -nto: cha-nto [BOTH.LEGS-PRIV] ‘without the normal use of both legs’ and ji-nto [TAIL-PRIV] ‘without tail.’ You can read more about body-part beginning pieces in sections 7.3 and 8.2.6.

h: Nouns Denoting Parts of the Body (body-part words)
t: Genipa americana, Rubiaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).

h: Group Nouns (words for groups)
t:
A few nouns refer to groups of things of the same kind. These words are: tsamá ‘group of,’ tonbó ‘group of (monkeys),’ kai ‘flock,’ senbó ‘group of (small creatures),’ texkan ‘large bunch of,’ and bero ‘grain of.’ Tsamá is usually used for groups of peccaries (wild pigs) and tapirs: yawa tsamá ‘herd of white-lipped peccaries,’ awá tsamá ‘herd of tapirs.’ But tsamá can be used more widely, and may be seen as the general word for ‘group.’
Tonbó refers to a group of monkeys: iso tonbó ‘group of spidermonkeys,’ shino tonbó ‘group of capuchin monkeys,’ wasa tonbó ‘group of squirrel monkeys,’ roo tonbó ‘group of howler monkeys,’ shipi tonbó ‘group of tamarin monkeys,’ riro tonbó ‘group of musmuque¹⁰ monkeys;’ but you cannot say \yawa tonbó ‘herd of white-lipped peccaries’ (the star marks a wrong form).
The word kai is used at least for some birds. Unlike with tsamá and tonbó, the noun that goes with kai takes the -n form: manxaman [manxan + -n] kai ‘flock of herons,’ bawa-n kai ‘flock of parrots,’ abo-n kai ‘flock of manshacos,’ isko-n kai ‘flock of paucars,’ pitso-n kai ‘flock of parakeets,’ etc.
The word senbó refers to groups of small creatures such as insects and lizards: jima senbó ‘group of ants,’ jenen yawa senbó ‘group of esquila (k. water insect),’ xanbo senbó ‘group of lizards.’ Senbó can also mean a group or small bunch of

h: Group Nouns (words for groups)
t:
Aotus spp.
fruits: xankon senbó group of uvilla fruits, wanin senbó ‘group of pijuayo¹¹ fruits,’ xenan senbó ‘group of guaba¹² fruits,’ binon senbó ‘group of aguaje¹³ fruits.’
Texkan refers to large bunches of fruit (for example, harvested bananas are brought from the chacra, the farm plot, in texkan or large bunches): wanin texkan ‘large bunch of pijuayo (fruit),’ paranta texkan ‘large bunch of plantain,’ binon texkan ‘large bunch of aguaje,’ isan texkan ‘large bunch of ungurahui (fruit).’
Bero ‘seed, eye’ can be used for ‘grain (of corn).’ There is no special counting word for mashi ‘sand,’ aros ‘rice,’ asókaro ‘sugar,’ or tashi ‘salt.’

h: Origin / Augmentative -n Ewá (the ending meaning "from" or "big")
t:
In the Shipibo view of the world, animals and plants have a “mother” or “owner” (these words translate the Peruvian Amazonian Spanish madre and dueño).¹⁵ This “mother” or “owner” is not thought of as female or male. It is simply where its kind comes from. For instance, waka-n ewá [fish-n ewá] ‘saltón’ (Brachyplatystoma filamentosum, Pimelodidae, Siluriforme) is seen as the “mother” of all fish without scales (Tournon 1995, Appendix 4); iso-n ewá [spidermonkey-n ewá] is said to be the
Bactris gasipaes, Palmae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1). ‘Peach palm’ in English (Phil Young, p.c.)
Inga edulis, Leguminosae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
Mauritia flecuosa, Palmae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).
Another form is -n ewa, without stress on the last vowel. The -n form of ewá is ewakan, while the -n form of ewa is ewan.
Speakers I consulted disagree about whether all animals and plants have a “mother” or “owner”, or only some do.
ancestor that all kinds of monkeys came from. These first, original kinds are described as bigger or more important than the ones that came after them. They usually live in the forest or in the water. They may harm people who don't follow certain set rules. For example, the father of a newborn baby must stay away from certain trees, like xono ‘lupuna’ (Ceiba pentandra, Bombacaceae). He must also avoid animals such as rono-n ewá ‘aquatic boa’ (Eunectes murinus, Boideae). If he doesn't, these could harm his baby.

h: Origin / Augmentative -n Ewá (the ending meaning "from" or "big")
t:
To name the mother or owner of a plant or animal, Shipibo usually uses the pattern [N-n ewá]: the noun, then -n, then ewá. You can see it in (63). Here is something interesting. In two related languages, Yaminawa and Sharanawa, the matching word for ewá means ‘mother.’ In Shipibo-Konibo it does not. The -n is probably the same ending that means ‘of’ (like English 's). So, long ago, [N-n ewá] probably meant ‘X's mother / origin.’ Here are some examples:
In these names, Ewá can sometimes be replaced by ibo “owner.” There are also names made with N-n tita (tita means ‘mother’). One example is yawish-en tita [armadillo-n mother] ‘yanguaturi’
Electrophors electricus, Electrophoridae; Hypopomus brevirostris, Hypopomidae, Gymnotoidei, (Tournon 1995, Appendix 4).
Brycon spp., Characidae, Characiforme (Tournon 1995, Appendix 4).
Pterygoplichtys multiradius, P. spp., Loricariidae, Siluriforme (Tournon 1995, Appendix 4).
(Priodontes maximus, Tournon 1995, Appendix 3), which is also called yawishan ewá. Another is atsa-n tita [yuca-n mother] ‘yuca mama’ (Tapirira guianensis, Anacardiaceae, Tournon 1995, Appendix 1). A third is rono-n tita [snake-n mother] ‘mother of the snakes,’ the origin of all kinds of snakes. One speaker said it is the same as kamox ‘shushupe’.
In the examples below, -n ewá doesn't mean ‘mother’ at all. It just means ‘big’ (linguists call this an augmentative):

h: The Nominalizer -Ti (the -ti ending that turns a verb into a noun)
t: You can turn a verb into a noun by adding the ending -ti. The new noun is usually a tool, the thing you do the action with. English does something similar with -er: open gives opener.

h: Zero Nominalization on Verbs (verbs used as nouns with no ending)
t:
Some verbs can be used as nouns without adding anything at all. English does this too: to walk and a walk. Examples are keen- ‘to want / desire (noun),’ mawá- ~ mawat- ‘to faint or die / fainted (one), corpse,’ and shinan- ‘to think, to
remember / mind, thinking.’ In the next two examples, shinan- is used first as a verb and then as a noun:
(66) E-n-ra shinan-ai ja Ani Xeati Kanaria jema-n i-ní. | ‘I remember the Ani Xeati ceremony that took place in Kanaria village long ago.’
(67) Ja-ska-rain e-n rama nato shinan bi-i i-t-ai. | ‘In this way, I am now acquiring this experience.’

h: Participle Nominalizers (endings that turn verbs into describing words)
t:
Another way to make a noun is to add one of two endings to the bare verb: -ai or -a. These are the same endings that make verb forms like English eating and eaten. -ai is for an action that is still going on, and -a is for one that is finished (linguists call these participle markers):
(68) ...no-a i-ti atipan-ke benxoa-mis, isin-ai-bo benxoa-[a]i. | ‘...we can become medicine people and cure the sick (ones).’
(69) Jain-xon-ribi yoi-kan-ai, ja mawat-a-ki ka-[a]i reboki.... | ‘It is also said that the dead people go to the upper Ucayali....’

h: Zero Nominalization on Time-Location-Manner Expressions (time and place words used as nouns with no ending)
t:
Words that tell you when, where or how something happens can be used as nouns just as they are. You don't need to add anything to turn them into nouns. They can take noun endings directly. For example, the
expressions ransa-ti-ain [dance-INF-LOC] and aros bana-kan-a-ainko [rice sow-PL-PP2-LOC:LOC] both carry the ‘at / in’ ending. They can mean ‘the place to dance’ and ‘rice field.’ Like ordinary nouns, they can take the plural ending -bo and other noun endings; see exx. (106) and (107). For examples with the ‘from’ ending and the ‘like’ ending, see sentences (56) and (87).

h: The Instrumental Causativizer -N (the -n ending that means "use something as a tool")
t: You can add the ending -n to a noun to make a verb. The new verb means ‘to do something to someone using that thing’ (linguists call this an instrumental causative):

h: The Distributive -Ti(i)bi (the ending meaning "each" or "every")
t:
You can add the ending -tiibi ~ -tibi to a noun or pronoun. It means ‘each, every,’ as in English each day or every person (linguists call this a distributive):
(71) Apo-n-ra jema-tiibi jawéki-bo meni-ke. | ‘The President made a donation to each village.’
(72) Nete-tibi-ra e-a nashi-ai paro-n. | ‘Every day I bathe in the river.’
In the last example, the noun with -tibi is clearly not a main part of the sentence. It just adds extra information, like a time or place word.

h: Nominal Compounding (nouns made of two nouns)
t:
Shipibo can join two words to make one name, like English rattlesnake or bookshelf. In these compound words, the describing word almost always comes first and the main noun last. I have found only one exception: iso koro ‘Humboldt’s woolly monkey.’ Most compounds are noun + noun. Others are noun + -n + noun, where -n means ‘of’ (like English 's). There are also some adjective + noun compounds. And, as I said, there is at least one noun + adjective compound:
Most compound words are names of plants and animals, especially names for specific kinds. The compounds below are names for different kinds of snakes. A word-for-word translation is given for each one. In all of them, the describing word comes first and the main word rono ‘snake’ comes last:
As I said earlier, chaxo ino lit. ‘deer jaguar’ is a kind of jaguar, not a kind of deer. The last word tells you what kind of thing it is. Compounds of noun + noun and noun + -n + noun can also show what something is made of, or what it is a part of. I talked about this in the section on Modifying Nouns in 3.3.7.1.
Macfadyena unguis-cati (L.) Gentry, Bignoniaceae (Tournon 1995, Appendix 1).

h: The Proprietive -Ya and The Privative -Oma ("having" (-ya) and "not having" (-oma))
t: Two endings go on the end of a whole noun phrase (a noun plus any words describing it). They turn it into a describing word. The ending -ya means ‘having’ or ‘with.’ The ending -oma means ‘without’ (linguists call these the proprietive and the privative). English has similar endings: -ful and -less, as in hopeful and hopeless. See also (2) and (53):

h: The Diminutive -Shoko and The Deprecatory -Isi ~ -Osi ("little" (-shoko) and "bad/ugly" (-isi ~ -osi))
t:
Other endings also go on the end of a noun phrase. The ending -shoko means ‘little.’ It can also show love or tender feelings, like English doggy or sweetie (see also (10)-(12)). The ending -isi ~ -osi shows that the speaker looks down on something. You use the second form when the word ends in /i/:
As I said earlier, -shoko doesn't only go on nouns. Neither does the ‘looking down on it’ ending, which can also go on a verb.

h: The Legitimative -Kon and Its Negative -Koma ("real/genuine" (-kon) and "not genuine" (-koma))
t:
When you add -kon to a noun, it adds the meaning ‘core, legitimate, true, real, authentic, very good.’ For example, the Shipibo call themselves Joni-kon ‘Core People.’ This comes from joni ‘person’ plus -kon, Their language may be called Joi-kon ‘Core Language.’ And Shipibo personal names are called jane-kon ‘core name:’
(78) Nokon papa-n jane-kon i-káti-ai Kesin Tsoma. | ‘My father’s Shipibo name was Kesin Tsoma.’
Another example is piti-kon ‘very good / core food.’ The Shipibo use this word for fish and the other kinds of food they like to eat most.²⁰
You can add the ‘not’ ending -ma to -kon. This gives -koma, which means ‘bad:’
(79) Nato r-iki joni-koma. | ‘This is a bad person.’ (Faust 1973:98)
(80) Ne-ri-ra bai-koma iki. | ‘Over here the way is not good / is hard.’ (Faust 1973:98)
In her Lecciones para el aprendizaje del idioma shipibo-conibo, the SIL missionary linguist Norma Faust gives these examples: kirika-kon ‘authentic book, very good book, Bible’ and bai-kon ‘true way, very good way;’ These words were most probably made up for religious purposes (1973:97-98).
Remember that -ti turns a verb into a noun. When -kon and -koma are added to such a noun, they mean something new. -kon means ‘easy,’ and -koma means ‘difficult or impossible to do.’ Look at these examples:
(81) Ja-ská-shaman-xon e-n jene-ti-koma ik-á iki. | ‘In that situation it was impossible / hard for me to leave (him).’

h: The Legitimative -Kon and Its Negative -Koma ("real/genuine" (-kon) and "not genuine" (-koma))
t:
(82) Onan-ti-koma r-iki i-kon jawéki. | ‘It is hard to know the truth.’ (Faust 1973:98)
Some everyday words come from -kon too, as the example above shows. The verb ik- ‘be, do (intr.)’ plus -kon gives ikon ‘true.’ The verb ja- ‘exist, live’ plus -kon gives jakon ‘good.’ Its opposite is jako(n)ma ‘bad.’

h: The Plural / Collective -Bo (the plural ending -bo)
t:
The ending -bo means ‘more than one’ or ‘a group.’ It works a bit like English -s. It goes on pronouns, nouns and other noun-like words. As I said earlier, -bo is common in the names of peoples, such as Shipibo, Konibo, Xetebo, Kashibo. It is also in kaibo ‘co-member of the ethnic group.’ Even the words for one woman and one man come from it. ainbo ‘woman’ comes from awin-bo [female / wife-bo], and benbo ‘man’ comes from bene-bo [male / husband-bo]. -Bo is also used to make the word for ‘they,’ ja-bo.
The next example shows that -bo goes on the last word of the noun phrase. That word doesn't have to be the main noun. (English does something like this with 's: the king of England's hat.)
(83) Jain-xon-ribi [sapa kenchá ani-osi]-bo | ak-á iki. | ‘She also made large flat clay pots.’
In the example below, -bo shows up twice. First it goes on the group of words built around Kashibo. Then it goes on the describing word xapanantiyashoko, even though the noun it describes is left out. The whole word xapanantiyashokobores is the only main part of a sentence that has no verb ‘to be’ in it:
(84) Ja Kashibo-bo kikin joshin-res ik-á iki chopa-oma ik-ax, | xapananti-[y]a-shoko-bo-res. | ‘The Kashibos looked all red because they wore no clothes, they only wore loincloths.’

h: The Plural / Collective -Bo (the plural ending -bo)
t:
-bo doesn't only mean ‘many people or things.’ It can also mean ‘many kinds’:
(85) Ja-ríba-ra-ke meskó keská nawa-shoko-bo. | ‘There are also different kinds of mestizos.’
(86) Moa-tian-ronki ja-káti-ai meskó keská joni-bo.... | ‘It is said that long time ago there were different kinds of people...’
Below, -bo goes on a pronoun that already has the ‘like’ ending:
(87) Moa-tian i-káti-kan-ai ja-ska-ra-shaman-bo.... | ‘Long time ago such (things) existed....’
Usually -bo goes only once, on the last word of the noun phrase. But sometimes it shows up on a second word in the same phrase as well. In the next example, -bo is on the word jatíribi ‘all’ and also on the noun that comes right after it:
(88) Inka-n yoi-ni keská-bi ja-ke rama jatíribi-bo | ainbo-bo kikin jawéki-a-ti onan-ma. | ‘Just like the Inka Woman said, there are nowadays some women who don’t know at all how to do the things (that are proper of women).’
In the example above, there is no clear pause between the two words that carry -bo.
In the example below, -bo goes on a pronoun. (This use of -bo needs more study.)
(89) Mato-bo moa mawat-a pekáo ik-ai. | ‘This will happen after you (all) die.’
Remember that some ‘where’ and ‘from where’ words can be used as nouns as they are. In exx. (56), (106) and (107), -bo goes on such ‘from’ and ‘at’ words. In (87), -bo goes on a ‘like’ word used the same way.

h: Case-Markers (endings that show a noun's role)
t:
In Shipibo, many little endings on nouns show the noun's role in the sentence: who does the action, who receives it, where it happens, and so on (linguists call these case markers). Like -bo, these endings go on the last word of the noun phrase. In this section I look at these endings: the plain form (ABS), the calling form (vocative), the -n-form, the ‘for whose sake’ form (interessive), the ‘at / to’ form (locative-allative), the ‘from’ form (ablative), the ‘to’ ending -ki (dative), the ‘with’ form (chezative) and the ‘when’ form (temporal). I also
look at some other ways to show relationships that don't have a fully fixed ending yet. Examples are where something comes from, or what something is about.

h: 6.6.5.1. Absolutive
t:
Most nouns and pronouns have no ending at all in the plain form (ABS, the plain form). Only a few words add the ending -a: ‘I,’ ‘you’ (one person), ‘we,’ and the question word ‘who.’ What does the plain form do? It is used for the doer of an intransitive verb (whether the doer is active or not). It is used for the receiver of a transitive verb. It is used after little words like kopí reason / cause (linguists call these postpositions, like English prepositions but placed after the noun). And it may be used for the ‘what something is’ part of a sentence like ‘he is a teacher.’ But pronouns never appear in that last use. So I can't rule out that those words are just bare words with nothing on them at all.
(90) Bake-ra jo-ke. | ‘A / the child came.’
(91) E-n-ra bake kena-ke. | ‘I called the child.’
(92) Nato r-iki nokon bake. | ‘This is my child.’

h: 6.6.5.2. Vocative
t:
When you call to someone (‘John!’), the noun takes the stress on its last syllable (linguists call this the vocative):
(94) Saní, ne-ri jo-wé! | ‘Sani, come over here!’
(95) Ja-tian e-n nokon wetsa Kesten Koshi yoyo ak-á | iki: “wetsá, e-a Tashi onan-kas-ai”.’ | ‘Then I told my brother Kesten Koshi: “Brother, I want to know the Salt (Mountain)”.’
In one word, two sounds swap places in the calling form. The word is shino ‘capuchin monkey.’ In some traditional kinds of speech it also means ‘woman’ (while xawe ‘turtle’ means ‘man’). Its calling form is shino > shoní.
Some nouns used to have three syllables long ago. Today they have two syllables, and they end in a stressed vowel or in a consonant. These nouns get back their old third syllable in the -n form. They do the same in the calling form, and the stress moves to that last syllable. This gives us a clue about the past. Long ago, the language had a rule that dropped the last vowel or syllable of three-syllable nouns. Before that rule came in, the calling form may have been made simply by moving the stress to the last
syllable of the noun.²¹ The calling forms probably kept their three syllables because the last syllable was stressed, so it didn't get dropped (cf. Features of Proto-Pano Grammar in 1.5.2). Now look at the calling forms of nouns whose normal form has a written stress mark:

h: 6.6.5.2. Vocative
t:
Three-syllable nouns make their calling form just by moving the stress to the last syllable. They do not add the linking piece -ni that shows up in the -n form (see 2.3.2):
Words ending in -mis ‘one who always does it’ don't change at all in the calling form. Examples are pi-mis > pi-mis ‘one who always eats.’ A parent says this when pretending to call the jaguar to scare a child. Another is rete-mis > rete-mis ‘one who always kills, murderer.’
In some related languages, such as Kapanawa and Kashinawa, the -n form is also used for calling someone. So there is another possible story. Maybe the SK calling form came from the -n form, after it lost its nasal sound.
A white person who is believed to kill Indians to take their fat. People say this fat is sold in rich countries as fuel for different kinds of machines, e.g. airplanes.

The -n ending does many jobs. A noun with -n can be any of these: the doer of a transitive verb (the doer marker, ERG), the tool or means you use (‘with a knife’), the owner (‘the man's’), the place (‘at / to’), the time (‘when’), and some other roles. The examples in (99) show the tool use. In the (b) sentence, the tool word is followed by the ‘not’ ending -ma. Together they mean ‘without.’ Notice that the ending -bi, which adds emphasis, is also there (as with Negative Indefinites, see 3.6.9):
(99) Pia-n-ra rete-ke. | ‘(He) killed (it) with an / the arrow.’ | Pia-n-ma-bi-ra rete-ke. | ‘(He) killed (it) without an / the arrow.’
The next example shows -n used for time, for means, for the owner, and for place:
(100) Rominko nete-n-ra nashi-a iki waste-n Rama-n xobo-n. | ‘On Sunday (s)he bathed with piripiri in Rama’s house.’
In the sentence below, the -n piece does two jobs. It marks the owner, in the form -nin. And it marks the doer of a transitive verb. Notice that the doer marker appears only once. It goes after the whole doer phrase, a phrase made of two owned nouns joined by ‘and’:
(101) Ja pekáo, [xontako-nin [papa betan tita]]-n atsa xeati-a-[a]i. | ‘After that, the girl’s parents prepared the yuca beer.’

h: 6.6.5.4. Interessive
t:
Shipibo has a special form for the person someone feels an emotion about or for, as in ‘I feel sorry for you’ (linguists call this the interessive). Some pronouns have their own special form for this: ‘I,’ ‘we,’ ‘you’ (one person), and ‘he / she.’ But nouns, and the pronouns ‘you all’ and ‘they,’ just use the same form as the -n form (for the special forms, see 6.1.4; see also the sentences with intransitive verbs plus an extra person in 8.2.2).
(102) Tita-ra nokon wetsa-n raket-ai. | ‘Mother fears for my sister.’
This ‘for whom’ word can be followed by the ‘from’ ending, by the endings that agree with a person in the sentence, or by both, as in the example below:
(103) E-a-ra mi-on-mea-x axe-ai. | ‘I learn for you / from you.’
Finally, the noun that goes with the little word paranan also takes this same ‘for whom’ form. You can see this in ex. (81), repeated below:
(104) Ainbo-ra e-on paranan bachin-anan-ke. | ‘The women pulled each other by the hair because of me.’

h: 6.6.5.5. Locative-Allative
t:
To say ‘at’ or ‘to’ a place, Shipibo has three endings: -n (< -no),²³ -nko and -ain (linguists call this the locative-allative). Which one you use depends on the length of the word, counted in beats (linguists call them moras). A word with an even number of beats usually takes -nko or -n; you can pick either one. A word with an odd number of beats takes -ain. Some two-syllable words count as three beats: those ending in a stressed vowel, and those ending in a consonant (see also 3.1.6 and 3.2.3). Words that were made from other words take -ain (odd number of beats) ~ -ainko (even number of beats):
Even-numbered moras
(105) ….moa bo-kan-ai wetsa-nko / wetsa-n. | ‘They went somewhere else.’
Odd-numbered moras and derived nominals
(106) Ransa-ti-ain-bo ka-[a]i, Ani Xeati-ain-bo ka-[a]i,
In other Panoan languages, including the closely related Wariapano, ‘at / to’ is shown with the ending -no on the end of the phrase. There are also clues inside SK itself that -no was (once) the ‘at / to’ ending. Look at these expressions:
Also, in his “Idioma Schipibo” Armentia (1898:61) listed the phrase hema-no putaqui [out-LOC/ALL throw] ‘to send somebody outside.’ There the ‘at / to’ ending is -no, not -n as it would be today. So there is enough evidence to say that -no, not -n, used to be the general ‘at / to’ ending in SK. It also means that using one ending, -n, for ‘at / to,’ for the doer marker, etc. is a newer change,

h: 6.6.5.5. Locative-Allative
t:
(None) meskó keskát-i ni-kan-ke. | ‘(Widows nowadays) go to dances, to Ani Xeatis, they go wherever they want (i.e., the traditional mourning rites are not observed).’
(107) Nato isá-ra ja-ke icha mano piko-t-a | manish-ain-bo, aros bana-kan-a-[a]inko-bo. | ‘This bird lives in the weeded shores with black mud, in the rice fields.’
Look at the two examples just above. The plural -bo comes after the ‘at’ words. These ‘at’ words are being used as nouns without any extra ending.

h: 6.6.5.6. Ablative
t:
To say ‘from’ a place, Shipibo builds on top of the ‘at / to’ ending (linguists call the ‘from’ form the ablative). So you get one ending stacked on another. The ‘from’ endings are -nkonia, -ainoa, -ainkonia, -mea, and -kea. Here is how they are built. If the ‘at’ form ends in -nko, you add the linking piece -ni and then the ‘from’ ending. If the ‘at’ form ends in a nasal sound, that sound is dropped and you add -mea. Two of the endings can also go on words made from other words. These are -ainoa [-ain locative + -no locative + -a ablative] and -ainkonia [-ain locative + -nko locative + -ni ligature + -a ablative]. Some words already mean a place by themselves and need no ‘at’ ending. If such a word ends in a vowel or in the sound /ʂ/, it just adds -kea to mean ‘from.’ There are exceptions. meran ‘inside’ can also take -oa (so you get meramea ~ meranoa). And manaon takes -kea in
spite of ending in a nasal sound (see also Alternate Mora Timing in 3.2.3). If a place word ends in a stressed vowel, its stress moves to the first syllable when it takes the ‘from’ ending -kea. For example, chichó ‘inside’ > chichokea ‘from inside:’
(108) Jepe Ian ainbo-bo iki wetsa-nko-ni-a-bo keská-ma. | ‘The women from the village of San Francisco are not like those from other villages.’

h: 6.6.5.6. Ablative
t:
(109) No-n Inka iki manamamea-ma.... | ‘Our Inka is not from the Andes....’
In the example above, manamamea is built from three parts. First comes the base word manan ‘mountain.’ Then comes -man, one form of the -n ending. Last comes -mea, which means ‘at’ + ‘from.’ The next ‘from’ forms are built on the ‘at’ ending -ain:
(110) Biri-ra jo-ke Maioshiaino-a-x. | ‘Biri came from Pucallpa.’
(111) Ja mai kini-ainoa-x pikó-xon joni-n yatan-a | iki ja ainbo jo-a. | ‘Coming out of the hole, the man grabbed the woman who had come nearby.’
In the example above, mai kini takes the ‘from’ form built on -ain. That is odd, because it has an even number of beats. Maybe mai kini is treated as one compound word. Below, -ainoa is added to a word that was made from another word:
(112) ...ronin meno-t-aino-a-x piko-t-a iki | ja waste. | .’...from the yacumama’s ashes originated that piripiri.’
Sometimes you can use the ‘from’ form where you might expect the ‘at’ form. This shows that the person was already at the place when the action happened. Or it shows that the person is seen as belonging to that place, like English ‘the people from the village.’ In English or Spanish, both versions are translated with ‘at’ or ‘in.’ Compare these examples:
(113) Abion-ra paké-ke kachio. | ‘The plane fell in the forest.’ (the plane was flying over an unspecified location and then fell in the forest.)

h: 6.6.5.6. Ablative
t:
(114) Abion-ra paké-ke kachio-kea-x. | ‘The plane fell in the forest.’ (the plane was flying over the forest and fell there)
There is another reason to use the ‘from’ form instead of the ‘at’ form. It lets you say something about the doer of an intransitive verb. That's because only ‘from’ words can carry an ending that agrees with that doer. The next example uses the ‘from’ ending -ainkonia. It is built from the two ‘at’ endings -ain + -nko, then the linking piece -ni, then the ‘from’ ending -a:
(115) Ja-ská-ribi no-a i-ti ja-ke
A huge water-snake from myths.
(None) Jepe Iainko-ni-a-x-bicho-ma.... | ‘We must behave in this way (i.e., kindly) not only in Jepe Ian.....’
Finally, the next two examples show words that already mean a place by themselves. They take the ‘from’ ending -kea:
(116) Ja-ra naiki-ai bachi chichokea-x… | ‘He (received the spirit of the ayahuasca²⁵ plant and) travelled to the upper world from inside his mosquito net.’
(117) Ochíti mecha a-nonxon-ronki bi-ti iki sokota pani bero, | chosko “jono joboxko,” chonka nia boan'is pei, | kachiokea. | ‘To make a dog become a good hunter one has to bring from the forest six yahuarango seeds, four “collared-peccary testicles” plants, and ten sacha sanango leaves.’

h: 6.6.5.7. Dative -ki
t:
The ending -ki means ‘at, against.’ It marks the thing that causes a feeling, as in ‘angry at him’ or ‘afraid of the dog.’ It also marks some place words. For convenience, I call -ki the “dative” here. In the example just below, notice that -ki looks exactly like the short form of the ‘I heard it from others’ marker. It also looks like the question marker, although I don't show that here:
Banisteriopsis spp., Malpighiaceae.
(118) Rama kaman-bi-ki ino-ki xae sinat-ai. | ‘Even until today the ant-eater is angry at the jaguar.’
(119) ...no-n jawen kishi-bo taxkan-xon nexa-ti atipan-ke jiwi-ki. | ‘..holding (the dog) with its legs upwards we can tie its legs to a pole.’

h: 6.6.5.8. Chezative -iba
t:
The ending -iba means ‘to / at the place where X is / lives.’ It is like French chez ‘at the home of’ (linguists call it the chezative, from that French word):
(120) No-n onanya-bo-iba no-a isin-ai-tian bo-xon no-a | benxo-ma-[a]i, ja-bo-iba no-n bo-ai jawéki-nin kopi-ke-tian. | ‘When we get sick we are taken to our onanyas (healers) and they heal us, to them we take (a child) when something has caused her harm.’
The next example has both the ‘at someone's place’ ending -iba and the ‘at, against’ ending -ki:
(121) Jain-xon-ribi yoi-kan-ai, ja mawat-a-ki ka-[a]i reboki, | Para Inka Rios-iba, Inka-ki.... | ‘It is also said that the dead go to the upper Ucayali River, where the Para Inka God (lives), to the Inka....’

h: 6.6.5.9. Temporal -tian
t:
The ‘when’ ending -tian can be added to some nouns to talk about a stage of life, like ‘when I was a child’:
(122) Bake-tian nokon yoxaman e-a ese-katit-ai | ne-ská a-kin..... | ‘When I was a child my grandmother used to advise me in the following way...’
(123) Ja-ra teet-ai estudiante-tian-bi. | ‘S/he works since s/he was a student.’
But -tian is more often found in other places. On the pointing word ja ‘that,’ it makes the linking word jatian ‘then.’ On time words like moa ‘already’ or rama ‘now,’ it makes moatian ‘long time ago’ and ramatian ‘currently.’ It also goes on a sentence that has been turned into a noun, and then that part tells you when something happened. And -tian has taken on one more special job. It tells you that the next action is done by someone else (see 9.2).

h: 6.6.5.10. Other Types of Nominal Relationships
t:
Shipibo has no fixed ending for ‘from whom’ (source) or ‘about what’ (reference). If you ask speakers to make up sentences, you can get ones like (124a) and (125) below. But people more often say these things in other ways, as shown in (124b):
(124) Tsoma-iba-ke-a ninkat-a. | ‘I heard it from Tsoma.’ | Tsoma-n yoiy-ai ninkat-a. | ‘I heard it from Tsoma.’ (lit. I heard what Tsoma said.’)
(125) Nokon tee-kiri a-kin-ra e-n wisha-ke. | ‘I wrote (him) about my work.’
Shipibo has no special noun endings for these meanings: ‘part of’ (partitive), ‘how far / how much’ (extent, distance measure), ‘although’ (concessive), ‘including,’ ‘except,’ ‘besides,’ and ‘across.’ For the price or value of something, the word kopía is used. It probably comes from kopí reason / cause + -ya ‘having’:
(126) Rabé chonka soro kopía-ra e-n bi-ke. | ‘I bought it for 20 soles.’
(127) Westíora chopa kimisha chonka soro (kopía) iki. | ‘A cloth is worth 30 soles.’
For what something is made of and what it is a part of, see section 6.7.1. For the circumstances of an action, see 6.7.9.

h: Word Order in the Noun Phrase (word order inside a noun group)
t:
The words that describe a noun fall into two big groups. The groups differ in where the words go: before the main noun or after it. Describing nouns, owner words (‘my,’ ‘the man's’),
pointing words (‘this,’ ‘that’), amount words (except icha), and numbers above ‘two’ must always come before the main noun. The second group can come before or after the main noun. Moving them doesn't seem to change the meaning. This group includes describing words (adjectives), the amount word icha, the number ‘two’ and, less often, ‘one,’ the phrase meskó keská ‘different kinds of,’ and the ‘who/which…’ description parts. I will call the words in this second group “ambipositional modifiers” (describing words that can go on either side). When both orders are possible, I call that “doubling” (Hawkins 1983).

h: Nouns and Modifying Nouns (a noun describing another noun)
t:
As with compound words, a noun that describes another noun must come before it. These noun + noun pairs have different meanings. One of them is ‘a thing made of a material,’ like English a stone wall:
To say ‘not made of,’ you add -ma to the noun + noun pair:
To show that something is part of a whole, you can just put the two nouns side by side: [whole part]. Or you can use the owner pattern: [whole-n part], like English ‘the tree's branch.’ The first way seems to be more common:

h: Nouns and Possessive Modifiers (nouns with "my, your, his")
t:
To say who owns something, the ‘of’ ending goes on the owner. The thing owned gets no ending. It's like English the man's house: the 's goes on man, not on house. You can also use an owner pronoun like ‘my’ or ‘your’ (or a pronoun with the ‘of’ ending). Again, the thing owned gets no ending. The owner must always come before the thing owned:
(131) nato ainbo rabekan xobo | ‘these two women’s house’
(132) nokon tita-n chomo | ‘my mother’s jar’

h: Nouns and Demonstrative Modifiers (nouns with "this, that")
t:
The three pointing words nato ‘this,’ ja ‘that,’ and oa ‘that (far away)’ must always come before the noun. Look at these examples with oa, the one for things far away:
(133) Oa ainbo-ra nokon tita iki. | ‘That woman (over there) is my mother.’ | Ainbo oa-ra nokon tita iki. | ‘That woman (over there) is my mother.’ | Ainbo-ra oa nokon tita iki. | ‘The woman over there is my mother.’ (oa functions as locative)
In the (c) example above, oa comes after the noun, but it isn't really pointing at it. Here it means ‘over there,’ a place. It is not part of the doer phrase. How do we know? Look at the marker -ra, which shows how the speaker knows something. It always comes right after the first big part of the sentence. Here that first part is just the doer. So oa must be outside it. The next two examples show that the other two pointing words, for ‘that’ and ‘this,’ can't come after the noun either:
(None) Ja ainbo-ra nokon tita iki. /  ainbo ja-ra | ‘That woman is my mother.’
(None) Nato ainbo-ra nokon tita iki. /  ainbo nato-ra | ‘This woman is my mother.’

h: Nouns and Non-Numeral Quantifiers (nouns with "many, some, all")
t:
Jatíbi(ri) ‘all’ and jatíribi ‘some’ must always come before the noun. But icha ‘much, many’ can come before or after the noun, with no clear change in meaning:
(134) Jatíbi benbo-ra mecha i-kan-ai. | ‘All men are good fisher / hunters.’ | \Benbo jatíbi-ra mecha i-kan-ai. | ‘All men are good fisher / hunters.’
(135) Icha benbo-ra mecha i-kan-ai. | ‘Many men are good fisher / hunters.’ | Benbo icha-ra mecha i-kan-ai. | ‘Many men are good fisher / hunters.’
The next examples with icha come from real, everyday speech:
(136) Bo-xon oin-kan-a-ki ik-á iki, paranta pei-tii-bi | bina icha, pani pani-tin-res-a. | ‘When leaving they saw many wasps hanging on every plantain leaf.’
(137) Ja-tian-ki ik-á iki ja joni moa icha nete, ja bake | xontako bi-ma-kan-a-ki ik-á iki moa | westíora oxe. | ‘By then the man had already spent many days there, already a month had passed since he had married the girl.’

h: Nouns and Numerals (nouns with numbers)
t:
Only the numbers ‘one’ and ‘two’ are old Panoan words. The numbers above ‘two’ were borrowed from Quechua. Here is something interesting. Only ‘one’ and, even more, ‘two’ can go either before or after the noun. The numbers from Quechua must always come before it:
(138) Jawen bene-n-ra shino westíora rete-ke. | Jawen bene-n-ra westíora shino rete-ke. | ‘Her husband killed one capuchin monkey.’
(139) Jawen bene-n-ra shino rabé rete-ke. | Jawen bene-n-ra rabé shino rete-ke. | ‘Her husband killed two capuchin monkeys.’
(140) \Jawen bene-n-ra shino kimisha rete-ke. | Jawen bene-n-ra kimisha shino rete-ke. | ‘Her husband killed three capuchin monkeys.’
In Quechua, the number always comes before the noun. So SK may have borrowed two things from Quechua. It borrowed the numbers above two. And it may also have borrowed the rule that a number must come before its noun.

h: Nouns and Adjectives (nouns with describing words)
t:
Describing words (adjectives) can go before or after the noun they describe (from Valenzuela 2001a):
(141) joxo chitonti / chitonti joxo | ‘white pampanilla (Shipibo skirt)’
(142) Bo-ax nokó-kan-a iki ani manaman. | ‘After walking they arrived at a big mountain.’
(143) Jain ik-á iki manan keyá, tso-n-bi mapé-ti-ma. | ‘There stood a steep mountain that nobody could climb.’
Some linguists have said that putting the describing word after the noun makes it stronger, giving it extra weight (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:36). But my data don't support this. Look at the passage below, for example. There is no reason to think the size of the canoe is being stressed. The size of the canoe doesn't matter to the story, and the text never mentions it again. What might matter is the size of the person. The person who appears here is a child, the Inka’s son:
(144) Ka-xon oin-a-ki ik-á iki maxko-shoko joni, montária | anítama-shoko-tonin-ki, ja axa-n-a paen-ai-tian | tsaka tsaka-be-i jo-i. | ‘Once there he_{i} saw a little person_{j} in a small canoe, who approached him_{i} driving the fish he_{j} had previously poisoned with barbasco (k. plant poison).’
What happens when a noun has two describing words? People most often put one before the noun and one after it: describing word + noun + describing word. Linguists call this “simultaneous doubling” (Hawkins 1983). Take ‘dog’ with ‘fierce’ and ‘black’. The order in (145a) is the favorite: ‘black dog fierce’. Colors tend to come first. Other orders do show up too, as you can see in (145b–d):

h: Nouns and Adjectives (nouns with describing words)
t:
(145) E-n-ra oin-ke wiso ochíti siná. | ‘I saw a fierce black dog.’ | E-n-ra oin-ke siná ochíti wiso. | E-n-ra oin-ke ochíti wiso siná. | E-n-ra oin-ke wiso siná ochíti.
Does one describing word wrap around the other in the receiver part above? In English, “fierce black dog” could mean a black dog that is fierce. I have no evidence that Shipibo-Konibo builds it in layers like that. So in the (a) example I can't say whether it must be grouped as [[wiso [ochíti]] siná] or as [wiso [[ochíti] siná]]. Either grouping is possible as far as the data shows.
Three describing words with one noun almost never happens in real speech. But I asked speakers to try it anyway. They always put at least one describing word before the noun and at least one after it:
(146) Ani joxo ochíti siná | ‘a large, white, fierce dog’
(None) Nenké jiwi payo wiso | ‘a long, rotten, black log’

h: Coordination of Nominal Modifiers (joining describing words with "and")
t:
Two describing words can be joined with itan ‘and’. Then speakers prefer to put the whole “X and Y” group after the noun, not before it. So (147a) sounds better than (147b). The reason is probably simple: long, heavy groups of words like to come after the noun. You saw the same thing in (142) and (143), with ani manaman and manan keyá, tsonbi mapétima:
Number
(147) E-n-ra oin-ke ochíti wiso itan siná. | E-n-ra oin-ke wiso itan siná ochíti. | ‘I saw a fierce and black dog.’
The word itan can join other kinds of describing parts too, not just describing words.
Below, itan joins ochó merati (a verb turned into a describing part, ‘to find nearby’) with the amount word icha ‘many’:
(148) Moa-tian-ra i-káti-ai yoina-bo ochó-ma mera-ti itan icha. | ‘Long time ago, animals could be found nearby and in large numbers.’ | Lit. ‘Long time ago animals were (those) to find nearby and many.’

h: Nominal Modifiers and the Free Intensifier Kikin (describing words with "very" (kikin))
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has two endings that mean ‘very’: -yora and -shaman. It also has a separate word that means ‘very, extremely’: kikin. It most likely comes from Quechua (Quechua kiki ‘same’ + -n ‘his/her’). Kikin must always come before the describing word it strengthens, though not always right before it,
(149) Jain ik-á iki kikin ani chomo-bo. | ‘There there were extremely large jars.’
and it can be used together with one of the ‘very’ endings:
(150) ...ikaxbi bi-ma-pao-kani-ke rayá joni.... | kikin mecha-shaman.... | .’..but (our parents) made us marry a hard-working man....an extremely good fisher / hunter....’
Kikin can also strengthen longer describing parts, not just single words:
(151) ...ainbo-bo kikin [jawéki-a-ti onan-ma] | .’...women who don’t know at all how to do the things (proper of women).’
(152) Ja xebi-ana bi-kan-ai iki kikin
(None) [jawen tita-n rao-ak-á].... | ‘The girl whose clitoris they were going to extract had been very well adorned by her mother.’ (the SK sentence is active)
Kikin doesn't always sit right next to the word it strengthens. Here is why. The word kikin must come before the whole noun group. But, as we saw earlier, some describing words can come after the noun. So the noun can end up in between:
(153) Ka-xon oin-a-ronki ik-á iki kikin joni icha. | ‘Once arriving there, (s)he saw a large number of people.’

h: Nominal Modifiers and the Free Intensifier Kikin (describing words with "very" (kikin))
t:
(154) Jaa napomea-x-ki piko-t-a iki | kikin-shaman ainbo xontako metsá. | ‘From the center (of the lake) came out an extremely beautiful young woman.’
In the two examples just above, kikin goes with the amount word icha ‘many’ in (153) and with the describing word metsá ‘beautiful’ in (154). So in Shipibo-Konibo, words that belong together in meaning can be split apart in the sentence.
Here is one more example, with kikin used twice. The first kikin is separated from the word it strengthens by the place phrase ‘in the forest’. The second kikin comes after ponté, which is yet another separate word meaning ‘very’:
(155) Jato keshan-beiran-i jo-xon, jis-á-ronki ik-á iki | ja ainbo-ki kikin nii meran jawen shinan-'oma-bi | raka-t-a, ponté kikin pasná. | ‘When coming back from telling (her parents what had happened), he found the woman in the forest lying completely unconscious and extremely pale.’

h: Nouns and Circumstancial Modifiers (nouns with words for time and place)
t:
Describing parts that tell you about someone's features, like ‘with long hair’, can come before or after the noun. This is true even when the part itself is a noun plus a describing word, like boo nenké ‘hair long’:
Circumstance
(156) westíora joni boo nenké. | westíora boo nenké joni | ‘a man with long hair’
Negative circumstance
(157) westíora joni boo nenké-ma | westíora boo nenké-ma joni | ‘a man without long hair’

h: Nouns and Meskó Keská ‘Different Kinds of’ (nouns with "different kinds of")
t:
Here is another case of a word that can go on either side of the noun. It is meskó keská ‘different kinds of’. It is made from meskó ‘several’ and keská ‘like’:
(158) meskó keská isá / isá meskó keská | ‘different kinds of birds’

h: Nouns and Texkan ‘Large Bunch of’ (nouns with "a large bunch of")
t:
Texkan ‘large bunch of’ can also come before or after the noun:
(159) westíora texkan paranta / westíora paranta texkan | ‘a / one large bunch of plantain’

h: Nouns and Relative Clauses (nouns with "who/which" descriptions)
t:
A ‘who/which…’ description part (like “the peccary that father killed”) can come before or after the noun it describes:
Prenominal relative clause
(160) [Papa-n rete-ibat-a] jono-ra moa no-n keyo-ke. | ‘We already finished the collared-peccary father killed yesterday.’
Postnominal relative clause
(161) jono [(ja) papa-n rete-ibat-a]-ra moa no-n keyo-ke. | ‘We already finished the collared-peccary father killed yesterday.’
A ‘who/which…’ description part can also have its noun inside it; see section 10.2.

h: Comitative Postposition and Coordinating Conjunction: Betan (betan: "with" and "and")
t:
The word betan looks like another case of a word that can go on either side of a noun. You find [noun betan1] and [noun betan2 noun]. But really these are two different jobs. In the first, betan1 means ‘with’ (linguists call this a comitative postposition). In the second, betan2 means ‘and’, joining two nouns (a coordinating conjunction). Look at the next examples. In (162a) the person going is ‘father’. ‘Mother’ just goes along with him:
(162) Papa-ra wai-nko ka-[a]i tita betan | ‘Father goes to the chacra with mother.’
You can check this with a question. (162b) asks who is going to the chacra, and (162c) gives the right answer, ‘Father’:
(162) –Tso-a-ki wai-nko ka-[a]i? | ‘Who is going to the chacra?’
(None) –Papa. | ‘Father.’
(162d) asks about the ‘with’ part instead, ‘With whom?’, and the answer is in (162e):
(None) Tso-bé-ki ka-[a]i papa wai-nko? | ‘With whom is father going to the chacra?’
(None) Tita betan. | ‘With mother.’
Now compare (162 a-e) with (163 a-c), and you can see the two jobs of betan. In (163 a) the people going are ‘father and mother’ together. How do we know? Look at -ra, a marker that shows how the speaker knows something. It comes after the whole group ‘father and mother’. Also, any case ending goes on the end of the whole group. So with the doer marker it would be papa betan tita-n [[father and mother]-ERG (the doer marker)]:

h: Comitative Postposition and Coordinating Conjunction: Betan (betan: "with" and "and")
t:
(163) –Papa betan tita-ra wai-nko ka[a]i. | ‘Father and mother go to the chacra.’
Notice that when you ask who is going, the question word takes the plural ending -bo:
(163) –Tso-a-bo-ki ka-[a]i wai-nko? | ‘Who are going to the chacra?’ | –Papa betan tita. | ‘Father and mother.’
When betan means ‘and’, it sits between two nouns. These two nouns are almost always the same kind of thing. Both are people, for example, or both are not alive:
(164) Jawe-tian-bi no-n pi-osma iki | [xae betan ino]. | ‘We never eat either anteater or jaguar meat.’
(165) \[Papa betan ochíti]-ra yomera-i ka-[a]i | ‘Father and the dog are going hunting.’
When betan means ‘with’, it links two living beings. One of them is more involved in what is happening than the other.
(166) Tita-ra ka-[a]i papa betan /ochíti betan / \rario betan / rario-ya | ‘Mother is going with father / with the dog / with the radio.’
The ‘with’ betan can also mean ‘against’:
(167) Jain oa ainbo-bo no-a betan pota-kas-i-bo, | no-a bibo shiro bewakan ninká-ma-i-bo. | ‘There were the women who wanted to fight against us provoking us with their bibo shiro songs.’
Other Panoan languages (the language family of Shipibo-Konibo) have a related word that means ‘with’. Examples are Kashibo-Kakataibo, Yaminawa, Chakobo, and Matses. So I conclude that in Shipibo-Konibo, betan first meant ‘with’. Later it also came to mean ‘and’, but it kept its old ‘with’ meaning too. (Compare Stassen’s 2000 split between “AND-languages” and “WITH-languages”.)²⁶

h: Nominal Coordination (joining nouns with "and")
t:
As we saw above, betan ‘and’ almost always joins two nouns of the same kind, like two people or two things. The next sentence, from a story, is an exception. The two things joined are not the same kind. The sentence describes a moment in the Ani Xeati ceremony. This is a coming-of-age celebration for a girl. Her father shows his daughter to his guests. He also shows the animal he raised for the party:
(168) Jain-xon pishta ibo-n jawen bake xontako betan senen | yoina piko-ai. | ‘Then, the owner of the fiesta would present (to his guests) his daughter and the grown animal (he had raised for the occasion).’
The word betan is also related to the number ‘two’, which has been rebuilt for the older language as \raβïta (Shell 1975:168). The change probably went from ‘with’ to ‘two’, not the other way. The piece ra- is a beginning piece for body parts. It comes from the noun yora ‘body’ (or ‘person’ in other Panoan languages). So ra-beta meant ‘with body / person’, and that became ‘two’.
The girl is the main figure of the Ani Xeati ceremony. Its high point is the xebiana tsekati, the cutting of the girl's clitoris. But the animal raised for the party is the main figure of a smaller ceremony inside it. That ceremony is called yoina reteti ‘Animal Sacrifice.’

h: Nominal Coordination (joining nouns with "and")
t:
When you list several things, you can put the word jainoax ‘and’ just before the last one, as in English “X, Y, and Z”:
(169) Awá Mai a-kan-ai meráya-nin-ki jawen nishi paen meran | oin-a iki meskó yoina-bo: nato jono, awá, yawa, ano, | yawish, chaxo, jainoax mari. | ‘The great shaman called Awá Mai saw different animals during his ayahuasca vision: collared peccaries, tapirs, white-lipped peccaries, pacas, armadillos, deers, and agoutis.’
For more about jainoax, see 11.1.
You can also join nouns by simply putting them one after another, with no ‘and’ at all:
(170) Bo-xon oin-kan-a ik-á iki jatíbi pi-ti jawéki-bo: | nato wame, xawe, kabóri, sapen. | ‘When they arrived they saw all kinds of edible animals: paiche fish, charapa turtle, taricaya turtle, (and) manatee.’
Speakers can also use the Spanish word for ‘and’, “y.”
To say ‘or’ between nouns, Shipibo-Konibo uses iamax. Here it is in a ‘neither… nor’ sentence:
(171) Ja jawe-tian-bi joxo nawa-baon iamax oa ani | joni-baon-bi no-a bichin-ti atipan-yama-ke. | ‘Neither the mestizos nor any other powerful people can ever take it (i.e., our knowledge to make designs) away from us.’
Speakers can also use the Spanish word for ‘or’, “o.”

h: Recombinations of Different Modifier Types (mixing different kinds of describers)
t:
When several kinds of describing words come before a noun, they go in a fixed order. First come pointing words like ‘this’. Then come ‘my / your’ words. Then numbers that come before the noun. Then describing words that come before the noun. (But see below for moatian, which can act as a describing word and breaks this rule.)
(172) nato nokon rabé maxko bake-bo | ‘these two little children of mine’ | Nato rabé nokon....
As we saw earlier, describing words and some numbers can also come after the noun.
The word moatian normally means ‘long ago’. But it can also be a describing word meaning ‘old, traditional.’ When moatian is used with a ‘my / our’ word, both orders are possible: ‘our old customs’ and ‘old our customs’:
(173) Jatíbi-tian e-n shinan-ai no-n moatian axé-bo moa | keyo-t-a. Icha a-kin e-n yoiy-ai moatian no-n | axé-bo jakiribi no-n bená a-ti atipan-ke. | ‘Sometimes I think that our traditional customs have disappeared already. Many times I say that we could renew our traditional customs again.’
THE VERB AND THE VERB PHRASE:

h: The Verb (the action word)
t:
A Shipibo-Konibo verb is built from a bare verb plus at least one ending at the end. It can also carry many other endings. Bare verbs can be one syllable (beat) long, like pi- ‘eat’, or two, like koko- ‘eat sweet fruit.’ A very long one is onitsa- ‘become desperate, agitated.’¹ A couple of verbs change into a totally different word depending on how many people do the action, a bit like English go / went. So jo- means ‘come (one person)’, but be- means ‘come (more than one) / bring’. And ka- means ‘go (one person)’, but bo- means ‘go (more than one) / take.’ Verbs can also be joined to other words, or doubled. Doubling a verb shows that the action goes on, happens again and again, or is very strong (see 4.6). Most bare verbs are already either intransitive verbs or transitive verbs. To switch from one type to the other, you need to add a special ending.
Besides the bare verb, a Shipibo-Konibo verb can carry these pieces: beginning pieces made from body parts; endings that change how many people the verb involves; -kas ‘want to’; -yama ‘not’; a group of endings for direction and for adverb-like meanings; -pao ‘usually’; tense
Today, onitsa- can't be split into smaller pieces. But it may come from onis ‘sad’. A related verb is onitsapi- ‘suffer’, though I haven't been able to explain the piece -pi. As Phil Young pointed out to me (p.c.), /pi/ is also the verb ‘eat’. So maybe ‘suffer’ first meant ‘go without eating’?

h: The Verb (the action word)
t:
endings; small add-on pieces that can move around; the plural ending -kan; the ‘watch out, or else’ ending -na; and endings at the very end that show the aspect and whether you're stating, asking or ordering. Some of these can show up more than once in the same verb: the endings that change how many people are involved, the direction and adverb-like endings, the movable add-on pieces, and the plural. Below is the order in which all these pieces appear. Keep three things in mind. First, they never all appear at once. Second, the order can sometimes change a bit, and that changes the meaning slightly. Third, where I show only two or three slots for a type, there could be more, but I haven't heard more in natural speech. The direction and adverb-like endings are written ADV. The pieces every verb must have are underlined:
(1) 
In the next sentence, the bare verb has a body-part beginning piece in front of it, and many endings after it. (For a verb with two body-part beginning pieces, see ex. (105) in Chapter 8.)
(2) Nokon ochíti-ra e-a | ta-níni-nan-bain-kean-wan-kan-ke. | ‘They almost pulled my dog by the foot while passing earlier today to my detriment.’
The sentence above has three people or things in it. There is the doer (‘they’), the receiver (‘my dog’), and an extra person affected by the action (‘me’, to my detriment). Because the doer is ‘they’, the verb shows it with the plural ending -kan. But the other two must appear as separate words outside the verb. So Shipibo-Konibo verbs have lots of endings, but they don't show who does what to whom. The only partial exception is the plural -kan. Some languages, called polysynthetic, pack all the people into the verb itself. Shipibo-Konibo does not, so it fails one of the main tests for being that kind of language.

h: The Verb (the action word)
t: In Shipibo-Konibo, nouns, describing words and some other words can also act as the main verb of a sentence. You just add verb endings straight onto them. I showed this in 5.4.1, in the part on Predicative Function.

h: The Polyfunctional Auxiliaries Ik- and Ak- (the helper verbs ik- ("be/do") and ak- ("do to"))
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has two very general verbs that can stand in for others. Linguists call them “auxiliaries.” One is the intransitive verb ik- ‘be, do, say’. The other is the transitive verb ak- ‘do, make, tell.’ Almost any verb can be replaced by ik- or ak-. The exceptions are bi- ‘get,’ the pairs ‘come / bring’ and ‘go / carry,’ and the verbs for ‘there is’ and ‘there isn't’. (See Short Answers to Polar Questions in 8.5.)
These two general verbs are also used with short exclamations and sound words to make new verbs (see 8.2.7). The verb ak- can also be added to nouns, describing words and some other words to turn them into verbs. Rarely, it is added to an intransitive verb to make it a transitive verb. When that happens, -ak is often pronounced as part of the word before it. Still, there are
things you can do with them that show they are really two separate words, such as joining with ‘and’ or doubling. Look at the examples below. Two describing words are joined by itan ‘and’. Then ak- comes only once, after the second one, like English “make [long and wide]”:
(3) E-n-ra xobo nenké a-ke. | ‘I made the house long(er).’ | E-n-ra xobo nenké itan naxbá a-ke. | ‘I made the house long(er) and wide(r).’

h: The Polyfunctional Auxiliaries Ik- and Ak- (the helper verbs ik- ("be/do") and ak- ("do to"))
t:
So a describing word plus -ak is a kind of loosely joined double word (see also 16.2.5). Notice also that nenké ‘long’ and naxbá ‘wide’ can themselves be verbs meaning ‘become long’ and ‘become wide’. Nouns, describing words and some other words in Shipibo-Konibo can do this. Because of that, you never need to add ik- to them to make a verb.
Both ik- and ak- also show up in some verb expressions made of more than one word, as you will see in 7.12. Finally, the word iki ‘is’ most probably comes from ik-

h: Prefixes (beginning pieces on verbs)
t:
Short forms of nouns, usually body parts, can be placed at the front of a verb. I already listed these “beginning pieces” and the nouns they come from in 6.2.6. Sometimes the verb itself is also shortened (for example, in sentence (3) in Chapter 4).
Adding one of these beginning pieces almost never changes how many people the verb needs. It just adds a ‘where’ meaning: on the foot, on the hand, and so on. One exception: the body-part piece me(e)- ‘hand’ can be a verb all by itself, meaning ‘touch, hit with the hand’ (cf. ex. 29). You saw ta-, from tae ‘foot’, in (2). There is more on verbs with body-part beginning pieces in 8.2.6.

h: Valence-Changing Derivations (endings that add or remove a person from a verb)
t: Some endings change how many main people a verb needs. Some add a person. These are the ‘make someone do it’ endings -ma, -n, -a, and a(k)-. They also include the endings that bring in an extra person (for whom / against whom / with whom): -xon, -(V)naan ~ (V)n and -ki(i)n. Other endings take a person away. These are -t (the ‘to yourself’ ending) and -(ana)nan ~ -anan (the ‘to each other’ ending).

h: Causativizers ("make someone do it" endings)
t:
Most ‘make someone do it’ verbs in Shipibo-Konibo are built from an ordinary verb by adding an ending. Start with a plain verb, like ‘sleep’. Add -ma, -n, or -a, and a new doer comes in: the person who makes it happen. The people already in the sentence then shift roles. The person who makes it happen always gets the doer marker (ERG). The person made to do it, and anyone affected, appear in the plain form (ABS). So a Shipibo-Konibo sentence can have more than one noun in the plain form.
The most common ‘make someone do it’ ending is -ma. It works with every kind of verb. -Ma has a very broad meaning. It can mean anything from
forcing or persuading someone, to letting, helping or making it easy for someone to do something. -Ma can be added after any ‘make someone do it’ ending, even after another -ma. Look at these ‘which…’ description parts with the verb maxkat- ~ maxká- ‘lack’. In (4) it is plain ‘lack’. In (5) -ma turns it into ‘let lack’:
(4) [no-n jema maxkat-a] jawéki-bo | ‘the things our village lacks’
(5) [no-a jawe-bi maxká-ma-yama-[a]i] joni. | ‘a man who provides for us,’ lit. ‘a man who does not let us lack anything.’
A second ‘make someone do it’ ending, -n, only works with a small, fixed group of intransitive verbs (and with nouns, as shown in section 6.4.1).
