For example, oxa- ‘sleep’ becomes oxa-n- ‘put to sleep.’ tipi- ‘lie (several things or animals of the same kind)’ becomes tepi-n- ‘lay (several things or animals of the same kind).’ And pani- ‘hang’ (by itself) becomes pani-n- ‘hang (something).’ Here is oxa- ‘sleep’ without and with -n:

h: Causativizers ("make someone do it" endings)
t:
(6) Bake-ra oxa-[a]i. | ‘The child is sleeping.’
(7) Yabi-n-ra bake oxa-n-ke. | ‘Yabi put the child to sleep.’
Some bare verbs about body position or moving into a position (‘sit’, ‘lie’) are neither intransitive nor transitive verbs on their own. They take -n to mean ‘put someone in that position’, or the ‘to yourself’ ending -t to mean ‘get into that position yourself’. I introduced this in 4.3. Look at the next example
showing the ‘make someone do it’ forms of yaka-t ‘sit’ and raka-t- ‘lie’. (The ending -n, glossed as TRNZ, is underlined below.)
(8) ...joni mawá-ke-tian miin-kati-kan-ai yoxan-baon ak-á | maweta-nin, ponté na-yása-n-res-kin | maweta meran, raka-n-a-ma. | .’..when a person died (s)he was buried in a big jar which the elderly women had made, the dead was seated straight inside the big jar, (s)he was not laid.’
We can't tell where -ma and -n came from. But the third ‘make someone do it’ ending, -a, clearly comes from the general verb ak- ‘do, make’, which wore down into an ending over time:
(9) ...nokon tita-n e-a axe-a iki koton-a-ti.... | .’...my mother taught me how to manufacture the blouse....’
Nouns, describing words, words for time, place or manner, and some other words can also join with ak- ‘do, make’. Together they work like one verb meaning ‘make something be that way’. In (10), ani a- ‘big make’ means ‘raise (a child)’:

h: Causativizers ("make someone do it" endings)
t:
(10) Pikó-ke-tian-bi no-a ani a-kan-ai.... | ‘Since (we) are born (our parents) raise us.....’
In example (11), the ending -ma is added after such a joined verb:
(11) E-n-ra jato e-a mechá a-ma-yama-[a]i. | ‘I will not let them get me wet.’
Which 'make someone do it' ending Shipibo uses depends on the meaning. The key question is how much the person being made to act does on their own. If that person starts the action by their own power, Shipibo uses -ma. So -ma is for indirect causing: you get someone to do something, and they do it themselves. The other 'make someone do it' endings are for more direct causing. There the person being acted on does little by themselves.
Because there are several of these endings, speakers can use them to tell meanings apart. One base word may have several meanings, and each ending can pick out one of them. Or a base word with only one meaning can give several different transitive verbs. Look at these verbs made from the base word bake ‘child, become a child, behave like a child:’

h: Applicatives (endings that bring in an extra person)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has three endings that bring an extra person into the action (linguists call these applicatives). The first is -xon. It means 'for someone's benefit'. On an intransitive verb it can also mean 'to someone's harm'. The second is -ki(i)n, which means 'together with someone'. The third is -(V)naan ~ (V)n, which means 'to someone's harm'. Some of these endings have a short form and a long form. Which one you use depends on the length of the verb, counted in small beats of sound (linguists call them moras). As a rule, verbs with an even number of beats take the short forms -anan and -kin. Verbs with an odd number take the long forms -ananan and -kiin. Unlike the 'for someone' ending and the 'together with' ending, which can go on both intransitive verbs and transitive verbs,
the 'to someone's harm' ending goes only on transitive verbs. An intransitive verb with -xon can mean either 'for someone's benefit' or 'to someone's harm'. The situation tells you which one is meant:
(13) Nokon bene-n-ra moa e-a ka-xon-ke. (\-naan) | ‘My husband left already to my benefit / to my detriment.’ (Valenzuela 1999:357)
In the next sentence, both the 'for someone' ending and the 'to someone's harm' ending appear on a transitive verb, ‘abandon’:
(14) Nokon bene-n-ra e-a pota-xon-ke / pota-naan-ke. | ‘My husband abandoned me to my benefit / to my detriment.’ (Valenzuela 1999:357)

h: Applicatives (endings that bring in an extra person)
t:
Example (15) shows the 'together with' ending -kin added to an intransitive verb, ‘enter’:
(15) E-n-ra nokon bake bachi-n jiki-kin-ai. | ‘I am going into the mosquito net with my child.’
A 'make someone do it' ending and an ending that brings in an extra person can both appear on the same verb. In (16) and (17), look for two endings in a row right after the bare verb:
(16) E-n-ra mi-n bake mi-a nonti a-ma-xon-ke. | ‘On your behalf I made your son construct a canoe.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
(17) Wetsa joni-ra mi-a bi-ma-nan-kan-na-ke. | ‘Be careful she could be given in matrimony to another man to your detriment.’
Usually the 'make someone do it' ending -ma comes first, before the ending that brings in an extra person. But the order can also be the other way around. It depends on the meaning: which ending applies to which part of the action. Compare (18), where -ma comes first, with (19), where it comes last:
(18) Rona-n-ra Biri bake rao xea-ma-kin-ke. | ‘Rona helped Biri to give medicine to the child.’
(19) E-n-ra nokon bene xea-kin-ma-ke. | ‘I made him drink with my husband.’

h: The Middle Marker -T (the -t ending (doing something to yourself))
t:
A transitive verb can become an intransitive verb by adding the ending -t. The one person left can be either someone who acts or someone the action happens to. In almost every case, -t gives one of three meanings. It can mean doing something to yourself ('I comb myself'). It can mean something happens by itself ('the canoe straightens'). Or it can mean something is done to you by someone who is not mentioned ('I was found') (Valenzuela 1997; see also 18.1). One exception is noko-t- [meet:MID] ‘arrive.’ In the example glosses this ending is labelled MID (linguists call it the middle marker).
The ending -t has several different forms. Most base words with two syllables that end in a vowel take -t. But they may also take -kaa(t). Sometimes another ending that starts with a consonant comes after -t. Then the /-t/ drops out, and the vowel before it gets the stress instead. With some base words, -t also changes the last vowel of the word: the vowel sounds different, or becomes longer. Base words that end in /n/ lose the /n/ and take -mee(t). Other forms of -t are -(k)ee(t), -(k)oo(t) and -(k)ii(t). Now look at (20), which has no -t. There the word ja ‘him’ (in the plain form, ABS) cannot mean Tsoma himself. So the sentence cannot mean ‘Tsoma poked himself.’

h: The Middle Marker -T (the -t ending (doing something to yourself))
t:
(20) Tsoma-n-ra ja chachi-ke. | ‘Tsoma_{i} poked him_{j} (with an arrow, knife, something pointed).’
Now compare (21). Here the -t ending is added, and the meaning becomes 'to yourself':
(21) Ja-ra chachí-ke. | ‘He poked himself.’
In the examples below, -t gives a different meaning. Either something happens by itself, or it is done by someone who is not mentioned. The transitive verbs used are ponte- ‘straighten something’ and noko- ‘find:’
(22) Nonti bari-n yosho a-ibat-a-ra moa ponte-t-ai. | ‘The canoe that got warped by the sun is becoming straight (by itself) already.’²
(23) Nato bake-n tae-ra moa ja-n-bi-x ponte-t-ai. | ‘This child’s foot is becoming straight by itself already.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:331)
(24) Kachio jabat-i ka-[a]x-bi-ra e-a noko-kaa-ke. | ‘I hid in the forest, but I was found (by others).’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Example (24) above uses noko-kaa-. But noko- ‘find’ also has another intransitive form, noko-t- ~ nokó-. This form means ‘arrive.’ The next example was first given in Chapter 6 as (142):
(25) Bo-ax nokó-kan-a iki ani manaman. | ‘After walking they arrived at a big mountain.’
A small canoe bent by the heat of the sun can become straight again by itself if it is left in the shade for a while.

h: Reciprocal (doing something to each other)
t:
To say people do something to each other ("they comb each other"), Shipibo adds an ending to the verb. The ending has two forms, -anan and -(ana)nan. Which one you use depends on the length of the verb: count its syllables (beats). An even number gets -anan; an odd number gets -(ana)nan. This ending works like -t (the "to yourself" ending). Once people act on each other, there is no separate receiver anymore. So the doers lose the doer marker and appear in the plain form. Below, the verb boex- ‘comb’ appears three ways: combing someone else (26), combing yourself (27), and combing each other (28).
(26) E-n-ra bake boex-ai. | ‘I comb the child.’
(27) E-a-ra boexet-ai. | ‘I comb myself.’
(28) Oa rabé-ra boexeanan-ai. | ‘Those two comb each other.’
A 'to each other' sentence can also have just one doer, plus another person added with betan 'with'. Then it means 'I and that person did it to each other'. In the example below, the doer ea ‘I’ is left out:
(29) Jawe-tian-bi nokon bene betan mee-kanan-yosma | i-xon oin-a.... | ‘It was never seen that my husband and I hit each other...’ Lit. ‘It was never seen that I hit with my husband in a reciprocal way.....’
But a 'to each other' sentence may also have just one doer, with nobody else named at all. In that case the speaker knows the other person did the same thing back, or will do it later. That other person is simply left out. Something similar has been described for the related language Kashinawa, where it is called ‘response-reciprocal’ (Camargo, ms.):

h: Reciprocal (doing something to each other)
t:
(30) E-a-ra pota-anan-ke. | ‘I abandoned someone who also abandoned me.’
The actions in a 'to each other' sentence do not have to happen at the same time. They also do not have to be exactly the same action. And the person who acts back may not be the same one who received the first action.
In Shipibo-Konibo, one 'to each other' verb has become a word of its own. bi-ananan- [get / receive-REC] literally means 'receive each other'. It is now the normal verb for ‘get married:’
(31) Jain onan-ma-i ka-i xontako moa biananan-a. | ‘There it will be made public that the young girl has already gotten married.’
The 'to each other' ending can also go on intransitive verbs that have a second person attached with a special marker. Compare (32), ‘I feel embarrassed at you’, with (33), ‘They feel embarrassed at each other’:
(32) E-a-ra mi-on rabin-ai. | ‘I feel embarrassed at you.’
(33) Ja-bo-ra rabin-anan-kan-ai. | ‘They feel embarrassed at each other.’
When exactly two people do something to each other, the verb can take the ending -bekon. It means 'the two of them'. In the example below, -bekon appears together with the plural ending. So it works as a more exact kind of plural: 'more than one, namely two'. The plural ending -kan normally comes after the 'to each other' ending. But there are cases with the reverse order, as in (34),

h: Reciprocal (doing something to each other)
t:
(34) Ja-ska-raino-a-xonki ino betan xae-ki | rawi-kanan-bekon-a iki. | ‘Since this time, the jaguar and the anteater are enemies.’
and cases where -kan appears twice in the same verb, once before and once after the 'to each other' ending:
(35) Ja-bo-ra nonti yoká-kanan-kan-ai. | ‘They asked each other for the canoe.’
The 'want to' ending -kas can also partly turn a transitive verb into an intransitive verb. It comes after the endings that add or remove people, but before the 'not' ending -yama, if there is one. Section 8.2.8 on Desiderative Clauses explains this.

h: Deictive-Directive Markers: Core Verb Serialization (endings showing direction of movement)
t:
Some endings on Shipibo verbs look just like separate verbs. One is the 'not' ending -yama. It has the same form as the verb meaning 'there is not'. There are a few other word pieces that attach to a verb in the same way and are
the same as, or similar to, separate verbs with related meanings. These pieces tell you about direction: which way the action is going.

h: ‘Going Up’ and ‘Going Down’ (going up and going down (the river))
t:
First, look at three separate verbs: ina(t)- ‘go up (the river),’ pake-t- ‘go down (the river),’ and pake- ‘drop, cause to fall.’ The verb pake-t- ‘go down (the river)’ is made from pake- ‘cause to fall’ by adding the -t ending, which turns it into an intransitive verb.
When they are added to the end of another verb, -ina(t) and -paket mean what you would expect: ‘going up (the river)’ and ‘going down (the river),’ respectively. But -pake means something different. It shows that the action is done to things one by one (linguists call this distributive). Each piece also fits only certain verbs. -paket goes only on intransitive verbs. pake- goes only on transitive verbs. -ina(t) ‘going up (the river)’ goes on both kinds. The table below sums up these pieces. It shows each one as a separate first verb (Verb 1, or V1) and as a second verb attached to another one (Verb 2, or V2):
Only a small number of verbs can act as these attached second verbs (V2s). They are pronounced as one word together with the first verb (V1), and the main stress falls on the V1. Although there are some reasons to treat
It is not clear how the meaning of pake- ‘cause to fall’ is connected to the ‘one by one’ meaning of -pake.

h: ‘Going Up’ and ‘Going Down’ (going up and going down (the river))
t:
these V1-V2 pairs as single compound words, I prefer another view. I see them as two verbs placed side by side and tightly joined (linguists call this nuclear verb serialization). I have two reasons. First, only a small, fixed set of verbs can be a V2. Second, each V2 only fits a V1 of the right type (vis à vis the V1): an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. Both features are also found in looser chains of verbs (see 7.14 and 15.3.1). Look at the following examples:
-ina(t) ‘up (the river)’
(36) Jainoa-xa no-a jo jó-ina-ke, | jawé-bi wino-t-a-ma. | ‘From there we came up the river without any problem.’
(37) Sani-ra bewa-inat-ai. | ‘Sani is going up the river singing.’
(38) Sani-n-ra jawen bake moa-tian i-káti-ai jawéki-bo | yoi-[i]nat-ai. | ‘Sani tells his son old stories going up the river.’
In natural speech, I never heard -inat on an intransitive verb where nobody really acts, like 'sleep'. But one speaker I worked with offered the form oxa-inat- [sleep-going.up]. It describes someone sleeping in a canoe while another person rows up the river.
The next example does two things. First, it shows ina(t)- used as a separate verb. Second, it shows -paket ‘going down the river’ attached to another verb, as a V2.
ina(t)- ‘go up (the river)’ and -paket ‘going down (the river)’

h: ‘Going Up’ and ‘Going Down’ (going up and going down (the river))
t:
(39) Ja nonti-n wetsa ka-a iki inat-i, | wetsa ka-a iki toxbá-paket-i. | ‘With the canoes one (of the brothers) went up the river, while the second one floated down the river.’
The next examples show pake- as a separate verb (see also ex. (43) in Chapter 4). They also show -pake as the 'one by one' marker:
pake- ‘cause to fall’
(40) Ja-tian-ki Yoashi-kon Inka-n ani niweaba | pake-a iki, ja chii noka-a-kas-kin. | ‘Then the Stingy Inka caused a big strong wind trying to extinguish the fire.’
-pake distributive ‘one by one’ (ex. (41) was previously given in Chapter 4 as ex. (44); see also ex. (45) in that chapter)
(41) ...Bai Shita-n-ki jato yatan-xon jene
(None) rete-ma-pake-a iki. | ‘...the Bai Shita held them and drowned them one by one (lit. held them and caused the flowing water to kill (them) one by one).’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)
(42) Yometso-nin-ra jato koríki meni-pake-ke. | ‘The thief distributed the money among his fellows.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:314)
(43) Ja-ská-ke-tian-ki choro-pake-ni-ke.... | In that way (the sloth woman) disentangled (the thread)....

h: ‘Going’ and ‘Coming’ (going and coming)
t:
Some other movement verbs that always go in a set direction also show up in this kind of verb combination. They are probably slowly turning into verb endings. Look at the examples with -kawan. Its pieces look like ka-wan [go-earlier today past]. But notice that in these sentences the two actions happen right one after the other. So the ‘earlier today’ past meaning doesn’t seem to fit here:
-kawan ‘going, moving away’
(44) Ja kena-a jo-xon jawen awin bachi merano-a-x | pikó-kawan-xon ikot-a iki. | ‘When the one who had been called arrived, he came out of the mosquito net and embraced his wife.’
(45) “Mi-n bene-n-ra e-a paran-a iki”, nokon ini ainbo | yoiy-a iki. Bechiake-kawan-xon nokon rayos yoiy-a iki: | “Mi-n-ra e-a paran-a iki” i-xon rishki-a iki westíora jiwi-n. | ‘“Your husband lied to me,” she told my niece. Then turning towards the man she told my son-in-law (i.e., my niece’s husband): “You lied to me;” and hit him with a pole.’
Two more verbs can also join onto another verb in this way: -be ‘coming’ and -bo ‘going;’ They don’t stand as separate words here. They lean on the verb in front of them. So far I have only found them on transitive verbs. The next example was first given as (144) in Chapter 6:
(46) Ka-xon oin-a-ki ik-á iki maxko-shoko joni, montária | anítama-shoko-tonin-ki, ja axa-n-a pae-n-ai-tian | tsaka tsaka-be-i jo-i. | ‘Once there he_{i} saw a little person_{j} in a small canoe, who approached him_{i} driving the fish he_{j} had previously poisoned with barbasco (k. plant poison).’

h: ‘Going’ and ‘Coming’ (going and coming)
t: (47) No-n oin-patan-bo-a-bi r-iki, no-n iskóra-nko-bo | jainoax no-n jema-nko-bo no-n joi-n-bi-ribi-kaya | meskó keská jawéki-bo onan-ti yama yama-bi-res. | ‘We see continuously that neither in our schools nor in our villages in general are there varied pedagogical materials in our language.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:5).

h: Andatives and Venitives (endings meaning "on the way there" or "on the way back")
t: SK has two endings that mean ‘coming here’ and two that mean ‘going away’ (linguists call them venitives and andatives). In form and in meaning, they are close to the verbs jo- / be- ‘come, bring’ and ka- / bo- ‘go, carry;’ They also follow the same rules as those verbs. Which form you use depends on how many people are doing it, and on whether the verb has a receiver (see 4.5).

h: The Venitives -Kiran / -Beiran (-kiran / -beiran: "on the way here")
t:
The ‘coming’ ending has two forms. Use -kiran with an intransitive verb and a single doer. Use -beiran with a transitive verb, or when there is more than one doer (with either kind of verb). Mostly, these endings show movement toward a central point, the ‘here’ of the speaker or the story. But they can also show movement in time, or movement with no clear ‘here’. They can even show someone entering a state of body or mind. The following examples show when to use -kiran and when to use -beiran:
singular, intransitive
(48) westíora ainbo yamé merano-a-x pikó-kiran-xon | nokon ini ainbo bachin-a iki. | ‘…a woman came out from the darkness and pulled my niece by the hair.’
plural, intransitive (see also ex. (43) in Chapter 8)
(49) Ja beshé-a-ke-tian ainbo-bo tsamá-beiran-xon xoi-ti | bo-kan-ai. | ‘After (the meat) had been cut into pieces, the women got together and took the meat to roast.’
singular, transitive
(50) Ja-ská-xon ja koko-ai-tian-ronki ik-ai o-no-a-x-ki | rewe a-beiran-i jo-á iki awá-isi. | ‘While they were eating (guayaba), a tapir came playing the flute.’
(51) Jato keshan-beiran-i jo-xon, jis-á-ronki ik-á iki | ja ainbo-ki kikin nii meran jawen shinan-'oma-bi | raka-t-a, ponté kikin pasná. | ‘When coming back from telling (her parents what had happened), he found the woman in the forest lying completely unconscious and extremely pale.’

h: The Venitives -Kiran / -Beiran (-kiran / -beiran: "on the way here")
t:
plural, transitive
(52) Jato-ronki keshan-beiran-kan-ke. | ‘S/he said that they told them and came.’
In the next examples, the ‘coming’ ending shows something else. In (53) it shows someone entering a physical state. In (54) it shows movement through time:
(53) Kimisha-a-kin xea-[a]x-ronki ik-á iki jawen yora | saki ik-i.............pasná-kiran-i. | ‘After drinking (the medicine) three times, (she) began to tremble and turned pale.’
(54) Ja kené iki no-n moa-tian yoxan-baon no-a | yoi yoi-beiran-kan-a. | ‘These designs were passed on to us by our foremothers.’
You can find an example where -beiran shows someone entering an emotional state in (72).

h: The Andatives -Kain / -Bain (-kain / -bain: "on the way there")
t:
The ‘going away’ endings -kain and -bain follow the same rules as the ‘coming’ endings. -kain is used with an intransitive verb and a single doer. -bain is used with a transitive verb, or when there is more than one doer.
singular, intransitive
(55) Pake-t-ax-ki chi-chá-yaka-kain-a iki. | ‘When she fell to the ground, she fell on her buttocks.’
The next sentence was first given in Chapter 5 as (40b). It shows that -kain can also mean entering a state, here falling asleep:
(56) E-a-ra meran-kain-ke. | ‘I fell asleep.’
plural, intransitive
(57) Ja joni-n mishki mishki-kin oin-a-ki ik-á iki, | jawen bimi maan-ke-tian pi-ax-ki nato sipan, | noya-bain-katit-i. | ‘While fishing with hook, the man saw that the fruits fell down from the tree and after eating them the pilchards flew away.’
singular, transitive
(58) Ka-ax-ronki noko-t-a iki iaman; nokó-xon-ki | ak-á iki ian kexá bena bena-bain-kin. | ‘Walking, she arrived to the lake; once there she went searching along the shore.’
plural, transitive
(59) Neno-ra bena-bain-kan-ke. | ‘They searched here and left.’
For another example of -bain on a transitive verb with more than one doer, see ex. (31) in Chapter 4.
Very often, the ‘coming’ and ‘going away’ endings don’t just add detail to the action of the verb they are on. Instead, they add a separate action that happens next:

h: The Andatives -Kain / -Bain (-kain / -bain: "on the way there")
t:
(60) Xoi pi-á pekáo-ronki ka-a iki ainbo | metsá-yon-kain-i. | ‘After eating, the woman made herself beautiful (designing her body with genipa) and left.’
In the example above, the ‘going away’ ending that adds the next action appears together with the verb ka- ‘go;’ But it doesn’t have to, as the example below shows:
(61) No-a shinan-beno-yama-[a]i a-kon-bires-kin no-a Inka-n | onan-ma-bain-i kopí. | ‘We don’t forget (how to do these things) because the Inka Woman taught us very very well before leaving.’
The next example shows two ‘which direction’ endings in a row:
(62) ...tapiti keyan-tanan-ki nee-ina-kain-xon-ki.... | .’..placing the ladder vertically (against sth.), he climbed up....’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)
To sum up, all the ‘which direction’ word pieces I have described so far come from SK verbs that can also stand alone. There seems to be a sliding scale here. At one end, two verbs simply stand side by side. At the other end, one of them has become an ending (see also section 4.9). The verb endings -pake ‘one by one’, -paket ‘going down (the river), -inat ‘going up (the river),’ -be ‘coming (tr.)’ and -bo ‘going (tr.)’ look exactly like the separate verbs pake- ‘cause to fall,’ pake-t- ‘come out,’ inat- ‘go up (the river),’ be- ‘come (n.sing.), bring’ and bo- ‘come (n.sing.), take,’ in that order. (Here ‘tr.’ means ‘used with transitive verbs’ and ‘n.sing.’ means ‘more than one person’.) Notice, though, that pake- ‘cause to fall’ and -pake ‘one by one’ mean very different things. Also, the ‘coming’ and ‘going away’ endings no longer look exactly like the verbs they come from: they end in -ain. Still, remember that they can still add a separate action that happens next. I also said above that -kawan, is most likely made of ka- ‘go’ plus -wan, the ‘earlier today’ past ending.

h: The Andatives -Kain / -Bain (-kain / -bain: "on the way there")
t:
Finally, the ‘coming’ and ‘going away’ endings usually come after the endings that change how many people a verb involves. But this is not always so, as shown below:
(63) Mi-n koríki-ra mi-a bi-bain-nan-toshi-kan-na-ke. | ‘Beware, they could suddenly take your money to your detriment and leave.’

h: Adverb-Type Markers (endings that work like adverbs)
t: Besides the ‘which direction’ word pieces above, SK has about ten other verb endings. They work a bit like English adverbs such as ‘quickly’ or ‘again’. They tell us how something happens, whether it is finished, how many do it, how long it lasts, which way it goes, and so on. These endings are: -tan ‘go do something (tr.) (and return),’ -wetsa-yama- ‘not again,’ -yon ‘completely,’ -toshi ‘suddenly / surprisingly,’ -men ‘quickly,’ -patan ‘at intervals (in space / time),’ -shin ‘all night long,’ -bai(t) ‘all day long,’ -kean ‘tried but failed’ (linguists call this the frustrative), and -bekon, which shows the action is done by two people.

h: -Tan ‘Go Do Sth. (Tr.) (and Return)’ ("go do something (and come back)")
t:
The ending -tan means ‘go and do something, and come back’. It can go on both intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. Most often, though, you find it on verbs of movement. Unlike the endings above, -tan does not come from any separate verb.
(64) Jene-n ka-tan-ax jo-xon.... | ‘If when coming back from the fishing....’ lit. ‘If when going to the river, doing sth. (i.e., catching fish) and coming back....’
(65) Yabí, karo bi-tan-we! | ‘Yabi, go get firewood!’

h: -Toshi(t) ‘Suddenly, Surprisingly’ ("suddenly, surprisingly")
t:
Some have suggested that this ending comes from the bare verb toshi- ‘burst, pop up’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:414).
(66) Ja jo-xon iso pota-toshi-ke-bi-ronki | jawen yoxaman-ki yoiy-a iki.... | ‘After he arrived and suddenly dropped the spidermonkeys (he had killed, to the ground), his wife told him....’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)
(67) Jo-anan-ki re-keyan-me-toshit-i.... | ‘Coming towards the shore, (the alligator-canoe) landed suddenly....’
See also example (63).

h: -Bait ‘All Day Long’ ("all day long")
t:
The next example from a story shows the ending -bai ‘all day long:’
(68) ...moa nete-n xopainsi i-bait-i-bi-ki | moa ja yamé-ki moa ainbo. | .’..although during the day (she) was just a secana (k. gourd), at night she (turned into) a woman.’

h: -Shin ‘All Night Long’ ("all night long")
t: (69) Jain e-n oin-yam[a]-a iki ransa-kan-ai, ponté mashá | ik-ai-res, bewa bewa-shin-i-res nete-kan-ai. | ‘There I did not see anybody dancing according to the mestizo style, they only performed the mashá (traditional singing and dancing), they kept on singing all night long until dawn.’

h: -Bekon Action Carried Out by Two People (an action done by two people)
t:
Example (70) comes from a story about the old conflicts between the Shipibo and the Kashibo. In this scene, an old couple gets ready to go after the Kashibo who had killed their grandchildren. There are two people going, the two grandparents. Yet the verb ‘go’ is in its form for one person (ka- instead of bo-). This choice of ka- suggests what -bekon means: one person does the action, and a second person goes along. That meaning fits where -bekon probably comes from: -be ‘with’ + -kon ‘true, core, legitimate.’
(70) Ja-skat-ax-ki pia nea yatanan-ki ka-bekon-a iki, | [baba rete-xon bo-kan-a] chiban-i.... | ‘After grabbing the bundle of arrows, the two of them left, chasing those who had killed their grandchildren and taken their corpses with them...’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)
I will come back to this example when I talk about Overlapping of Subject Reference in 9.5.
One verb quite often has both a ‘which direction’ ending and one of these adverb-like endings. You can see this in ex. (2). There the ‘going away’ ending -bain and the ‘tried but failed’ ending -kean appear together. Ex. (2) is shown again below. Notice that the ‘going away’ ending comes first:
(71) Nokon ochíti-ra e-a | ta-níni-nan-bain-kean-wan-kan-ke. | ‘They almost pulled my dog by the foot while passing earlier today to my detriment.’

h: -Yon ‘Completely’ ("completely")
t:
In the next example, the ending -yon ‘completely’ comes before the ‘coming’ ending -kiran. Just as in ex. (53), -kiran shows someone entering a state:
(72) Rama kaman-bi chamá a-kin a-kan-a no-a | sinat-ai, jointi-ain-bi no-a jawe kesk-á-yon-kiran-ai. | ‘Even until today, when we are called “chama” we get angry, something hurts us very much in our hearts.’

h: -Patan ‘At Intervals’ ("now and then")
t:
Below, -patan ‘at intervals’ comes before the ‘going away’ ending -kain:
(73) No-a rao-meet-a ik-ax meskó keská | kené-bo no-n shinain pikó-patan-kain-ai... | ‘If we have been cured (with special piripiri) we imagine all kinds of designs...’
In the next example, -patan comes before two ‘which direction’ endings in a row. Notice something odd. There is more than one doer here: four children. Yet the ending is -kain, the form for one doer with an intransitive verb, and not -bain:
(74) Jaa-ki choron-patainai-kain-ax poyan-tii-bi | choron-patan-ina-kain-ax | nee-kan-ke ja chosko xoxo bake-bo. | ‘Very quickly they climbed up on different tree branches, the four illegitimate children.’
Why -kain here? Probably because the scene is made of four small events. Each grandchild climbs onto a tree branch on their own.

h: The Frustrative -Kean (-kean: "tried but failed")
t: The ending -kean shows that something did not happen, or was not finished. Someone tried, but it didn’t work out. Linguists call this the frustrative. You can see it in ex. (2).

h: -Men ‘Quickly’ ("quickly")
t: The verb ending -men ‘quickly’ is common in commands. See examples (209)-(211) in Chapter 8.

h: -Wetsa-yama ‘Not Again’ ("not again")
t: Finally, the pair wetsa-yama [other-NEG] ‘not again’ can also go on verbs (NEG is the ‘not’ marker). For example, tee-wetsa-yama- [work-other-NEG] means ‘do not work again.’ I have never found the piece -wetsa on its own.

h: Definite Tenses (endings that say exactly when something happens)
t:
SK also has a set of endings that say exactly when something happened. You don’t have to use them.⁴ One of them, -yat ~ -yá, means ‘tomorrow’, but it is rare nowadays. All the other time endings show
We still need more research on two questions. First, how do people understand the time of a verb that has no time ending? Second, when does a time ending have to be used?
different degrees of past, from very recent to very long ago. -wan means ‘earlier the same day’. -ibat ~ -ibá means ‘yesterday, a few days ago’. -yantan means ‘some months, a few years ago’. -rabe means ‘about nine months to three years ago’, for an action that went on or happened again and again back then. -kati(t) means ‘many years ago’; it becomes -kato when the ‘finished’ ending -ke follows it. And -ni means ‘in very remote times’. Only -wan is exact: the event really did happen earlier the same day. For the other past endings, the times are only rough. In fact, the same speaker, in the same story, may use different past endings for events that happened at the same time (cf. ex. (89)). The plural ending -kan comes after every time ending except -ni, the ‘very remote past’ ending.

h: -Yat ~ -Yá ‘Tomorrow’ Future ("tomorrow")
t:
(75) Bakísha Maioshiain ka-yá-ribi-ai. | ‘Tomorrow he will go to Pucallpa again.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:421)
(76) Bakish i-yat-ai. | ‘It is going to take place tomorrow.’

h: -Wan ‘Earlier Today’ Past ("earlier today")
t:
(77) Wetsa-tian ik-ai iki moa miin-wan-ke-tian bachi-bo
(None) ten ak-ai. | ‘Sometimes it happens that after having been buried in the day, the dead one moved the rope of the mosquito nets during the night.’
(78) Rama bariapan-ra ka-wan-ke. | ‘He left today at noon.’

h: -Ibat ~ -Ibá ‘Yesterday, A Few Days Ago’ Past ("yesterday or a few days ago")
t:
(79) Ikaxbi bakisha e-n manxaman kawáti ao-bo icha | oin-iba-ke. | ‘But yesterday I saw a lot of manxaman kawáti trees.’
(80) Jaino-a-x nokon papa manat-a iki moa westíora | oxe jawen wetsa-bo bo-iba-kan-ke-tian. | ‘Then my father waited one month after his brothers had left.’
In examples (79) and (80), -iba is used both for ‘yesterday’ and for ‘one month ago.’

h: -Yantan ‘Some Months, A Few Years Ago’ Past ("some months or a few years ago")
t:
Examples (81) and (82) come from the same speaker, but from two different stories.
In these examples, -yantan is used for events that happened two months ago and a
few years ago. In example (83), which a speaker made up when I asked, -yantan helps describe something that happened about a year ago:
(81) Rabé oxe ka-yantan-ke-tian e-n ninkat-a ik-á iki, moa ja | ainbo mawat-a.... | ‘Two months after she had left, I heard that that woman had already died....’
(82) E-n-ra oin-yantan-ke rabé bene-ya yoxan.... | ‘A few years ago I met a woman who had two husbands.....’
(83) Wetsa bari-tian-ra nokon wetsa-n yamékiri | jawéki-a pekáo kirika wisha-yantan-ke. | ‘Last summer after the morning meal my brother wrote a letter.’

h: -Rabe ‘Nine Months to Three Years Ago’ Past ("nine months to three years ago")
t:
The ending -rabe points to about the same time in the past as -yantan. But the two differ in how they look at the event. -rabe is for an action that went on for a while or happened again and again, like English ‘used to write’. -yantan is for a single, finished action, like ‘wrote’. Compare (83) with the example below:
(84) Wetsa bari-tian-ra nokon wetsa-n yamékiri | jawéki-a pekáo kirika wisha-rabe-ke. | ‘Last summer after the morning meal my brother (usually) wrote letters.’
(85) Maioshiain-ra pei xobo ja-rabe-ke, | rama-ra yama-ke. | ‘Around three years ago, there were houses with palm leaf roofs in Pucallpa, now there aren’t any.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:354)

h: -Kati(t) Distant ‘Many Years Ago’ Past ("many years ago")
t:
Ex. (86) talks about a time when the Shipibo had less contact with Spanish speakers, probably a couple of generations ago. But (87) talks about a far-off time from the myths, when the Agouti Man taught the Shipibo how to grow yuca:
(86) Moa-tian nawa-baon chopa no-n bi-ama-katit-ai. | ‘Long time ago, we did not buy pieces of cloth in the store.’
(87) Moa-tian-ronki no-n reken-baon xeati-a-kas-i | onitsa-pao-kati-kan-ai. | ‘Long time ago, when our forefathers wanted to prepare drink they suffered (since there were no chacras from where to obtain yuca).’

h: -Ni Remote Past ("long, long ago")
t:
(88) Moa-tian-ronki i-pao-ni-ke jema-bo yama. | ‘It is said that in remote times there were no villages.’
The next example shows the order of these endings. The plural -kan comes after the ‘many years ago’ ending -kati(t). But it comes before the ‘very remote past’ ending -ni, so it separates -ni from -pao, the ‘used to’ ending:
(89) Moa-tian a-káti-kan-ai besté-ti... Ani Xeati... Reken-pari | chopa a-pao-kani-ke. | ‘Long time ago (our ancestors) used to organize the Ani Xeati ceremony to cut the girl’s bangs ... First of all, they manufactured the clothes....’
In the example above, the Ani Xeati ceremony and the making of the clothes happen during the same period of time. Still, the speaker uses two different past endings.
The ending -pao shows that something happened regularly, like English ‘used to’. It can appear together with the past endings -kati(t) and -ni, as you can see in (87)-(89). In fact, I have only found -pao with these two past endings.

h: “Less-Fixes” Clitics (pieces that can move around)
t:
As I explained in 4.2.3, “less-fixed” clitics are little word pieces with no fixed place in the sentence. They can attach to many different kinds of words. They are: -ribi ~ -riba ‘also / again,’ -yora, which makes the meaning stronger, -tani, which softens it, -pacho ‘always,’ -res ‘just,’ -bicho ‘only,’ -bires ‘purely,’ -shoko ‘little’, -shaman, which also makes the meaning stronger, and -isi, which looks down on something. In this section I look at how these pieces combine with verbs.
In (1) I gave a place inside the verb for the “less-fixed” clitics. But that is only what usually happens. For example, in ex. (122) in Chapter 8, -shaman comes before the ‘not’ ending, so that it affects the right part of the meaning. In the next example, the helper verb ak- (the one used with transitive verbs) takes the “less-fixed” clitics -res and -bires. They come before -kin, the last ending, which shows this is not the main verb of the sentence:
(90) ....no-n yoina-bo a-res-bires-kin no-n rete-yama-[a]i, | jawen ibo-ya-bo-ribi i-ke-tian. | .’...we do not kill our animals indiscriminately, since they also have their owner.’
In the example above, -ribi ‘also’ sits on the noun jawen iboyabo ‘(those) having their owner;’ In the next example, this piece appears first on a main verb and then on nouns. But notice that the last time, ‘again’ comes out as -biri instead of -ribi:

h: “Less-Fixes” Clitics (pieces that can move around)
t:
(91) Jain-xon e-n yoi-ribi-ai nokon tita-shoko-n-a-ribi, | nokon tita-n tita-n-a-biri. | ‘Now I will also tell (you) about my grandmother, about my mother’s mother.’
On verbs, the choice between the two forms -ribi ~ -riba is especially interesting. It depends on the length of the bare verb, counted in beats. Only vowels count as beats (linguists call them moras; see the description of the repetitive in Alternate Mora Timing in 3.2.3). An even number of beats gets -ribi; an odd number gets -riba. So in the previous example, -ribi is used because yoi- has two beats. In the next example, the bare verb ja- ‘there is’ has only one beat, so it needs -riba:
(92) Jaino-a-x ja-ríba-a iki jato ani xobo-n bo-ai | joni. | ‘There, there was also a man in charge of taking the people to the large house.’
Examples (93) and (94) show two of these pieces on verbs: -isi, which looks down on something, and -yora, which makes the meaning stronger:
(93) Titá, samá-yama-isi-we! Mi-a-ra ii-kin | rete-mis a-kin a-kana-ke! | ‘Mother, don’t fast (to acquire special powers)! Or else people might say you are a murderer (a witch).’
(94) Xate-kan-a-kaya-ra e-n a-yora-ke ja-ska-ra | shinan-kin. | ‘But after my operation I think about that very much.’
Examples (95) and (96) show the piece -pacho ‘always’ attached to a verb and to a pronoun:

h: “Less-Fixes” Clitics (pieces that can move around)
t:
(95) Ja r-iki chiponki-a-x jo-ai no-n ninká-pacho-ai. | ‘He is the one (about whom) we always heard was coming from the lower Ucayali.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:208)
(96) ...ja oin-a-ki awakan bai-shaman-ki pues
(None) ja-n-pacho ka-[a]i. | ‘… they found the tapir’s way pues, along which he always walks.’
You can find more examples of verbs with “less-fixed” clitics in 4.2.3.

h: The Preventive -Na (-na: "so that it doesn't happen" / "watch out")
t:
The ending -na is added to a bare verb to give a warning: ‘watch out, this could happen!’ It shows something you should prevent or guard against (linguists call it the preventive). It can appear in positive or negative sentences. It always comes together with the ‘finished’ ending. Here are some positive warning sentences (see also (93) above):
(97) Mi-bé ainbo-bo-ra mi-ki shiro-na-ke, | mi-bé ainbo-baon-ra mi-a osan-na-ke, | yoxan i-xon-bi mi-n jawéki a-kin jakóma-[a]i-tian”. | ‘Beware that the women around you make fun of you, beware that the women around you laugh at you, when despite being an adult woman you don’t do your things well.’
(98) Mi-a-ra mi-n bene-n pota-na-ke. | ‘Beware that your husband leaves you.’
The following warning sentences are negative:
(99) Ja-ra no-n senen-a-yama-na-ke | ‘Beware that we do not finish it (on time).’
(100) Ja axa-n-kan-ke-bi joni ka-yama-a iki jawen awin | too-ya i-ke-tian; jawen awin too-ya i-xon yapa | pae-n-ma-yama-na-ke-tian. | ‘Although the people of the village were fishing with barbasco (fish poison), the man did not go because his wife was pregnant; fearing that being pregnant his wife would prevent the fish from getting poisoned.’
The next example shows that the warning ending comes after the plural -kan (see also ex. (93)):
(101) Ochíti-baon-ra mi-a natex-ka[n]-na-ke. natex-na-kan-ke | ‘Beware, the dogs could bite you.’

h: Final Suffixes (the last ending on a verb)
t: Final endings, the ones that close off a verb, come in two kinds. Some make a complete main verb (finite). Others don’t (non-finite).

h: Finite Final Suffixes (last endings for a complete sentence)
t:
Which finite final ending a verb takes depends on the kind of sentence. It may be a statement, a command, or a ‘let me / let’s’ sentence (linguists call these declarative, imperative, and prospective / jussive). In statements, the final endings are the ‘not finished’ ending, the incompletive -ai
(INC) and the completive -ke (CMPL). These two endings tell you about time. The ending -ai (INC, the "not finished" ending) can mean three things. The event takes place regularly. Or it is happening right now, as you speak. Or it will take place very soon after the person speaks. The ending -ke (CMPL, the "finished" ending) means the action is already done. Done by which point? Usually by the moment the person is speaking, like English -ed. There are a few other verb forms that end a plain statement. One is the ending -kato. It is really the past ending kati(t) joined with -ke. Another is the word iki ‘be,’ used as the main verb. A third is those forms where a verb is followed by iki, which functions as a helper verb, a bit like English "is going" or "has gone." Two of these only appear in plain statements: -ke, and iki when it means ‘be.’ (This is not true of iki as a helper verb.) Since that is so, they also serve as markers that signal: "this sentence is a statement."

h: Finite Final Suffixes (last endings for a complete sentence)
t:
Sometimes the verb comes first in a statement. Then a small extra piece can slip inside the verb. Shipibo has little pieces that normally sit in the second spot of the sentence (linguists call them second-position clitics). When the verb is first, the piece goes into the verb itself. It sits after the bare verb but before the "more than one" ending -kan (if there is one) and the final ending. These pieces include -ra, which means "I know this for sure." They also include -ronki and -ki, which mean "people say" (-ki can also go in other places). And there is -mein, which means "maybe." Why can a piece go inside a word? This suggests that the endings after it used to be separate words. They became endings fairly recently. So the piece got trapped inside the verb. In the next examples, look at where -ra and -ronki sit:
(102) Ja-ríba-ra-ke ainbo-bo, moa wetsa joni betan i-xon | jato-n bene pota-[a]i. | ‘There are also women who, having an affair with another man, abandon their husbands.’
(103) “Tita-shoko tene-non a-kan-we!” i-ronki-ai. | ‘“Let’s kill the grandmother!” they said.’
Orders and wishes have their own final endings. A verb that gives an order ends in -we (linguists call this the imperative). A verb that says ‘may it happen’ or ‘let it happen’ ends in (-ba) -non (glossed P/J, for prospective / jussive). These endings take the place of -ai and -ke. The example above is a ‘let’s do it’ sentence. It speaks to a group that includes the speaker: ‘we, you and I.’ In Shipibo, a ‘let’s’ sentence is really two parts put together: a ‘may it happen’ part and an order part (see 8.6.3). That is why in (103) the verb tene- has the ‘may it happen’ ending -non, while a-kan- has the order ending -we. The next examples show the other form of the ‘may it happen’ ending, -ba -non. Example (105) also has two orders in it:

h: Finite Final Suffixes (last endings for a complete sentence)
t:
(104) Mi-a yoi-ba-non, ne-skat-a-ronki ik-á iki ja cuento | ja Wishmabo. | ‘Let me tell you / I’m going to tell you, so was the story of the “Wishmabo”.’
(105) Baké, mapó tsaman-we, e-n mi-a wexa-xon-ba-non, oin-we! | ‘Daughter, shape the clay, I will teach you how to polish, look!

h: Non-Finite Final Suffixes (last endings for a linked or incomplete sentence)
t: Some verbs can't end a sentence on their own. They lean on another verb. Their final endings come in two groups. The first group are the ‘participle’ endings: one for an action not finished, and one for an action finished. The second group are the linking endings. They tell you whether the next action is done by the same person, by someone else, or by the person who was the receiver before (linguists call them reference markers).

h: 7.11.2.1. Participial Suffixes
t:
The two participle endings are -ai and -a. The ending -ai means ‘not finished.’ It looks just like the -ai that ends a plain statement. The ending -a means ‘finished.’ It is different from the statement ending -ke. Verbs in questions take these participle endings. But when you ask for permission (‘may I…?’), you can put -pan on the verb instead. A question can also use a two-verb form with the helper verb iki. Or it can have no verb at all, if it uses the question marker -ri(n), which works like ‘is it…?’
Questions work just like statements here. When the verb comes first in the sentence, the question piece -ki (the one used when the verb is not ‘be’) slips in before the participle ending (see ex. (147d) in Chapter 8).
Participle endings are not only found in questions. They also appear in ‘who/which…’ description parts. They appear in parts that complete another verb (‘I know that he came’). And they appear in parts that say when or why something happened, if those parts have no linking marker (see Chapter 10).

h: 7.11.2.2. Reference-Markers
t:
A verb that doesn't end the sentence can also take a linking marker. Some of these markers tell you whether two parts of the sentence have the same doer or different doers. Others tell you that the receiver in the marked part is the same person as the doer in the main part. Here is something rare among the world's languages, and typical
of Shipibo-Konibo and of Panoan languages in general: some of these markers must change to match the main verb. One form is used if the main verb is an intransitive verb, and another if it is a transitive verb (see 9.1).

h: Periphrastic Verb Forms (verb forms made with a helper verb)
t:
In Shipibo-Konibo it is very common to say something with two verbs instead of one. The first verb carries the real meaning (I will also call it the main-meaning verb). It appears in a form that can't end a sentence: with a participle ending or a ‘same person’ ending. The second verb is a helper verb. It carries the information about time, about whether the action is finished, and about how many people are involved. There are two helper verbs, both with very general meanings. One is the intransitive verb ik- ‘do (intr.), be’. The other is its transitive partner ak ‘do (tr.), make.’ This is a bit like English ‘she is going’ or ‘I do know.’ I will call these two-verb combinations ‘Periphrastic Verb Forms’ or ‘Periphrastic Verbs.’
Other helper verbs can be used in these two-verb forms too. They add meanings like ‘there is,’ ‘there isn't,’ or ‘can.’ They are the ‘there is’ verb ja-, the ‘there isn't’ verb yama-, and atipan- ‘can’. But I will deal with these meanings in a separate section (7.13).

h: Participial Periphrastic Verbs (verb + helper with a describing form)
t:
Some two-verb forms put a participle ending, -ai or -a, on the main-meaning verb. The helper verb is usually the intransitive verb ik-. Looking at the history of the language, ik- may once have been the verb ‘be,’ joined to a sentence that had been turned into a noun,
but in today's Shipibo it is better to treat each combination as one single two-word verb. Look at this example:
(106) [E-n yoi-kas-ai] r-iki. | ‘I want to tell (the stories).’
Look at the doer in the example above. Whether it gets the doer marker depends on the main-meaning verb, not on the helper verb. Notice also where the ‘I know this for sure’ marker sits: as usual, after the first big part of the sentence. If you took the sentence apart piece by piece, you could read it as ‘It is the case that I want to tell (the stories).’ But Shipibo speakers don't understand it that way. To them, it simply means the same as this:
(106) E-n-ra yoi-kas-ai. | ‘I want to tell (the stories).’
A two-verb form is one choice you can make when you describe an event. In principle, any verb can appear either alone or in a two-verb form. Speakers may pick the two-verb form for style, or for a special purpose in a story or a conversation. (Güldemann, forthcoming, discusses similar forms in some African languages.) In their structure, and probably in their history, these forms are a helper verb or “dummy verb” plus a sentence turned into a noun. This has a result. Other big parts of the sentence can come between the main-meaning verb and the helper verb. So can the little pieces that sit in the second spot of the sentence.

h: 7.12.1.1. The Narrative Past V-a iki
t:
Probably the most common two-verb form in Shipibo-Konibo stories is V-a iki. Storytellers use it to report finished past events that move the story forward. It appears both in personal stories and in traditional tales. V stands for the main-meaning verb. That verb decides how many people take part and who gets the doer marker. In the example below, a Shipibo woman has refused to give the Inka Woman roasted peanuts. The Inka Woman is angry and decides to leave the Shipibo. So she goes back home to persuade her husband to leave:
(107) Ja washit-a-ronki ka-ríba-a iki jawen xobo-n. | ‘Having been denied (the roasted peanut), (the Inka Woman) went back home.’
Below, the narrative past (the storytelling past) appears in a passage from a personal story:
(108) Jain-xon nokon papa-n ani wai ak-á iki.... | ‘Then my father cultivated a big chacra....’
As I said above, the helper verb and the main-meaning verb don't have to sit next to each other:
(109) No-a Shipibo-baon r-iki shino shipi-n jane bi-a. | ‘We, the Shipibo, got the tamarin monkey’s name.’

h: 7.12.1.2. The ‘Pluperfect’ V-a ik-á iki
t:
The ‘pluperfect’ is built by doubling the narrative past: [[V]-a ik]-a iki. The fixed string -a iká iki is added to the bare verb. It doesn't matter whether that verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. Just as in the narrative past, the main-meaning verb decides everything else: how many people take part, who gets the doer marker, and which matching forms other words take. The next example comes from a story about getting ready for the Ani Xeati ceremony (girls’ puberty rites). It has two verbs in the pluperfect: the intransitive verb tee- ‘work’ and the transitive verb tsinki- ‘gather.’ Because tsinki- has a doer and a receiver, the linking word jainxon takes the form that matches a doer (A agreement):
(110) Ja ik-á iki moa westíora oxe maxká-ke-tian. Ja moa | nokon papa rabé baritia teet-a ik-á iki. Jain-xon moa nokon | papa-n wai-nko-ni-a yoa-bo tsinki-a ik-á iki. | ‘This was just one month before (the Ani Xeati). By then my father had already worked for two years in the preparations. My father had already gathered the crops from the chacra.’
The example below takes us back to the story of the Inka Woman, which we met in (107). The Inka Woman arrives home looking for her husband, but she doesn't find him:
(111) Ja-tian jawen bene ka-a ik-á iki jato | onan-ma-i tsaka-ti, wina-ti, | pia-a-ti.... | ‘By then her husband had gone to teach them (i.e., the Shipibo men) how to shoot with arrow, how to row, how to make arrows.....’

h: 7.12.1.2. The ‘Pluperfect’ V-a ik-á iki
t:
Sometimes, though, the V-a iká iki form does not mean "had done." It is translated into English as a simple past instead ("saw," not "had seen"). This mostly happens with verbs of seeing and hearing: oin- ‘see,’ jisá- ‘see / notice,’ and ninkat- ‘hear / understand.’ These verbs come at the start of a chain of actions that opens a new scene. So in this setting the ‘pluperfect’ form may show surprise, something the speaker did not expect (linguists call this mirativity).⁵ Here is an example. The Inka Woman has already left the Shipibo women and is running away up the Ucayali River. The Shipibo women want her back, so they travel up the river following her traces. Of course, lighting the fire happened before anyone found the traces of it. But look at which verb gets the ‘pluperfect’ form. It is ‘(they) saw,’ not ‘lit the fire’:
(112) Mayá pekáo ka-xon jis-á-ki ik-á iki
Peruvian Spanish also uses "had done" verb forms to show that something was unexpected. This probably comes from the influence of Quechua. Look at this Peruvian Spanish example:
(i) ¡Resulta que Jorge había sido sobrino de Fujimori! | ‘Jorge turned out to be Fujimori’s nephew!’
(None) chii keté-a-bain-a.... | ‘Following the turns of the river, (they) saw the fire she had lit on her way...’

h: 7.12.1.2. The ‘Pluperfect’ V-a ik-á iki
t: Look at the glosses. The piece -ki in jisá-ki is the shorter hearsay marker (it shows the speaker heard this from someone else). It is not part of the "had done" ending. Markers like -ki that show how the speaker knows something never break into the middle of a single unit of the sentence. So if -ki can sit where it does in the example above, the whole form must have become one single verb form quite recently (linguists call this grammaticalization).

h: 7.12.1.3. Other Participial Periphrastic Verbs
t:
There are more two-word verb forms like this. In each one, the main verb has a participle ending (an "-ing" or "-ed" type ending), and a helper verb adds the time and type of action. We still need to learn more about what these forms do in SK, but we can see a few patterns. The first pattern appears in (113)-(115). It shows up just after a story begins. It describes the situation in the background, which becomes important for the main events that follow. In these cases the helper verb is always the intransitive helper, even when the main verb is a transitive verb. The past-time markers are also present. Here is a passage from a story about a man who married a secana (a kind of gourd / pumpkin) woman: she was a woman at night but a secana during the day. In both sentences, the helper verb clearly shows "long ago" and "ongoing, not finished":
(113) Xopan ainbo-ki bi-a i-káti-ai. | ‘(He) was married to a secana woman.
(114) Ja-tian yamé-bicho-ki i-káti-ai ainbo-ki | ja betan ox-ai... | Then only at night the woman slept with him....’
The first example above has a transitive main verb, bi- ‘get / receive.’ The second has an intransitive main verb, oxa- ‘sleep.’ Word for word, they could be translated as ‘He was one married to a secana woman’ and ‘The woman was one sleeping with him only at night.’

h: 7.12.1.3. Other Participial Periphrastic Verbs
t:
In the next example, the helper verb shows "far in the past" and "used to do it regularly":
(115) Moa-tian-ronki i-pao-ni-ke jema-bo yam[a]-a. | ‘It is said that long time ago there were no villages.’
A second pattern shows up in direct quotes that are part of the main story. Look at (116). Here the main verb is a transitive verb, and the helper verb is the transitive helper too. Compare (113): its main verb is also a transitive verb, but it used the intransitive helper. Also, in (116) the helper verb has no past-time marker:
(116) Jawe kopí-ki ak-ai mato-n bari noka[a]-a? | ‘Why have you extinguished the sun (causing the ongoing eclipse)?’
To sum up: in these two-word verb forms, when the main verb is a transitive verb, the helper can be the transitive ak-, but it doesn't have to be. When the main verb is an intransitive verb, only the intransitive helper ik- is possible: Vtr. + Aux intr. / tr.; Vintr. + Aux intr. / tr.

h: Same-Subject Marked Periphrastic Verbs (verb + helper with the "same person" ending)
t: Some two-word verb forms are built a different way. The helper verb ak- or ik- carries the information about time and type of action. The main verb takes a "same person" marker (a marker that says the same person does both actions).

h: 7.12.2.1. The Progressive V-i itai
t:
The form V-i itai is how you clearly say that an action is going on right now, like English "is doing" (linguists call this the progressive). The helper verb i-t-ai [do.I / be-PROG-INC] is an intransitive verb. So the main verb always takes the ending -i. This ending means "at the same time, by the same person," and it matches an intransitive verb.
(117) Ja moa no-a na-ne-t-i i-t-ai-tian, | jo-xon ainbo-nin nokon sobrina bachin-ribi-a iki. | ‘Just when we were embarking in the canoe, the woman came and pulled my niece by the hair again.’
The "is doing" form can partly take away the doer marker. In the examples below, the doers appear in the plain form (no marker), even though
the verbs ak- and koko- are transitive verbs. These verbs still keep their receiver. So both the doer and the receiver of ak- and koko- appear in the plain form:
(118) –Jawe ak-i-ki mato i-t-ai? | ‘What are you doing?:’
(119) –Binpish koko-i-ra no-a i-t-ai. | ‘We are eating guayaba.’
But with a transitive main verb in the "is doing" form, whether the doer gets the doer marker (ERG) or the plain form (ABS) can depend on the receiver. Desire sentences work the same way (section 8.2.8). If the receiver is vague, not a particular thing, or not a real known thing, the doer appears in the plain form. If the receiver is a particular, known thing, the doer usually gets the doer marker. You can see this second case in (120):

h: 7.12.2.1. The Progressive V-i itai
t:
(120) Ja keská-shaman jawéki no-n wisha-i i-t-ai. | ‘We are writing this kind of stories (like the one I have just described).’
The main verb can also be said twice (doubled) as another way of showing that the action keeps going on.

h: 7.12.2.2. The Future V-i kai
t:
In many languages of the world, the verb ‘go’ can be used to talk about the future. SK does this too, just as English says "I am going to eat" about a future meal.
The helper ka-[a]i [go-INC] is an intransitive verb. So the main verb always takes the same-person, same-time ending -i. But there is a difference from the "is doing" form above. Here, whether the doer gets the doer marker depends on the main verb. In (121) and (123) the main verbs are transitive verbs, so the doers have the doer marker (ERG). In (122) and (124) the main verbs are intransitive verbs, so the doers are in the plain form (ABS):
(121) Jain-xon no-n onan-an-i ka-[a]i, ainbo joni | bi-ma-ti bewá, joni wanomaat-a wano-ma-ti. | ‘Then we are going to learn the song to help a woman conquer a man, learn how to help a widower marry again.’
(122) Tita-ra keyo-t-ai, ja-tian no-a banet-i ka-[a]i | ja-n no-a axe-a-a jawéki-bo-ya. | ‘Our mother dies and we will be left with the things that she taught us.’
(123) Bakish-ra e-n xenan wai-nko-ni-a bi-i ka-[a]i. | ‘Tomorrow I am going to bring guabas from the chacra.’
(124) Bakish-ra e-a yamékiri-bi wenit-i ka-[a]i. | ‘Tomorrow I am going to wake up early in the morning.’
In the next example, "we" is in the plain form, and the main verb axe-a- ‘teach’ is a transitive verb. That tells us noa is the receiver here ("teach us"), not the doer:

h: 7.12.2.2. The Future V-i kai
t: (125) ...ja noi waste yoshin-baon-kaya no-a axe-a-i ka-[a]i... | .’..the spirit of the “love piripiri” will teach us....’

h: 7.12.2.3. The Indefinite Future V-nonx iki
t:
The two-word form V-nonx iki talks about something that will happen in the future. But it doesn't say exactly when. That's why I call it the "indefinite" future. It is different from the "definite" ‘tomorrow’ future, which uses the ending -yat ~ yá (see 7.8.1).
(126) E-n-ra mi-a bi-ai, mi-a-ra nokon awin i-nonx iki. | ‘I am going to marry you, you will be my wife.’
The next example comes from a story where the Canary Woman teaches a group of Shipibo children how to grow corn. But the children did not follow her instructions exactly. So the corn will take three months (instead of a couple of days) to be ready to eat:
(127) Ne-ská-bi-ra mato ja-nonx iki: mato-n xeki bana-a-ra | ishto-n i-ama-nonx iki, kimisha oxe-pari-ra mato i-nonx iki
(None) jawéki-a-kas-i manat-i. | ‘You will live just like this: when cultivating corn it will not grow quickly, you will first have to wait three months in order to eat it.’

h: 7.12.2.4. Other Same-Subject Marked Periphrastic Verbs
t:
Just as with the participle forms, we don't yet fully understand what some of these same-person two-word verb forms do. But I will point out a few patterns. Usually the helper verb matches the main verb: ik- goes with intransitive main verbs, and ak- goes with transitive main verbs. The same-person marker then has to match the helper verb. Still, as with some participle forms, ik- can go with a transitive main verb (see (136)). But ak- is never used with an intransitive main verb.
Helper verbs with only the endings -ai and -ke (which show the type of action) appear only in conversations or in direct quotes inside stories. The next sentence is a question:
(128) Tso-n-ki ak-ai neno bake pota-kin? | ‘Who leaves his / her child here?’ (Inuma 1993:18)
In the example above, the main verb pota- is a transitive verb, so it takes the transitive helper ak-. And because the helper is a transitive verb, the same-person marker is -kin, the form that matches a doer.
Example (129) also comes from the story about the Inka Woman. Here she tells her husband what had happened to her earlier. The verb washí- is a transitive verb:
(129) ...bake-baon-ra e-a a-ke tama toban | washí-kin. | ‘...(our female) children have denied me the roasted peanuts.’
In (130), the helper verb comes first in the sentence. So it carries the marker -ra, which shows the speaker knows this directly (this marker always sits after the first part of the sentence):

h: 7.12.2.4. Other Same-Subject Marked Periphrastic Verbs
t:
(130) A-rá-ke tsaka-kin no-n benbo-baon... | ‘Our men have shot it (i.e., the animal)...’
The examples below are different. They come from stories, and they give background information at the start of the text. The helpers ik- and ak- take the "long ago" ending -kati(t) and the plural ending -kan, before the ending that shows the action was ongoing:
(131) Moa-tian-ronki Shipibo-bo-ki Kashibo-bo betan | tekít-i jaa i-pao-kati-kan-ai Tawa-ya wean meran. | ‘It is said that long time ago, the Shipibo lived together with the Kashibo on the banks of the stream of Tawaya.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:16)
(132) Moa-tian-bi-ra nawa-baon no-a a-káti-kan-ai
(None) “chama” a-kin. | ‘Long ago the outsiders used to call us “chama”.’
The next examples come from the story about the Secana Woman. They contain the longer helper forms iká iki and aká iki. Which one is used depends on the main verb: intransitive verb or transitive verb. As I said above, the same-time, same-person markers -i and -kin have to match the helper. These forms are used to move the main story forward. The free translations are given line by line:
(133) Ii-kin-ki ak-á iki joni-n-ki too a-kin.... | ‘After some time, the man got her pregnant.... (lit., ‘After some time, the man did it (to her) getting her pregnant.’)
(134) ...jawen poi-n, bachi benxo benxo a-kin-bi-ronki | ...while his sister was tidying up his mosquito net, | ak-á iki xopan, xopan-ki toe-nan-kin, | she broke the secana (to his detriment),

h: 7.12.2.4. Other Same-Subject Marked Periphrastic Verbs
t:
(135) ja toe-nan-a-ki | after she broke it (to his detriment) | ik-á iki bake-ki piko-t-i chosko bake. | four children came out.’
In the next sentence, the meaning "had done" comes from combining the longer helper iká iki with a main verb that has a same-person marker meaning "before" (instead of "at the same time")
Notice that the intransitive helper is used here, even though the main verb is a transitive verb:
(136) Ja-tian ja-bo bo-kan-ke-tian, nokon tita ik-á iki | jatíbi ja-n nokon wetsa rabé raó a-ti bi-ax.... | ‘When they got back, my mother had already gotten all the adornments with which to embellish my two sisters....’
As I said before, two-word verb forms don't act like one single verb in every way. For example, other words can come between the main verb and the helper (see (109), (114)-(116), (128)-(129), and others). Also, a marker that always sits in second place in the sentence can come between them (see (106), (118)-(119), (130)). In the sentence below, the two-word verb is made of the helper akátiai and the main verb axeakin, which has a same-person marker. Between these two parts come several words that are receivers of the action:
(137) Benbo Inka-n-ki a-káti-ai pia-a-ti, | yomera-ti nonti-a-ti, xakiti-a-ti, | biski-a-ti, jato axe-a-kin. | ‘The male Inka taught them how to make arrows, fish / hunt, construct a canoe, make graters, mixers, those (things).’

h: Modality (ways to say "can", "must", "may")
t:
This section is about how to say that someone can do something, may do something, might do something, or must do something. These usually use the verbs atipan- ‘can,’ ja- ‘exist,’ and yama- ‘exist not.’ (For how to talk about wanting, see 8.2.8 and 10.3.1. For how speakers show how sure they are, see Chapter 13.)
Some verbs take a whole sentence as their receiver: verbs of saying, thinking, seeing or hearing, and wanting. atipan-, ja-, and yama- are different. They don't decide on their own who the doer and receiver are. The sentence attached to them is always in the plain form. But whether their doer gets the doer marker depends on the other verb that goes with them. So atipan-, ja-, and yama- can work as helper verbs, not as main verbs. Their doer really belongs to the helper plus the verb that carries the main meaning, taken together. It's just like with keen- ‘want’ and other similar verbs: here too the main verb takes the ending -ti, which is like English "to" in "to go," and means the action hasn't happened (yet).

h: V-ti Atipan ("can do it")
t: The verb atipan- is probably made of the Quechua root ati- ‘can’ plus the SK verb piece -pan. The piece -pan is used when asking for permission (see the examples in (145)).

h: 7.13.1.1. Capability
t:
The main job of atipan- ‘can’ is to say that someone is able to do something:
(138) Rama-ra nee-ti atipan-ke. | ‘Rama can climb.’
(139) Rama-n-ra bi-ti atipan-ke. | ‘Rama can get it.’
In the example below, the intransitive verb nashi- takes an ending that brings in an extra person. That turns it into a transitive verb. So the doer min gets the doer marker:
(140) ...mi-n pe-chi waste-n nashi-xon-ti atipan-ke. | .’..you can bathe with the “piripiri to be left behind,” to his detriment (i.e., to get rid of him).’
To say someone can't do something, add -yama to the verb that means "can":
(141) Rama-n-ra kirinko-nin joi ninká-ti atipan-yama-ke. | ‘Rama cannot understand English.’
(142) Jawen awin moa jene-n rete-a ik-á iki, nee-ti | atipan-yama-ke-tian tooya ik-ax. | ‘His wife had drowned already, she could not climb (up the tree) because she was pregnant.’
The next example combines the "can" verb atipan- with a two-word verb form that has a marker telling you whether the same person or someone else does the next action:
(143) Ja kopí-ra e-a yoyo-ik-ai no-n a-ti atipan-ke | Ani Xeati-a-kin. | ‘Therefore I say that we could celebrate the Ani Xeati ceremony again.’

h: 7.13.1.2. Permission
t:
Besides "can," atipan- can also mean "may" in ordinary statements, giving permission:
(144) Mi-a-ra jiki-ti atipan-ke. | ‘You can / may come in.’
The questions that could lead to the sentence above are:
(145) E-a jiki-pan? | ‘May I come in?’ | E-a-ki jiki-ti atipan-a? | ‘May I come in?’
The next example shows that the question marker -ki can't be used when you use the permission piece -pan instead of the full verb atipan-:
(None) E-a-ki jiki-pan? | ‘May I come in?’

h: 7.13.1.3. Possibility
t:
Sentences with atipan- can also say that something might happen or might be the case:
(146) Icha-a-kin no-n ninkat-ai Kosko-n Inka-bo, | jainoa-ribi i-ti atipan-ke, Paro rebon ka-ax ja-o | mayat-a. | ‘We hear a great deal about the Inkas in Cuzco, it is possible that those are our Inkas too, it is possible that once they got to the upper end of the Ucayali River (after having left the Shipibo) they turned (towards Cuzco).’

h: 7.13.1.4. Necessity
t:
This is not its usual job, but in the negative the verb atipan- can mean that something must be done:
(147) Benbo bake-baon mapó mee-ti atipan-yama-ke, bakeranon | ik-ax-bi boshí wacho-na-ke-tian, mapó keská. | ‘Male children must not touch the clay (to make pottery), since they are boys their penises could become fluffy just like the clay.’

h: 7.13.2.1. Necessity
t:
One job of the verb ja- ‘exist’ is to say that something must or has to be done:
(148) Kesin Beso-ra ka-ti ja-ke. | ‘Kesin Beso has to go.’
(149) Kesin Beso-n-ra wai oro-ti ja-ke. | ‘Kesin Beso has to weed the chacra.’
Look at the following example, part of which was given earlier as (125):
(150) ...ja noi waste yoshin-baon-kaya no-a axe-a-i ka-[a]i, | ikaxbi no-n samá-a-ti ja-ke. | .’..the spirit of the “love piripiri” will teach us, but we have to fast and abstain from having sex.’

h: 7.13.2.2. Negative Necessity
t:
To say that something does not have to be done, or must not be done, SK uses yama- ‘exist not.’ The examples below show the helper yama- together with different kinds of intransitive verbs: verbs where someone actively does something, verbs where something just happens to someone, and intransitive verbs that also take an extra participant:
(151) E-a-ra ransa-ti yama-ke. | ‘I don’t have to / must not dance.’
(152) E-a-ra ino-ti yama-ke. | ‘I don’t have to / must not turn into a jaguar.’
(153) No-a-ra westíora joni-n shiro-ti yama-ke, ja-ra | ochó i-ke-tian. | ‘We must not be unfaithful to a man when he is far away.’
In the sentences below, yama- goes with transitive verbs:
(154) E-n-ra yoá a-ti yama-ke. | ‘I don’t have to / must not cook.’
(155) No-n chomo ak-ai-tian bake-baon no-a korá-xon-ti | yama-ke. | ‘When we are making pottery the children must not make noise (to our detriment).’

h: V-ti Iki ("must" / "should")
t:
A second way to say that something must be done is the V-ti iki form. The following examples show it. They come from a story about how the Whismabo Constellation began. In this scene, the alligator has bitten off
the leg of one of the children born outside marriage. (-rin is the question marker used with "be" sentences.)
(156) –“Rama-ki jawe-keská-xon no-n kishi bi-ai? Rete-ti-rin?” | ‘“And now, how do we recover the leg? Do we have to kill (the alligator)?”
(157) –“Rete-ti r-iki!” i-ronki-a-kan-ai ja xoxo bake-bo. | “We have to kill it!” said the (other) illegitimate children.
(158) –“Ja-skat-ax chaikoni ponseman noati bi-ti r-iki”.... | “Then we have to borrow the sloth’s spear”....’
In the example below, the "must" form V-ti iki goes together with a two-word verb form that has a marker telling you whether the same person or someone else does the next action. Notice there is a pause between the long helper akanti iki and the part of the sentence with the main verb:
(159) Ja benbo-baon-bi-ribi-ra a-kan-ti iki, atsa wai-a-kin. | ‘Also the men have to cultivate yuca....’

h: Phasal Verbs (verbs like "start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
The verbs peo- ‘begin’, keyo- ‘finish’ and jene- ‘stop’ are transitive verbs by nature. They can be used as main verbs. But peo-, keyo- and jene- can also be helper verbs (linguists call them phasal verbs, because they talk about the stages of an action). When they are helpers, they must match the main verb. If the main verb is a transitive verb, the "begin / finish / stop" verb stays as it is
If the main verb is an intransitive verb, the "begin / finish / stop" verb takes the ending -t, which turns it into an intransitive verb. The main verb also takes -i or -kin, matching the type of the "begin / finish / stop" verb (see 9.1):
(160) E-a-ra ransa-i peo-koo-ke. | ‘I began to dance (e.g., at a party).’
(161) E-n-ra bana-kin peo-ke. | ‘I began to plant (it).’
The two examples just above differ in three important ways. First, the doer has a different marker. Second, the main verb has a different same-time, same-person marker. Third, the "begin / finish / stop" verb is a different type. All three differences come from the main verbs: ransa- is an intransitive verb and bana- is a transitive verb. Here are examples with the other "begin / finish / stop" verbs:
(162) E-a-ra ransa-i jené-ke. | ‘I stopped dancing.’

h: Phasal Verbs (verbs like "start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
(163) E-n-ra yoá a-kin jene-ke. | ‘I stopped cooking (it).’
(164) E-a-ra ransa-i keyó-ke. | ‘I finished dancing.’
(165) E-n-ra pi-kin keyo-ke. | ‘I finished the food.’
In the examples so far, the main verb has the same-time, same-person marker, and the "begin / finish / stop" verb carries the full verb endings. But you can also flip this around. The "begin / finish / stop" verb takes the same-person marker, and the main verb takes the full endings. This happens especially with the "begin" verbs peo- / peo-koot- and the "finish" verbs keyo- / keyó-. The "stop" verb jene- is less flexible here. First, let's look at the "begin" examples. For at least one speaker, the pattern below can also mean starting to do something for the very first time (Yoi Sani, p.c. 2000):
(166) E-a-ra peo-koot-i ransa-ke. | ‘I began to dance (at the party / for the first time in my life).’
(167) E-n-ra peo-kin bana-ke. | ‘I began to sow (it).’
The next examples show the same kind of sentences with the "finish" verbs keyo-(t-):
(168) E-a-ra keyo-t-i ransa-ke. | ‘I finished dancing (the piece of music).’
(169) E-n-ra keyo-kin bana-ke. | ‘I finished sowing (it).’
Speakers don't like the same kind of sentences with the "stop" verb jene-.
The next example comes from a story, and it builds up step by step. The transitive verb rete- becomes an intransitive verb when it gets the "each other" ending -anan. This new intransitive verb rete-anan- is part of a two-word verb form with a same-person marker. So it needs the intransitive helper ikátikanai. That helper, in turn, needs the intransitive same-person marker -i (not -kin) on the main verb, which gives rete-anan-i. Next, this whole intransitive form goes together with the "begin" verb peo-, which must now become an intransitive verb too. Finally, peokot- takes the intransitive same-person marker -ax, because ikátikanai reteanani is an intransitive form:

h: Phasal Verbs (verbs like "start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
(170) Ja-ska-r[a]-ai-n peokot-ax-kaya-ki i-káti-kan-ai | Shipibo-bo betan Kashibo-bo-ki rete-anan-i. | ‘It is said that because of this, the Shipibo and the Kashibo began to fight against each other.’
Now look at a transitive version of the example above:
(171) Ja-ska-r[a]-ai-n peo-xon-kaya-ki a-káti-kan-ai | Shipibo-baon Kashibo-bo-ki rete-kin. | ‘It is said that because of this the Shipibo began to kill the Kashibo.’
Two more verbs, senen-'ak- and janken-'ak-, show that an action is finished. But unlike the "begin / finish / stop" verbs in this section, they only go with transitive main verbs.
SIMPLE CLAUSES:

h: Ergative-Absolutive Case-Marking System (the "doer marker" system)
t:
SK follows one strict rule for marking who does what. The doer of a transitive verb gets the doer marker. The single person of an intransitive verb gets no marker, just like the receiver (linguists call this an ergative-absolutive system). In most languages of this type, including the other Panoan languages, this rule is broken in some places (Dixon 1994:83-104). For example, it may change with the kind of noun, with the time of the action, or with the type of sentence. In SK, as far as we can say, none of that happens. (There is one exception: the doer marker can come and go depending on the receiver in "is doing" sentences and desire sentences; see sections 7.12.2.1 and 8.2.8.) The doer marker is the ending -n, added to the end of the whole noun phrase. The plain form has the marker -a on "I," "you" (one person) and "we," and on the "who" question word tso-
‘who.’ Other pronouns and nouns have no marker at all in the plain form. The doer marker {-n} has several forms: -n; -an, -en, -in; -kan, -ten, -tan; -man; -nin. Which one you use depends on how many beats (linguists say moras) the base word has. Also, -ton and -tonin are used with nouns that have been built from other words or already have endings. And the plural -bo plus the doer marker usually becomes -baon (Faust 1973, Valenzuela 1998, section 3.2.2). The ending -n is interesting for another reason too: one ending does many jobs. It goes on the last word of the noun phrase and can mean the doer, "of" (whose), "with" (a tool), and other meanings like "to / at a place" and "at a time." It is the only way to mark the doer and the tool, and for most nouns the only way to say "of." But for "to / at a place" and time there are other ways too (Valenzuela 1998, see also sections 6.1 and 6.6.5). Look at the examples below, which show different forms and jobs of -n:

h: Ergative-Absolutive Case-Marking System (the "doer marker" system)
t:
(1) Sankeman-ra jawen piakan pia-n koyaparo | tsaka-ke, iaman-xon. | ‘Sanken killed a tucunaré fish with his nephew’s arrow, in the lake.’
(2) Inka-n shinaman manan-xawe-n pei-ki seke-nan-a iki. | ‘The Inka, with his mental power, broke the tortoise’s wings.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
(3) Jisis-in-ra Sankeman bake natex-ke. | ‘The ischimi ant bit Sanken’s child.’
(4) Cesar-nin-ra Maria-nin wai rera-ke machito-nin. | ‘Cesar cleared Maria’s field with a machete.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
(5) Sabado-nin-ra e-a paboro-nin ka-kas-ai. | ‘On Saturday, I want to go to the cove.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
The next examples show that SK markers go on the last word of the noun phrase. The plain-form marker is usually nothing at all, so I use the doer marker to show this. The doer marker comes after: two doers joined by "and," a noun with a describing word, and a "who/which…" description part. Notice also where the markers -ra (the speaker knows directly) and -ronki (the speaker heard it from others) go. They come right after the first big part of the sentence, that is, right after the doer with its marker:
(6) [Tita betan papa]-n-ra jato-n bake-bo ese-ai. | ‘The mother and the father advise their children.’
(7) [Wiso ino sina]kan-ronki joni rabé pi-ke. | ‘It is said that the fierce black tiger ate the two men.’
(8) [Joni Kako-nko-ni-a-x nokó-ibat-a]-tonin-ra rono | rete-ke. | ‘The man who arrived from Caco yesterday killed a snake.’

h: Ergative-Absolutive Case-Marking System (the "doer marker" system)
t:
In SK, the doer marker (in most cases) depends on the verb, not on what really happens. (Dixon calls this a syntactically based system, as opposed to a semantically based one, 1994:23-5.) Each verb has a fixed pattern, based on its usual meaning. It doesn't change with how the verb is used in a particular sentence. So the doer of verbs like ‘kill,’ ‘overcome’ or ‘throw’ always gets the doer marker, and the receiver always gets the plain form. This is true even if the doer didn't mean to do it, or isn't really in control. The next examples show doers that didn't act on purpose, doers that aren't human, doers that aren't alive, and sentences where the action fails:
Non-volitional, non-controller, non-initiator agent
(9) Reokoo-xon-ra e-n jene xea-ke. | ‘Falling (from the canoe), I drank water.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Non-human agent
(10) Jiwi-n-ra Sani rishki-ke. | ‘The tree hit Sani.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Inanimate agent
(11) Aros sako-n-ra e-a ares-ke. | ‘The sack of rice overcame me (with its weight).’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Missed target:
(12) Roniman-ra to’-a-ti-nin ino kene-ke. | ‘Wexá missed the jaguar with the shotgun.’ (Valenzuela 1997)

h: Intraclausal Split-Ergativity (where the doer marker system changes within a sentence)
t: The doer-marker rule holds almost everywhere. It works with all kinds of nouns, with statements, questions and commands, and with every time and type of action (except some two-word verb forms). It works in positive and negative sentences, and in parts of sentences without a full verb.
