As I said earlier, the marker can sometimes change depending on whether the receiver is specific or known, but this is not common. Even so, two things in simple sentences always follow a different rule. In them, the single person of an intransitive verb and the doer of a transitive verb are treated alike (linguists call this a nominative pattern). These two things are the markers on emphatic pronouns ("he himself") and the verb plural ending -kan. Emphatic pronouns are also different in whether they carry a visible "who is involved" ending (see 8.1.2.3).

h: 8.1.2.1. Case-Marking of Emphatic Pronouns
t:
As I explained in 6.1.2, emphatic pronouns ("he himself") have the -n form for both the doer of a transitive verb and the single person of an intransitive verb. They have the form without a marker for the receiver. So these pronouns follow a different rule from nouns: doers of all kinds are treated alike, and receivers are different (linguists call this nominative-accusative). In the sentences below, given before in Chapter 6 as (6b) and (9), the emphatic pronoun has the form ja-n. In the first sentence the verb has been made into an intransitive verb; in the second it is a transitive verb:
(13) Tsoma-ra ja-n-bi-x chachí-ke. | ‘Tsoma (himself) pinched himself.’
(14) Wesna-n-ra ja-n-bi rao xea-ke. | ‘Wesna herself drank the medicine.’
You can see an emphatic pronoun used as a receiver in (17).

h: 8.1.2.2. The Verbal Plural -Kan
t:
The verb plural ending -kan follows the same rule. It shows that the doer is more than one person, whether the verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb, but never for the receiver (see also 12.2.1):
(15) Ja-bo-ra pishiman yaká-kan-ke. | ‘They are sitting on the rush mat.’
(16) Ja-baon-ra joni osan-kan-ai. | ‘They are laughing at the man.’

h: 8.1.2.3. Tripartite and Marked-S Distributions
t:
Besides these small exceptions, several kinds of "who is involved" endings follow yet other patterns, not the doer-marker rule. Compare (13) and (14). Only the emphatic pronoun for the single person of an intransitive verb, in (13), has the visible ending -x. The doer of a transitive verb, in (14), has nothing. The sentence below (given before in Chapter 6 as (10)) shows that emphatic pronouns used as receivers also have no such ending:
(17) Nato r-iki e-n piti be-á, | ja-bi moa bo-tan-we. | ‘This is the fish I have caught, you better take THIS home already (rather than continue waiting for your father who also went fishing).’
So, all in all, emphatic pronouns have three different forms, one for each role (linguists call this tripartite). For "he/she himself/herself" they are: janbix for the single person of an intransitive verb, janbi for the doer of a transitive verb, and jabi for the receiver. The "who is involved" ending, on the other hand, marks only the single person of an intransitive verb
with the ending -x, while the doer and the receiver get nothing (-0). I deal with these endings in 8.3 and in Chapter 19.

h: Declarative Clause Types (kinds of statements)
t: This section covers the basic kinds of statements in SK, sorted by how many people the verb needs. These are: intransitive verbs, intransitive verbs that also take an extra participant, transitive verbs, and verbs that can be either. It also covers sentences with verbs whose receiver repeats the verb's own meaning (like English "sing a song"), verbs with a beginning piece, and sound-imitating verbs. Last come sentences with an unnamed doer and sentences about wanting.

h: Intransitive Clauses
t:
Sentences with intransitive verbs use verbs that need only one person, either by nature or because an ending made them that way. A typical intransitive verb has these features. Its single person¹ is in the plain form. Some words that go with it must carry the "who is involved" ending: words for "from where," for life stage, for "how many," for "how," and emphatic pronouns. But words for "to / at a place" carry no such ending. It can't take the ending -t (the "middle" ending), the "against someone" ending, or the "spread around" ending. It needs the intransitive forms of the special verb pairs for "go" and "come," which use completely different words. It
By "a person" a verb needs, I mean someone or something the verb requires (linguists call it an argument). It must be part of the meaning, even if it isn't said out loud. The verb decides what kind of thing it can be. It is a noun phrase, or a phrase with a word like "to" or "with".
goes with the intransitive forms of the "begin / finish / stop" verbs and with the intransitive helper ik-. And it can take the verb piece -paket ‘going down (the river).’
Below I deal with sentences whose verb is an intransitive verb by nature. These come in several kinds. There are "be" sentences ("She is a teacher"), "there is" sentences, and other intransitive sentences. In the last group, the person either just has something happen to them or actively does something. Two different ways of saying "have" fall under "be" and "there is" sentences. For verbs that were turned into intransitive verbs by an ending, see 7.4.3, 7.4.4, and Chapter 8.

h: 8.2.1.1. Copular Clauses
t:
In "be" sentences, who the sentence is about is in the plain form, and the second part has no marker either. (You could also say the second part is in the plain form.) Below I give examples of "be" sentences that define something, say who someone is, describe a quality, say where something is, and say who owns something. The word for "be" is iki. It comes from the intransitive verb ik- ‘do (intr.), be.’ It can stand alone. Or it can fuse with -ra, the marker that the speaker knows directly, to make the word -riki: -ra + iki > r-iki. The form iki stays the same for every person (I, you, she, and so on). It can come before or after what is said about the subject. In natural, everyday speech, who the sentence is about often comes after iki:
Defining Clauses:
(18) Ja-ra joni iki. | Ja r-iki joni. | ‘He / that one is a person.’
Identificational Clauses:
(19) Ja r-iki Tsoma. | Ja-ra Tsoma iki. | ‘He / that one is Tsoma.’
Quality Clauses:
(20) Ino-ra onsá yoina iki. | Ino r-iki yoina onsá. | ‘The jaguar is a dangerous animal.’
Locative Clauses:
(21) Pitso-ra xobo naman iki.
(None) Pitso r-iki xobo naman. | ‘The parakeet is under the house.’
Possessive Clauses:
Shipibo shows that someone has something by adding an ending to the thing they have. The ending -ya means ‘with / having’, and -oma means ‘without / not having’. So you say something like “I am dog-with” for “I have a dog.” Shipibo does not care what kind of owning it is. A body part you can never lose and an object you could give away are said the same way. Owning something for good and having it just for now are also said the same way:

h: 8.2.1.1. Copular Clauses
t:
(22) E-a-ra radio-ya iki | ‘I have a radio.’
(23) E-a-ra radio-oma iki. | ‘I don’t have a radio.’
(24) E-a-ra rabé meken-ya / rabé meken-oma iki. | ‘I have two hands. / I don’t have two hands.’
(25) Rabé paranta texkan-ya r-iki e-a. | ‘I have two large bunches of plantain.’
(26) E-a rabé texkan paranta-oma iki. | ‘I don’t have two large bunches of plantain.’
In the next examples, the verb ik- ‘be’ carries endings that show the time of the action (past, future and so on):
(27) No-n papa Bari-ronki i-pao-ni-ke yawa iná-ya... | ‘Long ago our father Sun used to have white-lipped peccaries...’
(28) Bakish i-yat-ai. | ‘It is going to take place tomorrow.’
The example just above was already given in Chapter 7 as (76).
Some illnesses are described with the same “having” pattern, as if you “have” the illness (but compare ‘have diarrhea,’ in ex. (40), which works differently):
(29) E-a-ra yoná-ya iki. | ‘I have fever.’
There is a second way to say that someone has something. I describe it below, in the part on Existential Clauses (“there is / there isn’t” sentences).
Verb-less Clauses:
In everyday speech, people sometimes leave out the word ‘be’ completely. English does this too in headlines like “Prices high.” (See also ex. (84) of Chapter 6.):
(30) Ne-ke-a nete keská-ribi-ronki-ki ja jene meran. | ‘It is said that inside the water it is just like on this world.’

h: 8.2.1.1. Copular Clauses
t:
In the example below, both parts of the sentence have no verb at all:
(31) Xono raston, jato-n ponyan senen-ma. | ‘The lupuna tree was too broad, their arms were not long enough (to embrace it).’
Also, questions of the “What is it? / Who is he?” type must always leave out ‘be’. Instead, they carry a special question ending, -ri(n).

h: 8.2.1.2. Existential Clauses
t:
To say that something exists or is there (“there is …”), Shipibo uses the bare verb ja- ‘exist, live’. To say that something does not exist (“there isn’t …”), it uses the special word yama-:
(32) Ne-ska-ra kopí icha moa-tian mawá ja-káti-ai. | ‘Because of this there were many deaths in those times.’
(33) Kikin-shaman jatíbi jawéki-ronki ja-ke. | ‘(She said that) there is absolutely everything (in the next life).’
The next sentence is the answer to the question ‘Have you seen your niece?:’
(34) Yama-ra-ke, e-n-ra oin-a-ma iki. | ‘She is not here, I have not seen her.’
(35) Benbo-n-a yama-katit-ai ja-n a-ti-ma jawéki-bo. | ‘There are no special restrictions for the husband to comply with (while his wife is pregnant).’
As I said above, ja- ‘exist’ can also mean ‘live’:
(36) Ne-no r-iki jakoinra ja-ti. | ‘This is a good place to live.’
These “there is” sentences are also a way to say someone has something (like saying “there is a dog for me”):
(37) Ja-ke nokon rayos. | ‘I have a son-in-law (lit. ‘exists my son-in-law).’
The very general verb ik- ‘do (intr.), be’ can also be used to mean ‘exist / there is’:
(38) Reken-pari-ronki i-káti-ai westíora joni-ki, wano-oma-shoko, | ikaxbi-ki i-káti-ai ja tiempo-ki xopan ainbo-ki. | ‘First there was a man, a single man, but there was in those times a secana (k. gourd) woman too.’

h: 8.2.1.2. Existential Clauses
t: Ja- and yama- are also used to talk about what someone must or must not do (see 7.13.2).

h: 8.2.1.3. Other Types of Intransitive Clauses
t:
Some intransitive verbs describe something that just happens to you (“fall”, “die”). Others describe something you actively do (“dance”, “run”). Many languages treat these two kinds differently. Shipibo-Konibo (SK) does not: they look and behave exactly alike.² In both kinds, the person has no marker (the plain form, ABS). And, as Chapters 16-17 will show, both kinds can take the same endings that change how many people a verb needs.
The examples below show intransitive verbs where the person just undergoes what happens, rather than doing it on purpose.
Inactive Intransitive Clauses
(39) Mi-a-ra yaka-t-ai / nomi-ai / niskan-ai / | oxa[a]i / xana-[a]i. | ‘You are sitting / thirsty / sweating / sleeping / hot.’
(40) E-a-ra chixot-ai. | ‘I have diarrhea.’
Now look at intransitive verbs where the person is actively doing something:
There is one small exception: the describing endings -mis, -kas, and -yosma tend to go with “active” verbs (section 5.2.2).
Active Intransitive Clauses:
(41) Pena-ra sai ik-ai. | ‘Pena is crying out for help.’
(42) E-a-ra jiwi bochiki nee-ke bonko meran jiki-i. | ‘I climbed up the tree hiding in the foliage.’
The next piece from a story has several intransitive verbs: ransa- ‘dance,’ rankó- ‘limp,’ bewa- ‘sing,’ be- ‘come (non-singular),’ and nashi- ‘bathe.’ Look at the main verb, nashikana iki. The people doing it have no marker (the plain form). The other verbs carry endings that tell you the same person does the next action too. The ending -i means “at the same time”, and -ax means “before that”. These particular forms are used because the main verb is an intransitive verb:

h: 8.2.1.3. Other Types of Intransitive Clauses
t:
(43) ...jatíribi-bo ransa ransa-beiran-i, rankó rankó-beiran-i, | bewa bewa-beiran-i; be-ax-ki kori jene-n | nashi-kan-a iki. | .’..some came dancing and dancing, limping and limping, singing and singing; once they had arrived, they bathed in the golden water.’
Above, the “coming” ending -beiran is used, not -kiran. That is because more than one person is coming. (See how the “going” and “coming” endings are shared out in 7.6.1 and 7.6.2.)

h: 8.2.1.4. Clauses with Meteorological / Nature Verbs
t:
Some verbs about weather and nature are used together with the special “more than one” verbs be- ‘come (non-singular), bring’ and bo- ‘go (non-singular), carry.’ It is a bit like saying the rain “comes along”:
(44) Oi-ra be-ai. | ‘It is raining / the rain is coming.’ | Oi-ra bo-ai. | ‘The rain is moving somewhere else / is stopping.’
(45) Jene-ra be-ai / bo-ai. | ‘It is flooding, the water level is increasing / the water level is lowering.’
(46) Wakanawa-ronki be-ai / bo-ai. | ‘The school of fish is approaching / is passing.’

h: Extended Intransitive Clauses (intransitive sentences with an extra place or thing)
t: Some intransitive verbs actually need a second thing in the sentence too. I call these “stretched” intransitive verbs (linguists call them extended intransitives). There are a few kinds. Verbs of ‘happening’ need two words that both have no marker <ABS ABS>. Verbs of feeling need one plain word and one word with the ending -ki <ABS -ki>. Verbs of ‘lacking’ need one plain word and one word with the ending -n <ABS OBL-n]. Finally, a couple of verbs can take either pattern: <ABS ABS> or <ABS INTRSS> (the second word gets the “interest” ending).

h: 8.2.2.1. Verbs of ‘Happening’
t:
A couple of verbs, like ik- ‘occur, happen’ and wino-t- ‘occur, happen, experience’, take two words that both stay in the plain form, with no marker:
(47) Kikin onis-ti-bires jawéki no-n axekan-bi-ribi | no-a ik-á. | ‘An extremely sad thing happened to us because of our custom.’
(48) Ja-ska-ra jawéki e-a wino-t-a iki. | ‘Such things I experienced / happened to me.’

h: 8.2.2.2. Verbs of Emotion
t:
A few verbs of feeling, like bene- ‘be happy,’ sinat- ‘be angry,’ and shiro- ‘make fun,’ work this way. The person who has the feeling is in the plain form, with no marker. The thing that causes the feeling gets the ending -ki, a bit like English “angry at” or “happy about”. Look at these examples (see also ex. (97) of Chapter 7, and ex. (95) below):
(49) E-a-ra mi-ki bene-ai mi-n e-a a-xon-a kopí. | ‘I feel happy because of you, thanks to what you did for me.’
(50) E-a-ra Yabi-ki sinat-ai. | ‘I am angry at Yabi.’
Some speakers can also add a word for who it is about or for whose sake to this kind of sentence, as the example below shows:
(51) E-a-ra ino-ki (mi-on) raké-ke. | ‘I am scared of the jaguar (for you; i.e., because it may attack you).’

h: 8.2.2.3. Verbs of ‘Lacking’
t:
The verbs yoron- ‘suffer from the need / lack of’ and maxkat- ‘lack’ need two words. The person who is missing something is treated like the one person of an intransitive verb, so it has no marker (the plain form). The thing that is missing gets the ending -n. Even with that ending, it is still one of the two main words the verb needs:
(52) No-a-ra jawekiati-nin yoron-ai. | ‘We suffer from the lack of food.’
(53) Mawat-ax...no-a jawe-n-bi maxká-yama-ke.... | ‘When we die...we lack nothing....’
But there are some signs that the marker on the missing thing may really depend on how important or new it is in the conversation (see ex. (132) and foonote 4).

Saying ‘be hot’ and saying ‘be cold’ work very differently. For ‘be hot’ (ex. (39)), the word xana- is the verb by itself and needs only one person. For ‘be cold’, Shipibo uses the verb ik- ‘do (intr.)’ with two words. The person who feels cold is in the plain form, with no marker. The word matsi ‘cold’ gets the ending -n. It is a bit like saying “I am with cold”. Here is an example:
(54) E-a-ra matsi-n ik-ai. | ‘I am cold.’
So ‘be cold’ works like the ‘lacking’ verbs above. The only difference is that its second word is always the same: matsin.

h: 8.2.2.5. Extended Intransitives Clauses with Alternate Case Frames
t:
The verbs keen- ‘want’ and shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind’ need two words. The first is the person who wants or forgets, and it is in the plain form. The second is the thing wanted or forgotten. That second word can either have no marker, or carry the “interest” ending (INTRSS). These verbs sit halfway between intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. In this book I treat them as a kind of “stretched” intransitive verb.
Does it matter which marker the wanted thing gets with keen-? In an earlier work (Valenzuela 1997), I gave examples from the story of the ‘Stingy Inka’. They suggest that the choice may not change the meaning or the focus. The sentence below lists what the animals wanted from the Stingy Inka: blood, bile, liver, and stomach. In this list, all four things are equally important in the story. Even so, inside the very same sentence, some of the wanted things get the “interest” ending and others stay in the plain form:
(55) Ja-ska-ra ninkat-ax, [jawen jimi-n, tawi-n, taka-n, | poko, ja-baon] keen-i, be-kan-a iki, jatíbi | yoina-bo. | ‘Hearing that, wanting his blood, bilis, stomach, all those, they came, all the animals.’ (Bardales 1979:11-12, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
The next two examples come from the same story. They are about new tools and inventions the Shipibo wanted to get from the Stingy Inka. Here ‘plantain’ and ‘fire’ get the “interest” ending, while ‘pineapple’ stays in the plain form:

h: 8.2.2.5. Extended Intransitives Clauses with Alternate Case Frames
t:
(56) [Paranta-nin-ra] no-a keen-ai papá, no-n-ra atsa
(None) a-yama-ke, bona icha-yora i-ke-tian. | ‘We want plantain father, we didn’t take the yuca because there were very many isula ants.’ (Bardales 1979:15, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
(57) Bo-xon kankan yoká-ribi-kan-a iki: | “[Kankan-bicho-ressa] no-a keen-ai papá,” | a-kin a-kan-a iki. | ‘Coming back, they asked (the Inka) for pineapple too: “At least we want pineapple, father,” they told him.’ (Bardales 1979:15, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
(58) Ja-tian-ronki ja Inka-bicho-res-ki chiia i-pao-ni-ke. | Ja chii-kan-kaya-ronki ikon-bi-res iki keen-kati-kan-ai | ‘In those times, the Inka was the only one who had fire. It is said that (they) really wanted the fire.’ (Bardales 1979:15, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
However, when keen- means ‘love,’ the loved one must always take the “interest” ending. Maybe this is because the loved one is usually a person or animal, not a thing. Ex. (60) was partly given in Chapter 7 as (140):
(59) E-a-ra mi-on keen- ai. / mi-a | ‘I love you.’
(60) ...joni-shoko mi-on keen-ai-bi mi-a ja-on keen-yama-kin,
(None) mi-n pe-chi waste-n nashi-xon-ti atipan-ke. | ‘Even if (that) little man loves you, if you don’t love him you can bathe with the “piripiri to be left behind,” to his detriment (i.e., to get rid of him).’

h: 8.2.3.1. Properties of Transitive Clauses
t:
A transitive sentence is built around a transitive verb. That verb can be one by nature, or one that was made into one with an ending. You can recognize such a verb by how it behaves. The doer gets the doer marker (ERG) and the receiver has no marker (ABS). Words saying where or how something is done must “agree” with the doer, by showing a matching ending. Words for “from where” and emphatic pronouns show no matching ending at all. The verb can take a special ending meaning “against someone” and the ending -t (“to yourself”). It must use the “transitive, many people” forms of the paired “go” and “come” verbs. It goes with the transitive forms of verbs like “start” and “finish”, and it can take the helper verb ak-. Finally, it can take the ending -pake, which spreads the action over many things or places.
In SK, when the doer or the receiver is simply left out, people understand it as “he / she / it”. That is, unless the situation shows otherwise (Valenzuela 1997). Look at the examples in (61)-(62), taken from Valenzuela (1997):
(61) Ja-n-ra e-a jamá-ke. | ‘(S)he kicked me.’ | E-a-ra jamá-ke. | ‘(S)he kicked me.’
(62) E-n-ra ja jamá-ke. | ‘I kicked him / her / it.’ | E-n-ra jamá-ke. | ‘I kicked him / her / it.’

h: 8.2.3.1. Properties of Transitive Clauses
t:
Sentence (62b) really does mean a particular ‘him / her / it,’ someone already known. We know this because it is a fine answer to the question:
(63) Tso-n-ki nokon ochíti jamat-a? | ‘Who kicked my dog?’
Verbs of touching or causing are the most typical transitive verbs. But verbs of saying, thinking and seeing or hearing behave just the same way. Below, the verb yoi- ‘tell’ has a doer with the doer marker and a receiver with no marker. Also, the other part of the sentence carries the ending -xon. This ending says that the same doer does that action too:
(64) ...noko-xon-ronki chaikoni joni-n yoiy-a iki ja joni... | .’... after finding him, the chaikoni (people who now live on a different layer of reality) told the Shipibo man.’
Verbs of saying, thinking, and seeing or hearing can also take a whole sentence as the thing said, thought or seen (“she said that he came”). I deal with this in 10.3.

h: 8.2.3.2. Ditransitive Clauses
t:
Some transitive verbs need two receivers, like “give”: you give something to someone. (Remember, though, that people often leave words out.) Many languages treat these two receivers differently. English, for example, can say “give the book to Maria”. Other languages treat them both the same. In SK, nothing in the grammar tells the two apart. Take a verb like meni- ‘give’. Both the thing given and the person who gets it stay in the plain form, with no marker. Putting any other marker on either one makes the sentence wrong. Look at the next example from a story:
(65) Tso-n-bira tita-shoko awá nami meni-a? | ‘Who could have given tapir meat to (our) grandmother?’
Also, the two receivers can swap places, and nothing else in the sentence changes:
(66) Tso-n-bira awá nami tita-shoko meni-a? | ‘Who could have given tapir meat to (our) grandmother?’
I say more about this in section 12.3, where I look at how receivers behave. Below are more sentences with verbs that naturally take two receivers. Sentences (67) and (68) have the speaking verbs yoká- ‘ask for’ and yoi- ‘tell;’ while (69) and (70) have the giving verbs bane- ‘return’ and inan- ‘give as present:’
(67) Jato-n jawékiati keyó-ke-tian jo-á iki jawen awin e-a | paranta yoká-ti. | ‘Once their food supplies were finished, his wife came to ask me for plantain.’

h: 8.2.3.2. Ditransitive Clauses
t:
(68) ...bakish e-a yoi-iba-kan-ke meskó keská shinan. | ‘Yesterday (during the meeting) people gave me all kinds of ideas.’
(69) Ino-n-ra xae jawen bichi kené-ya | bane-yama-ni-ke. | ‘The jaguar didn’t return the anteater his designed fur.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
(70) E-n-ra westíora koton nokon papa inan-ai. | ‘I am giving my father a shirt as a present.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
You can also make a two-receiver verb out of a verb with just one receiver, by adding an ending (see Chapter 16 on “make someone do it” endings and Chapter 17 on endings that bring in an extra person).

h: Ambitransitive Clauses (verbs that can be either transitive or intransitive)
t:
Most SK verbs are either transitive verbs or intransitive verbs by nature. To switch a verb from one type to the other, you normally have to add an ending. But a small group of verbs can be used both ways with no ending at all, like English “break” (“I broke the glass” / “the glass broke”). Linguists call these ambitransitive verbs. How do you know which way the verb is used in a sentence? You look at how many people or things go with it, at their markers, and at other clues. One such verb is mapet- ~ mapé- ‘go up (at a slant).’ In the sentence below, mapé- has just one person, in the plain form. The word for “where” after it shows the matching ending for an intransitive verb:
(71) E-a-ra mapé-ke jene merano-a-x. / e-n | ‘I came up from the water.’
But mapé- can also take a receiver: the place you go up, in the plain form. Then the person going up gets the doer marker:
(72) E-n-ra xobo mapé-ke. / e-a-ra | ‘I came up to the house.’ (Lit. ‘I came up the house.’)
The verb bepo- can also be used both ways. As an intransitive verb, it means ‘have sleep in the eye’. As a transitive verb, it means ‘cover somebody’s eyes:’
(73) Nato bake-ra bepo-ke. | ‘This child has sleep in his eyes.’

h: Ambitransitive Clauses (verbs that can be either transitive or intransitive)
t:
(74) E-n-ra bake bepo-ke nisakan. | ‘I covered the child’s eyes with little sticks / leaves.’
A third verb that works both ways is beso- ‘awake, wake up’, which also means ‘scrub somebody’s face:’
(75) E-a-ra beso-ke. | ‘I woke up.’
(76) E-n-ra nokon bake beso-ke. | ‘I washed / scrubbed my child’s face.’
Both bepo- and beso- start with the body-part beginning piece be-, which comes from bero ‘eye.’
Finally, the verb maro-, which people translate into Spanish as ‘sell, buy’, needs two words. But the person doing it can either have no marker or carry the doer marker:
(77) E-a-ra chopa maro-ke. | ‘I bought / sold clothes.’
(78) E-n-ra chopa maro-ke. | ‘I bought / sold clothes.’

h: Clauses with Cognate Object Verbs (sentences like "sing a song" (the object repeats the verb))
t:
Some verbs come with a built-in receiver that adds almost nothing to the meaning. English has these too: “sing a song”, “dream a dream”. Linguists call them cognate object verbs. These verbs are partly intransitive verbs and partly transitive verbs, by different amounts. Saying the receiver out loud sounds better when it has a describing word with it (“sing a sad song”). In such cases the describing word adds real meaning, a bit like saying how the action was done (Levin 1993:95-6). The name “cognate” means “related”: the receiver is a noun made from the same verb, or from a verb with a similar meaning. In many languages, these sentences use the same markers as a normal transitive sentence (Givón 1984:105). In this book I stretch the idea a little. I also include verbs whose receiver is very limited and adds nothing to the meaning, even when the verb and the noun are not related words. Some SK verbs of this kind are: bake-n- ‘deliver (a baby),’ bewa- ‘sing,’ ae ik- ‘burp / belch,’ joti- ‘smoke,’ bekan- ‘spread (cotton),’ axa-n- ‘poison (fish),’ beax- ‘mix (the new yuca beer with the fermented one),’ and beten- ‘cook beten (kind of thick
soup).’ The examples below show how these verbs are used with a receiver that is made by the action (the baby, the song, and so on).

h: Clauses with Cognate Object Verbs (sentences like "sing a song" (the object repeats the verb))
t:
Some of these verbs use the pattern <ABS ABS>: both the person and the receiver are in the plain form, with no marker:
(79) Nokon awin-ra westiora benbo bake-n-ke. | ‘My wife gave birth to a baby boy.’
(80) Papa-shoko-ra mashá bewai. | ‘Grandfather is singing a mashá (kind of traditional song).’
The sentences below show that a verb like ae ik- ‘burp, belch’ does not accept a bare receiver. The receiver has to have a describing word with it:
(81) E-a-ra naranshi-bires ae i-ke. | ‘I burped pure pop drink.’ | E-a-ra naranshi ae i-ke. | ‘I burped pop drink.’
Other verbs of this kind use the pattern <ERG ABS>: the person gets the doer marker and the receiver has no marker, as in a normal transitive sentence:
(82) Tita-n-ra waxmen bekan-ai. | ‘My mother is going to spread the cotton.’
(83) E-n-ra pichá, boe, moxo baton
(None) axa-n-ke. | ‘I poisoned palometa, boquichico and lisa fish.’
(84) E-n-ra wanin xeati beax-ke. | ‘I mixed the pijuayo (fruit of a palm tree, Bactris gasipaes, Palmae) beer.’
Another verb of this kind with the <ERG ABS> pattern is beten- ‘cook beten (k. thick soup).’ The verb looks exactly like the noun beten ‘k. of thick soup.’ Usually a noun needs an ending before it can work as a transitive verb. But beten- is special: it can work as one directly, with nothing added:

h: Clauses with Cognate Object Verbs (sentences like "sing a song" (the object repeats the verb))
t:
(85) Tita-n-ra beten-ke. | ‘Mother cooked beten soup.’
As (85) shows, the bare word beten- works as a transitive verb by itself. So the person cooking must get the doer marker. You could also say the same sentence with ‘mother’ in the plain form instead. But then it would mean the odd thing that someone else cooked mother! In the example below, beten- has a receiver said out loud:
(86) Tita-n-ra chaxo beten-ke. | ‘Mother cooked deer beten.’
As I said above, these “built-in receiver” verbs sit at different points between intransitive and transitive verbs. I showed that bake-n- ‘deliver a child,’ bewa- ‘sing’ and ae ik- ‘burp / belch’ use the <ABS ABS> pattern (no doer marker). On the other hand, verbs like joti- ‘smoke,’ bekan- ‘spread cotton,’ axa-n- ‘poison fish,’ beax- ‘mix the new drink with the fermented one,’ and beten- ‘cook beten soup’ use the <ERG ABS> pattern (with the doer marker). In the first group, bewa- ‘sing’ has two odd features. First, it can also use another pattern, <ABS OBL>, like some “stretched” intransitive verbs. Second, it can still take the ending meaning “against someone”, which normally only goes on transitive verbs:
(87) E-a-ra shiro bewakan bew-ai. | ‘I am going to sing a love song.’
The setting for the next sentence is a modern-style contest, where people take turns singing different songs:

h: Clauses with Cognate Object Verbs (sentences like "sing a song" (the object repeats the verb))
t:
(88) Mi-n-ra e-a i-kas-ai bewá-ribi mi-n-pari e-a | bewa-naan-ke. | ‘You sang first the same song I wanted to sing (to my detriment).’
Verbs with the <ERG ABS> pattern behave almost exactly like transitive verbs. There is just one difference: they cannot take the “to yourself” ending or the “to each other” ending. The exception is beten-, which can take the “to yourself” ending to become
betemee- with the extremely unusual meaning ‘turn into beten (k. thick soup)’ (Valenzuela 1997).

h: Clauses with Prefixed Verbs (sentences with body-part pieces on the verb)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo (SK) has a set of beginning pieces that stand for body parts. Each one is usually the first syllable of the noun for that particular body part (see 6.2.6). These pieces combine with many verbs, attaching to the front. They add information about where the action happens on the body, much like English "elbow" in elbow someone. The meaning of the resulting verb is generally easy to guess. The body-part piece does not count as an extra person in the sentence. So the verb keeps the same number of people it had before. An intransitive verb stays an intransitive verb. A transitive verb stays one too. Most of these sentences work in a special way. The owner of the body part becomes a main person in the sentence. The body part itself is pushed to the side, like "I hit him on the head" instead of "I hit his head." Linguists call this "possessor raising." In Shipibo it is required with these verbs.
There seems to be no single rule that tells you which verbs can take a body-part beginning piece. But the meanings of these verbs often share some features. They tend to involve touching, moving or position, making something happen, or a (change of) state. Some verbs get shorter when the body-part piece is added. In those cases, the new verb is a body-part piece plus a shortened bare verb. A list of body-part beginning pieces was given in 6.2.6.

h: Clauses with Prefixed Verbs (sentences with body-part pieces on the verb)
t:
Intransitive roots
a) (Change of) State: be- < bero ‘eye’ + jotit- ‘have a tic’
(89) E-a-ra be-otit-ai. | ‘I have a tic in the eye.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
b) Motion / Position: ne- < jene ‘flowing water’ + ni- ‘stand’
(90) Ja ani jema tenaman-ronki ik-á iki westíora jiwi kikin icha | bimi-ya ne-ni-t-a. | ‘On the shore of the large village there was a tree full of fruit standing in the water.’
te- < texkan ‘large bunch (e.g., of plantain)’ + piko-t ‘come out’
(91) Ja ani wai-nko moa xawi-bo wira-[a]x ik-ai-tian, | paranta te-piko-t-ai-tian, nokon tita-n | chopa-a-kin senen’-a iki. | ‘When in the large chacra the sugarcanes were already becoming thick and the plantain was coming out in large bunches, my mother finished manufacturing the clothes.’
c) Emotion: xe- < xeta ‘tooth’ + rabin- ‘be embarrassed at’
(92) Piko-ra xe-rábin-ai. | ‘Piko is embarrassed at his teeth.’
Transitive roots: ta- < tae ‘foot’ + nexa- ‘tie’
(93) ...ja ochíti no-n mecha-a-kas-ai-bo-ki yatan-ti iki | nishi-n, ta-nex-nonxon. | .’..the dogs we want to make good hunters must be held with a rope, tying them by the feet.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
na- < napo ‘interior’ + tsaka- ‘spear’ (ex. (31) from Ch. 4 is repeated below)
(94) Ka-kin no-n na-tsá’ na-tsá-bain-a iki, | na-tsá’ na-tsá-bain-a iki. | ‘While going (up the river) we kept on spearing (arrows) into the water.’

h: Clauses with Prefixed Verbs (sentences with body-part pieces on the verb)
t:
Some body-part beginning pieces are used with a less literal meaning. For example, ma- from mapo ‘head’ can also mean ‘surface, top’, just as English says “the head of the table”. Here is an example with ke-:
ke- < kexá ‘mouth, lips;’ also ‘edge’ + sika- ‘paint, put something liquid’
(95) ...mi-ki ainbo sinat-ai-tian, mi-n jawen chitonti xeni-n | ke-ski-nan-a, ja ainbo tsini-ti | ka-[a]i. | .’..if a woman gets angry at you, you put (river dolphin’s) fat on the edge of her pampanilla and then she will start having sex with any man.’
It doesn’t happen often, but a body-part beginning piece can appear together with a full body-part noun that says where:
(96) Nokon ochíti-ra jawen jina-nko ji-natex-ke. | ‘My dog bit its (own) tail.’
(97) Tsoma-n-ra Rona (meken-ki) me³-tsó a-ke. | ‘Tsoma kissed Rona on the hand / kissed Rona’s hand.’
As I explained in 2.2.6, SK words are usually stressed (said louder) on the first syllable, unless the second syllable is “heavy”. You would expect a verb with a body-part beginning piece to follow this rule too, so the stress would move to the beginning piece. But many verbs whose first syllable is “light” keep their own stress when the piece is added. So the whole verb does not act like one single word for the purposes of stress:

h: Clauses with Prefixed Verbs (sentences with body-part pieces on the verb)
t:
Some speakers treat the verb be-tsó- [FACE-ONOM:kiss] as one single word meaning ‘kiss’, with no separate pieces, and they do not accept the form me-tsó-.
na-yásan- [INTERIOR-‘to seat’] ‘put something in the interior of:’
(98) Ja-tian ani nonti-n westíora chomo na-yásan-kan-ai. | ‘Then, they put (sit) a jar in the interior of a big canoe.”
Sometimes the stress falls on the second syllable even though it is “light”. This seems to make up for sounds that were dropped from the bare verb (see also example (94) with na-tsá-). Compare the stress in the following pair, built on choka- ‘wash’ and its “to yourself” form chokii(t)- ‘wash oneself’. (To make things clear, I mark the stress on all the body-part verbs below, even where it just follows the normal rule.):
ra- < yora ‘body’ + choka- ‘wash’
The next sentence shows something similar. In jan-tsé-, which contains a shortened form of tseka-, the stress stays on the bare verb. But in ja-nia-, the stress falls on the body-part beginning piece:
ja(n)- < jana ‘tongue’ + tseka- ‘take out’ and nia- ‘introduce, keep’
(100) Jainoa-ki ja joni-n, bimi jan-tsé-ti shinan-kin,
(None) jawen metoti iso ja-nia-a iki. | ‘Then, planning to take the fruit out of the spidermonkey’s mouth, the man introduced his finger in its mouth.’ (Valenzuela 1997, Ministerio de Educación and ILV 1982:4)

h: Clauses with Prefixed Verbs (sentences with body-part pieces on the verb)
t:
There are also cases where the bare verb keeps all its sounds and its own stress. The verb forms below have the “not finished yet” ending -ai:
As I said earlier, adding a body-part piece usually does not change what kind of verb it is. An intransitive verb stays an intransitive verb. But there are exceptions. In the next example, the intransitive verb ik- ‘do (intr.)’ becomes a transitive verb when it gets the body-part piece ma-. You can tell because the doer now has the doer marker, and there is a receiver, panyon, in the plain form:
ma- < mapo ‘head’ + ik- ‘do (intr.), be’ ‘put something on one’s own head’
(102) [E-n panyon ma-i-ke-tian]-ra, e-a joni-baon | osan-ke. | ‘When I put a kerchief on my head people laughed at me.’ (Valenzuela 1997, Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:241)
Usually the action is done to someone else’s body part. For example, ki-pas- means ‘pad someone’s thigh’. But with some verbs, such as ki-pish- ‘to have one’s own thigh joint dislocated,’ the body part belongs to the doer (see also ex. (102)):
Both bare verbs, pisha- and patsa-, are transitive verbs. So nothing in the word tells you whether the action is done to yourself or to someone else.
There are also other combinations. A verb can have two body-part pieces plus a bare verb, or two body-part pieces and no bare verb at all, or a body-part piece plus a sound-word (like “splash”), and so on. Below, two body-part pieces that both show where are attached to the same verb:

h: Clauses with Prefixed Verbs (sentences with body-part pieces on the verb)
t:
(104) Pake-t-ax-ki | chi-chá-yaka-kain-a iki. | ‘When she fell to the ground she fell on her buttocks.’
The next example with two body-part pieces is especially interesting. Here ma- HEAD shows where the action happens, while me- HAND shows what it is done with:
(105) Rima-mea-x jo-xon-ra papa-shoko-n jawen baba-bo | ma-me-pas-ke. | ‘Returning from Lima, grandfather patted his grandchildren’s heads.’
The next sentences are unusual. The verb has two body-part beginning pieces, but no bare verb at all.
In (105), it is easy to see what pe- and chi- are doing. But in (106), it is not clear what job chi- is doing:
(106) Ja-ra pe-chi-ke. | ‘He is turning his back on someone.’ (the SK sentence is monovalent)
(107) E-n-ra jasin tsaka-kin kene-ke, wetsa-ori-res | me-chi-xon. | ‘Shooting the arrow towards the wrong point, I missed the paujil (kind of wild turkey).’ | Ja-ra neno me-chi-ke. | ‘She moved his hand towards here.’
The word piece me(e)- ‘hand’ can also work as a verb all by itself. Then it means ‘touch, do something bad to somebody.’ Usually the hands are used, but not always. You can see this in example (108):
(108) Kinan-a pekáo moa, jakiribi moa semana pia | me-yama[-a] pekáo, no-a ka-ríba-a iki. | ‘After throwing up (the plant preparation to become a good fisher / hunter) and after not having touched an arrow for a week, we went (to fish) again.’

h: Clauses with Onomatopoeic Verbs (sentences with sound words as verbs)
t:
Many Shipibo-Konibo verbs are built from a sound word, like English bang or creak. The sound word is followed by one of two helper verbs. The helper ik- ‘do (intr.)’ makes an intransitive verb. The helper ak- ‘do (tr.)’ makes a transitive verb. (See also Double Auxiliarization in 4.7.) Let's look at a few examples:
xonxin ik- ‘whistle’ vs. xonxin ak- ‘whistle at’
(109) Tsoma-ra xonxin i-ke. | ‘Tsoma whistled.’ | Tsoma-n-ra ainbo xonxin a-ke. | ‘Tsoma whistled at the woman.’
teash ik- ‘break (intr.) producing a noise’ teash ak- ‘break sth. by stepping on it and making it produce a noise’
(110) Xena-ra bochiki-a-x pake-t-i teash i-ke. | ‘Falling from upwards, the worm died producing a noise.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
(111) E-n-ra xena teash a-ke. | ‘I stepped on the worm producing a noise.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
In (111) and (112), nobody actually says ‘died’ or ‘stepped.’ You have to guess those meanings from the situation. Word for word, the sentences say something like ‘Falling from upwards, the worm produced a noise “teash” (dying);’ and ‘I caused the worm to produce a noise “teash” (by stepping on it).’
tii ik- ‘the horn blows’ vs. tii ak- ‘blow a horn’
(112) Moa-ra tii i-ke. | ‘(The horn) blew already.’ (Valenzuela 1997) | E-n-ra moa tii a-ke. | ‘I made the horn blow already.’ (Valenzuela 1997)

h: Clauses with Onomatopoeic Verbs (sentences with sound words as verbs)
t:
jojó ik- ‘bark’ vs. jojó ak- ‘bark at’
The next example comes from a traditional kind of speech. People use it when they treat a dog with plant medicine, so that the dog becomes a good hunter:
(113) ...mi-n jojó a-yama-[a]i-tian-ra e-n mi-a | rao-n-ribi-ai, mecha ochíti ik-ai kaman! | ‘If you do not bark (at animals) I will treat you with plant medicine again, until you become a good-hunter dog.’ (being told to a dog while “curing” it)
biski ik- ‘shake oneself’ vs. biski ak- ‘shake something’
(114) Ochíti jene-nko pota-kan-a mapet-ax-a | biski biski ik-ai. | ‘The dog that was thrown into the water climbed up (to the land) and is shaking.’
(115) Tita-n-ra paranta xea-ti biski biski ak-ai. | ‘Mother is beating the plantain drink.’
mox ik- ‘creak’ vs. mox ak- ‘chew’
(116) Ronon ewa-n peká-ronki mox ik-ai no-n jamat-a. | ‘It is said that the boa’s back creaks if we step on it.’
(117) E-n-ra paranta xoo mox a-ke. | ‘I chewed the raw plantain.’
Sometimes the intransitive helper ik- means ‘to yourself.’ This happens when the doer is a person. For example, to' ak- means ‘shoot,’ but to' ik- means ‘suicide, shoot oneself.’ In the same way, me-tsó ak- means ‘kiss someone on the hand,’ and me-tsó ik- means ‘kiss oneself on the hand.’ In me-tsó ak- / ik-, the sound word tsó comes after the body-

h: Clauses with Onomatopoeic Verbs (sentences with sound words as verbs)
t:
part beginning piece me- ‘on the hand.’ (To say ‘kiss on the face,’ you would use be-tsó instead.)
Some verbs of this kind use a short quoted phrase where the sound word would be:
“kawé” ak- ‘take someone somewhere’ vs. “kawé” ik- ‘say good-bye, leave’
(118) E-n mi-a “ka-wé” ak-ai | ‘I am taking you.’ (Lit. ‘I am telling you “go!”’). (Valenzuela 1997) | Ja-ra “ka-wé” ik-ai moa. | ‘He is leaving.’ (Lit. ‘He is saying “go!” already’). (Valenzuela 1997)
“kai” ak- ‘say good-bye to somebody leaving’ “kai” ik- ‘say good-bye when leaving’
(119) Ja-n-ra moa no-a “ka-[a]i” ak-ai. | ‘He is saying “good-bye!” to us already.’ (Valenzuela 1997) | Ja-ra moa “ka-[a]i” ik-ai. | ‘He is saying “good-bye!” already.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
“bewé” ak- ‘ask / order someone to bring something’
(120) E-n-ra “be-wé” a-ke yami rabé. | ‘I ordered (him / her) to bring the two axes.’ (Lit. ‘I told (him / her) “bring!” the two axes’). (Valenzuela 1997)
“iráke” ak- ‘thank someone’
(121) E-n-ra mi-a “iráke” ak-ai mi-n e-a a-kin-a kopí. | ‘I thank you for your help.’
Shipibo-Konibo speakers often make new words this way. They take a sound word and add a general verb like ‘do.’ For example, chaka chaka a-ti [ONOM do.T-INF] means ‘sowing machine.’

h: Desiderative Clauses (sentences about wanting)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has an ending, -kas, that means ‘want to.’ When you add it to a transitive verb, something can change. The doer may lose the doer marker (ERG) and appear in the plain form (ABS). (Sentences with the verb keen- ‘want’ are covered in 10.3.1.) Why does this happen? Hopper and Thompson (1980) say some sentences are “more transitive” than others. A sentence about wanting is weaker in this way than a normal one. Think about what a typical transitive sentence describes: someone really does something, and something really happens to the receiver. A ‘want’ sentence breaks all of these rules. Nothing actually happens yet. The person is not really acting, only wishing. And the receiver is not affected at all. We can also add that a
‘want’ sentence, unlike a normal one, does not tell us whether the action ever happens.⁴
(122) E-n onan-shaman-yama-ke o-ri-bo. | ‘I don’t know those (places) well.’
(123) Tashi-nko-ronki metsá iki, ja kopí-ra e-a onan-kas-ai. | ‘I heard that it is beautiful the place where the salt is, therefore I want to know it.’
There are exceptions to this rule. I have described them before (Valenzuela 1997, 2000b). Take the sentence below. The doer may keep the doer marker if the receiver, the ‘fish,’ is a particular fish. This is especially true if the speakers can see that fish while they are talking. But the doer may appear in the plain form if it is just ‘fish’ in general, or fish nobody can see:

h: Desiderative Clauses (sentences about wanting)
t:
(124) E-a-ra yapa pi-kas-ai. | ‘I want to eat fish.’ | E-n-ra yapa pi-kas-ai. | ‘I want to eat the fish (e.g., that is on the table).’
There is another way to explain why the doer appears in the plain form. It has to do with the history of the language. As I said in 3.2.2.2, the ‘want’ ending probably came from another ending, -kas, which turns verbs into describing words. So ‘want’ sentences may once have been sentences turned into nouns.
So the marker on the doer changes in the sentences above. This fits Hopper and Thompson’s idea: a sentence is more strongly transitive when its receiver is a clear, particular thing (see 15.1-15.2).
The same rule, more or less, shows up in the next two examples from real stories. In (125), the doer of yoikasai has the doer marker (ERG). That is because the receiver is a particular, clearly known thing:
(125) E-n-ra mato moa-tian joi-bo yoi-kas-ai, nokon | papa-shoko-n e-a oxe napon yaká-xon yoi-katit-ai-bo. | ‘I want to tell you the old stories that my grandfather used to tell me when we sat together in the moonlight.’
In the next example, the speaker talks about her adopted son. He wants to find a mestizo girlfriend. But he has no particular woman in mind. And sure enough, the doer is in the plain form (ABS):

h: Desiderative Clauses (sentences about wanting)
t: (126) Nokon onan bake-ra ik-á iki universidain kirika ak-í. | Ja-tian bake ik-á iki nawa merati a-kas-i. | ‘My adoptive son was studying at the university. Then he wanted to have a mestizo girlfriend.’

h: 8.2.9.1. Affirmative Indefinite Clauses
t:
Here is how to say ‘someone did it’ or ‘something happened’ when you don't know who or what. You use a question word, like ‘who’ or ‘what,’ plus the little ending -bira. This -bira means ‘probably’ or ‘about.’ It usually goes on the verb ik- ‘do (intr.), be,’ or on the word being stressed in the sentence:
(127) Tso-a-ra sai i-bira-[a]i. | ‘Somebody is crying out for help.’
(128) Nokon poi-ra beno-ai tso-betan-bira. | ‘My sister will marry somebody.’ (man speaking)
(129) Tso-a-ra jema-n rario-nin-bira yometso-ke. | ‘Somebody stole the village’s radio.’
(130) Tso-n-ra jema-n koshi-bira rishki-ke. | ‘Somebody hit the village chief (with a pole).’
(131) Kesiman-ra e-a bo-ma-iba-ke westíora | jawe-bira-ribi.... | ‘Kesin sent me something....’

h: 8.2.9.2. Negative Indefinite Clauses
t:
To say ‘nobody,’ ‘nothing,’ ‘nowhere’ and so on, you also use a question word. It is usually followed by the stress ending -bi. Then the main verb is put in the negative. People also often put the Spanish word ni ‘neither’ in front of the question word.
(132) Ka-xon oin-a iki jatíbi jawéki, moa jawe⁵-bi maxká-yama-[a]i... | ‘After having gone there I saw everything, nothing was missing...’
(133) Ja no-n joné meratibo tso-n onan-yama-[a]i. | ‘Nobody knows (about) our secret lovers.’
(134) Ja-ská-ribi jawe-tian-bi no-n ponsen pi-[y]ama-[a]i. | ‘Likewise, we never eat sloth.’
(135) Jawe-keská a-xon-bi pota-ma-ti atipan-yama-ke | jawen keen i-ke-tian. | ‘There is no way I can make her leave him since it is her will (to be with him).’
(136) E-a-ra moa jawe-keskat-ax-bi ka-yama-[a]i! | ‘There is no way I am going (back)!’
Look at the second person in this example, after the verb maxká-. Verbs of ‘lacking’ usually put a special marker on that person or thing. Here, though, it is in the plain form (ABS). This may be because the thing is not a particular, specific thing.

h: Participant Agreement (words that "agree" with who is doing the action)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has an unusual feature. Words that tell you where, how or how much (like ‘there,’ ‘well’ or ‘all’) change their ending. The ending depends on who the sentence is about, and what role that person plays. Parts of sentences that do this job change too. The same is true in other Panoan languages. This is a striking feature of Panoan grammar. Linguists used to describe it as agreeing with the verb's type (intransitive or transitive). But see the discussion in 15.3, 19.2.1 and 19.2.2, and examples (142a-b). It is surprising, because words like ‘there’ or ‘well’ are usually thought never to change form, or at least never to take endings.⁶ I will call this feature participant agreement (PA for short). It works inside one sentence, and also between sentences. In this section, I only look at how it works inside one sentence. How it works between sentences is covered in 9.1. Chapter 19 is all about this very interesting feature.
Inside one sentence, words telling place, manner, stage of life, and quantity change their endings. So do nouns used in these jobs. The ending depends on which person they describe (see also the emphatic pronouns in 6.1.2). Words for time do not change this way (Valenzuela 1999:358).
In some Australian Aboriginal languages, words like ‘there’ or ‘quickly’ also match the people they describe, by taking the same markers (Austin 1988 and 1995, Austin & Bresnan 1996, Goddard 1983:56-61). But in at least some of these languages, word order is very free. There, those markers are just the normal ones. So you can explain them simply as describing words matching the noun they go with (Givón 1990:886, see also Valenzuela 1999:366-8). In Maori, words telling how something is done match the verb in another way (Bauer 1993:92).

h: Locative-Allative Adjuncts ("in / at / to a place" phrases)
t:
Look at the words telling where to or where at. When they describe the doer of a transitive verb, they get an extra ending, -xon (138). With an intransitive verb, the place word can only describe that one person. So no extra ending is needed, or even allowed (137):
(137) Bake-ra xobo-n tsini-ai. / xobo-n-xon | ‘The child is playing at home.’ (Valenzuela 1999:358)
(138) Jatian ja bake-n-a ainbaon jawen bene-n | xobo-n-xon bake-shoko ani-a-[a]i. / xobo-n | ‘Then, the woman who delivers a baby raises the little child in her husband’s house.’

h: Ablative Adjuncts ("from a place" phrases)
t:
Now the words telling where from. With intransitive verbs, they need the ending -x. It shows they describe the one person (139). But with the verb ‘to be,’ they get no extra ending. That's because there they just act like describing words (140). In transitive sentences,
words telling where from always describe the receiver. So again, they show no extra ending (141):
(139) Jaino-a-x bewa-kan-ai ja iná | tsak[a]-ainko-ni-a-x... | ‘Then, they sang from (the place) where they shot at the animal...’
(140) Ma-péken-xon oin-a iki xoxo bake-bo nai-kamea ik-ai. | ‘Uncovering them, (he) saw the illegitimate children that were from the sky.’
(141) Jain-xon moa nokon papa-n yoa-bo tsinki-a ik-á iki | wai-nko-ni-a. | ‘By that time, my father had already gathered the crops from the chacra.’
The next examples show more clearly what these endings do. They tell you which person in the sentence the place word describes. In (142a-b), the same transitive sentence has two different endings on the place word:
(142) E-n -ra kachio-kea ninká-ke. | ‘I heard it from the forest.’ (the noise came from the forest) | E-n-ra kachio-xon ninká-ke. | ‘I heard it from the forest.’ (I was in the forest)

h: From Place Adjuncts to Conjunctions (how place phrases became linking words)
t: Place words built on jain ‘there,’ with the endings we just saw, are also used as joining words, like English then or and so. They join sentences, and parts of sentences. You can see jainoax, jainxon and jainoa joining sentences in examples (36), (110) and (121) of Chapter 7, and in examples (141) and (95) of this chapter. jainoax joins parts of one sentence in example (169) of Chapter 6, and example (47) of Chapter 7.

h: Quantity and Manner Adjuncts ("how much" and "how" phrases)
t:
Most words telling how or how much can take an ending showing who they describe. One ending is for the one person of an intransitive verb (S). Another is for the doer of a transitive verb (A). Look at these examples with jatik ~ jatí ‘altogether, all:’
(143) Ja-ská-ke-tian, jatik-ax-bi bo-kan-a iki, neet-i. | ‘Then, they started to go up altogether.’ (Valenzuela 1999:362)
(144) Jain-xon-ronki nami yoá a-káti-kan-ai jatí-xon-bi pi-ti. | ‘Then they cooked the meat in order to eat altogether.’ (Valenzuela 1999:362)
Examples (145) and (146) show the word for ‘well.’ It comes from the same base word as ‘good.’ It can take two different sets of these endings (Valenzuela 1999:362-3):
(145) Jakon-ax ja-kan-we! | ‘Live well!’ | Jakon-i ja-kan-we! | ‘Live well!’
(146) Jakon-a-xon yoá a-wé! | ‘Cook well!’ | Jakon-a-kin yoá a-wé! | ‘Cook well!’
In (145a) and (146a), the endings are -ax (for S) and -xon (for A). These are the same endings we saw on the where from and where at words. The endings in the (b) examples are different. They are the same as the markers that say ‘the same person is doing two things at once.’ (These are covered in section 9.1.2. See also the S ending in kikin-i̱, examples (2) and (27) of Chapter 4, and (20) and (37) of Chapter 5.)

h: Quantity and Manner Adjuncts ("how much" and "how" phrases)
t: In (146a-b), the ‘how’ word contains the transitive verb a(k)- ‘do (tr.), make.’ The where at and where from words don't have it. This fact suggests something about history. Some of these words may once have been two short sentences, or two verbs in a row (Valenzuela 1999).

h: Polar Questions (yes/no questions)
t:
Here is how to ask a yes/no question. You add the little ending -ki to the first important word or phrase of the sentence. This is usually the word being stressed. You cannot put -ki anywhere else. You also cannot use -ki twice in one question. In questions, the verb also takes a special, unfinished-looking form. (Sentences with the verb ‘to be’ work differently, as we'll see.) Questions in Shipibo-Konibo usually go up in pitch at the end, like in English. Look at these examples:⁷
(147) Mi-a-ra atsa wai-nko ka-[a]i. | ‘You are going to the yuca chacra.’ | Mi-a-ki atsa wai-nko ka-[a]i? | ‘Are you going to the yuca chacra?’ | Atsa wai-nko-ki mi-a ka-[a]i? | ‘Are you going to the yuca chacra?’
Most sentences showing questions were given to me by Mr. Yoi Sani (Luis Márquez Pinedo). So the less common ones still need to be checked with other speakers.
Sometimes the first or only important word is the verb. Then -ki goes inside the verb, just before the ending that marks the time of the action:
(None) Ka-ki-ai mi-a atsa wai-nko? | ‘Are you going to the yuca chacra?’
You can also leave out the question ending -ki. Then you can still tell it's a question by the way the voice rises. Sometimes you can also tell by the verb form, if it is different from the form used in a normal statement.

h: Polar Questions (yes/no questions)
t:
You can also ask about one specific word in the sentence. You say that word with strong force and a rising voice. And you mark it with the word piece -shaman:
(148) Mi-a-ki bewa-shaman-kas-ai? | ‘Do you want to SING? (rather than dance)?’
Questions with the verb ‘to be’ use a different question ending, -rin, instead of -ki:
(149) Wesna-rin jakon shinan-ya ainbo? | ‘Is Wesna a generous / smart woman?’
(150) Jawe ak-í-rin mi-a, ainbo? | ‘Woman, what are you doing?’

h: Content Questions (who/what/where questions)
t: Questions asking for information (who, what, where…) use question words. These are built from jawe ‘what’ and tso- ‘who.’ I gave the whole set, with examples, in 6.1.5, where I discussed question words. You can find more examples in the next section.

h: 8.4.2.1. Questioning Constituents of the Main Clause
t:
You can ask about any part of a main sentence. Just move that part to the very start of the sentence, and mark it with the question ending.
Declarative
(151) Wesna-n-ra sabado-nin atsa xeati Tsoma | xea-ma-iba-ke, escuelainko-xon | ‘Wesna invited Tsoma to drink yuca beer, on Saturday, in the school.’
Questioning the Transitive Subject:
(152) Tso-n-ki Tsoma atsa xeati xea-ma-ibat-a
(None) sabado-nin, escuelainko-xon? | ‘Who invited Tsoma to drink yuca beer on Saturday in the school?
Questioning the Patient Object:
(153) Jawe-ki Wesna-n Tsoma xea-ma-ibat-a | sabado-nin, escuelainko-xon? | ‘What did Wesna invite Tsoma to drink on Saturday in the school?
Questioning the Recipient Object:
(154) Tso-a-ki Wesna-n xea-ma-ibat-a atsa xeati, | sabado-nin, escuelainko-xon? | ‘Whom did Wesna invite to drink yuca beer on Saturday in the school?
Questioning a Time Adjunct:
(155) Jawe-tian-ki Wesna-n Tsoma atsa xeati | xea-ma-ibat-a escuelain-xon? | ‘When did Wesna invited Tsoma to drink yuca beer in the school?
Questioning a Locative Adjunct::
(156) Jaono-xon-ki Wesna-n Tsoma atsa xeati xea-ma-ibat-a | sabado-nin? | ‘Where did Wesna invite Tsoma to drink yuca beer on Saturday?
Questioning the Predicate::
(157) Wesna-n-ki Tsoma jawe ak-á escuelain-xon, Sabado-nin? | ‘What did Wesna do to Tsoma in the school, on Saturday?
Questioning Manner Adjuncts:
Asking ‘how?’ is more complicated. You need a stand-in verb, a bit like English do in ‘How did he do it?’, in a ‘like this’ phrase:

h: 8.4.2.1. Questioning Constituents of the Main Clause
t:
(158) Wesna-n-ra jakon a-kin yoa ak-ai. | ‘Wesna cooks well.’
(159) Jawe keská a-kin Wesna-n yoa ak-ai? | ‘How does Wesna cook?
(160) Wesna-n-ra yoa ak-ai jawen tita-n keská. | ‘Wesna cooks like her mother.’
(161) Tso-n yoa ak-ai keská a-kin-ki Wesna-n yoa ak-ai? | ‘Like whom does Wesna cook?’

h: 8.4.2.2. Questioning Two Sentence Constituents
t:
You can ask about two things at once, like ‘Who gave what?’ But -ki can appear only once. It goes after the first part of the sentence, which is also the first thing being asked about. Or you can leave -ki out completely:
(162) E-n-ra Wesna Ronóyain-xon onan-a iki. | ‘I met Wesna in Ronoya.’
(163) Jawerano-xon(-ki) mi-n tso-a onan-a iki? | ‘Where did you meet whom?’
(164) –Tso-a(-ki) mi-n jawerano-xon onan-a iki? | ‘Whom did you meet where?’
The answer to the last question would be:
(165) –Wesna, Ronóyain-xon. | ‘Wesna, in Ronoya.’

h: 8.4.2.3. Questioning Constituents of a Subordinate Clause
t:
Sometimes you want to ask about the doer or receiver inside a smaller sentence that sits within a bigger one. To do this, you put the question word at the start of the smaller sentence. But -ki stays where it always is: after the first big part of the whole sentence. So here it comes right after the whole smaller sentence:
(166) [Tsoma-n Wesna wame meni-a]-ra mi-n oin-ke. | ‘You saw that Tsoma gave paiche to Wesna.’
Questioning the Transitive Subject:
(167) [Tso-n Wesna wame meni-a]-ki mi-n oin-a? | Tso-n-ki Wesna wame meni-a mi-n oin-a? | ‘Who did you see gave paiche to Wesna?
Questioning the Patient Object:
(168) [Jawe Tsoma-n Wesna meni-a]-ki mi-n oin-a? | Jawe-ki Tsoma-n Wesna meni-a mi-n oin-a? | ‘What did you see that Tsoma gave Wesna?’
Questioning the Recipient Object:
There are two ways to ask about the person who receives something (like ‘to whom’), inside a smaller sentence. The first way is to put the question word at the start of the smaller sentence, and mark that whole smaller sentence with -ki. That is the same way we ask about doers and other receivers. The second way is to put the question ending on the question word itself. In other words, the question word has been pulled out of the smaller sentence:
(169) [Tso-a Tsoma-n wame meni-a]-ki mi-n oin-a? | ‘To whom did you see that Tsoma give paiche?’ | [Tso-a-ki] Tsoma-n wame meni-a mi-n oin-a? | ‘To whom did you see that Tsoma give paiche?’

h: 8.4.2.3. Questioning Constituents of a Subordinate Clause
t:
Sentences like (169b) may be the only grammar difference between the person receiving something and the thing being acted on. (This idea still needs to be checked.)
You can ask about time, place or manner inside a smaller sentence too. You do it by moving things to the front. That is, you put the question word at the start of the smaller sentence, and mark that whole smaller sentence with -ki.

h: 8.4.2.4. Questioning Noun Phrase Elements
t:
To ask whose something is, you can put -ki after the whole ‘owner + thing’ phrase, as shown below:
(170) [Tso-n ochíti]-ki mi-n oin-a? | ‘Whose dog did you see?’
You can also pull out just the question word for the owner:
(170) [Tso-n]-ki mi-n ochíti oin-a? | ‘Of whom did you see a dog?’
Now say you ask what of someone's it is, not whose. Then the whole ‘owner + thing’ phrase must get the ending -ki. You cannot pull out the thing by itself. The (b) sentence below is wrong, and that shows this:
(171) [Tsoma-n jawe]-ki mi-n oin-a? | [Jawe]-ki mi-n oin-a Tsoma-n? | ‘What of Tsoma did you see?’

h: 8.4.2.5. Questioning the Object of a Postpositional Phrase
t:
Some phrases have a little place word after a noun, like ‘house-in’ for ‘in the house.’ When you ask about the noun in such a phrase, -ki must come after the whole phrase:
(172) Tso-a kopí-ki mi-a jo-a? | ‘Because of whom did you come?’
(173) [Jawe patax]-ki Wesna yakat-ai? | ‘Next to what does Wesna sit?’

h: 8.4.3.1. Partial Echo-questions
t:
An echo question repeats part of what someone just said, like ‘The what?’ -Ki cannot appear in an echo question that is just the questioned word by itself:
(174) –E-a-ra bakish Maioshiain ka-[a]i. | ‘I am going to Pucallpa tomorrow.’ | –Bakish? | –Bakish-ki? | ‘Tomorrow?’
But -ki may appear if the verb comes along with the questioned word:
(None) –Bakish-ki ka-[a]i? | ‘Tomorrow (you) are going?’
The same is true for echo questions with a question word:
(None) –Jawe-tian? | –Jawe-tian-ki? | ‘When?’ | –Jawe-tian-ki ka-[a]i? | ‘When are (you) going?’
These examples suggest that the question ending can't come at the very end of what you say.

h: 8.4.3.2. Complete Echo-Questions
t:
Sometimes a person repeats the whole question that was asked of them. Then -ki is never found:
(175) –Mi-a-ki bakish Maioshiain ka-[a]i? | ‘Are you going to Pucallpa tomorrow?’
(None) –Jawe? E-a bakish Maioshiain ka-[a]i? | What? Am I going to Pucallpa tomorrow?
The same goes for echo questions that repeat a whole question with a question word. -ki cannot appear there either:
(None) –Jawerano-ki mi-a ka-[a]i? | ‘Where are you going?’ | –Jawerano e-a ka[a]i? | –Jawerano-ki e-a ka-[a]i? | ‘Where am I going?’

h: 8.4.3.3. The Confirmative Ikon
t:
Ikon is made from i- ‘do (intr.)’ plus the ending -kon (linguists call it the legitimative). You use it to check that something is true, when you already know it somehow. It is like English ‘right?’:
(176) Bakish mi-a ka-[a]i, ikon? | ‘You are leaving tomorrow, right?’

h: 8.4.3.4. The Conversation Reorientative -Kan
t:
The word piece -kan is used to change the topic of a conversation. You add it to the person or thing you want to start talking about, something that was not the focus until now. It is a bit like English ‘And what about…?’:
(177) Sani-ra jo-ai. | ‘Sani is coming.’ | Jawen awin-kan? | ‘And (what about) his wife?’
In the next bit of conversation, Rona asks Wexá about the crops he and his family are growing in their village. Then Rona asks whether there are fish in the area. Wexá switches to this new topic by using the marker -kan:
(178) Ya, xekia paranta ni-ai. | ‘O.K., he is going to sow corn and plantain.’ | Jen jen, xeki koséchan-ai paranta piko-t-ai. | ‘Yes, he harvests the corn and then the plantain comes out.’ | Yapa-ki ja-ríba-a jain? | ‘Is there also fish there?’ | Yapa-kan ja-[a]i. | ‘Fish there is too.’

h: 8.4.3.5. Leading Questions
t:
The question ending -tsi shows that the speaker expects the answer ‘yes.’ It works like English ‘You're leaving tomorrow, aren't you?’ You can ask the questions below when you already have a reason to think the other person is leaving tomorrow. Or when you have already heard about the theft and want to get the other person to tell you the story:
(179) –Mia-tsi bakish ka-[a]i? | ‘You are leaving tomorrow, aren’t you?’
(180) –Mi-a-tsi nawa-n yometso-a? | ‘So, the mestizo stole from you?’
In the next example, the speaker uses -tsi because he doesn't remember something well. He expects the listener to give him the details. The topic is a belief about the shansho bird. People believe that if you kill one and bury it, you can make those who moved away to other villages or towns come back home:
(181) –Jawe-tsi i-[y]antan-a Elva, nexnex, nexnex rete-anan | miin-ti no sé jawe keska-ra i-bira-[a]i. | ‘What did Elva say some time ago, that one should kill a shansho (bird) and bury it? How was it?’
The question endings can also be combined as -tsi-ki. This combination seems to do the same job as plain -ki.

h: 8.4.3.6. Alternative Questions
t:
‘This or that?’ questions usually use the Spanish word o ‘or.’ In the examples below, you can leave out the question ending -ki:
(182) Mi-n(-ki) e-a a-kin-ai o a-kin-yama-[a]i? | ‘Are you going to help me or not?’
(183) Mi-a(-ki) e-bé wano-ai o mi-a i-[y]ama-[a]i? | ‘Are you gonna marry me or not?’ (man speaking)
(184) Ikax ma akí iki o ak-á-ma-pari? | ‘But is he making (plantain chacra) already or not?’

h: 8.4.3.7. Courteous Questions and Requests
t:
The ending -tani makes something sound gentler. You can use it to ask for something politely:
(185) Jawe-tian-ki mi-n tari a-tani-ai? | ‘When could you make a cushma (for me)?’
The ending -shaman can also make a question sound polite. (The example below already appeared in Chapter 6 as (44).)
(186) Tso-bé-shaman-ki mi-a ka-ti iki Kontámanain? | ‘With whom are you going to Contamana?’
Another way to ask for something politely is to use the ending -mein. This ending normally shows that the speaker is guessing or isn't sure (linguists call it speculative or dubitative). Using it softens a request, a bit like English "would you perhaps…?" Compare the two sentences below. In (187a) -mein makes the request polite; in (187b) the plain question ending -ki is used instead.
(187) Mi-n-mein e-a nokon wai oro-kin-ti-ma iki? | ‘Would you please / perhaps help me clear my chacra?’ | Mi-n-ki e-a nokon wai oro-kin-ti-ma iki? | ‘Will you help me clear my chacra?’

h: Short Answers to Polar Questions (answering "yes" or "no")
t:
To say ‘yes’ and ‘no,’ Shipibo has the fixed words jenjen (used by men) and jojo (used by women) (see exx. (178) and (220)). But there is a second way to answer a yes-or-no question. You can reply with a very general verb meaning ‘do.’ There are two of these: ik- ‘do (intr.)’ for intransitive verbs and ak- ‘do (tr.)’ for transitive verbs. They stand in for the real verb of the question. English does the same thing: "Did you eat?" "Yes, I did." The ‘do’ verb must be the same type as the verb in the question. For a yes answer, you add the ending that means "same person, at the same time." So the yes answers are ik-i [do.I-SSSS]
for questions with an intransitive verb, and a-kin [do.T-SSSA] for questions with a transitive verb. The no answers are ik-á-ma [be-PP2-NEG] for intransitive verbs and ak-á-ma [do.T-PP2-NEG] for transitive verbs. To build them, you take the right ‘do’ verb, add the ending -a (which marks a finished action), and then the ‘not’ ending -ma. Look at the examples below (see also 15.3.4). In (188) the question has a transitive verb (‘eat fruit’), so the answer uses a-kin / ak-ama. In (189) the verb is an intransitive verb (‘dance’), so the answer uses ik-í / ik-áma.
(188) –Bima-n-ki xenan koko-ai? | – ‘Does Bima eat guaba?’ | –Bima-n-ki xenan koko-a? | – ‘Did Bima eat guaba?’ | –A-kin / ak-ama | – ‘Yes’/‘No.’

h: Short Answers to Polar Questions (answering "yes" or "no")
t:
(189) –Jisbe-ki ransa-shin-ai? | – ‘Does Jisbe dance all night long?’ | –Jisbe-ki ransa-shin-a? | – ‘Did Jisbe dance all night long?’ | –Ik-í / ik-áma | – ‘Yes.’/‘No.’
However, a small group of verbs about moving (going, coming, carrying and so on) do not follow this pattern. Instead of using the ‘do’ verbs ik- and
ak-, these few verbs answer with their own base word. Look at the answers in (190) and (191). The intransitive verbs add -i, the "same person, at the same time" ending for intransitive verbs. The transitive verbs add -kin, the matching ending for transitive verbs.
Two more verbs answer with their own base word: ja- ‘there is / exist’ and its opposite yama- ‘there isn't.’ As I said earlier in this chapter, these verbs can also be used to say what someone has. Unlike the moving verbs above, ja- takes its normal endings in an answer: -ai for an action still going on and -ke for a finished one. So it looks like an ordinary full verb. Yama- takes no ending for an action still going on, but takes -ke for a finished one. The forms jaráke and yamarake are also common. They contain -ra, a marker that shows the speaker knows something first-hand. You can see all these answers in (192):
(192) –Mi-a-ki mecha ochíti-a iki? | – ‘Do you have a good hunter dog?’ | –Ja-[a]i / ja-rá-ke. | – ‘Yes.’ | –Yama / Yama-ra-ke / -Ja-yá-oma | – ‘No.’

h: Directives (commands and requests)
t:
By "directive" I mean any way of telling someone to do something, or wishing something would happen. This covers four kinds of sentence: "let me / let him…" (jussive), "let's…" (exhortative), orders like "go!" (imperative), and "don't…!" (prohibitive). Saying something is possible, necessary or allowed is covered separately (see section 7.13). Shipibo greetings and goodbyes use these directive forms, so I have included them in this section too.
Two endings are used for directives: -we and (-ba) -non. Some verbs are just one short syllable, like pi- ‘eat’ or ka- ‘go.’ On these, the stress falls on the ending, so it is written with an accent: -wé and -bánon. -We is a single word piece. It gives an order to the person you are talking to ("you, go!"); linguists call this the imperative. (-Ba) -non means "let me…" or "let him…" (linguists call this jussive). You can even put other endings between its two halves: -kan (more than one person) or -tan ‘go do something and come back.’ (-Ba) -non is only used for "I," "he/she" and "they" and some kinds of "we." It can never be used when the order is aimed at the person you are talking to. That includes "we" meaning "you and I."
Markers that show how the speaker knows something are not used in directives. There is just one exception. You can add the short "so I've been told" ending -ki to an order. This shows that the speaker is passing on an order or request from someone else. (Speakers hesitate over, or simply reject, the longer "so I've been told" ending -ronki here.)

h: Jussive ("let him/her do it")
t:
To say "let me…" or "let him…," you add (-ba) -non to the verb. It is used only when the order is NOT aimed at the person you're talking to. So it works for "I," "he/she," "they," and "we" meaning "me and others, but not you" (linguists call this "first person plural exclusive"). As I mentioned earlier, (-ba) -non can also show that someone plans or intends to do something. -Non belongs to the set of endings that come last on the verb. Look at the example below, where -non appears three times:
(193) Moa-tian e-n oin-a jawéki-bo mi-a onan-ma-non, | mi-a yoi-non, ja-ribi mi-n bake-bo a-táanan | mi-n axe-a-non. | ‘I will teach you the things I saw long time ago, I will tell them to you, so that when you have your children you pass these things on to them too.’
Look at the last part of example (193). There the ending -non (glossed FDS) has another job. It marks an action done by a different person, which happens after the main action or follows from it. (This is a marker that tells you the next action is done by someone else.)
Usually these "let me / let him" sentences don't name the doer at all. Only the situation tells you whether it means "I" or "he." That is why (194)–(196) each have more than one translation:

h: Jussive ("let him/her do it")
t:
(194) Ka-bá-non! | ‘I am leaving! / Let me leave! / May he leave!
(195) Piti pi-bá-non! | ‘I will eat fish! / Let me eat fish! / May he eat fish!
(196) Piti piáma-ba-non! | ‘I will not eat fish! / May he not eat fish!’
"We" meaning "me and others, but not you" looks just like the "I" and "he" forms above. The only way to tell it apart is to say the word "we" out loud, as in (197) and (198):
(197) No-a-pari pikó-ba-non! | ‘We (exclusive) will come out first! / Let us (exclusive) come out first!’
(198) No-n-pari pi-bá-non! | ‘We (exclusive) will eat first / Let us (exclusive) eat first!’
But even with this "we, not you," the speaker may leave out the word for "we":
(199) I-bá-non nato Xetebo-bo, Xetebo Iain ja-bo ik-ax. | ‘We’ll call these ones “Xetebos,” since they live at Xetebo Lake.’
To say "let them…," you simply put the plural ending -kan between -ba and -non:
(200) Piti pi-bá-ka[n]-non! | ‘May they eat fish!’
(201) Piti piáma-ba-ka[n]-non! | ‘May they not eat fish!’
As (198) shows, a "let me / let us" sentence can name the doer, and the doer then has the doer marker.

h: Imperative (direct commands ("do it!"))
t:
Real orders are aimed at the person you are talking to ("you"). To make one, you add the ending -we to the verb. Like -non (the ending for plans), -we cannot be used together with -ai and -ke, the endings for actions going on or finished. It also cannot be used with iki, the word for ‘be.’
Orders with -we usually leave out the word "you." With an intransitive verb, you can say "you," but people usually don't, as in (202). With a transitive verb, you can name the receiver ("fish"). But you cannot name the doer with the doer marker. In (203b), mi-n can only mean "your" ("eat your fish!"), not "you eat fish!" Look at the examples below:
(202) (Mi-a) ka-tan-we! | ‘(You) go!’
(203) Piti pi-wé! | ‘Eat fish!’ | Mi-n piti pi-wé! | ‘Eat fish! / Eat your fish!’
So in an order, the plain-form person (the one in an intransitive sentence, or the receiver) can be named. The doer with the doer marker cannot. This is a sign that the doer marker system affects how Shipibo builds whole sentences, not just how it marks words (linguists call this "syntactic ergativity" inside the sentence).
To say "don't…!" you add the "not" ending to the verb. Linguists call this the prohibitive. In the next example, adding the ending -yama moves the stress to the first syllable of the verb. That is just what the stress rule predicts:

h: Imperative (direct commands ("do it!"))
t:
(204) Piti pi-yama-we! | ‘Don’t eat fish!’
When you give an order to more than one person, you must add the plural ending -kan before -we. Here are examples of "do!" and "don't!":
(205) Piti pi-kan-we! | ‘Eat fish (2p.)!’
(206) Piti pi-yama-kan-we! | ‘Don’t eat fish (2p.)!’
With ‘come’ and ‘go,’ an order to several people needs two things. You add the plural ending -kan. But you also switch to a completely different verb, the one used for more than one person (be- ‘come’ and bo- ‘go’), much as English go changes to went:
(207) Be-kan-we! | ‘Come (2p.)!’
(208) Bo-kan-we! | ‘Go (2p.)!’
The ending -men ‘quickly, right away’ is often added to orders aimed at "you." In (209) and (210) there are two verbs. The first one is a verb of movement (‘come,’ ‘go’), and it carries both -men and the order ending. The second verb carries the ending that means "same person, at the same time":
(209) Jo-men-we pi-i! | ‘Come quickly to eat!’
(210) Ka-men-tan-we bi-i! | ‘Go quickly and get (it)!’
Another ending with a similar meaning is -panon ‘quickly.’ It goes after the order ending, as in the next sentence:
(211) Pi-men-we-panon no-a ishto-n ka-men-non. | ‘Eat quickly so that we leave soon.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:312)
As I said earlier, the short "so I've been told" ending -ki can be added to an order. Then the sentence passes on an order from someone else:

h: Imperative (direct commands ("do it!"))
t: (212) Onpax-ki be-wé! | ‘Bring water on her / his behalf.’

h: Exhortative ("let's do it!")
t:
"Let's…" sentences are aimed at "we" meaning "you and I" (linguists call these exhortatives). Shipibo makes them with two verbs in a row. The first verb carries -non, the "let me" ending. The second verb carries -we, the order ending. The first verb is the real action, like ‘eat.’ The second verb is just a general ‘do’ verb, of the same type as the first one. The plural ending -kan can be added or left out:
(213) No-n-pari pi-non a-wé! | ‘Let’s eat first!’
(None) Piti pi-non a-kan-we! | ‘Let’s eat fish!’
You usually cannot swap the two verbs around. That is true even if you also swap the endings, putting the "let me" ending on ‘do’ and the order ending -we on the real verb. Sentences (c) and (d) are wrong; the star () marks them as unacceptable:
(None) Piti a-kan-we pi-non! | Piti a-non pi-kan-we! | ‘Let’s eat fish!’
So a "let's" sentence is really a "let me" part plus an order. Word for word, it means ‘I am going to eat the fish, you do it too.’
To say "let's not…," you put the "not" ending only on the real action verb. Again, you cannot swap the order of the two verbs:
(214) Piti piáma-non a-kan-we! | ‘Let’s not eat fish!’ (Lit. ‘I am not going to eat fish, you do it (like me).’) | Piti a-kan-we piáma-non. | Piti a-yama-non pi-kan-we. | ‘Let’s not eat fish!’

h: Exhortative ("let's do it!")
t:
Something special happens in "let's" sentences with the verb ka- ‘go.’ There are two options. First, the first verb can be ka- with the "let me" ending -non, followed by the general ‘do’ verb ik- with the order ending -we (215a). Second, both verbs can be ‘go’ (in its intransitive form) (215b):
(215) Ka-non i-wé! | Ka-non ka-wé! | ‘Let’s go!’
What's more, with ‘go’ you can also swap the two verbs. The order verb can come first and the "let me" verb second:
(None) Ka-wé ka-non! | ‘Let’s go!’
The next examples show yet another option. Here a real action verb with the "let me" ending is combined with kawé ‘go!’:
(216) Ka-non ka-wé, Inka bi-non ka-wé! | ‘Let’s go, let’s bring the Inka back.’
(217) Chibá-non ka-wé! | ‘Let’s follow (her/him/it).’
Finally, "let's go" can also use bo-, the form of ‘go’ for more than one person, instead of ka-:
(218) Moa bo-non bo-kan-we! | ‘Let’s go already!’

h: Polite Imperative (polite requests)
t:
Just like with polite requests, you can add the softening ending -tani to an order. This makes it more polite, like adding "please":
(219) Ishton-tani ka-tan-we! | ‘Please go and do (it)!’

h: Greetings and Leave-Takings (saying hello and goodbye)
t:
The Shipibo use the order form of ‘come’ ("Come!") to greet people and welcome them into their house. When someone says they are leaving, the right reply is the order form of ‘go’ ("Go!"), for one person or for several:
(220) –Jo-wé! | ‘Come!’ (greeting welcoming one person)
(None) –Be-kan-we! | ‘Come!’ (greeting welcoming two or more people)
(None) –Jenjen! | ‘Yes’ (answer by a woman) | –Jojo! | ‘Yes’ (answer by a man)
(None) –Ka-bá-non! | ‘I am leaving!’ | –Bo-bá-kanon! | ‘We are leaving!’
(None) –Ka-wé! | ‘Go (singular)’! | –Bo-kan-we! | ‘Go (plural)!’

h: Equal Comparison ("as big as")
t:
To say two things are equal ("as big as," "like"), Shipibo uses the word keská ~ -ská ‘like.’ It must come after a noun. It can also come after a part of the sentence that has been turned into a describing word (see 10.4.6, which deals with "like…" parts of sentences). Usually it is followed by a general ‘do’ verb with the "same person, at the same time" ending. That ‘do’ verb is the same type as the main verb of the sentence. Here are some examples:
(221) E-n noi-ke nokon rayos, nokon bake-n bene, | nokon bake-bi keská. | ‘I love my son in-law, my daughter’s husband like my own child.’
Example (222) has two comparisons. The first one is negative ("we don't do it like that"). The second one shows that you can leave out keská when the comparison is a whole described action ("like the panshin fish eats"):
