(222) No-n ja-ská-a-yama-[a]i; panshin yapa-n pi-ti-n pi-á | a-kin no-n ak-ai, too a-patan-bain-kin. | ‘We don’t pass (the soccer ball) like that (i.e., like the mestizo women do); we play like the panshin fish eats (i.e., very quickly), kicking the ball and carrying it across the field .’
The sentence below has no word for ‘be.’ Here keská is used together with the ending -ribi ‘also, again’:
(223) E-a-ra mi-a keská siná-ribi. | ‘I am as brave as you.’

h: Unequal Comparison ("bigger than")
t:
To say "bigger," "further" and so on, Shipibo adds a "little" ending, -shoko or -cha, to the describing word. Or it simply uses más ‘more,’ a word borrowed from Spanish:
When you also say what something is compared to ("braver than you"), you use the word bebon ‘in front of.’ It goes after the person or thing being compared to:
(225) E-a-ra mi-a bebon siná iki. | ‘I am braver than you.’
(226) Ja-ke nokon bake e-bebon onan... | ‘I have a daughter who knows more than me.’
(227) E-n-ra noi-ke nokon awin mi-n awin | mi-n ak-á bebon. | ‘I love my wife more than you love yours.’
(228) E-n-ra icha-ira siribisa xea-ke mi-n atsa xeati | ak-á bebon. | ‘I drank more beer than you yuca beer.’
Shipibo has no set way to say "less than."

h: Superlative ("the biggest")
t:
Shipibo has no set way to say "the bravest" or "the most." But the people who helped me offered the two sentences below:
(229) E-a-ra kikin siná iki. | ‘I am the bravest.’ Lit. ‘I am extremely brave.’
(230) E-a-ra mato xewin-a siná iki | ‘I am the bravest (among you all and I).’ Lit. ‘I surpass you (in being) brave.’

h: Voice (changing who the sentence focuses on)
t:
Many languages have ways to shift attention away from the doer and onto the receiver. English uses the passive: "The man was taken by the spirits." Shipibo-Konibo (SK) has no true passive like this (Derbyshire and Pullum 1986:19). It also has no form that does the opposite, pushing the receiver into the background with an extra marker (Dixon and Aikhenvald 1999:xxvii). Linguists think this is typical of Amazonian languages, and SK fits that pattern. Instead, SK gets the same effect in other ways. It can change the word order to receiver–doer–verb (OAV) or receiver–verb–doer (OVA). It can use a transitive verb with the plural ending and no doer named. And it can use the "to oneself" ending (linguists call it middle) with the receiver as the one the sentence is about
and no doer named (see also 14.2, on how the ending -a, which shows that the receiver of one part is the doer of the next, is used in stories). A few sentences suggest that something like a real passive may be starting to develop in some special parts of sentences without a full verb. On the other hand, a speaker can play down the receiver just by leaving it out. In that case the verb stays a transitive verb, and the doer keeps its doer marker.

h: Non-Basic Constituent Order (unusual word order)
t:
The example below is the start of a story about a man who was taken by the chaikoni or ‘hidden people’ to live in their world. The story puts the words in an unusual order: receiver–verb–doer (OVA). This order introduces the man and makes him the one the story is about. At the same time, it brings in the chaikoni. They are less central, but still worth mentioning:
(231) Westíora joni-ronki bo-a iki chaikoni joni-n, | iaman yomera-i i-t-aitian. | ‘It is said that a man was taken by a chaikoni while fishing in the lake (the SK sentence is active.’
The next phrase is the title of a story. It is about a man who tries to kill a paca agouti (a large rodent), but gets killed by it instead. The words are in the order receiver–doer–verb (OAV). This shows that the man, the receiver, is more important in the story than the paca:
(232) Joni ano-n rete-ni. | ‘The man who was killed by a paca agouti.’

h: Impersonal Passive ("it was done" with no doer named)
t:
In many languages, a common way to get the effect of a passive is to say "they" without meaning anyone in particular (Keenan 1985b:247). English does this too: "They say it will rain." SK has a sentence type like this. The verb is a transitive verb with the plural ending -kan, and the doer must be left out. It works like a passive with no doer: "it is done." Even though the verb is marked plural, it does not refer to any real group, and the doer need not be more than one person:
(233) Shee a-rá-kan-ai yapa. | ‘Fish is being fried / Someone is frying fish.’
(234) Ja-tian jain i-kan-ai ja xontako rabé tanti-ma-kan-a... | ‘And then there were the two young girls who had been put to rest...’
(235) Joni-bo benoya ainbo betan ik-ai-ra wexa-kan-ai. | ‘Men who have an affair with a married woman get cut with the wexati knife.’
In the examples above, the doer is not necessarily plural, even though the verb has the plural ending -kan (see also ex. (17) in Chapter 7):

h: Middle Voice (actions that happen to oneself)
t:
The ending -t (linguists call it middle) generally shows that the doer is affected by the action. As shown in 3.4.4.3, adding -t to a transitive verb can give three meanings: doing something "to yourself," something just happening on its own ("the door opened"), or a passive with no doer ("he got pulled") (see also 18.1.9). The example below shows this last meaning. It uses the verb bachin- ‘pull someone by the hair’ with the middle ending added. (-mee(t) is another form of the same ending -t):
(236) Yanka-biresa e-a bachimee-ke ikon-tani | i-ke-n-ma-bi. | ‘I was pulled by the hair unfairly, without it being true.’ (i.e., a woman thought I was having an affair with her husband and pulled me by the hair.)
Sometimes the middle ending seems to show that the doer does something for their own benefit (see ex. (1) in Ch. 18, but compare 18.1.6). The middle ending is also common on verbs of moving, of body position (sitting, standing), and of feelings (exx. (2)-(5) of Ch. 18).

h: Promotional Passive? (is there a true passive ("was done by")?)
t:
The next example was given in Ch. 6 as (55). It has a main part followed by two "because…" parts. Those two parts carry -ax, the "same person" ending. This tells us they are about the same people as the main part: the bad, unkind people. Now look at the elders, anibaon. The -n on this word means "of" (genitive) in the first "because" part. But in the second part it cannot mean "of." There, the elders must be the doers ("their elders never cured them"), marked like a doer in a passive:
(237) Ja-rá-ke joni-bo jakóma shinan-ya [jawen ani-baon | esé ninká-yosma ik-ax], itan-ribi [jawen ani-baon | rao-n-yosma ik-ax]. | ‘There are bad / unkind people either because they never listened to their elders’ advice or because their elders never cured them with plant medicine.’
The example just above is the only time I found what could be called a real passive.

h: Object Demotion (pushing the receiver into the background)
t:
You can push the receiver into the background just by not mentioning it. As I said earlier, the verb does not change in any way. It stays a transitive verb, and the doer keeps its doer marker:
(238) No-n-ra moa pi-ke. | ‘We have eaten already.’
This kind of sentence could be called the SK "antipassive" (a form that leaves the receiver out). But Shipibo also lets you drop any word that is clear from context. So (238) can also mean ‘We have eaten it already.’ See also examples (33) and (34) in Ch. 15. There I suggest that the verb rebes- ‘die’ grew out of one of these "antipassive" sentences and became a single word.
CLAUSE-CHAINING AND SWITCH-REFERENCE:
The main way SK keeps track of who is doing what is a rich set of markers that tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else (linguists call this switch-reference). These markers appear in long sentences built from several parts. There is a main part, and one or more extra parts that come right before or after it. Sometimes an extra part sits inside the main part. The extra part must always end with its verb. That verb carries an ending that shows whether its doer is the same as the doer of the main part or not. There is also an ending that shows that the receiver of the extra part is the doer of the main part.

h: Object Demotion (pushing the receiver into the background)
t: Usually the extra part sets the scene for the main part. But it does not say exactly how the two events are connected. The listener works that out from the context. The extra part can also tell the next event in a story, moving the story forward. So in English, an SK extra part can come out as many things: "when…," "in order to…," "if…," "because…," "although…," or even "and…".

h: Same-Subject Marked Clauses (linked sentences with the same doer)
t: Extra parts with a "same person" ending have no full verb ending of their own. In an ordinary statement, the verb has endings that show whether the action is going on or finished. Here, the "same person" ending replaces those endings, and shows that this part depends on the main part. (By "same person" I mean the doer of an intransitive verb or of a transitive verb.) The most interesting thing about these endings is this. There are different ones depending on whether the main verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. (The only exceptions are the "same person" endings -taanan and -anan.) The endings also show the order of the two events: whether the extra part happens before, during, or after the main part (see also 19.2.1).

h: Previous Events (something that happened before)
t:
Say the extra part happens before the main part. If the main verb is an intransitive verb, you use the ending -ax. If the main verb is a transitive verb, you use -xon instead. (You could also use -taanan in both cases, as I'll show in 9.1.4.) Sentence (1) has only one main verb, the intransitive verb manóresa iki. Before it and after it come extra parts marked with -ax (glossed as Previous, Same-Subject, S
agreement). Using -xon in either extra part would make the sentence wrong:
(1) [...bachi meran jiki-ax] Ashi manó-res-a iki [moa | ka-ax]. | ‘... Ashi entered into the mosquito net and disappeared, after leaving (for the upper world).’ (Soi Rawa 1995:27, analyzed in Valenzuela 2002a:427)
In (2), the main verbs ‘boil’ and ‘chew’ are transitive verbs. So you must use -xon (Previous, Same-Subject, A agreement), not -ax. Notice that the "main" verb can be the real main verb of the whole sentence, like nakakatikanai. Or it can be the verb of another extra part, like kobin axon:
(2) [[Jawen tapon bi-xon] kobin-'a-xon] naka-kati-kan-ai. | ‘After getting its (i.e., the yotokonti plant’s) root and boiling it, they chewed it.’
Sentence (3) shows again that the choice between -ax and -xon depends on the type of the verb that the extra part leans on. Here that verb also comes next in time. As (2) already showed, that verb can be the real main verb, like wexaanankatitai, or the verb of another extra part, like joxon and meraax. Remember that the "to each other" ending -anan turns a verb into an intransitive verb:¹

h: Previous Events (something that happened before)
t:
(3) [[[Jene-n ka-tan-ax] jo-xon] jawen awin
Notice from the English translation that the doer of merax is not exactly the same as the doer of wexaanankatitai. It is part of that group: one person (3 singular) versus several (3 plural). I come back to this later, when I deal with doers that are partly the same, in 9.5.
(None) mera-ax] wexa-anan-katit-ai joni-bo. | ‘If when coming back from the fishing he found his wife (with another man), then the men would cut each other with the wexati knife...’

h: Simultaneous Events (things happening at the same time)
t:
Now say the two events happen at the same time, or overlap. Then a different set of "same person" endings is used. Again, the choice depends on the type of the main verb. You use -i (Simultaneous, Same-Subject, S agreement) when the main verb is an intransitive verb. You use -kin (Simultaneous, Same-Subject, A agreement) when it is a transitive verb:
(4) Ikaxbi-kan ja pishta-nko chiban-res-kan-ai | oa iná-bo tsaka-kin. | ‘However, the other participants at the fiesta continued (it), sacrificing the domesticated animals.’
(5) Jaino-a-ki, ja mawá raka-t-a-bi, | papiake-beiran-i jo-a iki bene-shaman. | ‘Without delay, (the Deer) put the dead (Jaguar) on its back and went back home feeling very happy.

h: Following Events (something that happens after)
t:
Finally, say the extra part happens after the main part. Then -nox (Following, Same-Subject, S agreement) shows that the doer is the same and the main verb is an intransitive verb. -noxon (Following, Same-Subject, A agreement) shows that the doer is the same and the main verb is a transitive verb. Parts marked with -nox and -noxon often mean "in order to…".
(6) E-a-ra ka-ai, [oa joni-bo osan-nox].... | ‘I will go in order to laugh at those people.’
In (7), the "same person" part sits inside the main part:
(7) ....no-a i-ti ja-ke [westíora metsá ainbo i-nox] | raoti-a. | ‘....we must be adorned in order to be a beautiful woman.’
(8) Ono xeki ak-í-ra boan-kan-ke [joa-noxon]. | ‘They went (to the chacra) earlier today to harvest corn in order to cook it.’

h: The Previous Same-Subject Marker -Ta(a)nan (the "before, same person" ending -ta(a)nan)
t:
There is one more "same person" ending, -ta(a)nan (glossed as Previous, Same-Subject). It doesn't care whether the main verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. Compared with -ax and -xon, -ta(a)nan usually means the second action follows immediately, like English "as soon as" (Faust 1973:105). In (9) the main verb, iká iki manota iki, is an intransitive verb:
(9) [Jato a-taanan]-ki ik-á iki moa Chichíporo | Ainbo-ki manot-a iki. | ‘After telling them that, the Canary Woman disappeared.’
In the example below, the main verb of the -taanan part is sotameet-. It is an intransitive verb that was made from a transitive verb:
(10) Ja-skáa-xon joni-n oin-a-ronki ik-á iki Awá jo-i, | [ja jo-ai oin-taanan]-ki joni sotameet-a iki. | ‘Then the man saw the Tapir coming, seeing him coming the man hid to spy.’
In ex. (11), the main part non aki kai has a transitive verb, and yet -taanan is used:
(11) Ja-tian [no-n bake a-taanan] ja-ská-ribi no-n ak-í ka-ai. | ‘Then we will do the same when having our children.’

h: The Simultaneous Same-Subject Marker -Anan (the "at the same time, same person" ending -anan)
t:
The ending -anan means "same person, at the same time." Like -ta(a)nan, it doesn't care about the type of the main verb, so it is used with both intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. In the next two examples, parts marked with -anan go with an intransitive main verb (tsiniai) in (12) and a transitive main verb (aká iki potakin) in (13):
(12) No-a tsini-ai no-n chitonti-a-bi, [kikin-i nishi-n | chi-nexeet-anan]. | ‘We play (soccer) wearing our pampanillas, tying them very tightly with a rope.’
(13) Jain-xon-ronki ak-á iki kikin a-kin-ki yochi | motsá jato-ki pota-kin, [joné-anan]. | ‘Then, (the man) spread the (ground) chili pepper that had been well mixed with water on the place where they (i.e., the Nutrias) were, without being seen.’

h: Previous and Simultaneous Events (before and at the same time)
t:
Now for the "different person" parts. Unlike the "same person" parts, they can take the ordinary endings -ai (action going on) or -ke (action finished). So they are closer to full verbs. In
line with what these endings normally mean, -ai is used when the two events happen at the same time or overlap. -ke is used when the extra part happens first. But most of the time, these parts also carry another ending meaning "when" or "at." This is either -tian "when" or -n, which can also mean "when." Over time, these endings have become markers of "a different person." Choosing -tian rather than -n usually (but not always) means that the main event happened right after the other one. In (14) and (15), the verbs in the extra parts carry -ke (finished / happened first), while the main verbs carry -ai (going on). This shows that the two parts can differ in this way:
(14) [Pikó-ke-tian]-bi no-a ani a-kan-ai... | ‘From the moment we are born, they (our parents) take care of us....’
(15) [Xeta joxo-bicho i-ke-n]-ki osan-kati-kan-ai. | ‘If one had the teeth just white, then people would laugh at one.’
There is a second big difference between "same person" and "different person" parts. The "different person" parts never show what role the doer has in the main part. So they don't care about the type of the main verb. Compare (14) and (15), where the main verbs are transitive verbs, with (16), where the main verb is an intransitive verb:

h: Previous and Simultaneous Events (before and at the same time)
t:
(16) [Pi-kin senen-'a-kan-ke-n]-bi jenetia-a iki. | ‘When they had just finished eating, the flooding started.’
In (16), the ‘different person’ ending is -ken, not -ketian. That is surprising, because the second action clearly follows right away. Now let’s look at an example with two events happening at the same time:
(17) [Jene-n rete-ai-tian]-ra | ainbo sai ik-ai. | ‘Since (s)he_{i} was drowning, the woman_{j} cried out for help.’
Besides showing that the doers are different, -ken, -ketian, -ain and -aitian show one more thing. The receiver in the marked part can't be the same person as the doer in the main part (see also 9.3 below).
There is a third ‘different person’ ending for events at the same time: -nontian. It means that one event happens and is over while another, longer event is going on. Think of English ‘While I was cooking, the phone rang’:
(18) [...jema-n pishta i-nontian] ka-a iki alcalde, | jainoax wetsa koshi-bo-ribi. | ‘...during the fiesta of the village, the mayor and other authorities came.’
(19) Ja Ani Xeati ik-á iki Kanaria jema-nko, [ja-tian nokon
(None) ani-bo ja-pari-nontian]. | ‘That Ani Xeati took place in Kanaria village, at that time my parents were still alive.’
In the two examples just above, the part with -nontian is the longer event, the one that surrounds the other. The main part is the short event, which is over before the long one ends. This is exactly the opposite of what Faust (1973:109) describes. Faust gives examples like this one:

h: Previous and Simultaneous Events (before and at the same time)
t:
(20) [Ja jo-nontian]-ra, e-a nii meran iba-ke, Tito betan. | ‘When he came, I was in the forest with Tito (i.e., he came and left before Tito and I came back, or while we were in the forest).’ (Faust 1973:109)
Shipibo speakers accept Faust’s examples as correct. So -nontian must link two events that partly overlap: a short, finished event happens during a longer event that is still going on. Either event can be the one with -nontian, and the other one goes in the main part. Don't confuse -nontian with -nontianb; I deal with the latter in 10.4.
‘Different person’ parts (except those with -nontian) can also leave out -tian or -n. Then they look just like full sentences that could stand alone. In such cases, the fact that they
lean on the main part can be seen from the kind of sentence they appear in.²
(See exx. (66) and (100) in Ch. 7, as well as ex. (60) in Ch. 3.)

h: Following Events (something that happens after)
t:
Finally, -non tells you two things. The doers are different. And the marked event happens after the main event:
(21) [Bake-shoko oxa-non] e-a bewa-ba-non. | ‘So that the baby sleeps I am going to sing.’
The verb with -non is often followed by the intransitive helper verb ik-. That helper verb then takes a ‘same person’ ending. It takes -ax if the main verb is an intransitive verb, and -xon if it is a transitive verb:
(22) [[No-n oin-non] ik-ax], ochíti betan jo-wé. | ‘Come with the dog, so that we see it.’ (Faust 1973:111)
(23) Ja-shoko-bo onan-ma-kin no-a ani a iki, | [[no-n tita ke-ská-ribi no-a i-non] i-xon]. | ‘Our mother raised us teaching us those little things, so that we become like her too.’
For example, only a leaning part ending in -ai can be made negative by adding -ma, the ‘not’ marker used with words that aren't verbs. And only such a part can appear in a two-verb form with the helper verb iki.
This is the only ‘different person’ form where the ending changes to match the type of the main verb.

h: Previous Event (something that happened before)
t:
A more unusual linking ending is -a. It tells you that the receiver in the marked part is the same person as the doer in the main part (whatever the type of main verb). The marked part tells of an earlier event. In the glosses this ending is labelled PO>S/A (Previous Object-to-Subject Coreferentiality), roughly ‘earlier event; the receiver becomes the doer.’ Think of English ‘Bitten by the dog, the boy cried’: the boy is the receiver of ‘bite’ and the doer of ‘cry.’ Look at examples (24) and (25). In (24) the main verb is an intransitive verb; in (25) it is a transitive verb:
(24) [Ja-n rao-n-a]-ra e-a ka-wan-ke. | ‘(S)he treated me with plant medicine and I left.’
(25) [Ja-n e-a rao-n-a]-ra e-n nonti | bená-wan-ke. | ‘(S)he treated me with plant medicine and I looked for a canoe.’
Now take the reverse case: the doer in the marked part is the receiver in the main part. Then you must use a ‘different person’ ending. Example (14), shown again below, is like this. The doer of the earlier event is the receiver in the main part:
(26) [Pikó-ke-tian]-bi no-a ani a-kan-ai.... | ‘From the moment we are born, they (our parents) take care of us....’

h: Simultaneous Events (things happening at the same time)
t:
For events happening at the same time, there is no special ending like -a for the case where the receiver of one part is the doer of the other. But the rule still holds: a ‘different person’ ending also means that the receiver in the marked part is not the doer in the main part. Let’s go back to (17), shown again below:
(27) [Jene-n rete-ai-tian]-ra | ainbo sai ik-ai. | ‘Since she_{i} was drowning, the woman_{j} cried out for help. | Since she_{i} was drowning, the woman_{i} cried out for help.’
In the Shipibo sentence, the doer in the marked part is jene ‘flowing water.’ Word for word, (27) says ‘Since the flowing water was killing her, the woman cried out for help;’ Shipibo has no verb for ‘drown.’ Suppose -aitian only meant ‘at the same time, different doers.’ Then the second reading above would be perfectly possible.³ But the drowning woman is the receiver in the marked part. So she can't be the one who cries out for help. That would make the receiver in the marked part the same person as the doer in the main
One speaker accepted the second reading after thinking about it for a while. But the first reading is always the preferred one.
part, and the ending doesn't allow that. One way to say this kind of thing is with a ‘who/which…’ description part, or with a part saying when or why that has no linking marker, as in the next examples:

h: Simultaneous Events (things happening at the same time)
t:
(28) Ainbo jene-n rete-ai]-ra | sai ik-ai. | ‘The woman who was drowning cried for help.’
(29) Ja-n e-a xeyot-ai kaman-ra e-a bewa-[a]i. | ‘While he was massaging me, I kept on singing.’

h: Following Events (something that happens after)
t:
There is one exception. When the marked part tells of a later event, a ‘different person’ ending can be used even if the receiver in the marked part is the doer in the main part:
(30) [(E-a) xeyó-non (ik-ax)]-ra e-a bewa-ke. | ‘So that he massages me, I sang.’
So, for earlier events and for events at the same time, ‘different person’ in Shipibo-Konibo means two things. First, the doers are different. Second, the receiver in the marked part can't be the doer in the main part either, even though in that case the doers really are different too. This rule does not apply to parts that tell of a later event.

h: Syntactic Pivot (which person the grammar "keeps track of")
t:
Which person do the ‘same person’ endings really keep track of? So far I have used the idea of the subject, the one the sentence is about. But I haven't asked whether these endings might really be about meaning. Maybe -ax and -xon actually track the one who acts, or the one something happens to, and not the subject. This is not the case. In the examples below, -xon and -ax link parts where one subject is someone something happens to and the other is someone who acts (see also ex. (141) in Ch. 10):
(31) Ja-tian jawen bene-n raté-xon | ino to' a-ke | ‘Then her husband got scared and shot the jaguar.’
(32) Ikaxbi tita i-xon no-n axe-a-ti atipan-ke | no-n bake xontako-bo.... | ‘But being mothers we could teach our young daughters....’
(33) Jawe onan-ma ik-ax no-a jainka-ma | nokó-yamai. | ‘If we are not knowledgeable we will not meet our goals.’
A third possibility is that the ‘same person’ endings really track the topic, the person the talk is about. In the next example, the speaker is talking about himself. He is best seen
as the topic of all three parts. But the first part has no ‘same person’ ending, because its doer is not the speaker but xeta ‘tooth:’
(34) Xeta-n chexa-a-ra rimon bero chaka-xon rao-n-ke. | ‘Since I had a toothache, I ground lemon seeds and treated it.’

h: Syntactic Pivot (which person the grammar "keeps track of")
t:
The example above also shows an important job of the ending -a in storytelling. Same/different person endings follow the subject, not the topic. But with -a, a main character can stay at the center of the story even when they receive an action instead of doing it. So in this use, -a does in Shipibo-Konibo what the English passive does (‘he was bitten’ instead of ‘the dog bit him’).
In the next example, -a is used to bring in a new main character. Earlier in the text, a woman makes a preparation from a plant and bathes with it to win over a man. In the second part below, -a moves the focus from the woman to the man:
(35) Ja waste-n i-xon ainbo-nin joni noko-a, | keen-yama-pacho-kin-bi kikin a-kin noi ka-i. | ‘Making use of that piripiri, when the woman meets the man, even though he didn’t want her before, he is going to fall in love with her.’
The table below sums up which linking endings Shipibo-Konibo uses, and when. “Neutral” means the ending doesn't change to match the main verb. So it doesn't matter whether the main verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb.

h: Overlapping of Subject Reference (when the doers of two linked actions partly overlap)
t:
Suppose the marked part tells of an earlier event, and its doer is a group that includes the doer of the main part (for example, ‘we’ in the marked part and ‘I’ in the main part). Then
Comrie (1998) looks at this topic for Haruai, a Papuan language. In Haruai, a part in the middle of a sentence gets the ‘same person’ marker when the doer of the final part is included in the doer of the middle part. In the reverse case, the middle part gets the ‘same person’ marker only if both doers are the same grammatical person (both ‘I/we,’ both ‘you,’ or both ‘he/they’). Overlapping doers have also been discussed for Huichol (Uto-Aztecan), in Comrie (1983). The Shipibo data in this subsection come from Mr. Barin Meni (Carlos Panduro) and Mr. Yoi Sani (Luis Márquez Pinedo) for earlier events, and from Mr. Yoi Sani alone for events at the same time and later events. I must point out that Mr. Barin Meni and Mr. Yoi Sani agreed completely in their judgments about earlier events. This is so even though the first comes from Nuevo Edén (Piski River, Lower Ucayali), while the second is from “Dos Unidos” de Pachitea (Upper Ucayali).
the ‘same person’ ending is used. Now take the reverse: the event is earlier, and the doer of the main part is a group that includes the doer of the marked part. Then the ‘different person’ ending is required.

h: Overlapping of Subject Reference (when the doers of two linked actions partly overlap)
t:
But for events at the same time or later events, choosing between ‘same person’ and ‘different person’ is not so simple. With events at the same time, the ‘different person’ ending is also possible when the doer of the marked part is ‘they’ or, especially, ‘you (plural).’ This is true even if that group includes the doer of the main part. With later events, two more things matter: the type of the main verb, and the grammatical person (‘I/we,’ ‘you,’ ‘he/they’). Three things must all be true. The doer of the marked part is a group that includes the doer of the main part. The main verb is a transitive verb. And both doers are the same grammatical person. Then ‘same person’ is required with ‘I/we’ and possible with ‘he/they.’ In all other cases the marked verb takes the ‘different person’ ending. Table 9.2 sums this up.
The examples below are about earlier events. If the doer of the marked part is ‘we’ and the doer of the main part is ‘I,’ the ‘same person’ ending is used. If it's the other way round, the ‘different person’ ending is required:
(36) (No-a) jema-n nokó-xon-ra e-a koshi-bo bena-i | ka-[a]i. | ‘When we arrive at the village, I will look for the authorities.’
(37) E-n wame chachi-ke-tian-ra jatí-xon-bi no-n pi(-kan)-ai. | ‘Once / when I drive a paiche, we will eat altogether.’

h: Overlapping of Subject Reference (when the doers of two linked actions partly overlap)
t:
The next example has a marked part telling of a later event. Its doer is ‘we,’ a group that includes the doer of the main part, ‘you’ (one person). The main verb is a transitive verb. As the table above shows, this needs the ‘different person’ ending -non:
MAIN DEPENDENT
(38) Pi-men-we-panon no-a ishto-n ka-men-non. | ‘Eat quickly so that we leave soon.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:312)
Now let’s look again at example (3), shown again below. The marked verb meraax has the ‘same person’ ending -ax vis-à-vis (that is, in relation to) the main verb wexaanankatitai. That main verb is also the verb that ends the whole sentence:
(39) [[[Jene-n ka-tan]-ax jo]-xon jawen awin | mera]-ax wexa-anan-katit-ai joni-bo. | ‘If when coming back from the fishing he found his wife (with another man), then the men would cut each other (on the back of the head) with the wexati knife...’
Look at the English translation. The doer of the main part (jonibo ‘the men’) is a group that includes the doer of the marked part (the husband). So the marked part has a ‘he’ doer and the main part a ‘they’ doer, and so
the marker for "someone else" should be needed, not the "same person" marker. But that is not what happens. (Example (39) comes from a story told naturally, and two other native speakers confirmed it is correct.) There may be a reason for this. In Shipibo-Konibo, a single person can be the doer of a "to each other" action, as explained in 7.4.4. So the "same person" marker can be used here. Read that way, (39) literally means ‘If when coming back from the fishing he found his wife (with another man), then he would cut him with the wexati knife and this action would be reciprocated in turn....’ The "to each other" endings are discussed more in 18.2.

h: Overlapping of Subject Reference (when the doers of two linked actions partly overlap)
t:
Now let’s go back to example (70) from Chapter 7. It is shown again below as (40).
(40) Ja-skat-ax-ki [pia nea yatanan]-ki ka-bekon-a iki, | [baba rete-xon bo-kan-a] chiban-i.... | ‘After grabbing the bundle of arrows, the two (grandparents) left, chasing those who had killed their grandchildren and had taken their corpses with them...’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)
The story makes it clear that only the old man grabs the arrows. Then he and his wife leave the house together. So the first part of the sentence is about one person (he), and the main part is about more than one (the two of them). That should call for the "someone else" marker, not the "same person" marker. But remember what Chapter 7 said about example (70). The main verb kabekona iki is built on the form of ‘go’ used for one person (ka-), not on its separate form for more than one person
(bo-). Because of this choice, I suggested that the sentence literally means ‘After (he) grabbed the bundle of arrows, he left accompanied by a second participant, chasing those who had killed their grandchildren and had taken their corpses with them.’ Read this way, all the parts of the sentence have the same doer: the old man. That explains why the "same person" marker is used. There is more support for this idea. In a "to each other" sentence, the other person is named with a word marked betan ‘with’. The verb here ends in bekon. Both contain the same ‘together with’ piece, be(tan) (linguists call this the comitative). This shared marking supports my view. The doer of such sentences is just one person, and the second person is only someone who comes along.

h: Overlapping of Subject Reference (when the doers of two linked actions partly overlap)
t: NOMINALIZATION OF CLAUSES:

h: Nominalization (how a sentence becomes noun-like)
t: In Shipibo-Konibo, a whole sentence can be turned into something that works like a noun. I will call these "noun-like sentences" (linguists call them nominalized clauses). They do three jobs. They can be a "who/which…" description part ("the man who came"). They can be the thing you say, know or want ("I know that he came"). And they can tell when, why or where something happens. But first, let's look at what all noun-like sentences have in common. We will look at the endings on the verb, at who does what to whom and how they are marked, at the agreement markers, at the little markers that sit in second place, and at word order. The term nominalized verb is shortened to V_{NMLZ}.

h: Verb Morphology (the endings on the verb)
t:
A verb that is turned into a noun ends in one of these endings. First, the "ongoing" ending -ai (PP1). Second, the "finished" ending -a (PP2). Third, the storytelling past -a iki (PP2 AUX). Fourth, no ending at all, when the verb already has the long-ago past ending -ni (if the bare verb has only one syllable, the stress then moves to the second syllable). Fifth, the ending -ti (INF). It is used for purpose (‘in order to’), for what must happen, for the future, and for things that are generally true. In addition, a few verbs become nouns with no ending at all, which linguists call zero
nominalization. Some verb endings are used both in noun-like sentences and in ordinary full sentences that state something. Table 10.1 shows this with the verb pota- ‘leave, abandon’:
The forms in italics in the table look exactly the same. But they are used in different places and do different jobs. A verb that has been turned into a noun can behave like a noun; an ordinary verb can't. It can take noun endings, including a role marker when it is the last word of a noun group. And it can stand where a noun would stand. The next sentence is an ordinary full sentence ending in -ai. Before -ai come two verb endings: the verb's ‘not’ ending -yama and the verb's plural ending -kan:

h: Verb Morphology (the endings on the verb)
t:
(1) Shipi-baon-ra kapé pi-[y]ama-kan-ai. | ‘The Shipibo don’t eat alligator.’
Sentence (1) is a complete sentence that can stand on its own. Sentence (2) is different. It contains a noun-like sentence ending in ai. After it come the plural ending for nouns, -bo, and the
‘not’ ending for words that are not verbs, -ma. But notice that the verb's plural ending -kan stays, even after the verb has been turned into a noun:
(2) Shipibo-ra kapé pi-kan-ai-bo-ma iki. | ‘The Shipibo don’t eat alligator.’ More literally: “The Shipibo are not alligator-eaters.”
In (1), Kapé pi[y]amakanai works as a verb. It says something about who the sentence is about. In (2), kapé pikanaiboma works as a noun. It is what someone is said to be, like a teacher in English "he is a teacher". There is another difference. (1) can't be used as a noun, because it has -ra. This marker shows the speaker knows it directly. It never appears inside one of the big parts of a sentence.¹
A verb turned into a noun can still take many verb endings. The exceptions are the endings that close an ordinary full sentence: the ones that show whether the action is complete, and whether you are stating, asking or ordering.² Also, some mixes of a tense ending and a "turn into a noun" ending are not possible. Table 10.2 shows which:

h: Verb Morphology (the endings on the verb)
t:
The only exceptions are full verb forms that are the only part, or the first part, of the sentence (see also "who/which" description parts that don't point to a specific thing, in Valenzuela 2002b).
As Table 10.1 shows, a verb turned into a noun can't take the ending -ke, which full sentences use to show the action is complete. The "ongoing" ending is trickier. We could say there are two different endings that just sound the same. One is -ai_{1}, used in full sentences. The other is -ai_{2}, which turns the verb into a noun. The first can come after the long-ago past ending -ni; the second can't. The same could be said for -a iki.
The ending -ti (for purpose, the future and so on) works like -ai here. It can't be combined with the past tense endings.
As I said above, the long-ago past ending -ni doesn't need any extra "turn into a noun" ending. But when it is added to a bare verb of one syllable, -ni takes the stress. So how do you tell a full sentence from a noun-like one in the long-ago past? The noun-like one has no ending showing whether the action is complete (pota-ni-ke / pota-ni-ai versus pota-ni-0; see also Table 10.1). The pair -a iki is found much more often in ordinary full sentences than in noun-like ones.

h: Verb Morphology (the endings on the verb)
t:
The next example was made up for this book, based on (2) in Chapter 7. It has a verb turned into a noun. That verb has a beginning piece naming a body part. It also has several endings: some build a new word, and some add grammar information. (In Shipibo-Konibo, "who/which…" description parts are always noun-like sentences.)
(3) Nokon koka r-iki | [jawen ochíti ta-nini-nan-yama-bain-wan-kan-a] joni. | ‘The man whose dog they did not pull by the foot to his detriment while passing earlier today is my maternal uncle.’

h: Argument Structure, Alignment, and Adjunct Status (how the people and extra parts are marked)
t:
When a Shipibo-Konibo verb is turned into a noun, it keeps everything it had as a normal verb. It keeps all its people: the doer, the receiver, and so on. And they keep the same markers they have in a normal sentence. So these sentences are only partly noun-like. In some other languages, such sentences become much more like real nouns.³
The next example shows this with the transitive verb yoi- ‘tell.’ Even inside a noun-like sentence, it needs a doer with the doer marker (ERG) and a receiver with no marker (ABS). So in (4), yoi- takes jan, the ‘he/she’ word with the doer marker. It does not take jawen ‘his/her’, the form that shows who owns something:
(4) Jain ja-ke westíora yoxan [ja-n jato yoi-ai] | ‘There there was an old woman who told them/telling them…’
The same happens when ‘I’ is the doer in a noun-like sentence. We find en, ‘I’ with the doer marker, not nokon ‘my’:⁴
(5) [e-n atsa xeati a-ma-ibat-a] | ‘that I invited (to drink) yuca beer’
The next examples show two things. First, look at the words that say where, how or when (linguists call these adjuncts). In noun-like sentences they get the same agreement markers as in full sentences. These markers show what kind of doer the action has. Second, a verb turned into a noun can be the last word of a noun group. Then it takes that group's role marker, which shows the job of the group vis-à-vis the main sentence, that is, its job in the main sentence. In (6), the doer of nokota is the doer of an intransitive verb. So ‘from Kako’ must take the intransitive agreement (S agreement). At the same time,

h: Argument Structure, Alignment, and Adjunct Status (how the people and extra parts are marked)
t:
In Turkish and Cuzco Quechua, for example, noun-like sentences are built just like an ‘owner + thing’ phrase (compare English "the enemy's destruction of the city"). The doer gets the owner form, not the normal doer form, because it now describes the noun-like verb. And the whole noun-like sentence is marked as something owned.
Remember that all the other pronouns, and all nouns, look the same whether they are the doer or the owner.
the verb turned into a noun takes the doer marker (ergative case). That is because its noun group is the doer of a transitive verb in the main sentence:
(6) [Ainbo [Kako-nko-ni-a-x nokot-a]]-tonin-ra rao | kobin ak-ai. | ‘The woman who arrived from Kako is boiling the plant medicine.’ | Ainbo-ra Kako-nko-ni-a-x nokó-ke. | ‘The / a woman arrived from Kako.’
In (7), the doer of onanyantaana makes the ‘where’ word take the transitive agreement (A agreement), not the intransitive agreement (S). onanyantaana is the last word of its noun group. That group is who the main sentence is about, and the main verb is an intransitive verb. So onanyantaana gets no marker: it is in the plain form (absolutive):
(7) Ainbo [Makáyain-xon e-n onan-yantaan-a]-ra ne-no | nokó-ke. | ‘The woman I met in Makaya last year arrived here’. | E-n-ra ainbo onan-yantan-ke Makáyain-xon. | ‘I met a / the woman in Makaya last year.’

h: Argument Structure, Alignment, and Adjunct Status (how the people and extra parts are marked)
t:
Here are examples where the ‘how’ words carry these agreement markers:
(8) [jatik-ax-bi teet-ai] | ‘who / that work altogether’
(None) [jatí-xon-bi sepa-[a]i] | ‘who / that slash a chacra altogether’
Only these where/how/when words get agreement markers. Describing words like adjectives never do. So these words are still where/how/when words, even inside a noun-like sentence. They don't turn into describing words.⁵

h: Sentence Second Position Clitics (pieces that come second in the sentence)
t:
Some little markers always sit in second place in the sentence, right after the first big part. These are -ra (the speaker knows it directly), -ronki (the speaker was told), and the question marker -ki. A noun-like sentence is not a sentence of its own. It is only a part, or a piece of a part, of a bigger sentence. So it can't have one of these second-place markers inside it. But when a whole noun-like sentence comes first in the bigger sentence, the marker can come right after it. Many examples show this. For instance, compare (6a) and (7a) with (6b) and (7b). In (6a) and (7a), the ‘knows it directly’ marker -ra comes after the first part of the sentence, that is, after the whole noun-like sentence.
This makes Shipibo-Konibo noun-like sentences different from similar ones in English. In English, a ‘how’ word usually turns into a describing word (Givón 1990:507-8): i. a. The enemy rapidly destroyed the city b. The enemy’s rapid destruction of the city ii. a. She quickly departed b. Her quick departure. The same thing happens in Cuzco Quechua: the ‘how’ word stops being a ‘how’ word.

h: Constituent Order (word order)
t:
In ordinary sentences, the words can come in many orders. Noun-like sentences are different: the verb must always come last. Also, in the stories I recorded, almost every noun-like sentence with a transitive verb and both people named uses the order doer, receiver, verb (linguists call this AOV). (9a) is a noun-like sentence used as the thing being said or known, and it follows this preferred order:
(9) [Nawa profesor-nin bake-bo onan-ma-ti]-ra | a-ti-koma iki. | ‘That a mestizo teacher teaches (Shipibo) children is hard.’
(9b) puts the receiver first: receiver, doer, verb (OAV). Speakers like it less than (9a), but it is possible. However, the versions where the verb is not last are clearly wrong:
(9) [Bake-bo nawa profesor-nin onan-ma-ti]-ra.... | [Bake-bo onan-ma-ti nawa profesor-nin]-ra.... | [Nawa profesor-nin onan-ma-ti bake-bo]-ra.... | ‘That a mestizo teacher teaches (Shipibo) children is hard.’
Sentence (10) shows the possible orders in a "who/which…" description part. Again, you can see that the verb must come last in noun-like sentences:
(10) Nokon wetsa-n-ra [baikan nonti be-ai] | tsasi a-ke. | ‘My brother stopped the canoe that was being brought by the river current.’
Example (10b) can be understood in two ways. nonti ‘canoe’ can be inside the description part, or it can be the noun being described, standing before it. Both readings are correct, as we'll see in 10.2.1. Example (10d) works only if nonti is the noun being described:

h: Constituent Order (word order)
t:
(10) [nonti baikan be-ai] / nonti [baikan be-ai] | [nonti be-ai baikan] | [baikan be-ai] nonti / [baikan be-ai nonti] | ‘...the canoe that was being brought by the river current’ (elicitation)
(11) comes from a story. It has a "who/which…" description part with the doer, the receiver and the verb all present, in the order doer, receiver, verb (AOV):
(11) ...[nokon papa-n e-a yoi-katit-ai] jato yoi-ti ja-ke. | ‘...(I) have to pass on to them what my father used to tell me.’
In (12), the noun-like sentence has a verb with three people, like ‘give’ (giver, thing given, and the one who receives it). The one who receives it comes first in that sentence. This is clearly because that person is a living being and the focus of attention (linguists say it is high in animacy / topicality). Speakers accepted other orders, as long as the verb stayed last, but they liked them less than (12):
(12) [E-a maistoro-n taría a-ti meni-a-bi]-ra a-ti-koma iki. | ‘The work the teacher assigned me is difficult.’
In the stories I recorded, there are no noun-like sentences with all three people actually named.
Other words, which are not the doer or the receiver, can go in different places inside a noun-like sentence. The only place they can't go is the very end:
(13) [Bakish mi-n ainbo onan-ibat-a]-ra moa ka-ke. | ‘The woman you met yesterday left already.’ | [mi-n bakish ainbo onan-ibat-a]ra moa ka-ke. | [mi-n ainbo onan-ibat-a bakish]-ra moa ka-ke.

h: Constituent Order (word order)
t:
So we can conclude that Shipibo-Konibo noun-like sentences must end with the verb. With a transitive verb, the preferred order is doer, receiver, verb (AOV).
To sum up this section, I have shown the following. Shipibo-Konibo noun-like sentences have some limits. They can't take every full-sentence ending, and their word order is less free. But they keep important features of ordinary sentences. The verb keeps all its people (doer, receiver, and so on). And these keep the same markers they have in sentences of their own. Also, the where/how/when words in noun-like sentences keep their agreement markers. This shows they stay where/how/when words; they don't become more like describing words. The following table sums up how ordinary statements and noun-like sentences in Shipibo-Konibo are alike and how they differ.
As I said at the start of this chapter, noun-like sentences in Shipibo-Konibo do three jobs. They can be "who/which…" description parts. They can be the thing you say, know or want. And they can tell when, why or how something happens. For this last job, they usually carry an extra ending or a little word like ‘at’ or ‘after’ (linguists call these peripheral cases or postpositions). Let's now look at each of these jobs.

h: Relative Clauses ("who/which" descriptions ("the man who came"))
t:
In Shipibo-Konibo, "who/which…" description parts (Cl_{RELS}) are made with the partly noun-like sentences described above. In this section I describe them in
three ways. First, where they stand compared with the noun they describe. Second, which person in the description part can be the one described (the doer, the receiver, and so on). Third, how each of these is built. We will see that Shipibo-Konibo has description parts that come before the noun, after the noun, and around the noun (with the noun inside them). All three kinds are built in a similar way, which may be rare among the world's languages. I also want to stress something. This is the only area of Shipibo-Konibo grammar where the doer-marker pattern controls how sentences are put together (linguists call this syntactic ergativity). In this chapter, the nouns being described are underlined, and the description parts are in brackets. The short form V_{REL} means the verb of a description part.

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
A description part (Cl_{REL}) can stand in three places compared with the noun it describes, and all three are found in Shipibo-Konibo. It can come before the noun, as in examples (14)-(16). It can come after the noun, as in (17)-(19). Or it can wrap around the noun, with the noun inside it, as in (20)-(22) (linguists call this circumnominal or internally-headed). Examples (14), (17) and (20) were made up for this book and are included for comparison.
Prenominal relative clauses
(14) [Papa-n rete-ibat-a] jono-ra | moa no-n keyo-ke. | ‘We already finished the collared-peccary father killed yesterday.’
(15) [Jain jato bi-ai] joni-bo ik-á iki tanpóra-ya... | ‘The people who came to welcome them there had drums...’
(16) Tita-ra keyo-t-ai, ja-tian no-a bane-ti ka-[a]i | [ja-n no-a axe-a-a] jawéki-bo-ya. | ‘Our mother dies and then we are left with the things that she taught us.’
Postnominal relative clauses:
(17) jono [papa-n rete-ibat-a]-ra moa no-n keyo-ke. | ‘We already finished the collared-peccary father killed yesterday.’
(18) Ja iki Shipibo [mashá ik-í nena-ni]. | ‘Those (nena palm trees forming a circle) were the Shipibo who very long time ago, while performing the mashá (singing and dancing), turned into nena trees.’
(19) Jain-xon... mashá i-kan-ai... xeati [yaka-t-a]-ki, | ja xobo [yaka-t-a]-ki, | ja witá [ni-a-bo]-ki. | ‘Then, they performed the mashá honoring...the drink in the jars, the house standing there, and the logs (that hold the house) standing there.’

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
Circumnominal relative clauses:
(20) [Papa-n jono rete-ibat-a]-ra moa no-n
(None) keyo-ke. | ‘We already finished the collared-peccary father killed yesterday.’
(21) [No-n ja rao xea-a] ik-á iki | ja-skat-i kikin moka kinan-ti. | ‘The plant medicine we drank was extremely bitter so as to provoke vomiting.’
(22) [Mi-n yawa maan-ibat-a]-ra onsá-yora iki. | ‘The white-lipped peccaries you brought down [from the sky] are too dangerous.’
Shipibo-Konibo clearly has description parts with the noun inside them (Cl_{RELS}). So a question comes up. Could (17)-(19), which I called "after the noun" above, really be the "noun inside" kind? There are several reasons to think the "after the noun" kind does exist. First, in some cases the "noun inside" reading would break the usual order doer, receiver, verb (AOV). That order is preferred in description parts and in noun-like sentences in general. This is what happens in (23) and (24). There, manan keyá ‘steep mountain’ and nokon machíto ‘my machete’ are the receivers in the description part:
(23) Jain ik-á iki manan keyá, [tso-n-bi mape-ti]-ma | ‘There, there was a steep mountain that nobody could climb.’
(24) Meráya-nin-ra e-a namá-xon-ke nokon machíto | [e-n manó-ma-yantan-a]. | ‘The great shaman dreamed for me of the machete I had misplaced some time ago.’
Still, word order alone does not settle the question. As shown in 10.1.4, the order receiver, doer, verb (OAV) can occur, although speakers like it less. It shows up in made-up examples, or when the receiver is a living being or the focus of attention.⁶

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
The role markers give much stronger support for the "after the noun" reading. In some description parts that I treat as "after the noun", the noun being described does not carry the marker that its role vis-à-vis the description part would need. Look at the next sentence. The main verb group iká iki neeti is an intransitive verb, so who the sentence is about must have no marker (ABS). But the verb of the description part, shinan-, is a transitive verb, so its doer would need the doer marker (ERG). jonibo has no marker. So this noun must belong to the main sentence, as who it is about. That means the description part comes after the noun:
(25) ...jato-n xobo-n-bo-ki joni-bo [ja shinan-tani-ai-bo] | ik-á iki neet-i. | ‘Those who were a little bit conscious climbed up to their houses.’ (Inuma 1993:25)
DeLancey (1999) asks a similar question in a study of "who/which" description parts in Lhasa Tibetan. He looks at (iii), which he reads as having the description part (Cl_{REL}) after the noun. He asks whether it could instead be read as having the noun inside, like (iv) (from DeLancey, op. cit.):
(iii) mi [sha gtub=mkhan de] | ‘the person who chopped the meat’ (p. 243)
(iv) [nga-s sha btsos-pas de] | ‘the meat which I cooked’ (p. 246)

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
In Lhasa Tibetan, the receiver in a main sentence can come before the doer, to put the focus on it.
In (25), the word ja comes between jonibo and the verb of the description part (V_{REL}). This suggests another reading. Maybe (25) is a noun followed by a description part with no noun of its own (ja works like ‘the’ and as a word pointing back to something already mentioned; see 10.2.3). However, the same sentence is perfectly fine without ja. (26a) is a similar example. Again, the main verb is an intransitive verb, the verb of the description part is a transitive verb, and the noun being described has no marker (ABS). Compare yamekan ewa in (26a) and (26b). In (26b), it must take the doer marker:
(26) Ja-ská-xon jis-á-ki ik-á iki | yamekan ewa [moa bari noka ak-ai]. | ‘Then they saw the eclipse that shaded the sun already.’ | Yamekan ewa-n-ra moa bari noka ak-ai. | ‘The great darkness shaded the sun already.’
In some languages, certain kinds of dependent sentences stop using the doer-marker pattern. Nothing suggests that Shipibo-Konibo does this. Just the opposite: whenever a doer is clearly named in a description part (Cl_{RELS}), or in any noun-like sentence, it has the doer marker. So the doer-marker pattern (ergative) is kept.
There is one more reason to accept the "after the noun" reading. Description parts probably work in parallel with describing words (adjectives). In Shipibo-Konibo, an adjective can come before or after the noun it describes, with no clear difference in meaning. Both orders are common in everyday speech (see 6.7.6), with a

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
likely preference for putting long, heavy describing phrases after the noun (6.7.7). The examples below were first shown in Chapter 6 as (142) and (143):
(27) Bo-ax nokó-kan-a iki ani manaman. | ‘Getting there they arrived at a big mountain’.
(28) Jain ik-á iki manan keyá, [tso-n-bi mape-ti]-ma | ‘There, there was a steep mountain that nobody could climb.’
Adjectives and “who/which…” description parts do much the same job. Both are optional words that describe a noun. Adjectives can come after the noun. So it makes sense that description parts can come after the noun too. Description parts and adjectives would then behave alike. (Something similar may happen in Lhasa Tibetan, DeLancey 1999.)
Here is another strong reason to think a description part can come after its noun. Look at sentences like (29) and (30). (29) was shown earlier as (4):
(29) Ja-tian jain ja-ke westíora yoxan [ja-n jato yoi-ai].... | ‘And then there was an old woman who told them / telling them…’
(30) Jain iki pionis bepon [ja-n rao-n-kati-kan-ai]. | ‘There is the resin pionis with which they cured (the girls).’
Suppose we said that yoxan and pionis bepon were inside their description parts. Then the noun would be named twice inside the same part: once in full, and once again by the pronoun ja-n. That would be quite strange. It would be especially strange when the described noun is the doer (see also exx. (85)-(87), (89)-(96), among others).

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
Also, in some cases speakers pause between what I take to be the outside noun and the description part that follows it:
(31) ...jawe-ra i-bir[a]-ai tepacha a-ti iamax rapichi, | [ja-n xawi jene-bo potsi-ti]. | ‘...what will we use, a tepacha or a trapiche, to extract the cane juice (with it).’
Finally, look at the next sentence. Here it seems clear that the noun belongs to the main sentence, not to the description part. In (32), the noun westíora nawa carries the emphasis ending -bi. Together with yamarake ‘there is not’, this gives the meaning ‘there is not a single mestizo’. (A similar pattern appears with words like “nobody”, treated in 8.2.9.2.; see also ex. (45).)
(32) Yama-ra-ke westíora nawa-bi [no-n joi | jakon-i yoyo ik-ai]. | ‘There is not a single mestizo who can speak our language well.’
So I conclude that there is enough evidence for all three kinds in Shipibo-Konibo. The description part can come before the noun, after the noun, or wrap around it so the noun sits inside (linguists call these prenominal, postnominal and internally-headed relative clauses).⁷ All three show up in natural storytelling and in sentences I asked speakers for. None of them is rare.
Some linguists tell apart “internally-headed” and “circumnominal” relative clauses. In Shipibo-Konibo that difference doesn't matter.
Finally, a noun can have one description part before it and another one after it, at the same time:

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t:
(33) [Ja bi-ti] ainbo [jawen papa-n raan-a] i-ká iki | chi-yaká. | ‘The woman he had to take as wife and who had been sent by her father was seated in the back of the canoe.’
Again, description parts behave like adjectives. As shown in 6.7.6, when one noun has two adjectives, these are the preferred orders:
(34) wiso ochíti siná | ‘black fierce dog’ | mecha joni shinan-ya | ‘good fisherman / hunter, well-intentioned man’
Sometimes you can hear a pause after the noun:
(35) Inka-ronki i-ká iki [wai-n teet-ai] joni, [jatíbi jawéki | ban-ai]. | ‘The Inka was a man who practiced agriculture and grew all kinds of crops.’
In Shipibo-Konibo, the "who/which…" description part can come before the noun it describes, after it, or wrapped around it. This freedom is unusual and interesting to linguists. Here is what other languages tend to do (Keenan 1985a:144-5). Languages that put the verb first, or between doer and receiver like English, mostly put the description after the noun. English does this too: "the man who came." (Languages with English-like word order also often allow both positions.) Languages that put the verb last, like Shipibo-Konibo, mostly put the description before the noun. But other patterns are also common in them. What seems rare is for one language to use all three patterns regularly. Shipibo-Konibo uses before, after and wrapped-around descriptions that are built in a similar way. And it uses them to describe the very same kinds of nouns in the sentence.

h: 10.2.1.1. Headed Relative Constructions
t: Section 10.2.4.8 offers another possible argument about certain of these "who/which…" descriptions. It says they are best seen as coming after the noun, rather than having the noun inside them. Here is the reason. In the corpus of stories studied, descriptions that clearly have the noun inside them occur only when they describe the receiver of the action.

h: 10.2.1.2. Headless Relative Constructions
t:
Sometimes a "who/which…" description part has no noun at all to describe. English does this too: "whoever came left early." These descriptions work as a noun all by themselves. They can be the doer or the receiver of the main verb. The next example comes from a traditional story. In it, the only Shipibo man to survive a great flood is visited by two women: the Inka’s daughter and her servant. The man catches the servant. Then she says the sentence below, which contains two of these noun-less descriptions.
(36) E-a-ma r-iki [no-n Inka-n raan-a], | oa-kaya r-iki [mi-n bi-ti]. | ‘I am not the one sent by our Inka; it is the one over there that you must take as wife.’
The noun ainbo ‘woman’ could easily be added to one or both description parts above. But native speakers reject sentences where both description parts come after the noun:
(36) E-a-ma r-iki [no-n Inka-n raan-a] ainbo, | oa-kaya r-iki [mi-n bi-ti] ainbo. | E-a-ma r-iki [no-n Inka-n raan-a] ainbo | oa-kaya r-iki ainbo [mi-n bi-ti]. | E-a-ma r-iki ainbo [no-n Inka-n raan-a], | oa-kaya r-iki ainbo [mi-n bi-ti]. | ??E-a-ma r-iki ainbo [no-n Inka-n raan-a], | oa-kaya r-iki [mi-n bi-ti] ainbo. | ‘I am not the woman sent by our Inka, it is the woman over there that you must take as wife.’

h: 10.2.1.3. Relative Clauses that Interrupt a Determiner-Head Sequence
t:
In Shipibo-Konibo, pointing words like “this” and “that” always come first in a noun phrase. A very common kind of description part sits between such a pointing word and its noun, like saying “this [who was drowning] woman”. The examples below show all three pointing words: nato ‘this (near)’, ja ‘that (middle distance)’ and oa ‘that (far away)’ (linguists call them demonstratives). Each one is separated from its noun by a description part. Again, this matches adjectives. In the (a) sentences, the description part can easily be swapped for a simple adjective, as the (b) sentences show:
(37) Nato [jene-n rete-a] ainbaon-ra moa join-ai. | ‘This woman who was drowning is breathing already.’ (Lit. “The woman (whom) the flowing water had killed is breathing already.”) (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:230) | Nato yoashi ainbaon-ra moa join-ai. | ‘This stingy woman is breathing already.’
(38) Ja [wexa-anan-a] joni rabé raká-kan-ai | westíora oxé. | ‘The two men who cut each other with the wexati knife lay for one month.’ | Ja yopa joni rabé-ra raká-kan-ai | westíora oxe. | ‘Those two bad hunter / fisher men lay for a month...’
(39) Jain ik-á iki oa [no-a shiro bewakan ninká-ma-ai-bo] | ainbo-bo. | ‘There stood the women who provoked us with their shiro songs.’ | Jain ik-á iki oa siná ainbo-bo. | ‘There stood those brave women.’

h: 10.2.1.3. Relative Clauses that Interrupt a Determiner-Head Sequence
t:
A similar thing happens when a number comes before its noun (as section 6.7.5 shows, a number can come either before or after its noun):
(40) E-n-ra mato yoi-ai westíora [nokon yosi-shoko betan e-a | winó-ni] jawéki.... | ‘I will tell you one thing that happened to me and my grandfather...’ | E-n-ra mato yoiy-ai rabé onis jawéki. | ‘I am going to tell you two sad things.’

h: 10.2.1.4. Relative Clauses that Interrupt a Complex Predicate
t:
In the next example, a description part with no noun of its own sits in the middle of a two-part verb. The helper verb iká iki comes first. The verb that depends on it, biax, comes later. Together they make one verb, iká iki...biax:
(41) Ja-tian ja-bo bo-kan-ke-tian, nokon tita ik-á iki
(None) [jatíbi ja-n nokon wetsa rabé raó a-ti] bi-ax: | kori, nane, maxe, meskó keská jawéki-bo. | ‘By the time they (the uncles) left, my mother had already gotten all (those things) with which to embellish my two sisters: lip ornaments, genipa, achiote, all kinds of things.’

h: 10.2.1.5. Discontinuous Relative Constructions
t:
Sometimes a noun and its description part are split apart by another describing word. In (42), an adjective comes between the noun and its description parts:
(42) Ja-ke Shipibo jakon-ma-ribi [ja no-a oin-ax “jo-wé” | i-ama-[a]i-bo-ribi], [no-a oinn-a-ma jis-á-res | ik-ai]. | ‘There are also bad Shipibo (men) who do not greet us when they see us, who act as if they had not seen us.’
The noun and the description part can also be split apart by a number:
(43) Ja-tian jain i-kan-ai ja xontako rabé [tanti-ma-kan-a]... | ‘And then there were the two young girls who had been put to rest...’ (the SK sentence is active)
In the next example, the part kikin xeta wisobiribi iki ‘whose teeth were extremely black’ ends in -i. This is a “same person” marker. It shows that this part depends on a main sentence with an intransitive verb, here jakátiai. This piece breaks into the middle of the description part. It works like an extra description of the noun:
(44) Ja-káti-ai [yotokonti pi-á] kikin xeta wiso-bi-ribi ik-í joni-bo. | ‘There were people who ate yotokonti and whose teeth were extremely (shiny) black.’
Sometimes a description part is moved away from its noun, further along the sentence (linguists call this extraposition). In (45), the phrase westíora jonibi ‘a single man’ comes first. In meaning, it belongs together with the description parts that follow. But the doer and the verb come in between and break it up. Notice also the adjective mecha ‘good fisher / hunter’ between two description parts:

h: 10.2.1.5. Discontinuous Relative Constructions
t:
(45) Ikaxbi rama-tian westíora joni-bi no-n mera-yama-[a]i [wai-a-[a]i], mecha, [ja sapen rete-ai], [wame rete-ai]. | ‘But nowadays we can’t find a single man who knows how to make chacra, a good fisher / hunter, who kills manatee, kills paiche.’
Here are two more examples from stories where the description part is moved away from its noun:⁸
(46) ...jain-xon-ribi-ra a-ti iki mi-n wetsa-n | chomo ani a-kin, kentí ani a-kin, | [ja-n atsa xeati yasa-n-ti]. | ‘...also, your sister has to manufacture big jars and pots in which to put the yuca beer.’
(47) No-a ainbo-bo iki joxo nawa-bo keská-ma, | [koríki-nin-bicho jawéki ak-ai-bo]. | ‘We, Shipibo women, are not like the (female) white outsiders, who only know how to do things with money.’
A split-up description part can also be moved to the very front of the sentence:
(48) [Awaranpiti naman raka-t-a]-ra e-n mananxawe bi-ke. | ‘I caught a tortoise that was lying under the / one vine.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:87)
(49) [Taxbakan nono-ai]-ra epa-n ano rete-ke. | ‘Uncle killed a paca that was swimming in the tahuampa’⁹ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:91)
Sentences (46) and (47) are like these English examples, where ‘who was invited’ describes ‘everyone’ in the same way in both sentences (from Jacobson 1994:719): iii. a. Everyone who was invited arrived. b. Everyone arrived who was invited.

h: 10.2.1.5. Discontinuous Relative Constructions
t:
Seasonal flood plain.
Nothing in (48) and (49) openly shows which person in the main sentence is the noun being described. Each main sentence has a doer and a receiver. Still, only the receiver can be understood as the described noun. I deal with this in 10.2.4.8.
The next example, part of which was shown in (40a), is another split-up description part. The extra part yomerai kaax ‘once we went fishing’ ends in -ax. This is a “same person, earlier action” marker. It shows that this part shares its doer with the description part, whose verb is an intransitive verb. Two things are split here. The description part separates the number from its noun. And the noun separates the description part from the extra part that depends on it:
(50) E-n-ra mato yoi-ai westíora [nokon yosi-shoko betan e-a | winó-ni] jawéki yomera-i ka-[a]x]. | ‘I will tell you one thing that happened to me and my grandfather once we went fishing.’
A description part with no noun can also have its own smaller parts hanging on it. In (51), ainbo bikaskin ‘when one wants to conquer a woman’ depends on raonti ‘to cure’. You can tell from the ending -kin. This “same person” marker matches a doer who acts on a receiver. So the verb it leans on must be a transitive verb:

h: 10.2.1.5. Discontinuous Relative Constructions
t: (51) Koshoshka-nin xeni iki [[ainbo bi-kas-kin] rao-n-ti]. | ‘The river dolphin’s fat is (that which is used) to cure a woman when one wants to conquer her.’

h: The Absence of a Differential Nominalization Strategy (no special form just for descriptions)
t:
As I will show in 10.2.4, Shipibo-Konibo mostly builds description parts in two ways. Either it leaves a gap where the described noun would be (linguists call this gapping), or it puts a pronoun there. But first, this section deals with two related questions. One is whether the “turning into a noun” endings tell us anything about the described noun. The other is how the pointing word ja is used like “the”.
Many languages build description parts by turning a sentence into a noun. Some of them also use this to show the role of the described noun: is it the doer, the receiver, and so on? Shipibo-Konibo description parts are clearly turned into nouns. So we may ask: does Shipibo-Konibo use these noun-making endings to show the role of the described noun?
The examples below show that the answer is no. In Shipibo-Konibo, the noun-making endings tell you nothing about the role of the described noun. In (52) and (53), the same verb form pi-á ‘ate’ is used. In (52) the described noun is the doer (the people who ate). In (53) it is the receiver (what I ate). ((52) was shown earlier as (44).)
(52) Ja-káti-ai [yotokonti pi-á] kikin xeta wiso-bi-ribi | ik-í joni-bo. | ‘There were people who ate yotokonti and whose teeth were extremely (shiny) black.’

h: The Absence of a Differential Nominalization Strategy (no special form just for descriptions)
t:
(53) [Pi-á]-tonin-ra e-a kinan-ma-ke. | ‘What I ate made me vomit’.
In the next sentence, a part turned into a noun with -a describes the doer of an intransitive verb (‘the man who came’):
(54) E-a-ra beno-a iki [nokon papa yokat-i jo-a] | joni betan. | ‘I got married with the man who came to ask (my hand to) my father.’
The same is true of parts turned into nouns with -ai. Examples (55)-(57) show -ai parts describing the doer of a transitive verb, the doer of an intransitive verb, and a receiver, in that order:
(55) ...jain oa ainbo-bo [no-a ...shiro bewakan ninká-ma-ai-bo]. | ‘...there (were) the women who provoked us with their shiro songs.’
(56) Mapéken-xon oin-a iki xoxo bake-bo [naikamea ik-ai] . | ‘Uncovering (them) (he) saw the illegitimate children who were from the sky.’
(57) ...jain-xon [no-n tita-n a-káti-ai] jawéki-ribi no-n | chiban-ai. | ‘...and then we continue practicing the things that our mother used to do.’
The next sentences show the same three roles with parts turned into nouns by -ni:
(58) Ja-ki ik-á iki ja [Inka bake bi-ni] joni. | ‘He / this was the man who had rescued the Inka child long time ago’.
The next example was shown earlier as (18):
(59) Ja iki Shipibo [mashá ik-í nena-ni]. | ‘Those (nena palm trees forming a circle) were the Shipibo who very long time ago, while performing the mashá (singing and dancing), turned into nena palm trees.’

h: The Absence of a Differential Nominalization Strategy (no special form just for descriptions)
t:
(60) Ja-tian no-n tita no-n kikin a-kin shinan-ai | [ja-n no-a a-ma-ni] jawéki-bo. | ‘Then, we remember our mother very much and the things that she taught us.’
Below are parts turned into nouns with -ti, the “to do” ending (like English “to” in “something to drive with”). They describe an intransitive doer, a receiver, and a tool:¹⁰
(61) Ja r-iki [no-n axé i-ti]-n-a | ‘This is what belongs to our custom.’
(62) Payári r-iki [pia-n tsaka-ti]. | ‘The arahuana¹¹ is (something) to drive with.’ (Valenzuela 1998:239)
(63) ...ja iki [ja-n xawi jene potsi-ti]. | ‘...it (a tepachati) is (something) to extract the cane juice with.’
-Ti description parts are like English “to” description parts, which also don't show the role of the described noun (from Keenan 1985:169): iv. a. The man to see is Fred. b. The first man to cross the line will get a prize. Shipibo-Konibo -ti description parts seem to be more common than the English ones.
K. fish; Osteoglossum bicirrhosum.
In the examples above, -ti has a general or “for doing” meaning. In the sentence below, it means “had to”:
(64) [Ja bi-ti] ainbo-ki ik-á iki | chi-yaká. | ‘The woman he had to take (as wife) was sitting in the back of the canoe.’ (Inuma 1993:34; analyzed in Valenzuela 2002b:48)
So in Shipibo-Konibo, the noun-making endings tell you about time, and about whether something must or can happen. But they don't help you find the role of the described noun. Therefore I conclude that Shipibo-Konibo description parts are built as nouns, but this is not the way the language shows the role of the described noun. We can also conclude something else. When these endings do happen to show the role, that is a side effect. It is not one of their main jobs.

h: The Demonstrative Ja (the pointing word ja)
t:
One tricky question about Shipibo-Konibo description parts is how to understand the word ja. On the one hand, ja belongs to a set of pointing words (“this”, “that”). These can go before a noun or stand alone in place of a noun. In some uses ja works just like English “the” (see 6.1.6). On top of that, ja is also the word for “he / she / it”, with no difference for male or female (6.1.1).
Inside description parts, ja can do two jobs. First, it can come before the described noun (said or just understood) as a “the” word. This matters, because adding a word like “the” is one way that sentences turned into nouns can differ from normal sentences (Givón 1990). Second, ja can be a pronoun (“him / her / it”) in the plain form, inside the description part. But nothing marks exactly where a description part begins. So when ja comes before a description part with an intransitive verb, it is hard to decide which job it is doing. This leaves a number of unclear cases, like the ones below:
(65) ...ja [re-yaká]-ki ik-á iki Inka ainbo-ma. | ‘...the one sitting in the front of the canoe was not the Inka woman.’ | ...[ja re-yaká]-ki ik-á iki Inka ainbo-ma. | ‘...the one sitting in the front of the canoe was not the Inka woman.’

h: The Demonstrative Ja (the pointing word ja)
t:
With a transitive verb there is no such problem. There, a pronoun for the doer would carry the doer marker. It would be jan, not the plain form ja:
(66) ...ja joni-ki i-ká iki [ja-n bi-a]... | ‘...this was the man who rescued (him).’

h: Relativizability and Relativization Strategies (which nouns can be described this way, and how)
t: In Shipibo-Konibo, a description part can describe many kinds of nouns. The noun can be: the receiver; other kinds of receivers (someone who gets something, or the extra person brought in by an “extra person” ending); the doer of an intransitive verb (someone who acts, someone something happens to, or people doing something to each other); the doer of a transitive verb (including verbs like “give”); the second person of verbs like “be scared of”; extra parts like “with what”, “where”, “from where”, “because of” and “together with”; and the owner of something. I got the “scared of” type and the owner type only by asking speakers. All the others come from a collection of about 135 description parts taken from natural stories. They are listed in order of how often they appear there, most common first. All the numbers in this section refer to that collection.

h: 10.2.4.1. Relativization on Objects
t:
Most description parts in this group describe a receiver that is acted on. Only one describes an extra person brought in by an ending. Ones describing a person who receives something were easy to get by asking speakers. In the collection, receiver description parts come in all four kinds: with no noun, before the noun, after the noun, and with the noun inside. All of them seem fairly common. The favourite method is to leave a gap where the receiver would be (about 30 out of 43 cases). In a few cases (4), there may be a pronoun there instead. The sentences below show the different kinds of receiver description parts:
Description before the noun, describing the receiver, gap method (the next example was shown earlier as (57))
(67) ...jain-xon [no-n tita-n a-káti-ai] jawéki-ribi no-n | chiban-ai. | ‘...and then we follow the things that our mother used to do.’
Description after the noun, describing the receiver, gap method (see also exx. (71)-(73))
(68) Moa-tian-ra i-káti-ai yoinabo [[ochó-ma mera-ti] itan | icha]. | ‘Long time ago, animals could be found nearby and in large numbers.’
In the next example, the speaker talks about the neighbouring Kokama people, who have lost their own native identity. The sentence has two description parts. The first describes a receiver and has the noun inside it. The second has no noun at all. Both use the gap method:

h: 10.2.4.1. Relativization on Objects
t:
(69) Ja-tian [neno-n-xon bake-bo a-kan-a-bo] iki | [jato-n joi-n moa shinan-benot-a-bo]. | ‘Then, the children they procreated here have already forgotten their language.’
The next description part has no noun and describes a receiver. It can be understood in two ways. The reading in (a) uses the pronoun method:
No noun, describing the receiver, possible pronoun method
(70) Jaino-a-x-ki bewa bewa-kai[n]-ni-i ka-a iki, | onis onis-kai[n]-ni-i [ja joni-n bi-a-ma]. | ......ja [joni-n bi-a-ma]. | ‘Then she left singing and singing, feeling sad very sad, the one the man didn’t take as wife.’
Example (71) is interesting. Its description part has an “each other” verb that also carries -kin, an ending that brings in an extra person (“with / against whom”). This is the only description part in my story collection that describes such an extra person:¹²
(71) Ja iki koshi shinan-ya-bo ja ainbo-bo | [kopi-anan-kin-ai-bo]. | ‘Those were brave the women they competed against.’
The next examples, which I got by asking speakers, describe an extra person brought in by an ending. In (72) it is someone something is done for. In (73) it is someone something is done against:
(72) Oa joni [e-n rao a-xon-a] r-iki nokon koka. | ‘That man for whom I prepared medicine is my maternal uncle.’
(73) Oa joni [e-n atapa yometso:anan-a] r-iki nokon koka. | ‘That man to whose detriment I stole the chicken is my maternal uncle.’

h: 10.2.4.1. Relativization on Objects
t: Ainbobo cannot be read as the “each other” partner. If it were, it would carry the “together with” marker.

h: 10.2.4.2. Relativization on Intransitive Subjects
t:
Description parts about the doer of an intransitive verb come in two kinds. Some describe someone something happens to (S_{o}). Others describe someone who acts (S_{a}). The first kind is slightly more common.¹³ There is also one case with an “each other” verb, whose doer has therefore lost the doer marker. In the story collection, these description parts come both before and after the noun. But there is no clear case with the noun inside. Description parts with no noun are very common. The favourite method is to leave a gap:
Possibly a description before the noun, describing an intransitive doer something happens to (S_{o}), gap method
(74) Jain-ribi-ronki be-kan-a iki... oa bake | [moa xontako-ai]... | ‘There also came...those girls (who were) already turning into young women...’ | ....[bake moa xontako-ai]...
Description before the noun, describing an intransitive doer who acts (S_{a}), gap method (the next sentence was shown as (54))
(75) E-a-ra beno-a iki [nokon papa yokat-i jo-a] | joni betan. | ‘I got married with the man who came to ask (my hand to) my father.’
I sorted these by meaning, because Shipibo-Konibo has no general grammatical way to tell S_{a} from S_{o}. In a few cases the choice seemed rather arbitrary.
Description with an “each other” verb, describing an intransitive doer, gap method (ex. (76) was already shown as (38))

h: 10.2.4.2. Relativization on Intransitive Subjects
t:
(76) Ja [wexa-anan-a] joni rabé raká-kan-ai | westíora oxé. | ‘The two men who had cut each other with the wexati knife lay for one month.’
Sometimes we can say the description part has been moved to the front, as in the next example (shown before as (48)):
Description moved to the front, describing an intransitive doer
(77) [Awaranpiti naman raka-t-a]-ra e-n mananxawe | bi-ke. | ‘I caught a tortoise that was lying under the / one awaranpiti vine.’
Importantly, when I asked speakers, I did get clear cases with the noun inside the description part of an intransitive verb. Look at the example below:
