(78) E-n-ra bena-[a]i [Kako-nko-ni-a-x joni noko-t-a]. | ‘I am looking for the man who arrived from Kako.’
In (78), the verb of the description part is nokot- ‘arrive’, an intransitive verb. Its doer makes the “from” word Kako-nko-ni-a-x ‘from Kako’ take an intransitive agreement ending. So this “from Kako” part cannot belong to the main sentence, because the main verb (“look for”) is a transitive verb. That means the noun joni ‘man’ must be inside the description part. This fact will
become very important when we look at the limits on description parts with the noun inside.
The usual way to show the noun inside the description part is to leave a gap. But the pronoun method also seems possible, as the next sentences suggest. Notice that ja appears twice in the example below. Probably the first ja means “the”, and the second is the pronoun “she”:

h: 10.2.4.2. Relativization on Intransitive Subjects
t:
(79) Ja Mararina-ronki ik-á iki [ja ainbo | [ja chi-[y]aká]]. | ‘It is said that the woman who was seated in the back of the canoe was named Mararina.’ (Inuma 1993:34)
Here is a similar example I got by asking a speaker:
(80) Pena-ronki ik-á iki ja ainbo [ja Iparia-nko ka-a]. | ‘It is said that Pena was (the name of) the woman who went to Iparia.’
There is another way to read the bracketed parts above. They could be description parts with no noun, placed next to ‘the woman’ to say more about her. Then the second ja would mean “the”, not “she” (but compare these examples with ex. (83)). That reading doesn't work for the next example from a story. There the supposed pronoun is plural: jato ‘them’. Words like “the” have no plural form, so jato must be a pronoun:¹⁴
One speaker I consulted rejected the story example below. This may be part of a more general dislike of plurals as pronouns here, see exx. (84) and (86).
(81) Jain-xon.......mashá i-kan-ai [jato jo-a-bo]-ki... | ‘Then...they performed the mashá honoring those who had come...’

h: 10.2.4.3. Relativization on Transitive Subjects
t:
Now for description parts about the doer of a transitive verb, including verbs like “give”. Most have a noun outside, either before or after the description part. A few have no noun at all. As with intransitive doers, the story collection has no case with the noun inside. The only possible exceptions involve a word meaning “whoever”:
(82) [Jawerato-n-ki yokat-ai] ja meni-kati-kan-ai. | ‘They gave her (her daughter) to whoever asked for (her).’
The favourite method here is to leave a gap (25 of the 33 story examples). The pronoun method is clearly found too (7 cases), as below:
(83) Pena-ronki ik-á iki ja ainbo [ja-n mapó ak-ai]. | ‘Pena was the woman who made pottery.’
Speakers generally rejected plural pronouns in this method:
(84) ??Metsá-ronki i-kan-a iki ja ainbo-bo [ja-baon mapó ak-ai] | ‘These were beautiful the women who made pottery.’
When the description part comes before the noun, the pronoun method is rare, probably because a pronoun normally comes after the noun it points back to, not before it (Keenan and Comrie 1977, Keenan 1985a:149). Interestingly, Shipibo-Konibo does have clear cases of the pronoun method in description parts before the noun. Here is one that describes a doer:
(85) Nete be-ai-tian pikó-pao-ni-ke [ja-n ak-ai] | joni oxa oxa-yama-i. | ‘When the day arrived the organizer came out (of his mosquito net) without sleeping much.’

h: 10.2.4.3. Relativization on Transitive Subjects
t:
In the example below, jan is singular. Yet it clearly points to the plural noun jonibo ‘men’:
(86) [Ja-n jato bi-ai] joni-bo ik-á iki tanpóra-ya. | ‘Those men who welcomed them had drums.’
Similar cases are easy to find in newly made words, like this one:
(87) [Ja-n yoiy-a] ainbo | ‘the woman who told (the story) (i.e., the narrator)’
Description parts before the noun with a pronoun might also exist when the described noun is in the plain form (ABS). But as I said earlier, these are hard to pin down for sure. A pronoun in the plain form looks exactly like ja meaning “the”.

h: 10.2.4.4. Relativization on Obliques
t:
Here, “oblique” does not mean a person the verb needs. It means the extra, optional parts of a sentence, like “with what”, “where” or “from where”. Description parts about the second person of verbs like “be scared of” (which also carries a marker) are treated later.
My collection has 18 description parts about such extra parts. They break down like this: a tool (11), a “from” place (1), an “at / to” place (3), a “together with” person (1), a cause (1), and the thing something is about (1). The gap method is found with description parts that have no noun.¹⁵ The next example was shown earlier as (51):
No noun, gap method, describing a tool
(88) Koshoshka-nin xeni iki [[ainbo bi-kas-kin] | rao-n-ti]. | ‘The river dolphin’s fat is (that which is used) to cure a woman when we want to conquer her.’
Keenan (1985:154) mentions gaps in such low positions in older forms of English: ‘the village that I walked down the main street....’. You can hear similar sentences in spoken English today.
However, for these extra parts, leaving a gap is not the favourite method (only 3 cases). These parts sit low on a scale of how easily languages can describe nouns (the Accessibility Hierarchy, Keenan and Comrie 1977). Instead, the pronoun method is common, with description parts that have no noun, come after the noun, or come before it:

h: 10.2.4.4. Relativization on Obliques
t:
No noun, pronoun method, describing a tool
(89) Rama a-non a-wé [ja-n no-n jato kena-i ka-ti]. | ‘Now let’s prepare what we are going to invite them with (i.e., manioc beer).’
In my story collection, all description parts about extra parts with an outside noun use the pronoun method:
After the noun, pronoun method, describing an “at / to” place
(90) Jain-xon-ribi-ra a-kan-ti iki, kawin [ja-n yawa | raka-n-ti]... | ‘Also they have to make rush mats on which to place the white-lipped peccaries.’
After the noun, pronoun method, describing a “from” place
(91) No-n mapo r-iki westíora kirika [jainoa oin-xon a-ti] | keská-ribi. | ‘Our heads are like a book from where (we) see (the designs we imagine) and then reproduce (them).’
The next example shows a description part about an extra part, moved away from its noun, using the pronoun method:
Moved away, pronoun method, describing an “at / to” place (shown earlier as (46))
(92) ...jain-xon-ribi-ra a-ti iki mi-n wetsa-n | chomo ani a-kin, kentí ani a-kin, | [ja-n atsa xeati yasa-n-ti]. | ‘...also, your sister has to manufacture big jars and pots in which to put the yuca beer.’
Description parts before the noun with a pronoun are also found for these extra parts:
Before the noun, pronoun method, describing an “at / to” place
(93) No-a [jain wirákocha-bo keská rao-meet-[t]i] | xobo-oma iki, ospital-oma iki. | ‘We have no houses where we can get cured, like the White people; we have no hospitals.’

h: 10.2.4.4. Relativization on Obliques
t:
The next example is a similar one that describes a cause.
Before the noun, pronoun method, describing a cause
(94) [Ja kopí e-a tima-nan-a] ainbo-ra moa ka-ke. | ‘The woman because of whom I fought already left.’
Before the noun, pronoun method, describing a tool
(95) [Ja-n nokon poi-n awá rete-ibat-a] to'ati-ra... | ‘The rifle with which my brother killed the tapir...’
Now look at the “together with” example below. Here the pronoun does not come at the start of the description part:
Before the noun, pronoun method, describing a “together with” person
(96) Nato r-iki [mi-a ja-bé ik-ai] joni, nato r-iki koshoshka | ‘This is the man you are having an affair with, this is a river dolphin.’
Description parts for extra parts with the noun inside came only from asking speakers:
Noun inside, describing a tool
(97) [E-n ja machíto-nin oro-ibat-a]-ra nokon papa-n-a | iki. | ‘The machete with which I cleared the chacra yesterday is my father’s.’
To sum up, Shipibo-Konibo can easily describe nouns that play these extra roles. Tools are the most common. Leaving a gap is possible. But the pronoun method is clearly preferred at this point on the scale. My collection has description parts before the noun, after the noun, and moved away from it. Ones with a tool noun inside came from asking speakers.

h: 10.2.4.5. Relativization on Second Argument of Extended Intransitives
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has a set of verbs, mostly about feelings, that involve two persons but still count as intransitive verbs. The one who feels is in the plain form (ABS). The thing that causes the feeling is marked with -ki (see 8.2.2.2). For example, in “we are scared of the jaguar”, “we” is plain and “jaguar” gets -ki. My story collection has no description part about this second person. For completeness, here is an example I got by asking:
(98) No-a-ra ino-ki raket-ai. | ‘We are scared of the jaguar.’ | Ino [no-a ja-ki raket-ai]-ra, kikin siná iki. | [Ja-ki no-a raket-ai] ino-ra kikin siná iki. | ‘The jaguar we are scared of is extremely fierce.’
I still need to check whether the pronoun in the (b) and (c) examples above is optional or required.

h: 10.2.4.6. Relativization on Possessors
t:
My story collection has no description parts about an owner (“whose”). But I easily got them by asking speakers. They need a pronoun inside the description part (jawen ‘his / her’). This fits the fact that owners sit quite low on the Accessibility Hierarchy (AH), the scale of how easily nouns can be described. Look at the examples below (see also ex. (3)):
(99) Oa ainbo [jawen bake mawat-a]-ra nokon awin-wetsa iki. | ‘That woman whose child died is my sister-in-law.’
(100) Ja joni [jawen ochíti e-n rete-a]-tonin-ra e-a tima-kas-ai. | ‘The man whose dog I killed wants to hit me.’

h: 10.2.4.7. Case Attraction?
t:
Sometimes, when describing a tool, something like “case attraction” seems to happen. That is, the noun that looks like it is outside gets the marker for its role vis-à-vis the description part, that is, its role inside it. These are not cases where the noun simply has the same role in both parts, because in the main sentence it is the doer of an intransitive verb.¹⁶ Unfortunately, there is no clear proof that
Similar sentences have been reported for Huallaga Quechua, where a marker “appears to have floated up to the head of the RC” (Keenan 1985:154-5, data from Weber 1978). In both Shipibo-Konibo and Quechua, the examples that allow this “case attraction” reading describe extra parts like tools.
the head nouns really sit outside the Cl_{REL} (the ‘who/which…’ description part). Still, I think it is unlikely that the head would appear inside that part twice: once as the full noun and once as a pronoun pointing back to it at the same time. In the examples below, the head noun takes the marker that belongs to its job inside the description part, here the ‘with’ marker (linguists call this case attraction). (Ex. (99) was rejected by a second language consultant.):
(101) To'ati-nin [e-n (ja-n) shino rete-ai]-ra nokon-a iki. | ‘The rifle with which I kill monkeys is mine.’
(102) ??Winti-n [e-n (ja-n) wina-ai]-ra nokon-a iki. | ‘The paddle with which I row is mine.’

h: 10.2.4.8. Disambiguation in Internally-Headed Relative Clauses and Syntactic Ergativity
t:
Sometimes the noun being described sits inside the ‘who/which…’ part (linguists call this an internally-headed relative clause). In many languages this causes confusion. There may be no way to tell which person or thing in that part is the one the main sentence is about.¹⁷ Shipibo-Konibo (SK) doesn’t have this problem. When the description part (Cl_{RELS}) has a transitive verb, the described noun is always the receiver (the O). That receiver is the one that also plays a role in the main sentence. Look at the following examples:
You can see this in the following Diegueño examples: v. [Xatəkcok-0 wi:-m ʔtuc-pu-c] nyiLy dog-DO rock-COM I hit-DEF-SUBJ was black ‘The rock I hit the dog with was black.’ ‘The dog that I hit with the rock was black.’ (Keenan 1985:163)
(103) [Joni-n ino rete-a]-ronki kikin siná ik-á iki. | ‘The jaguar that the man killed was extremely fierce’ | ‘The man who killed the jaguar was extremely brave’
(104) [Pitso-n bake natex-a]-ra nokon-a iki. | ‘The child the parokeet bit is mine.’ | ‘The parokeet that bit the child is mine.’
The next sentence shows that the receiver (O) of an inside-noun Cl_{REL} is read as the described noun even when that reading makes little sense in real life:
(105) [Joni-n yawa rete-ibat-a]-ra nokon koka iki. | ‘The white-lipped peccary the man killed is my maternal uncle.’ | ‘The man that killed the white-lipped peccary is my maternal uncle.’

h: 10.2.4.8. Disambiguation in Internally-Headed Relative Clauses and Syntactic Ergativity
t:
In (103)-(105) the main sentences have intransitive verbs. So you might wonder: is the receiver chosen just because both roles take no marker (the plain form, ABS)? No, that is not the reason. In (106) the receiver is still read as the described noun, even though that same participant is the doer (the A) of the main sentence:
(106) [Pitso-n bake natex-a]-tonin-ra joshin pi-ke. | ‘The child the parokeet bit ate the banana.’ | ‘The parokeet that bit the child ate the banana.’
To describe the doer (the A) instead, you have to put the noun outside the description part (linguists call this an externally-headed Cl_{REL}):
(107) [Yawa rete-ibat-a] joni-ra nokon koka iki. | ‘The man who killed the white-lipped peccary is my maternal uncle.’
(108) [Bake natex-a] pitso-n-ra joshin pi-ke. | ‘The parokeet that bit the child ate the banana.’
The next example shows that the inside-noun pattern also works for the single person of an intransitive verb (the S). Note that the verb of the description part (V_{REL}) describes an action someone actively does. So what counts here is the role, O or S, and not whether the person is someone things happen to (a patient):
(109) [Mi-bé ainbo jo-a]-ra no-n onan-yama-ke. | ‘We don’t know the woman who came with you.’
So the inside-noun pattern always picks the receiver of a transitive verb or the single person of an intransitive verb. These are the two roles that take no marker (the plain form). This is probably the only place in SK where the doer-marker system controls how two sentences link up (linguists call this interclausal syntactic ergativity). That is surprising, because the rest of SK sentence structure works like English: the doers of both kinds of verbs are treated alike (a nominative-accusative pattern). Still, it fits with the main jobs that ‘who/which…’ parts do in languages, and with how they relate to S and O (Fox 1987:861-864).¹⁸ Other languages where the inside-noun pattern picks S and O are

h: 10.2.4.8. Disambiguation in Internally-Headed Relative Clauses and Syntactic Ergativity
t:
According to Fox, a main job of Cl_{RELS} is to fit a newly mentioned person or thing into the ongoing conversation. This can be done in two ways. (a) “The Cl_{REL} provides a stative description of some aspect of the referent that situates it, and justifies its introduction.” This usually uses an intransitive-verb sentence, where the described noun is the doer; that is why S-relatives are so common. (b) “The Cl_{REL} provides a link via a referent that has already been introduced into the discourse”. This usually uses a transitive verb. The doer tends to be a pronoun (especially ‘I’ or ‘you’) and the described noun is the receiver; that is why O-relatives are so common.
Tibetan, Belhare (Tibeto-Burman), and probably Korean (Van Valin and LaPolla 1997:304 and references therein).

h: 10.2.4.9. Disambiguation in Fronted and Extraposed Relative Clauses
t:
Sometimes the ‘who/which…’ part (Cl_{REL}) is moved to the front of the sentence or to the end (linguists call this fronted or extraposed). Suppose the main sentence has a transitive verb, and nothing shows which noun is being described. Then listeners take it to be the receiver (the object). Example (48) is shown again below as (110a):
(110) [Awaranpiti naman raka-t-a]-ra e-n mananxawe | bi-ke. | ‘I caught a tortoise that was lying under an awaranpiti vine.’
Again, to describe the doer (the A) instead, you can put the ‘who/which…’ part right before the noun (a prenominal Cl_{REL}):
(110) [Awaranpiti naman raka-t-a] joni-n-ra mananxawe | bi-ke. | ‘The man who was lying under an awaranpiti vine caught a tortoise.’
The next example was shown earlier as (49):
(111) [Taxbakan nono-ai]-ra epa-n ano rete-ke. | ‘Uncle killed a paca that was swimming in the tahuampa.’
(None) ??[Taxbakan nono-ai] epa-n-ra ano rete-ke. | ‘Uncle swimming in the tahuampa killed a paca (not acceptable because people do not normally swim in the tahuampa).’
In the next example, the ‘who/which…’ part at the front (Cl_{REL}) has its own transitive verb. Again, the described noun must be the receiver (O) of the main sentence:
(112) [Atsa pi-ai]-ra epa-n ano oin-ke. | ‘Uncle saw the paca that was eating the manioc.’ | Uncle who was eating manioc saw the paca.

h: 10.2.4.9. Disambiguation in Fronted and Extraposed Relative Clauses
t:
The same rule holds if you swap the order of the two parts. So (113a) and (113b) can only mean that the manatee, not the man, was going up the river:
(113) Joni-n-ra sapen rete-ke [paro-n inat-ai]. | [Paro-n inat-ai]-ra joni-n sapen rete-ke. | ‘The man killed the manatee that was swimming up the river.’ | [Paro-n inat-ai] joni-n-ra sapen rete-ke. | ‘The man who was going up the river killed the manatee.’
In the next sentence, a ‘who/which…’ part (Cl_{REL}) with a transitive verb is moved to the end:
(114) Epa-n-ra ano oin-ke [atsa pi-ai]. | ‘Uncle saw the paca that was eating the yuca.’
To sum up: when a ‘who/which…’ part (Cl_{REL}s) is moved to the front or the end, and the main sentence has a transitive verb, the described noun is always the receiver (O) of the main sentence.
Table 10.4 shows which ways of building ‘who/which…’ parts SK uses for which roles. (Stimulus means the second participant of certain intransitive verbs that can take an extra participant.):
As I discuss in 12.2, there is strong evidence in SK for treating S and A together as the subject (the doer). If we add up S- and A-relatives, describing the subject is clearly more common than describing the object. Read this way, the data support the Accessibility Hierarchy Hypothesis of Keenan and Comrie (1977). Still, on their own, O-relatives are the most frequent of the three types, as I mentioned above, closely followed by S-relatives. Read that way, the data fit the Absolutive Hypothesis of Fox (1987). Now let’s look at complement clauses.

h: Complement Clauses (sentences that complete another verb ("I want him to go"))
t: Sometimes a whole sentence is turned into a noun and used as a main participant of another verb, as in English “I want to go” (linguists call this a complement clause). In SK this happens with the following verbs: keen- ‘want,’ raan- ‘send (sb. to do sth.),’ yono- ‘order / send sb. (to work), ask for sth.,’ axea- ‘teach / make sb. get used to do sth.,’ shinan- ‘think, remember, plan,’ onan- ‘know,’ yoi- ‘say to / tell (sb. to do sth.),’ oin- ‘see / realize,’ ninkat- ‘hear / understand,’ namat- ‘dream.’ All of these act like transitive verbs, except keen- ‘want’ (see Extended Intransitive Clauses with Alternate Case Frames in 8.2.2.5).

h: Non-Implicative Manipulation Verbs (verbs like "tell", "ask", "let")
t:
The verb keen- ‘want’ takes one of two marker patterns. The wanter is in the plain form (ABS). The thing wanted is either also in the plain form <ABS ABS>, or takes the OBL ending <ABS OBL>. keen- can also be used in two ways. If you want to do something yourself (“I want to go”), it works as a helper verb of wishing (a modality verb). If you want someone else to do something (“I want you to go”), it is a verb of getting others to act (a manipulation verb). In both uses, keen- may come before or after the other part:
Keen- ‘want’
(115) E-a-ra keen-ai [Kontámanain ka-ti]-n. | ‘I want to go to Contamana.’
(116) E-a-ra keen-ai [mi-n piti meni-ti]-nin. | ‘I want you to give (me) the food / fish.’
(117) E-a-ra [Sani rete-kan-ti] keen-ai. | ‘I want them to kill Sani.’
In all the examples above, the part that goes with keen- ends in -ti. This ending turns the part into a noun. It also shows that the action hasn’t really happened (yet). It is glossed as infinitive (INF), like English “to go.” Other verbs whose added parts take -ti are raan- ‘send (sb. to do sth.),’ yono- ‘order, send sb. to work,’ and axea- ‘teach, make sb. get used to sth.;’ as I show below, none of these verbs guarantee that the action really happens (linguists call them non-implicative verbs). Unlike keen-, the verbs raan-, yono- and axea- always need a different doer in the added part: you always send someone else. In the following examples with raan-, you can see again that the added part can come before or after the main sentence:

h: Non-Implicative Manipulation Verbs (verbs like "tell", "ask", "let")
t:
Raan- ‘send (somebody to do something)’
(118) Jain-xon-ronki raan-kan-a iki [samá-ti] | onanya i-ti kopí. | ‘Then they (i.e., the Inkas) directed her to abstain (from eating certain foods and having sexual intercourse), in order to become a shaman.’
(119) [Onibirisitáro a-ti-ra] nokon bake e-n Rima-n raan-ke. | ‘I sent my son to Lima in order to study at the university.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:354, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
In the next sentence, a father whose son does not come back home decides to send a second son to look for the first one:
(120) Moa basi manat-a-bi jo-yam-ai-tian, jawen chiní | bake raan-ribi-a iki, [jawen wetsa bena-ti]. | ‘Since (the oldest son) didn’t come back, after waiting for a long time (the father) sent his youngest son to look for his brother.’ (Ministerio de Educación and ILV 1982:33, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997).
Yono- ‘order / send someone (to work), ask for something’
(121) Ja-n-ra yono-ke [paranta bi-ti]. | ‘He ordered (them) to bring plantain.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:428; analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
(122) Ii-kin-bi-ronki beskon yono-kan-a iki, | [jaa chii bi-ti]. | ‘So, (they) ordered the chirriclés (kind of bird) to bring the fire.’
The verb axea- ‘teach’ is built from the bare verb axe- ‘get used to, learn’ plus the general transitive verb -a(k) ‘do’. Here -a(k) works as a ‘make someone do it’ ending. So axea- means ‘make someone get used to something’:

h: Non-Implicative Manipulation Verbs (verbs like "tell", "ask", "let")
t:
Axea- ‘teach, make someone get used to do something’
(123) Reken-pari nokon tita-n e-a axe-a iki
(None) [koton-a-ti]. | ‘First, my mother taught me how to manufacture the blouse.’
(124) Ja-n-ra e-a [atapa chachi-ti] axe-a-[a]i. | ‘(S)he will teach me how to vaccinate chickens.’ (Faust 1973:83, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)
All the verbs with added parts we have seen so far are about getting someone to do something. But getting them to do it doesn’t mean they actually did it (linguists call these non-implicative manipulation verbs). Look at the following examples, where the second action never happens:
(125) E-n-ra Wesna raan-ke [onpax bi-ti], ikaxbi | be-yama-ke. | ‘I sent Wesna to get some water but she didn’t bring it.’
(126) Inka-n-ronki joni-bo yono-a iki, [jaa jo-ai kaman | atsa xeati xea-ti-ma], ikaxbi senean-yama-n-a iki. | ‘The Inka ordered the people not to drink the yuca beer until his return, but they didn’t comply with this to his detriment.’
(127) E-n-ra Wesna axe-a-ke [jonxe a-ti], | ikaxbi axe-yama-ke. | ‘I taught Wesna how to make bracelets but she didn’t learn.’

h: Cognition and Utterance Verbs (verbs of thinking and saying)
t:
A second group of verbs can mark the added part in two ways. If the event is not real (yet), the part gets -ti. If it is real, it gets one of the describing endings -ai or -a. These verbs are yoi- ‘tell,’ onan- ‘know’ and shinan- ‘think, plan:’
Yoi- ‘tell’
(128) Nita-n-ra e-a yoi-ke [mi-a piróta-nin ik-ai]. | ‘Nita told me that you know how to play soccer.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Onan- ‘know’
(129) Ja-n-ra [raké-ti] onan-yama-ke. | ‘He never gets scared.’ (Lit. ‘He doesn’t know how to get scared.’) (Valenzuela 1997)
(130) E-n-ra onan-ke [nato ochíti-nin bake natéshama-a]. | ‘I know that this dog did not bite the child.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Shinan- ‘think, plan’
(131) E-n-ra shinan-ai [nokon papa-n nonti be-ai]. | ‘I think that my father is going to bring the canoe.’ (Faust 1973:89, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)

h: Perception Verbs and Namat- ‘Dream’ (verbs of seeing and hearing, and namat- "dream")
t:
A third group of verbs puts the endings -ai and -a on the added part. -ai is for an action that is still going on, and -a is for a finished one. These are the verbs of sensing, ninkat- ‘hear’ and oin- ‘see,’ plus namat- ‘dream.’ It is telling that namat- belongs in this group. It may show how dreams are thought of in Shipibo society. For example, through his dreams a shaman may be able to find a lost object or find out who committed a theft (see ex. (24)).
Namat- ‘dream’
(132) [Wakanawa be-ai-ra] e-n namá-ke. | ‘I dreamt that the school of fish is coming.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Ninkat- ‘hear’
(133) [Nawa-n Sani rete-a-ra] e-n ninká-ke. | ‘I heard that the outsider killed Sani.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
Oin- ‘see, realize’
(134) Wetsa nete-n-ki, ja nonon rabekan oinn-a iki, [jato-n | ian tsosin-ai]. | ‘One day, the two ducks realized that the water from their lake was lowering.’ (Valenzuela 1997)
The verb that takes the added part can also be made of more than one word (linguists call this a periphrastic verb).
In this case the added part may carry a marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else:
(135) Jain-xon-ronki oin-a iki, jaa koshi-ama-kin toxbá-xon | oin-a-ronki ik-á iki [westíora awá joni-ki jo-i]. | ‘From there (his canoe) he saw, without rowing just floating, he saw that a tapir man was coming.’

h: Adverbial Clauses (parts of a sentence about when, why and how)
t: Some parts of a sentence tell you when, why or how something happens (linguists call these adverbial clauses). Usually SK does this with a marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. But a sentence turned into a noun can do the same job. It often takes an extra ending or a small word after it that adds the exact meaning. Most kinds of these parts can be said in more than one way.

h: Purpose ("in order to")
t:
A purpose (‘in order to…’) can be said in three ways: with a part ending in the infinitive -ti, with -ti plus kopí, or with a same-or-different-person marker. Also, some of these same-or-different-person markers have more than one form. The purpose part in the example below can be said in four ways:
(136) Nokon yosi-n-ra e-a moa-tian joi-bo yoi-ke, | nokon bake e-n ja-ribi yoi-ti (kopi). | ‘My grandfather told me old stories, so that I tell them to my children afterwards.’ | Nokon yosi-n-ra e-a moa-tian joi-bo yoi-ke, | nokon bake e-n ja-ribi yoi-non (i-xon). | ‘My grandfather told me old stories, so that I tell them to my children afterwards.’
Here are more purpose parts turned into nouns. Notice that the small word kopi after them is optional. That is because the infinitive -ti can show purpose by itself, like English “to” in “I came to eat.”¹⁹ These parts can come before or after the main sentence:
(137) Nokon machíto e-n bi-ké ja-n bai a-ti (kopi). | ‘I grabbed my machete to clear the way with it.’ (speaker from Nuevo Edén, Piski)
(138) Xeta wiso-ti (kopi) moa-tian yoxan-baon | pi-káti-kan-ai yotokonti. | ‘Long time ago, adult women ate yotokonti in order to blacken their teeth.’
This second way, with the optional small word kopi, may have started with people who spoke two languages and said the same thing both ways at once. kopi most probably comes from Quechua. Today, kopi is felt to be a native word. See also footnote 20.

h: Purpose ("in order to")
t:
Intransitive verbs of moving or position (e.g., ka- / bo- ‘go,’ jo- / be- ‘come,’ yakat- ‘sit’ napokoo- ‘enter,’ neet- ‘go up’) often go with a purpose part marked with -i. This -i shows that the same person does both actions at the same time, and that this person is an intransitive-verb doer (S) (see also ex. (8) in Ch. 9, as well as exx. (50) and (54) in this chapter):
(139) E-a-ra [mi-a bena-i] jo-ke. | ‘I came to look for you.’

h: Reason ("because")
t:
In the examples below, kopí helps to give a reason (‘because…’):
(140) E-n i-rá-ke ak-ai ja-ska-ra joni e-a | meni-kan-a (kopí)… | ‘I am thankful because they (my parents) gave me (in matrimony) to a man like him…’
(141) Nokon tita noko-t-a kopí-ra rama no-n atapa | rete-ai. | ‘Since my mother arrived, now we will kill a chicken.’

h: ‘After’ ("after")
t:
To say something happens after something else, Shipibo turns that part into a noun and adds the small word pekáo ‘after.’ It is made of peká ‘back’ + -o, an ending meaning ‘around / near’:
(142) Kinan-a pekáo, jakiribi moa semana pia me-yama-a | pekáo, no-a ka-ríba[-a] iki. | ‘After throwing it up (the plant preparation to become good a fisher / hunter) and after not having touched an arrow for a week, we went (fishing) again.’
(143) Moa chaní-kan-a pekáo, joni-baon wino-ai, ja-yá | Ani Xeati-nin be-noxon. | ‘After having been invited, the men manufactured macanas to bring them to the Ani Xeati.’

h: ‘Before’ ("before")
t:
The ‘before’ part below is unusual. It is a sentence turned into a noun, but no case marker and no small word is added to it. Instead, the negative -ma ‘not’ and the emphatic -bi come after the describing ending -a. Together they give the meaning ‘before:’
(144) Yamet-a-ma-bi-ra jain oxa-ti bena-kan-ke. | ‘Before it became night, they looked for a place to sleep.’
This kind of time part can also be said with a same-or-different-person marker; see section 4.1.3.

h: Limitative ("until")
t:
To say ‘until,’ the part needs the small word kaman after it.²⁰ Before kaman is added, the verb in that part is either turned into a noun,
(145) Xontako-bo-ra jawen papa betan ik-ai beno-ai kaman. | ‘Young girls live with their parents until they get married.’
or else carries the word piece -non. Remember from 9.2.2 what -non normally does. It shows that someone else does the action in the extra part, and that it happens later than the main action. But in ‘until’ parts, -non can appear even when the same person does both actions:
(146) Kikin-i paen-a ik-á iki ja xontako rabé, | shinan-yama-non kaman... | ‘The two young girls had gotten completely drunk, until they became unconscious...’
The small word kaman clearly comes from the Quechua ending -kama, which does the same job. But unlike kopí, kaman can’t be left out (see footnote 19).

h: Similative ("like / as if")
t:
To say something is done ‘like’ something else, the part must be turned into a noun. It must also take the small word keskat- ~ keská ‘like’ (see also comparisons of sameness in 8.7.1):
(147) E-n-ra mapó ak-ai nokon yoxaman e-a | axe-a-ni keská. | ‘I make pottery like my grandmother taught me (long ago).’
(148) Tsoma-ra yoyo ik-ai Pishki-bo | yoyo ik-ai keská. | ‘Tsoma speaks like the Pishkibo people speak.’
(149) Ja no-n chitonti kewé-a-[a]i keská-ribi a-kin, | chomo-nko no-n raó ak-ai. | ‘In the same way we embroider our skirts, we decorate the jars.’

h: ‘Since’ ("since")
t:
A ‘since’ part is built from a ‘when’ part with a same-or-different-person marker, plus the emphatic -bi. The next example was given before in Ch. 9 as (14). The word ‘we’ is used in a general sense here, like English ‘one:’
(150) Pikó-ke-tian-bi no-a ani a-kan-ai.... | ‘Since (we) are born (our parents) take care of us.....’
Normally the marker -nontian means ‘while,’ and shows that someone else does the other action. But with the emphatic ending, -nontianbi can link two parts with the same doer:
(151) Koshoshka iki no-a joni-nontianbi no-n | pi-osma. | ‘Since the time we began to exist, we never eat river dolphin.’

h: Manner / Means ("by doing" / "how")
t:
Parts that tell how or by what means something is done can only be said with a same-or-different-person marker. The last part of the example below is one of these:
(152) Ja-tian ja-bo onan-ma-ti i-ke-n-bi, Inka raan-kan-a | iki tama toban washí-xon. | ‘Despite the fact that she still had to teach them (how to do things), they drove the Inka (Woman) away by denying her roasted peanuts.’

h: Irrealis Conditional ("if" (could still happen))
t:
‘If’ parts about things that may or may not happen also use a same-or-different-person marker:
(153) Nokon tita kai-n-ra e-a-ribi kai. | ‘If my mother is going, I am going too.’
The following sentence was given before in Ch. 9 as (3):
(154) Jene-n ka-tan-ax jo-xon jawen awin | mera-[a]x, wexa-anan-katit-ai joni-bo. | ‘If when coming back from the fishing he found his wife (with another man), the men cut each other with the wexati knife.’
(155) Ja-tian ja joni raké-ma ik-ax, chama ak-á | piko-t-ai. | ‘Then if the man was not a coward he would come out (from his house) when being called “chama”.’

h: Counterfactual Conditional ("if" (didn't happen: "if I had…"))
t:
‘If…had’ sentences about things that did not happen also use a same-or-different-person marker. In addition, the main verb takes the ending -kean, which shows that the event did not come true (linguists call it the frustrative):
(156) E-a bake i-ke-tian nokon papa-baon e-a raon-yama-a-ra, | kikin yopa i-kean-ke. | ‘If my parents had not treated me with plant medicine when I was a child, I would be a total incompetent (i.e., a bad fisher / hunter) now.’
(157) Nokon tita-n e-a meráya-iba bo-yama-a-ra | e-a moa mawat-a i-kean-ke. | ‘If my mother had not taken me to the great shaman, now I would be dead.’
(158) Bakish oi be-yama-iba-ke-tian-ra, | e-n moa pei bi-a i-kean-ke. | ‘If it had not rained yesterday, I would have gone to get palm leaf (for the roof).’
(159) Moa atsa wai a-xon-ra, no-n rama atsa xeati | a-kean-ke. | ‘If we had planted a yuca chacra, we would drink yuca beer now.’

h: Concessive / Adversative ("although" / "but")
t:
To say ‘although / even though,’ you add the emphatic -bi to a part that already has a same-or-different-person marker:
(160) Maioshiain ka-xon-bi-ra e-n chopa xate bi-ama-ke. | ‘Although I went to Pucallpa, I didn’t buy any / the piece of cloth.’ | ‘I went to Pucallpa, but I did not buy any / the piece of cloth.’
(161) Kikin icha nami-a i-xon-bi-ra e-a a-ma-yama-kan-ke. | ‘Even though they had a lot of meat, they did not invite me anything.’ | ‘They had a lot of meat, but they did not invite me anything.’
(162) Paxkin-a ik-ax-bi-ra Sani ni-wan-ke. | ‘Despite being tired, Sani kept on walking.’
(163) Mato r-iki e-n kena-a, pishta jakon-ma-shoko a-xon-bi. | ‘I have invited you in spite of having organized a not so good fiesta.’
To sum up: most kinds of these when/why/how parts can be built in more than one way. Only ‘like’ parts must always be turned into a noun and always take their own small word keská ~ keskat. Purpose (‘in order to’) can use an infinitive part turned into a noun, with kopí added if you like, or a same-or-different-person marker. Kopí can also appear in reason (‘because’) parts. Time parts mostly use a same-or-different-person marker. ‘After’ can also be said with a part ending in the finished-action ending -a, usually followed by the small word pekáo ‘after.’ ‘Since’ parts add the emphatic -bi to a time part with a same-or-different-person marker. To say ‘before,’ you add ‘not’ and the emphatic -bi to a part ending in the finished-action ending. ‘Until’ parts are either turned into a noun or marked with -non (which here does not mean that someone else acts), and they must take kaman. Finally, ‘how / by what means,’ ‘if,’ and ‘although’ parts must use a same-or-different-person marker. In ‘if…had’ sentences about things that didn’t happen, the main verb takes the frustrative -kean (‘it didn’t come true’). In ‘although’ parts, the emphatic -bi is added to the part with the same-or-different-person marker.

h: Concessive / Adversative ("although" / "but")
t:
COORDINATION OF CLAUSES:
This chapter is about joining sentences of equal rank, like English “I came and I saw” (linguists call this coordination). Keep in mind, though, that where English uses ‘and,’ SK often chains sentences together with same-or-different-person markers instead. Joined sentences can mean ‘and,’ ‘or,’ and ‘but.’

h: Juxtaposition (putting sentences side by side with no linking word)
t:
There are different ways to say ‘and.’ The simplest way is to put the two sentences side by side, with nothing added. The two sentences in (1) tell events that happen one after the other. Both are full sentences, and both end in -ke, the marker for a finished action:
(1) [Yoxan-shoko-ki rete-kan-ke], [paranta pei kakaa-kan-ke].... | ‘They killed the grandmother and extended the plantain leaves on the ground....’
In (2), the two joined sentences both end in -ai, the marker for an action still going on:
(2) [Ja-tian ja xeta kikin-i penet-ai], [payó-yama-ai]. | ‘Then, the teeth became extremely shiny, they didn’t get worn out.’
In (1) and (2), the doer is the same in both sentences, so it is left out of the second one. English does the same: “She came in and sat down.” Linguists call this “equi-subject deletion.” It follows the English-like pattern, where the doers of both kinds of verbs are treated alike (a nominative pattern). By contrast, in (3) and (4) the two sentences have different doers, so each doer must be named.
The example below (first given in Chapter 7 as (39)) is made of two longer sentences put side by side. Each one has a main verb in the storytelling past form kaa iki ‘went,’ plus an extra part with the ending -i. This -i shows that the same person does both actions at the same time, and that this person is an intransitive-verb doer (S):

h: Juxtaposition (putting sentences side by side with no linking word)
t: (3) [Ja nonti-n wetsa ka-a iki [inat-i]], [wetsa ka-a iki | [toxbá-paket-i]]. | ‘By canoe one went up the river and the other one floated down the river.’

h: -Ribi ‘Again, Also’ ("again, also")
t:
In (4), the two full sentences tell the same kind of event, done by different doers. The ending -ribi ‘also’ is attached to the doer of each sentence:
(4) [Ja-tian Ino-ribi jene-nko ka-ke], [Xae-ribi | jene-nko ka-ke]. | ‘Then the Jaguar went to the river and the Sloth went to the river too.’

h: Conjunctions (linking words)
t:
SK has a set of joining words (conjunctions) built from the demonstrative ja- ‘that.’ They usually take case markers and same-or-different-person endings. These joining words can link nouns, sentences, chains of sentences, and whole paragraphs. As in ex. (4), -ribi ‘also’ marks both doers in (5). But this time the joining word jatian also stands between the two sentences. (jatian also starts (4) and (5), linking them to the chain of sentences before.):
(5) [Ja-tian-ki Ino-n-ribi jawen tari jope-ke], | ja-tian [Xae-n-ribi jawen tari jope-ke]. | ‘Then the Jaguar took off his cushma, and the Anteater took off his cushma too.’
The joining word jatian contains the time ending -tian. In SK, -tian has become a marker that shows someone else does the next action (see 9.2). Besides that, jatian signals a break in the flow of the story in a wider sense (14.1).
Below, jainxon joins two parts that are receivers of the verb ‘think.’ The doer is the same in both, so it is left out of the second part. jainxon is followed by -ribi ‘also:’
(6) Ja-tian e-n shinan-ai, bake-ya i-xon, [[nokon bake-baon | onan-ti] jain-xon-ribi [no-n jawéki-bo sawe-ti]]. | ‘Therefore, as I have children of my own, I plan that they learn (our customs) and also that they wear our traditional clothes.’
Why is jainxon chosen in the example above? There are two reasons. First, the doer is the same in both parts (a kind of continuity in the story). Second, the next part, with sawe- ‘put on (clothes),’ has a transitive verb, and jainxon is the form that agrees with that kind of doer (A). The next example shows that the verb of the first part doesn’t matter. jainxon is chosen because the following part has a transitive verb, even though the first part has an intransitive verb:

h: Conjunctions (linking words)
t:
(7) Ja-tian westíora Ne-ino joni-a iki, | jain-xon yokat-a iki..... | ‘Then a Nutria turned into a man and asked him....’
On the other hand, the example below has jainoax, the form that agrees with an intransitive-verb doer (S). That is because the doers are the same and benxokaa- ‘get ready’ is an intransitive verb:
(8) [Kesin-ra nashi-ke] jaino-a-x [benxokaa-ke]. | ‘Kesin took a bath and got ready.’
In the next example, jainoax joins different doers who do the same thing; this is treated as a kind of continuity in the story. jainoax agrees with S here because bane- is an intransitive verb:
(9) Bane-ki-a-kan-a iki, westíora yosi-shoko, | yoxan-shoko jaino-a-x bake-bo-res. | ‘The only ones who stayed were an old man, an old woman, and the children.’
However, there are signs that jainoax is becoming a more general ‘and.’ It is losing the rule that it must agree with S. The next example (given in Chapter 6 as (169)) shows jainoax joining receivers (O) in a list:
(10) Wetsa nete, Awá Mai a-kan-ai meráya-nin-ki jawen nishi | paen meran oin-a iki meskó yoina-bo: nato jono, | awá, yawa, ano.... jainoax mari. | ‘One day, the great shaman called Awá Mai saw, in his ayahuasca vision, different kinds of animals: collared peccaries, tapirs, white-lipped peccaries, pacas....and agoutis.’
What’s more, in the sentence below jainoax joins doers of a transitive verb (A):

h: Conjunctions (linking words)
t:
(11) Iskorainko ik-á bake-baon yoyo a-ti, | koríjio ak-ai bake-ranon-baon itan
(None) xontako-baon-ribi yoyo a-ti, jainoax | jato axe-ai-baon-ribi yoyo a-ti kopí. | ‘So that the children in the elementary schools read it, secondary school boys and girls read it, and those who teach them also read it.’
The same thing has happened to the ‘but’ word ikaxbi, which I discuss below. It is also built with -ax, has become more general, and has lost its agreement with S.
Some joining words seem to come from three pieces put together: ‘that’ with a case marker, the general transitive verb ak- ‘do,’ and a same-or-different-person ending: ja-ská-ke-tian [that-SIML-P-DD] < ja-keská a-ke-tian [that-SIML do.T-P-DD].

h: -Kan ‘And’ ("and")
t:
Another way to join sentences is to add -kan ‘and, whereas’ to a sentence with no verb (see also 8.4.3.4). The sentence below has two ‘X is Y’ sentences. In the second one the word ‘is’ is left out, and the thing it is about carries -kan. Here -kan shows a contrast, like English ‘whereas’:
(12) [Shipibo-baon joi iki ponté-bicho], | [Konibo-baon-a-kan maké-ya]. | ‘The Shipibo’s speech is just straight whereas the Konibo’s speech has an accent.’
Describing parts that have been turned into nouns are joined with itan ‘and.’ itan is the word that joins describing words in general (see exx. (3a-c) in Chapter 5):
(13) Jatíribi Shipibo bake-ranon-bo no-n joi-n | yoyo ik-ai, ikaxbi jatíribi-bo-ra ja-ke | moa i-ama-[a]i-bo itan ninká-yama-[a]i. | ‘Some Shipibo young boys speak in our language, however there are some who don’t speak (in our language) anymore and who don’t understand it.’
For joining nouns (‘X and Y’), see 6.7.14, about the ‘with’ ending and the joining word betan.

h: Negative Conjunction ("neither / nor")
t:
To say the English ‘neither….nor,’ SK uses a joining word and a verb with ‘not’:
(14) No-n oin-patan-bo-a-bi r-iki, no-n iskóra-nko-bo | jainoax no-n jema-nko-bo no-n joi-n-bi-ribi-kaya | meskó keská jawéki-bo onan-ti yama yama-bi-res. | ‘We see continuously (when visiting the villages) that neither in our schools nor in our villages in general are there varied pedagogical materials in our own language.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:5).

h: Non-Restrictive Conjunction ("and also" (adding extra information))
t:
Look at the next sentence. It means ‘not only X but also Y.’ It is built almost exactly like the English and Spanish versions. The only difference is that in SK the ‘but’ word is not required:
(15) ...no-n joi-n-bi-ribi wisha-bo, bake-baon | yoyo a-ti iskoira-nko-xon-bicho-ma no-n xobo-nko-xon-ribi. | ‘Children should read books in our own language not only in the school but also at home.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:5)
People quite often add the Spanish word sino ‘but rather’ before the last item in sentences like (15).

h: Disjunction ("or")
t:
To say ‘or’ between two sentences with the same doer, you can use iamax / iamaxon. These are made of [be/do.I-NEG-PSSS] and [be/do.I-NEG-PSSA], respectively. Speakers can also use the Spanish word o ‘or.’
In the sentence below, iamax is used because it comes before a ‘to each other’ sentence. The ‘to each other’ ending takes away the separate receiver, so the verb becomes an intransitive verb:
(16) Ja-tian nawa-bo-bi-ribi jawen rawí noko-ax | [[tima-anan-kan-ai] iamax [tantash i-anan-kan-ai]]. | ‘Also the mestizos when encountering their rival hit each other or punch each other.’
In the next example, iamax comes before a verb made of two words. The main verb is a transitive verb with a ‘make someone do it’ ending added. After it comes the verb ‘go’, used here to talk about the future. Why is the intransitive form iamax used? Maybe because adding the ‘go’ future makes the sentence feel less like someone doing something to someone else:
(17) Rama-ra e-n nokon awin nashi-ma-i ka-[a]i, | iamax xea-ma-i ka-[a]i benxo-non i-xon. | ‘Now I will bathe my wife (with the plant preparation), or I will have her drink it so that she gets well.’
Now let's look at an example with iamaxon, the form used when the doer is acting on someone else:
(18) No-n awin no-a chota-nan-kan-ke-tian-ra no-n jato | tsewe-a-ti iki wexati-nin iamaxon wino-n.... | ‘If another man copulates with our wife to our detriment we must harm him with the wexati knife or with the macana (wooden club).’

h: Disjunction ("or")
t:
iamax and iamaxon can also mean ‘that is (to say)’ (Loriot, Laurialt, and Day 1993:193).
In the next example, the word itan plus the ending -ribi ‘also’ means ‘either… or’. It joins two reasons, and each reason has a different doer. (As I said earlier, itan can also mean ‘and’ between two describing words.)
(19) Ja-rá-ke joni-bo jakóma shinan-ya [[jawen ani-baon | esé ninká-yosma ik-ax], itan-ribi [jawen ani-baon | rao-n-yosma ik-ax]]. | ‘There are bad / unkind people either because they never listened to their elders’ advice or because their elders never cured them with plant medicine.’
Notice that in (11) itan was translated as ‘and’ in ‘secondary school boys and girls.’ But there ‘and’ simply covers both boys and girls. That's because Shipibo-Konibo has no single word for students of both sexes. It does not mean that the boys and girls would read the books together. To say that, you would use a different ‘and’ for nouns, betan. (betan grew out of the ending meaning ‘together with’.)

h: Adversative ("but")
t:
Shipibo-Konibo is turning ikaxbi [be/do.I-PSSS-EM] into a fixed word meaning ‘but.’ If you take it apart, ikaxbi is the verb ‘be/do’ with a same-doer marker. Then the emphasis ending -bi is added, and that is what gives the ‘but’ meaning. We saw the same thing in sentences meaning ‘even though’. Here is an example:
(20) [Maioshiain-ra ka-tan-ke no-n koráka], ikaxbi-ra | [nawa koshi-bo betan yoyo i-ama-ke]. | ‘Our chief went to Pucallpa but he did not speak with the mestizo authorities.’
ikaxbi contains the ending -ax. This same-doer marker is normally used only when the next part of the sentence has an intransitive verb. So, in theory, the part after ikaxbi should have an intransitive verb. But ikaxbi is becoming a fixed word, and one sign of this is that it often ignores that rule. Example (21) shows that ikaxbi can join two parts that both have transitive verbs. In fact, only the kind of verb in the second part matters:
(21) [Jain-xon moa beno-ma-kati-kan-ai], ikaxbi | [bi-ma-pao-ka:ni-ke rayá joni].... | ‘Then, they made (the girl) get married, but they married her to a hard-working man....’
But you can also find the other form of ikaxbi, the one used when the doer acts on someone else:
(22) Wetsa joni-ronki i-káti-ai mansána wai-a, i-xon-bi-ki | joni-n jawen bimi koko-yama-katit-ai. | ‘It is said that a man had an apple chacra long ago, but he could never eat his fruit.’ (Ministerio de Educación and ILV 1982:31)

h: Adversative ("but")
t:
Shipibo-Konibo speakers also often use the Spanish word for ‘but’, pero. Often they put it right after the Shipibo word ikaxbi, so they say ‘but’ twice, once in each language (linguists call this bilingual parallelism).
(23) [E-a-ra Maioshiain ka-tan-ke] ikaxbi pero | [chopa xate bi-ama-ke]. | ‘I went to Pucallpa, but I did not buy any piece of cloth.’
The next sentence (given in Chapter 7 as (147)) shows ikaxbi used the old way, as an ordinary verb form that has not become the word ‘but’:
(24) Ja-tian benbo bake-baon mapó mee-ti atipan-yama-ke; | bakeranon ik-ax-bi boshí wacho-na-ke-tian, mapó keská. | ‘Male children should not play with clay; being boys their penises might become fluffy, just like the clay.’
The next passage has ikaxbi meaning ‘but’. It also has two cases of -ribi joining parts of the sentence that carry a same-doer or different-doer marker:
(25) Nokon papa betan nokon tita-n e-a meni-a iki, | ikaxbi e-n shinan-yama-[a]i pota-ti, | [moa ja-bé icha bake-ya i-xon], | [icha-bi-res e-a ja-bé-ribi axe-a ik-ax],
(None) [jakoin-ra joni-ribi i-ke-tian]. | ‘My father and my mother gave me in matrimony, but I never considered divorce because I already have many kids with him, I have gotten very used to him, and he is a good man.’
FURTHER REFLECTIONS ON GRAMMATICAL RELATIONS:
This section is about how Shipibo-Konibo shows grammar roles, like ‘subject’ and ‘object’. These roles are about grammar. They are not the same as meaning roles, like ‘the one acting’ or ‘the one the action is done to’, or what the story is focusing on. Many languages show these roles in ways that don't work for Shipibo-Konibo, or work only a little. Some use word order. Some change the verb to match the doer or receiver. Some attach small pronoun pieces to the verb. Some have a passive, like English ‘The man was bitten by the dog’, where the receiver becomes the subject. None of these really apply here. Still, several other things in the language do show grammar roles (linguists call them grammatical relations).

h: Case-Marking System (the role-marking endings)
t:
As we have seen, Shipibo-Konibo uses the doer-marker system (linguists call it ergative-absolutive). With a transitive verb, the participant who is most like a doer gets the doer marker (ERG). The participant who is most
like a receiver gets no marker, the plain form (ABS). With an intransitive verb, the meaning makes no difference to the marking. The one person can be someone acting, someone feeling, or someone things happen to. In every case it gets the same plain form. This shows the marking follows grammar, not meaning. (Oddly, the evidence for this comes from intransitive verbs, not from transitive verbs.) As for meaning: the doer of a transitive verb (A) is usually someone acting, or a force. Sometimes it is someone feeling something. With the verb ‘ache’ it can even be the body part that hurts. But it is never the one the action is done to. The receiver (O) can be the one the action is done to, someone who gets something, or someone who feels something. But it is never the one acting (see also 8.1.1).

h: Case-Marking on Doubled Pronouns (role endings on pronouns said twice)
t:
As I showed in an earlier section with the same heading, you can say a pronoun twice for emphasis, a bit like ‘I, I did it’. When you do, the repeated pronoun keeps its form: with the doer marker or plain. Examples (11)-(13) from Chapter 6 are shown again below:
(1) E-n e-n a-res-ke. | ‘I defeated him / her (on my own). / Only I hit him / her.’
(2) E-a e-a a-res-ai. | ‘Only s/he is defeating / hitting me (I cannot hit back).’
With intransitive verbs things are different. Some speakers accept (3), where the verb is something you actively do (‘leave’). But every speaker I asked rejected (4), where the verb is something that happens to you (‘suffer’):
(3) E-a e-a ka-ke. | ‘I myself left.’
(4) E-a e-a onitsapit-ai. | ‘I myself suffer.’
So with intransitive verbs, everyone I asked rejected a repeated pronoun when the person just undergoes something. Some, but not all, accepted it when the person actively does something. Repeated pronouns are different from ‘emphatic pronouns’ (like ‘myself’), as we will see below.

h: Participant Agreement on Locative / Allative Adjuncts (place phrases that "agree" with the doer)
t:
Words that say where (‘in the house’, ‘to the middle of the river’) can carry a matching marker that points to one person in the sentence. This marker follows the doer-marker pattern. The ending -xon appears only when the ‘where’ word goes with the doer of a transitive verb, as in (5). When it goes with the one person of an intransitive verb, or with the receiver, there is no marker. See (6) and (7):
(5) Wesna-n-ra yoman ak-ai, xobo-n-xon. | ‘Wesna is spinning the thread in the house.’
(6) Bake-ra xobo-n tsini-ai. | ‘The child is playing in the house.’
(7) Joni-n-ra jawen nonti napon xoton-bain-a iki. | ‘The man pushed his canoe to the middle (of the river).’
You can find more examples of this matching marker on ‘where’ words in Chapter 19.

h: Internally-Headed Relatives (descriptions with the noun inside them)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has a kind of ‘who/which…’ description part where the noun being described sits inside the description itself (linguists call this an internally-headed relative clause). This kind follows the plain-form (ABS) pattern. It is the only known place in the language where joining two parts of a sentence follows the plain-form pattern instead of the subject pattern. (Probably the same is true for the ‘who/which…’ parts moved to the front or to the end; see 10.2.4.9.) As I discussed in 10.2.4.8, when the description part has a transitive verb, it is the receiver that belongs to the main sentence. In (8) that is the peccary, not the man:
(8) [Joni-n yawa rete-ibat-a]... | ‘The white-lipped peccary the man killed...’ | The man that killed the white-lipped peccary...’
These description parts can also have an intransitive verb. Then the one person in it is the same as someone in the main sentence:
(9) [Mi-bé ainbo jo-á].... | ‘the woman who came with you....’
Notice that the ‘white-lipped peccary’ in (8) is the one the action is done to, while the woman in (9) is more like someone acting. So what counts is not the meaning role. What counts is the grammar role: the receiver (O) or the one person of an intransitive verb (S).

h: Imperatives (commands)
t:
In commands with a transitive verb, only the receiver can be said out loud (‘Eat fish!’). In commands with an intransitive verb, the one person can be said. So the nouns you hear in commands follow the plain-form (ABS) pattern.
(10) Piti pi-wé! | ‘Eat fish!’ | Mi-n piti pi-wé! | ‘Eat fish! / Eat your fish!’
(11) (Mi-a) ka-tan-we! | ‘(You) go!’

h: Subjecthood (what counts as the "subject"?)
t:
So far we have seen several kinds of evidence that the plain form (ABS) matters as a grammar role in Shipibo-Konibo. But a handful of patterns treat the doer of a transitive verb (A) and the one person of an intransitive verb (S) the same way, and differently from everything else. They are: the plural verb ending -kan, emphatic pronouns (like ‘myself’), dropping the doer when it is the same person, and the same-doer markers -ax, -xon, -ta(a)nan, -i, -kin, -anan, -nox, -noxon. To a lesser degree there is also -a, which shows that the receiver of one part is the doer (S / A) of the main part. All of these were discussed in different
earlier sections. I go over them quickly here, so that all the evidence for a ‘subject’ group is in one place.

h: The Verbal Plural -Kan (the verb plural -kan)
t:
The verb ending -kan tells you that the doer (S or A) is more than one person. If the doer noun already shows it is plural, -kan is optional. What matters here is that -kan follows grammar, not meaning or what the story focuses on. It looks only at who the subject is (linguists call this a nominative pattern). Look at the examples below (see also 6.2.2):
S_{o} argument is plural
(12) Ja bari noka-[a]i-tian joni-bo onitsapi-kan-a iki. | ‘Since there was an eclipse of the sun, the people were suffering.’
S_{a} argument is plural
(13) Jaino-a-x bo-kan-ai chiponki.... | ‘Then they went down the river....’
A argument is plural
(14) Ja-tian ani nonti-n westíora atsa xeati chomo na-yásan-kan-ai... | ‘Then they put a jar of yuca beer in a big canoe.....’
O argument is plural (no -kan occurs)
(15) ...ja joni icha piti-a bané-ni-ke; | jatíbi roo rete-kin keyo-ax. | ‘And so the man remained with a lot of food, after having killed all the howler monkeys.’
The plural -kan isn't only used for the main characters of a story. It even shows up in sentences with no named doer, a bit like English ‘it is thought’ (linguists call these impersonal passives):
(16) Xate-kan-a-kaya-ra e-n a-yora-ke ja-ska-ra shinan-kin. | ‘But after my operation I think about that very much.’

h: Case-Marking on Emphatic Pronouns (role endings on "I myself"-type pronouns)
t:
As I explained in 6.1.2, emphatic pronouns (like ‘himself’) always come in the -n form. They point to the doer (S or A) of the same sentence. Below, janbix points to Mane, the one person of an intransitive verb that happens to him (an S_{o}):
(17) Mane-ra ja-n-bi-x mawá-ke. | ‘Mane himself died / died by his own action.’
In the next example, janbix points to the one person (S) of a ‘to yourself’ verb, which counts as an intransitive verb:
(18) Mane-ra ja-n-bi-x xaté-ke. | ‘Mane cut himself.’
The next examples clearly show that emphatic pronouns can also point to a one person who is actively doing something (an S_{a}):
(19) E-a-ra e-n-bi-x-bi-shaman beno-ama-[a] iki. | ‘I didn’t get married according to my own will.’
(20) Mane-ra ja-n-bi-x jabá-ke. | ‘Manera himself escaped.’
The next two examples show two things. First, emphatic pronouns also get the ending -n when they point to the doer of a transitive verb (A). Second, in that case they do not get the intransitive marker -x:
(21) Wesna-n-ra ja-n-bi rao xea-ke. | ‘Wesna herself drank the medicine.’
(22) Mane-ra ja-n-bi xeati mots-ai. | ‘Mane is preparing his banana drink himself (there is no woman to do it for him).’
In the next passage a woman tells how their mothers used to arrange their marriages for them:

h: Case-Marking on Emphatic Pronouns (role endings on "I myself"-type pronouns)
t:
(23) Jawen keen joni i-ke-tian, moa ja-n-bi
(None) bo-xon-bo no-a meni-i. | ‘Once they found a man they liked, they themselves would take us and give us in matrimony.’
Finally, the next sentence (given as (17) in Ch. 8) shows an emphatic pronoun that points to the receiver, the one the action is done to. The key point: there is no -n:
(24) Nato r-iki e-n piti be-á, | ja-bi moa bo-tan-we. | ‘This is the fish I have caught, you better take THIS home already (rather than continue waiting for your father who also went fishing).’

h: Deletion under Coreference (leaving out a person already mentioned)
t:
When two sentences with the same doer are put side by side, the doer of the second one is dropped, whether it is S or A. English does this too: ‘They killed the grandmother and (they) spread out the leaves.’ We saw this in Ch. 11 in examples (1) and (2), shown again below. Notice that the dropped doer is the doer of a transitive verb in (25), but the one person that things happen to in (26):
(25) [Yoxan-shoko-ki rete-kan-ke], [paranta pei kakaa-kan-ke].... | ‘They killed the grandmother and extended the plantain leaves on the ground....’
(26) [Ja-tian ja xeta kikin-i penet-ai], [payó-yama-ai]. | ‘Then, the teeth became extremely shiny, they didn’t get worn out.’
The same rule shows up with keen- ‘want.’ You can use it in two ways. If you want to do something yourself (‘I want to go’), the person is not repeated in the second part. English works the same way: we don't say ‘I want I to go.’ If you want someone else to do something (‘I want you to go’), that other person must be named. Examples (101) and (102) from Ch. 10 are shown again as (27a) and (28):
(27) E-a-ra keen-ai [Kontámanain ka-ti-n]. | ‘I want to go to Contamana.’ | E-a-ra keen-ai [e-a Kontámanain kati-n] | ‘I want to go to Contamana.’

h: Deletion under Coreference (leaving out a person already mentioned)
t:
(28) E-a-ra keen-ai [mi-n piti meni-ti-nin] | ‘I want you to give (me) the food / fish.’
In the next example, the other person in the second part is shown only by the plural ending -kan:
(29) E-a-ra [Sani rete-kan-ti] keen-ai. | ‘I want them to kill Sani.’

h: Same-Subject Markers ("same person" endings)
t:
The markers -ax, -xon, -taanan, -i, -kin, -anan, -nox, and -noxon tell you, among other things, that the marked part and the main part of the sentence have the same doer.
Under the heading Syntactic Pivot in 9.4, I showed that these word pieces follow grammar roles, not meaning or what the story focuses on. Here I just give more examples (and repeat one) to support my claim: ‘same doer’ works on the subject pattern, with S and A as one group. In the example below, the same-doer marker -xon is used. Yet the ‘I’ is someone experiencing something (seeing) in the first part, but someone things happen to in the marked part. (In Shipibo-Konibo, people who see or hear behave in the grammar just like ordinary doers of transitive verbs; see 10.3.3.)
(30) E-n oin-a iki Ani Xeati a-kan-ai | chonka rabé baritia-ya i-xon. | ‘When I was twelve years old, I saw how the Ani Xeati ceremony was practiced.’
Below, the same-doer marker -ax shows that the doer of ‘hit’ (A, someone acting) is the same as the one person of ‘fall’ (S, someone it happens to):
(31) E-a-ra [Mane tima-ax] paké-ke. | ‘I hit Mane and fell.’
In the next example, the same-doer marker -i links two parts. In one, the people are actively doing something (singing). In the other, they are more like someone something happens to:

h: Same-Subject Markers ("same person" endings)
t:
(32) ...bewa bewa-shin-i-res nete-kan-ai. | ‘Singing and singing all night long they received the new day.’
Example (33) shows that you cannot use a same-doer marker when the doers are different. This is true even if both parts are mainly about the same person:
(33) Xeta-n chexa-a-ra rimon bero chaka-xon rao-n-ke. | ‘Since I had a toothache, I ground lemon seeds and treated it.’

h: The Object-to-Subject Marker -A (the ending -a: the receiver becomes the next doer)
t:
Most of these markers follow the subject pattern. But we have seen that the marker -a is different. It shows that the receiver of the marked part is the doer (S / A) of the main part. In (33) above, -a links a receiver to the doer of a transitive verb (O > A). In the sentence below, it links a receiver to the one person of an intransitive verb (O > S):
(34) E-a bake i-ke-tian nokon papa-baon e-a raon-yama-a-ra, | kikin yopa i-kean-ke. | ‘If my parents had not treated me with plant medicine when I was a child, I would be a total incompetent (i.e., a bad fisher / hunter) now.’

h: Objecthood: Symmetrical Objects (what counts as the "object"? (when two objects behave alike))
t:
A receiver (an object) can be defined like this: in a transitive sentence, it is the plain-form (ABS) participant that is most like ‘the one the action is done to’. Also, the receiver of the smaller part is the key link in sentences joined with -a
. And it must be taken as the described noun in ‘who/which…’ parts with a transitive verb, whether the noun sits inside, is moved to the front, or is moved to the end.
But a sentence can have more than one receiver. For Shipibo-Konibo, I argue that the receivers in a sentence are equal (I call them ‘symmetrical objects’). I use this term a bit differently from Bresnan and Moshi (1990), who wrote about Bantu languages in Africa. In those languages two receivers can share receiver features, but there are still ways to tell a direct object from an indirect one. Think of English ‘give the girl a book’: ‘a book’ is the thing given and ‘the girl’ is who gets it. In Shipibo-Konibo, nothing in the grammar of ordinary statements separates those two (though see certain questions in 8.4.2.3). That is what I mean by ‘symmetrical object’ in this section. So with a verb like ‘give’, both the thing given and the person who gets it are in the plain form (ABS). They can also swap places with no change in form.

h: Constituent Order and Case-Marking (word order and role endings)
t:
The two examples right below show that with meni- ‘give’, both the thing given and the person who gets it are in the plain form (ABS). They can also swap places:
(35) Pena-n-ra bake-bo esé-bo meni-ai. | ‘Pena gives advice to the children.’
(None) Pena-n-ra esé-bo bake-bo meni-ai. | ‘Pena gives advice to the children.’
Still, people seem to prefer saying the person who gets it before the thing given.

h: Causativization ("make someone do it")
t:
The next sentence has a ‘make someone do it’ verb and two people as receivers. Notice that either of the two plain-form (ABS) words can be the one who is made to do something. (Given Shipibo customs, the first meaning is the more likely one.)
(36) Pena-n-ra ranon jawen xontako bi-ma-ke. | ‘Pena married her daughter to the young man (lit. made her unmarried daughter get / receive the young man). /Pena married the young man to her daughter (lit. made the young man get / receive her unmarried daughter).’

h: Applicativization (adding an extra person to the verb)
t:
Also, either one can be the receiver of an ending that brings in an extra person, such as the ‘for someone’ ending -xon:
(37) Pena-n-ra xontako joni mera-xon-ke. | ‘Pena found a man for the unmarried girl / Pena found an unmarried girl for the man.’

h: Object-to-Subject Coreferentiality (when the receiver of one action does the next)
t:
As we saw earlier, in one kind of long sentence the marker -a links two events in a row. It shows that the receiver of the first part is the doer of the main part. When the first part has a verb with two receivers (like ‘give’), either one can be picked: the person who gets it or the thing given:
(38) Pena-n bake-shoko meni-a-ra ainbo xobo-n ka-ke. | ‘After Pena gave (her) the baby, the woman went home.’
(39) Pena-n ainbo meni-a-ra bake-shoko wini-ke. | ‘After Pena gave (it) to the woman, the baby cried.’

h: Externally-Headed Relativization ("who/which" descriptions with the noun outside)
t:
Both receivers appear in the plain form, and both can also be described with a ‘who/which…’ part (‘the advice that Pena gives’, ‘the children to whom Pena gives advice’):
(40) Esé-bo Pena-n bake-bo meni-ai r-iki | moa-tian no-n axé. | ‘The advice that Pena gives the children is part of our traditional custom.’
(41) Bake-bo Pena-n esé-bo meni-ai r-iki jawen | baba-bo. | ‘The children to whom Pena is giving advice are her grandchildren.’

h: Internally-Headed Relativization ("who/which" descriptions with the noun inside)
t:
As I discussed earlier, in ‘who/which…’ parts where the noun sits inside, with a transitive verb, it is the receiver (O) that belongs to the main sentence. The examples below show that this works both for the person who gets something and for the thing given:
(42) [Tsoma-n joni koríki meni-a]-ra ono yaká-ke. | ‘The man to whom Tsoma gave money is sitting further over there.’ | [Tsoma-n joni koríki meni-a]-ra jawen pisha-n iki. | ‘The money that Tsoma gave to the man is in his bag.’
However, at least some speakers, when the verbs meni- ‘give’ and bichin- ‘take away’ were inside this kind of description part, tended to take the thing given or taken as the one being described.
This kind of description part treats ordinary receivers and receivers brought in by an extra-person ending the same way:
(43) E-n-ra bena-[a]i | [Beso-n nawa ainbo kena-xon-a]. | ‘I am looking for the woman that Beso called for the mestizo.’ | ‘I am looking for the woman for whom Beso called the mestizo.’ | ‘I am looking for the mestizo that Beso called for the woman.’ | ‘I am looking for the mestizo for whom Beso called the woman.’
To sum up, all the evidence in this section shows that the receivers in a Shipibo-Konibo sentence are equal. In many languages you can test which receiver is the ‘direct object’ with a passive, like English ‘The book was given to the girl’. But Shipibo-Konibo has no real passive of that kind, so that test isn't available.

h: Tripartite Alignment (marking the doer, the receiver and the lone person all differently)
t: We have looked at several patterns that pick out either the plain-form (ABS) group or the subject group. Now let's turn to emphatic pronouns (like ‘myself’). In their marking, they follow the subject pattern: for S and A they both get -n. But overall they follow a three-way pattern (linguists call it tripartite), because only the S emphatic pronoun gets the extra marker -x. So the three forms are: PRO-n + -x for S (exx. (19) and (20)), PRO-n + -0 for A (exx. (21)-(23)), and PRO-0 + -0 for O (ex. (24)).

h: S-Marked Alignment (marking only the lone person)
t:
By ‘S-marked alignment’ I mean a pattern where only the one person of an intransitive verb (S) gets a marker. The doer (A) and receiver (O) of a transitive verb get none. You can see this in the S marker on emphatic pronouns. You also see it on ‘from where’ words and other add-on words (for the ‘from where’ words, see 8.3.2; see also Chapter 9).
To sum up, Shipibo-Konibo marks these roles in many different patterns. However, almost all the rules for linking parts of a sentence work on the
subject pattern, where S and A count as one group (linguists call this nominative-accusative). So in Shipibo-Konibo, the grammar role ‘subject’ is S and A put together. On the other hand, nothing in the grammar separates different kinds of receivers. (Whether the two receivers behave exactly the same in certain questions still needs to be checked; see 8.4.2.3.)
EVIDENTIALITY AND EPISTEMIC MODALITY:
Shipibo-Konibo marks how the speaker knows something (linguists call this evidentiality). It does this at two levels. First there is a big split: -ra means ‘I know this first-hand’, and -ronki means ‘someone told me’. On top of that you can add -bira for ‘I conclude this’ or -mein for ‘I am guessing’. If you asked native speakers about (1a) on its own, they would call it ‘incomplete’. They would most likely offer (1b) instead:

h: S-Marked Alignment (marking only the lone person)
t:
(1) ??Jawen jema ani iki. | ‘Her village is large.’ | Jawen jema-ra ani iki. | ‘Her village is large.’ (I have been there.)
Another option is the ‘someone told me’ marker -ronki:
(1) Jawen jema-ronki ani iki. | ‘Her village is large.’ (I have not been there, I have been told that it is large.)
These two sentences clearly differ in how the speaker knows, as the notes in brackets show. Two more options use -bira and -mein. -Bira usually appears together with -ra. The guessing marker -mein is combined with -ra less often:
(None) Ani-ra i-bira-[a]i jawen jema. | ‘Her village must be large.’ (e.g., because it has a secondary school) | Ani-mein(-ra) iki jawen jema. | ‘Perhaps her village is large.’ (I am just guessing, “I ask myself”)
Also, -bira and -mein can be combined with -ronki:
(None) Ani-ronki i-bira-[a]i jawen jema. | ‘Her village must be large (from what I heard I infer).’ | Ani-mein(-ronki) iki jawen jema. | ‘Perhaps her village is large. (from what I heard I speculate)’
In many languages, ‘how I know’ markers are required endings on the verb. They often interact in interesting ways with other things the verb shows, like time, mood, person (I / you / he), and the type of verb (Aikhenvald, to appear). Shipibo-Konibo is different. Its ‘how I know’ markers are not verb endings, and few of those limits apply to them.

h: S-Marked Alignment (marking only the lone person)
t:
As in many languages with ‘how I know’ markers, some Shipibo-Konibo markers do two jobs. They show how you know something, and also how sure you are. These markers
are: -ra, for direct experience or certainty (the speaker saw it or is sure); -bira, for inference or probability (the speaker figured it out or thinks it likely); and -mein, for speculation or doubt (the speaker is guessing). However, -ra can be combined with -bira or -mein. This possibility shows that these markers cannot mainly be about how sure the speaker is. If they were, some real expressions in the language would have contradictory meanings, like ‘I am sure that I doubt’ (when combining -ra and -mein). It makes sense that direct sensory experience, like seeing something yourself, leads to being sure of it. The reverse situation seems less likely. The "someone told me" (hearsay) markers are special. Their only function is to show how the speaker knows something, never how sure they are.

h: The Direct Evidential / Certainty Marker -Ra (-ra: "I saw it / I'm sure")
t:
The marker -ra indicates that the speaker knows something first-hand (linguists call this the direct evidential). Maybe the speaker took part in the situation described, or was an observer. Or the speaker had direct sensory experience of it through vision, hearing, smell, taste or touch. -Ra is only used in statements, not in questions or commands. It is also used when referring to the future, to generally known facts, and in warnings and threats. In these instances -ra shows that the speaker is sure (certainty). -Ra always attaches in the same position: right after the first major part of the sentence, in second place. As expected, -ra appears all the time when people tell the story of their own lives. In (2a) and (2b), look for r (a short form of -ra) before iki. In the glosses it is labelled EV (the marker that shows how the speaker knows something).
(2) Nokon jane r-iki Inkan Soi. | ‘My name is Inkan Soi. | E-a r-iki Bawanixo-nko-ni-a. | I am from Bawanisho.
(None) E-n-ra mato yoi-ai westíora nokon yosi-shoko betan | e-a winó-ni jawéki yomera-i ka-[a]x. | ‘I’ll tell you what happened to me and my grandfather when we went fishing.’ | Westíora nete-n-ra ka-a iki nokon yosi betan e-a, piti | bena-i.... | ‘One day my grandfather and I went to look for fish....’

h: The Direct Evidential / Certainty Marker -Ra (-ra: "I saw it / I'm sure")
t:
The next examples confirm that -ra goes in second place in the sentence. It comes right after the first big chunk, whatever that chunk is (linguists call this a second-position clitic). In (3) it comes after a doer made of two nouns (‘father and mother’). In (4) it comes after a ‘who/which…’ description part. In (5) it comes after a whole ‘when…’ part. (In (5), -ra turns into -a after an s-like sound.)
(3) [Papa betan tita]-ra wai-nko ka-békon-ai. | ‘Father and mother (-RA) are going to the chacra.’
(4) [E-n xeati a-ma-ibat-a joni]-ra moa ka-ke. | ‘The man whom I invited beverage yesterday (-RA) already left.’
(5) [No-n papa nokó-ke-tian oin-ax]-a no-a raro-ke. | ‘When we saw that our father arrived (-RA), we became happy.’
If a sentence starts by calling someone (‘Father, …’), -ra skips that word. It comes after the next big chunk instead:
(6) Papá, mi-a-ra bake wetsa-baon kena-ma-ke... | ‘Father, my brothers sent me to call you....’
But when the first (or only) chunk is a verb, -ra goes inside the verb itself. It comes before the plural ending -kan (if there is one) and before the endings that show how the action unfolds. Look at these examples:
(7) toxbá-paké-yama-ra-kan-ai | ‘(they) do not go floating down the river’
(8) bi-bain-yama-ra-kan-ke | ‘they did not get it while going / they did not get it and left’

h: The Direct Evidential / Certainty Marker -Ra (-ra: "I saw it / I'm sure")
t: -Ra is also the ‘default’ marker for events the speaker might have seen. For example, ask a Shipibo speaker to translate “The dog caught a paca.” They will most likely use -ra without asking where the information came from. Why does -ra cover so much ground? Probably because it started out as a plain ‘this is a statement’ marker, and only later became a ‘seen it myself’ marker (Valenzuela 2003).

h: The Reportative -Ronki (-ronki: "they say")
t:
The reportative -ronki means the speaker got the information from someone else, known or unknown. -Ronki does not mean the speaker doubts it, or that it is less reliable. It just means ‘second-hand’. -Ronki is the usual marker in folk tales and other traditional stories, which often
start with Moatianronki ‘It is said that long time ago...’ or Nete benatianronki ‘It is said that when the world was new.’
Once it is clear that a story is second-hand, -ronki doesn't appear in every sentence or every turn of talk. Instead, it seems to mark certain chunks of the story. Look at this passage from a myth about how things began. In (9a) the storyteller uses -ronki to open the text, which describes how the Shipibo lived long ago. After it come several sentences with no ‘how I know’ marker:
(9) Nete bena-tian-ronki, no-n reken-bo onitsap-i-bires | ja-pao-ni-ke; wetsa-nko-bires rakat-ax oxa-ai-bo, | chopa sawe-ti onan-ma-bo, piti oa | jawékiati-bo onan-ma-bo, bimi-bicho | koko-ai-bo, boan-boan-res-i ja-kan-a-bo. | ‘When the world was new (-RONKI), our ancestors lived just suffering; they lay and slept anywhere, they didn’t wear any clothes, they did not know (how to obtain) fish or crops, they ate just fruit, they lived walking and walking.’
-ronki shows up again on the ‘when…’ part that opens (9b). Then the God Sun appears and the main story begins:

h: The Reportative -Ronki (-ronki: "they say")
t:
(9) Ja-ska-ra onitsap-i-bires i-t-ai oin-xon-ronki no-n
(None) Bari Rios-en jawen rabé bake no-a raan-xon-ni-ke: | Papa Inka Rios betan Xane Inka Rios. | Seeing that they were suffering (-RONKI), our God Sun sent us his two sons: Papa Inka God and Xane Inka God.
The next -ronki markers come where the story changes direction. The two Inkas sent by the Sun are compared, and -ronki comes after the mention of each one:
(None) Ja Papa Bari Inka Rios-ronki i-ni-ke jakon shinan-ya, ikaxbi | ja Xane Inka Rios-ronki i-ni-ke jakon-ma shinan-ya..... | Papa Inka Bari God (-RONKI) was generous, but Xane Inka God (-RONKI) was stingy....’ (Fucshico 1998:11)
So -ronki and -ra don't appear in every sentence or turn. But the ‘how I know’ marking is still ‘required’ in a sense. Earlier in the talk, the source of the information has always been marked, and native speakers know what it is. Once that's set up, -ra and -ronki can be left out of some sentences. Those sentences fall under the ‘scope’ (the reach) of an earlier marker. This fits another fact: a statement said on its own needs -ra or -ronki (280a). That's because there is no earlier talk to show how the speaker knows. When the source of the information changes, the speaker has to mark it again.
-Ronki is a small add-on piece that sits in the same spot in the sentence as -ra. It goes right after the first main part of the sentence (linguists call this kind of piece a clitic). There is more. Sometimes the first part, or the only part, is a full verb. Then -ronki comes before the endings that mean ‘many people’ (plural) and the endings that show whether the action is finished or ongoing (aspect):

h: The Reportative -Ronki (-ronki: "they say")
t:
(10) A-ronki-ai. | ‘It is said that she will do (it)./ She says that she will do it.’ | A-ronki-a iki | ‘It is said that she did (it)./ She says that she did (it).’
