However, -ronki cannot sit in the same word as the ‘finished’ ending -ke or the plural ending -kan. To use them together, you need a stand-in verb in between (linguists call it a pro-verb), much like English do in “she did”:
(10) A-ronki-ke. | ‘It is said that she did (it)./She says that she did (it).’ | A-ronki-a-ke. | ‘It is said that s/he did (it)./S/he says that s/he did (it).’ | A-ronki-a-kan-a iki. | ‘It is said that they did (it).’
-Ra is different. It can join the plural ending, the ‘finished’ ending -ke and the “narrative past” -a iki directly, with nothing in between. So -ra, -ronki and the question marker -ki (see 8.4.1-8.4.2) all take the
same spot in the sentence, apart from the small differences in (10c-e). Nothing points the other way, so I think these three add-ons form one set: you pick one of them for that slot.¹
SK -ronki has an interesting extra use. It marks reported speech: when you tell what someone else said or thought, in your own words (linguists call this indirect speech). Look at the part in square brackets in (11):

h: The Reportative -Ronki (-ronki: "they say")
t:
(11) Jain-xon nokon papa-n ninkat-a iki | [moa-ronki be-kan-a iki]. | ‘Then my father heard (from someone else) that they were coming already.’
In the next example both markers appear. The marker -ra marks the first part, because the speaker took part in that event himself: Beso told him something. The marker -ronki marks the second part, where the speaker passes on what Beso told him:
(12) Beso-n-ra e-a yoi-ke | [Kontámanain-ronki oi be-ai.] | ‘Beso told me that it is raining in Contamana.’
But you cannot use -ronki to report something you said yourself earlier. That is why (12b) is wrong:
(12) E-n-ra yoi-ke [Kontámanain-ronki oi be-ai]. | ‘I said that it was raining in Contamana.’
Compare Jaqaru, an Aymara language from Peru. There, the markers for questions, for first-hand information and for “someone told me” also form one set; Hardman (1986:129).
The “someone told me” marker -ronki is not a way to dodge blame or to keep your distance from what you say. Here is a telling case. Imagine a speaker talking about something that happened while she was drunk. She can use either -ra or -ronki. She picks -ra if she remembers what happened. She picks -ronki if she doesn't remember and others told her about it:
(13) E-a-ron i / -ra tima-nan-iba-ke. | ‘I had a fight.’ (I was told, I don’t recall it./ I recall it, although I was drunk.)

h: The Reportative -Ronki (-ronki: "they say")
t:
On its own, -ronki does not suggest that the information is unreliable. But it can be used sarcastically, together with other signals such as a special tone of voice, a gesture, and/or a smile. In (14) the speaker uses it to mean “I'm sure this isn't true”:
(14) Nato oxe-ronki mi-a sueldo neen-xon-ai apo-n, | oin-tan-we! | ‘(It is said that) this month the president will raise your salary. Go see it!’ (I am sure this is not true.)

h: The Reportative -Ki (-ki: "they say" (short form))
t:
There is a second “someone told me” marker, -ki. It may be a shorter form of -ronki. Notice that it looks exactly like the general question marker -ki. Like -ronki and the question marker -ki, this -ki can sit in the second spot of the sentence, and it also
comes before the plural and ‘finished/ongoing’ endings when it attaches to a full verb. But this -ki has something special: it can appear more than once in the same sentence. In (15) it shows up three times:
(15) Ii-kin-ki ak-á iki joni-n-ki too a-kin, | toya-ki moa. | ‘After some time, the man got her pregnant, she was pregnant already.’
-Ronki and -ki can both appear in the same chain of sentences, on different parts. The example below even has them stuck together, as -ronki-ki. The reverse order, -ki-ronki, never shows up:
(16) Ne-ke-a nete-keská-ribi-ronki-ki ja jene meran. | ‘(It is said that) inside the water it is just like on this world.’
Note that the expression above does not mean ‘someone told someone who told me’ (that kind of second-hand-of-second-hand report is covered in 14.3.3).
The short -ki can be used in a command, to pass on someone else's request. Here native speakers clearly preferred -ki, or simply rejected -ronki:
(17) Onpax-ki bi-wé! | ‘Bring water!’ (on her / his request)

h: The Reportative -Ki (-ki: "they say" (short form))
t:
As we saw, the short “someone told me” marker -ki looks exactly like the general question marker, which also sits in the second spot of the sentence. One way to explain this is to see the “someone told me” use and the question use as two
sides of a single word piece. Its bigger job would be to mark information that counts as second-hand for the speaker.

h: The Inferential / Probabilitive -Bira (-bira: "probably")
t:
-Bira is the “I figure / probably” marker. It works differently from all the other markers that show how the speaker knows something. It does not sit in the second spot of the sentence. Instead, it goes on the part the speaker wants to highlight. Very often that is the all-purpose intransitive verb ik- ‘be / do’. You find -bira both in statements and in questions. -Bira shows that the speaker has worked something out from good clues and has a fairly solid guess (linguists call this inference). It can also simply mean ‘probably’. In (18) the speaker guesses Beka is hungry, because everyone knows there is no fish in her village:
(18) Beka-ra pi-kas-i-bira i-t-ai. | ‘Beka must be hungry.’ (since everybody knows there is no fish in her village)
(19) “Janso-i-ra i-bira-[a]i mi-n bene ja-skat-i, | ja ikon i-ke-tian-ra moa ak-á i-kean-ke | yawa maan-kin” a-kin-ronki ak-á iki | jawen wetsa ja ainbaon. | ‘The woman told her sister: “Your husband must be lying, if it were true (that there are white-lipped peccaries in the upper world) he would have already brought them down.” (Soi Rawa 1995:25)
-Bira can also mean ‘about’ or ‘roughly’, when you aren't exact:
(20) Jaino-a-x kimisha oxe-bira ik-á iki. | ‘Then, about three months passed.’
-Bira also shows up when people hesitate while trying to remember something they might be able to recall.

h: The Inferential / Probabilitive -Bira (-bira: "probably")
t:
When -bira is not on a verb, you can usually swap it for the comparison word keská, which can be translated ‘it seems that, I think that.’ Keská can work like a marker of how you know something. But its basic meaning is ‘like, the same as’. So I see keská as a borrowed way of showing how you know something (an “evidential strategy” in the sense of Aikhenvald 2003), not as a true marker of that kind. The next example suggests that -bira and keská do the same job. The speaker first uses one, then rephrases with the other:
(21) Ja-o-bira-kan, osea ja-ó keska-ra | forestal-bo we-i-kan-ai. | ‘Hmm, I think in that area; that is, I think the forest policemen enter in that area.’
You can also use both the ‘like’ word and the “I figure” marker in the same expression, especially in the phrase jawe keskára ibirai ‘how might it be?’:
(22) Ikax ma akí iki o ak-á-ma-pari? | ‘But is he making (plantain chacra) already or not?’ | Ma ak-í r-iki jawe keska-ra i-bira-[a]i. | ‘He might be doing it already. How might it be?’
(23) Jawe-tsi i-[y]antan-a Elva, nexnex, nexnex rete-anan miin-ti | no sé jawe keska-ra i-bira-[a]i. | ‘What did Elva say, that one should kill a shansho (bird) and bury it? How was it?

h: The Inferential / Probabilitive -Bira (-bira: "probably")
t: (24) Joni jawe-keskat-a-ra no-n oin-bira-ke bai napon | raka-t-a. | ‘We saw a man lying on the road. What could have happened to him?’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:211)

h: The Speculative / Dubitative -Mein ~ -Main (-mein ~ -main: "maybe / I wonder")
t:
The word piece -mein ~ -main is the “I guess / I wonder” marker. Speakers use either form, freely. It also sits in the second spot of the sentence. On a full verb, it comes before the plural -kan and the ‘finished/ongoing’ endings. But -mein can be followed by -ra, or by the “someone told me” markers -ronki or -ki. Like -bira, -mein appears in both statements and questions. A sentence with -mein looks like an ordinary statement. It can even carry the ‘finished’ ending -ke, which is replaced by -a in questions and in other sentences turned into nouns. Yet native speakers hear it as a kind of question to oneself, or a guess. -Mein is used when the evidence for what you say is poor or missing altogether. It can also express doubt, or surprise at something unexpected (linguists call this mirativity). Here is an example. A man is fishing and sees a fruit
fall from a tree into the water. Next, some small fish (pilchards) swim towards the fruit. A few minutes later, the pilchards fly. At this moment the man “asks himself:”
(25) Nato jiwi bimi pi-ax-mein(-ra) sipan noya-ke. | ‘Having eaten the fruit from this tree perhaps the pilchards flew?’
In the sentence above, -mein shows not only guessing but also surprise. However, -mein doesn't have to express surprise. In the example below the speaker is just guessing what might happen:

h: The Speculative / Dubitative -Mein ~ -Main (-mein ~ -main: "maybe / I wonder")
t:
(26) Nato joxo koríki miin-kan-ni bi-ax-main, no-a | yometso i-ti iki. | ‘If we take these coins buried long ago, perhaps we would be taken as thieves.’
Besides -mein, there are other ways to show surprise: the emphatic -bi, the contrast marker -kaya, or a verb form that uses a doubled helper verb.
-Mein is also used in questions, to sound polite and to show that the speaker cares (see 8.4.3.7).
Table 13.1 shows which of these “how do you know” markers can appear in which types of sentences.

h: Evidentials and Cultural Attitudes (these markers and Shipibo values)
t:
The Shipibo use the “someone told me” marker -ronki when they tell their own dreams. At first sight this seems odd, because the marker's basic job is to mark information you heard from others. The following sentence could be used to tell a dream:
(27) E-a-ronki i-wan-ke ani aros wai napo chankat-a. | ‘(It is said that) I was standing in the center of a large rice chacra.’
Under the influence of the hallucinogen ayahuasca (Banisteriopsis spp., Malpighiaceae), the Shipibo shaman travels to a different layer of reality, the upper world. There he deals with beings such as the ‘hidden people’ or chaikoni, and with helpful and evil spirits. During a healing session with ayahuasca, the shaman sees designs and knots on the patient's face and body. His helper spirits help him find out what is wrong and heal the patient (Tournon 1991 and references therein). What follows is a very short piece of a song sung during a healing session (from Tournon 1991:196, my analysis):
(28) ...joni yora senen-ma, | ‘...the man’s body is not fully healed, | yora senen-mamea e-n-ra keyo-bo-ai jakon koshi bewakan, | I will complete the healing of the body with my good and powerful song, | ...e-n-ronki jakon ak-ai.... | ...they (my allied spirits) say that I do it well....’
So the Shipibo use the first-hand marker -ra for ayahuasca visions, but the “someone told me” marker -ronki for dreams. This tells us a lot about Shipibo culture. Ayahuasca visions count as part of reality, but at least some dreams do not. And this difference is built into the grammar.

h: Evidentials and Cultural Attitudes (these markers and Shipibo values)
t: Also, people use the “someone told me” marker, not the first-hand one, when they explain how something is done. They do this even if they have done it themselves.

h: Evidentials and European Innovations (these markers and new things from Europe)
t:
The Shipibo have stretched these markers to talk about things that came from Europe, such as books, radio and TV. Watching something on television counts as seeing it yourself, because you really “see” it happen. So when people watch a soccer match, they describe what is happening, and the score, with -ra. But if they heard the match on the radio, they must use the “someone told me” marker -ronki, because the reporter told them what happened:
(29) Penal r-iki. | ‘It is a penalty.’ (I am watching it on television) | Penal-ronki iki. | ‘It is a penalty.’ (I am hearing it on the radio)
But if you only hear the news on television, without seeing pictures of what is being reported, -ronki rather than -ra would be the right choice.
-Ronki is also used for things you hear on the telephone or read in the newspaper (because “the newspaper says it”) or in a book. In the bilingual primary schools, -ronki is everywhere when Peruvian history is taught:
(30) No-n reken Inka-ronki ik-á iki Manco Capac. | ‘(It is said that) our first Inka was Manco Capac.’
A teacher talked about geography classes. He explained that if you read in a book where a place is, you would use -ronki. But if you get the same information from a map, you would choose -ra instead:

h: Evidentials and European Innovations (these markers and new things from Europe)
t:
(31) Alemania-ronki Holanda patax iki. | ‘Germany is next to the Netherlands’. (I read it in a book) | Alemania-ra Holanda patax iki. | ‘Germany is next to the Netherlands’. (I saw it on a map)
How -ra is used with these European inventions supports my view of it as a first-hand marker: it marks information you got straight from the source. The marker -ronki, for its part, has been stretched from information you heard to information you read.
Within the Panoan family, having grammar markers for how you know something seems to be a new development. The languages seem to be building, or to have built, these systems more or less separately from each other (Valenzuela 2003).
NOTES ON DISCOURSE ORGANIZATION:

h: Narrative Organization (how stories are put together)
t:
Here is how a SK story is put together. It begins with one or a few sentences that describe the situation and/or introduce the important characters. The first of these sentences carries a marker showing how the speaker knows the story. Then, in the next group of sentences, or the next paragraph, the main storyline begins. SK paragraphs are usually linked in one of two ways. One way is a linking word like ‘then’, which carries case endings and a marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. The other way is a short sentence part with such a marker that sums up the scene before (‘having done that…’). Often a “how do you know” marker appears here too. The following piece of a story shows sentence parts that sum up the event before:
(1) Ja-tian ja keot-ai-tian-ki, ainbaon mawa mawa-a iki. | ‘Then, hearing (the black-jaguar bird) roaring, the woman imitated it.
(2) Ja mawa maw-ai-tian-ki, ja wiso-ino isá jo-a iki. | As she was imitating it, the black-jaguar bird came (to where the woman was).
(3) Jo-ax-ki ja isá-bi ino-a iki. | Once there, this same bird turned into a jaguar.
(4) Ino-xon-ki ja ainbo pi-á iki. | Turning into a jaguar, it ate the woman.’ (Ministerio de Educación and ILV 1979:10)

h: Narrative Organization (how stories are put together)
t:
Linking words are very important for holding a story together. And the ‘same doer’ and ‘different doer’ markers can do more than their name suggests: they can signal other kinds of continuity or break in the story. Look at the next piece of a story. It has jatian ‘then’ twice. The first time, it comes as the male Inka comes back into the story as the doer, so the doer changes. The second time, it does not. In fact, the doers in (c) and (d) are the same person. Here jatian marks a different kind of break: the switch from telling the story to quoting someone's exact words. Note that in (d) the doer ‘her husband’ is named, so that the listener does not take jatian to mean that the doer has changed:
(5) Ja washit-a-ronki ka-a iki. | ‘Being denied (the toasted peanut), (the Inka Woman) left.’ | Ja-tian jawen bene ka-a ik-á iki jato | onan-ma-i, tsaka-ti, wina-ti, | pia a-ti, yomera-ti axe-a-i. | ‘By that moment her husband had gone to teach them (i.e. the Shipibo men) how to shoot with arrow, row, make arrow, fish / hunt, to train them.’
(None) Jo-xon jis-á-ronki ik-á iki Inka Ainbo wini wini-i. | ‘When (he) returned, he saw the Inka Woman crying and crying.’ | Ja-tian jawen bene-n raté-xon yokat-a iki: | “Jawe-kopí-ki mi-a wini-ai?” | ‘Then her husband got scared and asked (her): ‘Why are you crying?’’

h: Narrative Organization (how stories are put together)
t:
In the next sentence, jainoax carries the ‘same doer’ marker even though the doers are actually different. Still, the sentence describes one single event, so here the marker shows a kind of continuity in the story, not literally the same doer.
(6) Bane-ki-a-kan-a iki, westíora yosi-shoko, | yoxan-shoko jaino-a-x bake-bo-res. | ‘The only ones who stayed were an old man, an old woman, and the children.’
Sentence parts with the ‘same/different doer’ markers often give background information. The next example is an unusually long chain. It describes how the ancestors of the Shipibo lived long ago, without farming and without fire. The first part sets the scene and gives background, “a framework within which the main predication holds” (Chafe 1976, Bickel 1999). Notice also that these sentence parts form groups, and each group paints one scene. The groups are closed off by the short “someone told me” marker -ki (the longer -ronki can't do this job). The single
full verb of the main sentence is underlined. The parts with ‘same/different doer’ markers are in square brackets, and the units marked with -ki are in simple brackets.
(7) [Ja-ska-ra i-xon-ronki] a-káti-kan-ai | {[yapa axa-n-xon] | [bi-xon-ki]} | {[makaman benes a-kin] | [chaka-xon-ki]} | {[bari-n raka-n-xon-ki]} | {[moshi-ke-tian bi-xon-ki]} | [pi-kin] no-n moa-baon, | [chii-oma i-xon]. | ‘Living in such conditions, our ancestors poisoned the fish and collected them, crushed them with a stone making them thinner, and lay them in the sun so that it dried; getting them they ate them, because they had no fire.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:9).’

h: Narrative Organization (how stories are put together)
t:
Sentence parts with ‘same/different doer’ markers can also move the story forward when they come before the main sentence. The next example is about two twin brothers who shoot arrows upward to build a ladder to the sky. The doers are the same all along: the two twin brothers.
(8) Ja pia-n-ribi, wetsa pia poinki tsaka-xon, | nenké-a-xon, mai-ki noko-ax, bo-ríba-kan-a iki,
(None) jakiribi, jato-n xobo-n. | ‘Again with this arrow they shot at another arrow’s end, and making (the arrow ladder) longer, they reached the ground, and then went back to their house.’
Some traditional stories end with a closing sentence that explains how the events just told led to the way things are today:
(9) Ja-skat-ax-ronki i-ni-ke no-a Shipibo jane-ti. | ‘And it was in this way how we were given the name Shipibo.’
(10) Ja-ska-raino-axonki ino betan xae-ki | rawi-kanan-bekon-a iki. | ‘In this way, the jaguar and the ant-eater became rivals.
(11) Rama kaman-bi-ki ja-ki xae sinat-ai. | And even until today, the ant-eater is mad at the jaguar.’
Most stories contain direct quotes, and reported speech can appear too.

h: Object-to-Subject Coreferentiality (when the receiver of one action does the next)
t:
As we saw in 9.3.1, the marker -a lets you keep a character as the main topic, or bring it in, or bring it back, even when that character is the one something is done to, not the one doing it. In
this way, sentences with -a do the same job as the passive in languages like English (“he was called”). The sentence below comes from a story about a great shaman. The main character is introduced at the start of the story. Then a few sentences describe how people used his services to talk with dead relatives. After that, the -a sentence brings the main character back into focus:
(12) Ja-ská-a-kin yoi-kan-a jo-ax-ki | yaka-t-ai bachi kexá. | ‘Once being called, he would come and sit at the edge of the mosquito net.’
You can see the same job, bringing the main character back, in the next piece of a story:
(13) Ja Inka Ainbo-ronki ik-á iki tama pi-kas. | ‘It is said that the Inka woman loved to eat peanut.’ | Ja i-t-ai-bi, westíora Shipibo ainbaon-ki | ak-á iki tama toban washí-kin. | ‘Then, a Shipibo woman denied her toasted peanut.’ | Ja washit-a-ronki ka-a iki. | ‘Being denied (the toasted peanut), (the Inka Woman) left.’
In the next example, the speaker is talking about himself, and he is the topic of all three sentence parts. The verb chexa ‘ache’ works in a special way: the aching body part is treated as the doer, and the person who feels the pain as the receiver (‘my tooth aches me’). So -a is used to keep the man as the topic:

h: Object-to-Subject Coreferentiality (when the receiver of one action does the next)
t:
(14) Xeta-n chexa-a-ra rimon bero chaka-xon | rao-n-ke. | ‘Since I had a toothache, I ground lemon seeds and treated it.’
In (15) a woman talks about her plans for the future. She explains how an operation she had is changing the way she sees things. The people who did the operation are only hinted at, through the plural marker -kan. And -a is used because the woman is the one the operation was done to:
(15) Xate-kan-a-kaya-ra e-n a-yora-ke ja-ska-ra shinan-kin. | ‘But after my operation I think about that very much.’
In (16) the -a sentence is used to change who the main character is:
(16) Ja waste-n i-xon ainbo-nin joni noko-a, | keen-yama-pacho-kin-bi kikin a-kin noi ka-i. | ‘Making use of that piripiri, when the woman meets the man, even though he didn’t want her before, he is going to fall in love with her.’

h: Direct Quotes (quoting exact words)
t:
Direct quotes, giving someone's exact words, are the most common way to pass on what someone else said or thought. But reported speech, in your own words, is not rare either. A direct quote inside a story comes between verbs of saying. These can also be the all-purpose verbs ik- (an intransitive verb) and ak- (a transitive verb), which here mean ‘say’ and ‘tell’. A direct quote often carries the add-ons that sit in the second spot of a sentence, especially -ra, the first-hand marker.
The following example shows a direct quote that opens with the verb yoi- ‘tell’ and closes with a two-word verb form built on the transitive verb ak-:
(17) Ja-n e-a yoi-katit-ai: “Moa-tian e-n oin-a jawéki-bo | mi-a onan-ma-non, mi-a yoi-non, ja-ribi mi-n bake-bo | a-taanan mi-n axe-a-non”, a-kin e-a a-káti-ai. | ‘He told me: “I will teach you the things I saw long time ago, I will tell them to you, so that when you have your children you will pass these things on to them too,” he told me.’
The next example also shows a direct quote. This time it opens and closes with the intransitive verb ik-:
(18) Ja-ská-ke-tian-ronki ja washit-a-ma-bo ik-á iki: “¡Ka-non | ka-wé, Inka bi-non ka-wé, chibá-non ka-wé!,” ik-í. | ‘Then the woman who had not denied her the roasted peanuts said: “Let’s go, let’s bring the Inka back, let’s follow her!” they said.’

h: Direct Quotes (quoting exact words)
t:
In the two examples just above, the direct quote has no second-spot add-on. That is because the quoted words are commands, and commands usually don't take these add-ons. The direct quote in the next example is different. It is a question, so it is marked by the question marker -ki. Here the transitive verb ak- comes before and after the quote:
(19) Ja-tian nokon papa-n-bi-ribi ak-á iki: “Moa-ki mi-n | ak-á Kesten Yabi senen-'a-kin?,” ak-á iki. | ‘Then my father asked (her) too: “Did you finish already Kesten Yabi?,” he told (her)’

h: Indirect Speech (reporting what someone said)
t:
As we saw when discussing how speakers mark the way they know things, reported speech is marked with the “someone told me” add-ons -ronki or -ki, and it is introduced by a verb of saying. The next example shows -ki doing this job:
(20) Joxo nawa-baon ne-ke be-xon no-a yoi yoi-kan-ai
(None) no-a-ki mai ibo-ma iki, | no-n-ki jawe onan-yama-ke]..... | ‘But when the mestizos come here they tell us that we are not the owners of the land, that we don’t know anything....’

h: Second Degree Hearsay ("they say that they said")
t:
The next example shows second-hand-of-second-hand information: a report of something that was itself reported. It is a piece of a story where the Shipibo plan to trick the Sun. They want the white-lipped peccaries (wild pigs) that he keeps in the upper world. The main character is the shaman Ashi. He is supposed to visit the Sun and get him to come down to the earth, and meanwhile Ashi will set the peccaries free. The piece contains a direct quote, closed by the stand-in verb ak-. Inside that direct quote there is a piece of reported speech. It is introduced by verbs of saying and contains the “someone told me” marker -ronki:
(21) “Ja noko-xon-ra e-n yo-i ka-[a]i ne-ská-a-kin: | “Papá, mi-a-ra bake wetsa-baon kena-ma-ke, | [mi-n-ronki xea-i ka-ti iki]”” a-kin ak-á. | ‘“Once I find him I will tell (him) the following: “Father, my brothers sent (me) to call you, they say that you have to go (down to the earth) to drink,”” he said’.

h: Conversation Sustainers (words that keep a conversation going)
t:
A listener can keep a conversation going by echoing what the speaker just said. Listeners echo exclamations, and also the verb forms with ‘same/different doer’ markers that end what was just said.
The following piece of a conversation comes from Illius (1999:113, glosses are mine):
(22) Yoi-yantan-ke-betin, amen-ronki a-tiki rete-kin], | ‘And the others say certainly that one has to kill the capybara. | rete-kin. | kill (them) | no-n-ronki rete-tiki. | that we have to kill them. | Mjm. | Rete-xon-ronki no-n a-tiki. Jawen poko | ja-ke-betin jawen beshe poko. | We have to kill them. There is as you know (as remedy against them) the intestines, the small intestines. | Mjm. | Ja-ronki a-tiki, no-n-ki xate-pake-kin— | This is what we have to do, cut the small intestine (of a dead capybara) into pieces | xate-pake-kin. | cut it into pieces’.
ISSUES IN TRANSITIVITY:
TRANSITIVITY:

h: The Notion of Transitivity (what "transitivity" means)
t: Transitivity is about whether, and how much, an action passes from a doer to a receiver. There are several ways to look at it. You can look at meaning, or at grammar (the word forms and word order). You can look at a whole sentence, or at the verb by itself; these two views go together (linguists call them “clause-level” and “inherent” verb-level transitivity). And you can treat it as a yes-or-no matter, or as a matter of more or less.

h: 15.1.1.1. Semantic Transitivity
t:
When we look at what verbs mean, we need to remember one thing. The roles people play in an event, like doer or receiver, describe how our mind pictures the event, not hard facts (DeLancey 1991:346). The way we picture an event in our head is not the same as reality, and does not match it exactly. These
roles are given out according to simple, fixed patterns of events, not according to the big, loose scenes that the verb's meaning brings to mind (1991:343). For example, the verb ‘buy’ involves four people or things: the seller, the buyer, the goods, and the money. Yet languages build sentences about buying with only two or three of them.
Givón (1995:76) describes a typical transitive event by its meaning, with three key features in the sentence (see also Hopper and Thompson's (1980) list of transitivity features in 15.1.2):
• The doer (Agent): “a volitional, controlling, actively-initiating agent who is responsible for the event, thus its salient cause.” In plain words, someone who acts on purpose, is in control, starts the action, and so is clearly its cause.
• The receiver (Patient): “a non-volitional, inactive, non-controlling patient who registers the event’s changes-of-state, thus its salient effect.” In plain words, someone or something that doesn't choose, doesn't act, isn't in control, and simply undergoes the change, so it clearly shows the effect.

h: 15.1.1.1. Semantic Transitivity
t:
• The kind of action (Verbal modality): a “perfective (non-durative), sequential (non-perfect) and realis (non-hypothetical) [event]. The prototype transitive event is thus fast-paced, completed, real, and perceptually-cognitively salient.” In plain words, the action is quick, finished, really happens, and is easy to notice.
In terms of meaning, an intransitive verb has only one main participant. That participant may be the one acting, the one changing, or the one simply being in a state. A transitive verb has two or more main participants, usually a doer and a receiver. The most typical transitive verb has a doer who starts the action, wants it, controls it and stands out. And it causes a physical, obvious, concrete,
visible change in the receiver; the receiver may be made, handled, or changed along the way (Givón 1984:96, Davidse 1996:98).

h: 15.1.1.2. Morpho-Syntactic Transitivity
t:
Transitivity in grammar is about how the roles in an event (doer, receiver) are matched to the slots in the sentence (doer slot, receiver slot). Transitivity has a big effect on how the main participants of a sentence, usually the doer and the receiver, are marked. It especially affects how this marking lines up with the slots of the sentence (linguists call these slots grammatical relations).
In grammar, verbs can be sorted by how many main participants they need. An intransitive verb needs just one, and it usually fills the subject slot (who the sentence is about). A transitive verb needs two or more, usually filling the subject slot and the object slot (the receiver).
Many languages show transitivity openly in their word forms. For example, languages with a doer marker (ergative languages) mark the doer of a transitive verb differently from the single person of an intransitive verb. Yup'ik, an Inuit language of Central Alaska, goes further. Besides the doer marker, it uses special endings on the verb that tell you whether the verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. The sentences below (taken from T. Payne 1997 and p.c. 1997) show this: intransitive verbs take the ending -u, while transitive verbs take the ending -a:
(1) Doris-aq aya-llru-u-q. | ‘Doris traveled.’ (T. Payne 1997:135)
(2) Tom-aq quyi-llru-u-q. | ‘Tom coughed.’ (T. Payne p.c. 1997)

h: 15.1.1.2. Morpho-Syntactic Transitivity
t:
(3) Nerre-llru-a-nga. | ‘I ate it.’ (T. Payne p.c. 1997)
The next examples show what happens when a verb loses its receiver. The verb nerre- ‘eat’ is by nature a transitive verb. But when the receiver is dropped or pushed into the background, the verb must take the intransitive ending -u (linguists call this antipassive). Compare ‘Yero ate the meat’ in (4) with ‘Yero ate (meat)’ in (5):
(4) Yero-m keme-q nerre-llru-a-0. | ‘Yero ate the meat.’ (T. Payne 1997:219)
(5) Yero-q (kemer-meng) nerre-llru-u-q. | ‘Yerro ate (meat).’ (T. Payne 1997:219)
In Panare (a Carib language of Venezuela), intransitive verbs use different endings for time and for finished/ongoing action, and different beginning pieces for person, than transitive verbs do (T. Payne 1990:431). For example, Panare has two different forms of the ‘ongoing’ ending. -nëpëj goes on intransitive verbs, and -mpëj goes on transitive verbs¹ (examples taken from Payne, Payne and Gildea 1992:176, 183):
The glosses for the Panare examples include the following: NEU neutral, DETRANS detransitivizer (takes away the receiver), IMPERF:I imperfective intransitive (ongoing, intransitive verb), NONSPEC:I non-specific intransitive, TRNS transitive (transitive), IMPERF:T imperfective transitive (ongoing, transitive verb), 1SG first person singular, OI object initial sentence (the receiver comes first).
(6) A-s-awantë-nëpëj ejkikë. | ‘Maybe he is sick.’
(7) Asoonwa wëënë y-uchi-n a-t-a'ma-nëpëj. | ‘For three months he will prepare (to get good aim with the blowgun).’

h: 15.1.1.2. Morpho-Syntactic Transitivity
t:
(8) A-y-itya-mpëj chu. | ‘I am listening to you.’
(9) Paamë y-akóika-mpëj e'ñapa. | ‘Someone is buying up all the salt.’
In Panare, the difference shows up in the endings for ongoing action. In Dulong / Rawang (a Tibeto-Burman language), it shows up in the past-tense endings instead (LaPolla 2000:293; see also Kittilä 2002:68). A rarer case is Wangkankurru (a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia). There, the command endings change depending on whether the verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb (Kittilä 2002:69):
(10) thadna-ru | ‘Leave it alone’ (Kittilä 2002:69, from Hercus 1994:180)
(11) kathi-ra | ‘Turn back’ (Kittilä 2002:69, from Hercus 1994:180)

h: Clause Level and Inherent Transitivity (at the sentence level vs. built into the verb)
t: In a very influential article, Hopper and Thompson (1980) question the traditional idea of transitivity. That old idea only asks whether the sentence has a receiver (a direct object), so that an action is “carried-over” or “transferred” from a doer to a receiver. For these authors, transitivity belongs to the whole sentence and has many parts. They list ten features that let you rank sentences from less to more transitive. Each feature “...involves a different facet of the effectiveness or intensity with which the action is transferred from one participant to another” (1980:242). In plain words, each one measures how strongly the action passes from one person to another. A sentence scores higher when it has: two or more participants (rather than one); an action (rather than a state); an action with a clear end point (rather than none); a quick, one-moment action (rather than a drawn-out one); a doer acting on purpose (rather than by accident); a positive sentence (rather than a negative one); a real event (rather than an imagined or possible one); a powerful doer (rather than a weak one); a clearly singled-out receiver (rather than a vague one); and a receiver that is completely affected (rather than partly or not at all). Kibrik (1996:279) suggests adding one more feature to Hopper and Thompson's list: how clearly singled-out, or definite, the doer is. Kibrik points out that many languages (such as Ute, Navajo, and Lithuanian) are known to pay attention to who the doer is. In these languages, a vague, unspecified doer (“actor”, Kibrik's word for the most doer-like role) makes the sentence less transitive in its grammar.

h: Clause Level and Inherent Transitivity (at the sentence level vs. built into the verb)
t:
So what does the most typical transitive sentence look like? The action really happens. It happens at one moment, and it gets finished. There are at least two people or things involved. The doer (A) is a clear, specific individual. The doer starts the action, controls it, and does it on purpose. The receiver (O) is also a clear, specific individual, and the action really affects it. Hopper and Thompson's idea has a surprising result. A sentence with only one person in it can count as "more transitive" than a sentence with two people. That happens if the intransitive sentence has more of the features on the list. They also argue that the markers and word order a language uses tend to follow how strongly the whole sentence has this transitive character.
D. L. Payne (1985) studied verbs in Yagua, a Peba-Yaguan language of Peru. She adds a second idea. Some of this transitive character belongs to the bare verb itself, not to the whole sentence. She calls it "inherent transitivity" and sets it against the sentence-level kind. In Yagua, she says, bare verbs come in degrees. She sorts them using three tests. First, how many people does the verb need? Some verbs must have a receiver, some may have one, and some have only one person. Second, what is the receiver? It may be something changed by the action, or a tool used to do it. Third, can the verb take the endings that add or remove a person? The first two tests work for any language. The third one is special to Yagua. Payne shows that the sentence-level idea cannot explain these facts. They don't depend on the meaning or the shape of the sentence around the verb. It is the other way round. What kind of verb it is partly decides where it can be used. Payne concludes that the two ideas are similar and partly overlap. A theory of transitivity that works for all languages needs both of them (see also Lemmens 1998).

h: Encoding Degrees of Transitivity (showing "more" or "less" transitive)
t:
All the writers I have mentioned agree on one main point. Being a transitive verb or an intransitive verb is not a yes-or-no thing. It is a matter of degree. It depends on a mix of things: how the sentence is built, what it means, how it is used in conversation, and maybe more. So we should expect some verbs and sentences to be better examples of each kind than others. There are no sharp boxes. As I explained in section 1.8.4 on Prototype Theory (the idea of "best examples" and "weaker examples"), this way of thinking is the heart of how I sort things in this book.
Languages often show these differences with some visible sign, when the difference matters enough to them. Not every language cares about the same differences, though. What change in meaning or use causes a change in form differs a lot from language to language (Kittilä 2002:63, 65). The visible sign can be the number of people actually named in the sentence. It can be a change in the markers on the nouns. It can be a change in the endings on the verb that point to the doer or receiver, or some other change on the verb. Finnish is a good example. It shows how strongly the receiver is affected by putting a different marker on the receiver. Below is the normal Finnish pattern for a typical transitive sentence: the doer gets the plain form (nominative) and the receiver gets the receiver marker (accusative) (from Kittilä 2002):

h: Encoding Degrees of Transitivity (showing "more" or "less" transitive)
t:
(12) Mies tappo-i karhu-n. | ‘The man killed the bear.’ (Kittilä 2002:56)
(13) Mies näk-i karhu-n. | ‘The man saw the bear.’ (Kittilä 2002:61)
Sentence (12) is a strong transitive event: the man kills the bear, and the bear is badly affected. Sentence (13) is weaker: just seeing a bear doesn't change the bear. Still, Finnish uses the very same pattern in (13), with the same receiver marker. So we can say Finnish has stretched its normal transitive sentence to cover some less typical cases too. Now compare (12) and (13) with the Hunzib sentences below. Hunzib does not do this. In Hunzib, seeing is marked differently from a strong action like eating:
(14) sɨ-bur-la-l n-uq xo | ‘The bears eat meat.’ (Kittilä 2002:79, from Van den Berg 1995:42)
(15) ɑbu-u ãc'ə-r ože | ‘Father saw the boy.’ (Kittilä 2002:79, from Van den Berg 1995:42)
Back to Finnish. In the next two sentences, the difference is how much the receiver is affected. In (16) the receiver marker (accusative) shows the action was finished: the milk is all gone.
(16) Mies jo-i maido-n. | ‘The man drank the milk (up).’ (Kittilä 2002:62)
(17) Mies jo-i maito-a. | ‘The man drank (some) milk.’ (Kittilä 2002:63)
In (18)-(20), the verbs need two people by their meaning: someone who hates and something hated, and so on. But these are not strong transitive events. You can see this in how the receiver is marked. It gets a "some of it" marker (partitive) or an "into" marker (illative). The real receiver marker (accusative) can't be used here, because Finnish keeps it for strong transitive events:

h: Encoding Degrees of Transitivity (showing "more" or "less" transitive)
t:
(18) Mies viha-si maito-a. | ‘The man hated milk.’ (Kittilä 2002:63)
(19) Mies ajattel-i lapsi-a-an | ‘The man thought about his children.’ (Kittilä 2002:114)
(20) Mies rakastu-i naise-en. | ‘The man fell in love with the woman.’ (Kittilä 2002:57)
Last, look at these Turkish sentences. Here the receiver marker (accusative) shows that the receiver is a specific, known thing: the ox, not just an ox.
(21) Hasan öküz-ü aldı | ‘Hasan bought the ox.’ (Comrie 1989:132)
(22) Hasan bir öküz aldı | ‘Hasan bought an ox (non-specific).’ (Comrie 1989:132)
Now for SK (Shipibo-Konibo). Like Finnish, SK uses its normal transitive sentence for seeing, hearing, and the like. SK also uses that pattern for something like (19), 'think about'. But for the ideas in (18) and (20), SK would need two different kinds of "stretched intransitive" sentences. In these the doer gets the plain form, and the second person or thing is marked in another way: <absolutive -ki> and <absolutive
interessive>, one for each. In Finnish, (16) and (17) show a difference in how much the receiver is affected. SK has nothing like that. But SK has a different trick. In "want to" sentences with two people, the doer can either take the doer marker or not. This shows whether the receiver is a specific, known thing or not (see (24a-c)).

h: Transitivity in Shipibo-Konibo
t:
In Valenzuela (1997) I described transitivity in SK as a bundle of features that go together. Some verbs are the best examples of intransitive verbs or transitive verbs. Others are weaker examples. So we can't always expect a sharp line between the two groups.
The idea that the verb itself carries this character explains most of what happens in SK. Most bare verbs are fixed as either intransitive verbs or transitive verbs. Certain features are always true, or never true, whenever that verb is used. On the other hand, quite a few transitive verbs can be used in intransitive sentences, and the other way round. You just add the right ending. For example, noko- means ‘meet, find,’ but nokot- (noko- plus the "middle" ending) means ‘arrive.’ Besides the verb itself and these regular endings, we also need the wider sentence-level idea (cf. Hopper and Thompson 1980; as well as Lazard 1998). It explains some weaker examples. It also explains a small number of patterns where other things matter: whether the receiver is a specific thing, whether the doer is in control, and how the verb was built in the past (Valenzuela 1997). For example, as I said in section 8.2.8, the addition of
the "want to" ending -kas to a transitive verb usually changes how the doer is marked. The doer loses the doer marker (ergative) and appears in the plain form (absolutive):

h: Transitivity in Shipibo-Konibo
t:
(23) a. E-n-ra wame rete-ai. | ‘I kill paiche (k. fish, Arapaima gigas).’ | b. E-a-ra wame rete-kas-ai. | ‘I want to kill paiche.’
Why does the doer lose its marker in (23b)? Because a "want to" sentence is less of a transitive sentence. Nothing has actually happened yet. There is no real action. The doer is not really acting, and the fish is not affected. But there is a twist. A "want to" sentence can still have the doer marker. That signals that the receiver is one specific, known thing. Look at these examples:
(24) a. E-a-ra wame pi-kas-ai. | ‘I want to eat paiche (referential or non-referential).’ | b. E-n-ra wame pi-kas-ai. | ‘I want to eat the paiche (referential only).’
You would most likely say (24b) when you can see the fish right in front of you. Now imagine a Shipibo speaker in Lima, the capital city. There is no paiche there. So that speaker could say the next sentence, and the doer must be in the plain form (absolutive):
(24c) c. E-a-ra wame pi-kas-kiran-ke. / E-n-ra | ‘I would like to eat paiche when I come (to the Ucayali).’
This switch in marking can also be used to contrast things. The doer marker in a "want to" sentence sounds even better when you are choosing between two or more things. Then the point is to pick out one receiver from the others around it. (Notice also that in the second part of the sentence, the doer is in the plain form.)

h: Transitivity in Shipibo-Konibo
t:
(25) E-n-ra wame pi-kas-ai, wetsa piti-bo-ra | e-a a-kásham-ai. | ‘I want to eat paiche, other kind of food / fish I don’t want.’
In (24b) and (25) the doer gets the doer marker and the receiver stays plain (the <ergative absolutive> pattern). The other choice would be both plain (<absolutive absolutive>). This seems to support what Hopper and Thompson (1980) said. A sentence with a clear, specific receiver counts as more transitive, and the grammar shows it. Speakers did not accept the switch seen in (24a-b) with other transitive verbs. But I did find sentences like (25) with xea-kas- ‘want to drink’ and bi-kas- ‘want to get’ (Valenzuela 1997).
Here is another case that the "built into the verb" idea can't explain. It is about kinan- ‘vomit,’ and whether the person is in control of it or not. This verb acts like a typical transitive verb in terms of the
grammar tests I describe in 15.2.1. But kinan- has one odd feature. Verbs like this, whose receiver repeats the verb's own idea ("vomit vomit", like English "sing a song"), often have it. You can't give kinan- a plain receiver with nothing added to it. The only exception is when the vomiting was caused on purpose, so it was under control. I think we need to understand this odd feature through Amazonian cultures. There, people drink special drinks that make them vomit, in order to gain valued qualities or skills:

h: Transitivity in Shipibo-Konibo
t:
(26) a. E-n-ra kinan-ke aros. | ‘I vomited (the) rice.’ | b. E-n-ra kinan-ke aros-bires.. | ‘I vomited pure rice.’
(27) a. E-n-ra kinan-ke yapa. | ‘I vomited (the) fish.’ | b. E-n-ra kinan-ke yapa-bires. | ‘I vomited pure fish.’
Now look at these examples. Here kinan- ‘vomit’ means vomiting on purpose, under control, and a plain receiver is allowed:
(28) E-n-ra kinan-ke manxaman kawáti. | ‘I vomited the manxaman kawáti (lit. ‘heron’s bridge;’ i.e., a beverage drunk to become good fisher / hunter).’
(29) Bake-n-ra kinan-ke atsa-n tita. | ‘The child vomited the atsan tita (lit. ‘yuca’s mother;’ i.e., a beverage given to children in order to make them become fatter).’
There are other cases where the markers are unexpected. Some of these are better explained another way. Sometimes two different verbs look exactly alike, and the marking keeps them apart. Sometimes the answer lies in how the verb was built in the past (see 15.2.3).
There is one more advantage to thinking in terms of "best examples" and "weaker examples". It explains why some verbs belong to two groups at once. One such verb is keen- ‘want.’ It can be used in three ways. It can take a noun as the thing wanted, and then the people in the sentence can be marked in two ways (<absolutive absolutive> / <absolutive interessive>). It can take a whole sentence, when you want to do something yourself ("I want to go"). And it can take a whole sentence about someone else, when you want another person to do something ("I want you to go").

h: Properties of Transitive Verbs (what all transitive verbs have in common)
t:
What does a typical transitive verb mean? There is a doer who starts the action, wants to do it and controls it. The doer causes a real, visible change in the receiver. In the typical case, the doer is the subject and the receiver is the object of the sentence. In SK, this means the doer gets the doer marker and the receiver stays plain (<ergative absolutive>). As I said earlier, this pattern has also been stretched to other verbs: verbs of saying, seeing and hearing, thinking, and remembering. This happens even though
the subject of these verbs just experiences something instead of acting, and the object just causes the experience instead of being changed by it.
In SK, a typical transitive verb has all of the following features. It can have a receiver. Its doer must get the doer marker (ergative), and its receiver must be in the plain form (absolutive). Some extra words in the sentence have endings that match the doer: words for "where" or "where to" and words for "how" get a visible matching ending, while words for "from where" and the emphatic pronouns get none. The verb can take the "against someone" ending (the malefactive). It can take the "middle" ending -t to mean "to yourself". It needs the special transitive forms of the "going" and "coming" endings, which also serve as plural forms. It goes with the transitive forms of the verbs for "begin", "finish" and "stop". It can be used with the transitive helper verb ak-, and it can be replaced by a stand-in verb of the same form. It can take the "here and there" ending -pake. Finally, when such a verb takes a whole sentence as its receiver, that sentence ends in -ti, -ai, or -a.

h: Properties of Transitive Verbs (what all transitive verbs have in common)
t:
Some of these features matter more than others for deciding if a verb is a transitive verb. In Valenzuela (1997) I found that two tests are the strongest. Can the verb take a receiver? Can it take the "to yourself" ending?
Some transitive verbs take two receivers, like English "give" ("give her a book"). Linguists call these ditransitive verbs. In SK, the two receivers don't seem to be marked differently in any regular way (but cf. 8.4.2.3 and footnote 11 of Ch. 17).

h: Properties of Intransitive Verbs (what all intransitive verbs have in common)
t:
An intransitive verb has only one person or thing in the sentence, and it is always in the plain form (absolutive). That person can be the one acting. It can also be someone in a state, or someone going through a change. As I showed in 8.2.1, SK has many kinds of intransitive verbs. There is the verb "be", and the verbs for "there is" and "there isn't". There are some verbs of moving and position, and verbs about weather and nature. There are verbs meaning "become something", made from nouns or describing words with nothing added. And there are movement verbs made the same way from place words. Verbs of moving in a set direction can take a place or a whole sentence after them. Small groups of these verbs have different bare verbs for one person and for more than one. They can also take a place as a kind of receiver.
A typical intransitive verb has the following features. Its one person must be in the plain form (absolutive). Some extra words in the sentence get a visible ending that matches that person: words for "from where", for stage of life, for "how many" and "how", and the emphatic pronouns. Words for "where" and "where to" get no matching ending. It cannot take the "middle" ending meaning "to yourself", nor the endings for "to each other", "against someone", or "here and there". With one person, it needs the intransitive, singular forms of the "going" and "coming" endings. It goes with the intransitive forms of the verbs for "begin", "finish" and "stop". It goes with the intransitive helper verb ik-, and it can be replaced by a stand-in verb of the same form. It can take the ending -paket ‘going down (the river).’ When such a verb takes a whole sentence after it, that sentence ends in -i.

h: Non-Prototypical Intransitive and Transitive Verbs (verbs that don't fit neatly)
t:
Some verbs are not typical intransitive verbs or typical transitive verbs. They come in several groups, and some have more transitive features than others. Here are the groups. First, verbs whose receiver repeats the verb's own idea, like English "sing a song" (and these don't all behave the same). Second, keen- ‘want’ and shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind.’ These allow two patterns of marking: both people plain (<absolutive absolutive>), or the second one with a different marker (<absolutive interessive>). Third, verbs that usually have only one person named, but that person gets the doer marker (ergative). Fourth, feeling verbs: the one who feels is in the plain form, and the cause of the feeling takes the "to" marker -ki. These verbs differ in their marking pattern and in which matching endings go with it. They also differ in whether they can take the "to yourself" ending, the "to each other" ending, the "against someone" ending, and other verb endings. Table 15.1 sums up how each type of verb behaves on these tests.
I must point out one more thing. Even verbs that seem to belong to the same group can behave differently on these tests. Take rabin- ‘be ashamed of’ and raké- ‘be afraid of.’ Or take keen- ‘want / love’ and shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind.’ In each pair, the two verbs don't follow the same pattern. Only rabin- and keen- can take the "to each other" ending.

h: Non-Prototypical Intransitive and Transitive Verbs (verbs that don't fit neatly)
t:
The verbs wina- ‘row’ and jono- ‘pole (a raft or canoe)’ seem to belong to the same small group. They mean similar things. With both, the doer gets the doer marker (ergative), and there is no second person or thing in normal everyday
speech. Still, wina- has more transitive features than jono-. wina- can take the "middle" ending and the "to each other" ending, but jono- can't. Looking closer, we find another difference. wina- can have a person as its plain-form receiver (you can "row" someone, that is, take them by canoe). jono- can only have a raft, canoe or boat as its receiver.
The verbs join- ‘breathe’ and rebes- ‘die’ don't allow a receiver. Even so, the one who breathes or dies must get the doer marker (ergative). (Some speakers do allow nouns like niwe ‘wind’ and jakonma koin ‘harming smoke’ as a second thing with join; see ex. (117) in Ch. 17.) join- ‘breathe’ is really closer to a typical intransitive verb. Apart from the doer marker and the matching endings that go with it, it has none of the other transitive features. For example, it can't take the "against someone", "middle", or "to each other" endings. The next sentence shows join- with only one person named. That person, the one breathing, has the doer marker:
(30) Nato jene-n rete-a ainbaon-ra moa join-ai. | ‘This woman who almost drowned is breathing already.’ (Lit. ‘The woman whom the flowing water killed is breathing already.’) (Loriot, Lauriault and Day 1993:230, analyzed in Valenzuela 1997)

h: Non-Prototypical Intransitive and Transitive Verbs (verbs that don't fit neatly)
t:
The sentences below show that the one breathing with join- can't be in the plain form (absolutive) (from Valenzuela 1997):
(31) a. E-n-ra join-ai. | ‘I breathe.’
(31b) b. E-a-ra join-ai. | ‘I breathe.’
Sentence (31b) is wrong if you want to say ‘I breathe.’ But the very same string of sounds is a good sentence with a different meaning. It is just built from different pieces:
(32) E-a-ra joi-n-ai. | ‘S/he is criticizing me.’
Why does join- need the doer marker? I have two possible answers. First, imagine the one breathing were in the plain form, as you'd expect for ‘breathe’. Then (31a) could be confused with (32). Using the doer marker could avoid that mix-up. Second, (32) hints that ‘breathe’ may be built from joi- ‘word’ plus the ending -n. This -n is a "make it a transitive verb" ending, linked to using something as a tool. If this second idea is right, the verb's history explains the doer marker (Valenzuela 1997).
Like join- above, the verb rebes- ‘die’ needs the doer marker on the one who dies. Yet it allows no receiver (from Valenzuela 1997):
(33) Moa-ra papa-n rebes-ke. | ‘My father died already.’
Here the likely reason for the surprising doer marker is different. The intransitive verb rebes- ‘die’ seems to come from the transitive verb rebes- ‘reach the end of.’ You can see that verb in this example (from Valenzuela 1997):

h: Non-Prototypical Intransitive and Transitive Verbs (verbs that don't fit neatly)
t:
(34) Moa-ra e-n paro rebes-ke. | ‘I reached the end of the river already.’
So ‘die’ was probably once ‘reach the end (of something)’ with the receiver left out. Over time, that use became fixed as a word of its own (linguists call a sentence that drops the receiver this way an antipassive) (Valenzuela 1997).

h: Other Verb Classes (other kinds of verbs)
t:
In Valenzuela (1997) I also grouped some verbs in ways that have nothing to do with how many people they take. Here are some of these groups. The helper verbs atipan- ‘can’ and ja- ‘have to’ have no people of their own. They borrow them from the main verb that goes with them. Sound-imitating verbs (like English "buzz" or "splash") are very common in SK. They are usually made by adding a general verb to a sound word. Adding -ik ‘be, do (intransitive), say’ makes an intransitive verb. Adding -ak ‘make, do (transitive), tell’ makes a transitive verb. There is also a small, fixed set of "flexible" verbs. They can be used either with one person or with a doer and a receiver, with no ending added (English "break" works like this: "I broke the cup" / "the cup broke"). Also, some verbs can take beginning pieces that name a body part. A verb with such a piece usually stays the same kind of verb as before. Intransitive verbs with these pieces seem to be about moving, position, or a (change of) state. Transitive verbs with them seem to be about events
where something causes something or touches something. There is more. In SK, you can answer a yes/no question briefly with a stand-in verb, a bit like English "Did you go?" "I did." But a few verbs of moving in a set direction don't use the usual intransitive or transitive stand-in for this. Instead, they answer with an unfinished form of their own bare verb. The verbs for "there is" and "there isn't" also answer with their own bare verb. But unlike the moving verbs, they use the normal, finished verb forms. I covered the kinds of verbs in SK in Chapter 8. Endings that add or remove people are covered in detail in Chapters 16-18.

h: Transitivity Agreement (verb forms that change depending on whether the main verb is transitive or intransitive)
t:
In grammar, "agreement" means one word changes its form to match another. In Steele's words, it is “some systematic covariance between a semantic or formal property of one element and a formal property of another” (Steele 1978:610). English has a little of this: "she walks" but "they walk". SK has unusual kinds of matching. They are connected to whether the verb is an intransitive or a transitive verb, and they don't happen inside the noun phrase (the noun and the words that go with it). Earlier work treated them together (see e.g. Valenzuela 1999 and Loos 1999). Here I suggest we must separate two basic kinds, in SK and in Panoan languages in general. I call them "transitivity agreement" and "participant agreement". Transitivity agreement depends on what kind of verb the main verb is: intransitive or transitive (sometimes together with other things, like number). Participant agreement depends on the job of the person the word matches: doer, receiver, and so on. Also, transitivity agreement shows up on the verb and the words right around it. Participant agreement shows up on
the extra words in the sentence, the ones that say where, when or how. Each pattern with transitivity agreement (TA) gets its own chapter in this book. So in this section I just give a short overview of all of them together. Participant agreement is the main topic of Chapters 19 and 20.

h: Phasal Verbs ("start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
The verbs peo- ‘begin,’ keyo- ‘finish,’ and jene- ‘stop’ are transitive verbs by nature. They can be the main verb of a sentence. But peo-, keyo- and jene- can also team up with another verb, the one that says what is begun or finished. This is a kind of verb chain, where verbs line up one after another (Foley and Olson 1985; see also 7.14). When they team up, the "begin/finish/stop" verb must match the other verb's type. If the other verb is a transitive verb, the "begin" verb stays as it is. If the other verb is an intransitive verb, the "begin" verb takes the "middle" ending -t, which turns it into an intransitive verb too. Also, one of the two verbs takes a marker meaning "at the same time, by the same person". That marker is -i or -kin, depending on the type of the other verb. The other verb is the finished one, with the full verb endings. Look at -i and -koo in (35), and -kin in (36):^{2}
(35) E-a-ra ransa-i peo-koo-ke. | ‘I began to dance (e.g., at a party).’ | E-a-ra peo-koot-i ransa-ke. | ‘I began to dance (at the party / for the first time in my life).’
(36) E-n-ra bana-kin peo-ke.
A marker meaning "before, by the same person" may also be found.

h: Phasal Verbs ("start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
(None) ‘I began to sow (it).’ | b. E-n-ra peo-kin bana-ke. | ‘I began to sow (it).’
The two sentences below come from stories. They show the transitive verb peo- ‘start, begin’ teamed up with another transitive verb. In the first sentence, peo- has the full verb endings and is the main verb. The other verb, xobo a(k)- ‘build a house’, takes the matching "same time, same person" marker -kin:
(37) Wetsa nete winó-ke-tian, xobo a-kin peo-kan-a iki. | ‘On the next day, they started building the house.’
The next sentence is especially interesting. The verb Ani Xeati-a(k)- means ‘to organize, celebrate the Ani Xeati ceremony.’ It hangs on peo- ‘start’. Together they form one verb group. That whole group then hangs on the transitive stand-in verb akana iki, which has the full verb endings. What decides that the whole group is transitive? The verb Ani Xeati-a(k)-:
(38) Ja-ska-rain-xon-ronki a-kan-a iki no-n reken-baon | [[Ani Xeati-a-kin] peo-kin]. | ‘And it was in this way that our ancestors started celebrating the Ani Xeati ceremony.’
In the next example, the verb group is an intransitive group. What makes it so is the intransitive verb tsinkit- ‘to gather (intr.),’ as in "people gather". This verb is made from the transitive verb tsinki- ‘to gather (tr.),’ as in "gather things", by adding the ending that removes the receiver. Because of this, the intransitive general verb ik- is chosen as the stand-in verb. And peo- ‘begin’ must also take the ending that makes it an intransitive verb:

h: Phasal Verbs ("start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
(39) Ja-ska-ra i-t-i-bi-ronki ik-á iki, joni-bo | [[Komankaya mai-n tsinki-t-i] peo-koot-i]. | ‘Then, people began to gather in Komankaya forming a village.’
Examples (40) and (41) below show the transitive keyo- ‘finish’ and its intransitive form keyó- ~ keyo-t-. In (40) it goes with a transitive verb, ‘kill’. In (41) it goes with an intransitive verb, ‘go down (water)’:
(40) Ja-ská-a-xon-ki ja joni icha piti-a bané-ni-ke; | jatíbi roo rete-kin keyo-ax. | ‘And so the man got a lot of food, having killed all the howler monkeys.’
(41) Jato meni-a bi-xon, ian napon ne-níchin-kan-a, | jene tsosin-i keyo-t-a iki. | ‘Taking (the spear) they were given, they inserted it in the middle of the lake and the water lowered completely.’
We find the same kind of matching in Dulong / Rawang. This is a Tibeto-Burman language spoken on both sides of the border between China and Myanmar. It has some helper verbs that are transitive verbs by nature. When they go with an intransitive main verb, they must take a "to yourself / middle" ending that makes them intransitive verbs too. These helper verbs mean ‘continue,’ ‘begin to,’ ‘be finished,’ ‘be about to,’ and ‘be willing to.’ Look at the next pair. The helper mv̄n ‘continue’ gets the ending -shì only when the main verb is an intransitive verb (‘sleep’ in (b), not ‘carry’ in (a)):

h: Phasal Verbs ("start", "keep on", "finish")
t:
(42) à:ngí shǿng rímā:nòē | ‘He is continuing to carry the wood.’ (LaPolla 2000:293) | àng yøpmv̄nshìē | ‘He is continuing to sleep.’ (LaPolla 2000:294)
You can also see two other things in these examples. In Dulong / Rawang, the doer of a transitive verb may take a doer marker, -i, while the single person of an intransitive verb can't. Also, transitive verbs need a marker for a third-person receiver in the present (ò), placed before the ending for ordinary present statements (ē) (LaPolla, ibid.:283-284).
So in these patterns, verbs that mean "begin", "continue", "be able" and the like change to match the main verb's type. This suggests the two verbs are closely bound together. They must share the same set of people: the same doer, and the same receiver if there is one.

h: ‘Going Down’ and Distributive Suffixes ("going down" and "each" endings)
t:
The transitive verb pake- ‘drop, throw’ and the intransitive verb made from it, pake-t- ~ paké ‘fall’, are slowly turning into verb endings. The first one goes only on transitive verbs. The second goes only on intransitive verbs. This need to match types reminds us of the "begin / finish / stop" verbs above. So these endings probably also started out as verbs lined up in a chain.
The following examples show pake- ‘drop’ and pake-t- ‘fall’ used as ordinary, separate verbs:
(43) Abioni-n-ra kirika pake-ke. | ‘The small airplane dropped a letter.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:314)
(44) Yaká yaká-kin oin-a-ronki ik-á iki | westíora bimi ani jiwimea-x pake-t-i | jene-nko-shaman. | ‘Just when he was sitting there he saw that a fruit fell from a big tree into the water.’
The last example also has the intransitive verb yaka- ‘sitting position’. Its transitive partner is yasa-.
The next sentence shows the "one by one" ending -pake. It goes only on transitive verbs:
(45) Ja-skat-ai-tian-ronki ak-á iki, ja joni-n-ki | jiwi bi-xon ma-rishki-pake-kin keyo-kin. | ‘Then the man grabbed a pole and killed all the monkeys hitting them on the head one by one.’
As I said above, -pake can't go on intransitive verbs. But SK has at least two other ways to say "one by one" (see 4.6). In example (46), the number westíora ‘one’ is said twice, giving the meaning ‘one by one’. (Notice also that the "finish" verb matches the intransitive verb maan- ‘come down’.)

h: ‘Going Down’ and Distributive Suffixes ("going down" and "each" endings)
t:
(46) Westíora westíora-bo, maan-i keyó-kan-a iki. | ‘One by one, they finished coming down.’
The example below has the ending pake-t- (or V2) ‘going down (the river)’ twice. It goes only on intransitive verbs:
(47) Tii i-paket-i jato yoi yoi-paket-i. | ‘Playing the horns, they went down the river inviting the people (to the Ani Xeati ceremony).’
The intransitive verb inat- ‘go up’ can also be used as a verb ending. But unlike pake-t-, -inat can go on both intransitive verbs and transitive verbs.

h: ‘Come’ and ‘Go’ ("come" and "go")
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has two pairs of verbs for ‘come’ and ‘go.’ Which one you use depends on how many people are moving. It also depends on whether someone is bringing or carrying something along:
jo- ‘come (sing.)’ ka- ‘go (sing.)’ be- ‘come (non-sing.), bring’ bo- ‘go (non-sing.), carry’
These are the only verbs in the language with two completely different words for one mover and for many movers. English does something a little like this with go and went: two unrelated words for the same verb. You use jo- and ka- when one person or thing comes or goes. You use be- and bo- when many come or go. You also use them for things that come as a mass, like ‘rain,’ ‘flooding,’ ‘clouds,’ ‘school of fish,’ ‘wind,’ and ‘waves.’ The next two examples show be- and bo- used for more than one mover:
(48) a. Koshi mee-anan-kan-ax bo-kan-ai [atsa xeati xea-[a]i]. | ‘After trying their strength against each other, they went to drink yuca beer.’ | b. Jain-xon-ribi iná tsaka-kan-ai, ja Ani Xeati-nin | be-a joni-baon. | ‘Afterwards, those people who had come to the Ani Xeati ceremony shot arrows at the animal.’
Now look at be- ‘bring’ and bo- ‘carry, take,’ where someone moves something else. At first it looks like two separate pairs of words that just happen to sound the same. One pair is ‘come (many)’ and ‘bring.’ The other is ‘go (many)’ and ‘carry’:

h: ‘Come’ and ‘Go’ ("come" and "go")
t:
(49) No-n-ra joni be-ke no-n jema-nko. | ‘We brought the man to our village.’
(50) No-n-ra joni bo-ke jawen jema-nko. | ‘We carried / took the man to his village.’
But I think there is more going on. The choice between jo- / be- and ka- / bo- is not only about how many people move. It is also about whether someone is moving something else, or making it move. In this view, be- ‘come (n.sg.) / bring’ and bo- ‘go (n.sg.) / take, carry’ are one word each. They are the forms for many movers _and_ for moving something along. The plain one-mover forms are jo-‘come’ and ka- ‘go.’ So the forms split up like this:
So part of the meaning of be- would be ‘cause sth. / sb. to come, come with sth. / sb.,’ i.e. ‘bring;’ Part of the meaning of bo- would be ‘cause sth. / sb. to go, go with sth. / sb.,’ i.e. ‘carry, take.’ In other words, bringing is ‘making something come,’ and carrying is ‘making something go.’
Two facts support the idea that be- and bo- are also the ‘moving something’ partners of jo- and ka-. First, these four verbs belong to a small group of verbs that do not need an all-purpose verb to
stand in for them when you answer a yes/no question. (The other verbs in this group are ja- ‘there is,’ yama- ‘there isn’t,’ and bi- ‘get;’ see section 8.5.) With most Shipibo-Konibo verbs, you answer a yes/no question with an all-purpose verb. You use ik- if nobody is acted on, and ak- if someone does something to something. It is a bit like English Did you eat it? Yes, I did, where did stands in for ate. But these four verbs repeat their own form in the answer instead. And they follow the same split as in Table 15.2 (see also 8.5). You can see this below. (For the usual pattern, see exx. (55) and (56).)

h: ‘Come’ and ‘Go’ ("come" and "go")
t:
(None) -Tita-n-ki bo-ai? | -‘Is mother carrying (it)?’
(None) -bo-kin / bo-ama | -‘yes / no’
Look at the ‘yes’ answers. When be- means ‘come (n.sg.)’ and bo- means ‘go (n.sg.),’ the answer takes the ending -i. That is the ‘same person does the next action’ ending used with intransitive verbs. When be- means ‘bring’ and bo- means ‘carry,’ the answer takes -kin instead. That is the same ending’s form for transitive verbs. So the language treats ‘bring’ and ‘carry’ as transitive verbs.
The second fact comes from some verb endings: -kiran / -beiran ‘coming’ and -kain / -bain ‘going.’ They mean coming or going toward or away from a place mentioned in the story (7.6.1-7.6.2). These endings probably grew out of the verbs jo- / be- and ka- / bo, over time. They mean roughly the same as those verbs, and they also look like them. (The one exception is -kiran; from the verb you would rather expect j(e)iran.) But here is the strongest part of the argument. Which ending gets used looks strange at first. It makes perfect sense, though, once we accept one idea. The main verbs be- and bo- are the forms for many movers, and also the forms for moving something along. In other words, be- ‘come (non-singular)’ and be- ‘bring’ are really the same word. The same goes for bo- ‘come (non-singular)’ and bo- ‘carry.’ The endings split up like this:

h: ‘Come’ and ‘Go’ ("come" and "go")
t:
These endings add extra meaning to the verb they are attached to. But often they still do what they probably did in the past: they show that one event comes after another. How these endings, and the matching verbs, change with the number of movers and the kind of verb is covered in 7.6.1 and 7.6.2. Here are a few more examples. First, the ‘coming’ endings. In the example below, -kiran is used because one person does the last action. Also, the verb it attaches to, xoo i-, is a sound-word verb with no receiver:
(51) Ja-ská-tian jo-ai oin-a-ronki ik-ai, ja-skat-i | kapé-isi xooo i-res-kiran-i. | ‘When (they) saw what was coming, it was a huge alligator approaching producing a noise xooo in the water.’
In the next example, one person also does the action of rewe a- ‘play the flute.’ But this verb has a doer and a receiver, so the ‘coming’ ending -beiran is needed:
(52) Ja-ská-xon ja koko-kan-ai-tian-ronki ik-ai | o-no-a-x-ki rewe a-beiran-i, jo-a oin-a-ki
() awá-isi | ‘While they were eating fruit, a tapir appeared and came playing the flute.’
Now look at the ‘going’ endings. In the example below, one bird does the flying, and noya- ‘fly’ is an intransitive verb. So the form -kain is used:
(53) Paké-ke-tian-ki ik-á iki yapa-bo | tsamá-boan-i. Ja basi-ma-bi-ronki | ik-á iki pichá noya-kain-i. | ‘When (the fruit) fell (into the water) all the fish gathered around it. A little bit later a palometa (fish) flew away.’

h: ‘Come’ and ‘Go’ ("come" and "go")
t:
The next example comes from a story where the Jaguar threatens to eat the Deer if he does not bring meat. Only one person is involved here. Even so, the ending -bain is used, not -kain. That is because it attaches to (masá-)shinan- ‘be sad:’, which works as a transitive verb:
(54) Ja-tian Chaxo masá-shinan shinan-bain-i ka-a iki, | piti bena-i. | ‘So the Deer went to look for meat, feeling very sad and scared.’
So I conclude that be- and bo- are the forms of jo- and ka- used for many movers and for ‘making something come or go.’ This makes sense if you think about it. When you bring or carry someone or something, you come or go together with it.

h: Semantically Generic Verbs (general verbs like "do" and "be")
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has two all-purpose verbs with very general meanings. One is ik- ‘do (intr.), be, say,’ used when nobody is acted on. The other is ak- ‘do (tr.), make, tell,’ used when someone does something to something.^3 These two can stand in for most other verbs, like English do in Did you see it? Yes, I did. You can see this, for example, in short answers to yes/no questions (from Valenzuela 1997; see also 8.5):
(55) a. -Mi-n chai-ki moa neno noko-t-a? | -‘Did your brother-in-law arrive here already?’ | b. -Ik-í / Ik-ama | -‘Yes / No’
(56) a. -Mi-n papa-n-ki wiso ino rete-a? | -‘Did your father kill the black puma?’
Wistrand (1969:157) says that the related language Kashibo-Kakataibo has three all-purpose verbs that act as helper verbs or stand-ins. They are ʔi- ‘be’ (nobody acted on), ʔa- ‘do’ (someone acted on), and o- ‘make, do’ (two people acted on). Wistrand adds that o- is ‘one type of causative’ (a ‘make someone do it’ form). Interestingly, the Tukanoan languages, which are not related to ours, have a similar three-way split. For example, in Secoya: më-i ‘go up,’ më-a ‘raise,’ and më-o ‘cause to raise;’ dai ‘come,’ da ‘bring,’ dao ‘make bring’ (Johnson and Levinsohn 1990:59). In the languages of the Eastern branch of that family, these three pieces come at the start of the word (Gómez-Imbert, p.c.).

h: Semantically Generic Verbs (general verbs like "do" and "be")
t:
(b) -A-kin / Ak-ama | ‘-Yes / No’
The next two examples show how the general verbs share out the work. The main verbs rete- ‘kill’ and ishto- ‘run (away)’ appear in an unfinished form, with no time or number information. That information is carried instead by a general verb. ‘Kill’ is a transitive verb, so it takes a(k)-. ‘Run’ is an intransitive verb, so it takes i(k)-. Other words in the sentence have to match too. The linking word jain(oa) ‘then’ and the word jati(k) ‘altogether’ take a matching ending: -xon goes with a(k)-, and -(a)x goes with i(k)- (see 19.2.2.8 and 19.2.2.11). Finally, the main verb carries a marker that says “the same person does the next action.” This marker must also match the general verb: -kin goes with the transitive type, and -i goes with the intransitive type. Compare (57) and (58):
(57) Jain-xon-ronki a-kan-a iki jatí-xon-bi awá rete-kin. | ‘Then, it is said that altogether they killed the tapir.’
(58) Jainoa-x-ronki i-kan-a iki jatik-ax-bi ishto-i. | ‘Then, it is said that altogether they ran (away).’
Over time, the pairing of ik- or ak- with an unfinished main verb has turned into fixed two-word verb forms (7.12). Speakers may choose these forms for style, or to give a part of a story a special role. Some of them, such as the “narrative past” used in telling stories, have become a regular tense of the verb.

h: Semantically Generic Verbs (general verbs like "do" and "be")
t:
The general verbs can also join with words that are not verbs at all, to make a new verb meaning. The first word can be a noun, an adjective, a sound word, a short exclamation, or a word borrowed from Spanish (see also ex. (38)):
(59) mashá ik- | ‘perform the mashá (traditional singing, dancing) | Ani Xeati ak- | ‘organize, carry out the Ani Xeati (girls’ puberty rites) | bake ak- | ‘engender, have a child’ | ani ak- | ‘raise, enlarge’ | yoyo ik- | ‘say’^{4} | yoyo ak- | ‘tell’ | shee ik- | ‘fry (intr.)’ | shee ak- | ‘fry (tr.)’ | “ka-wé” ik- | ‘say good-bye, leave’ | “i-rá-ke” ak- | ‘thank sb.’ | sonso ak- | ‘be unfaithful to sb.’ | kirika ak- | ‘study, read’
The intransitive verb ik- is used less often this way. Part of the reason is that many non-verb words can already act as verbs on their own, meaning “become” that thing. For example, bake means ‘child,’ but also ‘become a child’ or ‘behave like a child,’ and ani means ‘big’ or ‘become big’
The transitive verb ak- can also join with a noun to mean “make” that thing (see ex. (37)):
(60) xobo ak- | ‘build (a) house’ | pia ak- | ‘make (an) arrow’ | nonti ak- | ‘make (a) canoe’ | mapó ak- | ‘make pottery’ | chitonti ak- | ‘manufacture chitonti (traditional skirt) ’

h: Semantically Generic Verbs (general verbs like "do" and "be")
t:
Finally, the general verbs i(k)- and a(k)- are often used to report what someone said, like English go in “and she goes, ‘Hi!’” They can replace a real verb of saying, or appear next to one. Examples (61) and (62) show the transitive kind used to report speech:
The verb yoi- ‘tell’ may itself have come from the sound word yo ‘speak’ joined with the intransitive verb i(k)-.
(61) E-n nokon tita yoká-katit-ai: “Titá, jawe kopí-ki | moa-tian Ani Xeati a-káti-kan-ai? E-a-ra onan-kas-ai | jawe-kaya-rin ja i-xon,” a-kin a-káti-ai. | ‘I asked my mother: “Mother, why was the Ani Xeati celebrated in the past? I want to know what is the meaning of the Ani Xeati.”’
(62) a. -“Xoxo bake-bóoo!” a-ronki-ai jato, | “jawe ak-í-ki mato i-t-ai?” | ‘“Illegitimate childreeen,” he called them, “What are you doing?” | b. -“Binpish koko-i-ra no-a i-t-ai” | a-ronki-a-kan-ai. | ‘“We are eating guayaba,” they answered (him).’
In the next two examples, the intransitive verb ik- is used to report speech:
(63) Ja-ská-ke-tian-ronki ja washit-a-ma-bo ik-á iki: | “Ka-non ka-wé, Inka bi-non ka-wé, chibá-non ka-wé!” ik-í. | ‘Then, the ones who had not denied (the Inca Woman the roasted peanut) said: “Come on, let’s go get the Inca Woman, let’s follow her”.’
(64) “Jeee” i-ronki-ai ja-skat-i “tita-shoko-n-ra awá
(None) piti-a-ke. Tso-n-bira awá meni-a” i-ronki-ai. | “‘Jee,” said one of the grandchildren, “grandmother has cooked tapir meat. Who might have given her the tapir meat?,” he said.

h: Semantically Generic Verbs (general verbs like "do" and "be")
t:
To sum up, the general verbs ak- ‘do (tr.), make’ and ik- ‘do (intr.), be’ have three jobs. They stand in for other verbs. They join with other words to make new verb meanings. And they report speech. Joined with non-verb words, they also turn those words into verbs. Which one you use depends on the type of verb involved: ak- goes with transitive verbs, and ik- goes with intransitive verbs. People often use ak- and ik- to report speech, so they are often translated as “say.” But I think this is a later use that grew out of their main job of standing in for other verbs.^5 Ik- also works as the verb “be,” as treated in 8.2.1.1.
Interestingly, Güldemann (forthcoming) describes something very similar in languages of Northeast Africa. There, a new verb meaning is built from two parts: a “content sign” plus a general verb. The content sign can be a sound word (or a similar one-word expression); a short quote, such as an exclamation or a command; a borrowed word; a word used elsewhere as a noun, adjective or adverb; or a word used elsewhere as a verb. Look at the examples below (from Güldemann, forthcoming, and the works he cites). The general verb is labeled AUX in the word-by-word line:
Güldemann (2001) argues in detail that the speech-reporting words in Northeast African languages come from general verbs. However, the picture in Northeast Africa might be different from the one I suggest here.

h: Semantically Generic Verbs (general verbs like "do" and "be")
t:
