(65) kowkàw-iyy- | ‘chatter’ | tàssa-iyy- | ‘become happy’ | katábō-da | ‘write’ | óo-da | ‘cry’ | bárē-da | ‘tear apart’ | ‘ellé-ydi | ‘move, travel rapidly’ | ‘eró-ydi | ‘obey, agree’
These African verb forms look very much like the Shipibo-Konibo ones in (59) and (60).
In Northeast African languages, the general verbs have a second job too. They can join with other verbs to put special weight on something: to make it stand out, put it in focus, or soften it. Over time, these special forms can turn into ordinary verb forms. This is like what ak- and ik- do in the Shipibo-Konibo two-word verb forms (see exx. (57)-(58) and section 7.12). Third, the general verbs in Northeast African languages can also report speech (labeled QV in the examples):
Shona (Benue-Congo)
(66) va-bereki vaka-ti v-ana chi-mbo-garai pano | ‘The parents said, “Children, just sit down here!”’
What is more, some Northeast African languages have one general verb for transitive verbs and another for intransitive verbs, just like Shipibo-Konibo. Examples are Afar (Cushitic), Tigre (Semitic) and Dongola (Nubian) (see Güldemann, op. cit.). The main difference seems to be this: in those languages the general verbs cannot stand in for any verb, while Shipibo-Konibo ik- and ak- can.

h: Malefactive Marking ("against someone" endings)
t:
There is one more place where Shipibo-Konibo makes words match the type of verb. It has to do with endings that show an action was done “for” or “against” someone. Shipibo-Konibo has two such endings. The first, -xon, can mean either “for someone's good” or “to someone's harm.” The second, -(V)naan ~ -(V)n, only means “to someone's harm.” To say “to someone's harm” with an intransitive verb, you can only use -xon. With a transitive verb, you must use the second ending (see 17.2 and 17.3). Look at the next two sentences. korá- ‘make noise (several people)’ is an intransitive verb, so it takes -xon (67). keyo- ‘finish off, wipe out’ is a transitive verb, so it takes -nan (68):
(67) Bake-baon-ra no-a korá-xon-ke. | ‘The children made noise to our detriment.’
(68) Moa-tian joxo joni-bo jo-xon no-a
(None) keyo-nan-kean-kan-a iki no-n yoina-bo. | ‘Long time ago the white people came and almost exterminated our animals to our detriment.’
You cannot put the “harm only” ending on an intransitive verb like the one in (67). But the opposite works. Example (68) could take -xon instead of -nan and still be a correct sentence. It would just mean something odd: ‘Long time ago the white people came and almost exterminated our animals to our benefit.’
CAUSATIVIZATION:

h: Introduction (introduction)
t:
This chapter is about ‘making someone do something’ (linguists call this causation). Some linguists describe the most typical kind of causing as a bundle of features of how people act on the world around them (‘properties characterizable only in terms of the interaction of human beings as part of their environment,’ Lakoff 1987:56). Other kinds of causing are then seen as departures from this typical case. In the most typical case, a person acts directly on someone or something. That causes a change you can see. And the action and its result feel like one single event^1 (Lakoff 1987:55, Lemmens 1998:21). Lakoff also says that in a typical case the person causing it ‘is looking at the patient,’ meaning the one affected, and sees the change happen. Good examples are verbs like ‘hit,’ ‘kill,’ and ‘break.’ But in these verbs the idea of
A typical doer has these features: they act on purpose, they start the action, they are in control, they are responsible, and they are a clear, single human being. A typical receiver is affected by the action, is a different person from the doer, and is clearly a single individual. ‘Acting directly’ means using physical energy, with your hands, your body, or a tool, with nothing in between (Hopper and Thomspon 1980, Givón 1984, Lakoff 1987).
causing is built into the word itself. It is not expressed by a separate piece (Langacker 1991:408, see also Lemmens 1998:27). English kill already means ‘cause to die’; you don’t need to add a separate word for ‘cause.’

h: Introduction (introduction)
t:
Many schools of linguistics have looked at ‘make someone do it’ sentences (for example Transformational Grammar, Generative Semantics, Relational Grammar, Incorporation-Government and Binding Theory, and Lexical-Functional Grammar). Most of them see such a sentence as two smaller sentences, or two smaller meanings, glued into one (Baker 1988:154; see also Kemmer and Verhagen 1994:115-6, Dixon 2000:30).² Kemmer and Verhagen (1994) see it the other way around. For them, a ‘make someone do it’ sentence is modelled on ordinary, simple sentences, both in its shape and its meaning. It is not a shrunken version of something bigger underneath. Instead, it is a stretched version of a normal sentence. It can be built like a transitive sentence. Or it can be built like a sentence with three people, such as ‘give someone something,’ or one with a tool, such as ‘cut something with a knife.’³ So the markers
Here is one example of such a theory. In Lexical-Functional Grammar, a ‘make someone do it’ sentence is a combined verb. It joins a main ‘cause’ verb with a smaller base verb. The ‘cause’ verb has two parts: the one who causes, and the event that is caused. The causer acts on one of the people in that event. Each theory has its own rules for how these parts end up in the sentence and which markers they get. A combined verb can be one single word or several separate words. Either way, all such sentences are assumed to have the same underlying parts. But the joining of the two verbs is said to happen in a different place in each case. When the result is one word (as in Chicheŵa), it happens in the dictionary of the language. When it is separate words (as in Catalan), it happens when the sentence is put together (Alsina 1992, 1997).

h: Introduction (introduction)
t:
Kozinsky and Polinsky (1993:235) point out that Nedjalkov and Sil'nickij (1969) had already noticed that ‘make someone do it’ sentences look like other kinds of sentences; see also Shibatani (1976:29-31).
that change in ‘make someone do it’ sentences are seen as tied to what those markers mean in ordinary sentences.^{4}
This chapter is based on Valenzuela 2002a. It looks at ‘make someone do it’ sentences in Shipibo-Konibo. As I will show, the language does some interesting things here. This is especially true of how these sentences interact with transitive verbs and intransitive verbs. I also want to see how well current ideas about causing explain what we find in Shipibo-Konibo. And the other way around: how the facts of Shipibo-Konibo grammar can help us understand causing better, and the ways languages express it.
Section 16.2 covers the different ways the language has to build ‘make someone do it’ sentences. It shows where each one is used. It also shows how they interact with transitive verbs, with the markers that tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or someone else (switch-reference), and with the way words agree with the people in the sentence. In section 16.3, I look at differences in meaning. In particular, I look at how the language tells apart causing something directly and causing it indirectly. Section 16.4 is about words that describe how or where something happens, and how far their meaning reaches in the sentence. Finally, section 16.5 sums up what this chapter has found.

h: Introduction (introduction)
t: Cole (1983) also discusses what particular markers mean, and how the markers that change in ordinary sentences relate to the ones that change in ‘make someone do it’ sentences.

h: Causativization: Forms and Structures (the forms used)
t: In section 10.3.1, I described three groups of verbs that can take a whole sentence as their receiver. One group is verbs of getting someone to do something, without saying whether they actually did it. These are keen- ‘want, wish;’ raan- ‘send (sb. (somewhere) to do sth.);’ yono- ‘order / send sb. (to work), ask for sth.;’ yokat- ‘ask (for) sth.,’ and axea- ‘teach, make sb. get used to sth.’ I don’t cover sentences with these verbs in this chapter. Still, they may be the only clear cases in Shipibo-Konibo where ‘make someone do it’ is said with a separate verb. English does this all the time: ‘I made him go,’ ‘I had her cook.’

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
In Shipibo-Konibo, you can turn a verb into a ‘make someone do it’ verb by adding the general ending -ma to it.^5 The meaning of -ma is very broad. Depending on the sentence and the situation, it can be translated into English as ‘make,’ ‘have,’ ‘cause,’ ‘let,’ ‘allow,’ and even ‘contribute’ and ‘invite.’ The examples below show the different kinds of pushing and allowing that -ma can express (Talmy 1985 calls these ‘force-dynamics’):
Interestingly, David Payne (1990:77-8) lists a ‘make someone do it’ piece of the form /mV/ as one of five grammar forms found widely across South America. And indeed, the ending -mV is found not only in the Panoan and Takanan languages. It also appears in the Carib languages Apalaí and Hixkaryana (where it is listed as meaning ‘for someone’), and others. The ending -miti is found in Aguaruna (Jivaroan). As a beginning piece, mV- is found in some Arawakan languages of the Pre-Andine and Southern branches, in the Tupi languages Tupinambá and Munduruku, and in Yuracaré, Ona, Pirahã, Nadëb and Yanomama. The form m- is found in Tehuelche and Trumai, and ɨm- in Mapudungun.
(1) ...ja-ská-xon-ki xea-ma-kan-a iki meskó xeati... | ‘...then, they invited (him) different kinds of drinks...’
(2) ...paro rebo-n ka-xon.... jato noko-ma-yama-a iki. | ‘...getting to the end of the (Ucayali) river... (she) didn’t let them find her.’

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
The next sentence comes from the ceremony where a girl’s fringe is cut. This is part of the traditional coming-of-age rites:
(3) Ja r-iki nokon bake, jakon-tani-shoko i-ke-ma-bi | mato be-ste-ma-kas-kin e-n a-t-ai, kena | kena-ma-kin. | ‘This is my daughter, and although she is only a bit good / pretty, I have invited you all, wishing to have you cut her fringe.’
(4) Ja-tian ja xontako jawen tita-n | xoi meni-ma-[a]i keen-yama-[a]i-bi... | ‘Then, her_{j} mother_{i} makes the unmarried girl_{j} give roasted meat / fish (to the man who had asked her in matrimony) even though she_{j} doesn’t want to...’
You can say exactly what kind of pushing or allowing happened by adding a second part to the sentence. That part has the ‘same person’ marker and tells you how the causing was done, as in (5b-d):
(5) a. E-n-ra jo-ma-ke. | ‘I made / had / allowed / invited him (to) come.’
(b) E-n-ra nini-xon jo-ma-ke. | ‘I forced / obliged him to come, by pulling him.’
(c) E-n-ra tea-res-kin jo-ma-ke. | ‘I obliged / demanded him to come (by bothering him / insisting on it).’
(d) E-n-ra mee-res-kin jo-ma-ke. | ‘I insisted / begged him to come (no physical contact necessarily).’
The weakest kinds of causing can be said even more indirectly. The result you want is put in a separate part of the sentence. So in the next example, the ending -ma is not attached to the verb for the result. It is attached to shinan- ‘think, plan, consider:’

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
(6a) E-n-ra mi-a shinan-ma-kas-ai jo-ti. | ‘I suggest that you come (lit. I wish to make you consider come).’ | (Also, ‘I want to remind you to come.’)
An even more indirect way is to use -kin instead of -ma. The ending -kin brings in an extra person who takes part with you:
(6b) E-n-ra mi-a shinan-kin-kas-ai jo-ti. | ‘I’d suggest that you come (lit. I wish to accompany you in considering to come. / I wish to consider with you the possibility of coming).’
The endings -ma and -kin overlap in one area. Dixon (2000:62, 73) calls it the ‘involvement
parameter’ of the causer: is the causer taking part in the action too? Shibatani and Pardeshi (2002) call it ‘sociative causation.’ So a sentence like (7) can mean three things. It can mean ‘make someone do it while doing it with them,’ ‘do it together with someone,’ or ‘help someone do it.’ (Example (6) could also be read as a case of making someone do something while doing it with them.)
(7) Yoxaman-ra bake bachi-n jiki-kin-ke. | ‘The old woman made the child enter the mosquito net (by entering herself). / The old woman accompanied the child into the mosquito net. / The old woman helped the child enter the mosquito net.’
In Shipibo-Konibo, the thing that causes something can be a force of nature. That is something that doesn’t act on purpose and isn’t alive, like the weather, seen as the final cause. In fact, the language has no intransitive verb for ‘drown,’ as in ‘he drowned.’ The only way to say it is with ‘kill’: the flowing water^6 is the doer, and the person who drowns is the receiver. So you literally say ‘the water killed him’:^7

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
Jene ‘flowing water’ is different from onpax ‘contained water,’ see exx. (9), (59), and (68).
DeLancey (1984:208) noted that languages such as English and Hare (Athabaskan) allow a force to be the doer. That is because a force is seen as the direct, final cause. But a force cannot act on purpose. So both languages prefer other ways of saying it, where the force is not the doer (English and Hare examples from DeLancey 1984:208): | POSSIBLE | (i) Lightning killed him. (ii) ‘idikóné’ ye-wéhxį / lightning 3OBJ-killed / ‘Lightning killed him.’ | PREFERRED | (iii) He was killed by lightning. (iv) ‘idikóné’ k'é lánįwe / lightning died / ‘He died from / due to lightning.’ | So what is special about the Shipibo-Konibo ‘drown’ is not that flowing water can be the doer. It is that this is the only way to say it. This is connected to the fact that the language has no passive, like English ‘he was killed by.’
(8) Jene-n-ronki bake-bo rete-ke. | ‘(I heard that) the children drowned (lit. the flowing water killed the children).’
Now, to say ‘drown (somebody),’ you take ‘kill’ and add the ‘make someone do it’ ending. The flowing water is the one made to do the killing, and the causer is a living being:
(9) ...Bai Shita-n-ki jato yatan-xon jene | rete-ma-pake-a iki. | ‘...the Bai Shita held them and drowned them one by one (lit. held them and caused the flowing water to kill (them) one by one).’ (Soi Rawa 1995:17)

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
Here are two more examples where a force is the one made to act:
(10) E-n-ra koshon-xon oi be-ma-ke. | ‘Bewitching with tobacco smoke, I caused the rain (to come).’
(11) Yobekan-ra mayan niwe xontako a-ma-ke. | ‘The sorcerer caused the whirlwind to harm the unmarried girl.’^8
Shipibo-Konibo -ma can be added to every kind of verb. So far, I have shown it added to a verb with a doer and two receivers, such as ‘give’ (ex. (4)). I have shown it with transitive verbs (exx. (1), (2), (3), (6), (9), and (11)). And I have shown it with intransitive verbs where the person does something actively (exx. (5) and (10)).
The whirlwind is believed to be a bad spirit. When the whirlwind reaches someone, it makes that person ill.
Below are examples with intransitive verbs where the person does not really act. Instead, something happens to them:
The person feels or experiences something:
(12) E-a-ra xontako-nin waste-n-xon | keen-ma-ke / shinanbeno-ma-ke. | ‘The unmarried girl made me love / forget her by treating me with piripiri.’
(13) Mi-n-ra tita siná-ma-ke koríki yoi-xon. | ‘You made mother get angry, telling her about the money (e.g., that you lost).’
(14) Mi-n-ra tita bene-ma-ke koríki yoi-xon. | ‘You made mother feel happy, telling her about the money (e.g., you earned).’
(15) Mi-n-ra tita rabin-ma-ke yometso-xon. | ‘You made mother feel ashamed, having stolen.’

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
Something happens to the person or thing:
(16) Ja-n-ra e-a niskan-ma-ke tobí a-xon. | ‘S/he made me sweat massaging the area of my dislocated bodypart (to reset it).’
(17) E-a-ra nokon patóro-nin nomi-ma-ke. | ‘My master made me undergo thirst (he didn’t give me anything to drink while working the whole day).’
(18) E-a-ra piti tashianka-nin nomi-ma-ke. | ‘The salty fish (I ate) made me feel thirsty.’
(19) E-n-ra Piko neté-ma-ke. | ‘I made Piko become quiet (either by asking him to shut up or by putting my hand on his mouth.’
(20) ...nishi xea-xon-ki Iskon Niwe-n jawen yora | yoshin-ma-[a]i, saki saki-i i-non kaman. | ‘...drinking ayahuasca, Iskon Niwe made his body turn into spirit until it trembled repeatedly.’
Note that in ex. (18), the one who is made to change is affected by the action, and the causer is not alive.
Transitive verbs can become intransitive verbs by adding the ending -t, which has different forms. The new verb can be about someone who acts (S_{a}) or someone something happens to (S_{o}). But usually adding -t gives a meaning like ‘to yourself,’ or ‘it happened on its own,’ or even something like the English passive ‘it was done’ (ex. (32), 7.4.3 and 18.1). The ending -ma can then be added on top of these new verbs, as Table 16.1 shows. Many other languages, such as Japanese, don’t allow this (see Shibatani and Pardeshi 2002:86-87):

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
Look back at the sentences in this section. When you add -ma, the person who would normally do the action becomes the receiver of the new verb. So that person always appears in the plain form, with no marker. You can see this clearly when the base verb is a transitive verb. There, the doer normally has the doer marker (ERG). Once -ma is added, the same person loses it and appears in the plain form (ABS):
(21) Rabi-n-ra bi-ke mecha joni. | ‘Rabi got (as husband) a good fisherman / hunter.’
(22) Tita betan papa-n-ra Rabi bi-ma-ke | mecha joni | ‘Mother and father made Rabi get (as husband) a good fisherman / hunter.’
Adding -ma turns a verb into a transitive verb. You can also see this in which all-purpose verb is used to answer a yes/no question,
(23) a. Rabi-ki beno-a? | ‘Did Rabi get married?’ | b. Ik-í / ik-[y]áma | ‘Yes / No’
(None) c. Rabi-ki beno-ma-a? | ‘Did s/he make Rabi get married?’ | d. A-kin / ak-[y]áma | ‘Yes / No’
and in which form of the ‘then / when’ linking word is chosen. Ex. (24a) has the intransitive verb benxokaa- ‘get ready’ (‘get yourself ready’). But in (24b), the verb takes the ending -ma (‘get someone ready’). So the linking word changes too, to match the new transitive verb that follows:

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
(24) a. Kesin-ra nashi-ke jainoa-x benxokaa-ke. | ‘Kesin took a bath and got ready.’ | b. Kesin-ra nashi-ke jain-xon benxokaa-ma-ke. | ‘Kesin took a bath and made (her / him) get ready.’
You can add the ‘make someone do it’ ending -ma twice, as below (‘make someone make someone do it’):
(25) E-n-ra mi-a kirika bo-ma-ma-ma-ke. | ‘I had her / him have her / him send you a letter.’
-ma can also appear in the same verb as the endings that bring in an extra person (for whom, with whom, etc.). In these cases, -ma usually comes first (but see ex. (193) in Ch. 17):
(26) Moa-ra mi-n e-a chomo toe-ma-anaan-ke. | ‘Already you made the jar break, to my detriment.’ (Valenzuela 1997:128-9)
(27) E-n-ra mi-n bake mi-a nonti a-ma-xon-ke. | ‘On your behalf I made your son construct a canoe.’ (Valenzuela 1997:129)
The person who is made to act always appears in the plain form. That is true whatever kind of verb they are made to do. So when someone is made to do a transitive verb, two people are marked the same way. One is the person made to act. The other is the one that action ends up on (the “affectee”^9). Here Shipibo-Konibo is unusual. In most languages of the world, these two get different markers. And in most languages, someone made to do an intransitive verb is marked differently from someone made to do a transitive verb (Comrie 1976). It is easy to explain the Shipibo-Konibo pattern if we see these sentences as stretched versions of ordinary sentences with a doer and one receiver, or with a doer and two receivers, like ‘give’ (Kemmer and Verhagen 1994:123-4). Remember that in a ‘give’ sentence, both the thing given and the person it goes to are in the plain form.^10 Also, the language allows -ma twice, and allows -ma together with the endings that bring in an extra person. So you can have several people in the plain form in the

h: The General Causativizer -Ma (the main "make someone do it" ending -ma)
t:
Kemmer and Verhagen (1994) define the affectee as ‘the endpoint of the energy (physical or metaphorical) expended in the entire causative event...’ (p. 119). In other words, it is the person or thing that the whole chain of causing finally lands on.
I am leaving out here a few verbs and sentence types that let the person made to act be marked with betan ‘with.’ The sentence below shows one of these cases. Here the ‘with’ marking seems to happen partly because there are so many people in the sentence (see also ex. (206a) in Ch. 17):
(v) Joni-baon-ronki jato-n papa mawat-a-ton kaya kena-ma-kan-ai | meráya betan. | ‘The people have their late fathers’ souls called by the meráya.’
same sentence, as in example (27) above. (Compare Givón 1976:333-5 and 339-40, on limits on such sentences in some Bantu languages.)

h: Other Causativization Strategies (other ways to say "make someone do it")
t:
Shipibo-Konibo has an interesting feature. Nouns, describing words, and even words for place and manner can take verb endings directly, without any change first. But most verbs DO need a special change before they can be used as anything other than a verb. So a root such as nenké can be a describing word, ‘long.’ It can also be an intransitive verb where something changes: ‘become long.’^11 To get a ‘make it so’ verb from such words, you add /ak/. It also appears as just /a/, especially in the Shipibo dialect rather than the Konibo dialect. This piece almost certainly comes from the all-purpose verb ak- ‘do (tr.), make, tell.’ Examples (28) and (29) show /nenké/ used as a describing word and as a verb. Example (30) shows the ‘make it long’ form:
(28) Westíora nishi nenké-pari e-a bi-xon-we! | ‘First, get me a long rope!’
(29) Tita-n mapó taran-a-ra nenké-ke. | ‘The clay that mother had kneaded became long(er).’
Notice that in English you need several words to say nenké- (‘become long’). When English turns a describing word into a verb with an ending, the result is usually a transitive verb: short/shorten, sick / sicken, dark / darken (which can also be an intransitive verb), large / enlarge.
(30) Joni-boan-ra jato-n-bi tsinkíti nenké a-kan-ai. | ‘The people themselves make the meeting (become) longer.’

h: Other Causativization Strategies (other ways to say "make someone do it")
t:
Besides describing words, words for place and manner can also take /ak/ to mean ‘make it so.’ So can a group of nouns and verbs.^12 For example: bebon ‘in the front, in front of,’ bebon- ‘get to the front,’ bebon a(k)- ‘put something in the front;’ ota ‘shadow,’ ota- ‘become shadowy,’ ota a(k)- ‘shade (tr.).’
A third ‘make someone do it’ ending is -n, It is added to a small number of nouns and intransitive verbs, and turns them into transitive verbs. When it is added to a noun, -n means ‘affect someone using the thing the noun names.’ So it is a kind of ‘do it with this tool’ ending (6.4.1). Look at the following example with the noun rao ‘medicine (generally plants):’
(31) Moa-tian nawa-n rao-bo yama-katit-ai, no-n | rao-n-bi-ribi payó-bo rao-n-kati-kan-ai. | ‘Long time ago, there were no Western medicines, and they (our ancestors) cured the (infected) wounds with our own medicine.’
In (32), rao-n- ‘treat someone with medicine’ is turned back into an intransitive verb. The result is raomeet- ‘be treated (with medicine)’ (the form rao-n-ma- is found in ex. (55)):
I am not including here the cases where /ak/ comes after a noun for a concrete thing and means ‘build, make;’ e.g., xobo ak- ‘build (a) house,’ nonti ak- ‘build a canoe,’ chopa ak- ‘make cloth.’

h: Other Causativization Strategies (other ways to say "make someone do it")
t:
(32) No-a jain wirákocha-bo keská raomeet-[t]i | xobo-oma iki, ospital-oma iki. | ‘Unlike the white people, we have no houses where to be treated; we have no hospitals.’
Here are more examples of this “do it with this tool” ending: axa ‘kind of plant poison’ / axa-n- ‘(to) poison fish,’ joi ‘word’ / joi-n- ‘criticize,’ xeni ‘fat’ / xeni-n- ‘grease something,’ waste ‘piripiri’ / waste-n- ‘change somebody’s behavior by treating him / her with piripiri’ (ex. (12)), bata ‘sweet, sugar’ / bata-n ‘sweeten.’ -N can also be added to a few intransitive verbs, like oxa- ‘sleep’ / oxa-n- ‘put to sleep,’ pani- ‘hang (intr.)’ / pani-n- ‘hang (trans.),’ kesha- ‘confess (intr.)’ / kesha-n- ‘tell, give notice:’
(33) Ani texó jiwi-n-ra nato shino pani-ai. | ‘This monkey (usually) hangs on the big quinilla tree.’ | Nokon koka-n awinin-ra jawen chopa patsa-a | pani-n-ai. | ‘My maternal uncle’s wife is hanging her recently washed clothes.’
As I described in 4.3., the ending -n is also used in a two-way process with a small group of roots. These roots name body positions, or movements into a position. On their own they are neither intransitive verbs nor transitive verbs. The ending that goes the other way, turning them into intransitive verbs,
is -t. The root raka- ‘lying position’ shows how this works: ‘lay someone down’ versus ‘lie down’:

h: Other Causativization Strategies (other ways to say "make someone do it")
t:
(34) ...bo-xon kawin taraman-ki raka-n-kan-a iki. | ‘...carrying [the white-lipped peccaries] they laid them on the extended rush mat.’
(35) Nato yawa rabé rete-kan-a raka-t-a | chopa bi-xon mapo-we! | ‘Get a cloth and cover these two white-lipped peccaries that [they] have killed and that are lying (there)!’

h: Alternate Auxiliarization (using different helper verbs)
t:
As I described in 4.7 and 8.2.7, there is also a set of sound-words (often easy to recognize) that can be used either way. Whether they are intransitive or transitive depends on which all-purpose helper verb they take. So a root such as kobin with the intransitive helper ik- means ‘boil (intr.),’ as in ‘the water boils.’ The same root with the transitive helper ak- means ‘boil (tr.),’ as in ‘I boil the water.’ Two more examples are biski ik- ‘to shake oneself’ versus biski ak- ‘to shake something;’ shee ik- ‘fry (intr.) versus shee ak- ‘fry (tr.).’
I will come back to this way of switching helper verbs in 16.3.4.

h: ‘Come’ / ‘Bring’ and ‘Go’ / ‘Carry’ ("come / bring" and "go / carry")
t: As I explained in 4.5 and 15.3.3, the choice between the verb pairs jo- / be- and ka- / bo- depends on two things. One is how many people move. The other is whether someone is moving something else along. So jo- ‘come (singular)’ and ka- ‘go (singular)’ are used for one mover going on their own. Their partners be- ‘come (non-singular), bring’ and bo- ‘go (non-singular), carry’ are used for many movers, or for ‘making something come or go.’

h: On the Syntactic Status of Causatives (is it one sentence or two?)
t:
Shipibo-Konibo clearly shows when something is one sentence and when it is several. The key clue is that a sentence part can never end in a bare verb. It must end with a final ending of some kind. By that test, all the ‘make someone do it’ verbs we have seen are clearly one sentence. But another question comes up. Are all of them single words, with the cause and the result as two pieces of one word, like English shorten? Or are some of them separate words, one for the cause and one for the result, like English make short?
In most cases /ak/ is pronounced as part of the word before it. Even so, it seems to behave a bit differently in the sentence from the other ‘make someone do it’ endings.^{13} Unlike -ma and -n, /ak/ acts, at least to a certain
-ma and -n are clearly endings, pronounced as part of the word they attach to. With /ak/, this is not so clear. For example, Loriot, Lauriault, and Day (1993:96-7) tell apart xobo a-ti ‘build a house’ (two words) and xobo-a-ti ‘house build’ (one word). This suggests that /ak/ is at different stages of
extent, more like a separate word. Look at the examples below. Two words for the result are joined with itan ‘and.’ The ‘make it so’ piece then comes only once, after both of them. It is like saying ‘make it long and wide’ instead of ‘make it long and make it wide’:^{14}

h: On the Syntactic Status of Causatives (is it one sentence or two?)
t:
(36) E-n-ra lejía-nin soro pené itan | bená a-ke. | ‘I made the sol coin look shiny and look like new.’
(37) E-n-ra xobo nenké itan naxbá a-ke. | ‘I made the house longer and wider.’
(38) E-n-ra bake mankoa-nin potó itan | keras a-ke. | ‘With the mangos, I made the child become stuffed and dirty.’
With -ma it is different. You cannot join two result verbs with ‘and’ unless you repeat -ma on each one.^{15} The sentences below show two ways to try to say ‘Jisbe made them burn the chacra and build the house.’ Notice that only the sentences where -ma is repeated after each verb are correct:
turning from the full verb ak- ‘do (tr.), make’ into a grammar piece. See Shibatani and Pardeshi (2002). They suggest that these forms lie along a scale, from separate words to endings, both across languages and within one language. For a fuller comparison of ‘make someone do it’ endings versus ‘make someone do it’ separate words, see Alsina 1997:221). [continuation of footnote 13 from previous page]
The describing word plus /a(k)/ is pronounced as one word. But I write it as two separate words to show how unusually it behaves in the sentence.
(39) Jisbe-n-ra jato wai meno-ma-xon xobo | a-ma-ribi-ke. | Jisbe-n-ra jato wai meno-xon | xobo a-ma-ribi-ke. | Jisbe-n-ra jato wai meno-ma-ke jain-xon | xobo a-ma-ribi-ke. | Jisbe-n-ra jato wai meno jain-xon | xobo a-ma-ribi-ke. | ‘Jisbe made them burn the chacra and build the house.’

h: On the Syntactic Status of Causatives (is it one sentence or two?)
t:
The sentences below show the same thing, this time with intransitive verbs. The English meaning is ‘Jisbe made the child cry and dance:’
(40) Jisbe-n-ra bake wini-ma-xon-bi | ransa-ma-ribi-ke.
I was trying to get speakers to say sentences such as (39b) and (39d) below. One speaker who was helping me explained that those sentences were wrong because ‘the meno (part) is incomplete’ (Ronon Meni, p.c. 2000).
(None) b. Jisbe-n-ra bake wini-xon-bi ransa-ma-ribi-ke. | c. Jisbe-n-ra bake wini-ma-ke jain-xon | ransa-ma-ribi-ke. | d. Jisbe-n-ra bake wini jain-xon ransa-ma-ribi-ke. | ‘Jisbe made the child cry and dance.’
You can also use -ma instead of /ak/ to make a ‘make it so’ verb from a describing word. The meaning is slightly different (see section 16.3.1). But in that case, you cannot join two result words with ‘and’ and use the ending only once:
(41) a. E-n-ra bake ani-ma-ke jain-xon | xoa-ma-ke. | b. E-n-ra bake ani jain-xon xoa-ma-ke. | c. E-n-ra bake ani itan xoa-ma-ke. | ‘I caused the child to grow and get fat.’
So /ak/, at least with describing words, is more independent than the general ending -ma. Other words can come between it and the result word. This fits with another fact. The meaning of /ak/ is easy to see (‘do, make’), while the meanings of -ma and -n are not. Nevertheless,

h: On the Syntactic Status of Causatives (is it one sentence or two?)
t:
the helper verb ak- (the one used with transitive sound-words) is not this independent. That is surprising. It looks the same as /ak/ and comes from the same source. And it is not even pronounced as part of the word before it: speakers often make a small catch in the throat, or a little pause, between the word and ak-. Still, the sentences below show that you cannot join two such words with ‘and’ unless you repeat the helper verb:
(42) E-n-ra yapa kobin ak-ai jain-xon | xeni shee ak-ai. | E-n-ra yapa kobin jain-xon xeni shee ak-ai. | ‘I boiled the fish and fried the fat.’
(43) E-n-ra nami shee ak-ai ja-pekao kobin ak-ai. | E-n-ra nami shee ja-pekao kobin ak-ai. | ‘I fried the meat and then boiled it.’
There is one more thing about ‘make it so’ verbs built from a describing word plus /ak/. You can put certain small, movable pieces in between. Examples are -shaman ‘very,’ -shoko ‘a little’ (a ‘small’ ending), and -tani ‘somewhat’:
(44) Mi-n-ra papashoko raro-tani a-ke. | ‘You made grandfather a little bit happy.’
(45) E-n-ra tapo keyá-shoko a-ke. | ‘I made the palm-bark floor somewhat high.’
(46) E-n-ra xobo kikin ani-shaman ak-ai. | ‘You made the house quite large.’
The root bata ‘(become) sweet’ can become ‘sweeten’ in two ways: with /ak/ or with -n. With /ak/, you can put the ‘a little’ ending -shoko right after the root. With -n, you can’t:

h: On the Syntactic Status of Causatives (is it one sentence or two?)
t:
(47) E-n-ra xeati bata a-ke. | E-n-ra xeati bata-n-ke. | ‘I sweetened the drink.’ | E-n-ra xeati bata-shoko a-ke. | E-n-ra xeati bata-shoko-n-ke | ‘I sweetened the drink a little bit.’
So in how it is built, ‘make it so’ with /ak/ is different from the other ways of doing this in Shipibo-Konibo. You could call the /ak/ form a kind of two-part verb. It is like the French faire ‘make’ construction. In French, faire usually comes right next to the other verb. But some words, like certain manner words and ‘not,’ can come in between.

h: Causativization and the Determination of Reference (how "make someone do it" helps show who is who)
t:
Does Shipibo decide "same person or someone else?" before or after it adds a "make someone do it" ending? In Huallaga Quechua, the "same person / someone else" marker is chosen first, using the plain verb, before the "make someone do it" ending is added (Weber 1989:306; see also pp. 12, 292-3). In SK it is the other way around: the marker is chosen by looking at the person who makes something happen. Look at the long sentence below. Each of its two parts has a "make someone do it" form: one uses the helper verb ak- (a transitive verb meaning 'do'), and the other uses the ending -ma. In both parts, the thing that changes is the sugar cane juice. And in both parts, the people making it happen are "they." So a simple "same person" marker alone would not tell us which comes first. But remember that SK "same person" markers also tell you what kind of verb comes in the main part of the sentence. The marker -xon says the shared person is a doer with a receiver, so the main part must have a transitive verb. That is why, in (48) below, we can see that the "make someone do it" ending is added first, and the "same person" marker is chosen afterwards:
(48) ...xawi jene kobin a-xon | pae-ma-kan-a iki. | ‘...they boiled the cane juice and let it ferment.’

h: Causativization and the Determination of Reference (how "make someone do it" helps show who is who)
t:
In the next sentence, the "same person" marker -ax tells us something. The people going to Caco are the same people who made something happen in the first part. So again, the "make someone do it" ending comes first, and the marker is chosen afterwards:
(49) Rabi beno-ma-[a]x-ra Kako-nko bo-kan-ke. | ‘After making Rabi get married, they went to Caco (maybe with Rabi and her husband too).
The word piece -a shows that the receiver of one part is the doer of the other part. It also shows that, in the example below, the "make someone do it" ending comes before the "same person / someone else" choice:
(50) Tita betan papa-n beno-ma-a-ra Rabi | Kako-nko ka-ke. | ‘After mother and father made her get married, Rabi went to Caco.’

h: Semantic Aspects: Direct versus Indirect Causation (meaning: doing it yourself vs. getting someone else to do it)
t:
This section is about two differences in meaning that come with "make someone do it" forms. First, Shipibo has more than one way to say that someone makes something happen. Sometimes the person causing it does it with their own hands. Sometimes they only get it going, or let it happen. Linguists call this direct versus indirect causation, and I look at what meanings decide the choice. Second, I discuss limits on when each method can be used. I think these limits mostly depend on how alive and active the person or thing being made to act is, and so on whether it could start an action by itself.
So far, I have looked at different "make someone do it" endings that never compete. Roughly, the kind of word they attach to decides which one you use. But, not surprisingly, SK can also make the same verb into a "make someone do it" verb in more than one way. Many linguists say that two such forms never mean exactly the same thing. They show two different ways of picturing the same event in your mind (Fodor 1970; Shibatani 1976:28-38; Hetzron 1976; Wierzbicka 1980; Cole 1983; Haiman 1983; Lemmens 1998:21; inter alia). These differences are usually grouped under one contrast: "direct" versus "indirect" causation. Direct means you make it happen yourself, like pushing a door shut. Indirect means you get it going in a less hands-on way, like asking someone to shut the door. Kemmer and Verhagen (1994:120) give three ways to tell them apart: physical or not physical, done yourself or done through someone else, and really causing it versus just allowing or permitting it (per se). Dixon (2000:61-78) lists nine related features found in many languages. First, he separates states from actions. Next, he looks at the person being made to act: are they in control, do they want it, and are they changed by it? For the person causing it, he looks at how direct it is, whether they mean to do it, whether it is natural, and how involved they are. Finally, Shibatani and Pardeshi (2002) build the contrast on two basic situations. The other cases come from these two. The difference lies in how the person being made to act is seen. In direct causation, an active causer acts on someone or something that just undergoes the change. In indirect causation, both the causer and the one being made to act are active people.

h: Semantic Aspects: Direct versus Indirect Causation (meaning: doing it yourself vs. getting someone else to do it)
t: Languages show this direct / indirect difference in several well-known ways. One is a single word versus a phrase of several words (like English kill versus cause to die). Another is an ending versus a phrase. A third is marking the person being made to act in different ways. In his survey of "make someone do it" forms, Dixon (2000:63-77) adds other ways found in the world's languages. These include different endings, endings in a different order, an ending versus a separate little word, an ending versus a sound change, repeating part of the word, and marking of time or mood. As I will show, SK can mark direct versus indirect causation by choosing different "make someone do it" methods. A second way puts two steps on the same verb: first an ending that takes away the receiver, then an ending that adds a causer. I think this softens a verb that normally means doing it directly, so it comes to mean "let it happen." Also, some verbs have more than two different forms, made with different words or different endings.

h: Alternate Causativizers (different "make someone do it" endings)
t:
In section 16.2.1, I described -ma as the most general "make someone do it" ending. It can go on the widest range of words, and it can show the widest range of ways of causing something. Also, -ma is the only one of these endings that can be added twice, or after another such ending. Here I will show something more. When a verb has two possible "make someone do it" forms, the one with -ma shows the least direct kind of causing. To return to a classic example, the verb mawá-ma- (‘die’ + -ma) is best translated as ‘let someone die,’ not as ‘kill.’ For instance, mawá-ma- would fit when somebody is
taking care of a sick person and this person dies. The idea of ‘kill’ uses a completely different verb, rete-:^{16}
(51) E-n-ra nokon bake mawá-ma-kean^{17}-ke ishton | onanya-iba bo-yama-xon. | ‘I almost caused my son to die, by not taking him to the onanya quickly.’
(52) E-n-ra misho rete-kean-ke nokon kawá pi-ke-tian. | ‘I almost killed the cat for having eaten my patarashca (fish wrapped in a leaf and roasted).’
The same kind of difference shows up between -ma and /ak/. It seems that forms with -ma always show less direct causing than forms with /ak/. Look at the examples below. The verb benxo-ma- means ‘to have someone cured (by somebody else),’ for example by taking her or him to the shaman. But benxo a(k)- means ‘to cure somebody’ yourself, for example if you are a shaman or know how to use plants:

h: Alternate Causativizers (different "make someone do it" endings)
t:
(53) No-n onan-ya-bo-iba no-a isin-ai-tian bo-xon
It is interesting to compare related languages. In SK, ‘die’ and ‘kill’ are two different words. In the related language Kashibo-Kakataibo, ‘kill’ is made by adding an ending to ‘die’: bama- ‘die’ vs. bama-mi- (die-CAUS, where CAUS is the "make someone do it" ending) ‘kill’ (Shell 1987:91-2). In a third Panoan language, Marobo, ‘die’ and ‘kill’ are also two separate words, but not the same ones as in SK: /‘vupi/ ‘die’ vs. /yamama/ ‘kill’ (Costa 1998:pp.68, 76). However, in SK the form /yamama/ would clearly look like a "make someone do it" form: yama- 'there is none' + –ma, the "make someone do it" ending.
The meaning ‘almost’ is shown by an ending added to the verb. I will come back to this in the next section.
(53) no-a benxo-ma-i / \benxo a-[a]i | ‘When we get sick (our parents) take us to the onanya and have us cured.’
(54) Ikaxbi ja-ska-ra jakon-ma shinan-ya joni-bo no-n | benxo a-ti atipan-ke rao-n-xon. / \benxo-ma-ti | ‘But we can cure this kind of bad men by treating them with (plant) medicine.’
(55) Nokon bene mee-mis i-ke-tian-ra e-n nokon | tita rao-n-ma-ke. | ‘Since my husband used to beat me, I had my mother cure him with (plant) medicine (in order to change his behavior).’
In (54) and (55), the women are talking about a Shipibo belief. A man who behaves badly can be made to change. You have him drink, without him noticing, a drink made with the right medicinal plant.

h: Alternate Causativizers (different "make someone do it" endings)
t:
In (56) and (57), two nouns are used like verbs. xono ‘(become) lupuna tree’ is turned into a "make it happen" verb with /ak/. But yoshin ‘(become) spirit’ takes -ma instead ((57) was shown before as (20)):
(56) Binpish jamá-xon-ronki awakan xono a-ni-ke. | ‘Kicking the guayaba (tree), the tapir turned it into a lupuna (tree).’
(57) ...nishi xea-xon-ki Iskon Niwe-n jawen yora
(56) yoshin-ma-[a]i, saki saki-i i-non kaman. | ‘...drinking the ayahuasca, Iskon Niwe made his body turn into spirit until it trembled repeatedly.’
The story around (56) makes it clear that the tapir did not mean to cause the change. It did not even know what could happen when it kicked the guayaba tree. The shaman is different. He drank ayahuasca on purpose, knowing what he was doing, to do his job. There is another difference too. The tapir acts by itself on something that does nothing at all. But when the shaman drinks ayahuasca, people think of the spirit of the plant as the one that is really active and makes things happen.
Loriot, Lauriault, and Day (1993:417) give another example of two "make it happen" endings with different meanings. The intransitive verb tsasi- ‘stop’ has two "make it stop" forms: tsasi a- and tsasi-ma. They say that both can be translated as ‘stop (something),’ but tsasi a- “implies an intercepted object,” for example a canoe being carried down by the water. tsasi-ma- instead “refers to the fact of stopping the movement, e.g., of a horse...” (my translation). Here the thing being stopped is clearly much more, or much less, active in each case: a horse moves by itself, a canoe does not.

h: Alternate Causativizers (different "make someone do it" endings)
t:
In section 16.2.2, I said that /ak/ is the "make it happen" form used with describing words that mean "become ___". So a word such as ani ‘(become) big, grow’ usually takes /ak/ to make ‘raise.’ But in section 16.2.5, I mentioned that ani can also take the general
"make it happen" ending -ma, again with a slightly different meaning. Compare these two sentences:
(58) E-n-ra bake ani a(k)-ai. | ‘I raise the child.’ | E-n-ra bake ani-ma-ai. | ‘I make / help the child grow (taking special care of her / him; e.g. by giving her / him special food or vitamins).’ (Valenzuela 1997:108)
The word xana ‘(become) hot’ (another "become ___" describing word) changes in the same way:
(59) E-n-ra onpax xana a(k)-ai. | ‘I heat the water (put it on the fire and probably leave it).’ | E-n-ra onpax xana-ma-ai. | ‘I heat the water (taking constant care of it, by using a fan to keep the fire high, etc.).’ (Valenzuela 1997:109)
Here is how to read (58) and (59) above. With /ak/, the person causing it makes the change happen. The thing that changes is seen as just undergoing it. With -ma, the person causing it is seen more as a helper. They make something that was about to happen anyway happen faster, better, or more.

h: Alternate Causativizers (different "make someone do it" endings)
t:
Here is something interesting. When a verb can take either -ma or /ak/, the more independent piece (cf. 16.2.5), which is also the one whose origin is easy to see,
is the one that shows more direct causing. In other words, what is closer in meaning is not closer in form. You might expect the more direct meaning to use the piece more tightly attached to the verb, but it is the other way around.
Some verbs can take either -ma or -n. The same basic difference applies here: the form with -n means more direct causing than the form with -ma. In the examples below, native speakers often understand nee-n- as touching someone physically, with the other person just undergoing it. The form with -ma rather means persuading or urging someone, so that person must be more active:
(60) a. E-n-ra bake nee-n-ke jiwi bochiki. | ‘I put the child up on the tree (I hold the child and put in on the tree).’ | b. E-n-ra bake nee-ma-ke jiwi bochiki. | ‘I caused the child to go up on the tree (e.g., by asking her / him to do it).’
Having different "make it happen" endings can also help when the base word has two possible meanings. For example, the describing word menkó means ‘upside down’ but also ‘laying (hen).’ menko-n- means ‘put someone upside down,’ while menkó-ma- means ‘place a hen in its nest so that it lays eggs’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:259). Different endings can also make different verbs from a word with only one meaning. For example, bake ‘child’ can take -n to make bake-n- ‘deliver a child,’ or /ak/ to make bake a- ‘engender / have a child.’ In general, -n seems to have a more physical meaning (cf.

h: Alternate Causativizers (different "make someone do it" endings)
t: the examples of two steps of word-building in 4.3, where -n turns words about body positions, or about moving into a position, into "make someone do it" verbs).

h: The Detransitivizing Strategy (the "removing a person" method)
t:
There is a second way to show direct versus indirect causing, besides choosing different endings. You take the same transitive verb and use it either bare or with two endings added one after the other. The bare verb shows direct causing. Indirect causing takes two steps. First, the middle ending -t removes the receiver, so the verb now means that something just happens. Second, the general "make someone do it" ending -ma is added to that new verb (Table 16.1). Again, the form with -ma is the one that shows indirect causing. So the word-for-word meaning of this form seems to be ‘to let someone or something go through the change.’
In the examples below, the speaker talks sadly about how the Shipibo are losing their traditional culture. She first uses the bare transitive verb keyo- ‘finish, kill, exterminate.’ It shows that the one causing it is actively involved and makes it happen. Then she uses keyó-ma-. This shows that the one causing it takes a less active part, and the event seems to happen by itself:
(61) ...no-a no-n-a-bi jawéki-bo keyó-ma-i | i-t-ai. Ja-ska-ra i-xon no-n Ani Xeati | oin-yam-ai, no-n be-sté-kan-ai-bo | oin-yam-ai, no-n mashá i-kan-ai-bo oin-yam-ai. | Rama-tian no-a jawe-oma-bi.... | no-n bake-bo jawe-bi onan-ma iki... | ‘...we are letting our customs disappear. Thus, we don’t see any Ani Xeati ceremony, we don’t see the cutting of the girls’ fringes, we don’t see those who perform the mashá. Nowadays we have absolutely nothing...our children are completely ignorant of this...’

h: The Detransitivizing Strategy (the "removing a person" method)
t:
As she goes on, the speaker finds reasons to blame the Shipibo themselves for losing their traditional culture. She thinks the Shipibo could stop losing their culture if they chose to. In this stronger statement, almost an accusation, she uses the bare verb keyo- instead. Notice also the strong pronoun nonbi ‘we ourselves:’
(62) No-a-ra jakiribi i-ti atipan-ke ne-skat-i, ikaxbi | no-n-bi-kaya-ra no-n axé-bo keyo-i | i-t-ai... joxo nawa-bo-res no-n onan-ma-[a]i.
(None) Ja-tian ja-bo-res no-n yo-i ka-[a]i, ja-tian moa | no-a ja-ska-ra-ton shinan-benot-ai. | ‘We could practice this again, but instead, we ourselves are finishing with our customs…we only show it to the white outsiders. Thus, we tell only them, and we are forgetting these things already.’
The next two examples show again how a bare transitive verb differs from its -ma form. In (63), menó-ma- is about something sad that happened by accident, without anyone meaning it. In (64), meno- is done on purpose. It follows the custom of burning or simply leaving the house after a relative dies:
(63) E-n-ra xobo menó-ma-ke mari bina | meno-kas-kin. | ‘I caused the house to burn wanting to kill the wasp (by burning it).’
(64) E-n-ra nokon xobo meno-ke jainoa-x nokon papa | mawá-ke-tian. | ‘I burnt my house because my father died there.’
Other pairs like this are rate- / raté-ma- and payo- / payó-ma:

h: The Detransitivizing Strategy (the "removing a person" method)
t:
(65) a. E-n-ra bake rate-ke. | ‘I scared the child (by hiding in the dark and coming out suddenly).’
(65b) b. E-n-ra bake raté-ma-ke. | ‘I let the child get scared’ (e.g., I left the child alone, and while I was away the child got scared; I feel responsible about it).
(66) a. E-n-ra chopa payo-ke. | ‘I wore out my clothes (through the normal daily use).’ | b. E-n-ra chopa payó-ma-ke. | ‘I let my clothes become worn out (by not taking appropriate care of them, by leaving them for too long in the water while washing, etc.).’

h: Combined Strategies (using more than one method together)
t:
Some verbs have not just two but even more "make it happen" forms, as Table 16.2 shows:
The form with the middle ending, paké- ('come down'), can be used as a command. You use it when you tell or ask a person or a dog to come down from a tree, a hammock or a house,^18 or to get out of a canoe. You would then use paké-ma- when you tell someone else about your order or request. Usually you cannot use paké-ma- to report making
something fall that cannot move by itself, such as money or a cup. (A fruit is different, because fruits can fall by themselves.) Paké-ma- can also be used when you are looking after a child and, while you are busy with other jobs, the child falls to the ground. Or when you are swinging a hammock and the child falls out of it. In general, paké-ma- means that the speaker feels responsible for what happened, even though they did not cause it directly.
On the other hand, pake- is the better choice when you physically act on the child. For example, you take the child down from a tree, or you swing the hammock so hard that the child falls. It is also used if you tip the canoe over and the dog falls out. These last two can happen on purpose or by accident. In these last two cases, speakers also accept paké-ma-:

h: Combined Strategies (using more than one method together)
t:
(67) a. E-n-ra bake paké-ma-ke, yono-xon. | b. E-n-ra bake pake-ke, yono-xon. | ‘I had the child come down by ordering her / him to do it.’
(68) a. E-n-ra bake xobo-nko-ni-a | paké-ma-ke, onpax bi-i ka-xon. | b. E-n-ra bake xobo-nko-ni-a pake-ke, | onpax bi-i ka-xon. | ‘I let the child fall from the house while going to get water.’
Shipibo houses typically stand on poles.
In rough English, the next sentences mean: (69) ‘I caused the child to fall from the hammock,’ (70) ‘I caused the dog to fall from the canoe,’ and (71) ‘I caused the money to fall from (my) pocket:’
(69) E-n-ra bake paké-ma-ke | weyóti-aino-a. | E-n-ra bake pake-ke weyóti-aino-a.
(70) E-n-ra ochíti paké-ma-ke nonti-mea. | E-n-ra ochíti pake-ke nonti-mea.
(71) ??E-n-ra koríki paké-ma-ke | borosicho-nko-ni-a. | E-n-ra koríki pake-ke borosicho-nko-ni-a. | ‘I threw / dropped the money from the pocket.’
People often understand the difference between the (a) and (b) sentences like this. In one, the person causing it does it on purpose. In the other, it is an accident. This is just like (63) and (64).
Here is another example, this time with a "become ___" describing word:
(72) Nato xeati r-iki xawi jene kobin a-xon | pae-ma-kan-a. | ‘After boiling the sugar cane juice they let this drink ferment.’
(73) ...ja-n kikin-i pae-n-kan-a iki. | ‘...with it (sugar cane liquor) they got completely drunk.’

h: Combined Strategies (using more than one method together)
t:
(74) Moa a-ti nete xabat-ai-tian, nokon wetsa rabé | pae-n a-kan-a iki. | ‘When the day (to carry out the Xebiana Tsekati ceremony) cleared, they got my two sisters drunk.’
(75) Nokon xobo-n ka-xon-ra e-n jato | pae-n-ma-res-ke. | ‘I went home and just let them get drunk.’
The examples in Table 16.4 use the noun bake ‘child,’ which can also mean "become a child":
Finally, look at the next sentence (shown before as (24) in Ch. 10):
(76) Meráya-nin-ra e-a namá-xon-ke nokon machíto | e-n manó-ma-yantan-a. | ‘The great shaman dreamt, on my behalf, of the machete I had misplaced some time ago.’
At first, you might explain the "make it happen" form in (76) like the combined forms above. That is, you would start with a transitive verb mano- ‘to lose something.’ Then the middle ending is added, and then -ma. If that were right, the direct meaning should just be the bare verb mano-. And SK does have the verb mano-. But it has a special meaning: ‘to look for somebody by asking others.’ To get a direct meaning, you would use a different transitive verb, such as pota- ‘to abandon, throw.’

h: Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
As I said in section 16.2.1 (see also footnote 7), SK can treat forces and ideas, such as an illness, as the doer of a transitive verb. Real objects that cannot move by themselves can also be the doer. But this happens only when they are the real starting point of the event, not a tool that someone uses (ex. (18)). DeLancey (1984:181) points out the difference. Neither forces nor tools want anything. But a tool is controlled by someone, and a force is not. For example, in SK you could say that a fruit hit Yoi on the head. But this means the fruit fell from the tree, not that somebody threw it at Yoi. Hare, an Athabaskan language, is similar. A gun that goes off by itself can be the doer of the verb ‘kill,’ but a gun that someone fires cannot (DeLancey ibid.:187).
A body part can also be the doer of the verb chexa- ‘ache.’ Look at the example below (see also ex. (34) in Ch. 9):
(77) E-a xeta-n chexa-ke-tian-ra, e-n rokotoro | tseka-ma-ke | ‘Because my tooth was aching, I had the dentist pull it out.’ (Valenzuela 1997:144; see also Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:162)
In an earlier work (Valenzuela 1997:110-11, 230-2), I noticed that some "make it happen" endings cannot go with some words. I explained this by the kind of person or thing that is made to act. In the section above, I compared pake- (‘bring down, throw, drop’) and paké-ma- (‘cause to come down, cause to fall’). The second form is usually not accepted when the thing that falls is money (ex. (71)). But paké-ma- can be used with a fruit, because fruits can fall by themselves. The next examples show something similar, using the same word with different endings:

h: Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
(78) a. E-n-ra bená a-[a]i soro. / bená ak-ai | ‘I make the coin (look) new.’ | b. E-n-ra soro bená-ma-ai. | ‘I make the coin (look) new.’
But:
(79) a. E-n-ra kaimito bimi-ma-ai. | ‘I am taking care of the caimito (e.g. by treating it with snail egg or by not letting anybody touch it) till it yields fruit.’ | b. E-n-ra kaimito bimi a-ai. | ‘I made the caimito yield fruit.’
Several of the people who helped me with the language did not accept ex. (78b). It would mean that the coin could somehow become new by itself, without anyone doing it. This fits with what I said about -ma: it marks indirect
causing, where the thing being made to act is seen as active itself. As for bimi- ‘yield fruit,’ I argued that it takes -ma and not /ak/ because trees bear fruit by themselves, without anyone making them do it (Valenzuela 1997:110-11).^{19} But there are cases like raké a- ‘frighten, threaten,’ where /ak/ is used even though the one frightened is a person. Still, here is one way to see it. Like bená a-, and unlike bimi-ma-, the event in raké a- could not have happened without someone else causing it. Or simply, some events with a person who could act can still be pictured as direct causing. To sum up: in 16.2 I explained which "make it happen" endings go with which words using grammar rules (roughly, the type of base word). But a closer look shows that these grammar facts also work together with meaning.

h: Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
Limits based on meaning also show up with the helper verbs. Here the base words are sound words, like English woof or bang. They can join either the intransitive helper verb or the transitive helper verb. The pair below is the model for these forms. The sound word jojo plus the intransitive helper ik- means ‘bark.’ But jojo plus the transitive helper ak- means ‘bark at,’ which adds a receiver (Valenzuela 1997:229):
(80) a. Ochíti-ra jojo ik-ai joni-bo kopí. | ‘The dog is barking because of the people.’
I wish to thank Inkan Soi (Kruger Pacaya Cruz) for sharing with me his insights on this particular issue.
(80b) Ochíti-nin-ra joni-bo jojo ak-ai. | ‘The dog is barking at the people.’
(80c) E-n-ra ochíti jojo i-ma-[a]i joni-bo kopí. | ‘I make the dog bark because of the people.’
(80d) E-n-ra ochíti joni-bo jojó a-ma-[a]i. | ‘I make the dog bark at the people.’
(80e) E-n-ra ochíti jojo ak-ai. | ‘I make the dog bark.’
As (80a) and (80b) show, a sound word plus ik- makes an intransitive sentence, and a sound word plus ak- makes a transitive sentence. The dog is the one acting in both. The same is true for sound words about a person acting, such as betsó ‘kiss’ and too ‘shoot.’ But with a person, the intransitive helper gives a "to yourself" meaning.

h: Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
It is different with other animals and things that are not human. Like the dog, and unlike people, their sound words with the intransitive helper do not mean "to yourself." They just mean the thing does the action:
(81a) Xena-ra tiash i-ke. | ‘The worm produced a noise tiash (e.g. when falling from a branch).’
However, (80e) is correct with the less likely meaning ‘I bark at the dog.’
(None) b. Atapa bachi xaká-ra moish i-ke. | ‘The chicken egg shell produced a noise moish (e.g. when breaking).’ | c. Motóro-ra tokotoko ik-ai. | ‘The engine is producing a noise tokotoko (when starting or working).’
But unlike dogs and people, here you cannot use the sound word with the transitive helper (that is, you cannot add a receiver):
(82) a. Xena-n-ra tiash a-ke. | b. Atapa bachi xakakan-ra moish a-ke. | c. Motóro-nin-ra tokotoko ak-ai.
One way to make a "make it happen" form is to add -ma to the sound word plus the intransitive helper,
(83) a. E-n-ra xena tiash i-ma-ke. | b. E-n-ra atapa bachi xaká moish i-ma-ke. | c. E-n-ra motoro tokotoko i-ma-[a]i. | ‘I caused the worm / chicken egg shell / engine to produce a noise tiash / moish / toko toko.’
or to add a new doer and turn the one who was acting into the receiver:

h: Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
(84) E-n-ra xena tiash a-ke. | E-n-ra atapa bachi xaká moish a-ke. | E-n-ra motoro tokotoko a-ke. | ‘I made the worm / chicken egg shell / engine produce the noise tiash / moish / toko toko (e.g., by stepping on it, by starting it, etc.)
These examples do not cover all the sound verbs in SK. But they suggest something. How these words combine depends on how alive and active the one doing the action is.

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
Some linguists have argued about whether single-word "cause" verbs (like English kill) come from hidden longer phrases (like cause to die). Part of that argument looked at how far a describing word or phrase reaches in the sentence (Hochster 1974, Shibatani 1976:9-13). The SK facts in the last section strongly support one idea. When a language has several ways to say that someone causes something, the ways show different pictures of roughly the same real event. This is true whether they are single words, words with endings, or longer phrases. Still, how "make it happen" forms work with describing words is worth studying for other reasons, not just for the
argument about where they come from. For example, we could compare how different languages make clear which part of the sentence a describing phrase belongs to. Languages do this with the order of words or word pieces, with the tune of the voice,^{21} with different ways of keeping track of who is who, and with different word forms, like klugerweise / klug in German and Dutch (Dik et alia 1990:36-7). For example, Fodor (1970) points out the following. In sentence (85a), the phrase ‘by swallowing his tongue’ can describe either the causing or just the result. In (85b), it can only describe the causing:
(85) 
In SK, it can be unclear what such extra phrases (which I have called adjuncts) belong to. This can happen even when "cause" is said with a longer phrase. One way SK can solve this is with the markers that tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. Sentence (86) has the marked part imakaskinmabi. It is the closest thing to English ‘involuntarily, against somebody’s will:’

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(86) Tita-n-ra Chonon Biri bewa-ma-ke,
In fact, Dik et alia (1990) separate two kinds of extra phrases: ones that describe the event, and ones that show the speaker's view. These match Quirk et alia’s (1985) adjuncts and disjuncts. Dik et alia claim that only the first kind is said with the same voice tune as the main part of the sentence (p.41).
(86) i-ma-kas-kin-ma-bi. | ‘Mother_{i} made Chonon Biri_{j} sing against her_{i} will (lit. ‘w/o wanting to cause it’).’
At first, it seems this extra phrase could describe either of two things. It could describe the action itself (Chonon Biri didn't want to sing). Or it could describe the causing (the mother didn't want to make Chonon Biri sing). The English translation ‘against her will’ can mean either one. But imakaskinmabi is not unclear in SK. The "same person" marker and the "make someone do it" ending -ma show exactly what it describes. Compare (87) below. There, a phrase with the same meaning describes the result, so the "someone else" marker is used instead:
(87) Ja-tian ja xontako jawen tita-n | xoi meni-ma-[a]i keen-yam[a]-ain-bi... | ‘Then, her_{j} mother_{i} made the unmarried girl_{j} give roasted meat / fish (to the man who had asked her in matrimony) even though she_{j} didn’t want to...’
A language can also make this clear in other ways. Spanish, for example, can use the male or female ending of a word. Look at these Spanish sentences, said by a woman:

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(88) a. Le hice pag-ar la cuenta por tont-o. | ‘I made him pay the bill because he is stupid.’ | b. Le hice pag-ar la cuenta por tont-a. | ‘I made him pay the bill because I am stupid.’
In (88a), the best reading is that the man paid the bill because he himself was stupid. In (88b), the woman was stupid to make him pay the bill.
Hindi works differently. In the examples below, the place of the word ‘slowly’ in the sentence decides what it describes. In (89a) it describes only the result. In (89b) it describes the whole sentence (from van Olphen 1975:199, see also Kulikov 1993:146-7):^{22}
(89) a. Admī-ne mātā-se bacce-ko dhīre khil-vā-yā | ‘The man had the mother feed the child slowly.’ | b. Admī-ne dhīre mātā-se bacce-ko khil-vā-yā | ‘The man slowly had the mother feed the child.’
Asheninka is a language that uses the order of word pieces to show what such describing words apply to in "make someone do it" forms (David Payne 2002).
In SK, the meaning ‘almost’ is an ending added to the verb. You saw this in sentences (51) and (52), shown again here as (90) and (91):
(90) E-n-ra nokon bake mawá-ma-kean-ke ishton | onanya-iba bo-yama-xon. | ‘I almost caused my son to die for not taking him to the onanya quickly.’

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(91) E-n-ra misho rete-kean-ke nokon kawá pi-ke-tian. | ‘I almost killed the cat for having eaten my patarashca.’
In the first example, the part that gives the reason makes it clear what -kean 'almost' applies to. I did something (I waited a long time before taking my son to the onanya) that almost caused my son to die. The second sentence seems unclear. It is probably unclear in the same ways as the English sentence ‘John almost killed Harry’ (Shibatani 1976:9). Did John almost do something, or did he do something that almost killed Harry?
(92) 
As for ishton ‘quickly’ in (90), its place in the sentence makes clear what it describes.
Next, I will look at a method that seems to be very special to SK (and maybe to Panoan languages in general). SK can change the ending of some extra phrases to agree with the person they describe. This makes clear what the phrase applies to.
Many parts marked as "same person" take different endings depending on the role of the person they describe. Extra phrases without their own verb do the same. In the intransitive sentences below, the place words can only be the forms for an intransitive doer or a receiver: tapon, bachin, and nii meran. The forms used for a doer with a receiver, tapon-xon, bachin-xon, and nii meran-xon, would make the sentences wrong:

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(93) Nokon ochíti-ra tapo-n ransa-[a]i. | ‘My dog is dancing on the palm-bark floor.’
According to Olphen (1975), this freedom of position is only possible with “second causatives.”
(94) Nokon bake-ra bachi-n oxa-[a]i. | ‘My child is sleeping in the mosquito net.’
(95) Nokon ochíti-ra jojo ik-ai nii meran. | ‘My dog is barking in the forest.’
But when the intransitive verb ransa- ‘dance’ gets a "make someone do it" ending, both forms of the place word are possible: the intransitive form and the doer-with-receiver form:
(96) E-n-ra nokon ochíti ransa-ma-[a]i tapo-n. | ‘I make my dog dance on the palm-bark floor.’ (specifies location of causee) | E-n-ra nokon ochíti ransa-ma-[a]i tapo-n-xon. | ‘I make my dog dance on the palm-bark floor.’ (specifies location of causer)
As you would expect, (96a) and (96b) mean different things. (96a) says that the dog is on the palm-bark floor, but the person causing it is not. (96b) says that the person causing it is on the palm-bark floor, and does not say where the dog is. So the intransitive form tapon gives the place of the one who does the result (the dog). The doer-with-receiver form tapon-xon gives the place of the one who does the causing. The next pairs of sentences show the same kind of difference:
(97) E-n-ra nokon bake oxa-ma-[a]i bachi-n. | ‘I make my child sleep in the mosquito net.’ (specifies location of causee)

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(97) b. E-n-ra nokon bake oxa-ma-[a]i bachi-n-xon. | ‘I make my child sleep in the mosquito net.’ (specifies location of causer)
(97a) says that the child sleeps in the mosquito net. (97b) says that both people are in the mosquito net, and the one causing it puts the child to sleep. In the same way, (98a) says that the person causing it stays somewhere else but sends her or his dog into the forest to bark (at animals). In (98b), both the person and the dog are in the forest, and the person makes the dog bark (at animals):
(98) a. E-n-ra nokon ochíti jojo i-ma-[a]i nii-meran. | ‘I make my dog bark in the forest.’ (specifies location of causee) | b. E-n-ra nokon ochíti jojo i-ma-[a]i nii-meran-xon. | ‘I make my dog bark in the forest.’ (specifies location of causer)
The next pair is especially interesting. Here, both the causing and the result are packed into a single base word. Even so, the extra phrase can still take either form:
(99) a. E-n-ra bake pake-ke weyóti-aino-a. | ‘I made the child fall from the hammock.’ (only the causee was in the hammock) | b. E-n-ra bake pake-ke weyóti-ain-xon. | ‘I made the child fall from the hammock.’ (the causer was also in the hammock.)
In example (100), an intransitive verb about body position gets the ending -n, which turns it into a transitive verb. The sentence also has a phrase telling where something goes, ani nontin. It has the receiver form (the doer form would be ani nontin-xon):

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(100) Ja-tian ani nonti-n westíora atsa xeati chomo | na-yása-n-kan-ai. | ‘Then, they put a jar of yuca beer inside the big canoe.’
So the phrase in (100) says that the jar is put inside the big canoe. It does not say that the people were in the canoe when they put the jar there. Compare (100) with (101) below. There, both the people drinking the yuca beer and the drink are inside the big canoe:
(101) a. ...ani nonti-n-xon westíora atsa xeati chomo keyo-kan-ke. | b. ...ani nonti-n westíora atsa xeati chomo keyo-kan-ke. | ‘...they finished a jar of yuca beer in the big canoe.’
You can read more about how "make someone do it" forms work with this agreement in 19.2.2.2. Here is my point. Even when the causing is packed into one word, or even into the base word itself, the grammar still seems to see two layers. That matches the event, which has two parts: the causing and the result. In this way, "make someone do it" forms (probably including single-word
"cause" verbs in general) do not seem to behave like any other kind of sentence in the language that describes a simple, single event.
This choice was not possible with the phrase ‘three times’ (cf. Shibatani 1976:15). The sentences below show that kimishai is the form for an intransitive doer, and kimishaakin is the form for a doer with a receiver:

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
(102) Bake-ra choron-ke kimisha-i. | ‘The child jumped three times.’
(103) Ochíti-nin-ra bake natex-ke kimisha a-kin. | ‘The dog bit the child three times.’
But in a "make someone do it" sentence like (104a) below, only the doer-with-receiver form is possible:
(104a) a. Sani-n-ra bake choron-ma-ke kimisha a-kin. | ‘Sani made the child jump three times.’
The sentence above means that both events happened three times: Sani handling the child, and the child jumping. The intransitive form kimishai cannot be used here to describe only the child's action in a "make someone do it" sentence:
(104b) b. Sani-n-ra bake choron-ma-ke kimisha-i. | ‘I made the child jump three times (I told him once to jump three times).’
I asked one of the people who helped me with the language how to say that Sani acted only once, but the child jumped three times. They gave me the sentence below, where ‘three times’ describes only the result:
(105) E-n-ra bake yoi-ke (westíora a-kin-bicho) | kimisha-i choron-ti. | ‘I told the child (once) to jump three times.’
Why does ‘three times’ behave differently from the place words? It is not the type of sentence, the base verb, or the roles of the people. In all these ways, (104b) is the same as (96a) and (98a). Instead, the reason may lie in the kind of phrase itself (see Ch. 19 on the difference between phrases of place and phrases of manner and amount). Note one thing here. Unlike place phrases, phrases of manner and amount always show by their ending whether they describe an intransitive doer or a doer with a receiver. The same phrase can even have two sets of such endings. These endings look like the "same person" markers of the PSS and SSS types.

h: Adverbial Scope and Causativization (which part an adverb applies to)
t:
I began this section by saying that we need to learn more about what describing phrases apply to, by comparing many languages. I focused on a way of making this clear that is special to Panoan languages. It uses the markers that tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else, and agreement with the person in general. We still need to learn more about how agreement and describing phrases work together. But the facts here show
a method that is rare among the world's languages and that, as far as I know, no one had written about before.

h: Summary
t:
In this chapter, I have looked at the main facts about "make someone do it" forms in SK: their word pieces, their sentence patterns and their meanings. I have also shown the many ways they connect with the difference between intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. I have not covered everything.
SK can say "make someone do it" with a single different word, and with a longer phrase using verbs like 'order' or 'ask' that do not guarantee the result. Besides these, SK has several grammar methods. At first, each seems to have its own job and not to compete with the others. The most general one is the ending -ma. When it is the normal or the only choice, -ma has a broad meaning. It can mean forcing, persuading, allowing, letting, or helping. -ma can go on any kind of verb. It can also follow any other "make someone do it" ending, even another -ma. A second ending, -n, goes only on a small, fixed set of nouns and intransitive verbs. Together with -t, it also takes part in two steps of word-building, using words about body position that are neither intransitive nor transitive verbs by themselves. In general, -n seems to have a more physical meaning.
-ma and -n cannot stand alone, and their meaning is not obvious. The "make it happen" form /ak/ is different. Its meaning is clear ('do'), and with some

h: Summary
t:
base words it is more independent in the sentence. /ak/ goes with nouns, "become ___" describing words, and the base words of extra phrases and of place words. These could be seen as verbs made of two words joined together. A different method, using one of two helper verbs, is found with sound words. In section 16.3.4, I suggested that which helper they take, and what they mean, depends on the people or things involved. Probably the most unusual method is the pairs of completely different verbs jo- / be- and ka- / bo-. For these, I suggested a link between "more than one" and "make someone do it." Finally, a vowel change inside the word can come together with an ending (yaka-t- ‘sit’ vs. yasa-n- ‘seat’). Verbs that can be used both ways with no change are rather rare.
Let us set aside the verbs that can be used both ways, the pairs of different verbs, the two-step forms and the helper verbs. Then SK "make someone do it" sentences are more complex than the plain sentences they come from, both in form and in meaning. In fact, they are built on top of the plain verb. When you add -ma, -n or /ak/ to a plain verb, a new doer comes in, and the old people in the sentence change roles. The one causing it always gets the doer marker (ERG). The one made to act, and anyone affected, get no marker, the plain form (ABS) (but see footnote 10). SK is quite relaxed: it allows more than one person in the plain form in the same sentence. So far, I have found no regular grammar method that marks different kinds of receivers differently. So it is easy to explain the markers in (most) "make someone do it" sentences. They follow the same pattern as ordinary transitive sentences and sentences with two receivers.

h: Summary
t:
A "make someone do it" ending and an ending that brings in an extra person can both appear on the same verb. In the natural speech I studied, the extra-person ending comes after the "make someone do it" ending.
Looking at the meanings in SK confirms earlier findings by other linguists. One is the difference between the true starting point of an event and a mere tool. Only the starting point can be the doer of a transitive verb. In 16.3.4 I also said that the choice between "make it happen" methods seems to depend on meaning. Does the change clearly need someone outside to make it happen? Then /ak/ is preferred. Or can the thing that changes be seen as somehow starting the event by its own inner force? Then -ma is chosen.
Many linguists have been interested in the idea that different "make someone do it" forms never mean exactly the same thing, and that they are used to tell “direct” from “indirect” causing. Whatever form the methods take, the SK facts support this idea. The different forms show different ways of picturing roughly the same real situation. When more than one method is possible, it is clear that these endings carry their own meaning and their own sense of force, just like the doer and receiver markers and ordinary words do. As I said above, when -ma is the only choice, its meaning is broad. But when it competes with another method, it clearly shows indirect causing, and the one made to act must be more active. Then -ma means ‘cause,’ ‘have,’ ‘allow’ or ‘contribute (to a process).’ On the other hand, -n and /ak/ express more

h: Summary
t:
direct ways of making someone do something. Here the person made to do it is more passive, more like something being handled. Shipibo-Konibo also uses these different endings to tell apart the meanings of a verb with several meanings. For example, menko-n- means ‘put sb. upside down’, but menkó-ma- means ‘place a hen in its nest so that it lays eggs’. They can also make two different transitive verbs from a verb with only one meaning. For example, bake a(k)- means ‘engender / have a child’, but bake-n- means ‘deliver’ a child’.
There is one interesting way to show the difference between direct and indirect causing. It was discussed in 16.3.2. First, an ending is added to a transitive verb that takes away its doer (the middle ending). Then the "make someone do it" ending -ma is added on top. Without these endings, the bare verb would indicate direct causing, by its own inherent force. The first ending cancels that force out. The result means that the receiver goes through the change of state by itself, without any obvious causer. (Linguists call this an anticausative construction.) Then -ma introduces a new, unusual kind of doer. This doer does not act directly. Instead, they allow the process to happen or contribute to it. And in this situation the person who changes plays a rather active part.

h: Summary
t:
