Shipibo-Konibo marks the doer with a special doer marker (the ergative), while the receiver takes the plain form (the absolutive). Languages that mark things this way are especially sensitive to how many people a verb involves. Adding a "make someone do it" ending adds one more person. Changes like this are expressed all over the grammar of Shipibo-Konibo. In most respects, "make someone do it" sentences appear to be modeled on simple sentences with the same number of people. As mentioned above, take an intransitive verb plus -ma. In how its people are marked, it acts just like a transitive verb. And a transitive verb plus -ma acts just like a verb with a doer and two receivers (like "give"). In many other ways, too, the grammar treats the "make someone do it" sentence as one single unit. This is true for keeping track of who is who, for choosing the small stand-in verb, for joining sentences together inside one sentence and across sentences, and
the markers on attached sentence parts that show who is doing what. Still, at least one process treats 'make someone do it' sentences differently from ordinary ones. In SK, words added to a sentence to say where or how someone is acting take a form that agrees with one person in the sentence (linguists call this participant agreement). In a 'make someone do it' sentence, this lets us say separately where the person causing it is, and where the person made to do it is. So each of them can be tied to their own action. More research is needed here. But simple sentences without a 'make someone do it' ending do not seem to allow these choices of form. Through these choices, SK grammar seems to say that at least some 'make someone do it' sentences are basically different from other sentences. We can see them as one “single complex macro-situation” made up of smaller “micro-situations” (to use Comrie’s 1989:165 terms). Each smaller situation can be described on its own. Most languages do not mark this difference in their grammar.

h: Introduction (introduction)
t:
This chapter describes the endings in Shipibo-Konibo that bring an extra person into the sentence (linguists call them applicatives). I base it on about 150 such sentences taken from natural speech, plus many examples I asked speakers for.
SK has three endings that bring an extra person into the sentence. The first is -xon, the “affective” ending: the action is done for someone’s good or to someone’s harm. The second is -kin ~ -kiin, the associative ending: the action is done together with someone. The third is -(V)naan ~ -(V)n, which means the action is done against someone. The second and third endings each have different forms. Which form you use depends partly on the length (in beats) of the verb they go on.^{1} These three kinds of ending are common in the world’s languages. So the SK system is not especially rich, either in the number or in the kinds of these endings. Still, these sentences in SK are interesting in several ways. Sometimes you can say the same thing without the ending, and sometimes you can’t. The receivers they bring in behave in special ways. And they interact with how many people the verb takes,
with what the people in the sentence must be like, and with which meaning is preferred for a given verb. Also, no one has yet studied these endings in detail in any Panoan language. So this book will help us understand Panoan grammar better. It will also add to what linguists know about endings that change how many people a verb takes.

h: Introduction (introduction)
t: In the rest of section 17.1, I give a general introduction to these endings, based on how they work in the world’s languages. This sets up what follows. I also look at how these endings relate to 'make someone do it' endings, and how this shows up in SK. (This will matter most for the 'together with' ending in section 17.4.1.) Section 17.1 ends with an introduction to the SK endings themselves. Sections 17.2, 17.3, and 17.4 are the heart of the chapter. They describe how the SK endings work today: how often they appear in texts, which verbs they go with, how the added receivers behave, and whether you can say the same thing without them. In section 17.5, I briefly show sentences with more than one such ending. Section 17.6 sums up what I found.

h: Definition of Applicative Construction (what this kind of sentence is)
t:
An applicative is a sentence with a special ending on the verb. The ending lets a person or thing who would normally sit at the edge of the sentence become the main receiver (Peterson 1999:1). It is a bit like English turning “I baked a cake for her” into “I baked her a cake.” Across languages, these sentences are
As Faust (1973:70-72) says, -kiin and -naan or -n go on verbs with an even number of
usually ones that add a receiver to the sentence (but see 17.1.2.6). Some languages are especially rich in these endings: Kinyarwanda (Bantu; Kimenyi 1980), Nez Perce (Sahaptian; Rude 1986), Nomatsiguenga (Maipuran Arawak; Wise 1971, David Payne 1990), Caquinte (Maipuran Arawak, Swift 1988), and Haka Lai (Tibeto-Burman; Peterson 1999).
Look at the following examples from Haka Lai. In this language, nouns mostly use a doer marker (ERG, the doer marker) and a plain form (ABS, the plain form), like SK. But the small pieces on the verb that point to the people in the sentence follow a different pattern, more like English. Sentence (1a) has an intransitive verb. So its only person is in the plain form, and the verb does not (and cannot) take a piece pointing to a receiver. In (1b), the ending -piak is added. It brings in a receiver, and the verb now carries a piece pointing to that receiver. Because there is now a receiver, the doer gets the doer marker. In meaning, -piak tells us that the added person is affected by the action. Here, that person benefits from it:

h: Definition of Applicative Construction (what this kind of sentence is)
t:
(1) tsewmaŋ door=ʔaʔ ʔa-kal | ‘Tsewmang went to the market.’ (Peterson 1999:11) | tsewmaŋ=niʔ door=ʔaʔ ʔa-ka-kal-piak | ‘Tsewmang went to the market for me.’ (Peterson 1999:11)
beats (syllables). -kin and -Vnaan or -Vn go on verbs with an odd number of beats. But see example (114).

h: Typological Variation (how languages differ in this)
t: This section gives an overview of the ways these endings can differ from language to language. Three of these ways will matter most for this book: how the endings relate to markers on nouns, whether you must use the ending or can choose to leave it out, and limits on which kinds of verbs they go with.

h: 17.1.2.1. Applicative and Oblique Nominal Markers: Cognate versus Alternative Forms
t:
In some languages, the verb ending has a twin: a marker on nouns that comes from the same source. Wise (2000) points out that this happens in some languages of the Peruvian Amazon, such as Yagua (Peba Yaguan), Arabela (Zaparoan), and Nomatsiguenga (Arawak Maipuran). Look at the Arabela examples below. They use -ta ~ -tia, a kind of 'with' ending: together with someone, or using something (from Rich 1999:54-57; also Wise 2000). Look for -ta or -tia in each sentence:
(2) kua morehaka tiurii-tia-ree-nihia | ‘I stumbled while carrying my load of yuca.’ (Rich 1999:55, Wise 2000)
(3) a. haniya kia-ta kia-nu pani-ya-ni | ‘I want to go with you.’ (Wise 2000) | b. kia kia-a-re kia nukua-ta | ‘Go with your mother!’ (Rich 1999:403)
Something similar has been reported for Warrwa (Eastern Nyulnyulan, Australia). There, the ending -ngany can go on both nouns and verbs. On a noun, -ngany mainly means 'using something'. On a verb, -ngany is the 'with / using' ending that brings in an extra person or thing^{2} (McGregor 1998:171).

h: 17.1.2.2. Encoding of Applicative Object
t:
In Warrwa, sometimes both the verb and the noun carry -ngany (or another edge-of-sentence marker) at the same time (McGregor ibid.). But first, let’s look at a sentence that follows the normal pattern. In the examples below, adding -ngany brings a second person into the sentence, with no marker. It also changes the doer: the doer goes from the plain form to the doer marker:
(4) a. linyju nguy jina. | ‘The policeman returned.’ | b. linyju-na nguy jina-ngany-jirr, kuya jirra. | ‘The policeman brought back their mother.’ (McGregor 1998:174)
Now look at (5) and (6). They break the normal pattern. Here, the added person or thing does not appear as a plain receiver with no marker.
It also marks something planned or intended for the future. In McGregor’s words, it marks “an implicated construction, which basically signals that the referent situation is projected or intended for the future” (McGregor 1998:171).
(5) biina jirrwadaj jan-ngany, bakal-ngany, | ‘She yandies (separates by shaking) the ant eggs in a coolamon.’ (McGregor 1998:191)
(6) ngayi-na nganjalany-ngany kinya wamba wariny-warri wamba | ‘I saw him with his mate.’ (McGregor 1998:185)
The Haka Lai sentence below shows another way the added receiver can differ from a normal receiver. The added receiver is in the plain form, not marked as an edge-of-sentence noun. Even so, the verb has no piece pointing to it. This is probably because those pieces on the verb only work for certain kinds of beings (Peterson 1999:13). Remember from (1b) that on the verb, the piece for the doer comes before the piece for the receiver:

h: 17.1.2.2. Encoding of Applicative Object
t:
(7) ka-naam khaa tsewmaŋ=niʔ ʔa-ń-tshuʔn-naak. | ‘Tsewmang stabbed you with my knife.’ (Peterson 1999:13)
Still, an ending on the verb can show that the added receiver is more than one:
(8) tsewmaŋ=niʔ ka-naam khaa ʔa-ń-tshuʔn-naak-hnaa | ‘Tsewmang stabbed you (sg.) with my knives.’ (Peterson 1999:14)

h: 17.1.2.3. Monofunctional versus Polyfunctional Applicative Forms
t:
Languages also differ in another way. Some use one single ending for several different roles of the added person. Others use a separate ending for each role.3 For example, Haka Lai has seven such endings, each with its own meaning. In Kichaga (Bantu), one single ending gives a whole range of meanings. A language can also have both kinds (e.g., Tukang Besi, Donohue 1999; see also Peterson 1999:4-8, 31-33).
In some Arawak languages of Peru, such as Pajonal Asheninka and Yanesha, one verb ending can have a rather vague meaning. It can be translated as “with reference to, including, or concerning X” (Wise 1986:592). Look at the Yanesha examples below with the ending -amʸpʸ (unless I say otherwise, they come from Wise 2000, originally in Duff-Tripp 1997:100):
(9) 0-kow-een-aan chesha-tʸoll | ‘S/he is looking at the small child.’ | 0-kow-amʸpʸ-een-aan chesha-tʸoll | ‘S/he is caring for the small child.’
(10) ye-maʔyoch-een-s-a | ‘We pray to you (pl).’
Linguists have also called these two kinds “homophonous” and “non-homophonous” applicative forms: one form that sounds the same for every meaning, versus different-sounding forms (Peterson op. cit).
(10) b. ye-maʔyoch-amʸpʸ-een-s-a | ‘We pray for you (pl) (along with others).’
(11) a. 0-chekmʸ-et-een tʸooñ-o | ‘It’s dark / night along the trail.’ | b. ye-chekmʸ-et-amypy-es tʸooñ-o | ‘The darkness overtook us (while we were still) on the trail.’

h: 17.1.2.3. Monofunctional versus Polyfunctional Applicative Forms
t:
(12) a. 0-ahn-om-a | ‘It (the bird) flew.’ | b. y-ahn-om-amʸpʸ-s-a | ‘We flew (in the plane).’
(13) a. ne-maht-a | ‘I run.’ (Wise 1986:592) | b. ne-maht-amʸpʸ-s-apy-a | ‘I run away from you.’ (Wise 1986:592)
(14) y-atʸoor-amʸpʸ-een-ʸ ony | ‘We fan the fire to heat the water.’ (lit. ‘we blow / fan the water contained’)
(15) 0-aʔnos-amʸpʸ-s-aan-a rreera po-choy-oor | ‘He climbed up to where the hawk’s chicks were.’
A similarly vague ending that “adds a person” to the sentence has been found in Tariana, a Northern Arawak language (Aikhenvald 2000:166-170). As for the Arabela ending shown in (2), Rich (1999:54) describes it as a general way of adding a receiver,
a tool that can do several different jobs. It can mean a passive kind of 'with someone', containing something, or being in an unusual state. It can even show that the speaker feels pity.

h: 17.1.2.4. Symmetry versus Asymmetry of Objects
t:
As discussed in 12.3, linguists who study Bantu languages use the term “symmetrical object.” It describes a language where two receivers can both behave like main receivers at the same time. This happens even though the language has ways to tell a direct receiver from an indirect one (in English “give the boy a book”, the book and the boy) (Bresnan and Moshi 1990). SK is different. It has no regular grammar tool to tell direct and indirect receivers apart.
These sentences differ, both between languages and inside one language, in how the added receiver and the normal receiver share the features of a receiver. They also differ between sentences with different endings. As mentioned above, in Haka Lai the pieces on the verb that point to people only work for certain kinds of beings. An added receiver who benefits from the action gets a piece on the verb showing who it is (ex. (1b)). An added tool does not (ex. (7)). But the tool can still get an ending after the verb showing that it is more than one (ex. (8)). Normal and added receivers can also differ in other features. These include word order, markers on the noun, whether they can become the subject of a passive sentence (“the book was given”), whether they can be described by a 'who/which…' part, whether they control who is meant in the next part of the sentence, whether they can be used with 'to yourself' and 'to each other' endings, and so on.

h: 17.1.2.4. Symmetry versus Asymmetry of Objects
t:
In Tukang Besi, the kind of base verb helps decide how the added receiver behaves (Donohue 1999). The role of the added receiver matters too. Tukang Besi has one ending, -ako, with several meanings: giving to someone (dative), using a tool (instrument), the thing moved or talked about (theme), a cause, and a purpose. Sentences (16)-(18) show that an added receiver with the 'to someone' meaning can become the main person of the sentence (the nominative, exx. (18a-b)) and be shown on the verb by receiver endings. An added receiver with the 'theme' meaning cannot:
Dative:
(16) a. No-ala te kau. | ‘She fetched the wood.’ | b. No-ala-ako te ina-su te kau. | ‘She fetched the wood as a favour for my mother.’ (Donohue 1999:231)
Theme:
(17) a. No-balo te ama-no | ‘She answered her uncle.’ (Donohue 1999:231) | b. No-balo-ako te kampo te ama-no. | ‘She answered her uncle with the (name of the, information about the) village.’ (Donohue 1999:232)
Addition of object suffix to the verb
(18) a. No-ala-ako-'e na ina-su. | ‘She fetched (it) as a favour to my mother.’ (Donohue 1999:232) | b. No-balo-ako-'e na kampo. | ‘She answered with the (name of the, information about the) village.’ (Donohue 1999:232)
The normal receiver also behaves differently depending on the role of the added receiver. For example, take a sentence with the 'to someone' (dative) ending. Its normal receiver can be described by a 'who/which…' part. In a sentence with the 'theme' ending, it cannot. Donohue (op. cit.:268) concludes that “rather than classifying a language, or even a construction, as symmetrical or asymmetrical, each individual combination of grammatical construction, semantic role, and transitivity needs to be separately examined.” In other words, we have to look at each case on its own.

h: 17.1.2.5. Obligatory versus Optional Applicative Types
t:
The definition in 17.1.1 doesn’t say so, but a typical sentence with this kind of ending has an ordinary alternative without it. English works the same way: “I baked a cake for her” and “I baked her a cake.” You can see this in the Kinyarwanda examples below:
(19) a. Umugóre a-rá-vug-a n’âgahiinda. | ‘The woman is talking with sorrow.’ (Kimenyi 1980:84)
(None) b. Umugóre a-rá-vug-an-a agahiinda. | ‘The woman is talking with sorrow.’ (Kimenyi 1980:84)
However, some languages have one or more of these endings that you must use. That is, there is no ordinary sentence without the ending that means about the same. Tzotzil is like this. The only way to say who receives something is to add the ending -be to the verb:
(20) a. Ba y-ak’-0 ʔune. | ‘He went to give it.’ | b. ti mi č-av-ak’-b-on ʔep tak'ine | ‘if you will give me a lot of money’ (Aissen 1983:280)
Once -be is added, the person who receives works as the main receiver. The verb shows its person and number, and it can become the subject of a passive sentence. Nouns in Tzotzil have no markers like the doer marker (Aissen 1983).

h: 17.1.2.6. Valency-Increasing versus Semantic Role Rearrangement Applicative Types
t:
This point will not matter for SK, but it should be mentioned. In many languages, adding such an ending does not always add a person to the sentence, especially with a transitive verb. That is why
some linguists describe these endings as shuffling the roles of the people already in the sentence, rather than adding one (Comrie 1985:312-319).
Doris Payne (2000) points out that in Yagua the ending -ta sometimes adds no receiver and does not change the role of a receiver. Instead, it makes the verb’s meaning stronger, more “intense.” We can see the same thing if we compare the Yanesha examples (9a) and (9b). In (9b), the ending did not add a piece on the verb pointing to a receiver, unlike in (13b). Instead, it added the greater “intensity” that Payne mentions. In the same way, I said above that the Arabela ending can add unusual meanings, such as an unusual state or even the speaker’s pity. Such uses have also been reported in Bantu languages (D. L. Payne op.cit.).

h: 17.1.2.7. Transitivity Restrictions
t:
There are two kinds of limits on which verbs these endings go with. Either the verb must have at least a certain number of people, or it may have at most a certain number.
In Tzotzil, the 'for someone' ending -be can only go on transitive verbs (Aissen 1983:294-296). Something similar has been noted for Matses, a Panoan language (Kneeland 1979). Shibatani (1996) explains why the 'for someone' ending in many languages needs such a minimum. It is based on the idea of ‘give’, and giving needs three people: a giver, a thing, and a receiver.
On the other hand, some languages do not allow these endings on verbs that already have two receivers, like ‘give’. These include the Papuan languages Yimas and Alamblak, and Sesotho (Narrow Bantu) (Peterson 1999:47). The examples below are from Sesotho:
(21) a. ntate o-f-a bana lijo | ‘My father gives food to the children.’ (Peterson 1999:47, from Machobane 1989:109) | b. ntata o-f-el-a morena bana lijo | ‘My father gives food to the children for the chief.’ (Peterson 1999:47, from Machobane 1989:111)

h: Functions of Applicative Constructions (what it is used for)
t:
Why do languages have these endings? From the point of view of how we think, they are different ways of looking at the same scene (Croft 1994). They bring a person from the edge of the scene onto center stage (T. Payne 1999), by making it the main receiver. The doer is where the event starts, its “ultimate cause.” The receiver is where it ends, its “final result.” Other nouns, marked at the edge of the sentence, are things more or less involved in the event. With one of these endings, the person from the edge, not the normal receiver of the verb, becomes the endpoint of the action. It becomes the “chief locus of the effect of the action” (Croft op.cit.): the main place where the action has its effect.
Rude (1986) studied how these sentences are used in Nez Perce (Sahaptian) talk and stories. He shows that added receivers are more often what the story is about (more “topical”) than other receivers. Rude used Givón’s (1983) way of measuring “topic continuity”: how recently a person was mentioned, and how long they keep being mentioned. With a similar goal, Peterson (1999:49-77) studied stories in Haka Lai and Wolof (Niger Congo). He used two methods: Givón’s (1983) “topic continuity” and Thompson’s (1990) “topicworthiness.” Peterson’s results suggest one key difference: whether the added receiver is a living being or a thing. Added receivers that are living beings are talked about as much as people who receive things, and more than things that are simply acted on. They are also far more topical than the same people marked at the edge of the sentence. Added receivers that are things are usually not very topical. In those cases, the ending seems to be used for grammar reasons. It lets the thing be replaced by a pronoun. It is also the preferred way to make it a receiver in 'who/which…' descriptions, in “it was X that…” sentences, or when it is moved to the front. Similar reasons have been found in Olutec (Mixean). There, the ending is required when the edge-of-sentence person is described by a 'who/which…' part, put in focus with “it was X that…”, or asked about. It is also required “when it is part of conjoined clauses in which the extra-thematic argument acts as clausal topic” (Zavala 2002), that is, when it is what the joined sentences are about. So making an edge-of-sentence person into the main receiver can be a way to put it in the right slot, so that other grammar rules can work on it. Or it lets that person become what the conversation is about (see also Dixon 2000:32).

h: Functions of Applicative Constructions (what it is used for)
t:
Peterson (op. cit.:37-38) also points out that in some languages, the main reason to use these endings may be meaning. For example, they can tell 'being at a place' apart from 'moving toward a place'. As mentioned earlier, these endings can also add shades of meaning, such as greater intensity, the speaker’s pity, and maybe doing something on purpose.
In general, sentences with these endings are more unusual than the ordinary sentences without them (where those exist). They are more unusual both in form and in use. They may also be less frequent (McGregor 1998:194).

h: Applicativization and Causativization (adding a person vs. "make someone do it")
t:
Endings that bring in an extra person and 'make someone do it' endings usually do the same basic job: they add someone to the sentence. The difference is who they add. The first kind adds a receiver who is not simply acted on. The 'make someone do it' ending adds a new doer, the one who causes the action. Many languages that are neither related nor near each other use the same ending for both jobs, especially for 'for someone' and 'make someone do it'.4 According to Song (1990:181-9), this is common in North and Central American languages such as Sierra Miwok (Miwok), Jacaltec (Mayan), Maidu (Penutian), and the Uto-Aztecan family. The same is found in certain Aboriginal
Shibatani and Pardeshi (2002) discuss the ideas behind this link between the two kinds of endings; see also 16.2.1. More research is needed to find out which of these endings can also mean 'make someone do it'.
languages of Australia, in the Austronesian family, in Khasi (Mon-Khmer), and in Wolof (Niger Congo) (Comrie 1981:176).
In South America, the Yagua ending -ta may come from the same source as the 'make someone do it' ending -tániy. But in Yagua today, they are best treated as two different word pieces (T. Payne 1999).
In some languages, the meaning of such a double-job ending depends on the kind of verb it goes with. For example, Asheninka (Maipuran Arawak) has an ending -akag, called the “inflectional causative.” On most verbs of physical activity, it can mean two things: 'make someone do it' or 'do it together with someone'. In real stories and talk, the 'together with' meaning is the most common (David Payne 2002:490-491):

h: Applicativization and Causativization (adding a person vs. "make someone do it")
t:
(22) j-atai-t-aka-an-ak-e-ri jenoki panko-tsi-ki. | ‘They climbed up with him / caused him to climb up high in the house.’
But on verbs like ‘live,’ only the 'make someone do it' meaning is possible, as shown below:
(23) j-aña-aka-ak-e-ri | ‘He caused them to live on’ (i.e. did something dramatic, perhaps even sacrificing his own life, to enable his family to go on living). ‘he lived with them’
In the same way, in Seko Padang (Western Austronesian), the ending -ing is said to add an extra receiver on transitive verbs, but to mean 'make someone do it' with certain
intransitive verbs (T. Payne 1999, exx. 16-17). Austin (1993:5) says that some Australian languages have a single ending that does either job, depending on the kind of verb. Other Australian languages have two or more endings. One goes on intransitive verbs where something just happens to you (like ‘fall’) and makes 'make someone do it' verbs. The other goes only on intransitive verbs where you act on purpose (like ‘dance’) and adds an extra person. In Hualapai (Yuman), the same verb ending makes 'make someone do it' verbs from verbs of being, but 'for someone' verbs from verbs of action (Ichihashi-Nakayama 1996:232).
As I showed in earlier work (Valenzuela 1997:100-131), SK uses different endings for 'make someone do it' and for bringing in an extra receiver. This suggests that SK sees adding a new doer as different from adding a new receiver. Still, as shown in 16.2.1, there are sentences where the two meet. In the sentence below, the 'together with' ending -kin is used instead of the 'make someone do it' ending -ma. It expresses a special, indirect kind of making someone do something. Unlike (20b), (20a) means that the old woman also goes into the mosquito net:

h: Applicativization and Causativization (adding a person vs. "make someone do it")
t:
(24) a. Yoxaman-ra bake bachi-n jiki-kin-ke. | ‘The old woman made the child enter the mosquito net (by entering herself). / The old woman accompanied the child into the mosquito net. / The old woman helped the child enter the mosquito net.’ | b. Yoxaman-ra bake bachi-n jiki-ma-ke. | ‘The old woman made / had the child enter the mosquito net (but she did not enter herself).
I will come back to this kind of causing, where the causer joins in (linguists call it sociative causation), in section 17.4.1, with the verb tee- ‘work.’

h: Applicatives in Shipibo-Konibo (these endings in Shipibo)
t:
As I said in the introduction, SK has three different endings that bring in an extra person. They are the affective ending -xon (for someone’s good or harm), the associative ending -kin ~ -kiin (together with someone), and the specific 'harm' ending -(V)naan ~ -(V)n (against someone). These endings come right after the bare verb. They usually come before the other endings: the 'modifying' endings,^5 and the endings for time, number, and aspect (whether an action is finished or ongoing). The next sections will show that each of the three endings adds one person to the sentence. Another feature of SK, and probably of all Panoan languages, is this: these endings have no twin marker on nouns (see 17.2.5, 17.3.6, and 17.4.4). Table 17.1 shows that the three endings differ a lot in how often they appear in texts. They also go with intransitive verbs and with transitive verbs in different amounts. The intransitive column also includes intransitive verbs that take an extra edge-of-sentence noun, and 'to each other' verbs. The transitive column also includes verbs with two receivers, like ‘give’. Under “others” I put (more) unusual verbs that do not fit well in either group:
By “modifying” endings on the verb I mean endings such as 'not' and 'want to'. I also mean other endings whose meanings other languages usually express with separate words, like ‘quickly’ or ‘again’ (see 7.7).

h: The Affective -Xon (-xon: doing something for or about someone)
t:
Adding -xon to a verb brings in a receiver. That person is helped or harmed by what the verb describes (linguists call this person the beneficiary or maleficiary). Across the world’s languages, the 'for someone’s good' ending is said to be the most common of these endings (Croft 1994:95, Peterson 1999:4 and Chapter 5).
As Table 17.1 shows, -xon is by far the most frequent of these endings. It can go on both intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. But it is used far more often with transitive verbs. Table 17.2 lists the verbs that -xon goes on in my texts. The number of times each verb appears is given in brackets.^6
The lists of verbs and numbers in Tables 17.2, 17.4, and 17.6 come from my own collection of texts. I don’t claim anything about which verbs these endings might go with in a different collection. Still, I decided to include this information to show which verbs the endings do occur with. These endings can be used freely with new verbs. But that does not mean that in real talk they appear with every possible verb. The numbers give a general idea of how often these sentences occur.
I count the verb wina- ‘row’ as an unusual transitive verb, for these reasons. wina- makes other words in the sentence take their transitive forms. Its doer must get the doer marker (ERG, the doer marker), and words that agree with the doer take the doer forms. Also, when I ask speakers, wina- allows a receiver in the plain form: a means of transport such as a canoe, or a person. However, in all the texts I have seen so far, wina- never has a receiver (see also Valenzuela 1997:181-184).

h: -Xon with Intransitive Stems (-xon with intransitive verbs)
t:
When -xon goes on an intransitive verb, it turns it into a transitive verb by adding a second person. The person who was already there now gets the doer marker (ERG). The added receiver is in the plain form (ABS). Look at the examples below. In (25), the doer has no marker. In (26), once -xon is added, the doer gets the doer marker -n.
(25) Pexé Piko-ra tee-ke. / Pexé Piko-n-ra | ‘Pexé Piko worked.’
(26) Pexé Piko-n-ra e-a tee-xon-ke. / Pexé Piko-ra | ‘Pexé Piko worked for me (e.g., in my chacra).’
(27) Kashibo joni-ra reken-ke. | ‘The Kashibo man led (the way).’
(28) Kashibo joni-n-ra Shipibo reken-xon-ke jawen | kaibo betan rete-anan-ti-nko-bo. | ‘The Kashibo man led (the way) for the Shipibo during the confrontations against his fellow Kashibos.’
With some verbs, a -xon sentence can mean that the doer does the action in place of the person -xon refers to. English “I’ll work for you” can mean the same thing:
(29) E-a isin-ai-tian-ra nokon wetsa-n e-a | tee-tan-xon-ke. | ‘Since I was sick, my brother went to work for me.’
Whether -xon means 'for someone’s good' or 'to someone’s harm' is often decided by the situation. Of course, the meaning of the verb matters a lot too, because it makes one reading more likely. For example, on verbs such as tee- ‘work’ or jo- ‘come,’ -xon most likely means 'for someone’s good' (ex. 29). On verbs such as isin- ‘get sick,’ mawat- ~ mawá- ‘die,’ rabin- ‘feel embarrassed,’ or jison- ‘urinate,’ the 'to someone’s harm' meaning is the most likely. Look at the example below (see also (38)):

h: -Xon with Intransitive Stems (-xon with intransitive verbs)
t:
(30) Bake-n-ra e-a isin-xon-ai. | ‘My child is sick on me.’
In the sentence below, either meaning is possible, good or harm. It depends on the situation and on the culture:
(31) Nokon bake-n-ra e-a kinan-xon-ke. | ‘My child vomited (to my benefit / detriment).’
Shipibo parents and grandparents treat their boys with plant medicine so that they become good fishers and hunters. This treatment makes the child vomit. The vomiting is meant to free the child from bad traits such as laziness or poor shooting. In that situation, the sentence above would mean 'for my good'. But if the child throws up for no clear reason, the same sentence would mean harm, since it could mean the child is sick. In the same way, if we replace the verb kinan- in (31) with oxa- ‘sleep,’ we get ‘My child slept (to my benefit / detriment).’ Again, which meaning is meant would depend on the situation.
Examples (32)-(34) show -xon used in my texts to mean harm to someone. In (32), a woman is advised to use a certain piripiri^8. She would use it if she wants to leave her partner but thinks he will not agree. So using the piripiri is seen as harmful to the man’s interests:
The pechi waste is a type of piripiri (a plant with special powers). It is used when you want your husband, wife, or lover to leave you.

h: -Xon with Intransitive Stems (-xon with intransitive verbs)
t:
(32) Ja joni-shoko mi-on keen-ai-bi | mi-a ja-on keen-yama-kin, | mi-n pe-chi waste-n nashi-xon-ti atipan-ke. | ‘Even if that little man loves you, if you do not love him, you can bathe with the “to be abandoned” piripiri (to his detriment).’
The example below uses the intransitive verb korá- ‘to be noisy, make noise (said of several people).’ A woman needs to concentrate when she makes pottery. So children making noise around her clearly harms her work:
(33) No-n chomo ak-ai-tian bake-baon no-a korá-xon-ti | yama-ke. | ‘When we are making pottery, the children must not produce noise (to our detriment).’
In Shipibo culture, the father of a newborn baby must carefully follow a set of rules. He must avoid certain activities so as not to harm the baby’s healthy growth. For example, he must not eat certain kinds of meat, touch certain trees in the forest, lift heavy things, have sex (especially with a woman other than the baby’s mother), or play soccer. In (34), the father broke one of these rules, so his child has been harmed:
(34) Jawen papa-n yora-n i-xon-a bicha-bo | kinan-ai ja bake-shoko-n. | ‘Because his father had sexual intercourse (to the baby’s detriment), the baby is vomiting phlegm.’
Example (35) says the same thing as (34) in another way. Here it is clear that the baby is the added receiver in the part of the sentence that gives the cause. Notice also something in both examples. The ending -a shows that the receiver of one part is the one the next part is about. In both sentences, that receiver is the person affected by -xon (cf. 17.2.3.4):

h: -Xon with Intransitive Stems (-xon with intransitive verbs)
t:
(35) Bake-shoko jawen papa-n yora-n i-xon-a | bicha-bo kinan-ai. | ‘Because its father had sexual intercourse to its detriment, the baby is vomiting phlegm.’
The ending -isi, which makes something sound bad or pitiful, can force the 'harm' meaning of -xon. Without it, the sentence would most likely mean 'for someone’s good':
(36) a. Oa-tonon-ra jo-xon-ke. | ‘Those (people) came (to my benefit).’ | b. Oa-tonioinsi-ra jo-xon-ke. | ‘Those (people) came (to my detriment).’
The next examples show -xon meaning 'for someone’s good' (37) and 'to someone’s harm' (38). Here it goes on intransitive verbs where the person does not act on purpose: things just happen to them (like ‘grow’ or ‘die’). Once -xon is added, the whole sentence becomes a transitive sentence. So the person who was already there gets the doer marker (ERG):
(37) Nokon choncho-baon-ra moa e-a ani-xon-ke. | ‘My chickens grew already (to my benefit).’
(38) Nokon shino-n-ra e-a mawá-xon-ke. | ‘My monkey died on me.’9
Examples (39) and (40) show -xon on these 'things just happen' verbs, even when the one the sentence is about is a thing, not a living being:
(39) Atsa xeati-nin-ra moa no-a pae-xon-ke. | ‘The yuca beer already fermented to our benefit.’
(40) Nonti-n-ra e-a payó-xon-ke. | ‘(My) canoe became rotten to my detriment.’
These examples are especially interesting when we compare other languages. Some languages only allow the doer of such a sentence to be someone who acts on purpose, like a person (Austin 1997, Ichihashi-Nakayama 1996, Shibatani and Pardeshi 2002). SK does not have this limit.

h: -Xon with Intransitive Stems (-xon with intransitive verbs)
t:
Intransitive verbs made from a noun, a describing word, or even a place word (like ‘in the middle of’), with no added ending, can also take the affective ending -xon (see also exx. (28) and (39)):
The form mawá-xon- cannot be used when the one who dies is a person (Yoi Sani, p.c. 2000).
() shino | ‘monkey’ | shino- | ‘turn into a monkey, behave like a monkey’
(41) Ranoman-ra bake-bo shino-xon-ke. | ‘The young man behaves like a monkey to please the children.’
() napon | ‘in the middle / center of’ | napon- | ‘get to the middle / center (e.g. of the river or lake)’
(42) Nokon bake-n-ra e-a napon-xon-ke e-n | rishki-kas-a-bi. | ‘My child got to the middle (of the river / lake) to my detriment, because I wanted to hit him.’
As I will discuss in 17.2.2 and 17.3.1, -xon can mean both good and harm for a reason: intransitive verbs usually cannot take the special 'harm' ending.

h: -Xon with Transitive Stems (-xon with transitive verbs)
t:
So far, I have shown that -xon can go on different kinds of intransitive verbs. But in natural speech, -xon mostly goes on transitive verbs. There, -xon almost always means 'for someone’s good'. Look at these examples from my texts:
(43) E-a nonti a-xon-we! | ‘Make a canoe for me!’
(44) “E-n mi-a raan-xon-i jo-bá-non westíora nonti ani bocho kabóri.” | Jain-xon-ronki napó-xon-a iki kabóri... | ‘“I am going to send you (with sb. else) a big canoe full of taricayas (k. turtle);” (he said). Then he placed the taricayas inside (the canoe)...’
(45) Ja-tian jawe-bi maxká-yam[a]-ai: wetsa-n-ki piti | bena-xon-ai, wetsa-n wai oro-xon-ai; ja-ska-ra. | ‘Then, (the shaman woman with two husbands) did not lack anything: while one (husband) searched for food / fish (for her), the other one cleared the chacra (for her); so it was.’
The next two sentences from my texts go against the rule that -xon on a transitive verb always means 'for someone’s good'. Both include the 'not' ending -yama:
(46) Ja-tian ja bake-shoko jawen ani-baon jawe-bi | a-xon-yama-a jakon-shoko ani-ai, wini-yam-ai. | ‘Then, if its parents have not done anything (prohibited) to its detriment that baby will grow nicely, it will not cry.’
(47) No-n bene pota-bain-a noibati-shoko, no-n | ja-ská-a-xon-ti atipan-yama-ke. | ‘And as to the poor husband whom we have left (in the village), we cannot do this (i.e. be unfaithful) on him.’

h: -Xon with Transitive Stems (-xon with transitive verbs)
t:
There is one more thing to notice. In both sentences above, -xon is added to the same verb, a(k)-. This is the general ‘do’ verb that can stand in for other transitive verbs (linguists call it a pro-verb). So maybe these two odd cases are not real exceptions. One idea is that a-xon- has frozen into a fixed word with its own meaning. Another idea is that ak- simply can't take the ‘against someone’ ending (linguists call it the malefactive applicative), so -xon fills in for it (but see 17.2.2).^{10}
Here are more cases where -xon plus the ‘not’ ending -yama gives a ‘to someone's harm’ meaning. The ending -yama is added to a verb that already has -xon-. One of them, ninká-xon- in (48), seems to be turning into a fixed expression in SK. People who speak both languages translate ninká-xon- with the Spanish hacer caso ‘pay attention, listen to, follow somebody’s advice:’
(48) Piróta a-ti-n no-a a-kan-ai alcalde i-táanan; jakon a-kin | no-a ninká-xon-yama-kan-ai no-n jema maxkat-a jawéki-bo | no-n yoiy-ai-tian. | ‘Once elected mayor (the former candidates) treat us like a ball (i.e. they send us from one office to the next one); they don’t listen to us when we expose to them the necessities of our town.’
The expression senen a-xon-, shown below, also seems to have frozen into a fixed meaning: ‘comply with something:’

h: -Xon with Transitive Stems (-xon with transitive verbs)
t:
(49) Moa no-a senen'a-xon-yama-kan-ai-tian no-n xepo-ti ja-ke
Phil Young (p.c.) pointed out to me that in both cases the harmful thing does not actually happen. That is, both are about something harmful __not__ happening.
(None) karaboso-ain westíora nete. | ‘When people don’t comply with their obligations towards us, we have to lock them in the village jail for one day.’
The doer in these sentences does not have to be a person. It can even be a force of nature, like the wind or the river. This works when -xon is added to a transitive verb:
(50) E-a oi jene-n nokon nonti choka-xon-a. | ‘The rain washed my canoe well to my benefit.’
(51) Bai koshi-n-ra e-a nokon pisha be-xon-ke. | ‘The water current brought my bag (to the shore) to my benefit.’
(52) Bari-n-ra nokon chopa e-a ishton manxan a-xonke. | ‘The sun dried my clothes very quickly to my benefit.’
The doer does not need to be a person or even a living thing. But the extra person who gets the benefit does seem to have to be alive (a person or an animal). The same goes for the person who is harmed (see 17.3.3):
(53) E-n-ra joshin pitso / shino be-xon-ke. | ‘I brought ripe banana for (my) paroqueet / capuchin monkey.’
(54) E-n-ra pei xobo be-xon-ke. | ‘I brought leaves for my house (i.e. for the roof).’ | E-n-ra pei be-ke xobo jakon a-noxon. | ‘I brought leaves to improve my house.’

h: -Xon with Transitive Stems (-xon with transitive verbs)
t:
(55) E-n-ra iskoira kirika-bo be-xon-ke. | ‘I brought books for the school.’ | E-n-ra kirika-bo be-ke iskoira-na i-ti. | ‘I brought books for the school (lit. so that they are of the school).’
Transitive verbs come in two kinds. Some have one receiver (‘cut something’). Others have two, like ‘give something to someone’ (linguists call these ditransitive verbs). In the stories I recorded, -xon appears only once on a two-receiver verb. Here too, -xon adds one more person to the sentence. This example is given as (58) in the next section.

h: Object Properties in -Xon Applicative Constructions (how the new receiver behaves)
t: When -xon is added to a transitive verb, the sentence ends up with two receivers. One is the ordinary receiver of the verb (the thing cut, the canoe made). The other is the extra person brought in by -xon (the person it is done for). In this section I ask a simple question: does Shipibo treat these two receivers the same way, or differently? Linguists test this in many languages with several checks. Some of those checks don't apply to SK. SK verbs don't change their form to agree with the receiver (or the doer). SK also has no ordinary passive (like English ‘was cut’), nor its mirror image. So I will use only the checks that make sense for SK. These are: the order of the words, the markers they carry, whether each one can be described by a ‘who/which…’ part, which one can mean ‘each other’, and which one can be picked up by a linked sentence.

h: 17.2.3.1. Coding Properties: Case-Marking and Constituent Order
t:
When -xon is added to a transitive verb, the verb ends up with two receivers. Both receivers appear in the plain form, with no marker (ABS). And their order in the sentence is not fixed. So neither word order nor markers can tell you which one is which. Look at example (56). The two receivers are equally ‘alive’ (both are people). Either one can be understood as the person the action is done to, or as the person it is done for:
(56) E-n-ra Rawa Piko kopi-xon-ke. | ‘(In return) I cast a spell on Rawa to Piko’s benefit.’ / | ‘(In return) I cast a spell on Piko to Rawa’s benefit.’
At least when I asked speakers directly, either receiver could come first. This was true even when one receiver was clearly a person and the other was a thing:
(57) a. Ainbo-nin-ra meráya tari a-xon-ke. | b. Ainbo-nin-ra tari meráya a-xon-ke. | ‘The woman made a tari (traditional men’s clothes) for the great shaman.’
The next sentence is the only case in my recorded stories where -xon is added to a two-receiver verb. As usual in real stories with many people involved, not every receiver is actually said out loud in the sentence:
(58) Awakan yoiy-a iki, “mi-n ibo e-a yoi-xon-tan-we,” | a-kin-ki ak-á iki, kimisha-a-kin. | ‘The tapir told (the fish), “go tell your owner for me!” So he said (to it) three times.’

h: 17.2.3.1. Coding Properties: Case-Marking and Constituent Order
t:
Still, when I asked speakers, they easily accepted sentences with all three people said out loud, all of them in the plain form with no marker:
(59) Nokon papa-n-ra e-a Kesten Beso jawen baba | yoká-xon-ke, e-n awin a-ti. | ‘My father asked Kesten Beso for his granddaughter for me, so that I could marry her.’
Linguists have another test to tell the two receivers apart. They check which one can be moved to the very front of the sentence, set off from the rest (linguists call this left-dislocation). Peterson (1999:16-22) found this in Haka Lai, a language of Burma. There, only the extra receiver brought in by the ending can be moved to the front, not the ordinary receiver. (The ordinary one can be moved only if the other one has a ‘this/that’ word with it.) Look at the next Haka Lai examples:
(60) tsewmaŋ=niʔ taaynaamkooŋ niihuu ʔa-0-tshiʔm-piak | ‘Tsewmang said it to Niihuu for Taaynaamkoong.’
(61) taaynaamkooŋ tsewmaŋ=niʔ niihuu ʔa-0-tshiʔm-piak | ‘Tsewmang said it to Niihuu for Taaynaamkoong.’ |  ‘Tsewmang said it to Taaynaamkoong for Niihuu.’
(62) niihuu tsewmaŋ=niʔ taaynaamkooŋ ʔa-0-tshiʔm-piak | ‘Tsewmang said it to Niihuu for Taaynaamkoong.’ | ‘Tsewmang said it to Taaynaamkoong for Niihuu.’
In SK, though, either receiver can be moved to the front:
(63) a. E-n-ra bake tita raan-xon-ke. | b. Bake-ra e-n tita raan-xon-ke. | ‘I sent my child for mother (e.g. to accompany her).’ / | ‘I sent mother for my child.’)

h: 17.2.3.1. Coding Properties: Case-Marking and Constituent Order
t:
or moved to the end of the sentence:
(64) a. Ainbo-nin-ra tari a-xon-ke, meráya. | b. Ainbo-nin-ra meráya a-xon-ke, tari. | c. Tari-ra ainbo-nin a-xon-ke, meráya. | d. Meráya-ra ainbo-nin a-xon-ke, tari. | ‘The woman made a tari for the great shaman.’

h: 17.2.3.2. Relativization
t:
Both receivers can also be pulled out of the sentence and talked about on their own. When this happens, what's left works like a ‘who/which…’ description part (‘the man who came’). So I will deal with both things together. The examples in (65) show that either receiver can be described this way: the thing the action is done to, or the extra person brought in by -xon:
(65) a. Nato r-iki tari [ainbo-nin meráya a-xon-a]. | ‘This is the tari that the woman made for the great shaman.’ | b. Nato r-iki ja^{11} meráya [ainbo-nin tari a-xon-a]. | ‘This is the great shaman for whom the woman made a tari.’
Sometimes the same sentence can be read two ways. So in (66a), the described word is understood as the thing the action is done to. In (66b), it is understood as the person the action is done for:
(66) a. Joni [yobekan kopi-xon-a]-ra | moa mawá-kas-ai. | ‘The man on whom the sorcerer cast a spell (in return) (to sb. else’s benefit) is dying.’
Notice that the extra receiver (the person it's done for) is also more ‘alive’ than the other receiver. And it is the one that takes the ‘that’ word ja. One more question worth looking at: do ‘this/that’ words help tell the two receivers apart in real speech? In Haka Lai, for example, the ‘that’ word khaa is used more with the extra receiver than with the others. This suggests that the receiver with the ‘that’ word is more often what the speaker is talking about (Peterson 1999:14-16).

h: 17.2.3.2. Relativization
t:
(b) Joni [yobekan kopi-xon-a]-ra | raro-shaman iki. | ‘The man for whom the sorcerer cast a spell (on sb. else) (in return) is happy.’
In English, a ‘who/which…’ part always comes after the word it describes (‘the canoe that I made’). In SK it can also come before that word, or wrap around it, with the word sitting inside it. When the word sits inside, only a receiver (or the one person of an intransitive verb, see 10.2.4.8) can be the word being described (linguists call it NP_{REL}). The following examples show the same basic sentence with the description part before the word, around it, and after it. With the ‘around’ type there are two choices: the person it's done for can come before the thing it's done to, or the other way round. In each case the word understood as the described one is underlined:
(67a) E-n-ra oin-ke tari | [ainbo-nin ja meráya a-xon-a].
(67b) E-n-ra oin-ke | [ainbo-nin ja meráya tari a-xon-a].
(67c) E-n-ra oin-ke | [ainbo-nin tari ja meráya a-xon-a].
(67d) E-n-ra oin-ke
(None) [ainbo-nin ja meráya a-xon-a] tari. | ‘I saw the tari that the woman made for the great shaman.’
All four sentences above are correct SK. A speaker I worked with always understood them in one way: as describing the thing the action is done to. This fits the four sentences below, which are also correct in principle. But (68c) and (68d) were always rejected when they were meant to describe the extra person, the one the action is done for:

h: 17.2.3.2. Relativization
t:
(68) E-n-ra oin-ke ja meraya | [ainbo-nin tari a-xon-a]. | E-n-ra oin-ke | [ainbo-nin tari a-xon-a] meraya. | E-n-ra oin-ke | [ainbo-nin ja meraya tari a-xon-a]. | E-n-ra oin-ke | [ainbo-nin tari ja meraya a-xon-a]. | ‘I saw the great shaman for whom the woman made tari.’
In other words, look at the ‘around’ type, where the described word sits inside the description part. When both receivers were said out loud, the speaker understood the ordinary receiver as the described word (NP_{REL}). I got similar results when the same speaker looked at sentences (69a)-(69f):
(69) a. E-n-ra benai [Beso-n __kirika__ bake be-xon-a]. | b. E-n-ra benai [Beson bake __kirika__ be-xon-a]. | c. E-n-ra benai [Beson bake be-xon-a] __kirika__. | d. E-n-ra benai __kirika__ [Beso-n bake be-xon-a]. | ‘I am looking for the book that Beso brought for the boy.’ | ‘I am looking for the boy for whom Beso brought a / the book.’ | e. E-n-ra benai __bake__ [Beso-n kirika be-xon-a]. | f. E-n-ra benai [Beso-n kirika be-xon-a] __bake__. | ‘I am looking for the boy for whom Beso brought a / the book.’
I should point out one thing about (69b). I tested it four times on different days. Three times, the speaker picked kirika as the described word, so that is the one I underlined. The fourth time he picked the extra receiver instead. So here is what this test shows. With -xon, when the described word sits inside the description part, it is usually the ordinary receiver (the thing the action is done to). I must stress that these results come from the judgements of only one native speaker. Still, his answers were fairly

h: 17.2.3.2. Relativization
t: consistent.^{12} But this test can't tell us one thing. Is it the ordinary receiver's place in the sentence that matters here? Or is it its meaning, the fact that it is the thing the action is done to?

h: 17.2.3.3. Reciprocalization
t:
A receiver can usually be the same person as the doer, as in ‘to yourself’ or ‘to each other.’ So we can ask: with two receivers, which one can mean ‘each other’? When the doer and both receivers are people, the meaning can be unclear. Look first at these English examples (from Peterson 1999:23):
(70) 
In both sentences above, ‘each other’ refers back to the doers. But in (70a), ‘each other’ is the ones the action is done to. In (70b), it is the ones it's done for. Now here is the key point about Haka Lai. When the same idea is said with an ending that brings in an extra person, only that extra person can mean ‘each other’ with the doer. (The ‘with a tool’ ending is the one exception.) (1999:22-24):
I found the same pattern with two other verbs that take two receivers: meni- ‘give’ and bichin- ‘take away;’. With these too, when I gave the speaker a sentence with the described word sitting inside, he understood it as the thing the action is done to. But other two-receiver verbs, like bi-ma- ‘cause to receive (e.g. someone in matrimony)’, show no difference: either receiver can be described this way. I admit this example is tricky. bi-ma- already has an ‘each other’ feel to it. If I make X receive Y in marriage, I also make Y receive X.

h: 17.2.3.3. Reciprocalization
t:
(71) tsewmaŋ ʔan-ʔii-tshoʔn-piak | ‘They talked to Tsewmang for the benefit of each other.’
In my recorded stories there are sentences where both -xon and the ‘each other’ ending are added to a verb, in that order: first -xon, then ‘each other’. In all of them, ‘each other’ means the extra person, the one the action is done for:
(72) Ja-bo-ra kokoti-bo be-xon-anan-ai. | ‘They bring fruit for each other.’
(73) Ja-bo-ra bi-xon-anan-ai. | ‘They buy from each other / for each other.’
(74) Oa rabé-ra ia bi-xon-anan-i iki. | ‘Those two are searching each other for lice.’
But in the recorded stories there is no sentence with -xon and the ‘each other’ ending on the same verb where all the people involved are human. So the rest of this section is based on sentences I made up and checked with one native speaker. That means these results are only a first guess. I gave example (75b) to a speaker, who translated it freely. ((75a) is shown here to compare.):
(75) a. Nokon bake-bo noko-ananan-ke. | ‘My children met each other.’
(None) b. E-a-ra nokon bake-baon noko-ananan-xon-ke. | ‘My children met each other for me.’
The speaker accepted the sentence above right away. He understood that the ones the action is done to are ‘each other’ (see also ex. (87)). Then I asked if ‘each other’ could instead be the ones it's done for. To make the sentence work that way, he added extra words. So this meaning seems possible, but speakers don't like it much:

h: 17.2.3.3. Reciprocalization
t:
(76) E-a-ra nokon bake-baon noko-ananan-xon-ke, | jato-n-a jakon jawéki. | ‘My children met me for each other, for their own benefit.’
Then I gave him a second sentence of the same kind. Again, he readily accepted the reading where the ones the action is done to are ‘each other’ with the doers. But he rejected the other reading, where the ones it's done for are ‘each other’. In fact, he said the SK sentence was wrong even with extra words added, as in (77b):
(77) a. Ja-baon-ra e-a pota-anan-xon-ke. | ‘They separated (lit. left each other) for me.’ | They left me for each other.’ | b. Ja-baon-ra e-a pota-anan-xon-ke, jato-n-a jakon jawéki. | ‘They left me for each other, for their own benefit.’
These are only first results. But they suggest that either receiver can be ‘each other’ with the doers. Which one it is seems to depend on the order of the two endings on the verb: the ‘each other’ ending and -xon.

h: 17.2.3.4. Interclausal Coreferentiality Control
t:
Shipibo has a way to join two sentences where the first action happens before the second. It uses the marker -a. Here, the receiver of the first sentence is the same person as the doer (or the one person) of the main sentence. When the first sentence has two receivers, either one can be the person shared with the main sentence. It can be the one who receives something, or the thing that is given (from Valenzuela 2002):
(78) Pena-n (bake-shoko) meni-a-ra ainbo xobo-n ka-ke. | ‘After Pena gave (her) the baby, the woman went home.’ (Valenzuela 2002:422)
(79) Pena-n (ainbo) meni-a-ra bake wini-ke. | ‘After Pena gave (it) to the woman, the child cried.’ (Valenzuela 2002:422)
So for sentences with -xon we can ask the same question. Can either receiver (the extra person or the ordinary receiver) be the same person as the doer of the main sentence? Look at the following example:
(80) E-n-ra Rono tita raan-xon-ke. | ‘I sent Rono for my mother’s benefit.’ / ‘I sent my mother for Rono’s benefit.’
Let’s imagine this situation. The speaker’s old mother lives alone in another village. The speaker sends Rono to take care of her. Here Rono is the ordinary receiver (the one sent), and the mother is the extra person (the one he is sent for). Now look at the following sentences:

h: 17.2.3.4. Interclausal Coreferentiality Control
t:
(81) E-n raan-xon-a-bi-ra nokon tita isin-ke. | ‘Even though I sent him (for her), my mother got sick.’
(82) E-n raan-xon-a-bi-ra Rono ka-yama-ke. | ‘Even though I sent (him) for her, Rono did not go.’
So in a sentence joined with -a, either receiver can be the same person as the doer of the main sentence: the extra person or the ordinary receiver.
The following table sums up what we found in section 17.2.3 about how the two receivers behave.
To sum up, the two receivers behave the same in most ways. They have the same markers and the same freedom of word order. Both can be described by a ‘who/which…’ part that comes before or after them. Both can be the person shared with a linked sentence. There is one difference. When the described word sits inside the ‘who/which…’ part, the extra person brought in by -xon behaves less like a normal receiver. With ‘each other’, either receiver can be ‘each other’ with the doers. This may depend on the order of the two endings on the verb. So my conclusion is this. The ordinary receiver passes one more receiver test than the extra person brought in by -xon. But overall, the two behave very much alike.

h: The Applicative -Xon and Other Valency-Changing Devices (-xon and other person-changing endings)
t:
-xon can be combined with other endings that add a person to the sentence. When it is, -xon always comes after them. The most common case is -xon added after the ‘make someone do it’ ending. Speakers rejected sentences with the two endings in the other order:
(83) No-n joi-n-bi-ra no-n profesor-baon no-a | onan-ma-xon-ti atipan-ke. / onan-xon-ma-ti | ‘In our own language the teachers can teach (our children) (to our benefit).’
(84) E-a jo-ma-xon-we. / jo-xon-ma-we | ‘Make him / her come for me.’
(85) E-a ani a-xon-we. / ani-xon-a-we | ‘Grow it for me.’
(86) E-a chopa pani-n-xon-we. /  pani-xon-n-we | ‘Hang the clothes for me.’
As examples (72)-(77) showed, -xon can come before or after the ‘each other’ ending. The example below shows another case of -xon added to a verb that already has the ‘each other’ ending. (That ending takes away the receiver, so the verb has become an intransitive verb):
(87) Ja-baon-ra e-a bi-ananan-xon-ke. | ‘They got married for me.’
In general, -xon seems to be rare on verbs that already have an ending that takes away the receiver, such as the ‘to yourself / for yourself’ ending (linguists call it the middle). In fact, the ‘each other’ verb in the example above may simply be a fixed word, meaning ‘get married’. Take an English sentence like ‘He washed for me.’ To say this, speakers prefer a different way: they put kopi ‘because of’ after the word for the person who benefits (see 17.2.5.3). Still, here is one case where -xon can be added to a verb with the middle ending (-kaa is the middle ending):

h: The Applicative -Xon and Other Valency-Changing Devices (-xon and other person-changing endings)
t:
(88) Kaisi-nin-ra mi-a ishton benxokaa-xon-ke. | ‘Kaisi got ready quickly for you.’
Why does -xon so rarely appear with the middle ending? Maybe because the middle ending already says that the doer is the one affected. So bringing in another affected person would clash with it.

h: Obligatoriness of -Xon Applicative Constructions (when -xon must be used)
t:
Languages differ in another way too. In some, you must use the ‘extra person’ ending to say a certain thing. In others, it is optional. By ‘optional’ I mean this. There is another way to say almost exactly the same thing, without the ending. You use a plain verb and put a marker on the word for the person who is helped or harmed. So the same idea can be said in two ways, and only one of them uses the ending.
At first glance, sentences with -xon are quite common in the stories. Also, it is not easy to find another way of saying the same thing. (If such a way existed, we would expect it to be more common than the -xon sentence; see 17.1.2.) Still, there are three possible candidates that might help build a sentence without -xon. These are: words showing ‘in whose interest’, the ‘my / your / his’ words, and words marked with ‘because of’. Let’s look quickly at each one.

h: 17.2.5.1. Complements of Interest
t:
Some SK verbs have one person plus a second word that is not quite a receiver. When that second word is a pronoun (like ‘me’ or ‘you’), SK uses a special set of pronouns. These are different from every other set of pronouns in the language. But when the second word is a noun, it takes the ending -n. This same -n is also used for the doer marker, for ‘of’ (possession), for ‘with a tool’, for ‘in / to a place’, and for time
(6.1.4, 6.6.5, and 8.2.2). These verbs are mostly about feelings or changes in feeling. The word with this “interessive” marker (meaning ‘in someone’s interest’) usually names the person the feeling is about or for. For example: be happy about something for X, be angry at somebody for X, love X, forget X, feel jealous about X, ask X in matrimony.
Still, I tried to use these ‘in someone’s interest’ words to say the same thing as a sentence with -xon. It didn’t work. In fact, every sentence I built this way was wrong:
(89) a. Ainbo-nin-ra e-a bewa-xon-ke. | ‘The woman sang for me.’ | b. Ainbo-ra e-on bewa-ke.
(90) a. E-a nonti a-xon-we. | ‘Make a canoe for me.’ | b. E-on nonti a-we.
(91) a. Rono-n-ra mi-a paranta be-xon-ke. | ‘Rono brought you plantain.’ | b. Rono-n-ra mi-on paranta be-ke. / Rono-ra

h: 17.2.5.1. Complements of Interest
t:
Now let's go the other way. Take a correct sentence with an ‘in someone’s interest’ word and say it with -xon instead. The meaning changes, as in the following pair of sentences:
(92) a. E-a-ra mi-on keen-ai. | ‘I love / want you.’ | b. E-n-ra mi-a keen-xon-ai. /  E-ara | ‘I want (it) for you (e.g., a piece of clothing).’
One speaker, Mr. Yoi Sani, felt that the two ways of saying it could mean the same thing:
(93) a. E-a-ra mi-on raket-ai. | ‘I fear for you.’ / ‘I am afraid of you^{13}.’ | b. E-n-ra mi-a raké-xon-ai. / E-ara | ‘I fear for you.’
But other native speakers did not agree that (93a) is correct. To say ‘for someone’, they gave (93b) instead.
In 19.2.2.3 I discuss some extra words that show who is affected. They are made from an ‘in someone’s interest’ pronoun plus an ending that matches the person in the sentence. These words could say the same thing as sentences with -xon. But these pronoun forms
One speaker told me this sentence can be read two ways. But usually the person or thing you are afraid of is marked with the ‘to’ ending -ki.
came up only when I asked speakers directly while comparing languages. They never appear in the recorded stories. More study is needed here. For now, I don't think these pronouns are a real other way to say what -xon sentences say. The main reason is that they are probably very rare in real speech.

h: 17.2.5.2. Possessive NPs Marked by -A
t:
Words with the ‘owner’ ending -a are usually translated as ‘something for X’ / ‘something of X.’ But sentences with this -a word (when speakers accepted them at all) meant something a bit different from the sentence with -xon:
(94) ?nonti a-wé nokon-a
If speakers accepted the sentence above, it would mean ‘make the canoe that was / is mine’, not ‘for me.’ The better way to say (94a), though, is:
(94) Nokon-a-bi-pari nonti a-wé. | ‘Make first the canoe that I was doing (lit. that was mine).’
In the same way, native speakers felt that the next two sentences mean different things, though both are correct:
(95) a. E-n-ra nokon tita karo xate-xon-ke. | ‘I cut firewood for my mother.’ | b. E-n-ra karo xate-ke nokon tita-n-a. | ‘I cut the firewood that belonged to my mother.’
Only the sentence with -xon meant that the mother is the one who benefits. Ex. (95b) could be used in a different case. Say the speaker goes to his mother’s house, cuts the firewood she had stored there, and takes it home for himself. Also, one sentence can have both -xon and the ‘owner’ ending -a:
(96) a. E-n-ra karo xate-xon-ke nokon tita-n-a. | ‘I cut the firewood that belonged to my mother for her.’
Speakers said that Ex. (96a) means the same as (96b):

h: 17.2.5.2. Possessive NPs Marked by -A
t: (96) b. E-n-ra nokon tita-n karo xate-xon-ke. | ‘I cut my mother’s firewood for her.’

h: 17.2.5.3. The Reason Markers Kopí / -N Paranan
t:
SK has two ways to mark a word as the cause or reason (‘because of X’). The “neutral” one is kopí. It goes after a word in the plain form, with no marker. The other one is paranan, which has a negative feel. It goes after a word with the ‘in someone’s interest’ marker. Sometimes you can say the same thing as a -xon sentence with kopí and / or paranan:
(97) Yobekan-ra Rawa Piko kopi-xon-ke. | ‘The sorcerer (in return) cast a spell on Rawa for Piko.’ (or ‘cast a spell on Piko for Rawa’).’ | Yobekan-ra Rawa kopi-ke Piko kopí. | ‘The sorcerer (in return) cast a spell on Rawa because of Piko.’ | Yobekan-ra Rawa kopi-ke Pikon paranan | ‘The sorcerer (in return) cast a spell on Rawa because of Piko’s fault.’
(98) E-a nonti a-xon-we! | ‘Make a canoe for me.’ | E-a kopí nonti a-wé. / eon paranan | ‘Make a canoe for / because of me.’
(98a) and (98b) can be translated the same way into English, but they don't describe the same situation. From (98a) we understand that the listener will make a canoe for the speaker to use, or instead of the speaker making it. Sentence (98b) fits a different case. Say a father asks his son to learn to make canoes, so that he has this skill in the future. The canoe may be for the son to use. But the son makes it to please his father. Also, (98b) can't mean that the son makes the canoe instead of his father. So speakers clearly tell apart a sentence with kopí from what looks like the same sentence with -xon.

h: 17.2.5.3. The Reason Markers Kopí / -N Paranan
t:
Again, (99a) means that the taricayas are for the father, or that Rawa is putting them in the canoe instead of the father. (99b) does not mean either of these. In (99b), Rawa puts the taricayas inside the canoe because of his father. Maybe his father is traveling by canoe with a group of people, and the taricayas are a way to pay for his trip. Or maybe they are to make sure the group doesn't go hungry on the trip, since his father is part of it. So the two kinds of sentences clearly mean different things:
(99) a. Rawa-n-ra papa kabóri napó-xon-ke. | ‘Rawa put the taricayas inside the canoe for father.’ | b. Rawa-n-ra kabóri napó-ke papa kopí. | ‘Rawa put the taricayas inside the canoe because of father.’
(100a) can be translated into English in two ways. But only one of them, the one without ‘for someone’, can also be said with (100b), which uses kopí:
(100) a. Rawa-ra e-n rabin-xon-ai. | ‘I feel embarrassed by Rawa (because of something negative he has done).’/ | ‘I feel embarrassed for Rawa (because of sth. negative that was done to him).’ | b. E-a-ra rabin-ai Rawa kopí. / Rawan paranan | ‘I feel embarrassed (because) of Rawa (because of something he has done).’
So here is my conclusion from this section. There is no other way of saying exactly what a -xon sentence says without the ending. That means the -xon ending must be used

h: 17.2.5.3. The Reason Markers Kopí / -N Paranan
t: whenever you want to say that something is done for someone or against someone. More study is needed about the ‘in someone’s interest’ pronouns with the matching ending.

h: The Malefactive -(V)na(a)n ~ -(V)n (-(V)na(a)n ~ -(V)n: doing something against someone)
t: SK has a second ending that brings in an extra person. It is the ‘against someone’ ending -(V)naan ~ -(V)n (linguists call it the malefactive). It means that the action is bad for someone else. Table 17.4 shows the verbs that take this ending in my recorded material:

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t:
Let's go back to Table 17.1. The first thing we see is that the ‘against someone’ ending is fairly rare in the stories. It appears 17 times, compared with 84 for -xon and 45 for the ‘together with’ ending. Also, every verb in Table 17.4 is a transitive verb. So unlike -xon, the ‘against someone’ ending goes only on transitive verbs. This confirms what earlier work had already said: this ending needs a verb with a receiver (Faust 1973:72, Valenzuela 1997:126). Just to show this, below is a list of intransitive verbs with the ‘against someone’ ending. Native speakers said all of them were wrong. Instead, they offered the same verb with -xon to give the ‘against someone’ meaning:
The list above has both kinds of intransitive verbs: ones where the person actively does something and ones where something just happens to them. So the rule depends on whether the verb has a receiver, not on that difference between intransitive verbs (see Peterson 1999:45-46). But speakers did accept one verb that is usually an intransitive verb with the ‘against someone’ ending. The next sentence (given as (88) in Ch.
8) comes from a modern kind of contest, where people take turns singing different songs:
(102) Mi-n-ra e-a i-kas-ai bewá-ribi mi-n-pari e-a | bewa-naan-ke. | ‘You sang first the same song I wanted to sing (to my detriment).’

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t:
Bewa- ‘sing’ is a special kind of verb. It can take a receiver in the plain form, which names a kind of song (one of the different kinds of traditional Shipibo songs). But its doer still has no doer marker, and it behaves like the person of an intransitive verb in other ways too (section 8.2.5). We will look at this and other kinds of transitive verbs below.
Table 17.4 shows one more thing. The ‘do’ verb a(k)- never appears with the ‘against someone’ ending in my recorded material. This is very surprising. a(k)- is also the general verb that can stand in for any transitive verb, and such verbs are expected to be very common. But when I asked speakers, a(k)- with the ‘against someone’ ending came up easily:
(103) a. Ja-n-ra e-a a-anan-ke. | ‘S/he did it on me.’
With other verbs, the ‘against someone’ ending must come right after the bare verb. So it comes before other endings, like the ‘not’ ending -yama and the plural ending -kan (in this
order). But with a(k)-, the plural ending must come before the ‘against someone’ ending. The ‘not’ ending, though, stays in its usual place:
(b) Ja-baon-ra e-a a-kan-an-ke. /  a(a)nan-kan-ke | ‘They did (it) on me.’
(c) Ja-baon-ra e-a a-kan-an-yama-ke | ‘They did not do (it) on me.’

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t:
Both the ‘for someone’ ending -xon and the ‘against someone’ ending can also come after the ‘do’ verb a(k)- when it is attached to the word jaská- ‘like that’ (see also ex. (47)):
(104) a. Jato-n rika ja-ská-a-xon-ti jakon r-iki. | ‘It is a good idea to do their net in this way for them.’ | b. Jato-n rika ja-ská-anan-ti jakon r-iki. | ‘It is a good idea to do their net in this way on them (i.e., to their detriment).’
In (104a), the ‘do’ verb could be used, for example, instead of benxoa-xon-ti (fix-xon-INF) ‘to fix something for someone.’ In (104b), ak- could replace jonan-an-ti (hide-MAL-INF) ‘to hide something on someone.’
Finally, the ‘against someone’ ending can also go on a(k)- when it is part of a combined verb, like senen-'a-naan- ‘to complete something, to comply with something’ (cf. ex. (49)):
(105) Ja-baon-ra e-a senen ‘a-naan-ke. | ‘They took a little bit (of my chacra) on me (i.e., they made their chacra right on the border with mine, and it even overlaps a bit with mine).’
Now we can go back to sentences (46)-(47). There, -xon with the ‘do’ verb a(k)- meant ‘against someone’ instead of the expected ‘for someone’. I suggested there that this might be because a(k)- can't take the ‘against someone’ ending. But (103)-(105) show that a(k)- takes it with no problem. So that idea must be dropped. What may matter instead is that both (46) and (47) are ‘not’ sentences.

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t:
Still, some transitive verbs give wrong sentences with the ‘against someone’ ending. One is be- ‘bring’ (it also means ‘come’ for more than one person). It can only take -xon, whether the meaning is ‘for someone’ or ‘against someone’:
(106) Joxo nawa-baon-ra no-a rao/ jakon joi/ | jakon-ma isin be-xon-ke. / be(e)naanke | ‘The white outsiders brought us medicine / good news / bad illnesses.’
In 17.2.1 I talked about how the meaning of an intransitive verb decides whether -xon means ‘for someone’ or ‘against someone’. I also said that jo- ‘come (sing.),’ with -xon most likely means ‘for someone’. jo- is the intransitive, singular form of be-: the two are different words for the same idea (linguists call this suppletion). Following that, I suggest this. ‘Bring’ is very often used with a ‘for someone’ meaning, by its very nature. Its probably
frequent use this way froze be-xon- into a fixed combination. That would explain why be- plus the ‘against someone’ ending is not allowed (cf. kene- in (112) below). SK has another pair of verbs that works the same way as jo- ‘come (sing.)’ / be- ‘come (non-sing.), bring,’. It is ka- ‘go (sing.) / bo- ‘go (non-singular), carry.’ But unlike be-, bo- can take both endings: -xon and the special ‘against someone’ ending -(V)naan:
(107) Ainbo jakon i-ke-tian-ra jawen tita-n bo-xon-ai, | jawen bake pota-ma-kashama-kin. | ‘When a woman_{i} is good, his (the husband’s) mother_{j} takes her_{i} (where her_{j} son is), because she_{j} doesn’t want to let her_{j} son abandon her_{i}.’

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t:
(108) Jato-n xobo patax ik-á bakeranoman-kaya bo-onaan- | ik-á iki jawen bake xontako. | ‘Instead, a young man who lived next to their house had taken his young daughter with him.’
More examples from the recorded stories are given below. In all of them, the verbs are typical transitive verbs, and the ‘against someone’ meaning is clear:
(109) Ja-tian mi-ki ainbo sinat-ai-tian, mi-n jawen chitonti | xeni-n ke-ski-nan-a, ja ainbo tsini-ti k-ai. | ‘If a woman is angry at you, you can apply (dolphin’s) fat on the edge of her chitonti (traditional skirt) to her detriment, and she will become an easy woman.’
(110) Moa-tian joxo joni-bo jo-xon no-a | keyo-nan-kean-kan-a iki no-n jono... | no-n awá, no-n mari, meskó keská mebi-a-bo. | ‘Long ago when the white people came they almost exterminated our peccaries... our tapirs, our agoutis, and all kinds of monkeys (to our detriment).’
(111) Ja-ská-ke-tian-ki, wetsa-o-ri-kea kishi-ki, | kapetan tseka-nan-a iki, | jawen ibo-n joi ninká-xon-yama-ke-tian. | ‘And so it is said that the alligator on the other side (of the lake) bit off his leg to his detriment, for not having followed its owner’s warning.’
There is only one exception in my recorded texts. In it, the “to someone’s harm” ending adds a good effect instead of a bad one:
(112) Maxokan-ra e-a atapa kene-nan-ke. | ‘The opossum failed (to catch) my chicken (to my benefit).’

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t:
I offered the combination kene-xon- to a speaker, and it was rejected. The verb kene- usually means that you missed your prey when you shot at it or threw a hunting weapon (see also Lauriault, Loriot, and Day 1993:339). So kene- is nearly always used for something bad. One could argue that this is why the combination kene-nan- became fixed. Then the “harm” ending, which is usually about harm, was
given a wider job: showing that someone is affected, for good or for bad. In other words, this is the reverse of what happened with the verb be- ‘come (non-singular), bring.’
Here are other verbs that can take the “to someone’s harm” ending. Some were offered by speakers; others come from other texts:
(113) pota- ‘leave, abandon’ | raan- ‘send (someone to do something)’ | pi- ‘eat’ | koko- ‘eat (fruit)’ | xea- ‘drink’ | toe- ‘break’ | meno- ‘burn’ | chiban- ‘follow, chase’ | yoká- ‘ask, request’ | bena- ‘search, look for’ | mera- ‘find, meet’ | osan- ‘laugh at’ | rete- ‘kill’ | mecho- ‘worsen, spoil’ | kobin-a(k)- ‘boil (tr.)’ | paen a(k)- ‘get someone drunk’ | rami a(k)- ‘spoil, ruin, insult’
The “harm” ending has several forms. Which form a verb takes mostly depends on how long the bare verb is. A very short verb (one beat, or mora) takes a form that starts with a vowel. A verb with two beats takes a form that starts with the sound n (see footnote 1). With bo- ‘carry’ the vowel of the ending also seems to change a little to match the verb. Still, the list below also has some forms that don’t follow this rule:

h: The Malefactive Applicative Construction (how "against someone" sentences work)
t: (114) pi- ‘eat’ pi-ana(a)n- ~ pi-an | rete- ‘kill’ rete-na(a)n- ~ rete-n-

h: The Malefactive and Verbs of Intermediate Transitivity ("against someone" with verbs that are only partly transitive)
t:
Now let’s look at in-between verbs. These are verbs that are not clearly transitive verbs, and not clearly intransitive verbs either. In 17.3.1 I showed that the “to someone’s harm” ending needs a verb with at least some receiver-like quality. When you add it to a clear intransitive verb, the result is wrong. In this section I check whether the in-between verbs can take this ending. These verb types, and the sentences they appear in, are described in sections 8.2.1-8.2.7.
Some Shipibo-Konibo verbs are odd. Their doer must take the doer marker (ERG). The verb also agrees with the doer the way transitive verbs do (A-agreement). But in other ways they don’t act like transitive verbs. Can these verbs take the “harm” ending? One example is wina- ‘row.’ As I said in footnote 7, the doer of wina- always has the doer marker, and the verb agrees like a transitive verb. When I ask speakers directly, wina- can even take a receiver, like a canoe or a person (‘row the canoe’, or ‘take someone somewhere by rowing’). But so far I haven’t found a receiver with wina- in real stories or conversations. Interestingly, wina- is like an intransitive verb in one way: it can’t take the “harm” ending (\wina-naan- is wrong),
but it is like a transitive verb in another way: wina-xon- can only mean doing it for someone’s good.

h: The Malefactive and Verbs of Intermediate Transitivity ("against someone" with verbs that are only partly transitive)
t:
Look at these examples:
(115) Neeri e-a wina-xon-we, baba-shoko! | ‘Row for me over here, grandchild.’
(116) E-a jain ka-ti-n raket-ain-bi Koriman e-a wina-xon-ke. | ‘Even though I was afraid of getting there, Korin rowed (me) to my detriment.’
The verb join- ‘breathe’ is a bit like wina-. Its doer must take the doer marker, and the verb agrees like a transitive verb. Again, when I ask speakers directly, a few receivers in the plain form (ABS) are possible:
(117) Ainbo-nin-ra (niwe / jakonma koin) join-ai. | ‘The woman breathes (air / the harming smoke).’
Breathing for someone’s good, or to someone’s harm, may seem like a strange idea. Still, the next examples suggest that speakers like join- with -xon a little better (or rather, dislike it a little less) than with the “harm” ending:
(118) a. Jene-n rete-kean-a-bi-ra ainbo-nin join-ai. | ‘After almost drowning, the woman is (now) breathing.’ | b. ?Jene-n rete-kean-a-bi-ra ainbo-nin e-a
(None) join-xon-ai. | ‘After almost drowning, the woman is (now) breathing to my benefit.’ | c. Jene-n rete-kean-a-bi-ra nokon rawikan e-a | join-naan-ai. | ‘After almost drowning, my enemy is (now) breathing to my detriment.’
The verb kinan- ‘vomit’ also acts like a transitive verb, both in how its doer is marked and in how the verb agrees. But some receivers are only allowed if something is added to them, for example -bires ‘purely, just (see also 15.2):’

h: The Malefactive and Verbs of Intermediate Transitivity ("against someone" with verbs that are only partly transitive)
t:
(119) a. E-n-ra aros / piti / yapa kinan-ke. | ‘I threw up the rice / the food / the fish.’ | b. E-n-ra aros-bires / piti-bires / yapa-bires kinan-ke. | ‘I threw up just the rice, just the food, just the fish.’
In 17.2.1 I showed that kinan-xon- (vomit-xon-) can mean either ‘for someone’s good’ or ‘to someone’s harm.’ Which one depends on the situation and the culture. Here is example (31) again:
(120) Nokon bake-n-ra e-a kinan-xon-ke. | ‘My child vomited (to my benefit / detriment).’
