But kinan- is different from the other verbs in this section. It can also take the “harm” ending:
(121) Rao e-n xea-ma-a-ra, bake-n e-a | kinan-naan-ke. | ‘My son threw up the medicine I gave him to my detriment.’
The verbs keen- ‘want, love, like, need’ and shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind, forget’ are special. Each can be used in two patterns. In one, both people are in the plain form: <ABS ABS>. In the other, one person is in the plain form and the second is the thing you are interested in: <ABS complement of interest> (8.2.2.5). Interestingly, keen- can only take -xon, whether you mean for someone’s good or to someone’s harm:
(122) Roniman-ra wetsa ainbo e-a keen-xon-ke. / keen-naan-ke | ‘Ronin wants / likes another woman (to my benefit / detriment).’

h: The Malefactive and Verbs of Intermediate Transitivity ("against someone" with verbs that are only partly transitive)
t:
So keen- is different from noi- ‘love.’ The two are close in meaning, but they behave differently in the sentence. noi- is a typical transitive verb. So it takes both endings that bring in an extra person: -xon for someone’s good, and -naan for someone’s harm:
(123) a. Roniman-ra e-a wetsa ainbo noi-xon-ke. | ‘Ronin loves another woman to my benefit / to my detriment.’ | b. Roniman-ra e-a wetsa ainbo noi-naan-ke. | ‘Ronin loves another woman to my detriment / to my benefit.’
shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind, forget’ is different from keen-. It does take both of these endings:
(124) Roniman-ra e-a nokon bake xontako moa | shinan-beno-xon-ke / shinan-beno-naan-ke. | ‘Ronin already forgot my unmarried daughter to my benefit / to my detriment.’
Finally, let’s look at a few verbs of feeling. In most ways they act like normal intransitive verbs: the doer gets no marker, and the verb agrees like an intransitive verb. But unlike other intransitive verbs, they have a second person: the one the feeling is aimed at (what you fear, who you are angry with). This second person usually has the ending -ki ‘at, to’ (linguists call it the dative). I looked at seven verbs of feeling. Only one of them, raket- ~ raké- ‘fear, be afraid of,’ can take the “harm” ending:
(125) Ronin-ra ino-ki raké-ke. | ‘Ronin was afraid of the jaguar.’ | Roniman-ra e-a ino-ki raké-xon-ai / | raké-enaan-ke^{14}. | ‘Ronin was afraid of the jaguar to my benefit / to my detriment.’

h: The Malefactive and Verbs of Intermediate Transitivity ("against someone" with verbs that are only partly transitive)
t:
In another session, the same speaker, Mr. Yoi Sani, rejected the form rakéenaanke. But he confirmed that rakéxonke cannot mean ‘to someone’s harm.’
Two other verbs of feeling, rabin- ‘feel embarrassed’ and sinat- ~ siná- ‘be angry,’ could only take -xon. With the “harm” ending, speakers said they were wrong:
(126) Roniman-ra e-a rabin-xon-ai. / rabin-(a)naan-ai | ‘Ronin feels embarrassed (towards others) in relation to me.’
(127) Roniman-ra e-a siná-xon-ke. / siná-(a)naan-ke | ‘Ronin got angry (at others) in relation to me / in my benefit.’
The other verbs of feeling I looked at are listed below. Again, with the “harm” ending they are all wrong. With -xon, they are all fine:
(128) 
As expected, things change when rabin- and sina(t)- are first turned into transitive verbs by adding a(k)- ‘do (tr.), make.’ Then they mean ‘make someone feel embarrassed’ and ‘make someone angry,’ and they can take the “harm” ending.
The table below sums up which in-between verbs can take which of the two extra-person endings we have seen so far.
In short, these verbs are transitive verbs to different degrees. This shows in whether they can take the endings -xon and -(V)na(a)n ~ -(V)n, and in what the result means when they can. Even verbs from the same small group can behave differently. For example, raket- ‘be afraid of’ is different from the other verbs of feeling, and keen- ‘want’ is different from shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind.’ We should expect speakers to disagree sometimes. The same speaker may even judge a word differently on different days.

h: Malefactive Applicative Constructions and Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
With the “harm” ending, the doer doesn’t always have to be a person. Some of these sentences allow a doer that is not human. Interestingly, the matching “for someone’s good” sentences, the (b) sentences, were judged unacceptable.15
The (b) sentences are not acceptable because jene, kinan and akonten would then be understood as if they were people (Yoi Sani p.c. 2000, and Ranin Nita p.c. 2001).
(129) a. Jene-n-ra e-a bake rete-naan-ke. | ‘My child drowned to my detriment (lit. the flowing water killed my child).’ | b. Jene-n-ra e-a nokon rawí rete-xon-ke. | ‘My enemy drowned to my benefit.’
(130) a. Kinaman-ra e-a bake rete-naan-ke. | ‘My child died from vomit to my detriment (lit. vomit killed my child).’ | b. Kinaman-ra nokon rawí e-a rete-xon-ke. | ‘My enemy died from vomit to my benefit.’
(131) a. Akonteman-ra e-a bake kopi-naan-ke. | ‘The akonten tree affected my child negatively to my detriment.’ | b. Akonteman-ra e-a nokon rawí kopi-xon-ke. | ‘The akonten tree affected my enemy negatively to my benefit.’
(132) a. Nokon jawéki bana-a-ra e-a niwe-n poxa-naan-ke. | ‘My planted trees were overcome by the wind (to my detriment).’ (the SK sentence is active) (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:211) | b. Nokon rawikan jawéki bana-a-ra e-a niwe-n poxa-xon-ke. | ‘My enemy’s planted trees were overcome by the wind to my benefit.’

h: Malefactive Applicative Constructions and Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
Sentences (133) and (134) show why the (b) sentences above are bad. The problem is not adding -xon to those verbs; that part is fine. Instead, the next examples suggest that the problem is the kind of doer:
(133) Epa-n-ra nokon rawí e-a rete-xon-ke. | ‘My paternal uncle killed my enemy to my benefit.’
(134) Ja-n-ra nokon rawí e-a kopi-xon-ke. | ‘S/he returned it (a negative behavior) to my enemy to my benefit.’
Remember, though, that some -xon sentences did allow a thing as the doer, with both intransitive and transitive verbs (exx. (39)-(40) and (50)-(52)). But in those cases the event is good for someone in an obvious, expected way. So it seems some verbs are strongly tied to a certain kind of event. With those verbs, an unexpected “for someone’s good” or “to someone’s harm” meaning is impossible, even when the right ending is added.
The extra person brought in by the “harm” ending can be an animal, just like the one brought in by -xon:
(135) Bake-n-ra paranta joshin pitso pi-anaan-ke. | ‘The child ate the ripe banana to the paroqueet’s detriment.’
But there is a difference. The extra person brought in by the “for someone’s good” ending must be alive (exx. (53)-(55)). The one brought in by the “harm” ending can be a thing:
(136) Iskoira-n kirika-ra oi-n biblioteca mechá a-nan-ke. | Lit. ‘The rain made the school books wet to the library’s detriment.’

h: Malefactive Applicative Constructions and Semantic Restrictions (limits on meaning)
t:
(137) ?Iskoira-n kirika-ra profesor-nin biblioteca bi-xon-ke. | ‘The teacher got the school books to the library’s benefit.’
Sentence (138) shows why (137) sounds rather bad. Most likely the problem is what kind of thing the one who benefits is:
(138) Iskoira-n kirika-ra profesor-nin bake-bo bi-xon-ke. | ‘The teacher got the school books to the children’s benefit.’
The same thing happens in the following examples:
(139) Meskó keská yoina-ra joxo joni-baon nii | keyo-naan-kean-ke. | ‘The white people almost exterminated different kinds of animals to the forest’s detriment.’
(140) ?Meskó keská yoina-ra joni-baon nii koiran-xon-ke. | ‘The people protected different kinds of animals to the forest’s benefit.’
(141) Meskó keská yoina-ra joni-baon no-a koiran-xon-ke. | ‘The people protected different kinds of animals to our benefit.’
So examples (136)-(141) suggest this: the “harm” ending is less strict than the “for someone’s good” ending about whether the extra person must be alive.

h: Object Properties in Malefactive Applicative Constructions (how the new receiver behaves)
t: As in 17.2.3, in this section I compare the two receivers in “harm” sentences. One is the verb’s own receiver (the base object). The other is the extra person added by the “harm” ending. Do the two behave differently in any important way?

h: 17.3.4.1. Coding Properties: Case-marking and Constituent Order
t:
In Shipibo-Konibo, sentences with two receivers (like sentences with ‘give’) put both receivers in the plain form (ABS). The same is true here: the verb’s own receiver and the harmed person are both in the plain form. They can come in either order before the verb:
(142) a. Mari-baon-ra no-a atsa pi-anaan-kan-ke. | b. Mari-baon-ra atsa no-a pi-anaan-kan-ke. | ‘The agoutis ate the yuca to our detriment.’
(143) a. Ino-n-ra tari kené-ya xae sawe-naan-ke. | b. Ino-n-ra xae tari kené-ya sawe-naan-ke. | ‘The Jaguar put on the designed tari to the Anteater’s detriment.’16
Both receivers can also be moved to the front of the sentence,
(144) a. Tari kené-ya-ra ino-n xae sawe-naan-ke. | b. Xae-ra ino-n tari kené-ya sawe-naan-ke.
or moved to the end, after the verb:
(144) c. Ino-n-ra xae sawe-naan-ke, tari kené-ya.
The story behind the example above: long ago, the Jaguar managed to steal the Anteater’s beautifully patterned fur.
(d) Xae-ra ino-n sawe-naan-ke, tari kené-ya.
(e) Ino-n-ra tari kené-ya sawe-naan-ke, xae.
(f) Tari kené-ya-ra ino-n sawe-naan-ke, xae. | ‘The Jaguar put on the designed tari to the Anteater’s detriment.’

h: 17.3.4.2. Relativization
t:
Next, I looked at “who/which…” description parts (linguists call them relative clauses). The noun being described can come before the description, after it, or inside it. Again, I tested this with only one native speaker. I asked this speaker which person or thing each sentence in (145) below was describing. The sentences came in a different order each time, mixed in with other sentences. I tested each one on at least two different occasions. I got three different answers: the dog (the verb’s own receiver), the man (the harmed person), or the whole event (the sentence read as a ‘that…’ sentence instead of a ‘who/which…’ one). Only the receivers given as possible answers are underlined:
(145a) E-n-ra oin-ke [ja-n ochíti joni boonaan-a] | ‘I saw the dog that he took to the man’s detriment.’ / | ‘I saw that he took the dog to the man’s detriment.’
(145b) E-n-ra oin-ke [ja-n joni ochíti boonaan-a]. | ‘I saw the dog that he took to the man’s detriment.’ / | ‘I saw that he took the dog to the man’s detriment.’
(c) E-n-ra oin-ke ochíti [ja-n joni boonaan-a]. | ‘I saw the dog that he took to the man’s detriment.’
(d) E-n-ra oin-ke [ja-n joni bonaan-a] ochíti. | ‘I saw the dog that he took to the man’s detriment.’
(e) E-n-ra oin-ke joni [ja-n ochíti bonaan-a]. | ‘I saw that he took the dog to the man’s detriment.’

h: 17.3.4.2. Relativization
t:
(f) E-n-ra oin-ke [ja-n ochíti boonaan-a] joni. | ‘I saw the man to whose detriment he took the dog.’
As expected, when ‘dog’ comes before or after the description part, it is the only noun that can be the one described (NP_{REL}); see (c) and (d). When the noun sits inside the description part, again only ‘dog’, not the man, can be the one described. In (a) and (b) the speaker could also read the sentence as a ‘that…’ sentence. The harmed person ‘man’ is chosen as NP_{REL} only when it comes after the description part. When it comes before, the speaker felt that the pointing word ja ‘that / the’ was needed to read ‘man’ as the one described: Enra oinke ja joni [jan ochíti boonaana]. So when the noun is inside the description part, only the verb’s own receiver, not the harmed person, can be the one described. This matches what I found for -xon sentences in 17.2.3.2.
Still, a sentence similar to (145) got somewhat different results from the same speaker:
(146) a. E-n-ra onan-ke xontako [bakeranoman joni
(a (cont.)) bo-onaan-a]. | ‘I know the girl that the young man took to the man’s detriment.’ | ‘I know that the young man took the unmarried girl to the man’s detriment.’/
(b) Enra onanke [bakeranoman joni boonaana] xontako. | ‘I know the girl that the young man took to the man’s detriment.’ BASE OBJ

h: 17.3.4.2. Relativization
t:
(c) E-n-ra onan-ke joni [bakeranoman xontako boonaan-a]. | ‘I know the man to whose detriment the young man took the girl.’ APPL. OBJ
(d) E-n-ra onan-ke [bakeranoman xontako boonaan-a] joni. | ‘I know the man to whose detriment the young man took the girl.’ APPL. OBJ
(e) E-n-ra onan-ke [bakeranoman xontako joni boonaan-a]. | ‘I know that the young man took the unmarried girl to the man’s detriment.’
(f) E-n-ra onan-ke [bakeranoman joni xontako boonaan-a]. | ‘I know that the young man took the unmarried girl to the man’s detriment.’
As you can see, in (e) and (f) both receivers are inside the description part. There the speaker read the sentences only as ‘that…’ sentences (complement clauses).
So the data above lead to this conclusion. When the noun is inside the description part, only the receiver that the action is done to (the patient) can be the one described (NP_{REL}). In some cases, though, the ‘that…’ reading is preferred.

h: 17.3.4.3. Reciprocalization
t:
Adding the “harm” ending to a verb that already has the “to each other” ending gives a wrong sentence. The reverse order (verb + harm + each other, V-MAL-REC) has not been found either. So I couldn’t test whether “each other” would link the doers with the verb’s own receiver, with the harmed person, or with both. Just to show what this looks like, here are some examples:
(147) a. Ja-bo-ra pota-anan-ke. | ‘They separated (lit. left each other).’ | b. Ja-baon-ra bake-bo pota-anan-naan-ke. | / pota-(a)naan-anan-ke. | ‘They abandoned each other to the detriment of the children.’ / | ‘They abandoned the children to each other’s detriment.’
(148) a. Ja-bo-ra rishki-anan-ke. | ‘They hit each other (with a pole).’ | b. Ja-baon-ra e-a rishki-anan-naan-ke. / rishki-(a)naan-anan-ke. | ‘They hit each other to my detriment. / They hit me to each other’s detriment.’
Why is this combination wrong? The “to each other” ending takes away the receiver: once people act on each other, there is no separate receiver anymore. But the “harm” ending needs a verb with at least some receiver. So the two don’t fit together.

h: 17.3.4.4. Interclausal Referentiality Control
t:
Shipibo-Konibo can join two parts of a sentence with the marker -a-. With it, the receiver of one part can be the same person as the doer of the next part. Examples (c) and (d) below show that either receiver can play this role:
(149) Sankeman-ra ainbo rao-n-ke. | ‘Sanken_{i} treated the woman with medicine (to have her fall in love with him_{i}).’ | Sankeman-ra joni jawen awin rao-n-naan-ke. | ‘Sanken, to the man’s detriment, treated his wife with medicine.’ | Sankeman rao-n-naan-a-ra joni jawen awinin | pota-ke. | ‘After Sanken treated (her) with medicine (to her husband’s detriment), the woman left her husband (lit. his wife left the man).’ | Sankeman rao-n-naan-a-ra joni-n Sanken | wexa-ke. | ‘After Sanken_{i} treated (her) with medicine (to his_{j} detriment), the man_{j} cut Sanken_{i} with a wexati knife (on the back of the head).’
The sentences in (150) come from a traditional story. A man felt embarrassed after his sister-in-law painted part of his face black with genipa. So he went up to the sky and became the moon. That is why the moon can’t be seen completely at night: the Shipibo say the man is showing the painted part of his face:
(150) Wesna-n-ra joni (nane-n) be-ski-ke. | ‘Wesna painted her brother in law on the face (with genipa).’ | Wesna-n-ra ainbo jawen bene be-ski-naan-ke. | ‘Wesna_{i}, to the woman_{j}’s detriment, painted her_{j} husband on the face.’ | Wesna-n be-ski-naan-a-ra ainbo siná-ke. | ‘After Wesna_{i} painted (her_{j} husband) on the face (to her_{j} detriment), the woman_{j} got angry.’ | Wesna-n be-ski-naan-a-ra bene rabin-ax | naikan ka-ke. | ‘After Wesna painted (him) on the face (to his wife’s detriment), the man felt embarrassed and went up to the sky.’

h: 17.3.4.4. Interclausal Referentiality Control
t:
Table 17.6 sums up how the verb’s own receiver and the added receiver behave in “harm” sentences.
In short, the two receivers in “harm” sentences behave much like those in -xon sentences. The main difference is this: when the noun is inside a “who/which…” description part, only the verb’s own receiver can be the one described (NP_{REL}).

h: The Malefactive Applicative and Other Valency-Changing Devices ("against someone" and other person-changing endings)
t:
In my data, the “harm” ending comes after other endings that add a person. These are the general “make someone do it” ending -ma, and also -n and a(k):^{17}
(151) Ja-n-ra e-a nawa jiki-ma-naan-ke. / jiki-naan-ma-ke | ‘He let the outsider enter to my detriment.’
(152) Ja-n-ra no-a bachi mape-n-naan-ke. / mape-naan-nVn-ke | ‘S/he lifted the mosquito net to our detriment.’
(153) Ja-n-ra e-a kochi ani a-naan-ke. / ani-naan a-ke | ‘S/he (taking it from me) raised the pig to my detriment.’
As I said in 17.3.4.3, the “harm” ending can’t come after the “to each other” ending. That’s because “to each other” takes away the receiver, and the “harm” ending doesn’t usually attach to
Note, however, that the bare verbs in (151)-(153) are not transitive verbs. That is why they can’t take the “harm” ending directly. Perhaps the order transitive verb + harm + “make someone do it” (V(tr.)-MAL-CAUS) is possible in the right context.
intransitive verbs. In the same way, adding the “harm” ending to a verb with the middle ending was judged wrong. (The middle ending takes away the doer, so the event seems to happen by itself.) Look at these examples:18
(154) a. Bake-n-ra meno-ke. | ‘The child burned (it).’ | b. Bake-ra menó-ke. | ‘The child burned himself.’ | c. Bake-n-ra e-a meno-naan-ke. | ‘The child burned (it) to my detriment.’ | d. Bake-n-ra e-a menó-(o)naan-ke. / meno-naamee-ke. | ‘The child burned himself to my detriment.’

h: The Malefactive Applicative and Other Valency-Changing Devices ("against someone" and other person-changing endings)
t:
(155) a. Bake-n-ra sika-ke. | ‘The child painted it.’ | b. Bake-ra sikí-ke. | ‘The child painted himself.’ | c. Bake-n-ra e-a sika-naan-ke. | ‘The child painted (it) to my detriment.’ | d. Bake-n-ra sikí-(i)naan-ke. / sika-naamee-ke. | ‘The child painted himself to my detriment.’
The middle ending has several different forms. In the (d) sentences below, the second option uses the form that goes with verbs ending in a nasal sound.
Example (155d) above shows both possible orders of the middle ending and the “harm” ending. I did the same for the “to each other” ending in (147) and (148). Why are all of these wrong? Probably because the “harm” ending needs a verb with at least some receiver, and these endings take the receiver away (see also ex. (170), with a “to each other” verb and the “together with” ending). This rule explains why some situations that make perfect sense can’t be said with the “harm” ending. Examples are English ‘They left each other to the children’s detriment’ or ‘The child burned her / himself to my detriment.’

h: Obligatoriness of the Malefactive Applicative Construction (when it must be used)
t:
As with -xon, there is no simple way to say the same thing without the “harm” ending. One possible candidate is the ending -ki (linguists call it the dative), which means ‘at, to, against’ in English. Look at the examples below:
(156) Ja-n-ra mesa-ki kenchá toe-ke. | ‘S/he broke the dish against the table.’
(157) Nokon bake-ra mai-ki paké-ke. | ‘My child fell to the ground.’
(158) E-a-ra Yabi-ki sinat-ai. | ‘I hate Yabi. / I am angry at Yabi.’
(159) E-a-ra ino-ki raket-ai. | ‘I am afraid of the jaguar.’
So a noun with -ki is the third person with a transitive verb, or the second person with an intransitive verb (see 17.2.2.2). Sometimes -ki can be translated as ‘against’, which sounds like it could mean harm. But every attempt to get a “harm” meaning from a noun with -ki, without the “harm” ending, failed. There is no other close way to say what a “harm” sentence says.

h: The Associative -Kin ~ Kiin (-kin ~ -kiin: doing something with someone)
t:
A third ending that brings in an extra person is the “together with” ending -kin ~ -kiin (linguists call it the associative). Here is how often it appears with different kinds of verbs:
Intermediate Transitivity Stems: 1 instance
Transitive Stems: 23 instances
The first important point: the “together with” ending appears equally often with intransitive verbs and with transitive verbs. This is unlike the general -xon ending and the special “harm” ending.

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t:
Like the other endings that bring in an extra person, -ki(i)n adds a person to the sentence. Added to an intransitive verb, it adds a second person, usually understood
This verb needs a doer with the doer marker, but it can take very few kinds of receivers. Usually there is no receiver at all.
as someone who is “accompanied” or “helped”;^{20} added to a transitive verb, it gives a verb with a doer and two receivers. In the examples below, the verb yakat- ~ yaká- has just one person, in the plain form. But when -kin is added, the sentence gets a doer and a receiver:
(160) Jawen baba-ra yaká-ke. / jawen baba-n-ra | ‘Her granddaughter is sitting.’ | Jawen baba-n-ra [jawen yoxan pashkin-ke-tian] | yaká-kin-ke. | ‘Since her grandmother was tired, the granddaughter sits with her (Valenzuela 1997:121).’
Here are more examples from texts, with intransitive verbs that describe states rather than actions. Sentences (161) and (162) use ja- ‘be, exist’, and (163) and (164) use the small intransitive stand-in verb ik-. Notice that in some sentences, like (161) and (164), the two people play different roles: the doer helps or goes along with the added person. In others, like (162) and (163), the two people seem equally involved in the event, at least judging from how native speakers translated them:

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t:
(161) Baké, nato joni-ra mi-a no-n bi-ma-[a]i; | nato joni-ra mecha iki, mi-a ja-n-bi-ribi
Note that the “together with” ending may also have a bit of a “for someone’s good” meaning.
(None) jawéki a-xon ja-kin-ti jisá oin-xon. | ‘Daughter, we will make you receive this man (in matrimony); this man is a good fisher / hunter hence we believe that he, performing the activities (proper of men), might be able to support you (lit. might help you live / exist).’
(162) ...jakiribi xobo-a-xon ja-kin-a-bi-ronki i-káti-ai | kikin jakon-ma. | ‘Building a house again it is said that they lived together very badly.’
(163) ...ja bo-xon-ronki westíora shanka kini meran i-kin-ai | ‘(The Yonkexta woman) took him and they stayed together in the rock cave.’
(164) Ja-bo-ra jo-ai mato i-kin-i. | ‘They will come to stay with you.’
The next sentences show the “together with” ending with intransitive verbs of feeling:
(165) Rama-ra e-n raro-kin-kas-ai mato Piró-ma | ik-á-bo. | ‘In this moment I want to greet you, (indigenous peoples) who are not from Peru.’
(166) Axeamis-bo jakon-shaman, non koshi-bo jakoin-ra, | noa bene-bene-kin-shaman-ai. | ‘The teachers are very good, our authorities are very good too, and therefore we are totally satisfied with them.’
The next sentences have intransitive verbs of action. You can see that the doer and the added person play different roles. In (167) a newly married man goes back to his village, taking his new wife with him. In (168) the shaman woman is in charge of dealing with the ayahuasca spirits, and her two husbands help her in different ways:

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t:
(167) Jawen jema-n nokó-kin-ke-tian jawen reken merati-baon | ja ainbo bachin-i bo-kan-ai. | ‘And when (the newly married woman) arrives to his (i.e. the husband’s) village with him, his former lovers will pull that woman by the hair.’
(168) Ja-tian nishi xea-nko, wetsa-n bewa-kin-ai, | wetsa-n shini tapon keté a-xon-ai. | ‘During the ayahuasca drinking sessions, one (husband) helped her sing while the other one lighted up the pipe for her.’
With the action verbs ‘go’ and ‘come,’ -kin needs the special forms bo- and be-. These are the forms used for more than one person, or with a receiver. The forms for one person alone, ka- and jo-, can’t be used (see 4.5):
(169) a. Rama-n-ra Yabi ka-kin-ai / bo-kin-ai. | ‘Rama goes with Yabi.’ | b. Rama-n-ra Yabi jo-kin-ai / be-kin-ai. | ‘Rama came with Yabi.’
Choosing bo- and be- makes sense. -kin adds a receiver to the sentence, and the doer does not act alone.
With the “together with” ending we find the only sentence in my texts where an extra-person ending is added to a verb with the “to each other” ending:
(170) Ja iki koshi shinan-ya-bo ja ainbo-bo | kopi-anan-kin-ai-bo. | ‘Those were brave the women that competed against each other.’
Finally, the next text examples show the “together with” ending with transitive verbs. Sentence (171) comes from the talks between two sets of parents who are arranging a marriage between their daughter and son. As the culture expects, at some point the future groom’s father describes his son as lacking the skills and knowledge men should have:

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t:
(171) Bo-tan-we! Jawe a-ti onan-tani-ma i-ken-bi | mato-n atapa xepo-kin-ti-bires. | ‘Take him with you! Although he hardly knows how to do anything, at least he can help you lock up your chickens.’
(172) Ja-ská-a-xon jawen poi-n yatan-a iki, | xea-kin-kin nete-a iki. | ‘And so her brother kept him there, drinking together until it dawned.’
(173) Bi-xon-ronki, kena-ti iki westíora joni, ja-n ochíti | yatan-kin-ti. | ‘After getting (the medicine), one has to call another person so that s/he helps hold the dog (in order to cure it).’
(174) ...bake-baon-ki ishton rene-kin-a iki | ‘...the children helped her grind (the corn) quickly.’
As I said above, most “together with” sentences seem to have a built-in relationship where one person depends on the other. Usually the added person is the one more involved in doing the action. The doer of the sentence, the one with the doer marker, just helps or goes along. For example, (173) comes from a description of how to “cure” your dog to make it a good hunter. The “together with” ending says that at some point you should get help to hold the dog. In (174) the Canary Woman introduces herself to a group of Shipibo children and makes corn beer for their parents. The children help her grind the corn so that she can finish on time.

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t:
But with the verb tee- ‘work’ the expected meaning ‘the doer helps the added person to work’ is rejected. Instead, the doer is seen as mainly responsible for the work, and the added people are helpers who are pushed to help:
(175) E-n-ra mi-a tee-kin-ai. | ‘I help / accompany you to work.’ | ‘I make you work with me.’
(176) E-a-ra Rawa-n tee-kin-ai jawen wai-n. | ‘Rawa helps me work...’ | ‘I help Rawa work in his chacra.’ (Rawa indirectly obliges me to do it)
(177) Juan Melendres-nin-ra e-a tee-kin-ai. | ‘Juan Melendres helps me work.’ | ‘I work for / with Juan Melendres.’
Here is one likely explanation. At least with tee-, -kin works mainly as a “make someone do it together with you” ending. The person with the doer marker makes the added person act, and both take part in the event. In other words, the doer works too. (Linguists call this sociative causation.) The extra information in parentheses in (176), given by a native speaker, supports this idea. I also noted this meaning of tee-kin- in Valenzuela (1997), with examples from a different speaker. The English translations in (178)-(180) are a bit misleading. But the extra information in parentheses makes clear that someone is being made to work together with the doer:
(178) Sani-n-ra Wexá tee-kin-ai | ‘Sani works with Wexá (but for Sani’s benefit, probably in Sani’s chacra).’

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t:
In the sentence below, look at the marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. It shows that the doer of jawe ayamai it- ‘have nothing to do’ is not the same as the doer of the main verb. The first is the son; the second is the father. Because the son had nothing to do, his father made him work with him. So the father made it happen, but he worked too:
(179) Papa-n-ra jawen bake jawe a-yam-ai it-ai-tian | tee-kin-ai. | ‘Because his son has nothing to do, the father is working with him (probably the father asked the son for help).’ (Valenzuela 1997:123)
Now compare the next example. Here the verb in the first part carries the "same person" marker. This tells us that the one who ‘wants to leave soon’ is the same person who does the main verb:
(180) Wesna-n-ra ishton ka-kas-kin Rama tee-kin-ai. | ‘Wesna_{i} is working with Rama_{j} (probably asked Rama for help) because she_{i} wants to leave soon.’ (Valenzuela 1997:123)
We still need more research to see if other verbs act the same way. When -kin is added to verbs other than tee- ‘work’, does it also have to mean "make someone do it while you do it with them"? We don't know yet (see also ex. (196)).

h: The Associative Applicative Construction (how "with someone" sentences work)
t: One more point. As far as other studies show, the "make someone do it" endings in the Panoan languages all come from the same old source. They look like -mV, -n, and ak- or wa-. None of them looks anything like the "with/helping" ending -kin. So when we compare related languages, we find no proof that -kin grew out of an old "make someone do it" ending (cf. Shibatani and Pardeshi 2002, Payne 2002).

h: 17.4.2.1. Coding Properties: Case-Marking and Constituent Order
t:
With the "with/helping" ending, a sentence can have two receivers: the one the action is done to, and the one you help. When both are named, both appear in the plain form, with no little word after them. Again, they can swap places, so the sentence can be read two ways. In (181) you can't tell who was cured and who was helped:
(181) Wesna-ra e-n Tsoma rao-n-kin-ke. | ‘I helped Wesna to cure Tsoma. / I helped Tsoma to cure Wesna.’
But in real stories, people usually leave out one or more of the people involved. They can do that because the listener already knows who they are. In my recordings, sentences that name all three people are extremely rare. Here is one of those rare cases:
(182) ...yoman maban-xon mi-n chopa mi-n bake-bo mi-n | chiton-kin-ti... | ‘...spinning the thread (and manufacturing cloth) you can dress with your daughters your own (resulting) chitontis...’
There is another option. The thing the action is done to can get a marker after it instead of staying plain. The examples below suggest that speakers prefer this marked version when that thing is more important in the conversation (from Valenzuela 1997:124-125):
(183) a. E-n-ra jatíbi jawéki ak-ai. | ‘I make everything / all kinds of things.’ | b. E-n mi-a jatíbi jawéki-nin a-kin-ti iki. | ‘I will help you with everything.’

h: 17.4.2.1. Coding Properties: Case-Marking and Constituent Order
t:
(184) a. E-n-ra pei bi-ai xobo a-ti. | ‘I am bringing leaves in order to build a house.’ | b. Maistoro-ra e-n pei bi-kin-ai xobo a-ti. | ‘I am helping the teacher to bring leaves in order to build a house.’
The helped person can also be marked differently. Instead of the plain form, it can get the "with" word betan. This happens when a verb has more than one "extra person" ending, probably to avoid confusion about who is who. You can see this in ex. (206a) in 17.5 (see also footnote 10 in Ch. 16).

h: 17.4.2.2. Extraction and Relativization
t:
As with the other "extra person" endings we looked at, both receivers can be moved to the front of the sentence. Both can also be the person described in a "who/which…" description part:
(185) a. Nato r-iki ochíti [e-n joni rao-n-kin-a]. | ‘This is the dog that I helped the man cure.’ | b. Nato r-iki joni [e-n ochíti raon-kin-a]. | ‘This is the man whom I helped cure the dog.’
(186) a. Joni [e-n (meráya) raon-kin-a]-ra moa jakon-tani iki. | ‘The man that I helped (the great shaman) to cure is a bit better already.’ | b. Joni [e-n raon-kin-a]-ra moa jawen awin jakon iki. | ‘The man whom I helped to cure (his wife), his wife is well already.’
Also, both receivers can be described by a "who/which…" part, whether that part comes before or after the noun it describes:
(187) a. E-n-ra bena-ke ochíti [Wesna-n joni raon-kin-a]. | b. E-n-ra bena-ke [Wesna-n joni raon-kin-a] ochíti. | ‘I looked for the dog that Wesna helped the man to cure.’
(188) a. E-n-ra bena-ke joni [Wesna-n ochíti raon-kin-a]. | b. E-n-ra bena-ke [Wesna-n ochíti raon-kin-a] joni. | ‘I looked for the man whom Wesna helped to cure the dog.’
But the results here are different from the other two "extra person" endings we looked at (especially the "for/against someone" ending -xon). Sometimes the "who/which…" part has the described noun sitting inside it. In that case there is some

h: 17.4.2.2. Extraction and Relativization
t:
evidence that speakers prefer to take the helped person as the one being described (NP_{REL}):^{21} In (189) both readings are possible, but in (190) only the reading with the man works.
(189) E-n-ra bena-ke [Wesna-n ochíti joni raon-kin-a]. | ‘I looked for the man whom Wesna helped to cure the dog.’ / | ‘I looked for the dog that Wesna helped the man to cure.’
(190) E-n-ra bena-ke [Wesna-n joni ochíti raon-kin-a]. | ‘I looked for the man whom Wesna helped to cure the dog.’ / |  I looked for the dog that Wesna helped the man to cure.’

h: 17.4.2.3. Interclausal Referentiality Control
t:
Sometimes the doer of one sentence is the receiver of the sentence before it. With the "with/helping" ending, that earlier receiver can be either one: the person the action was done to, or the person who was helped. In (191), ‘he’ can be the shaman or the man:
(191) E-n onáya joni rao-n-kin-a-ra | xobo-nko ka-ke. | ‘After I helped the shaman_{i} treat the man_{j} with plant medicine, he_{i/j} went home.’
The table below sums up how the helped person and the plain receiver behave in the grammar.
Still, I must say again that my judgements about "who/which…" description parts in this chapter come from only one native speaker. Also, the kind of test itself is, I admit, open to debate.
So with the "with/helping" ending, both receivers behave in roughly the same way. There is one difference. When the described noun sits inside the "who/which…" part, speakers may prefer to take the helped person as the one being described (NP_{REL}).

h: The Associative Applicative and Other Valency-Changing Devices ("with someone" and other person-changing endings)
t:
The "with/helping" ending can be combined with "make someone do it" endings, and their order matters. The ending -ma can come before or after it. The order changes which part of the meaning covers which. But the other "make someone do it" endings, a(k) and -n, must always come before the "with/helping" ending. If you put them after it, the sentence is wrong:
(192) Rona-n-ra Wesna bake rao | xea-ma-kin-ke. | ‘Rona helped Wesna give medicine to the child.’
I don't have full data on whether the helped person can be the "each other" partner of the doer. But ex. (198) shows that this is possible.
(193) E-n-ra nokon bene xea-kin-ma-ke. | ‘I made (him) drink with my husband.’
(194) Rona-n-ra jato mechá a-kin-ke. | ‘Rona helped them to make (it) wet.’
(195) Rona-n-ra e-a chopa pani-n-kin-ke. | ‘Rona helped me to hang the clothes.’
The "to someone's harm" ending can't be used with verbs that already carry the "each other" or "to yourself" endings. The -xon ending rarely appears with such verbs. The "with/helping" ending is different: it combines with them easily. In the next examples, the "to yourself" or "each other" ending comes before the "with/helping" ending:
(196) Ja pae-n-a-nin-ra e-a paké-kin-ke. | ‘That drunk (person) made me fall (falling with me).’
(197) Rona-n-ra nokon bake boexee-kin-ke. | ‘Rona helped / told my child to comb (combing herself too).’

h: The Associative Applicative and Other Valency-Changing Devices ("with someone" and other person-changing endings)
t:
(198) Joni-n-ra jawen rawí i-ananan-kin-ke | kopi-anan-kin-ke. | ‘The man confronted his enemy as an equal.’
In the next example from a story, the "with/helping" ending -kin comes before the "each other" ending:
(199) ...tee-ain-bo a-kin-anan-i no-n bake-bo | ja-ská-a-xon ani a-ti kopí. | ‘...we (my husband and I) help each other in our work in order to be able to raise our children.’

h: Non-Applicative Associative Constructions ("with someone" sentences that don't add a person)
t:
Of all the "extra person" endings, only the "with/helping" one has a close way of saying the same thing without it. In that version, the extra person is simply followed by a little word meaning "with". Compare the examples below:
(200) Tita-n-ra papa wai oro-kiin-ai. | ‘Mother helps father clear the chacra.’ / | ‘Mother clears the chacra with father.’ | Tita-n-ra wai oro-ai papa betan. | ‘Mother clears the chacra with father.’
The "with" word betan joins things of the same kind: people with people, animals with animals. The examples below have a human doer, so the one marked by betan must also be human. If it isn't, you use -ya to say ‘along with’ instead. (None of these word pieces can mean "with" in the sense of a tool, as in "cut with a knife".)
(201) E-a-ra kachio ka-i | ‘I go to the forest....’
The next sentence (shown earlier as (177)) uses the "with/helping" ending. After it comes a version that says the same thing without the ending. (Juan Melendres is the name of a local patron, a boss.)
(202) Juan Melendres-nin-ra e-a tee-kin-ai. | ‘I work for / with Juan Melendres (we both work).’
(203) Juan Melendres betan-ra e-a teet-ai. | ‘I work for / with Juan Melendres (we both work).’
Both versions mean the same thing here. Both say that the two people, the doer and the one marked by betan, take part in the action of the verb.

h: Non-Applicative Associative Constructions ("with someone" sentences that don't add a person)
t:
The next example from a story is especially telling. The speaker first uses the "with/helping" ending. Then the speaker says the same idea again, this time using betan instead.
(204) Ja-tian Ne-ino-nin shinan-a iki, ja i-kin-ti, no?;
(None) o sea, ja-bé i-ti. | ‘Then, the Nutria_{i} thought that (the woman) was going to be with him_{i} (join him_{i}), right?; that is, that she was going to be with him_{i}.’
Sentence (204) strongly supports my claim. Native speakers see the betan sentence as meaning almost the same as the "with/helping" one. We still need more research to explain when people choose one or the other.

h: Multiple Applicative Constructions (adding more than one extra person)
t:
You can put more than one "extra person" ending on the same verb, at least when I ask speakers to make up sentences. In the example below, Rono is the person helped. The person who benefits, mia ‘you’, is left out because it is understood:
(205) E-n-ra Rono shinan-kin-xon-ke | [mi-a ja-ská-kin a-xon-ti]. | ‘I gave Rono the idea so that he made it that way for you (lit. I thought with Rono on (your) behalf...).’ (Valenzuela 1997:127-128)
Examples (206a-b) show two ways to mark the helped person. In (206a), Wexá gets the "with" word. That makes the meaning clear. In (206b) it doesn't, so the sentence can be read two ways:
(206) a. E-n-ra Tsoma nonti rabi-kin-xon-ai Wexá betan. | ‘I praise the canoe for Tsoma with Wexá.’ | b. E-n-ra Wexá Tsoma nonti rabi-kin-xon-ai. | ‘I praised the canoe for Tsoma with Wexá.’ / | ‘I praised the canoe with Tsoma for Wexá.’
The example below combines the "with/helping" ending and the "to someone's harm" ending. The "with/helping" ending refers to the son. The "to someone's harm" ending refers to the owners of the canoe. Again, the "with/helping" ending comes first:
(207) Kesten Beso-n jawen bake jato-n nonti yoká-ti raan-a-ra | e-n yoká-kin-naan-tan-ke. | ‘Kesten Beso sent his son to ask for their canoe, and I accompanied him to ask for it to their detriment (probably they did not want to lend their canoe).’

h: Multiple Applicative Constructions (adding more than one extra person)
t:
Another speaker gave me the verb below. It has the same two endings, but in the opposite order. (This speaker said (207) was wrong.)
(208) pi-anaan-kin-ke / pi-kin-naan-kan-ke | ‘eat with somebody to somebody else’s detriment.
These data suggest that the order probably depends on which ending's meaning covers which. This point needs more research.

h: Summary
t: Let's sum up. SK has three "extra person" endings (applicatives). The first is -xon, the "for/against someone" ending. The second is -(V)naan ~ -(V)n, the "to someone's harm" ending. The third is -kin ~ -kiin, the "with/helping" ending. For the last two, which form you use depends partly on the length and weight of the verb. All three are textbook examples of this kind of ending. Each one is added to the end of the verb. Each one brings a new person into the sentence, with a clear role. This new person appears in the plain form, so it acts like an ordinary receiver. (The only exception: the helped person can get betan when the verb already has a doer and a receiver and all three people are named.) The sentence gains one more person. And the doer must carry the doer marker. Two of the endings, -xon and the "to someone's harm" ending, have no other way of saying the same thing. Only the "with/helping" ending has a close version without the ending, using the word betan. Since you can't avoid using the first two, they can't just be a stylistic choice for seeing an event in a different way (cf. Croft 1994). As for the "with/helping" ending, we still don't know why speakers choose it over betan, or the other way around. So far, no other Panoan language has had a detailed study of these endings. Still, it seems to be a general Panoan feature that the endings don't come from the little words that mark nouns.

h: Summary
t:
When I look at my recordings, I see that the three endings are used very differently. Some are much more common than others. They also combine differently with intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. For example, -xon goes easily with all kinds of verbs. But in real speech it shows up mostly with transitive verbs. There, -xon usually means "for someone's benefit". This fits Shibatani's (1996) idea that "for someone" endings are modeled on the verb ‘give’. With intransitive verbs, -xon can mean "for someone" or "against someone". Often the situation decides which. The meaning of the verb also helps make one reading more likely. Compare ‘work to someone’s benefit’ with ‘get sick to someone’s detriment’. To force the "against" reading, speakers can add the "poor/bad" marker -isi. Or they can use the combination V-xon-yama (i.e., VERB-BEN-NEG, "verb, not for the benefit of").
The "to someone's harm" ending -(V)naan ~ -(V)n is fairly rare in stories. As its label says, it brings in a person who is hurt by the action. It may be less picky than -xon about who or what can be the doer and especially the receiver. That is, objects and other non-living things can appear in some sentences with this ending, but not in the matching -xon sentences. This idea needs more research. Also, some verbs seem strongly tied to a "for someone" or an "against someone" situation. With these verbs, the other meaning is not accepted, even when you add the matching ending.

h: Summary
t:
One special thing about the "to someone's harm" ending: it only goes on transitive verbs. If you put it on an intransitive verb, the sentence is wrong. (Remember that -xon on an intransitive verb can mean either "for someone" or "against someone".) I have shown that the choice between the two endings really depends on whether the verb has a receiver. It does not depend on whether the doer is active or not.
Simplifying a bit, here is how the general "for/against someone" ending and the "to someone's harm" ending compare:
Some verbs sit halfway between intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. They behave in mixed ways that are hard to predict. You can't always tell if they take -xon or -(V)na(a)n ~ -(V)n, or what the result will mean. Even verbs of the same type can behave very differently. Take keen- ‘want, love, like, need’ and shinanbenot- ‘slip the mind, forget’. Both can mark their people in two ways: <ABS ABS> or <ABS INTRSS>. Keen- acts like an intransitive verb here. It can only take -xon, to mean either "for" or "against" someone (the combination keen-MAL- is
wrong). So keen- is different from noi- ‘love’. The two mean almost the same thing, but they work differently in the grammar. Noi- is a typical transitive verb. So it can take -xon to mean "for someone" and -(V)na(a)n to mean "to someone's harm". And the other verb of the pair, shinanbenot-, is unlike keen-: it does take both endings.

h: Summary
t:
The verb be- ‘bring’ is a typical transitive verb. Yet it can't take the "to someone's harm" ending. It needs -xon for both the "for" and the "against" meaning. Here is a possible reason. When you bring something, you usually bring it to someone. So ‘bring’ already carries a "for someone" idea. People use it with that meaning all the time. That may have fixed the form be-xon- and made be-enaan- unacceptable. (Unlike be-, bo- ‘carry, take’ can take both endings.) The opposite happens with kene- ‘miss, fail’. When you miss or fail, it is usually you who is hurt. So kene- can only take the "to someone's harm" ending, even when the meaning is "for someone". If I'm right, these verbs show how the way we usually picture an event, and the way we use the language, can shape the grammar and override its normal rules.
Finally, the "with/helping" ending goes equally well with intransitive verbs and transitive verbs. -Kin ~ -kiin usually adds a person who is accompanied or helped. With -xon and the "to someone's harm" ending, only the doer actually does the action. The "with/helping" ending is different. It always means that both the doer and the helped person take part. This shared action
may explain something odd. Some verbs have two completely different forms: one for a single person doing it alone, and one for several people or for use with a receiver. With -kin, you must use the second form. This is true even when only one person is the doer and the bare verb would normally have just one person. Another possibility is that the second form is needed because -kin adds one more person to the sentence.

h: Summary
t:
Most of the time, the "extra person" endings come after the other endings that change the number of people. These are the "make someone do it" endings, the "each other" ending, and the "to yourself" ending. The "extra person" endings come before the endings that add other meanings and the endings for time. However, with the "make someone do it" ending -ma, a different order is possible. The order shows which part of the meaning covers which. We have also seen -xon and the "each other" ending in different orders. Now remember two facts: where the "to someone's harm" ending sits in the verb, and that it needs a transitive verb. Because of this, it can never follow the "to yourself" or "each other" endings, since those always remove the receiver. So a grammar rule blocks some ideas that would make perfect sense, like ‘They left each other to the children’s detriment’ or ‘The child burned her / himself to my detriment.’
I also noted that -xon rarely comes after the "to yourself" ending, even though it combines easily with all kinds of verbs. The reason may be that the "to yourself" ending already shows that someone is affected, namely the doer.
-xon is much more common in stories than the "to someone's harm" ending. One reason may be that the latter needs a transitive verb. Another may be that -xon has two jobs: "for someone" and "against someone".

h: Summary
t:
In this chapter I have also looked at how the two receivers behave: the ordinary receiver and the person added by the ending. Both appear in the plain form (ABS, no marker). Both can stand anywhere between the doer and the verb. So neither word order nor markers tell them apart, and you may not know which is which. Also, both can be moved to the front or tacked on at the end. Both can be described by a "who/which…" part placed before or after the noun. And both can be the "each other" partner of the doer (where I have data). Both can also be understood as the doer of the main sentence in sentences joined with -a. Still, one early result shows that speakers make small distinctions between them. It comes from "who/which…" parts that have the described noun inside them. With the "to someone's harm" ending and especially -xon, speakers prefer to take the ordinary receiver as the one being described (NP_{REL}). So the ordinary receiver seems to be the more "real" receiver. But with the "with/helping" ending, speakers seem to prefer the helped person as the one being described.
In general, SK uses different tools for adding an extra person and for "make someone do it". Still, the "with/helping" ending is used for making someone do something while you do it with them. So in a way, it steps into "make someone do it" territory. This is especially true when it goes on the verb tee-

h: Summary
t:
‘work’ (and maybe also paké- ‘fall’). With these verbs, it must mean "make someone do it while you do it with them". The doer, with the doer marker, is the one who makes it happen. The helped person is the one made to do it. Both take part in the action. Compare this with the other endings. The other "extra person" endings mean that only the doer does the action. The "make someone do it" endings mean that only the person made to do it does the action. The "with/helping" ending means that both the doer and the added person really take part. However, there is no evidence that the "extra person" endings and the "make someone do it" endings come from the same source.
DETRANSITIVIZATION:
This chapter is about saying that you do something to yourself and that people do something to each other in SK. For "to yourself", SK usually (but not always) adds the ending -t. For "to each other", it must add a special "each other" ending to the verb. Adding either ending to a transitive verb takes away the separate receiver. The sentence then has fewer people in it.

h: The Middle Marker -T (the -t ending)
t:
The ending -t shows that the action mainly affects the doer. In the words of one linguist, the doer is the “principal locus of the effects” (Klaiman 1988:36). Linguists call this the "middle". Around the world, verbs that use such endings fall into several groups of meaning. These include: grooming or body care (washing, combing), moving in place (turning), changing body position (sitting down), doing something for yourself,
actions that are naturally done to each other, moving from place to place, feelings, thinking, things that just happen by themselves, and pointing back to the speaker in reported speech (Kemmer 1993:16-19).
Many SK verbs naturally have a doer and a receiver. They can become intransitive verbs by adding the ending -t. I call -t the "middle" ending. That is because it does jobs very similar to the "middle" verb forms of some old European and Indian languages, like Classical Greek and Classical Sanskrit (Klaiman 1988 and references therein, Kemmer 1993). One big difference: in SK, "to each other" uses a separate ending. In SK, adding -t can show several things. It can mean you do the action to yourself or to part of your body, as in combing your hair. It can mean the doer changes by itself, with no one causing it. It can mean the doer changes because of someone who is not mentioned. It can also be used for physical actions, feelings or changes in feelings, and doing something for yourself. To put it all together: -t “indicates broadly that the action is performed with ‘special reference’ to the subject”, that is, the action is mainly about the doer (Smyth 1974, in Klaiman 1993:33).

h: The Middle Marker -T (the -t ending)
t:
The ending -t has different forms. Which form you use goes back to the history of the language.^1 Usually, a two-beat bare verb ending in a vowel takes the form -t. With some of these verbs, -t changes the last vowel, making it sound different or longer. When the verb plus -t is followed by an ending that starts with a
For a discussion of the “reflexive” ("to yourself") marker in Panoan languages, see Loos (1985).
consonant, the /t/ drops out. The last vowel of the bare verb gets extra stress to make up for it (for example, ‘burn,’ ‘hide,’ and others). Other forms of -t are -meet, used when the verb ends in /n/ (for example, ‘open,’ ‘hang’), -(k)oot, -(k)eet (‘turn over’), -(k)iit and -(k)aat.
To keep things simple, I translate the SK forms for unfinished actions into English present tense, and the forms for finished actions into English past tense.
As I said above, the "middle" ending does more than mean "to yourself", as in the translations in Table 18.1. In the next example, it seems to mean doing something for your own benefit (but cf. 18.1.6):
(1) Jawe onan-ma ik-ax no-a jain kaman | nokó-yamai. | ‘If we are not knowledgeable we will not meet our goals.’
In the sentences below, the "middle" ending goes on verbs of movement, body position, and feelings.

h: The Middle Marker -T (the -t ending)
t:
(2) [Jato a-taanan]-ki ik-á iki moa Chichíporo | Ainbo-ki manot-a iki. | ‘After telling them that, the Canary Woman disappeared.’
(3) [Pikó-ke-tian]-bi no-a ani a-kan-ai... | ‘From the moment we are born, they (our parents) take care of us....’
(4) Jawe-tian-ki no-n Inka jo-ai, ja-tian-ra | no-a i-nox iki weni-t-i. | ‘The day our Inka comes back, we will stand up (from among the dead).’
(5) Ja-tian jawen bene-n raté-xon | ino to’-a-ke | ‘Then her husband got scared and shot the jaguar.’
The "middle" ending has more jobs, which I will cover later in section 18.1.9. One is for things that happen by themselves: the doer changes, and no one causes it (linguists call this "anticausative"). Another is for things that happen to the doer because of someone who is not mentioned ("agentless passive", like English "the window was broken").

h: Reflexive and Emphatic Subject Senses ("to yourself" and "by yourself" meanings)
t:
A "to yourself" sentence (linguists call it "reflexive") is one where the doer and the receiver are the same person. The doer acts on itself. Around the world, languages do this in two main ways. One way is to put a "self" word in the receiver's spot, like English himself. The other is to add a special ending to a transitive verb. That turns it into an intransitive verb that means "to yourself" (Dixon and Aikhenvald 2000:11). As we have seen, SK uses the second way. It adds -t to a verb that normally has a doer and a receiver. The verb often becomes an intransitive "to yourself" verb. Because of this, the doer loses the doer marker (ERG) and appears in the plain form (ABS). SK also has a set of "emphatic" pronouns, meaning "by my own action, I myself". Earlier writers called them “reflexive pronouns” (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:67). But these pronouns are usually not needed in "to yourself" sentences. And they also appear in many sentences that are not about doing something to yourself. Look at this ordinary transitive sentence:
(6) a. Tsoma-n-ra ja chachi-ke. | ‘Tsoma poked him (with an arrow, knife, something pointed).’
In the sentence above, the plain-form pronoun ja ‘him’ can't mean Tsoma. So the sentence can't mean ‘Tsoma poked himself.’ Now look at the "to yourself" version of (6a). Tsoma has no doer marker anymore, and the verb has the middle form:

h: Reflexive and Emphatic Subject Senses ("to yourself" and "by yourself" meanings)
t:
(6b) b. Tsoma-ra chachí-ke. | ‘Tsoma poked himself.’
Here is another pair like that: a transitive verb and its version with the "middle" ending:
(7) a. Mi-n-ra shino chekeren-ke. | ‘You tickled the capuchin monkey.’ | b. Mi-a-ra chekeremee-ke. | ‘You tickled yourself.’
As I said, the emphatic pronouns are optional in most "to yourself" sentences. In the English translations of (8) and (9), the words in brackets show what the optional emphatic pronouns add:
(8) Tsoma-ra (ja-n-bi-x) chachí-ke. | ‘Tsoma pinched himself (by his own action).’
(9) Mi-a-ra (mi-n-bi-x) chekeremee-ke. | ‘You tickled yourself (by your own action).’
The emphatic pronouns historically contain the emphatic marker -bi ('self, very'). Yet they can take -bi again, as you can see here:
(10) Wesna-ra ja-n-bi-x-bi topomee-yama-ke. | ‘Wesna didn’t count herself (e.g. when counting the people present in the meeting).’
Here is a surprise. rete- ‘kill’ is a typical transitive verb. Yet it can't take the "middle" ending to mean ‘kill oneself’. Sentence (12) is wrong:
(11) Tsoma-n-ra Mane rete-ke. | ‘Tsoma killed Mane.’
(12) Mane-ra reté-ke. | ‘Mane killed himself.’
You can still say ‘kill oneself’, though. You use the intransitive verb mawat- ‘die’ together with the right emphatic pronoun:
(13) Mane-ra ja-n-bi-x mawá^{3}-ke. | ‘Mane himself died / died by his own action.’
Reté-, the "middle" form of rete- ‘kill,’ does exist, but it means something else:

h: Reflexive and Emphatic Subject Senses ("to yourself" and "by yourself" meanings)
t:
(14) Tsoma-ra reté-kain-ke. | ‘Tsoma fainted falling to the ground.’
Another way to say ‘kill oneself’ is to say how it was done, as in (15b). The emphatic pronoun is optional here:
(15) a. Joni-baon-ra to' a-kan-ke. | ‘The men shot at him / her / it.’
I can't tell for sure whether mawat ~ mawá ‘die’ itself has the "middle" ending. SK has a transitive verb mawa- ‘imitate’, but it might not be related to ‘die.’
(b) Ja-bo-ra (jato-n-bi-ni-x) to' i-kan-ke. | ‘They shot themselves (by their own action).’
You will find more examples with sound-imitating verbs like to' a(k)- and to' i(k)- in section 18.1.3 below.
Intransitive verbs, including those that can take a second person, usually can't take the "middle" ending to mean "to yourself".^4 Instead, verbs of the second kind get a "to yourself" meaning simply by leaving out the second person. When that second person is there, it carries the "to" marker -ki or the marker -n:
Extended intransitive
(16) Wesna-ra Tsoma-ki siná-ke. | ‘Wesna got angry at Tsoma.’
(17) Wesna-ra Tsoma-n rabin-ai. | ‘Wesna is embarrassed about Tsoma.’
Reflexive sense
(18) Wesna-ra siná-ke. | ‘Wesna got angry at herself.’ Also ‘Wesna got angry.’
(19) Wesna rabin-ai. | ‘Wesna is embarrassed about herself.’ Also ‘Wesna is embarrassed.’
In some languages, some intransitive verbs that can take a second person also have a "to yourself" form. Think of English sentences like I talked to myself and I laughed at myself.

h: Reflexive and Emphatic Subject Senses ("to yourself" and "by yourself" meanings)
t:
Shiro- ‘laugh at, make fun of’ is an intransitive verb that can take a second person. It marks its people as <ABS -ki>. That means the one doing the laughing is in the plain form, and the one laughed at gets -ki:
(20) Wesna-ra Tsoma-ki shiro-ke. | ‘Wesna made fun of Tsoma.’
Something special about shiro-: according to one speaker I worked with, you must add an emphatic pronoun to get the "to yourself" meaning:
(21) Wesna-ra ja-n-bi-x shiro-ke. | ‘Wesna made fun of herself.’
You can also add the meaning "I did it myself" to a shiro- sentence. This is the same meaning the emphatic pronouns gave in earlier examples. To do this, you add the emphatic -bi to the doer:
(22) Wesna-bi-ra Tsoma-ki shiro-ke. | ‘Wesna herself made fun of Tsoma.’
Another verb that seems to need an emphatic pronoun instead of the "middle" -t to mean "to yourself" is keen- ‘want / love.’ Keen- sits halfway between an intransitive verb and a transitive verb. It marks its people as <ABS ABS / INTRSS>. But note that example (24) can also be read another way, without "to yourself":
(23) Wesna-ra Tsoma(-n) keen-ai. | ‘Wesna loves / wants Tsoma.’
(24) Wesna-ra ja-n-bi-x keen-ai. | ‘Wesna loves / wants herself. / Wesna herself loves / wants (him / her / it).’

h: Reflexive and Emphatic Subject Senses ("to yourself" and "by yourself" meanings)
t:
Native speakers did not like the "to yourself" reading of (24). But they easily accepted noi-kaat-, the "middle" form of the transitive verb noi- ‘love.’ This suggests why the "middle" form of keen- sounds bad. The reason is the kind of verb keen- is (halfway to an intransitive verb), not its meaning or use. (These two verbs also differ in how they say "to someone's harm"; see 17.3.2, especially exx. (122)-(123).)
Usually, the "middle" ending can't go on a verb that already has a "make someone do it" ending. One exception is bo-ma ‘send’. Probably this is because it is now treated as one ordinary word:
(25) Wesna-ra kirika bo-ma-kaa-ke. | ‘Wesna sent a letter to herself.’
Later in this chapter I give examples of the opposite order: a "make someone do it" ending added to a verb with the "middle" ending.

h: Reflexive Onomatopoeic Verbs ("to yourself" with sound-word verbs)
t:
SK has a group of verbs made from a sound-imitating word plus a general verb. That verb is ak- ‘do’ (with a doer and a receiver) or its intransitive partner ik-. What's interesting is that
these sound-imitating verbs can have a special "middle" form to mean "to yourself". This form can't be split into smaller pieces (I mark it REFL, the "to yourself" form). Compare barking at someone (26), just barking (27), and barking at yourself (28):
(26) Ochíti-nin-ra joni jojó a-ke. | ‘The dog barked at the man.’
(27) Ochíti-ra jojó i-ke. | ‘The dog barked.’
(28) Ochíti-ra jojó iaká-ke. | ‘The dog barked at itself (e.g. at its own shadow).’
The verb ‘kiss (on) the hand’ has a body-part beginning piece before the sound-imitating word:
(29) Tsoma-n-ra Wesna me-tsó a-ke. | ‘Tsoma kissed Wesna’s hand / kissed Wesna on the hand’
(30) Wesna-ra me-tsó iaká-ke. | ‘Wesna kissed her own hand / kissed herself on the hand.’
I have not found forms like these with any other kind of verb.

h: Locative Reflexives ("to yourself" in place phrases)
t:
In SK, a phrase about place, like the one below, can't show whether "him/her" means someone else or the doer. A pronoun meaning "him" and one meaning "himself" look the same:
(31) Wesna-n-ra chomo ja pekáo a-ke. | ‘Wesna put the jar behind her(self).’

h: Possessive Reflexives ("to your own" (body part or thing))
t:
To show that the owner is the same person as the doer ("her own brother"), Shipibo often uses -bi, an ending that adds emphasis. This matters most with 'he', 'she' and 'it'. In English, "she killed her brother" can mean her own brother or someone else's. Shipibo has the same problem, as (32) shows. Adding -bi points to her own brother. You can also put the word kikin ‘own, legitimate, elegant’ before the owned thing. (kikin can also make a word stronger, like 'really'.) Compare (32) and (33):
(32) Ja-n-ra jawen poi rete-ke. | ‘She_{i} killed her_{i} brother. / She_{i} killed her_{j} brother.’
(33) Ja-n-ra jawen (kikin) poi(-bi) rete-ke. | ‘She killed her own brother.’
But these tricks are not fixed rules yet. They don't always give the 'her own' meaning. Speakers often leave out -Bi, and kikin even more often. And even when both words are there, ‘her own’ in (33) might point to someone other than the doer. Examples (34)-(41) show more sentences meaning 'my own', 'her own', and so on (that is, adding -bi and kikin):
(34) Jawen (kikin) xobomea-x(-bi)-ra jo-ke. | ‘(She) came from her own house.’
(35) Jawen (kikin) ochíti(-bi)-ra yoina a-ma-i ka-ke. | ‘(He) went to hunt with his own dog.’ Lit. ‘He went (to the forest) making his own dog obtain game.’
In examples (36)-(39), the verb has a beginning piece that names a body part, like 'hand', 'leg' or 'hair'. These sentences can match English sentences like 'he burned his own hand'. In each pair, (a) has someone doing something to another person. In (b), the verb has MID (the 'to yourself' ending, which linguists call the middle). So the person does it to their own body:

h: Possessive Reflexives ("to your own" (body part or thing))
t:
(36) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma me-méno-ke. | ‘Wesna burned Tsoma on the hand / burned Tsoma’s hand.’ | Tsoma-ra me-ménoo-ke. | ‘Tsoma burned himself on the hand / burned his own hand.’
(37) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma ki-xonin-ke. | ‘Wesna rubbed Tsoma on the leg /rubbed Tsoma’s leg.’ | Tsoma-ra ki-xonimee-ke. | ‘Tsoma rubbed himself on the leg / rubbed his own leg.’
(38) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma ja-no-ke. | ‘Wesna introduced her finger in Tsoma’s mouth.’ | Tsoma-ra ja-nokoo-ke. | ‘Tsoma introduced his finger in his own mouth.’
(39) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma bo-chó-ke. | ‘Wesna washed Tsoma’s hair.’ | Tsoma-ra bo-chokí-ke. | ‘Tsoma washed his own hair.’
But some verbs with a body-part beginning piece cannot take the 'to yourself' ending. In (40b) and (41b), the forms with a star are not possible:
(40) a. jina-ki natex-ke ~ ji-natex-ke | ‘bit X on the tail, bit X’s tail’ | b. jina-nko natex-ee-ke but ji-natex-ee-ke | ‘bit oneself on the tail, bit self’s tail.’
(41) a. mapo-nko rishki-ke ~ ma-rishki-ke | ‘hit X on the head, hit X’s head’ | b. mapo-nko rishki-kaa-ke but ma-rishki-kaa-ke | ‘hit oneself on the head, hit one’s own head.’
We still need more research to find out exactly when the 'to yourself' ending can go with these body-part verbs.

h: Benefactive Reflexives ("for yourself")
t:
As we saw in the last chapter, you can add a person for whom something is done. You do this by adding the ending -xon to the verb. (It is an ending that brings in an extra person.) Now the verb has one more person in it. So the doer always gets the doer marker (ERG). The person helped, and the thing acted on if there is one, both stay in the plain form (ABS). Look at these examples. tee- ‘work’ is an intransitive verb, and xoi- ‘roast’ is a transitive verb:
(42) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma tee-xon-ke. | ‘Wesna worked for / instead of Tsoma.’
(43) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma atsa xoi-xon-ke. | Wesna roasted yuca for Tsoma.’
What if you do something for yourself? Then you don't use -xon. Instead you add a phrase meaning ‘for herself, what is of herself.’ It is the word for 'her' followed by -bi, the emphasis ending. The verb has no extra ending, so no extra person is added to it:
(44) Wesna-ra jawen-a-bi tee-ke. | ‘Wesna worked for herself / what is of herself.’
(45) Wesna-n-ra jawen-a-bi atsa xoi-ke. | ‘Wesna roasted manioc for herself / roasted her own yuca.’
Look at the English translations of (44) and (45). They can also mean 'her own' thing, like 'her own yuca'. So, to sum up: the Shipibo 'to yourself' ending (the middle) does not regularly mean 'for yourself' (compare ex. (1)).

h: Reflexives without an Antecedent ("to yourself" with no one named)
t:
Shipibo can also have 'to oneself' sentences where nobody is named as the one doing it:
(46) Neno-ra yama-ke to' iaká-kas-ai. | ‘Here there has been no suicide attempt.’
(47) Jakon-ma r-iki no-n-bi-x-bi namakaat-a. | ‘It is bad to dream about oneself.’

h: Reflexives and Complex Sentences ("to yourself" across linked sentences)
t:
The next sentence has two parts, each with its own verb. The second part says why I am going: to look at myself. The 'myself' there points back to the doer of the main part, 'I':
(48) E-a-ra nokon xobo-nko kai [ispíko-nin oinmee-ti]. | ‘I am going to my house to look at myself in the mirror.’
Unlike (48), the main part of (49) has a doer and a receiver: Wesna asks Kate. Notice that 'herself' in the 'which…' description part can point to either woman. It can be the jar Wesna made, or the jar Kate made:
(49) Wesna-n-ra Kate yoká-ke [ja-n(-bi) chomo ak-á]. | ‘Wesna_{i} asked Kate_{j} for the jar she_{i} had made herself_{i} / the jar she_{j} had made herself_{j}.’
In the next example, the 'to yourself' verb sits inside the part that says what I think:
(50) E-n-ra shinan-ai [Tsoma ja-n-bi-x menot-a]. | ‘I think that Tsoma burnt himself.’

h: Reflexive, Anticausative, and Agentless Passive Senses ("to yourself", "it just happened", and "it was done")
t: Adding -t to a transitive verb can give several meanings. It can mean doing something to yourself (reflexive). It can mean something just happens on its own (anticausative). Or it can mean something is done to someone, by a doer who is not named (agentless passive). The 'to yourself' meaning is possible when the one the sentence is about is alive (but remember reté- in (12) above).

h: 18.1.9.1. Anticausative Sense
t:
Linguists use the word “anticausative” for something that happens to a person or thing by itself. Nobody, or almost nobody, seems to cause it. English has this too: 'the door opened', 'the glass broke'. A verb with -t can mean 'to yourself', or 'it just happened', or both. The examples below show this:
Transitive
(51) Joni-n-ra koríki miin-ke. | ‘The man buried the money.’
(52) Wesna-n-ra Tsoma xe-tse-ke. | ‘Wesna took something out from (between) Tsoma’s teeth.’ |  ‘Wesna took out Tsoma’s teeth / tooth.’
Detransitivized reflexive sense
(53) E-a-ra mashi-n miimee-ke. | ‘I buried myself in the sand.’
(54) Wesna-ra (xeta) xe-tsekee-ke. | ‘Wesna took out her denture.’
Detransitivized anticausative sense
(55) Mashi-n meosoti pake-kan-a-ra miimee-ke. | ‘The ring that they dropped in the sand got buried.’
(56) Wesna-ra (xeta) xe-tsekee-ke. | ‘Wesna’s denture fell.’
Some sentences with the 'to yourself' ending are read only, or mostly, as 'it just happened'. This is especially true when the thing affected is not alive, like clothes:
Transitive
(57) Wesna-n-ra chopa kato-ke. | ‘Wesna folded the clothes.’
Detransitivized anticausative sense
(58) Nokon papa-n tari-ra niwe-n ak-á kato-kaa-ke. | ‘My father’s tari folded due to the wind.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:142)
Loriot, Lauriault, and Day (1993:270) give mishkí- as the only 'to yourself' form of mishkí- ‘fish with hook.’ They say mishkí- has two different

h: 18.1.9.1. Anticausative Sense
t:
meanings, ‘hook oneself’ and ‘choke.’ The speakers I worked with know two different 'to yourself' forms for mishki-: mishki- ~ mishki-t- and mishki-kaa-:
Transitive
(59) Nima-n-ra sipan mishki-ai. | ‘Nima is fishing sardines.’
Detransitivized reflexive sense
(60) Yomera-i ka-i-ra e-a e-n-bi-x-bi | mishki-kaa-ke / mishkí-ke. | ‘While going fishing I hooked myself (I had the hook hanged on the shoulder).’
Detransitivized anticausative sense
(61) E-a-ra boe-n xao-n mishki-kaa-ke / mishkí-ke. | ‘I choked with the boquichico’s (kind of fish) bone.’
Most speakers I asked said the two forms mishki- and mishki-kaa- mean the same thing. But for one speaker they are different. For this speaker, mishki- can only mean 'it just happened' (choking). And mishki-kaa- can only mean 'you did it to yourself' (hooking yourself) (Yoi Sani, p.c. 2000).

h: 18.1.9.2. Agentless Passive Sense
t:
First, what is a “passive”? In a passive sentence, the one something is done to becomes the main topic. The doer becomes less important. English does this: 'The cake was eaten (by the kids).' A typical passive has three parts: a) the doer is pushed into the background, b) the receiver moves into the spotlight, and c) the verb describes more of a state than an action. Each of these can make the sentence lose its receiver (Givón 1990:chapter 14). Some languages have a passive where the doer must be left out. We know someone did the action, but who did it doesn't matter. This is called an “agentless passive.” English 'I got robbed' is like this.
Shipibo 'to yourself' verbs (middle verbs) have a third meaning too. Besides 'to yourself' and 'it just happened', they can mean 'it was done to me by someone' (the agentless passive). Take bachin- ‘pull by the hair’ and osan- ‘laugh at.’ Their middle forms can mean doing it to yourself. Or they can mean having it done to you, by someone not named:
Transitive
(62) Nato ainbaon-ra jawen bene-n merati bachin-ke. | ‘This woman pulled her husband’s lover by the hair.’^{5} (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:99)
(63) Bake-n-ra oa pae-n-a-bo osan-ai. | ‘The child is laughing at those drunk ones over there.’
If a woman finds out or thinks her husband is cheating on her, it is very common for her to pull her husband’s lover by the hair. People expect this, since a woman must be siná ‘brave.’

h: 18.1.9.2. Agentless Passive Sense
t:
Detransitivized reflexive sense:
(64) Nokon mapo-nko ia chaba chaba ik-ai-tian, bi-ti shinan-i-ra | e-a bachimee-res-ke. | ‘Since the lice were making my head itch and itch, trying to catch it I pulled myself by the hair.’
(65) Ispijo-nin oimeet-ax-ra e-a osamee-ke. | ‘Looking (at myself) in the mirror, I laughed at myself.’
Detransitivized agentless passive sense:
(66) Yanka-bi-res-a e-a bachimee-ke ikon-tani | i-ken-ma-bi. | ‘I was pulled by the hair unfairly, without it being true.’ (i.e., a woman thought I was having an affair with her husband and pulled me by the hair.)
(67) Nokon kené jakon-ma-shoko icha napon piko-ax-a, e-a | osamee-ke. | ‘Because I ended up with a little ugly pottery design in front of many people, I was laughed at.’
In (67), 'I' is the doer of both parts of the sentence. We know this from the ending -ax, a marker that says the same person does the next action. This ending also fits the main verb osameeke, which is an intransitive verb. So in the second, main part, 'I' is the one being laughed at. The one doing the laughing is not named. Compare the sentence above with
(68). There, the plural ending on the verb shows that the main part is about 'they', or 'people' in general. Also, the ending -ketian shows that the two parts have different doers. (It is a marker that tells you the next action is done by someone else.)

h: 18.1.9.2. Agentless Passive Sense
t:
(68) Nokon kené jakon-ma-shoko icha napon piko-ke-tian-ra, e-a | osan-kan-ke. | ‘Because I ended up with a little ugly pottery design in front of many people, they laughed at me.’
Two more verbs work the same way. They can mean 'to yourself' or 'done to you by others': yoi- ‘tell’ > yoi-kaa- ‘tell oneself / be talked about’ and ninká- ‘hear’ > ninka-kaa- ‘hear oneself / be heard about (i.e., others hear something about the subject).’
Speakers all agree that these middle verbs can mean 'to yourself'. But they don't always agree that a verb can also mean 'done to you by others'. This suggests that the passive meaning is not the basic one. For example, the transitive verb potsi- ‘squeeze, milk (a cow)’ becomes potsi-t-:
(69) Yamékiri-tibi-ra waka xoma potsi-t-ai. | ‘Every day at dawn the cow is milked.’ (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:334)
One speaker accepted the sentence above. But two others rejected it. For them, potsi-t-ai can only have the 'to yourself' meaning.
The verb noko- ‘find, meet somebody’ also has two different 'to yourself' forms, just like mishki- ‘fish with hook.’ But this time everyone agrees that each form means something different: noko-t- ‘arrive’ and noko-kaa- ‘be found.’
Transitive
(70) Kachio ka-xon-ra kamox no-n noko-a iki. | ‘Going to the forest, we found a shushupe snake.’

h: 18.1.9.2. Agentless Passive Sense
t:
Detransitivized, motion
(71) E-a-ra yamé nokó-wan-ke. | ‘I arrived at night.’
Detransitivized agentless passive sense
(72) Kachio jabat-i ka-[a]x-bi-ra e-a noko-kaa-ke. | ‘I hid in the forest but was found (by others).’
Klaiman (1988:36-38) studied the middle in the Indo-European languages. In those languages, the basic job of the middle is this: the one the sentence is about is affected by what happens. Klaiman sees what I call here the “anticausative sense” ('it just happened') as a stretch of that basic job. The one the sentence is about is affected by the action, but plays no part in making it happen. According to Klaiman, the passive came fairly late in Indo-European history. It is found in only two branches: Greek and Indo-Iranian. And it may have grown out of stretching the 'it just happened' (anticausative)
use even further. That is, the one the sentence is about is affected by an action that someone else does.
Look at these Sanskrit sentences (from Klaiman 1988:36-37):
Sanskrit
(73) a. devadatto namati daṇḍam | ‘Devadatta bends the stick.’ | b. namate daṇḍaḥ | ‘The stick bends.’ | c. namyate devadattena daṇḍaḥ | ‘The stick is bent by Devadatta.’
In (b) and (c), the verb has the middle form. In (a), it has the normal form, which linguists call the active. The table below shows how the uses of the middle grew over time in Indo-European:

h: 18.1.9.2. Agentless Passive Sense
t:
Klaiman (1988:37) concludes that the Indo-European middle shows that the one the sentence is about is affected by the action. This is true even if that one also does, starts, controls or sets off the action. In Klaiman's words, subjects “have affected entity conceptual status, irrespective of their possible concomitant status as actors, sources, controllers, or catalysts of action.”
What we have seen in this section suggests that the Shipibo middle is now spreading from stage (2) to stage (3) in the table. In both stages, the one the sentence is about is affected by the action. The verbs describe more of a state than in the matching transitive sentence. And no other hidden person takes over the spotlight from the one the sentence is about.

h: Middle Stems and Causative Constructions (-t verbs with "make someone do it")
t:
'To yourself' verbs can also take the 'make someone do it' ending. The English translations below give the meaning native speakers liked best:
(74) Wasaman-ra miimee-ma-yama-ke. | ‘Wasan didn’t let someone bury himself.’
(75) Wasaman-ra Rono noko-kaa-ma-ke. | ‘Wasan allowed / contributed (so) that Rono be found.’
(76) Wasaman-ra Rono katokoo-ma-ke. | ‘Wasan allowed / contributed (so) that Rono be chosen.’
The next sentence can have a 'make it happen' meaning even though it has no 'make someone do it' ending. Here the doer just sets things off:
(77) Bake-bo-ra jato-n-bi-ni-x kikin-i rishki-kaa-kan-ke. | ‘The children themselves caused that they be hit (e.g. by their parents) with a pole (as punishment). / The children hit themselves with a pole.’
We have also looked at 'to yourself' verbs with the 'make someone do it' ending -ma in 16.3.2.
In this book I have described two more jobs of the middle ending -t. First, 'start' and 'finish' verbs (phasal verbs) must match the verb they go with: both must be intransitive verbs, or both transitive verbs. -t helps them match (15.3.1). Second, -t can weaken a strong transitive verb. Then -ma can express a less direct kind of 'making someone do it' (16.3.2).

h: Reciprocalization (doing something to each other)
t:
To say people do something to each other, Shipibo adds the ending -(ana)nan ~ -anan to the verb. It means that two similar actions are happening. The doer of the first action is the receiver of the second, and the other way around. So the two people act on each other (linguists call this reciprocal). Usually, once people act on each other, there is no separate receiver anymore. So the doers lose the doer marker and appear in the plain form (ABS). Which form do you use? According to Faust (1973:73), count the syllables (beats) of the verb. An even number gets -anan; an odd number gets -ananan. But this is a strong habit, not a strict rule. Speakers may use both forms with the same verb; e.g., rete-ananan-kan-ai ~ rete-anan-kan-ai ‘they kill each other;’ see also the examples with noko- ‘meet’ in (78) and (79) below.
