Shipibo 'each other' sentences can be sorted by how the doers are shown: two names joined by 'and'; a plural doer; no doer named, but a plural ending on the
verb; one doer plus a 'with someone' phrase; and one doer with nothing else. Here are examples of each type:
Coordinated NP subject:
(78) [Yawish betan mari]-ra atsa wai-nko noko-ananan-ke. | ‘The Armadillo and the Agouti met (each other) in the yuca chacra.’

h: Reciprocalization (doing something to each other)
t:
The next example shows that an 'each other' verb can also take -bekon, an ending meaning that two people do the action (7.7.5). Notice too that the 'each other' ending has a different form here than in (78), even though the verb is the same:
(79) [Kate betan Rono]-ra noko-anan-bekon-ai. | ‘Kate and Rono met (each other).’
Plural subject:
Most plural doers in my data include the number rabé ‘two.’ In the next example the plural ending -kan is optional, because the number already tells us there is more than one:
(80) [Ainbo rabé]-ronki bachin-anan(-kan)-ai. | ‘(I heard that) two women are pulling each other by the hair.’
(81) [Bake-bo]-ra chiban-anan-kan-ai. | ‘The children are chasing each other. / The children are competing against each other in a race (e.g., between two schools).’
The next example comes from a story about a woman shaman who had two husbands. It is interesting because three people are involved:
(82) Ja-bo-kaya kimisha noi-anan-kan-a. | ‘But the three of them loved each other.’
In the sentence below, the plural ending -kan comes before the 'each other' ending. We would not expect this:
(83) No-a ninká-kanan-ti ja-ke; ainbaon ninkat-ai | benbo-n-ribi ninkat-ai iki. | ‘We have to understand each other; women have to understand (men) and men have to understand (women) too.’
Unexpressed subject with plural-marked verb:

h: Reciprocalization (doing something to each other)
t:
In the sentences below, no doer is named. The plural ending -kan on the verb gives them a general meaning, like English 'people' or 'they' in 'they say':
(84) Rinko-baon jema-n-ronki rete-anan-kan-ai. | ‘(I heard that) there is a war in foreign countries.’
(85) Ono-ra rami-anan-i tsamá-kan-ke. | ‘A group of people are insulting each other over there.’
Singular subject and comitative complement:
(86) [Kesten Beso]-ra Wano betan pota-ananan-ke. | ‘Kesten Beso and Wano separated.’
-ra is a marker that shows how the speaker knows something. It always comes right after the first main chunk of the sentence. So in (86), Wano betan ('with Wano') is not part of the doer. Ex. (87) comes from a story where the shaman Ashi is the main character:
(87) ...bechi-ax-ki [Bari betan] Ashi rete-ana[n]-ni-ke... | .’..after finding (him) Ashi and the Sun fought against each other...’
In ex. (87), the first part has -ax, the marker that says the same person does the next action. Remember Table 9.2 on doers that partly overlap in linked sentence parts. Say the first part has one doer, and the main part has that same person plus others. Then you would normally need the 'someone else' marker instead.
Singular subject:
These examples are almost the same as the ones with one doer and a 'with someone' phrase. The difference is that the 'with someone' phrase is missing. So the sentence is fine without naming the second person. That means a better translation of these Shipibo 'each other'

h: Reciprocalization (doing something to each other)
t:
sentences might be ‘to do an action in a reciprocal way (with X),’ that is, back and forth with someone. Look at these examples:
(88) E-a-ra keen-anan-ai. | ‘I love someone (who also loves me).’
(89) E-a-ronki tima-nan-wan-ke. | ‘(I was told) I had a fight.’ (I don’t remember it, I was drunk). Lit. ‘(I was told) I hit (with somebody) in a reciprocal way.’
(90) E-a-ra wisha-anan-ai. | ‘I write to someone (who will also write to me afterwards).’
Sentences like these, with one doer and no one else named, have also been found in Kashinawa, a language related to Shipibo (Camargo, ms.). There they were called “response reciprocal.” In every case, the one doer knows that the action is returned, or will be returned later. I have found other examples like (88)-(90). They use the word ea 'I' (the plain form) with the 'each other' forms of these verbs: bena- ‘look for,’ noko- ‘meet,’ tima- ‘hit w/fist,’ nini- ‘pull,’ tsaka- ‘hit with arrow,’ ikoko- ‘embrace,’ pota- ‘abandon,’ osan- ‘laugh at,’ sika- ‘paint,’ natex- ‘bite,’ roto- ‘miss,’ shinan- ‘remember,’ bane- ‘make stay,’ a-kin- ‘help,’ axe-a- ‘teach,’ keen- ‘want / love,’ shinanbenot- ‘forget / slip the mind,’ shiro- ‘make fun of,’ joe ik- ‘greet,’ yoyo ik- ‘talk to,’ etc.
Because of this possible “response reciprocal” meaning, a sentence like (91) can be understood in two ways:

h: Reciprocalization (doing something to each other)
t:
(91) Nato joni-bo-ra a-kin-anan-ai. | ‘This men are helping each other.’ / | ‘This men are helping someone / others who will later help them too.’
The example above shows that the 'response' meaning is not only for single doers. But with a single doer, the 'response' meaning is the only one possible.
The two (or more) actions in an 'each other' sentence may happen at the same time, or not. The actions may also be a bit different. Say one person gives another some clothes and gets a chicken back. You could describe that as:
(92) No-a-ra meni-anan-ai | ‘We give each other (something).’
Also, the action may be returned by the one who received the first action, or by someone else. For example, the sentence below fits this situation: Wexá takes Beso across the river in a canoe. Afterwards, a third person takes Wexá back across, and so on:
(93) Bake-bo-ra shita-ananan-kan-ai. | ‘The boys crossed each other (to the opposite bank of the river).’
You can also have 'each other' sentences where no doer is named at all.
Look at sentences (94)-(95):
(94) Neno-ra tima-anan-a yama-ke. | ‘Here there hasn’t been any fight.’
(95) (No-a) a-kin-anan-a-ra jakon iki. | ‘It is good to help each other.’
In the next sentence, the doer is a word like 'nobody':

h: Reciprocalization (doing something to each other)
t:
(96) Neno-ra tso-a-bi tima-anan-a-ma iki. | ‘Here nobody has hit each other.’
The example below shows that you can add an extra phrase to an 'each other' sentence, here saying by means of whom:
(97) Ainbo betan joni-ra bake-n nini-anan-kan-ai. | ‘The woman and the man are pulling each other (by means of) the child.’
Emphatic pronouns (words like 'we ourselves') can appear in 'each other' sentences. They give the meaning ‘do something oneself in a reciprocal way:’
(98) No-n-bi-x-ra no-a rao-n-anan-kan-ai. | ‘We ourselves cure each other with plant medicine.’
(99) No-n-bi-x-ra no-a a-kin-anan-ai. | ‘We ourselves help each other.’
In Shipibo, the 'each other' form bi-ananan- [get / receive-REC] has become a word of its own: it means ‘get married.’ According to Camargo (op. cit.), in Kashinawa the same form has become the word for ‘exchange.’

h: Reciprocalization and Transitivity Classes of Verbs ("each other" with transitive and intransitive verbs)
t: So far, the examples used typical transitive verbs. There were also a couple of less transitive verbs with two people: keen- ‘want / love’ and shinanbenot- ‘forget / slip the mind.’ With these verbs, the one who wants or forgets is in the plain form (ABS). The second person or thing can be in the plain form or take -n. Now I turn to the 'each other' ending with other kinds of intransitive verbs: those that have an extra person, and plain ones.

h: 18.2.1.1. Extended Intransitive Verbs
t:
As I noted in an earlier paper (Valenzuela 1997), the 'each other' ending works with some verbs that have two people but behave like intransitive verbs (linguists call them extended intransitive verbs). Take raket- ~ raké- ‘be scared, be afraid of.’ It has two people, like a transitive verb: someone is afraid, and someone is feared. But it acts like an intransitive verb in several ways. The one who is afraid gets no doer marker, and the feared one gets another marker (<ABS OBL> rather than <ERG ABS>). It cannot take the 'to yourself' ending or the 'against someone' ending (both of these only go on verbs that are at least a bit like transitive
verbs); it follows the intransitive pattern for matching doers inside a sentence and between sentence parts; and in short answers to yes/no questions it uses the intransitive forms iki / ikama. This example comes from my earlier paper (Valenzuela 1997):
(100) Joni rabé-ra tima-nan-kas-i-bi raké-anan-ke. | ‘The two men, wanting to fight, became afraid of each other.’
Other such verbs can take the 'each other' ending too: Other extended intransitive verbs that can take the reciprocal suffix are rabin-ananan- ‘feel embarrassed about each other,’ yoashi-anan- ‘be stingy towards each other,’ wini-ananan- ‘cry for each other,’ raro-anan- ‘be happy about each other,’ bene-anan- ‘be happy about each other,’ keras-anan- ‘feel disgusted about each other.’ But native speakers may disagree about whether most of these forms are acceptable.

h: 18.2.1.2. Intransitive Verbs
t:
Usually, plain intransitive verbs cannot take the 'each other' ending. So it sounds wrong to add it to verbs like ja- ‘exist / live,’ jo- ‘come,’ ka- ‘go,’ nokó- ‘arrive,’ mapé- ‘go up,’ nee-t- ‘climb up,’ ni- ‘walk,’ weni-t- ‘stand,’ raka-t- ‘lie,’ oxa- ‘sleep,’ etc. But at least two intransitive verbs can take it, and then they get a more specific meaning: jiki- ‘enter’ and ishto- ‘run:’
(101) Ino betan Xae-ra jiki-anan-a iki. | ‘The Jaguar and the Anteater competed against each other as to who could remain longer inside the water.’
(102) Mananxawe betan Chaxo-ronki ishto-anan-a iki. | ‘The Tortoise and the Deer ran against each other in a competition.’
The two examples above come from two well-known folk stories.
However, speakers prefer another way to say these sentences. There, the intransitive verb does not take the 'each other' ending. Instead, the ending goes on tana- ‘try’, which is a transitive verb:
(103) Ino betan Xae-ra jiki-i tana-nan-a iki | ‘The Jaguar and the Anteater competed against each other as to who could resist longer inside the water.’
(104) Mananxawe betan Chaxo-ronki ishto tana-nan-a iki. | ‘The Tortoise and the Deer ran against each other in a competition.’

h: Benefactive Reciprocal ("for each other")
t:
Usually, a verb with the 'for someone' ending -xon cannot also take the 'each other' ending. This is true both for intransitive verbs and for transitive verbs. Remember that -xon adds an extra person to the verb. The forms with a star below are not possible: tee- ‘work’ > tee-xon- ‘work for someone’ but tee-xon-anan- ‘work for each other,’ bewa- ‘sing’ > bewa-xon- ‘sing for someone’ but bewa-xon-anan- ‘sing for each other,’ ninká- ‘listen to’ > ninká-xon-
‘follow someone’s advice’ but ninká-xon-anan- ‘follow each other’s advice,’ karo ak- ‘cut firewood’ > karo a-xon- ‘cut firewood for someone’ but karo a-xon-anan- ‘cut firewood for each other,’ piti bena- ‘look for food’ > piti bena-xon- ‘look for food for someone’ but piti bena-xon-anan- ‘look for food for each other,’ etc.
Still, with a couple of verbs it is fine to combine the 'for someone' ending with the 'each other' ending (the examples below were given as (72)-(74) in Ch. 17):
(105) Ja-bo-ra kokoti-bo be-xon-anan-ai. | ‘They bring fruit for each other.’
(106) Ja-bo-ra bi-xon-anan-ai. | ‘They buy from each other / for each other.’
(107) Oa rabé-ra ia bi-xon-anan-i iki. | ‘Those two are searching each other for lice.’
Be-xon- and bi-xon- are used very often. Because of this, speakers may now feel them as simple, single words, not as a verb plus an ending. That would fit with the fact that they can take the 'each other' ending.

h: Benefactive Reciprocal ("for each other")
t:
You can also do it the other way around: first add the 'each other' ending, then the 'for someone' ending -xon. Here is an example (see also 17.2.3.3):
(108) Ja-baon-ra e-a pota-anan-xon-ke. | ‘They separated (lit. left each other) for me.’

h: Dative Reciprocal ("to each other" (giving, telling))
t:
Some verbs have three people: a giver, a thing given, and a receiver (like 'give'). When the 'each other' ending goes on such a verb, the doers are also the ones who receive. Look at these examples with verbs that naturally have three people. The verbs have INC (the 'not finished' ending). So they can mean the action is going on now, or that it happens regularly:
(109) Ja-bo-ra piti meni-anan-ai. | ‘They give fish to each other.’
(110) Ja-bo-ra winti bichin-anan-ai. | ‘They take away the paddle from each other.’
(111) Ja-bo-ra (jawéki-bo) inan-anan-ai. | ‘They give presents to each other.’
(112) Ja-bo-ra kirika wisha-anan-ai. | ‘They write letters to each other.’
(113) Ja-bo-ra joi yoi-anan-ai. | ‘They tell stories to each other.’
(114) Ja-bo-ra nonti yoká-kanan-kan-ai. / yoká-kan-an-ai. | ‘They ask for the canoe to each other.’
The example above is interesting: the plural ending -kan can appear twice, once before the 'each other' ending and once after it. Below, the 'each other' ending goes on verbs that got their third person from the 'make someone do it' ending -ma:
(115) Ja-bo-ra nami bo-ma-anan-ai. | ‘They send meat to each other.’
(116) Ja-bo-ra xea-ma-anan-ai. | ‘They invite yuca beer to each other.’
(117) Ja-bo-ra foto-bo oin-ma-anan-ai. | ‘They show pictures to each other.’

h: Possessive Reciprocal ("each other's")
t:
Some 'each other' sentences have a second noun in the plain form (ABS), and it may have an owner word like 'their'. This matches English sentences like ‘Those two know each other’s secrets.’ But look at the literal translations: 'They know each other their secrets.' So in Shipibo, the owners are treated as the receivers of the action, not just the owned things (linguists call this possessor raising):
(118) Oa rabé-ra jato-n joné jawéki-bo onan-anan-kan-a iki. | ‘Those two know each other’s secrets.’ Lit. ‘They know each other their secrets.’
(119) Oa rabe-ra jato-n santíra kaxke-ananan-ke. | ‘Those two cut each other’s watermelons in halves / cut their watermelons in halves for each other.’ Lit. ‘They cut along each other their watermelons.’
(120) Ja-bo-ra jato-n foto-bo oinyanan-ai. | ‘They saw each other’s pictures.’ Lit. ‘They saw each other their pictures.’
(121) Oa rabé-ra jato-n merati-bo onan-anan-kan-a iki. | ‘Those two know each other’s lovers.’ Lit. ‘Those two know each other their lovers.’
(122) Ja-bo-ra jato-n ochíti meni-anan-ai. | ‘They lend their dogs to each other (when hunting).’ Lit. ‘They give each other their dogs.’
Or the extra noun can take a marker instead of staying in the plain form:
(123) Kate betan Pena-ra bake / bake-n koiran-anan-ai. | ‘Kate and Pena take care of each other’s child.’ | Lit. ‘Kate and Pena take care of each other the child / by means of the child.’

h: Possessive Reciprocal ("each other's")
t:
(124) Kate betan Pena-ra bene / bene-n bichi-nanan-ai. | ‘Kate and Pena steal each other’s husband.’ Lit. ‘Kate and Pena take away from each other the husband / by means of the husband.’
(125) Oa rabé-ra mapo-nko xo-ananan-ai. | ‘Those two scratched each other’s head.’ Lit. ‘Those two scratched each other on the head.’
You can also say 'each other's face', 'each other's feet' and so on with a body-part beginning piece on the verb:
(126) Nato rabé-ra be-choki-ananan-kan-ke. | ‘These two washed each other’s face.’
(127) Nato rabé-ra ta-nexa-nan-ai. / tae nexa-nan-ai. | ‘These two tie each other’s feet.’
(128) Nato rabé-ra ke-pé-anan-ai. | ‘These two perforate each other’s lips.’
(129) Nato rabé-ra pe-ní-anan-ai. | ‘These two stand on each other’s back/surface (taking turns).’

h: Summary
t:
Many languages of the world use one marker for both 'to yourself' and 'to each other'. Shipibo doesn't. Its middle ending -t has many meanings: 'to yourself', 'it just happened', and 'it was done to me by someone'. But it never means 'to each other'. Also, some -t verbs simply become intransitive verbs with a plain doer (e.g., noko-t- ‘arrive’ and piko-t- ‘come out’). Shipibo also has a set of words that were called “reflexive” pronouns before (Loriot, Lauriault, and Day 1993:67). But you usually don't need them to say 'to yourself'. They even show up in other kinds of sentences, including 'each other' sentences. I call them “emphatic pronouns,” like English 'herself' in 'she did it herself'. Often they stress that the doer did the action by herself. Also, they contain the emphasis piece -bi. In fact, -bi has become a fixed part of these words, because another emphasis ending can be added after the whole word.
When the middle ending -t goes on a transitive verb, the new verb often means 'to yourself'. Sometimes, though, the meaning can't be predicted; e.g., rete- ‘kill’ > rete-t- ‘faint / kill oneself,’ noko- ‘meet
somebody’ > noko-t- ‘arrive.’ The ending -t usually does not go on intransitive verbs. Verbs with an extra person (extended intransitives) usually get a 'to yourself' meaning just by leaving out the second person. An emphatic pronoun can help show the 'to yourself' meaning. With some verbs you may even need one (cf. shiro- ‘make fun of’). Also, adding the emphasis ending -bi to the doer gives the meaning ‘do something oneself.’ Some sound-imitating verbs have their own special 'to yourself' form.

h: Summary
t:
Usually, the middle ending does not go on verbs that have the 'make someone do it' ending. One exception is bo-ma- [carry-CAUS-] ‘send.’ This is probably because it now works like a single word. But the other order is fairly common: you can add 'make someone do it' to a verb that has already lost its receiver.
With 'he', 'she' and 'it', Shipibo has no way to tell 'him' from 'himself' in place phrases like ‘He put it next to him(self).’ To say 'her own' thing, you can put the emphasis ending -bi after the owned thing, and / or the word kikin ‘own’ before it. These tricks are common, but they are not fixed rules yet. English sentences like 'he burned his own hand' can be said in Shipibo with a body-part beginning piece on a verb that has lost its receiver. However, speakers I worked with disliked or rejected a few of these body-part verbs.
To say you did something for yourself, you use an owner word ('her') plus the emphasis ending -bi. These two pieces mean ‘for herself, what is of herself.’ Here the verb takes no 'for someone' ending, so no extra person is added. Together with self-
benefactive meaning, the sentence can also be read as being about something of your own (“her own”). I have also found these “to yourself” forms with no earlier word for them to point back to.

h: Summary
t:
I have also included longer sentences made of two parts, each with its own verb. Sometimes a “to yourself” form in the smaller, attached part points back to a person in the main part. If the main part has both a doer and a receiver, the “to yourself” form can point back to either one. “To yourself” forms appear in main sentences, and also in attached parts that have been turned into nouns.
The ending -t- can mean more than “to yourself.” A verb with this ending can also mean that something just happens on its own (“the door opened”). Or it can mean that something was done to someone, without saying who did it (“she was pulled”). Sometimes “to yourself” or “it just happened” is the only meaning, or the preferred one. But often more than one meaning is possible. Take the verb bachin- ‘pull someone by the hair,’ which normally has a doer and a receiver. With the ending, it becomes bachimeet-. This can mean ‘she pulled herself by the hair’ or ‘she was pulled by the hair.’ A few verbs have two different forms with this ending, and speakers may give each form its own meaning. One speaker told me, for example: mishki- ‘fish with hook’ > mishki-t- ‘choke’ / mishki-kaa- ‘hook oneself.’ In other cases, most speakers agree on what each form means. For example: noko- ‘meet someone’ > noko-t- ‘arrive’ and noko-kaa- ‘be found.’ I think the “was done to someone” meaning in SK is probably growing out of the “it just happened” meaning. In both, the person in the sentence is affected, but does not cause the action. The difference is whether someone else is understood to have done it. Speakers all agree that these verbs can mean “to yourself” and “it just happened.” But they may disagree on whether a given form can also have the

h: Summary
t:
“was done to someone, by someone unnamed” meaning. This suggests that this meaning is not the basic one; it came later (e.g., potsi-t-ai). Linguists have suggested that the same kind of change happened in some Indo-European languages (the family that includes English and Spanish).
The ending -t has two more jobs, which I describe in other chapters. First, it can be added to a verb that means “begin” or “finish” so that it matches the verb that goes with it: if that verb has no receiver, the “begin/finish” verb loses its receiver too (15.3.1). Second, it can weaken a transitive verb, so that adding -ma then means “cause something indirectly” (16.3.2).
Sentences with the t ending can mean “to yourself,” “it just happened,” or “it was done to someone.” They all have three things in common. The person the sentence is about is affected by the action. The action is less of a “someone does something to someone else” action than with the plain verb. And no other person in the sentence is more important than that person.
To say people do something to each other, SK has its own ending: -(ana)nan ~ -anan. The ending has different forms. Which one you use depends on the length of the verb: count its syllables (beats). An even number usually gets -anan; an odd number gets -ananan. This ending works like -t (the “to yourself” ending). Once people act on each other, there is usually no separate receiver anymore. So the doers lose the doer marker and appear in the plain form (linguists call this the absolutive).

h: Summary
t:
We can sort SK “each other” sentences by who the doers are. The doers can be two names joined by “and.” They can be a group with a number word, or with the plural ending -bo. The doers can be left out, if the verb has the plural ending -kan (which adds the sense “people, someone”). There can be one doer plus a “with someone” phrase. Or there can be just one doer on his or her own. That last type works because the SK “each other” ending can also mean “to pay someone back” (linguists call this a “response reciprocal”). It means the doer knows her action is, has been, or will be returned. But the person who does the
second action is not named. Camargo (ms.) was the first to describe this “pay back” meaning in a Panoan language, Kashinawa, spoken along the Purus River.
The two actions in an “each other” sentence may happen at the same time or not. The actions can also be a bit different. Or the action may be returned by someone who was not the receiver of the first action. An “each other” sentence can also have a second plain-form noun, or a “by means of” phrase. In English this is like ‘They pull each other (by means of) something / someone.’ There are also “each other” sentences with no earlier word naming the people involved. In SK the verb bi-ananan- [get / receive-REC] (“get each other”) has become a fixed word meaning ‘get married.’

h: Summary
t:
The “each other” ending usually goes on transitive verbs. But unlike the -t ending, it also goes on most intransitive verbs that take an extra “to/at someone” phrase. Plain intransitive verbs, with only one person involved, don’t usually take it. Still, at least two such verbs can take it, and then they get special meanings (exx. (101)-(102)). Verbs with the “for someone” ending -xon usually don’t take the “each other” ending. And sometimes the ending goes on giving verbs, which have a doer, a thing given and a receiver: “they give each other things.”
The plural ending -kan normally comes after the “each other” ending. But sometimes the order is reversed. There are even verbs where -kan appears twice, once before and once after the “each other” ending. When there are just two people involved, the verb can also take the ending -bekon, which means “the two of them.”
Some “each other” sentences have a second plain-form noun, and that noun can have an owner word with it. This is like English sentences such as ‘They saw each other’s pictures.’ Or the second noun can take a “by means of” ending instead. Word for word, that would be ‘They saw each other (by means of) their pictures.’ You can also say “each other’s” by putting a body-part beginning piece on the verb.

h: Summary
t: PARTICIPANT AGREEMENT:

h: The Notion of Participant Agreement (what this means)
t:
In SK, extra words that describe a person in the sentence change their ending depending on that person’s role. Is the person the doer of an intransitive verb? The doer of a transitive verb? Or the receiver? Each gets a different ending. I call this “participant agreement” (PA for short). These endings appear on words and phrases that add optional, adverb-like information about one of the main people in the sentence. That includes words about place, manner, amount, stage of life, feelings, and having or lacking something. PA also shows up on emphatic pronouns (“she herself”). It shows up too on place words like “there,” when they are used to link sentences and parts of sentences. Finally, PA shows up on attached parts that end in a “same person” marker. Their ending depends on whether the main doer is the doer of an intransitive verb (S) or of a transitive verb (A).
As I explained in 15.3, agreement is when one word changes its form to match something about another word: a “systematic covariance between a semantic or formal property of one element and a formal property of another” (Steele 1978:610). English has a little of this: we say “he walks” but “they walk.” Corbett (2001, 2002) suggests a first way to describe all kinds of agreement. It has the

h: The Notion of Participant Agreement (what this means)
t:
following parts. The controller is the word that decides the agreement. The target is the word whose form changes to match. The domain is the place in the sentence where this happens. We also talk about agreement features: what exactly is being matched. And if something else decides the agreement without being marked itself, these are agreement conditions.
Here is how SK participant agreement fits that picture. The controller is one of the main people in a simple sentence: the doer of an intransitive verb (S), the doer of a transitive verb (A), or the receiver (O). In a longer sentence with attached parts, the controller is the doer (S or A) of the main part. The target is a word, phrase or part of the sentence about time, place or manner; an emphatic pronoun; or a linking word. The domain is the agreement between the people in the sentence and these extra words. What is being matched is which person the extra word describes: S, A, or O. Nothing else affects it, so there are no agreement conditions. I must point out that PA is not a typical kind of agreement, like the way Spanish words for “the” and “red” match the gender of the noun (see Corbett 2001). Still, Corbett’s way of describing agreement helps us understand PA better. I will come back to this in 19.4, near the end of this chapter.

h: Interclausal and Intraclausal Participant Agreement (agreement between and within sentences)
t:
In this section, we look at PA between sentence parts and inside a single sentence part. By a sentence part, I mean a stretch that has its own verb, or the verb “be.”
Table 19.1 shows the PA endings found in SK. It also shows where each ending can appear: on words and phrases, or on whole sentence parts with their own verb.
As Table 19.1 shows, the endings -ax, -i and -nox point to the doer of an intransitive verb (S). The endings -xon, -kin, and -noxon point to the doer of a transitive verb (A). Pointing to the receiver (O) never gets any ending at all. So the system splits three ways: S, A, and O each behave differently (linguists call this tripartite). I must also
point out that these PA endings can’t be broken into smaller pieces in SK. (You can split -no(n)xon into -no + -xon, but it isn’t clear what these two pieces mean.) One more thing, though it isn’t central here. Most of these endings have no other job in the language. But -xon and -kin look the same as, and fit in meaning with, two other endings: the “for someone” ending and the “together with someone” ending (Valenzuela 1999:368-369; see also 7.4.2, 17.2 and 17.4, as well as ex. (72) in Ch. 17).

h: Interclausal Participant Agreement (agreement across linked sentences)
t:
SK has attached sentence parts whose verb is not complete on its own. Their ending tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. These parts usually set the scene for the main part of the sentence. But they don’t say exactly how the two events are connected; you work that out from context. Sometimes, instead, the attached part tells an event that moves the main story forward. So these SK parts can match English parts starting with “when,” “in order to,” “if,” “because,” “although,” and even “and” (see Chapter 9 and Valenzuela 1999).
Between sentence parts, PA shows up in most of the “same person” markers. Each of these endings does several jobs at once. It says the same person does both actions. It says which event comes first, or how they are logically linked. And it says what role that shared person plays in the main part: S or A. Between sentence parts, being the A or the S simply matches the kind of main
verb. A goes with main transitive verbs, or with giving verbs, whether they are like that naturally or because an ending made them so. S goes with intransitive verbs, or with verbs that have lost their receiver. As I will show later, these “same person” markers are basically the same as the agreement endings on extra words and phrases. Importantly, the “different person” markers do not show PA in SK.

h: Interclausal Participant Agreement (agreement across linked sentences)
t:
Let’s see how PA works between sentence parts. In (1a) and (1b) the event in the attached part happens first. It is done by the same person who does the main action. The difference is the main verb: in (1a) it is an intransitive verb, but in (1b) it is a transitive verb. The agreement follows the doer of the main part. So (1a) uses the “same person” marker -ax, which points to S. And (1b) uses -xon, which points to A. In the glosses, PSSS means “previous event, same person, S in control,” and PSSA means “previous event, same person, A in control.” Put more simply: use -ax when the main verb is an intransitive verb, and -xon when the main verb is a transitive verb. (The attached parts are shown in square brackets.)
(1) Nokon papa-ra [wai meno-ax] kachio ka-ke. -xon | ‘After burning the chacra my father went to the forest.’ | Nokon papa-n-ra [wai meno-xon] atsa bana-ke. -ax | ‘After burning the chacra my father sowed the yuca.’
Notice that in (1a-b) the attached parts sit inside the main part of the sentence. We can tell because ‘my father’ gets its marker according to the main verb (vis-à-vis the main verb, as linguists put it). Also, the marker -ra, which shows how the speaker knows something and always comes second in the sentence,

h: Interclausal Participant Agreement (agreement across linked sentences)
t:
shows that ‘my father’ is one of the main pieces of the whole sentence. If ‘my father’ belonged to the attached part, it would have the doer marker in both sentences. And -ra would come after the whole attached part (see 4.2.2 and 13.1).
Ex. (2) was given as (1) in Ch. 9; I repeat it here to make things easier. It has two attached parts ending in -ax, both linked to the same main part. Notice that attached parts can come before or after the main part:
(2) [...bachi meran jiki-ax] Ashi manó-res-a iki | [moa ka-ax]. | ‘... Ashi entered into the mosquito net and disappeared, leaving (for the upper world).’ (Soi Rawa 1995:27, analyzed in Valenzuela 2002a:427)
Ex. (3) has two main parts. Each one has an attached part with a “same person, at the same time” marker. -kin is used when the doer of the main part is an A (transitive verb). -i is used when that doer is an S (intransitive verb). So again, you could just say that -kin goes with transitive main verbs, and -i with intransitive main verbs:
(3) a. E-a-ra nokon tita-n [ese-kin] ani-a iki. | ‘My mother raised me giving me advice. | b. E-a-ra esé-ya iki | I am wise | [nokon tita-n yoiy-ai ninká-xon-katit-i]. | because I listened to what my mother used to tell me.’ (Valenzuela 1999:365)

h: Interclausal Participant Agreement (agreement across linked sentences)
t:
Finally, examples (4)-(5) show the “same person” markers for an event that happens afterwards. One points to S and the other to A. Again, they match intransitive and transitive main verbs:
(4) ....no-a i-ti ja-ke [westíora metsá ainbo i-nox] raotia. | ‘...we must be adorned in order to be a beautiful woman.’
(5) Westíora nete winó-ma-xon, kachio bo-ti iki | [xete-ma-noxon]. | ‘After one day, one takes (the dog being treated with a special plant preparation in order to make it a good hunter) to the forest and has it smell (at animals).’
I said this when I introduced each pair of examples above. With the “same person” markers, pointing to S or A is just the same as matching an intransitive or a transitive main verb. That is the main reason PA was described before as “transitivity agreement” (Valenzuela 1999) or “transitivity concord” (Loos 1999): agreement with the type of verb. Linguists studying Panoan languages had looked almost only at the same/different person system (but cf. Valenzuela 1999). But when we look at PA inside a single sentence part, it becomes clear that the type of verb is not what decides it. This is especially clear where two different endings are possible.

h: Intraclausal Participant Agreement (agreement within one sentence)
t: With the “same person” markers there are three pairs of PA endings. On extra words and phrases, though, we find only two of these pairs: -ax versus -xon and -i versus -kin.

h: 19.2.2.1. Locative / Allative -xon (A-orientation) vs. -0 (S- / O-orientation)
t:
Words that say where something happens, or where it goes to, get the ending -xon when they describe the A (the doer of a transitive verb). When they describe an S or an O, they get no ending. So, looking at which ones get an ending, this works just like the doer marker: A is marked, and S and O are plain (linguists call this ergative-absolutive). In the following examples the place words describe an S: the doer of an intransitive verb, whether that person acts (S_{a}) or just undergoes something (S_{o}).
S-orientation
(6) Jawerano-ki Inka-bo ja-a? | ‘Where do the Inkas live?
(7) Bochiki-ra e-a oxa-[a]i / tsini-ai / bewa-[a]i. | ‘I sleep / play / sing high up (e.g., in a higher area inside the house).
(8) Nashi-ra e-a jene-nko paké-ke. | ‘While I was bathing, I fell in the water.’ (I was in the water already)
Examples (6)-(8) have different kinds of intransitive verbs. Examples (9)-(19) have transitive verbs. In (9)-(11) there is no -xon. This shows that the place words are
about the receiver (O), and that the doer (A) is not at the same place. (I show this “no ending” in the glosses here to make it clear.)
O-orientation (exclusive)
(9) E-n-ra yami kentí bochiki a-ke. | ‘I placed the metal pot high up.’ (only the pot is high up)

h: 19.2.2.1. Locative / Allative -xon (A-orientation) vs. -0 (S- / O-orientation)
t:
(10) Ja-tian ani nonti-n westíora atsa xeati chomo | na-yásan-kan-ai. | ‘Then, they put a jar of yuca beer inside the big canoe.’ (the agents are not in the canoe; Valenzuela 2002a:469)
(11) Jain-xon Ashi-n jato yoiy-a iki, | [bake-bo bochiki, tapo-n nee-n-ti] | yawa be-ax onsat-ai-tian. | ‘Then Ashi told them to place the children up, on the palm-bark floor, since the white-lipped peccaries would come and they could be dangerous.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:28, Valenzuela 2002a:469-470)
Examples (12)-(15) also have transitive verbs. But here -xon is present. This shows that the place word describes the doer (A). The receiver (O) is at the same place too:
A-orientation (non-exclusive)
(12) E-n-ra yami kentí bochiki-xon tan tan a-ke. | ‘I hit the metal pot (being) high up.’ (I am high up with the pot)
(13) Jawerano-xon-ki epa-n pi-ai? | ‘Where does paternal uncle eat?’
(14) ...ani nonti-n-xon westíora atsa xeati chomo keyo-kan-ke. | ‘...they finished a jar of yuca beer in the big canoe.’ (Valenzuela 2002a:469)
(15) Westíora a-kin e-n oin-a iki ani tsinki-ti-ain-xon | Kashinawa, Wanbisa, Aguaruna; ja-bo-res e-n oin-a iki. | ‘Once I saw in a big meeting Kashinawas, Wanbisas, Aguarunas; only them / these I saw.’
In the examples above, both the doer and the receiver are at the place named. But in (16)-(19), the place words tell us where only the doer is:

h: 19.2.2.1. Locative / Allative -xon (A-orientation) vs. -0 (S- / O-orientation)
t:
A-orientation (exclusive)
(16) E-n-ra yami kentí bochiki-xon tsaka-ke, kochára-nin. | ‘I hit the metal pot from high up with the spoon.’ (I was high up and the pot was down, and I threw the spoon against the pot.)
(17) Bake-n-ra e-a bimi-n tsaka-ke jiwi bochiki-xon | wino-t-ai-tian. | ‘The boy up in the tree hit me with a fruit while I was passing by.’
(18) E-n-ra oin-ke [joni wino-t-ai] jene-nko-xon. | ‘I_{i} saw someone_{j} passing (in a canoe) in the water_{i}.’ (I was bathing in the water, and I saw someone passing in a canoe).
In example (18), the place word describes the doer of the main part of the sentence. In the next example it describes the doer of the attached part:
(19) Ja-tian nokon tita-n e-a yoiy-a iki | [ja tenaman-xon mana-i ka-ti]. | ‘Then my mother told me to go wait for him on the shore.’
Exx. (9)-(19), among others, show that -xon does not depend on the type of verb, since all those verbs have a doer and a receiver. It depends on which person the place word describes. To sum up: the A-ending -xon tells you the doer is at the place where the event happens. The receiver may or may not be there too. No ending means the place word describes either an S or an O.

h: 19.2.2.2. Ablatives -x (S-orientation) vs. -0 (O-orientation)
t:
Unlike place words for “where” and “to where,” words for “from where” have an extra ending, -x, to show they describe an S. But they get no ending at all when the “from” word
describes the receiver (O). A “from where” word can never point to the doer of a transitive verb (A); for that you have to use a “where” phrase. Look at the following examples:
S-orientation
(20) Jawerano-a-x-ki mi-a jo-a? | ‘Where do you come from?’
(21) E-a-ra bochiki-a-x / nontime-a-x paké-ke. | ‘I fell from high up / from the canoe.’
(22) E-a-ra jene merano-a-x mapé-ke | ‘I went up from the water.’
O-orientation
(23) E-n-ra yami kentí bochiki-a be-ke. | ‘I brought the metal pot from high up.’
As I said above, a “from where” phrase can’t take the A ending. But a “where” phrase with -xon can be used for this instead. So in (24a-b) and (25a-b), the English translations use the word ‘from.’ But in the (b) examples, SK actually uses a “where” phrase, not a “from where” phrase:
(24) a. E-n -ra kachio-kea ninká-ke. | ‘I heard it from the forest.’ (the noise came from the forest)
(None) E-n-ra kachio-xon ninká-ke. -kachiokea-xon | ‘I heard it from the forest.’ (I was in the forest; the noise may have come from the forest or not; lit. ‘I heard it in the forest.’)

h: 19.2.2.2. Ablatives -x (S-orientation) vs. -0 (O-orientation)
t:
(25) E-n-ra bake pake-ke weyóti-aino-a. | ‘I (accidentally or purposefully) caused the child to fall from the hammock.’ (only the child was in the hammock) | E-n-ra bake pake-ke weyóti-ain-xon weyótiainoa-xon | ‘I caused the child to fall from the hammock (I was in the hammock too; lit. ‘I caused the child to fall in the hammock.’)
This swap between “where” and “from where” is not possible with the verb be- ‘bring,’ a movement transitive verb. It only allows a “from where” phrase with no ending, which therefore describes the receiver (O):
(26) E-n-ra ian napo-ri-kea onpax be -ke. | ‘I brought water from approximately the middle of the lake.’ | E-n-ra ian napo-ri-xon onpax be-ke. naporikeaxon | ‘I brought water from approximately the middle of the lake.’
Here is a guess at why. When you bring something from one place to another, you and the thing you bring both start and end in the same places. In this case, the language has settled on the form that describes the thing being brought (the receiver) as the fixed rule.^1
In contrast, the form that describes the doer is possible in the related languages Matses (as shown in ex. (60) of Ch. 20) and Sharanawa (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes).
We just saw a “where” phrase used to mark A openly. The opposite also happens: a “from where” phrase can be used instead of a “where” phrase to mark S openly. In fact, sometimes you can use either a “where” or a “from where” phrase for S, and unlike (24) and (25), the meaning doesn’t clearly change. In the next examples, where the S person is located is shown with a “where” phrase in the (a) sentences, but with a “from where” phrase in the (b) sentences. (Native speakers offered (27a) and (28b) on their own while we were talking about something else. I asked about (27b) and (28a) so I could compare.)

h: 19.2.2.2. Ablatives -x (S-orientation) vs. -0 (O-orientation)
t:
(27) a. E-manaon-ra popo keo keo-wan-ke nete xabat-ai-tian. | ‘The owls cried above me (i.e. on top of my house) very early in the morning.’ | b. E-manaonkea-x-ra popo keo keo-wan-ke | nete xabat-ai-tian. | ‘The owls cried above me (i.e. on top of my house) very early in the morning.’
(28) a. E-naman-ra ashá keo keo-wan-ke yamé. | ‘The ashá toads sang and sang under my house (lit. under me) last night.’ | b. E-namamea-x-ra ashá keo keo-wan-ke yamé. | ‘The ashá toads sang and sang under my house (lit. under me) last night.’
Now let’s see how PA on place words works with the “make someone do it” ending and with endings that bring in an extra person. This continues what I discussed in 16.4. First, look at the following sentences built on an intransitive verb, with and without the “make someone do it” ending. Exx. (29a-b) and
(30a-b) differ only in the ending on the place word: -0 (no ending) vs. -xon. The change in meaning is clear. Sentence (29a) means the speaker stays out of the forest, but sends his dog into the forest to bark (at animals). In (29b), by contrast, both the speaker and the dog are in the forest, and the speaker makes the dog bark (at animals):
(29) a. E-n-ra nokon ochíti jojo i-ma-[a]i nii meran. | ‘I make my dog bark in the forest.’ (specifies location of causee) | b. E-n-ra nokon ochíti jojo i-ma-[a]i nii meran-xon. | ‘I make my dog bark in the forest.’ (specifies location of causer)

h: 19.2.2.2. Ablatives -x (S-orientation) vs. -0 (O-orientation)
t:
Exx. (30a-b) also differ in meaning. The first one means that only the dog is on the palm-bark floor. The second means that the speaker is (also) up there. (Shipibo houses usually stand on poles, so the floor and the ground are at different heights.)
(30) a. E-n-ra nokon ochíti ransa-ma-[a]i tapo-n. | ‘I make my dog dance on the palm-bark floor.’ (specifies location of causee) | b. E-n-ra nokon ochíti ransa-ma-[a]i tapo-n-xon. | ‘I make my dog dance on the palm-bark floor.’ (specifies location of causer).
The exx. in (29) and (30) fit what I have said so far. The place word gets -xon when it describes the A, the one who makes someone do something. It gets no ending when it describes the O, the one who is made to do it (on the role of this person, see Ch. 16; cf. also exx. (33a-b) below). But now look at the next examples. Here the “from where” phrase ‘from
Kako' gets the S ending. Yet Wesna is the receiver in the sentence: in (31) because of the “make someone do it” ending, and in (32) because of an ending that brings in an extra person. (Remember that pointing to O is shown by -0, no ending.)
(31) E-n-ra Wesna jo-ma-ke Kako-nko-ni-a-x. | ‘I made Wesna come from Kako.’

h: 19.2.2.2. Ablatives -x (S-orientation) vs. -0 (O-orientation)
t:
(32) E-n-ra Wesna nokó-kin-ke | Kako-nko-ni-a-x. | ‘I came with Wesna from Kako.’
Different Shipibo helpers gave me the examples above, and Mr. Sanken Bari later confirmed them. I asked him whether (31) and (32) could take the form with no ending, Kakonkonia. He thought about it for a short while. Then he explained that Kakonkonia is actually the “correct” form, but that speakers normally say Kakonkoniax in these sentences. This was a very sharp observation. It suggests that Wesna makes the “from where” word agree because of its meaning: Wesna really is the S, the one doing the plain intransitive action of the bare verb.
Another way to explain the ending in (31) and (32) is this: in these combined verbs, the extra word may agree with a person who belongs to the bare verb. I will come back to this point shortly.
I just showed something about sentences with the “make someone do it” ending, or an ending that brings in an extra person, built on an intransitive verb. There, a “from where” phrase can openly take the S ending -x
to show that it describes the doer of the bare verb. But this doesn’t work when the bare verb has a doer and a receiver. For example, you can’t put the A ending -xon on a “where” phrase to show it describes the person who is made to do the action:

h: 19.2.2.2. Ablatives -x (S-orientation) vs. -0 (O-orientation)
t:
(33) a. E-n-ra nokon ochíti pi-ma-[a]i tapo-n. | ‘I make my dog eat on the palm-bark floor.’ (specifies location of causee) | b. E-n-ra nokon ochíti pi-ma-[a]i tapo-n-xon. | ‘I make my dog eat on the palm-bark floor.’ (specifies location of causer).
In the sentence just above, -xon can only mean that the place word describes the person who makes someone do the action. One possible conclusion is this. With the “make someone do it” ending, and probably also with the endings that bring in an extra person, an extra word can’t describe a person of the bare verb. The exception is agreement based on meaning, with the doer of an intransitive bare verb, as in (31) and (32). Another explanation is also possible. Maybe a person of the bare verb can control PA. But when the bare verb has a doer and a receiver, there are two doers competing to be the A. And the A ending on extra words always goes with the more important A. I haven’t found specific tests that would help me choose between these two ideas. Still, I lean towards the agreement-by-meaning idea, because of Mr. Sanken Bari’s judgements that I quoted above.

h: 19.2.2.3. Complement of Interest -ax (S orientation) vs. -xon (A- / O-orientation)
t:
A “for whose sake” phrase names the person for whom, or because of whom, someone changes inside (feels something) or does something. These phrases are usually the second person in intransitive verbs that take an extra “to/at someone” phrase (see section 8.2.2.2). For example:
(34) E-a-ra ja-on keen-ai. | ‘I love him.’
(35) Ja-tian joni mi-on shinan-benot-i ka-[a]i | ‘Then the man is going to forget you.’
(36) E-on-ra joni yoben-wan-ke. | ‘The / a man asked me in matrimony (to my parents).’
These “for whose sake” phrases can take PA endings. When they do, they usually have an emotional meaning: doing something for someone’s good, or to their harm. I must point out that I got exx. (37) and (39)-(41) by asking speakers directly. Ex. (38) comes from a story told naturally, but there the “for whose sake” phrase seems to mean “from” rather than “for” or “against.”
S-orientation
The S ending -x has been found on pronouns with the “for whose sake” ending. But first these pronouns need to take the “from” ending (which is itself built on the
“at / in” ending) before -x is added. So the pronouns in (37a) and (38)-(40) are made of these word pieces: the pronoun + the “for whose sake” ending -on + the “at / in” ending -me + the “from” ending -a + the PA ending. -Me is a form of the “at / in” ending that comes before the “from” ending on words ending in a nasal sound (like n). I first introduced the “at / in” + “from” sequence -mea in 3.2.3.2, where I describe how the “from” ending is used.

h: 19.2.2.3. Complement of Interest -ax (S orientation) vs. -xon (A- / O-orientation)
t:
Or you could say that the pronouns in (37a), (39) and (40) take the S ending -ax. Then -a would be part of the agreement ending, not the “from” ending. But this second explanation can’t account for the piece -me:
(37) a. E-a-ra mi-onmea-x axe-ai. | ‘I learn for you / I learn from you.’^2
Exx. (37a) and (37b) look almost the same. But in (37b) the pronoun does not have the “from” ending, so it can’t take PA. As a result, (37b) can’t mean “for someone’s good”:
(37) b. E-a-ra mi-on axe-ai. | ‘I am going to get used to you.’^3
Speakers differ about which meaning they prefer for this sentence. For example, Mr. Yoi Sani preferred the “for someone’s good” meaning, while Mr. Sanken Bari only accepted the second meaning.
One speaker offered this other form: i. E-a-ra mi-ki axe-ai. | 1-ABS-EV 2-DAT learn / get.used.to-INC | ‘I am going to get used to you.’
Compare (37a) also with the example below. Here e-onmea has the “from” ending but no agreement ending. In (38), the spirit of the Sun Medicine plant talks, in her dreams, to a woman who has drunk a drink made from that plant:
(38) Jawe kopí-ki mi-n e-a xea-a, | e-onmea onan-kas-kin...? | ‘Why did you drink me, wanting to learn from me....?
In the next examples the “for whose sake” pronouns have the “from” ending. With intransitive verbs, they openly show the S ending. Adding the emphatic -bi makes the meaning “to someone’s harm” rather than “for someone’s good”:

h: 19.2.2.3. Complement of Interest -ax (S orientation) vs. -xon (A- / O-orientation)
t:
(39) Ja-ra e-onmea-x-bi wano-ke. eonbi | ‘He got married in spite of being with me.’
(40) Mi-onmea-x-bi bake mawat-a. mion | ‘The child died being under your care.’ (It is an accusation; maybe you didn’t take good care of the child, or you didn’t take it to the onanya in order to be treated).
These examples suggest that the “from” ending in (37a), and especially in (39) and (40), is there for a grammar reason. It doesn’t really mean “from” here. It is simply needed so that the phrase can take the S agreement ending.
A-orientation
The next example openly shows A agreement. That is because the verb kinan- has a doer and a receiver, and its doer must take the doer marker:
(41) Mi-on-xon bake-n kinan-a. | ‘The child vomited being under your care.’

h: 19.2.2.4. Life Stage -x (S-orientation) vs. -xon (A-orientation)
t:
Words for a stage of life (“as a child,” “as a young man”) can also openly show S or A agreement. After these agreement endings comes the emphatic -bi.
(42) Ja-ríba-ke bake chea-a-ti, bake-x-bi | too-ke-tian poko-mea-bi bake maxko a-ti. | ‘There is also (a plant with special powers) to make the fetus very very skinny, to make the fetus small when a girl becomes pregnant at / from a very early age.’
In (53), when I deal with words for “having something,” I give an example of agreement with a specific age. The next example has a transitive verb. So the S ending is not possible, and the time ending -tian (“when”) is used instead:
(43) Ja-n-ra mapó ak-ai bake-tian-bi. bake-x-bi | ‘She makes pottery since (being a) little girl.’
But the S ending does show up in a version of (43) with an intransitive verb:
(44) Bake-x-bi mapó a-ti onan r-iki ja. | ‘She knows how to make pottery since (being a) little girl.’
The time ending -tian can be used on stage-of-life words that refer to the A or the O of a transitive verb. In other words, these words don’t point to a particular person. Look at the next sentence, which has two people as main participants:
(45) E-n-ra onan-ke Sanken Bari bake-tian-bi. | ‘I know Sanken Bari since I was a child / since he was a child.’

h: 19.2.2.4. Life Stage -x (S-orientation) vs. -xon (A-orientation)
t:
In the example below, bake-shoko gets the ending -xon:
(46) Mapó a-kin peo-ti r-iki bake-shoko-xon-bi. | ‘To make pottery one has to begin at a very young age.’
As (44) shows, stage-of-life words with an agreement ending can mean the same as English ‘since,’ a “from that time on” meaning, even though there is no “from” ending. Compare the following pairs of sentences with intransitive verbs:
‘Since’
(47) a. E-a-ra teet-i peo-koot-a iki bake-tian-bi. | ‘I began to work when (being a) child.’ | b. E-a-ra teet-i peo-koot-a iki bake-x-bi. | ‘I began to work since (being a) child.’
(48) a. Biri-ra Rima-n ka-a iki bake-shoko-tian-bi. | ‘Biri went to Lima when (being a) little girl.’ | b. Biri-ra Rima-n ka-a iki bake-shoko-x-bi. | ‘Biri went to Lima since (being a) little girl.’
Some speakers think (47a) and (48a) are better when the situation is no longer true at the time of speaking. The (b) sentences, on the other hand, probably mean that the speaker is still working and that Biri is still in Lima. What matters here is this. It seems right to separate two kinds of expressions. True time words with -tian don’t point to any person. Stage-of-life words with -x and -xon do point to a person.
‘Although, in spite of’
A stage-of-life word with the S ending can also mean “although” or “in spite of.” This is probably because the emphatic -bi is often used with this meaning. Speakers understood the expressions below in the “although” sense:

h: 19.2.2.4. Life Stage -x (S-orientation) vs. -xon (A-orientation)
t:
(49) E-a-ra teet-ai bake-x-bi. | ‘I work in spite of (being a) child.’
(50) Ja-ra teet-ai estudiante-ni-x-bi estudiante-x-bi | ‘S/he works although (s/he is a) student.’
(51) Nato-ra mapet-ai maxko-shoko-x-bi. | ‘This one goes up in spite of (being) very small.’
(52) Ja-ra ransa-[a]i ochíti-ni-x-bi. | ‘It dances in spite of (being a) dog.’
Stage-of-life words raise an important question, which shows how strongly they point to a person. The S ending -x appears on them without the “from” ending. As I will show in 19.2.2.6, the same is true of emphatic pronouns.

h: 19.2.2.5. Proprietive and Privative -xon (A-orientation) vs. -0 / -x (S-orientation)
t:
PA also shows up on words that describe having or lacking something (“with a radio,” “without a radio”). But the open S ending has only been found with age expressions like the one in ex. (53),
S-orientation
(53) Pichika baritia-ya-ni-x moa shinan-ai mishki-ti, | pia a-ti, kanóti a-ti. | ‘At five years of age, (the boy) already thinks of fishing with hook, making arrows, making bows.’
but not with other kinds of intransitive sentences:
(54) Tita-ra ka-[a]i rario-ya. rario-ya(-ni)-x | ‘Mother is going taking the radio with her (lit. is going with (a) radio).’
One could say that a person’s age is part of who that person is, while a radio is not.
But look at exx. (56) and (57). Both have A agreement:
A-orientation
(55) Nato joni-n-ra e-a oin-ke siná-ya-xon. | ‘This man looked at me (and he was) angry (lit. ‘looked at me with anger’).’
(56) Mi-n-ra machíto-ya-xon pi-ai-pan. | ‘You are eating holding the machete (you forgot to put in on the floor).
(57) Xawe Ainbaon-ronki machítoma-xon-bi wai a-káti-ai. | ‘It is said that the Turtle Woman worked in the chacra without a machete.’
O-orientation
The next two examples show “having something” words that describe the receiver (O):
(58) Ja iná piko-xon koros kené-ya nichin-kan-ai. | ‘After presenting the domesticated animal (to the guests), a designed cross was inserted in the soil.’

h: 19.2.2.5. Proprietive and Privative -xon (A-orientation) vs. -0 / -x (S-orientation)
t: (59) Jain-xon ja moxó-ya-bi bo-kan-ai | xebinanti a-xon-xon. | ‘Then, they took (the circumcized girls) with the piece of topa wood (serving as stretcher), after having placed the xebinanti⁴ (in their wounds) to their benefit.’

h: 19.2.2.6. Empathic Pronouns -x (S-orientation) versus -0 (A- / O-orientation)
t:
Emphatic pronouns (“she herself”) stress that the person did the action her / himself. Or they set that person against the receiver, for contrast. Some emphatic pronouns take PA endings. This suggests that in SK they work as extra words in the sentence, not as main participants. An emphatic pronoun is made like this. Start with a pronoun in its -n form or in its plain form (linguists call these nominative and accusative). Add the emphatic -bi. Then add -x to show it describes an S, or nothing at all when it describes an A or an O (see also 6.1.2, 12.2.2, and 12.5):
Xebinanti is a special mud. It is put on the wound left by female circumcision (clitoridectomy) to help it heal (Valera and Valenzuela, ms.).
S-orientation:
(60) Wesna-ra ja-n-bi-x pikó-ke. | ‘Wesna freed herself / came out herself.’
(61) Mato-n-bi-ni-x mato rami-t-ai. | ‘You yourselves get harmed / You harm yourselves.’^{5}
(62) E-a-ra e-n-bi-x-bi-shaman beno-[y]ama-a iki. | ‘I didn’t get married according to my own will.’
Compare (62) with the next piece of a story. Here a woman talks about the old days, when their mothers used to arrange their marriages for them:
A-orientation:
(63) Jawen keen joni i-ke-tian, moa ja-n-bi | bo-xon-bo no-a meni-i. | ‘Once they found a man they liked, they themselves would take us and give us in matrimony.’

h: 19.2.2.6. Empathic Pronouns -x (S-orientation) versus -0 (A- / O-orientation)
t:
(64) No-n-bi tari a-xon-yama-kin no-n benbo-baon
A speaker fluent in both languages gave this Spanish translation (the emphasis is mine): ‘Entre ustedes mismos se hacen daño.’ The word entre ‘among’ here shows that the phrase tells us how the action is done. We see the same thing when people translate the quantity words jatikax [all-S] ~ jatixon [all-A] as ‘entre todos.’ That means ‘all acting together,’ not simply ‘todos’ ‘all.’
(None) axé no-n keyo-ai. | ‘Because we ourselves do not manufacture taris (i.e., traditional men’s clothes) for (them), we are finishing with our husbands’ traditional customs.’
O-orientation:
(65) Nato r-iki e-n piti be-á, | ja-bi moa bo-tan-we. | ‘This is the fish I have caught, you better take THIS home already (rather than continue waiting for your father who also went fishing).’

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
Words that tell how something is done (manner words) are a bit more complicated. They can take two sets of agreement endings. When the word goes with the doer of a transitive verb (A), it takes -xon or -kin. When it goes with the doer of an intransitive verb (S), it takes -ax or -i. The examples below use the question word jawe keská ~ jawe keskat ‘how, why:’
S-orientation:
(66) Jawe keskat-ax-ki mi-a jo-a / piko-t-a? | ‘How did you come / escape?’
(67) E-a-ra moa jawe keskat-ax-bi ka-yama-[a]i! | ‘There is no way I will go back!’
(68) Ja-ska-ra i-ke-tian-ki be-kati-kan-ai Ashi-iba,
(None) jato-n papa, jato-n tita, jato-n bake mawá-ke-tian | jawe keskat-ax-ki mawat-a i-xon onan-kas-i. | ‘Because of this, (many people) came to his place to know how their father, their mother, their child had died.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:25)
But the ‘how’ question word does not take the S ending when the verb describes a state (how someone is). It only takes it when the verb describes something that happens, or some other intransitive action:
(69) Jawe keská-ki mato i-t-ai? | ‘How are you (pl)?’
Examples (70) and (71) show the second S ending, -i. It looks exactly like the -i we saw in (3b). That one marks an action happening at the same time, done by the same person, who is the doer of an intransitive verb. In (71), the S ending appears in a comparison (‘like single women’):

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
(70) Jawe keskát-i mato i-t-ai? | ‘What is going on with you (pl.)?’
(71) E-a-ra icha ni-ke benoma keskat-i, | ik-ax-bi e-a beno-yama iki. | ‘I have walked a lot like single women (do); however, I never had a lover.’
The next example has the expression neté-shaman-ax ‘quietly:’
(72) Ja oin-taanan, neté-shaman-ax ka-xon, joni-n jawen nonti, | napon xoton-bain-a iki.... | ‘Seeing that, getting closer (acting) very quietly, the man pushed his canoe to the middle (of the river) (Ministerio de Educación and ILV 1982:3)
But words of time, place and manner can also act like verbs and take verb endings directly. So there is another way to read this word: as ‘behaving very quietly.’ Then -ax would be the ending that means ‘after the same person did this,’ used with the doer of an intransitive verb (S):
A-orientation:
The first two examples below show the A ending -xon (for a word that goes with the doer of a transitive verb). Example (73) comes from a story in which the Shipibo learn from the white monkey how to have sex:
(73) Chaikoní, jawe keská-xon-ki a-ti iki no-n awin | chota-kin? | ‘Brother in law, how do we have to do to have sexual intercourse with our wives?’
(74) Ikaxbi rama-tian xontako-baon onan-yama-ke mapó a-ti, | ja-ská-shaman-xon meskó moa-tian kené-bo a-ti. | ‘But nowadays young girls do not know how to make pottery; similarly, (they do not know how) to make traditional designs.’

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
This is a bit like netéshamanax in (72). The word ja-ská-shaman-xon may be a short form of ja-ská-a-shaman-xon [that-SIML-do.T-INTENS-PSSA]. If so, it may also be a little sentence with its own verb. Examples (75)-(77) show the A ending -kin:
(75) Jawe keská-kin-ki mi-n pi-káshamai? | ‘Why don’t you want to eat?’
(76) ....jawe keská-kin shee ak-á-ki jakon-shaman | piko-t-ai. | ‘...how to varnish the hot pottery so that it turns out pretty.’
Like sentence (71), the next example contains a comparison.
This is a message from Mrs. Ranin Ama to indigenous peoples outside Peru:
(77) Icha-bi-res e-n mato yoiy-ai, keyó-ma-yama-kan-we | mato-n axé, mato-n joi; no-n ak-ai keská-kin-ribi | a-kan-we! | ‘I beg you not to let your customs and your languages disappear; keep them just like we keep ours!
Again, some cases of jawe keská are said with a long /a/. Perhaps these are really followed by the general verb ak- ‘do (tr.),’ a verb that can stand for many transitive actions. If so, these ‘like’-marked expressions would really be little sentences with their own verb. This cannot be decided
for sure, however, because the vowel might (also) be longer simply because it is stressed.
You can also make manner words from describing words (adjectives) by adding -n. These words do not take agreement endings:
(78) Ishto-n jo-wé! | ‘Come quickly!’

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
(79) Ishto-n be-wé! | ‘Bring (it) quickly!’
But, as I said earlier, in SK these extra words can also take verb endings and act as intransitive verbs. So ishto-n can also be used as the verb ‘to hurry.’ Then ishton- takes agreement through the ‘same person’ endings described earlier, just like any other verb:
(80) Ishto-n-i-ra e-a paké-ke. | ‘Being in a hurry, I fell.
(81) Ishto-n-ax-ra e-a shinan-beno-ke. | ‘Being in a hurry, I forgot (it).’
(82) Ishto-n-kin-ra e-n be-yama-ke. | ‘Being in a hurry, I didn’t bring (it).’
In sentences where someone makes someone else do something, built on a transitive verb, extra words without their own verb agree with the one who causes the action (see ex. (33)). In the same way, ishto-n-xon in the example below agrees with the one who makes the other act:
(83) Ishto-n-xon-ra e-a be-ma-yama-ke. | ‘Being in a hurry, he didn’t let me bring (it).’
Now let’s look at how the word kikin behaves. Kikin can make a describing word stronger, like English ‘very.’ Then it takes no ending. (In SK, describing words can come before or after their noun, but kikin must come before the whole [noun adjective] group):
(84) kikin siná | ‘extremely brave’
(85) kikin ainbo metsá | ‘extremely beautiful woman’
The word kikin also takes no ending when it describes a noun and means ‘true, legitimate, elegant, luxurious:’

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
(86) kikin xobo | ‘good, luxurious house’
But kikin can also be an extra word outside the noun group. Then it does take the agreement endings we are discussing. Here kikin is translated as ‘extremely:’
S-orientation:
(87) Kikin-i pake-t-a. | ‘He fell hurting himself hard.’
(88) Kikin-i keyo-t-a. | ‘It finished (disappeared) completely.’
(89) Kikin-ax chankat-a. | ‘He is standing very elegantly dressed and / or posing.’
(90) Kikin-ax yaka-t-a. | ‘He is sitting like posing (e.g., crossing his legs).’
The examples above show a clear difference in meaning. The form kikini describes the event itself (how the falling or finishing happened). The form kikinax instead says something about the person, the S doer. So it may help to separate two jobs: describing the event, and describing a person. Now let’s turn to sentences with a transitive verb.
A-orientation:
(91) Kikin-a-kin keyo-a. | ‘He finished (it) completely.’
(92) Kikin-a-kin rete-a. | ‘He really killed (him).’^6
(93) Kikin-xon pi-ke. | ‘He ate elegantly (like the mestizos, with tablecloth, silverware, taking out the bones from the fish....), or ‘He was dressed elegantly and ate.’
Again, there seems to be a difference in meaning. The form kikin-a-kin is more about the event, while kikin-xon is more about the person. Notice something else in the examples above. Before kikin can take -kin, the general transitive verb a(k)- must be added. This is not needed before -xon. This difference suggests two things. First, expressions with the ‘like’ ending

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
that take -kin might really be little sentences with their own verb too (see the discussion above). Second, at least some words taking -kin and -i work differently, in meaning and in sentence structure, from those taking -xon and -ax. (Notice that -i looks exactly like the general intransitive verb ik- ~ i-.)
Now let’s look at the SK word for ‘well.’ It is based on the describing word jakon ‘good.’ When jakon is used as an extra word in the sentence, it also takes agreement endings. The examples below show S agreement (with the doer of an intransitive verb). I have not been able to find any difference in meaning between (94a) and (94b).
(94) a. Jakon-ax ja-kan-we! | ‘Live well!’ | b. Jakon-i ja-kan-we! | ‘Live well!’
With transitive verbs, things change. The general transitive verb a(k)- must be added before any A ending. So the sentences below should be seen as little sentences with their own verb:
(95) a. Jakon-a-xon yoá a-wé | ‘Cook well!’ | b. Jakon-a-kin yoá a-wé! | ‘Cook well!’
For one speaker, the two sentences above mean slightly different things. The (a) version means ‘cook carefully.’ The (b) version is about how good the food turns out (Mr. Sanken Bari, p.c. 2002). We can explain this the same way as with kikin. Then jakon-a-xon points to the A

h: 19.2.2.7. Manner -ax / -i (S-orientation) vs. (-a)-xon / (-a)-kin (A-orientation)
t:
A Spanish version given by a speaker fluent in both languages is: Lo mató bien matado.
participant, the doer who is going to cook well or carefully. On the other hand, jakon-a-kin describes the event, which results in good food. But kikin and jakon still differ in one way. With kikin, only the -kin forms need the transitive verb ak-. With jakon, both the -kin forms and the -xon forms need ak-. The story example below has two S endings in the same sentence: -i on kikin, which tells how much, and -x on the word for the stage of life (‘child’):
(96) Ja-tian kikin-i bake-x-bi no-a xeta keyo-t-ai. | ‘Then, in spite of being very very young we lose our teeth.’

h: 19.2.2.8. Quantity
t:
Words of quantity follow at least two different patterns. The word jatik ~ jati ‘all’ shows one pattern. The number kimisha ‘three’ shows the other.
Jatik ~ jati ‘altogether’ -ax (S-orientation) vs. -xon (A-orientation)
(97) Ja-ská-ke-tian, jatik-ax-bi bo-kan-a iki, nee-t-i. | ‘Then, everybody started to go up.’
(98) Ja-skáa-xon-ki, jatí-xon-bi jato-n bake-bo-ki | notsi-n-kan-a iki. | ‘Then, they scolded their children altogether.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:16)
Numeral -0 / -i (S-orientation) vs. -xon / -a-kin (A-orientation)
Like manner words, numbers can take two different S endings and two different A endings. There is one small difference. On numbers, the S endings are -0 (no ending) and -i, not -ax and -i. The A endings are the same as for manner words: -xon and -kin. As with kikin, the two S endings and the two A endings carry a clear difference in meaning. Look at examples (99)-(102), with the number kimisha ‘three:’
(99) Ja-bo-ra kimisha-bo jiki-ke. | ‘They entered in groups of three.’
(100) Ja-baon-ra kimisha-xon-bo naransha bi-ke. | ‘They got oranges acting in groups of three.’
(101) Ja-ra kimisha-i pake-t-a iki. | ‘He fell three times.’
(102) Ja-n-ra kimisha-a-kin pi-a iki. | ‘He ate three times.’
The forms kimisha-bo and kimisha-xon-bo describe the people (‘in groups of three’). The forms kimisha-i and kimisha-a-kin instead describe the event (‘three times’). Notice too that only kimisha-a-kin is a little sentence with its own verb.

h: 19.2.2.9. Comitatives
t:
Phrases with betan ‘with’ (as in ‘with father’) do not take agreement endings in SK. Look at the examples below. One has an intransitive verb (‘go’) and one has a transitive verb (‘slash’):
(103) E-a-ra wai-nko kai papa betan. | ‘I go to the chacra with father.’
(104) E-n-ra wai sepai papa betan. | ‘I slash the chacra with father.’
Still, as I will show in 20.3.6, ‘with’ phrases do take agreement endings in some related languages. So the lack of agreement here may be something new that developed in SK.

h: 19.2.2.10. Temporals
t:
Like ‘with’ phrases, time words take no agreement endings at all. This is probably because they describe the whole event, not one of the people in it. (But see the time words in Matses, exx. (86) and (87) of Ch. 20.) This fits with what happens in
the Australian language Warlpiri. There, time words may match the doer of the sentence in their case marking, but they don’t have to. Place and manner words, however, must always match (Simpson 1991:208). The next examples use the time words rama ‘now’ and bakish ‘one day from today:’
(105) Rama-ra oxa-[a]i / ka-[a]i / pi-ai. rama-xon ramax ramai ramakin | ‘Now I am going to sleep / to go / to eat.’
(106) Bakisha e-a yamékiri-bi weni-t-ai. | ‘Tomorrow I am going to wake up early in the morning.’
(107) Bakisha e-n xenan wai-nko-ni-a | bi-i ka-[a]i. | ‘Tomorrow I am going to bring guabas from the chacra.’

h: 19.2.2.11. Conjunctions
t:
In SK, some joining words (like ‘then’ or ‘and so’) are made from the word ja ‘that’ plus a place ending or a ‘like’ ending. Because they started out as place or manner words, these joining words can take the whole range of agreement endings described above. In the story below, the joining word jainoax links one sentence to the next. The story is about the Yoina Reteti or Animal Sacrifice Ceremony, which is part of the girls’ puberty rites, the Ani Xeati:
(108) a. Ja tsaka-[a]i ibo iki kanóti kené-ya, pia | chi-kené-ya jonxe kené-ya, wexati | ba-pani-a. | ‘The man in charge of directing the shooting had a designed bow, arrows with designs on the non-pointed end, designed bracelets, and a wexati knife hanging on the shoulder. | b. Jaino-a-x ja tsaka-[a]i betan ik-á joni-bo | iki wiso tari-ya, joshin tari-ya, joxo tari-ya-bo. | Then, the men accompanying him were dressed in black, red, and white taris (men’s traditional clothes). | c. Jaino-a-x bewa-kan-ai ja iná | tsak[a]-ainko-ni-a-x... | Then, they sang from (the place) where they shot at the animal (w/arrow)...’
In the next story excerpt, jainxon also links sentences:
(109) a. Ja moa nokon papa rabé baritia teet-a ik-á iki. | ‘My father had already worked for two years (organizing my sisters’ Ani Xeati ceremony). | b. Jain-xon moa nokon papa-n yoá-bo tsinki-a ik-á iki | wai-nko-ni-a. | By then, my father had already gathered the crops from the chacra.

h: 19.2.2.11. Conjunctions
t:
(c) Jain-xon-ribi jatíbi jawen iná bi-ní-bo | yatan-a iki.... | Also he had gathered the animals he had raised (for the occasion)....’
In 19.2.2.3 we saw something similar with phrases of interest. Joining words take either the ‘from’ ending (as in jainoa) or the ‘at’ ending (as in jain). The choice seems to depend on the grammar: it lets the S or A ending appear. An S ending only appears on joining words with the ‘from’ ending. (Remember that the ‘from’ ending must always come after an ‘at’ ending.) An A ending only appears on joining words with the ‘at’ ending. Jainoax and jainxon can also join parts inside a single sentence, and even inside a single part of a sentence. The examples below show the first use:
(110) No-a jimi-i jene-t-ai, jaino-a-x jo-ai bake | joni a-ti. | ‘Once we stop menstruating, comes the pregnancy.’
(111) Ja-tian rao-n-noxon waste xaki-ai ja joni | shinan shinan-anan-bi, jain-xon samat-i kai. | ‘In order to treat (a man to make him love you), you grind the piripiri (i.e., plant with special powers) concentrating on that man, and you abstain from eating (certain foods) and from having sex.’
The next two examples show joining words with the ‘like’ ending:
(112) Ja-ská-kin ja joni-n jato yoiy-a iki. | ‘Then / so the man communicated them (that).’

h: 19.2.2.11. Conjunctions
t: (113) Ja-skat-i-kaya-bira mi-a pikó-yora-[a]i | xobome-a-x. | ‘This is probably why you go out from home so much.’

h: Participant Agreement: Further Examples (more examples)
t:
This section gives a few more examples from real stories. They show how the different kinds of agreement work together in speech. In (114), two extra words without their own verb carry the S ending (for the doer of an intransitive verb): ‘from Pucallpa’ and the word for ‘extremely.’ The part ‘When he returned from Pucallpa’ has the ‘same person’ ending -ax (PSSS). This ending also shows that the person it goes with is an S: the doer of the main intransitive verb ‘be thirsty.’ The part ‘feeling extremely thirsty’ has a marker that tells you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else. So no agreement is needed there, and none is possible:
(114) [[Maioshiainoa-x jo-ax] kikin-i nomi-ai-tian]] | ‘When (he) returned from Pucallpa feeling extremely thirsty, | e-n xea-ma-a iki ja e-n rao kobin ak-á. | I had him drink the plant medicine I had previously boiled.’
In (115a) we again see the S ‘same person’ ending -ax, here with the intransitive verb ‘sleep.’ The A partner of -ax is -xon. It appears on three parts that have their own verb. Notice that oxa-xon and onan i-xon in (115b) go with the same A doer: the doer of the transitive verb ‘dig.’ In (115c), napokoo-xon also goes with the A doer, the doer of ‘see.’ Some extra words without their own verb take no agreement ending: mashi-n ‘on the sand / beach’ and jain ‘there.’ They describe the S doers of ‘slept’ and of ‘enter’ (an intransitive verb made from another verb). On the other hand, jain-xon ‘there’ and choska chonka-xon ‘forty’ take the A ending.

h: Participant Agreement: Further Examples (more examples)
t:
(115) [Ka-ax] mashi-n oxa-kan-a iki. | ‘Once they arrived they slept on the beach. | [Mashi-n oxa-xon], [yosi-bo moa onan i-xon], | After sleeping on the beach, since the elders were experienced (in warfare), | mashi chini-kan-a iki. | they dug the sand. | [Jain napokoo-xon] oin-kan-a-ronki ik-á iki | There, entering (into the holes), they saw | Kashibo-bo be-i... | the Kashibos approaching | Jain-xon-ki yatan-kan-a iki jato-n tokoriko, | ja chosko chonka-xon. | There they captured their chief, those forty men (lit. ‘in a group of forty’).’
The chains of sentences in (115) are fairly short. Each has one main part with a full verb, joined to at most two parts with ‘same person / someone else’ markers. But in real speech, much longer chains are found, as in (116) (given earlier in Ch. 14 as ex. (7)). The one full verb is underlined. The parts with ‘same person / someone else’ markers are in square brackets. Larger chunks of the story are in simple brackets. These chunks (roughly one scene each) are marked by the short ending -ki, which shows the speaker heard the story from others:
(116) a. [Ja-ska-ra i-xon-ronki] a-káti-kan-ai | b. {[yapa axa-n-xon] c. [bi-xon-ki]} | d. {[makaman benes a-kin] e. [chaka-xon-ki]} | f. {[bari-n raka-n-xon-ki]} | g. {[moshi-ke-tian bi-xon-ki]} | h. [pi-kin] no-n moa-baon, i. [chii-oma i-xon]. | ‘Living in such conditions, our ancestors poisoned the fish and collected them, crushed them with a stone making them thinner, and lay them in the sun so that they dried; getting them they ate them, because they had no fire.’ (Soi Rawa 1995:9).’

h: Participant Agreement: Further Examples (more examples)
t:
The first part sets the scene by giving background information. The second part has the full general verb akátikanai. This verb is separated from its A doer by several parts with ‘same person / someone else’ markers. These parts move the
description of the process forward. The last part gives the reason why the Shipibo prepared the fish this way. That reason had already been given in an earlier chain.

h: Agreement Patterns and Adjunct Types (agreement patterns and the kinds of extra phrases)
t:
We can now sum up participant agreement in SK in a new way. First, there are three basic patterns of agreement endings on the extra words:
Pattern 3 is clearly just -no plus the endings in Pattern 1.
Second, the extra words can be split into four groups, based on which agreement endings they take (see sections 19.3.1-19.3.4). A fifth group takes no agreement endings at all (19.3.5). Third, the groups are ranked. Words that take the Pattern 2 endings also take the Pattern 1 endings. Words that take the Pattern 3 endings also take the Pattern 2 endings: Pattern 1 > Pattern 2 > Pattern 3.
Fourth, we can tentatively link the different groups of extra words to differences in meaning (19.3.6).

h: Adjunct Type 1 (kind 1)
t:
Emphatic words like ‘she herself’ and life-stage words like ‘as a child’ have something special. (Life-stage words include ‘having’ phrases that give a specific age.) They can take the S ending -x directly. They do not need the ‘from’ ending -a in front of it. (That -a itself always has to be built on the ‘at’ ending.) But these two kinds of words take different A endings. Emphatic words take -0 (no ending), while life-stage words (and ‘having’ phrases) take -xon.
(None) ja-n-bi-x | ‘she herself (S-oriented)’ | ja-n-bi-0 | ‘she herself (A-oriented)’ | bake-x-bi | ‘as a child (S-oriented)’ | bake-shoko-xon | ‘as a little child (A-oriented)’

h: Adjunct Type 2 (kind 2)
t:
Type 2 words take -ax for S agreement. (That means the ‘from’ ending -a must come before -x.) For A agreement they take -xon. This group includes place words (the ‘at / to’ ending together with the ‘from’ ending), affective words (like ‘on me’), and jati ~ jatik ‘altogether.’
(None) xobo-nko-ni-a-x | ‘from the house (S-oriented) | xobo-n-xon | ‘in the house (A-oriented) | e-on-mea-x | ‘on me (S-oriented) | e-on-xon | ‘on me (A-oriented) | jatik-ax | ‘altogether (S-oriented)’ | jatí-xon | ‘altogether (A-oriented)’

h: Adjunct Type 3 (kind 3)
t:
Words of manner or reason and number words form one group here. They take endings from both Pattern 1 and Pattern 2. Adding -kin seems to need the general transitive verb ak-, but this is not always true for -xon:
kimisha ‘three’
jawe keská ~ jawe keskat ‘how / why’
kikin ‘extremely’
jakon ‘good, well’

h: Adjunct Type 4 (kind 4)
