t: Type 4 contains parts of a sentence with a ‘same person’ marker. They describe events that happen before, at the same time as, or after the event of the main sentence. All three agreement patterns are used.

h: Adjunct Type 5 (kind 5)
t: ‘With’ words and time words take no agreement endings at all. So they form one group, Type 5.

h: Adjunct Types and Semantic Criteria (the kinds of extra phrases and their meanings)
t:
As I said above, we can tentatively link these groups to meaning. The question is how much a word describes a person, and how much it describes the event. This idea comes from the difference in meaning we found in some words that take both Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 endings (Type 3). Emphatic words and life-stage words (Type 1) describe a person the most. They can take the ending -x directly.⁷ Place words, affective words and ‘altogether’ (Type 2) are also
This will matter in 20.4 and 20.5, where I argue that -x used to be a case marker for S, the doer of an intransitive verb. So Type 1 words once took the marker of their S controller directly.
about a person, but they cannot take -x directly. Manner/reason and quantity words (except ‘altogether’) can go either way. With -ax and -xon they describe a person. With -i and -kin they describe the event. The same may be true of parts of a sentence with a ‘same person’ marker. Finally, ‘with’ words and time words take no agreement endings at all. (Neither do life-stage words with -tian.) This may show that they cannot describe a person. We can sum up this idea as a scale (PO stands for Participant-Orientedness, how much a word describes a person; EO for event-orientedness, how much it describes the event; and AT for Adjunct Type, the group of the extra word):

h: Adjunct Types and Semantic Criteria (the kinds of extra phrases and their meanings)
t:
There is, however, another way to explain why life-stage words seem special. Remember, they don’t need the ‘from’ ending -a before the S ending -x. Recall that in SK a noun can act as a verb meaning ‘become’ by taking verb endings directly. So bake-ax [child-ax] means ‘after becoming / behaving as a child.’ What I would like to suggest here is
that life-stage words may take the S ending -x, and not -ax, for a reason: to avoid mixing up the two meanings, ‘after becoming a child’ and ‘as a child.’

h: Participant Agreement as a Non-Canonical Type of Agreement (why this is an unusual kind of agreement)
t:
At the start of this chapter, I named the parts of SK participant agreement, following the framework of Corbett (2001, 2002). These are the controller (the noun that decides the ending), the target (the word that takes the ending), the domain (where the agreement happens) and the agreement feature (what the ending shows). In this section I use the same framework to place participant agreement among the kinds of agreement found in the world’s languages. I also want to show exactly what makes it an unusual kind of agreement. (Linguists call the most typical kind ‘canonical’ agreement.)
First I give the criteria for canonical agreement put forward by Corbett (2001). Then I check SK participant agreement against each criterion, and point out where it differs from canonical agreement.

h: Defining Canonical Agreement (what "normal" agreement looks like)
t: Corbett (2001) gives several criteria for what canonical (most typical) agreement looks like. I list them or briefly introduce them below. Some may become clearer when I describe SK participant agreement in 19.4.2. (See Corbett op.cit. for fuller definitions and more examples.) The symbol ‘>’ means ‘more canonical than.’

h: 19.4.1.1. Criteria that Relate to the Controller
t:
Criterion-1: controller present > controller absent
Agreement is more canonical when the controller must be there. For example, think of a verb agreeing with its doer. This is more canonical in a language where the doer must always be said, like English. It is less canonical in a “pro-drop” language, where the doer can be left out.
Criterion-2: controller has overt features > controller has covert features
Agreement is more canonical when the controller clearly shows its features. Take French. Describing words agree in gender (masculine or feminine) with the doer. This agreement is more canonical with a ‘he/she’ doer (117) than with an ‘I’ doer (118). That is because the pronouns for ‘he’ and ‘she’ show a gender, but the pronoun for ‘I’ does not:
(117) Elle est content-e. / Il est content. | ‘She is happy.’ / ‘He is happy.’
(118) Je suis content-e. / Je suis content. | ‘I am happy (of a woman).’ / ‘I am happy (of a man).’
Criterion-3: consistent controller > hybrid controller
A consistent controller always causes the same agreement pattern. A hybrid controller causes different forms on different words. Corbett (op. cit.:5) gives an example of a hybrid controller from the Talitsk dialect of Russian. There, a plural verb can be used with a singular noun to talk about that person plus other people.

h: 19.4.1.1. Criteria that Relate to the Controller
t:
Criterion-4: controller’s part of speech irrelevant > relevant (given the domain)
In the canonical case, once you know the domain, you don’t need to know the controller’s part of speech. Take a verb agreeing with its doer in Russian. It doesn’t matter whether the doer is a noun or a pronoun. But in Bayso, pronouns and nouns need different rules.

h: 19.4.1.2. Criteria that Relate to the Target
t:
Criterion-5: expression of agreement on the target is bound > free (affix > clitic > free word)
Criterion-6: obligatory > optional
Agreement that must always be marked is more canonical than agreement that is optional.
Criterion-7: regular > suppletive
In the canonical case, agreement is shown with regular endings. Corbett (op. cit.) gives examples from Norwegian, where agreement can be shown by a completely different word form instead (linguists call this suppletion, like English go / went):
(119) en liten øl / to små øl | ‘one small beer’ ‘two small beers’
alliterative > opaque:
In the canonical case, the agreement ending on the target sounds the same as a piece of the controller. And the same ending is used on different targets.
productive > sporadic:
In the canonical case, every possible target of a given kind shows agreement. For example, in Russian every verb agrees in number (singular or plural). But in Chechen and Ingush (Nakh-Daghestanian languages) only about 30% of verbs show agreement.
doubling > independent:
The agreement shows up whether or not the controller is present. This criterion is related to Criterion 1, but here it is about the target.
target agrees with a single controller > agrees with more than one controller:
In the canonical case, the target has one controller, even if the agreement is marked more than once. It is less canonical for a target to agree with more than one controller.

h: 19.4.1.2. Criteria that Relate to the Target
t:
target’s part of speech irrelevant > relevant (given the domain):
In canonical agreement, you can describe the targets in general terms, as one broad part of the domain. You don’t need extra rules for different kinds of target.

h: 19.4.1.3. Criteria that Relate to the Domain
t:
Criterion-13: asymmetric > symmetric
In the canonical case, agreement goes one way: one word decides, and the other follows. Corbett points out a problem with case agreement inside the noun group (NP). It can be a problem for linguists who see sentences as built from nested groups of words. For them, the matching inside the noun group comes from one outside word that controls all of its words. But it is not a problem for linguists who see sentences as words depending on other words. For them, the noun is the head of the noun group, and the describing words depend on it.
Criterion-14: local > non-local
Agreement inside one part of a sentence (with its own verb) is more canonical than agreement that reaches beyond it.
Criterion-15: domain is one of set > single domain
A language can have several areas of agreement (for example, verb with doer, describing word with noun, a ‘who/which…’ part with the noun it describes, etc.). Such a language is a more canonical case than a language with only one area of agreement.

h: 19.4.1.4. Criteria that Relate to Features
t:
Criterion-16: feature is lexical > non-lexical
Canonical agreement is about a feature that belongs to the word itself (for example, gender). The target could not carry that feature on its own; it gets it only from the controller. This is linked to the direction of agreement.
Criterion-17: features have matching values > non-matching values
Agreement where the feature values match is more canonical than agreement where they don’t (for example, agreement based on meaning rather than form).
Criterion-18: no choice of feature value > choice of value
In Russian, under certain conditions, the words for ‘five girls’ can go with either a singular or a plural verb. This is less canonical than languages where only one form is possible. In a similar sentence, English uses only the plural verb, and Hungarian only the singular (Corbett op.cit.:18-19).

h: 19.4.1.5. Conditions
t:
Criterion-19: no conditions > conditions
In Hungarian, two singular nouns joined by ‘and’ can go with a singular or a plural verb. Which one you use depends on a condition: whether the nouns are living beings or things. Such conditions are common when agreement is non-canonical.
Corbett also gives three general principles of canonical agreement, which sum up the criteria above:
1- Canonical agreement is redundant rather than informative. In other words, it repeats information the sentence already gives. This may be why canonical agreement is fairly rare in the world’s languages (criteria 1, 2, 16, 17, 18 and, less directly, 15).
2- Canonical agreement is syntactically simple. That is, it follows simple sentence rules. This principle sums up several of the criteria above (3, 4, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, and partly 6).
3- The closer the expression of agreement is to canonical (i.e. affixal) inflectional morphology, the more canonical it is as agreement. Put simply: the more agreement is shown by regular endings, the more canonical it is. Several criteria point to this principle (namely 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9).
In the next section, I give a first description of participant agreement using these criteria.

h: 19.4.2.1. Controller
t:
In SK participant agreement, the controller is one of the main people in the sentence: the doer of an intransitive verb (S), the doer of a transitive verb (A), or the receiver (O). Or it is the doer (S or A) of the main sentence. The controller may be said or left out. It may show its features openly
(through its case marker, see the discussion in 20.4 and 20.5) or not (if it is left out). It always controls the same agreement patterns, even though there are different patterns and smaller patterns (‘from’ words, ‘at’ words, manner words, emphatic words, etc.). And its part of speech doesn’t matter, because this noun group can be built on either a noun or a pronoun.

h: 19.4.2.2. Target
t: The target is a word, phrase, or part of a sentence that is an extra part attached to the verb. Agreement on it is shown by endings attached to the whole phrase. The marking must always be there. It appears whether or not the controller is said, so it can repeat the controller’s marking. The marking is regular but ‘opaque’: it does not sound like the marker on the controller. It is fairly productive, since it does not affect all extra parts. (This depends on how we define an extra part, especially on the difference between describing a person and describing the event.) Different kinds of targets need extra rules. The target agrees with only one controller. The target’s part of speech doesn’t matter.

h: 19.4.2.3. Domain
t:
The domain is agreement between a person in the sentence and an extra part. It goes one way, since the ending on the extra part depends on the role of the controller in the sentence. It is not necessarily local (that is,
it is not always kept inside one part of the sentence). This kind of agreement is the only area of agreement in the language.

h: 19.4.2.4. Agreement Features
t: The agreement features are not part of the word itself. They come from its role in the sentence (S, A, O). Their values match, so there is no choice of values. (A possible exception is agreement based on meaning on ‘from’ words. This may happen in sentences with a ‘make someone do it’ ending or an ending that brings in an extra person, built on an intransitive verb.)

h: 19.4.2.5. Conditions
t:
No conditions are found.
In short, SK participant agreement differs from canonical agreement in these ways (C = criterion). C-8: it is opaque, since the endings on the extra parts differ from the markers on the nouns that control them. C-12: different kinds of targets need extra rules. C-14: agreement can reach beyond one part of the sentence, because the ‘same person’ markers on chained parts are chosen according to the role of the main sentence’s doer. C-15: it is the only area of agreement in the language (leaving aside transitivity agreement). C-16: the feature comes from sentence role, not from the word itself. That is, the target is not marked for a built-in property of the controller, but for the specific grammatical role it
has with other words in a particular sentence. Also, there seem to be some cases of agreement based on meaning, C-17.
So SK participant agreement differs from canonical agreement in several ways. But these criteria miss what is probably its most striking feature. The agreement appears in the “wrong place”: on the extra parts of the sentence. And there is no agreement at all in the “right place”: inside the noun group (NP). So participant agreement cannot be explained as having spread from the noun group to the extra parts.

h: Summary
t:
In this chapter I have shown that in SK certain extra parts of a sentence get a special ending. The ending depends on the role of the person they describe. This person (the controller) can be one of the main people in a simple sentence. Or it can be the doer of the main sentence in a longer sentence, where one or more parts are chained to it. I found three basic agreement patterns. All three follow the same overall three-way split: an ending for S (the doer of an intransitive verb), an ending for A (the doer of a transitive verb), and no ending for O (the receiver), when that applies. I also proposed four basic groups of extra parts, based on the agreement patterns they take. A fifth group is made of the words that cannot take these endings. Finally, I offered a tentative link between these five groups and how much they describe a person or the event.
Finally, I have shown that this participant agreement differs in several respects from more usual kinds of agreement. Here is the main point. A noun decides the shape of the extra describing words in the sentence. But it does not affect the shape of the words that describe it inside its own noun group (its noun phrase). This situation is quite unusual, because it is the only kind of agreement in the whole language.

h: Summary
t:
Where these agreement endings come from is not clear. But there are hints that they are related to the markers on nouns that show the doer and the receiver. The endings -xon and -kin, used when the describing word goes with the doer of a transitive verb, end in /n/. That /n/ is the basic form of the doer marker (ERG). Also, describing words that go with the receiver, and sometimes with the doer of an intransitive verb, get no ending at all. This matches the plain form (ABS), which also has no marker. But the piece -xo and the ending -x cannot be explained from today’s language. The hardest one is -(a)x, used when the describing word goes with the doer of an intransitive verb. That is odd because such doers have no marker in Shipibo-Konibo. (The only exceptions are the words for ‘I’, ‘you’ and ‘we’, which take -a.)
This book raises some big questions. Why do the extra describing words agree with a noun, when words inside a noun group never agree with each other? Where do these agreement endings come from? How did this unusual feature develop? Do other languages of the same family (the Panoan languages) have it too? The next chapter tries to answer these questions by comparing related languages and looking at the history of the language.

h: Summary
t:
PARTICIPANT AGREEMENT IN PANOAN:
Participant agreement may be the most striking feature of the grammar of the Panoan languages. (Panoan is the language family that Shipibo-Konibo belongs to.) Participant agreement means that an extra describing part of the sentence takes an ending that matches the person it goes with. In this chapter I compare the Panoan languages and look at their history. I want to find out what these agreement endings really are, and how this unusual feature might have grown over time. I will show that participant agreement is found in all the different branches of the Panoan family. I will also show where the endings come from. Long ago, each one was two markers stuck together: a marker for place or direction, plus a marker showing the main roles in the sentence (doer or receiver). This matters a lot for rebuilding Proto-Pano, the old language that all Panoan languages come from. It shows that Proto-Pano most probably already had participant agreement. It also shows that, in some parts of its grammar, Proto-Pano marked three roles in three different ways: the doer of a transitive verb, the doer of an intransitive verb, and the receiver. Along the way, I rebuild a handful of new old word pieces. This adds to the pioneering work of Olive Shell (1965 / 1975).

h: Summary
t: Because this chapter compares languages, I use data from a number of chosen Panoan languages. Their sounds may be quite different from those of Shipibo-Konibo. So in the following sections I write all of them the same way, using a spelling very close to the IPA (the international phonetic alphabet).

h: Panoan Languages (the related languages)
t:
The Panoan family has about 28 languages. They are (or used to be) spoken in neighboring parts of the Amazon in Peru, Brazil, and Bolivia. The list below gives some key features that Panoan grammar has, and some that it lacks. Features (d) to (i) will matter most for this chapter:
(a) The basic word order is doer–receiver–verb (AOV) in sentences with a transitive verb, and doer–verb (SV) in sentences with an intransitive verb.
(b) Words are mostly built by stringing pieces together, each piece with one job. Verbs sometimes pack in a lot of pieces.
(c) Only endings are used, never beginning pieces (except the body-part “prefixes”). Words like ‘on’ and ‘in’ come after the noun, not before it.
(d) The verb (or helping verb) has no well-developed set of endings showing who is doing the action, of a kind shared across the family.
(e) Words inside a noun group never agree with the noun.
(f) The doer of a transitive verb gets a special doer marker (ergative), but this pattern is split in different ways in different languages.
(g) One marker often does several jobs. The same form can mark the doer (ergative), the tool used (instrumental), the owner (genitive), and other roles.
(h) Role markers tend to appear only once in a noun group, on its last word.

h: Panoan Languages (the related languages)
t:
(i) Sentences are chained one after another, with a fairly complex system of markers that tell you whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else.
This study relies mainly on data from Chakobo, Yaminawa, Amawaka, Shipibo-Konibo, Kashibo-Kakataibo, and Matses. Together they represent the different branches of the Panoan family (see section 1.5). Table 20.1 sums up
where these languages are spoken and roughly how many people speak them. (The population numbers are not always up to date.)
I should explain a couple of choices. First, I have not included any language from the South Western branch of Panoan, because there are no useful data for any of them. Second, I have chosen to show Yaminawa
and Amawaka separately. Both may belong to the same “Purus” branch. But they differ in an important way: they mark the doer and the receiver differently. I also use data from other languages, especially when I rebuild old word pieces and discuss role markers. I always say where the data come from. Only Sparing-Chávez’s (1998) article on Amawaka gives examples with a word-by-word breakdown. The other sources don't. So the breakdowns I give here are my own reading of the grammar information in those or other sources. They are somewhat provisional, but this does not affect the points I am making.

h: Interclausal Participant Agreement and the Panoan Switch-Reference System (agreement across sentences and the "same/different person" system)
t: In this section I only look at sentence parts that carry a “same doer / different doer” marker and that also show participant agreement. Most parts marked “same doer” fit this description. Their endings are shown in Table 20.2 below.

h: Panoan Same-Subject Markers ("same person" endings in related languages)
t:
All the Panoan languages here have clearly similar “same doer” endings, and a similar participant agreement system in general. In fact, these endings come from the same old forms in all the sister languages (linguists call such related forms “cognates”).
All the endings in Table 20.2 say that the extra part of the sentence has the same doer as the main sentence. They also say something more. The endings in columns 1 and 2 are used when the action in the extra part happens before the action in the main sentence. Which of the two you use depends on the main verb. -aʂ is used when the shared doer is the doer of an intransitive verb, so the main verb is an intransitive verb. -ʂon is used when the shared doer is the doer of a transitive verb, so the main verb is that kind of verb. Columns 3 and 4 hold the endings for actions that happen at the same time. Again, which one you use depends on the role of the shared person in the main sentence, and so on what kind of verb the main verb is. Finally, columns 5 and 6 hold the endings for actions that happen afterwards, again one for each kind of doer.
Over time, the sounds of the old parent language, Proto-Panoan, changed in different ways in each daughter language. Here are some of these changes (see also Shell 1975). The old sound ʂ stayed /ʂ/ in Chakobo, Yaminawa, Shipibo-Konibo (SK), and Kashibo-Kakataibo. In Amawaka it became /x/,¹ and in Matses it became /ʃ/. Chakobo has one special change. It has probably lost the /n/, or the nasal sound, on some endings. These are the endings that point to the doer of a transitive verb, or show that someone is in control (the ones in columns 2 and 4). Now for the vowels. Old i turned into both /i/ and /e/ in Matses. Old o turned into both /o/ and /u/ in Matses and Kashibo-Kakataibo.

h: Panoan Same-Subject Markers ("same person" endings in related languages)
t:
Table 20.2 shows a general pattern. The endings that go with the doer of a transitive verb (columns 2, 4, and 6) end in a nasal sound or /n/. Chakobo is the exception (and so is Pakawara, another Southern language). That fits the sound change I just described. By contrast, the endings that go with the doer of an intransitive verb end in /ʂ/ or /i/ (or the sounds that replaced them). Note also that in Kashibo-Kakataibo the ending in column 1 (labeled PSSA) is just -ʂ, not -aʂ.
In the next sections I show how participant agreement works in parts of the sentence marked “same doer”. I use examples from the different languages. The languages I chose are typical for each pattern, unless I say otherwise. I already dealt with participant agreement in Shipibo-Konibo in the previous chapter. But I include Shipibo-Konibo examples here too, to make comparing easier.
Sparing-Chávez (1998:477) says that in her spelling <x> stands for the sounds [x] and [ç], and <tz> stands for [ts] and [tθ]. I do not know whether both sounds occur in the endings discussed here. So I have kept the symbols used in her work.

h: 20.2.1.1. Marked Clause Codes Previous Event
t:
The examples in this section show the “same doer, earlier action” endings in the chosen languages. Each language has one ending for the doer of an intransitive verb and one for the doer of a transitive verb.
Southern Pano: Chakobo (Zingg 1998)
Chakobo is special. Its “same doer” endings have a short form and a long form. Which one you use depends on whether the marked part comes before or after the main sentence. The short form is used when the marked part comes first, as in the (a) examples. The long form is used when it comes after the main sentence, as in the (b) examples. (In (1a-b), notice that ‘in the hammock’ also has a long and a short form. It depends on where it stands compared to the verb.)
(1) [kaʔɨʔ-aʂ] tsi ha oʂa-kɨ niʃí no. | niʃí tsi ha oʂa-kɨ [kaʔɨʔ-aʂ na.] | ‘He slept in the hammock [after having arrived].’ (p. 31)
(2) [pi-ʂo] tsi hawɨ poroma ha kɨno-kɨ. | poroma ha kɨno-kɨ [pi-ʂo na]. | ‘[After having eaten] he sharpened his ax.’ (p. 31)
Purus Pano 1: Yaminawa (Eakin 1991):
(3) [mã pi-aʂ] nõ ka-i. | ‘After having eaten, we’ll go.’ (p. 124)
(4) [ʂoo mɨ̃ra tsao-ʂõ] ɨ koma õita. | ‘After sitting on the bench, I saw a partridge yesterday.’ (p. 124)
Purus Pano 2: Amawaka (Sparing-Chávez 1998):

h: 20.2.1.1. Marked Clause Codes Previous Event
t:
(5) [jantan ʔoro-ʔax]-mɨn hatzanamɨ-ɨ-jama-ʃin-kɨ-ʔnɨ. | ‘Cultivating till late yesterday, I didn’t get tired. / Although I cultivated till late yesterday, I didn’t get tired.’ (p. 457)
(6) [niʔii ka-xon]-mɨn ʔɨn ʔaa rɨtɨ-kɨ-ʔnɨ. | ‘Having gone hunting, I killed a tapir./ I went hunting and killed a tapir.’ (p. 458)
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo (Valenzuela 1997):
These examples were already given in Chapter 9 as (1a)-(1b).
(7) nokon papa-ra [wai mɨno-aʂ] katʃio ka-kɨ. | ‘My father, after burning the garden, went to the forest.’
(8) nokon papa-n-ra [wai mɨno-ʂon] atsa βana-kɨ. | ‘My father, after burning the garden, sowed the yuca.’
Western Pano: Kashibo-Kakataibo (Wistrand 1969)
(9) [aa-ʂ kwan-ʂ]-βi ka-ísa nɨtɨ-akɨʂin. | ‘He went away but disappeared.’ (p. 166)
(10) [βi-ʂun] kaa piti ʔikɨn. | ‘He takes it and (then) will eat it!’ (p. 166)
Northern Pano: Matses (Kneeland 1979)
(11) [pi-aʃ] uʃ-eβi. | ‘After having eaten, I will sleep.’ (p. 105)
(12) [ɨnapen nid-ʃun] anseme-p-omβi. | ‘After having gone far, I fished a lot (with hook).’ (p. 106)

h: 20.2.1.2. Marked Clause Codes Simultaneous Event
t:
In the following long sentences, the action of the extra part happens at the same time as the action of the main sentence, or overlaps with it.
Southern Pano: Chakobo (Zingg 1998)
(13) [tʃama-jama-ʔi] tsi ha mɨmɨ-mɨmɨ-kɨ. | ‘Not having the strength, he trembled.’ (p. 31)
(14) [tʃama-jama-kí] tsi ha tɨro-jama-kɨ. | ‘Not having the strength, he did not lift it.’ (p. 30)
Purus Pano 1: Yaminawa (Eakin 1991):
(15) [mɨ o-i] pakɨ-a. | ‘When I was coming, I fell.’ (p. 124)
(16) [ka-kĩ] nõ ʂafɨ fich-ita. | ‘While we were going, we found a tortoise.’ (p. 124)
Purus Pano 2: Amawaka (Sparing-Chávez 1998):
(17) [hii rɨra-rɨra-ʔi]-mɨn han pakɨɨ-xo-ʔnɨ | ‘[While cutting down trees], he fell.’ (p. 460)
(18) [hiri-kin]-mɨn non hato ninkaa-kɨ-ʔnɨ. | ‘[While eating], we heard them.’ (p. 460)
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo (Valenzuela 1997):
(19) [karo βɨna-i]-ra pakî-kɨ. | ‘While s/he was looking for firewood, s/he fell.’
(20) [karo βɨna-kin]-ra rono mɨra-kɨ. | ‘While s/he was looking for firewood, s/he found a snake.’
Western Pano: Kashibo-Kakataibo (Wistrand 1969)
In Kashibo-Kakataibo and other Panoan languages, the ending -i can come before a verb of motion (like ‘go’). Then it means ‘in order to’, or an action still to come:
(21) [ka-na kwan-i] kwan-in. | ‘I am going (to one place) to go (from there to another place).’ Lit.: ‘going I go’

h: 20.2.1.2. Marked Clause Codes Simultaneous Event
t:
(22) [kwan-kin] kaa isa-kɨɨʂin. | ‘While he was going, he saw.’
Northern Pano: Matses (Kneeland 1979)
The Matses sentence below has three actions happening at the same time. ‘Eating’ hangs on ‘sit’, which has a “same doer” ending but is an intransitive verb. In turn, ‘sitting’ hangs on the transitive sentence ‘I saw it:’
(23) [[p-eʔ] tsad-kin] is-omβi. | ‘While I was eating sitting, I saw (it).’

h: 20.2.1.3. Marked Clause Codes Subsequent Events
t:
Finally, the examples below show cases where the action in the marked part happens after the action of the main sentence. Not all languages have this set of “same doer, later action” endings. Sometimes they may seem to be missing only because of a lack of
good descriptions. (For example, Table 20.2 doesn't list it, but Prost (1965:95) records the ending -noʂ in Chakobo and translates it as ‘before’.)
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo
(24) [[mi-a βi-i] ho-noʂ]-βi-ra papa ʂatɨ̂-iβa-kɨ. | ‘Right before coming to get you, father cut himself.’
(25) [[mi-a βi-i] ho-no(n)ʂon]-pari-ra papa-n hiwi rɨra-kɨ. | ‘Before coming to get you, father cut down a / the tree.’
Northern Pano: Matses (Kneeland 1979)
Matses has two sets of “same doer, later action” endings: -nuʃ versus -nun, and nueʔ versus -nuen:
(26) [nid-nuʃ] uʃ-eβi. | ‘I will sleep, [before leaving].’ (p. 128)
Note one difference from Shipibo-Konibo (ex. 25). In the example below, the ending for the doer of a transitive verb (labeled FSSA) does not have the piece -ʂon:
(27) [ʃuβu ua-nun] aiaʃ tɨs-eʔ nid-o-ʃ. | ‘[Before building the house], he went to pull the vines away.’ (p. 128)
The ending below is for the doer of an intransitive verb (labeled FSSS). It is made of -nu + -eʔ. The second piece looks exactly like the “same doer, same time” ending for intransitive verbs (labeled SSSS) shown in ex. (23):

h: 20.2.1.3. Marked Clause Codes Subsequent Events
t:
(28) tʃɨʃɨid se-nueʔ nid-o-ʃ. | ‘He went to shoot a spidermonkey (with arrow).’ (p. 129)
(29) tʃɨʃɨid se-nuen pia ua-o-ʃ. | ‘Before shooting the spidermonkey, he² made arrows.’ (p. 129)
Purus Pano 2: Amawaka (Sparing-Chávez 1998)
Amawaka also has two “same doer, later action” endings for intransitive verbs (labeled FSSS): -katzi and -xanʔni. Most probably, both end in the “same time” ending for intransitive verbs, -i, shown in ex. (17). In turn, -xanʔni contrasts with -xanʔkin in ex. (32), which goes with the doer of a transitive verb. -xanʔkin carries the “same time” ending for such doers, -kin, shown earlier in (18):
(30) [hiri-katzi]-mɨn naʃi-ʔi ka-ʔi ʔɨn-ʔka-nɨ | ‘I am going to bathe, and then I will eat.’ (p. 462)
(31) [[mapoki ka-şon] miʃki-xanʔni]-mɨn ka-ʔi ʔɨn-ʔkai. | ‘I am going fishing downriver.’ (Lit.: ‘Having gone downriver in order to fish I am going.’) (p. 462)
(32) [tʃiʔi pima-xanʔkin]-ko-mɨn karo xatɨ-xan. | ‘Chop wood to make a fire.’ / ‘Chop wood and make a fire.’ (p. 462)
The verb ending -ʃ marks a third person (he, she, it). So I have slightly changed Kneeland’s translation, which reads “Antes de flechar al maquisapa, hice flechas”. ‘Before shooting the spidermonkey (with arrow), I made arrows.’
In short, the Amawaka “same doer, later action” endings end in /i/ and /kin/. These are the same as the “same doer, same time” endings. So we can say that Amawaka did not develop its own special agreement endings for later actions.

h: Different-Subject Markers ("different person" endings)
t:
In all the languages I looked at, parts of the sentence marked “same doer” show participant agreement. But only Kashibo-Kakataibo also shows it on parts marked “different doer”. These endings are shown in Table 20.3. Notice that only the endings in the first two columns carry the pieces -ʂ and -ʂun, which are also found in the “same doer” endings. On the other hand, the pieces /βɨ/ and /βɨtan/ are identical to the forms of the “with” marker (comitative) found in the different languages (see exx. (75)-(85)).
The following examples (taken from Wistrand 1969) show Kashibo-Kakataibo “different doer” endings:
(33) [ʔa-kɨʂ]-βi ka-ísa ina-ñu ʔi-akɨʂa. | ‘He made them, but they had tails.’ (p. 167)
(34) [ka-kɨʂun] ka-ísa ka-akɨʂa... | ‘He_{i} said, (then) he_{j} said... (p. 167)
(35) [kwain-kɨβɨ] ka-ísa aa-bɨ-iʃi tiiki-akɨʂa. | ‘As he_{i} circled around, he_{j} just stayed with him_{i}.’ (p. 167)
(36) [pɨkara-kɨβɨtan] kaa is-akɨʂin. | ‘When it was light, he saw.’ (p. 167)

h: Interclausal Participant Agreement in Panoan: Conclusion (conclusion)
t:
I have shown that all the chosen languages have participant agreement on parts marked “same doer” when the action happens before or at the same time as the action of the main sentence. (The “same time” set is missing in Kapanawa, an Ucayali Pano language, according to Loos 1999.) Shipibo-Konibo, Matses, and Amawaka have also developed special “same doer” endings for later actions. But in their make-up, the Amawaka endings and some of the Matses ones use the same agreement endings found for actions at the same time. The Shipibo-Konibo ending for the doer of a transitive verb (FSSA) differs from one of the matching Matses endings: Shipibo-Konibo adds the piece /ʂon/. So Matses has -nun, while Shipibo-Konibo has -no(n)ʂon.
Kashibo-Kakataibo is the only language with agreement on “different doer” endings. Most likely this is something new that Kashibo-Kakataibo developed on its own, not something the sister languages once had and then lost. In Kashibo-Kakataibo, only the “different doer” endings for earlier actions carry the agreement pieces. The “different doer” endings for actions at the same time take the “with” marker instead, which we will look at below.

h: Intraclausal Participant Agreement (agreement within one sentence)
t: Inside a single sentence, participant agreement shows up on extra describing parts of several kinds: place and direction (‘in / to’), starting point (‘from’), reason, ‘for / against someone’, manner (‘how’), and company (‘with’). It may also appear regularly on other kinds, for example ‘as a child / as an adult’. But for now there are no data on them. Time expressions usually don't take this kind of agreement (but see exx. (86) and (87)). Sadly, no earlier studies have looked at participant agreement inside single sentences in Panoan languages. So I can't show every type with an example from each language.

h: Locative-Allative ("in / at / to a place")
t:
We saw this for Shipibo-Konibo: words of place or direction (‘in / to’) have no ending when they go with the doer of an intransitive verb or with the receiver. But they take the extra ending -ʂon (or a related form) when they go with the doer of a transitive verb. In the previous chapter, sentences (29), (30), and (33) showed the same place word with different agreement in Shipibo-Konibo. Such examples are not available for the other languages.
Southern Pano: Pakawara (East and East, ms.)
Pakawara is a close relative of Chakobo. Like Chakobo, it has lost the /n/ or nasal sound on the endings that go with the doer of a transitive verb. The next examples show the question word ‘where’. It agrees with the doer of an intransitive verb in the first sentence, and with the doer of a transitive verb in the second:
(37) hawɨra oşa ʔaiʔ? | ‘Where do you sleep?’
(38) hawɨra kaʔai? | ‘Where are you going?’
(39) hawɨra şo piʔaiʔ? | ‘Where do you eat?’
Purus Pano 1: Yaminawa (Eakin 1991)
(40) ono ɨfɨ kanõa. | ‘My canoe is there.’ (p. 87)
(41) na paşta na pɨşɨ namã-şõ pi-i. | ‘The dog being under the house eats.’ (p. 89)
In (41), Eakin translates the place expression into Spanish with the verb form ‘being’, so he treats it as a little sentence of its own. He may have chosen this because

h: Locative-Allative ("in / at / to a place")
t:
Yaminawa sentences of the type ‘X is Y’ have no separate word for ‘is’, as you can see in ex. (40) (but compare the Shipibo-Konibo and Kashibo-Kakataibo examples (42) and (44)).
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo:
(42) winti-ra βɨβon iki. | ‘The paddle is in the front.’
(43) Sankɨman-ra βɨβon-ʂon atsa ʂɨati ʂɨa-i. | ‘Sanken is drinking yuca beer in the front (row).’
Western Pano: Kashibo-Kakataibo (Wistrand 1969):
(44) motora kaa βaka-nu ʔi-aşin | ‘There was a motorboat at the river.’ (p. 153)
(45) papa-n kaa aa-nu-şun piɨşanşin. | ‘Father ate there.’ (p. 153)
Northern Pano: Matses (Kneeland 1979):
(46) umanuʔ matses taβad-p-o-ʃ. | ‘The people were outside.’ (p. 74)
(47) umanuʔ-ʃun p-enda. | ‘Don’t eat it outside.’ (p. 74)

h: Ablative ("from a place")
t:
We saw for Shipibo-Konibo in sections 19.2.2.1 and 19.2.2.2 how ‘from’ expressions work (see also exx. (52) and (53) below). The sister languages work the same way. When the ‘from’ expression goes with the doer of an intransitive verb, it shows this with an ending. When it goes with the receiver, there is no ending. And when it goes with the doer of a transitive verb, this can only be shown by using a place (‘in / at’) expression instead. But Chakobo and Matses have some special features, which I will point out with the examples.
Purus Pano 1: Yaminawa (Eakin 1991)
(48) fanĩ-a-ş mĩ o-i-mɨ̃? | ‘Where do you come from’? (p. 73)
(49) manãkiri-no-a-ş ɨ̃ o-a. | ‘I came from up the river.’ (p. 73)
Looking at its history, manãkiri-no-a-ş is the noun manã ‘hill’ with five different role markers added: -ki ‘in / at’ + -ri ‘towards / about’ + -no ‘in / at’ + -a ‘from’, and, as I will show later, -ş, a marker for the doer of an intransitive verb.
(50) fanĩ-a mĩ fɨ-a-mɨ̃? | ‘From where did you bring it?’ p. (74)
(51) manãkiri-no-a ɨ̃ fɨ-a. | ‘I brought it from up the river.’ (p. 74)
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo:
(52) ha-ra ßɨßomɨa-ʂ ho-kɨ. | ‘He came from the front (row).’
(53) mɨrája-nin-ronki naikamɨa jawa ßɨ-ʂon-kɨ. | ‘The great shaman brought the white-lipped peccaries from the sky (for us).’

h: Ablative ("from a place")
t:
Western Pano: Kashibo-Kakataibo (Wistrand 1969):
(54) ɨ-nu-a-ʂ kwan-in | ‘goes from here’ (p. 152)
(55) ʂußu-nu-a-ʂ aßat-in | ‘runs from the house’ (p. 152)
Sometimes, as in (56), a ‘from’ structure is used to agree with the doer of an intransitive verb even though nobody seems to move from anywhere. In such cases, the only job of the ‘from’ structure may be to let the agreement show openly. (Remember also the Shipibo-Konibo exx. (27)-(28) in the previous chapter):
(56) ka-nanuna ßaka-nu-a-ʂ kwa-in. | ‘We play at the river.’ Lit. ‘We play from at the river.’ (p. 160)
Sadly, I have not been able to find a Kashibo-Kakataibo example with a ‘from’ expression in a simple sentence with a transitive verb.
Southern Pano: Chakobo:
Chakobo is different from the languages above. In sentences with a transitive verb, the word that the English translation renders with ‘from’ carries the marker şo (see also the Matses examples with transitive verbs below). There are two ways to read this. One is that şo means ‘from’. Then the extra part would show no open agreement. The other is that şo is the ending for agreeing with the doer of a transitive verb (as in other Chakobo sentences and in Panoan in general). But then the meaning ‘from’ or ‘in / at’ would have no marker at all. (In the Chakobo example (1b), notice that ‘in’ on ‘hammock’ is shown only by stress or tone: niʃi ‘hammock’ vs. niʃi ‘in the hammock.’

h: Ablative ("from a place")
t:
But no stress or tone is marked for garden in ex. (58)):
(57) a. nɨ-a aş | b. nɨ-a-na aş na | ‘from here’ (most probably in combination with an intransitive verb)
(58) a. wai şo tsi karo βi-kia. | b. karo βi-kia wai şo na. | ‘I obtain firewood from my garden.’ (Zingg 1998:26)
Northern Pano: Matses (Kneeland 1979):
Matses sentences with a transitive verb have a special feature. The word that the English translation renders with ‘from’ is really built as an ‘in / at’ word, with the ending -no.
As expected for ‘in / at’ words, tied-no takes the ending -ʃon in this case, to agree with the doer of a transitive verb. Comparing the languages, Matses expresses ‘from’ in two ways. With the doer of an intransitive verb, it uses a ‘from’ form with agreement. With the doer of a transitive verb, it uses an ‘in / at’ form with agreement:
(59) aton tied-no-ɨ-ʃ tʃo-eʔ. | ‘He comes from his chacra.’ (p.1)
(60) tied-no-ʃon patʃid βɨ-oʃ. | ‘S/he brought yuca from the chacra.’ (p.35)
The ending -mi also works this way. It means roughly ‘around / toward somewhere’. It takes open agreement with either kind of doer, again mixing ‘from’ forms and ‘in / at’ forms:
(61) taɨ-mioɨʃ tʃo-ʃ. | ‘He came from downriver.’ (Kneeland 1979:110)

h: Ablative ("from a place")
t:
(62) taɨ-mi-ʃun ʃɨkten βɨ-oʃ. | ‘He brought peccary from downriver.’ (Kneeland 1979:110)
So the Matses ‘from’ and ‘in / at’ forms in (59)-(62) show agreement openly, both with the doer of an intransitive verb and with the doer of a transitive verb.

h: Reason ("because")
t:
Parts of the sentence that give a reason (‘why’) can agree with either kind of doer. Look at the following Chakobo examples. The question word hɨni appears with -ʔaş (for the doer of an intransitive verb) and with -şo (for the doer of a transitive verb). (See also the Shipibo-Konibo sentences with hawɨ keskat ‘how, why’ in examples (66)-(71) in Chapter 19, and examples (69)-(70) below.)
Southern Pano: Chakobo (Zingg 1998:42)
(63) hɨni-ʔaş tsi mi ho-ʔa? | ‘Why did you come?’
(64) hɨni-şo şoβo a-jama-ʔai? | ‘Why don’t you build a house?’

h: Affective (feelings and attitudes)
t:
The agreement endings can also appear on parts of the sentence that say who something is good or bad for (‘for someone’ or ‘against someone’). This kind of agreement has been found
so far only in Yaminawa and Shipibo-Konibo. In fact, I first found these sentences in Yaminawa (Valenzuela 2000c). Later I got them for Shipibo-Konibo, but only by asking speakers to produce them.
Purus Pano 1: Yaminawa (Eakin 1991)
(65) ɨfã ɨ-õ-no-a-ʂ ratɨ-a.... | ‘Mother feared for me...’ (p. 111)
(66) ɨ~ a-õ-ʂõ tãp-i. | ‘I am learning for him.’ (‘learn’ is transitive in Yaminawa) (p. 111)
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo (given in Ch. 19 as examples (39) and (41)):
(67) ha-ra ɨ-on-mɨa-ʂ-βi wano-kɨ. ɨonβi | ‘He got married in spite of being with me.’ (woman speaking)
(68) mi-on-ʂon βakɨ-n kinan-kɨ. mion | ‘The boy threw up despite being under your care.’

h: Manner and Quantity ("how" and "how much")
t:
Words that say how something is done, or how many, also show open agreement with either kind of doer.
Southern Pano: Chakobo (Zingg 1998)
(69) hɨnawa-ʔaʂ βakɨ pistia koʔa? | ‘How was the baby born?’ (p. 43)
(70) hɨnawa-ʂo marakati mi ak-á? | ‘How did you make the roof?’ (p. 43)
Northern Pano: Matses (Kneeland 1979)
(71) daɨd-daɨd-eʔ tʃo-ʃ. | ‘They came in groups of two.’ (p. 110)
(72) daɨd-daɨd-en tʃɨ! | ‘Eat them in groups of two.’ (p. 110)
The number words above have the “same doer” endings for intransitive verbs (labeled SSS). (See also the Shipibo-Konibo sentences (99)-(102) in Chapter 19, which use the number kimisha ‘three’.)
Ucayali Pano: Shipibo-Konibo
(73) ha-ská-kɨ-tian, hatik-aʂ-βi βo-kan-a iki, nɨɨt-i. | ‘Then, they started to go up altogether.’ (Valenzuela 1999:362)
(74) hain-ʂon-ronki nami joá a-káti-kan-ai hatí-ʂon-βi pi-ti. | ‘Then they cooked the meat in order to eat altogether.’ (Valenzuela 1999:362)

h: Comitative ("with")
t:
All the languages except Shipibo-Konibo have different ‘with’ (company) forms for the doer of an intransitive verb and for the doer of a transitive verb. Shipibo-Konibo instead uses different ‘with’ forms for pronouns (like ‘me’, ‘you’) and for nouns. Chakobo does both: it has participant agreement, and it also tells pronouns and nouns apart. Note that only the Chakobo forms for the doer of a transitive verb have an ending related to the agreement endings found on other extra parts, namely şo.
Below I only show the ‘with’ forms that have participant agreement.
Southern Pano: Chakobo
Pronouns with S-orientation vs. Pronouns with A-orientation (Zingg 1998:27)
(75) ka-kia ha βɨta. | ‘I go with him.’
(76) no βɨta-şo şɨki tima-ki. | ‘He grinds maize with us.’ | şɨki tima-ki no βɨta-şo na. | ‘He grinds maize with us.’
Nouns with S-orientation vs. Nouns with A-orientation (Zingg 1998:27-28):
(77) papa ja ha ka-kɨ. | ‘He left with his father.’
(78) Kako ja-şo tsi wai patsa-ki. | ‘He slashes the garden with Caco.’ | wai patsa-ki Kako ja-şo na. | ‘He slashes the garden with Caco.’
Purus Pano 1: Yaminawa (Eakin 1991):
(79) afɨ paşta-fɨ otʃi fɨ katananĩ. | ‘His dog also went with the older brother.’ (p. 68)
(80) ɨ̃ ania fɨta pi-i. | ‘I am eating with my brother in law.’ (man speaking) (p. 68)

h: Comitative ("with")
t:
Western Pano: Kashibo-Kakataibo (Wistrand 1969)
(81) aa-βɨtan ka-na ʔa-in. | ‘I am doing it with him.’ (p. 154)
(82) mii-βɨ kaa kwan-kas-in. | ‘He wants to go with you.’ (p. 154)
Finally, Matses is the only known Panoan language where ‘with’ forms have three different shapes: one for the doer of an intransitive verb, one for the doer of a transitive verb, and one for the receiver (according to the data in Kneeland 1979):
Northern Pano: Matses
(83) kon tʃu-βɨdtan pachid βe-omβi. | ‘I brought yuca with my sister.’ (p. 33)
(84) kon tʃu-βɨd nes-oβi. | ‘I bathed with my sister.’ (p. 33)
(85) kon ku-βɨdta kon tʃu is-omβi. | ‘I saw my uncle and my sister.’ (p. 33)
In short, ‘with’ forms show agreement in most of the languages. But only Chakobo has agreement endings related to those found on other kinds of extra parts. Remember also that the Kashibo-Kakataibo “different doer, same time” endings are built on ‘with’ forms (20.2.2). Shipibo-Konibo has no participant agreement on ‘with’ forms.

h: Temporal ("when")
t:
Only one case of participant agreement on time words has been found. It is the Matses pair aβadiadaʃ ~ aβadiadʃun, translated by Keeland (1979) as ‘the day after tomorrow.’ Notice that both forms carry open agreement endings:
(86) aβadiad-aʃ tʃo-eβi. | ‘I will come the day after tomorrow.’ (p. 205)
(87) aβadiad-ʃun βɨ. | ‘Bring it the day after tomorrow.’ (p.205)
Perhaps this expression did not start out as a time word.

h: Participant Agreement in Panoan: Conclusions (conclusions)
t:
This comparison of the languages leads to two important conclusions. First, participant agreement is found in languages from all the different branches of the Panoan family. This is true both inside single sentences and across linked sentences. So it seems safe to say that the old parent language (Proto-Pano) already had it.
Second, the agreement endings have the same or very similar forms in all the sister languages. Usually the endings on simple extra words are the same as the “same doer” endings. Also, the overall pattern marks three roles in three ways. Endings that go with the doer of a transitive verb end in a nasal sound or /n/ (except in the Southern languages). Endings that go with the doer of an intransitive verb end in /ʂ/ or /i/, or related sounds. And agreement with the receiver, where it exists, has no ending at all.
I have also noticed some special points. First, the “same doer, later action” endings vary more across the sister languages that developed them. Second, participant agreement on “different doer” endings may be something Kashibo-Kakataibo developed on its own. There, the endings for earlier actions have the same endings as the “same doer” ones, but the endings for actions at the same time take the ‘with’ marker instead. Third, except in Chakobo, agreement on ‘with’ forms uses endings that differ from those on other extra parts, so they must have come from somewhere else. Fourth, having no agreement on ‘with’ forms is special to Shipibo-Konibo. Finally, agreement on time words has so far been found only in Matses.

h: Reconstruction of Agreement Markers (working out the original agreement endings)
t:
In this section I try to rebuild the oldest forms of the matching endings that the Panoan languages share. These are -aʂ-, -ʂon, -kin, -noʂ and no(n)-ʂon, or their relatives in each language (see Table 20.2). By "rebuild" I mean working out what they probably looked like in the ancestor language, by comparing its living daughter languages. In today's languages you can't split these endings into smaller pieces, or you can only split them partly. Starting from SK (Shipibo-Konibo) is especially hard. In SK, the bits -ʂo, -ʂ, and -no don't exist as separate word pieces on their own. (The last one, -no, only shows up inside a few fixed combinations.) But that is not true in all the sister languages, as we will see below.
When we compare the languages, we find that each matching ending was built from two layers. The first layer is an ending for place or time (like 'at', 'from', 'to'). The second layer is one of the main markers that show who did what (like the doer marker). The forms I propose for the ancestor language follow the sound matches between the languages and the rebuilt word pieces worked out by Shell (1975).

h: Peripheral Cases: First Layer (first layer: the extra-phrase endings)
t:
Most linguists agree that languages tend to change from concrete meanings to more abstract ones. Here, the change also goes from nouns to verbs. A word piece meaning 'from (a place)' on a noun, for example, can later come to mean 'after (an action)' on a verb. Following this idea, I propose that the ancestor language, Proto-Pano, had the following place endings:
-ʂo (ablative? >) sequential > past, completive
In every language I looked at, the sound sequence /ʂo/ (or its local equivalent) is part of a "same-doer" marker. This is a marker on a verb that says "the same person then did the next thing", and it carries the meaning 'first this, then that' (linguists call this sequential). The form -ʂon and its variants always point to a doer of a transitive verb (an A). But the forms that come straight from -ʂo can also point to the receiver (an O).
In the Purus branch of the family, the forms -ʂo ~ -xo ~ -ʂu are endings that show time or whether an action is finished. In Kashinawa, -ʂu has been described as a 'finished, in the past' ending (Montag 1981:563). In Amawaka, -xo is a past ending used for third persons when telling stories, for actions seen as complete (Sparing-Chávez 1998:447; see also ex. (17)).
In Chakobo, a Southern language, ʂo is a small "equals" word (Prost 1965). It helps build sentences like "X is Y", much like English is. Something similar happens in two South American languages not related to Panoan, Canela Krahô (Jê) and Paumarí (Arawak). There, similar "equals" words can be traced back to an ending meaning 'from' (Stassen 1997:90). In the Australian language Yankunytjatjara, a 'then, after' ending is added to verbs turned into nouns, and also to nouns. On nouns, its meaning fits well with 'from' (Goddard 1985:134). Also, remember that sentence (58) could be read with -ʂo meaning 'from'. Even so,

h: Peripheral Cases: First Layer (first layer: the extra-phrase endings)
t:
there is no solid proof that ʂo- meant ‘from’ in Proto-Pano, the ancestor language. So I will simply call it the ‘then, after’ marker (linguists call this a sequential marker). Its meaning probably changed later in the Purus languages. There it seems to have come to mean that something happened in the past, or that it is finished. Before this book, nobody had rebuilt ʂo on its own for the ancestor language. Now let's look at -ʂon, the ending that points to the doer of a transitive verb. I think it was once two separate pieces: ʂo + -n. In other words, it is the ‘then’ piece plus the doer marker.
-ʔa ablative ‘from’ > sequential > perfect of result, past
-ʔa (or its relative) means 'from' in every language I looked at. In Matses it has the form /ɨ/. All these languages share an interesting habit. To say 'from a place', they first add the 'at' ending and then the 'from' ending on top of it, so two place endings are stacked (linguists call this case stacking). Besides meaning 'from', -ʔa has picked up other jobs on verbs. In Yaminawa it marks a finished action (Eakin 1991). In Kashinawa it marks a resulting state, like English 'has done' (Montag 1981). In Amawaka it marks a result of a past action, and also a very recent past for 'I' (Sparing-Chávez 1998:447). In SK it is a 'finished' verb form (Valenzuela, this work). In Matses it is a negative ending for earlier events, used when the main verb is a helper verb (Kneeland 1979).

h: Peripheral Cases: First Layer (first layer: the extra-phrase endings)
t:
So I think the ancestor language had a ‘from’ ending of the form -ʔa. Over time, this ‘from’ ending may have turned into related endings. They meant ‘in the past’, ‘finished’, and ‘with this result’ (linguists call them past, completive, and resultative markers). This explains -(ʔ)aʂ, the ending that points to the one person of an intransitive verb. Long ago it was two pieces stuck together: -(ʔ)a + -ʂ. Like -ʂo above, -ʔa on its own had not been rebuilt for the ancestor language before. I also think the ancestor language could already stack role endings, one on top of another (see the examples in (90)).
-ki Non-specific locative ‘at, towards, to, on’ > simultaneous, incompletive
Shell (1975:143) already rebuilt this place ending for the ancestor language. He gives these forms: SK -ki, a general 'at / to' ending; Kapanawa -ki ‘towards’; Kashinawa -ki ‘at, on’; Amawaka -ki (no meaning given); Chakobo -ki ‘in the direction of, towards.’ Shell usually includes Kashibo-Kakataibo in his work. But he left it out for -ki given that it lacks any locative marker of this shape. Nevertheless, there is a locative of the form -mi not only in Kashibo-Kakataibo but also in Matses that seem to play the same function. It may be the case that these forms are cognate with the -ki ending of the other sister languages, that is, related to it by descent. But for now I can't explain why the first sound is different.

h: Peripheral Cases: First Layer (first layer: the extra-phrase endings)
t:
Besides the place meanings Shell lists, -ki has other jobs. It marks the person who receives something (like 'to him' in 'give it to him') in Chakobo and Kashinawa. It also marks the thing that causes a feeling (like 'of the dog' in 'afraid of the dog') in SK,
Chakobo, and Kashinawa. -ki also turns up on verbs. There it marks an unfinished action in Chakobo. In Amawaka it marks an action going on right now, and also a very recent past with 'you' and 'he/she' (for Amawaka, see Sparing-Chávez 1998:447).
-no locative / allative > subsequent > purposive, prospective
The form -no (-nu in Matses, -anu in Kashinawa) means ‘in, at, to’ in all the languages I looked at. (In Chakobo it appears in the long forms of the place endings, and it is also used for time.) In SK, -no has shrunk to -n, except in a few fixed combinations. These are the 'from' ending and the 'where?' and 'there' words. In several languages, -no or -nu also means 'in order to' or 'about to happen'. Nobody had proposed this word piece for the ancestor language before.
The short phrases below show what became of -ki, -no, and -ʔa on nouns in several Panoan languages:
The Non-specific Locative -ki (including -mi from Kashibo-Kakataibo and Matses)
(88) 
Locative / allative -no

h: Peripheral Cases: First Layer (first layer: the extra-phrase endings)
t:
(89) 
Ablative -a: Notice that all the languages below build their 'from' ending on top of the 'at' ending -no. In other words, they all stack two place endings (“case-stacking”).
(90) 
For Chakobo I don't have clear examples of -no meaning 'at' and -no-a meaning 'from'. As I said above, in Chakobo -no is often used for time, which is probably an extension of its place meaning. Also, the 'at' ending -ki seems to be used more in Chakobo than in its sister languages. Maybe in Chakobo the place ending -no shrank to -n, as in SK, and then this nasal sound disappeared. (Remember that the Southern languages also lost the nasal sound or /n/ in the matching endings that point to a doer.) Also, the pieces no and xo na appear in the long forms of the 'at' and 'from' endings. These points need more research. But this exception involves only Chakobo, so it is limited to the Southern languages.
I think it is likely that place endings such as -ki, -no, -ʔa, and also -ʂo (though there is no firm proof that -ʂo was a place ending too) were added on
verbs that had no tense of their own. There they showed how two actions done by the same person were linked in time or logic. The meanings fit together nicely. The 'from' ending -ʔa and the sequential -şo came to mark actions that were finished and so happened first. Think of 'from' turning into 'after'. The general 'at / to' ending -ki came to mark unfinished actions and actions happening at the same time. And the 'at / to' ending -no came to mark actions that come later.

h: Core Cases: Second Layer (second layer: the doer and receiver endings)
t:
Comparing the languages also shows a second layer. On top of these verbs that already had a place ending, another ending was added. This one is one of the main markers that show who did what. It is one of the proto-word pieces -n, -ş and -0, which I rebuild below.
-n A marker > ergative (all languages), nominative (Purus languages and Wariapano)
The ending -n (or a nasal sound) marks the doer of a transitive verb (A) in every language I looked at. -N is the doer marker (ergative) in most, if not all, Panoan languages. In KK, Amawaka, and maybe Iskonawa, it also marks the one person of an intransitive verb (S), because these languages have three separate markers (20.4.3). Besides that, -n marks every kind of doer in sentences that follow an English-like pattern (where 'he' is the same whether he runs or hits someone) in Kashinawa, Yaminawa and other Purus languages. It is also part of some of those doer pronouns in the Ucayali language Wariapano (Valenzuela 2000a, 2000b). This
idea is different from Shell's (1975:103). He proposes the old word piece -mã as the marker for “transitive reference”, that is, for sentences with a doer and a receiver.
-∅ O marker
In all the languages I looked at, most receivers of an action have no marker at all. The only exceptions are some pronouns in SK that take -a. (You could also see this -a as part of the pronoun itself.)

h: Core Cases: Second Layer (second layer: the doer and receiver endings)
t:
-ʂ S marker
Most daughter languages no longer use -ʂ as a main role marker. But a few still do: KK, Amawaka, and maybe Iskonawa. These languages have three separate markers, and they use -ʂ for the one person of an intransitive verb. Shell (1975:115) did not rebuild this marker as an old word piece on its own. He only saw it inside the matching ending -ʔaʂɨ. As I said above, I think this matching ending was built from two pieces: the ‘from’ ending -ʔa and the intransitive marker -ʂ. Shell reconstructs this combination as ʔaʂɨ, that is, with an extra vowel at the end. He does this because Marinawa, a language of the Purus branch, says -aʂɨ rather than -aʂ. As far as I know, only Marinawa and its very close relative Sharanawa (very
likely two dialects of the same language) have this extra vowel at the end (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes). So, at least for now, I prefer the old form -ʂ rather than -ʂɨ as the marker for the one person of an intransitive verb. To be complete, here are some examples of -ʂɨ in Sharanawa:
(91) βaʃaro hihiki fasi-koin dii-bera-do-a-ʂɨ. | ‘The jaguar roars very loudly in the forest.’ (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes)
(92) ɨ-wɨn ɨpa dii-bɨra ka-ʂɨ fɨdo-a. | ‘My father went to the forest and got lost.’ (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes)

h: Tripartite Case-Marking Systems in Panoan (marking doer, receiver and lone person all differently)
t:
Some Panoan languages, at least in some parts of their grammar, really do use three separate markers built from the main markers above: one for the doer of a transitive verb, one for the receiver, and one for the one person of an intransitive verb. Notice that here the one person of an intransitive verb gets its own visible marker. That is probably unusual in three-marker systems.
Purus Pano 2: Amawaka:
Sparing-Chávez (1998:446) says that Amawaka uses three separate markers in two situations. One is when the doer is being highlighted in the conversation. The other is with certain verb forms that show an action someone is busy with or will be busy with (“aspects encoding events that
someone is actually engaged in or will be engaged in”).³ Otherwise, Amawaka uses either the usual doer-marker pattern or no markers at all. Look at these examples:
(93) Xano-n-mɨn maninʔa-0 bi-ʔaʂ-ki-ʔnɨ. | ‘It is the woman who has gotten / brought bananas.’ (Sparing-Chávez 1998: 446)
(94) Honi-x-mɨn ka-ʔaʂ-ki-ʔnɨ. | ‘It is the man who has gone.’ (Sparing-Chávez 1998:446)
(95) Wakɨwaɨ-x mɨn nonti-n nanɨɨhi kankiʔnɨ. | ‘The children board the canoe.’ (Loos 1978:159)
The sources for these examples don't say this directly. But it seems that in Amawaka the three separate markers are only used on nouns.
But three-marker systems are not found only in the Purus branch. In fact, the Western language KK uses this feature even more, because it also uses three separate markers on pronouns. KK might also be the only language that still keeps the actual sound of the old marker ʂ:

h: Tripartite Case-Marking Systems in Panoan (marking doer, receiver and lone person all differently)
t:
Western Pano: Kashibo-Kakataibo
(96) Papa-n kaa aa-nu-şun piɨşanşin. | ‘Father ate there.’ (Wistrand 1969:153)
In ordinary main sentences, where nothing is being highlighted, Amawaka uses the doer-marker pattern with plain verb forms, but no markers at all with the special verb forms (Sparing-Chávez 1998:445-446).
(97) Pinu-ş kaa ßaka-nu-a-ş a-in. | ‘Humingbird (name) is coming from the river.’ (Wistrand 1969:153)
(98) ʔɨɨ-n ka-na piti ʔaru-an | ‘I cooked food (earlier today).’ (Wistrand 1969:160)
The next examples show that pronouns in Kashibo-Kakataibo also have three separate forms. Exx. (99)-(101), (104) and (105) show 'I' as the one person of an intransitive verb (S), as the doer of a transitive verb (A), and as the receiver (O):
(99) ʔɨɨ-ş ka-na kwan-ɨşan, ʔɨɨ-n nɨtɨ-nu. | ‘I went (in the near past) to my land.’ (Wistrand 1969:161)
(100) ʔɨ-n ka-na Jorge ɲuká... | ‘I asked George...’ (Shell 1978)
(101) Jorge-nen ka ʔɨ kaşa... | ‘George told me...’ (Shell 1978)
Exx. (102)-(104) show 'you' (one person) as the doer (A), as the one person of an intransitive verb (S), and as the receiver (O):
(102) Mi-n ka-is-mina ʔɨ-n lápiz tsasia. | ‘I heard that you broke my pencil.’ (Shell 1978)
(103) Mi-x ka-ra-mina kuan? | ‘Are you going?’ (Shell 1978)
(104) ʔɨ-n ka-na mi koon ʔɨ-n lápiz is-na tsasia kişun. | ‘I told you yesterday that I broke my pencil.’ (Shell 1978)

h: Tripartite Case-Marking Systems in Panoan (marking doer, receiver and lone person all differently)
t:
Exx. (105)-(108) show 'he/she' as the doer (A), as the one person of an intransitive verb (S), and as the receiver (O). Also, (109) shows the question word ui ‘who’ as the one person of an intransitive verb:
(105) A-n ka ʔɨ ɲukáşa uinu ka-ra-is-na kuani kişun. | ‘He asked me where I was going.’ (Shell 1978)
(106) A-ş-βi ka taramɨtia. | ‘He rolled over and over.’ (Loos 1978:159)
(107) A-ş ka lápiz ʔisɨn. | ‘It is a pencil.’ (Shell 1978)
(108) aa pain ka-na piisa tanin. | ‘I want to eat that first.’ (Wistrand 1969:234)
(109) Ui-ş ka-ra mi-bɨ kuan? | ‘Who is coming with you?’ (Shell 1978)
We still need to find out exactly when Kashibo-Kakataibo uses its three separate markers. Wistrand (1969) found nouns used as the one person of an intransitive verb that do not have the marker -ş. I included sentence (107) to show that the split does not depend on whether the noun is alive or not. It also does not depend on whether the verb describes an action or a state.
A few nouns in KK follow the usual doer-marker pattern instead. So when they are the one person of an intransitive verb, they get no marker. These are motora ‘motorboat’ (see ex. (44)), otʃiti ‘dog,’ and kanino ‘jaguar.’ The first two are clearly borrowed, from Spanish and from an Arawak language. All three have three syllables (beats) and the same three-unit length. These facts may explain why they don't use the three-marker system seen in (96)-(109) (see the discussion of three-syllable nouns and borrowed words in 3.1.6.4).

h: Tripartite Case-Marking Systems in Panoan (marking doer, receiver and lone person all differently)
t:
Finally, Iskonawa may also use three separate markers. In the example below, the pronoun 'I' carries an extra -h when it is the one person of an intransitive verb. (Remember from footnote 1 that this marker in Amawaka is also a breathy sound of this kind, not an 's' or 'sh' sound.) Sadly, we have very little data on Iskonawa. We don't even know yet where it fits in the Panoan family.
Iskonawa
(110) ʔɨa-h ka kai. | ‘I am going.’ (Loos 1978:159)

h: Possible Historical Scenario (how it might have developed)
t:
In this section I suggest, carefully, how the matching endings might have developed in the Panoan systems that track whether the doer stays the same. I also look at how they developed on describing words and phrases that are not full sentences.
Stage 1: Case-Markers in the Ancestor Language:
The ancestor language used three separate markers, like Kashibo-Kakataibo, in at least some parts of its grammar. These were its main markers:
-n for A, -ş for S, and -0 for O.
The ancestor language also had these place endings and related markers:
-şo SEQ (ABL), -ʔa ABL, -ki DAT / LOC, and -no LOC / ALL (and possibly the predecessor of -tian TEMP).
Stage 2: Addition of Peripheral Cases to Non-finite Clauses:
The place endings are put to work on verbs without tense, in a part of the sentence that hangs on another part. There they show how two situations are linked in time or logic. The two situations probably shared the main person being talked about. So the speaker could drop that person in the second part, the way English says "After eating, he left" instead of "After he ate, he left" (linguists call this “equi-subject” deletion). The meanings of the place endings fit very well with the time and logic links they came to show:
In today's languages, these place endings have mostly kept their old jobs.

h: Possible Historical Scenario (how it might have developed)
t:
Stage 3: Reinterpretation of Peripheral Cases:
Next, people start to hear these place endings on verbs as a sign that the doer stays the same. Place endings turning into such "same doer / different doer" markers has been seen before, in Aboriginal languages of Australia. There, the 'at' ending became a same-doer or different-doer marker, and the 'to' ending came to mean 'different doer' (Austin 1981). Maybe in Panoan, place endings such as -ʂo, -ʔa, and -ki split up the work between them. In the end, each one marked the place of a noun only when that noun played a certain role in the sentence. For example, -ʂo may have been an 'at' ending that took turns with -ʔa. Notice that no Panoan language combines -ʂo with -ʂ, or -ʔa with -n. In the same way, no language has the sequence -ki-ʂ. There is also some evidence that these
markers can show place in a way that depends on the rest of the sentence. For example, the 'from' ending can mark 'at a place' in a sentence with an intransitive verb. You can see this in ex. (56) of this chapter and examples (27)-(28) of Chapter 19.⁴
This sharing of the work may be linked to another fact. Besides showing time and logic links and 'same doer', these markers also tend to limit what role the shared person plays in the main sentence. (Linguists call this shared person the controller.) Remember that these languages use three separate markers. So 'same doer' in Panoan really splits in two. One kind of marker needs the shared person to be the doer of a transitive verb (A). The other needs that person to be the one person of an intransitive verb (S). (But see -no.)

h: Possible Historical Scenario (how it might have developed)
t:
In general, when they mark 'same doer', -ʂo and -ki need the shared person to be the doer of a transitive verb (A). -ʔa needs the shared person to be the one person of an intransitive verb (S). Some single languages have their own quirks. In Amawaka and Matses, the forms that came from -ʂo can link a person in the marked part to the receiver in the main sentence (Sparing-Chávez 1998:458, Kneeland 1979:129). You could see this as a rule that -ʂo only goes with a main transitive sentence.
In the Australian languages Wagaya and Warlpiri, nouns with the 'to' ending can be used in transitive sentences that are not about movement. There they give only the location of the receiver; Austin 1981:331-332.
In SK and Matses, the forms that came from -ʔa can link a receiver in the marked part to the main person of the main sentence (S or A). On the other hand, in SK and Matses the 'at / to' ending works with either kind of shared person, S or A. Also, in SK -no can be followed by -ʂon.
(In SK, the time ending -tian comes to be used only for "same doer / different doer" marking. In other languages, the 'at' ending -no or -nu may do this job.)
Stage 4: Addition of Core Cases:

h: Possible Historical Scenario (how it might have developed)
t:
Next comes a second layer. The side part of the sentence already has a role marker. Now one of the main role markers, \-n, \-ʂ, or \-0, is added on top of it. Which one you add depends on the shared person: the person who appears both in the side part and in the main sentence. The marker matches the role this person plays in the main sentence. This raises a question: why add a second layer at all? One possibility is that it just repeats information. Matching endings often do that (Corbett 2001). A second possibility is that these main role markers helped show whether the next action is done by the same person or by someone else (linguists call this switch-reference). Compare, e.g., -xo vs. -xo-n in Amawaka, -a vs. -aʂ in SK, and -nuʃ vs. -nun in Matses. In fact, this very change has happened in some Native North American languages. In Muskogean and Yuman, the main role markers turned into ‘same doer’ and ‘different doer’ markers. The forms used for the doer came to mean ‘same doer’, and the other forms came to mean ‘different doer’ (Jacobsen 1983). These two ideas can both be true in the system as a whole;
that is, these markers may have helped show 'same or different doer' in some cases, but just repeated information in others.

h: Possible Historical Scenario (how it might have developed)
t:
Fusion and Spread of Same-Subject Markers:
The two layers, place ending plus main marker, then melt together into a single ending. This one ending now shows three things at once: that the doer is the same, which action came first, and what role the shared person plays in the main sentence.
Next, some describing parts that once had their own verb start being heard as having no verb at all. Maybe their verb was invisible, or very general, like 'be' or 'do'. So a sentence that had two parts, each with a verb, is now heard as a single sentence. You can see this most clearly with words that say how, why, and how much. After that, the same-doer markers spread to some describing words that are not sentences at all (see, for example, the feeling words in SK and Yaminawa).
Stage 6: Loss of Intransitive Subject Marking:
Most languages lose the marker for the one person of an intransitive verb, either in some sentence types or everywhere: -ʂ > -0. So that person now looks just like the receiver and different from the doer. That gives the doer-marker pattern (linguists call it ergative-absolutive). But the old -ʂ form and the three-way split survive in the matching endings on describing parts. This gives an unusual mixed system: the nouns follow one pattern and the matching endings follow another.

h: Possible Historical Scenario (how it might have developed)
t: Some languages lose the 'then, after' marker -ʂo. In SK, -no > -n. The full form -no survives only in fixed spots, such as the stacked 'from' ending.

h: Possible Alternative Development (another possible path)
t:
Some words take the marker -ʂ directly, without the 'from' piece first. These include the emphatic pronouns (like 'I myself') and words for stages of life (like 'as a child'). This suggests that some describing parts may have developed differently, inside a single sentence. They might simply copy the marker of the person they describe. Interestingly, these may be the describing words most closely tied to a person. (Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann, to appear, treat life-stage words as the best examples of words that describe a person's state during an action.) Still, when they point to the doer of a transitive verb, life-stage words take the matching ending -ʂon, not just -n. This development probably happened after -ʂon could no longer be split into pieces; this
fits with another fact. In SK, the ending for 'same doer, later action' is -noʂon, not -non. The form -non would match Matses -nun .

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
As I discussed in Valenzuela (1999), the Panoan matching endings look a lot like something found in some Aboriginal languages of Australia. These include languages of the Mantharta and Kanyara groups from northwestern Australia (Austin 1988, Austin 1995, Austin and Bresnan 1996). In that work I gave the following examples of “double case” (two markers stacked on one word) in Jiwarli, a Mantharta language (from Austin, 1988; emphasis added):
(111) Thuthu-ngku juma-rti-nha yanga-rninyja warlpari-lu. | ‘The dog chased the children south.’ [N13p18s1]
(112) Juma-ngku ngatha-nha nhanya-nyja maya-ngka-nguru-lu. | ‘The child watched me from the house.’ [N10p10s3]
In the sentences above, the 'to' and 'from' endings also carry the doer marker. That's because they tell us which way the doer of a transitive verb was moving (Austin 1988). Just as in Panoan, words that say how something was done also carry a matching marker:
(113) Wurnta-nma nhapa pirru tharti-ngku. | ‘Cut this meat quickly.’ [N5p71s1]
The plain form has no marker at all. So sentences with an intransitive verb need no extra ending.
Jiwarli also has a kind of extra sentence part with a verb that has no tense of its own. It gives background about the event in the main sentence it hangs on. In English we would translate it with words like 'while…' or 'who…'. The verb in this extra part shows whether the doer stays the same. It also carries a marker that matches the role of the shared person in the main sentence. When the two parts have the same doer, the extra part takes either no marker or the doer marker. Which one depends on whether the main verb is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb (Austin 1988, Austin and Bresnan 1996:254-5). These Jiwarli examples show this:

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Matrix clause is transitive (from Austin 1988, emphasis added)
(114) Warlka-rninyjalu-ru ngatha-nha wantha-nma-rni. | ‘After you have opened it give it to me!’ [T10s2]
(115) Mantharta-lu kurrpirli-nha pinya-nyja yanga-rnu-ru. | ‘The man speared a kangaroo as he was chasing it.’ [N11p31s2]
In (114) the main verb is an intransitive verb, so no visible matching marker appears (from Austin and Bresnan 1996:255, emphasis changed):
(116) Walangu ngunha kumpa-ira ngunhi-rru-pa
(None) papa-wu paja-rnu. | ‘The birds will sit there drinking the water.’ (JIT57s14)
Panoan and these Australian languages share two key features. First, the verb (or helper verb) doesn't show who the doer and receiver are. Second, the doer of a transitive verb gets its own marker, unlike the English pattern. (If the doer had no marker, a matching marker would have almost nothing to copy.)
But there are some important differences between SK and Jiwarli. First, Jiwarli is a language with very free word order (linguists call it “non-configurational”). The words that belong to one noun phrase don't have to stay together. So each word carries its own marker to match the main noun it goes with. In other words, Jiwarli puts markers on every word (“word-level case-marking”) (Austin 1988, Austin 1995, Austin and Bresnan 1996). Jiwarli also adds matching markers to describing words, and to the markers that show if the doer stays the same, even to 'different doer' (Austin 1988, Austin and Bresnan 1996:252). So in Jiwarli, matching markers on extra sentence parts might just be one case of a general rule. That rule is that every describing word matches its noun (Givón 1990:886). SK is different. In SK, the words of a noun phrase stay neatly together. The marker comes only once, at the end of the group. The words inside the group don't match each other.⁵ Also, in the Australian languages, extra sentence parts with a matching marker can also work as 'who…' description parts, but

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Bernard Comrie pointed out to me (p.c., 2003) that in some Australian languages, such as Warlpiri and probably Pitjantjatjara, describing words usually don't match their noun if they stay inside the noun phrase. They match only if they move outside it. This is still different from what I describe for SK, but it certainly starts to look more alike.
apparently not in Panoan (see 10.2 and Valenzuela 2002b for SK; this point needs more comparison). This may matter, because 'who…' description parts describe nouns (cf. Hale 1976). But unlike in the Australian languages, in Panoan (or at least in SK) these parts don't match the noun they describe in any way.
Second, in Jiwarli the doer marker and the plain form on extra words are the same as the ordinary markers. In Panoan, though, the matching endings do not look like the ordinary markers. The historical change in Panoan's marker system can't fully explain why the two groups of languages differ here. In Panoan, the matching endings on describing words are usually the same as the same-doer markers. They also have an extra layer, a place ending, which the Australian languages usually don't have. In Panoan the place endings fit very well with the time and logic links between the actions in the two parts. But it is hard to explain why this place layer also shows up on describing words that aren't sentences. Compare these examples of extra words in Jiwarli and Panoan:

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Locative / allative adjuncts
(117) warlpari-lu | ‘(to the) south’ (ex. (122))
(118) ʂoβo-n-ʂo-n | ‘at home’
Manner adjuncts:
(119) tharti-ngku | yaparru-lu | ‘quickly’ (Austin 1994:375)
(120) kikin-ʂo-n | ‘extremely’ | nɨtɨ-ʃaman-a-ʂ | ‘very quietly’ | hawɨ kɨskat-a-ʂ | ‘how’
Affective adjuncts::
(None) takara-õ-no-a-ʂ | ‘(be scared) for the chickens’
See also the Chakobo example (57b). There, a phrase that already has the 'from' ending takes the matching ending -aʂ ('from' + the marker for the one person of an intransitive verb), not just -ʂ. Another point that needs attention is this. In Sharanawa, describing words that point to the one person of an intransitive verb must add the 'at' + 'from' sequence (LOC-ABL), even to words that are already
marked with an 'at' ending. For example: iwi-wɨ-do-a-şɨ [tree-LOC-LOC-ABL-S] ‘in / from the tree’ (Tournon and Valenzuela, fieldnotes).
But Warlpiri does have one structure like this. Something that looks like a describing word, not a full sentence part, must take the 'to' ending before it gets its matching marker. (Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann, to appear, treat it as a word describing someone's state during the action.) The 'to' ending limits the shared person to a receiver. In Warlpiri the receiver can have no marker or a 'to someone' marker. Then the main marker is added to match the marker of that shared person:
