h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Warlpiri (Pama-Nyungan, Australia)
(121) Ngula=rla nyiya wanti-ja langa-kurra karnta-ku-ju jarda-kurra⁶-ku | ‘Then something fell into the woman’s ear (while she was) asleep’ (lit: ‘something fell (to) the woman into the ear (while she was) asleep’) (Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann op. cit.:38, from Warlpiri dictionary)
Still, in the Australian languages it seems rare for these describing words (“depictives”) to take both a place ending and a main marker.
Third, as I said above, in the Australian languages the matching markers also show up on 'different doer' markers. In Panoan this usually doesn't happen.
-Kurra attaches to verbs without tense. It shows that the doer of the hanging part is the same as the receiver of the main sentence. So it limits the shared person to a receiver, or to a 'to someone' person. The 'to' ending can be followed by a matching marker, but doesn't have to be (Hale 1976, Austin 1981:325, Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann to appear:38).
“Euphoric” element.
Finally, SK (at least) has a second kind of extra sentence part. Its verb takes a participle ending (like English -ing or -ed forms), and it is often followed by place endings or small place words. In fact, you can often say the same optional describing idea in two ways. You can use a part with a same-doer marker, or a part with a participle (10.4). Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann (to appear) treat describing parts with matching markers in Australian languages as "depictives", words that describe someone's state during an action. If we follow them, same-doer parts would be real depictives, focused on the person. Participle parts would be focused on the event instead. But remember that words for how and how much, marked by -i and -kin, also feel focused on the event. This is clearest when you compare them with the other forms that take -aʂ and -ʂon (see exx. (87)-(102) in Ch. 19).

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Also, Schultze-Bernd and Himmelmann (op. cit.) point out that it is somewhat hard to treat same-doer parts as depictives. In fact, in SK these parts are a big, separate piece of the sentence. They have their own intonation. Other sentence parts can come between them and their main sentence. And, though it's rare, they can even name their own doer (so they don't always need to share a person).
Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann (op. cit.) studied depictives in many languages. They conclude that “In all languages that allow agreement of depictive constituents, modifiers in a noun phrase also obligatorily agree with their head noun...” (op. cit.:35). In other words, if a describing word outside the noun phrase matches its noun, then describing words inside the noun phrase must match too. They see a matching marker on a word outside the noun phrase as a sure sign that it is a depictive. So Panoan clearly breaks their proposed rule. As far as I know, Panoan is the only known case where
the less typical describing words got matching markers, while the typical ones inside the noun phrase did not. This surprise may come from a Panoan rule. Markers go on the whole phrase, not on each word. As I said at the start of this chapter, the markers in these languages come only once, at the end of the last word in the noun phrase. Interestingly, Panoan noun phrases stay neatly together. But the parts with "same doer / different doer" markers can come before the main sentence, inside it, or after it. They don't even have to sit next to their main sentence, and more than one of them can hang on the same main sentence. In this situation, it makes more sense for a language to build its matching system between sentence parts.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Today, Panoan and Australian languages such as Jiwarli look quite alike in their matching endings, or “referential double case” (Austin 1995). But they may have got there by different historical paths. Still, the main reasons were probably about the same. For example, they help the listener keep track of who is who and what each describing part belongs to. That matters in languages where the verb doesn't show who the doer and receiver are. It also matters when word order and other clues don't make clear which noun a describing word goes with. If my historical story here turns out to be basically right, the Panoan languages may be unique in how this unusual feature developed.
CONCLUSIONS:
In this last chapter I point out some of the main findings of this book. I also raise questions that need more research.
One finding has big consequences for the study of Panoan languages. It is that we must tell apart two different things: “transitivity agreement” and “participant agreement”. Transitivity agreement means changes and limits that depend partly or fully on the kind of verb, whether it is an intransitive verb or a transitive verb. Participant agreement means endings on extra describing parts that match one of the main people in the sentence. It is tied to the kind of verb only through the role of the person it matches. The two differ in four ways. First, transitivity agreement affects the verb, while participant agreement affects the describing parts. Second, verbs can be more or less "transitive", so transitivity agreement has to be checked verb by verb. Participant agreement, by contrast, can be read straight from the marker on the matched person. (The link isn't obvious, though, because the ordinary markers and the matching endings look different.) Third, transitivity agreement changes the verb or the whole event in different ways. Participant agreement shows which main person a describing part is about.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
As I said in 15.3 and 19.2.1, these two really different kinds of agreement used to be treated as one thing. It was called “transitivity agreement” (Valenzuela 1999) or “transitivity concord” (Loos 1999). Two things led to this mistake. First, when matching endings link two sentence parts, they always go along with the kind of main verb. Second, linguists studying Panoan languages focused almost only on the rich "same doer / different doer" systems. They mostly ignored matching endings inside a single sentence. In Ch. 19 I showed clearly that the kind of verb cannot explain participant agreement. Two almost identical sentences can differ only in the ending on the describing part, while the verb form and the markers stay the same. It is worth noting that SK and the Panoan languages in general have these unusual kinds of agreement. Yet they lack the more common kinds, like a verb matching its doer.
I have argued that in SK most bare verbs can be sorted into intransitive verbs and transitive verbs by their very nature. You can tell them apart by several grammar tests:
how many main people go with the verb; which markers those people take; the matching endings; which stand-in verb is used (like English do in 'he did'); the form of the 'go and do' / 'come and do' pairs; the form of verbs for 'start' and 'stop'; whether the verb can take the 'to someone's harm', 'to each other', middle ('to yourself') and 'here and there' / ‘going down’ endings; and, for some verbs, which joining word introduces a following sentence part. Some of these tests are common in the world's languages, such as how many main people there are and which markers they take. Others are rarer or even special to SK, such as the form of 'start' and 'stop' verbs and the 'here and there' / ‘going down’ endings. As you might expect, this grammar-based sorting of SK verbs mostly matches meaning. A verb with a doer acting on a receiver usually counts as a transitive verb. But we can't fully predict which changes in meaning or use will cause a change in grammar. For example, seeing and feeling are treated very differently, though both have someone who experiences something and a thing that causes it. I have also shown in different chapters that even verbs from a small, closed, fairly uniform group can behave differently on these tests.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Participant agreement is different. It is a side effect of the role and marker of the person it matches, and you can predict it from them. In other words, there are no cases where the doer of an unusual transitive verb has no marker but the describing part takes a doer-matching ending, or the other way around. The matching endings follow role and marker this strictly. The “transitivity agreement” idea can't explain that. That idea would probably expect the endings on describing parts to show, somehow, that verbs are more or less "transitive".
Some things about how Shipibo-Konibo (SK) handles transitive verbs are special to this language. SK uses different general-purpose verbs (verbs like “do”) depending on the kind of verb. The “to someone's harm” ending only goes on verbs that have at least a doer and a receiver. Stage verbs (like “begin” and “finish”) and some verb endings must match the main verb: if the main verb has a doer and a receiver, they must too. Most important of all is what I call participant agreement: describing words get special endings that match the person they describe. All of these features are very interesting to linguists who compare languages. They help us understand what “transitive” really means, and the many ways languages show it.
Each verb has its own built-in type (intransitive or transitive). But a wider idea of how “strong” an action is also explains a fairly small number of sentence patterns. In these, three things seem to matter. How much control the doer has (in relation to cultural practices). How important or noticeable the receiver is. And the history of the particular verb. For example, in sentences meaning “want to” or “be doing”, the doer can get a different marker. This can signal that the receiver is very specific, or is being contrasted with something else. But this trick is not a fixed rule of the grammar. It may only work for certain verbs in a certain sentence pattern.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
These findings matter for theories of grammar. To describe SK properly, a theory has to look at two things together: the built-in type of each verb, and the whole sentence. It must also show that verbs can be more or less “transitive”. This is true between different groups of verbs, and even between verbs in the same group. What's more, we have to check each verb one by one, in every sentence pattern. Seeing where a verb can and can't be used tells us how speakers picture the event behind it. The verb's type alone can't explain everything. For example, it can't explain why a verb such as be- ‘bring’ cannot take the special “to someone's harm” ending but takes the
extra-person ending -xon to say either “for someone's good” or “to someone's harm.” And the opposite: kene- ‘miss, fail’ takes only the “to someone's harm” ending, and not -xon. I think these limits come from the meaning of the verbs themselves. Each verb calls up a typical scene, and that scene usually already includes someone who gains or someone who loses. Also, because speakers keep using these verbs in their typical scenes, some verb-plus-ending combinations may have become fixed, and others unacceptable. So the way people usually picture events, and the way they actually talk, can shape grammar. This can override the plain rules about word pieces and sentence structure.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Sometimes two verbs are joined into one unit. This happens when a stage verb (like “begin”) goes with a main verb. It also happens when the bare verb pake- ‘cause to fall’ is stuck onto another bare verb. I have treated both as cases of “verb chaining” (linguists call this verb serialization), one looser and one tighter. In SK, chained verbs have a special rule: both verbs must be of the same type. Either both are intransitive verbs, or both are transitive verbs. This suggests that they share the same set of participants. Something similar has been described for languages such as Ngan'gityemerri and Amharic. There, the two verbs that together make one complex verb must also match in this way (Kittilä 2002:71). So this kind of matching seems to go with two verbs that together describe a single event.
SK has two general-purpose verbs, ik- and ak-, a bit like English “do.” Which one you pick depends on the main verb they stand in for, go with, or help to build. If that verb is an intransitive verb, you use one; if it is a transitive verb, you use the other. I have grouped what these verbs do into four jobs. They can stand in for another verb. They can report what someone said (like “she goes, ...”). They can join another verb to make a bigger verb. And they can turn a word that isn't a verb into one. Except for the first job (standing in for another verb), these

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
jobs are roughly the same as those of similar verbs in some languages of northeast Africa. Interestingly, in some of those languages, the choice between two such general verbs also depends on the type of verb (Güldemann, to appear). In Ch. 15 I suggested how the “reporting speech” job in SK may have come about. It may have grown out of the wider “stand-in verb” job, by narrowing it down. So I don't think verbs of saying are the original source of these general verbs, in any of their jobs. (Others have proposed that ‘say’ turned into a verb-making word; see Güldemann forthcoming and the works it cites.) My idea fits with Güldemann’s (2001) conclusion that ‘say’ may not be the origin of the verb-making word in northeast African languages. But the path he proposes is a bit different. As I said, the general verbs in those languages don't seem to work as stand-in verbs. Back to SK: we still need more research on how these general verbs are used in real speech, and how they changed over time. In footnote 3 of Ch. 15 I pointed out that general verbs look and work strikingly alike in Panoan and Tukanoan languages. So it might be worth checking whether this feature spread across a whole geographic area.
Another big topic in several chapters of this book is how receivers behave in a sentence. Some languages have two kinds of receivers. English has “direct” and “indirect” objects: in “I gave her a book,” book is the thing given and her is the person receiving. SK makes no such split. So the question is this: when a sentence has two (or more) receivers, do they behave the same way or not? I have looked at this question, although with

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t: different amounts of detail, in several kinds of sentences. I looked at the thing given and the person receiving it, in plain “give”-type sentences. I looked at the person made to act (with a “make someone do it” ending) and the person affected. And above all, I looked at the original receiver versus the extra person brought in by an extra-person ending. To compare them, I checked many things. Which marker each gets. Their order between the doer and the verb. Whether each can be moved to the front, or tacked on at the end. Whether each can be described with a “who/which…” part. Whether each can be read as acting “to each other” with the doer. And whether each can be picked up as the doer of a following sentence. My conclusion is that SK is a very good example of a language whose receivers are “equal” (linguists call them symmetrical objects). Neither word order nor markers tell the different receivers apart. So, all else being equal, a sentence can be ambiguous. All receivers can be described with a “who/which…” part, placed either before or after the noun. At least with extra-person endings, any receiver can be read as acting “to each other” with the doer. And any receiver can become the doer of a following sentence. Still, there is one early hint of a difference. One special kind of “who/which…” part (where the noun sits inside the description) seems to prefer the original receiver (the thing given) over the extra person or the person receiving. We need more research to test this, ideally with methods other than asking speakers to make up sentences. Future research should also look at the role of the word ja (‘that’), which comes before some receivers. We also need to test further the different ways to ask a question about the receiver of an inner part of a sentence (8.4.2.3).

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Linguists use the term “symmetrical objects” (“equal receivers”) in two different ways. In the first sense, it means two receivers can both act like receivers at the same time. Even so, some grammar processes may still tell them apart. In the second sense, it means a language makes no regular
grammar distinction between kinds of receivers at all. SK receivers are “equal” in this second sense (unless future research clearly shows otherwise). I also suggest a link between the two senses. If a language has equal receivers in the second sense, then it has them in the first sense too. In other words, if grammar has no way to tell receivers apart, then the receivers should be able to share receiver properties at the same time.
SK is quite relaxed here. It lets up to three nouns in the plain form (with no marker) appear in the same sentence. This can cause confusion about who is who. In “make someone do it” sentences, and in “do it together with someone” sentences, there is a way out. You can mark the person who is made to act, or the companion, with the word betan ‘with’. But remember: people are often simply left out when the context makes them clear. Leaving them out does not change the type of the verb.
A large part of this book looks at endings that change how many people a verb involves. It also shows how often SK marks such changes in the form of its words and sentences. Chapter 16 looked at the main features of “make someone do it” sentences: their word pieces, their structure and their meaning. Two things stand out. First, in some verb pairs, “more than one person” goes with “making someone do something.” These pairs are jo- ‘come (sing.)’ / be- ‘come (non-sing.), bring’ and ka- ‘go (sing.)’ / bo- ‘go (non-sing.), carry, take;’. Second, the “make” piece /ak/ is halfway between an ending and a separate word. This supports the idea that “make someone do it” forms lie along a scale, not only in the

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
meaning but also in the form (Shibatani and Pardeshi 2002). I also showed that “make someone do it” endings easily attach to words that are not verbs. One of them, the “using something” ending -n, goes on a noun. It means doing something to someone by using the thing that noun names.
SK “make someone do it” sentences support the view of cognitive linguists. They say that different ways of saying “make someone do it” reflect different ways of picturing roughly the same real event. In SK, which “make” piece you choose depends on meaning. Mainly it depends on this: does the change need a clear outside cause to happen? Or can the person affected be seen as starting the event by their own inner force? (Shibatani and Pardeshi 2002). I also proposed a link between two things. One is where sound-imitating words (like “splash” or “thud”) are used and what they mean. The other is how alive or human the people or things involved are.
Two SK “make someone do it” sentences may differ only in which “make” piece they use. This shows that these pieces have their own meaning, just like markers and ordinary words. Each one carries its own built-in sense of force and pushing. SK has a clever way to show whether you caused something directly or indirectly. First you add a “happens by itself” ending, then the “make” ending -ma. Here's how it works. A transitive bare verb on its own suggests direct causing. Adding the “happens by itself” ending (linguists call it the middle) cancels that out. Now the sentence just says the original receiver goes through the change, with no outside cause. Then adding -ma brings in a new, weaker doer. This doer allows the process, or helps it along,

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
while the person changing plays a fairly active part. As far as I know, this strategy has not been described for any other language. It may even be found only in SK and not in the other Panoan languages.
The SK data also confirm some earlier findings by linguists. One is the difference between a true cause of something and a mere tool. Only a true cause can be the doer of a transitive sentence (DeLancey 1984). Most interestingly, sentences about how someone dies must be said in a particular way. This includes dying by drowning, by suffocation, from vomiting, and so on. The force or illness is the doer, and the person who dies is the receiver. What stands out in SK is that this is the only possible way to say it. The force gets the doer marker and the person gets no marker, the <ERG ABS> pattern: ERG (the doer marker), ABS (no marker / the plain form) (exx. (8)-(9) and footnote 7 in Ch. 16).
Chapter 17 looked at SK sentences with extra-person endings (linguists call them applicatives). Mostly they follow the usual pattern found in other languages. SK has three kinds. Two of them have no other way of being said without the ending: the general “affecting someone” kind, and the special “to someone's harm” kind. So these endings are required. They are not just an optional way of presenting an event from a different angle (cf. Croft 1994). This means one of the main jobs of extra-person endings in other languages mostly doesn't apply in SK. For the third kind, the “together with someone” kind, we still don't know why speakers choose the ending in some cases and a plain sentence in others. Ch. 17 is the first detailed study of extra-person endings in any Panoan language. From what others have written, it seems that Panoan languages generally don't share the same, related extra-person endings and noun markers. Most interestingly, Panoan languages differ a lot in the

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
extra-person endings they have. This might be useful for working out how the languages of the family are grouped.
The numbers are too small to be statistically significant. Still, it was very helpful to list, for each kind of extra-person ending, the verbs it goes on and how often it shows up in my collection of recorded texts. First, this showed which verbs these endings actually appear with, and roughly how often. Counting showed that the -xon kind is the most common, with more than fifty percent of the cases. The “together with someone” kind is less common, but still about thirty percent. The special “to someone's harm” kind is fairly rare, with less than twelve percent. The three endings also differ in which kinds of verbs they go on. When I asked speakers to make up sentences, -xon attached easily to both intransitive and transitive verbs. But in real texts it nearly always goes on transitive verbs (ninety-three percent of all cases). The special “to someone's harm” ending appears only on transitive verbs. The “together with someone” ending appears equally with both types. Shibatani (1998) claims that “for someone's good” endings tend to go only on transitive verbs, since they are built on the idea of ‘give’. If we look only at what is possible, SK seems to go against this claim. But if we look at how “for someone's good” sentences are actually used in texts, SK fits it.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
As for meaning, there is some evidence of a difference. The special “to someone's harm” ending may be less strict about having living beings as its doers and
especially as its receivers, compared with the general -xon. That is, things that are not alive can appear as doers or receivers with some “to someone's harm” endings, but not with -xon. This idea needs more research. Also, some verbs seem tied more strongly to a typical scene with someone who gains or someone who loses. With these verbs, the other reading is not accepted, even when the grammatically correct ending is added.
On transitive verbs, the general -xon mostly means “for someone's good.” On intransitive verbs, whether it means “for someone's good” or “to someone's harm” is often decided by the meaning of the verb, by the context, or by both.
Perhaps the most striking thing about SK extra-person endings is this: the “to someone's harm” ending only goes on verbs that have at least a doer and a receiver. Importantly, I showed in Ch. 17 that this really depends on the verb having a doer and a receiver. It does not depend on whether the person is active or not. One important part of this book looks at verbs that are halfway between the two types. I checked whether they can take the extra-person endings. These in-between verbs behave in a mixed way that you can't predict. This reflects the fact that verbs can be more or less “transitive”.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Another important question is what the “together with someone” ending adds to the meaning. Usually it brings in a person who is accompanied or helped. It is the only extra-person ending where both the doer and the extra person actively take part in the event. But they don't take part equally. In most cases I looked at, the extra person seems more responsible for the event, or more
directly involved in it, than the doer. But with the verb tee- ‘work’ (and probably some other verbs) the meaning is more like “make someone work alongside you.” The person with the doer marker gets the extra person to work while working too. So you could say this ending reaches into the “make someone do it” area. However, in Panoan languages there is no evidence from comparing the languages that extra-person endings and “make” endings come from the same source. Valenzuela (1999) pointed out that extra-person endings look and work much like same-doer markers. (To be exact, like the endings that match the doer of a transitive verb.) This important question needs research comparing the languages.
In SK you can combine several endings that change how many people a verb involves. Changing the order of an extra-person ending and the “make” ending -ma can change what each one applies to. But remember: the “to someone's harm” ending needs at least a doer and a receiver. So it cannot go on verbs that already have the “happens by itself” ending or the “to each other” ending, because these take away the receiver. This grammar rule makes it impossible to use the “to someone's harm” ending for some perfectly sensible situations. Examples are ‘They left each other to the children’s detriment’ or ‘The child burned her / himself to my detriment.’

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Also, -xon rarely goes on verbs with the “happens by itself” ending. This is surprising, because -xon combines easily with all kinds of verbs. My suggestion is this. The “happens by itself” ending already shows that the doer is affected. So adding another affected person with an extra-person ending may not fit.
The “happens by itself” ending -t (linguists call it the middle marker) has many meanings. It can mean doing something to yourself. It can mean something happens on its own (“the door opened”). And it can mean something was done, without saying by whom (“the door was opened”). But it never means doing something to each other. The ending can also go on verbs of position, movement and feeling, to make intransitive verbs. Sometimes it seems to mean doing something for your own good. This ending in SK needs more research.
When this ending goes on a transitive bare verb, the result often means doing it to yourself. With several verbs, though, there is more than one possible meaning. It can mean “to yourself” or “on its own.” Or it can mean “to yourself” or “was done (by someone unnamed).” It seems likely that the “was done” meaning in SK is growing out of the “on its own” meaning. In both meanings, the person or thing is affected but doesn't cause the action. The difference is whether an outside doer is understood or not (cf. Klaiman 1988). Speakers agree on the “to yourself” and “on its own” readings of these verbs. But they may disagree about whether a given verb can also have the “was done” reading. This suggests that the “was done” meaning is not the basic one. The ending seems to be spreading into this new meaning right now.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
I have also looked at how the emphatic pronouns (words like “myself” in “I did it myself”) relate to the meaning “to yourself.” But I have argued that these words should not be called “reflexive” (“to yourself”) words. You usually don't need them to say “to yourself.” Also, they show up in many sentences that don't mean “to yourself,” including “to each other” sentences. SK emphatic pronouns are especially interesting, and I discuss them in several sections of this book.
I also covered other points about saying “to yourself.” One is how you say it with some intransitive verbs that take an extra noun, and with sound-imitating verbs. (Sound-imitating verbs have a special form used only for “to yourself.”) Another is that, in place phrases, SK doesn't tell “him/her/them” apart from “himself/herself/themselves.” I also covered how to say “your own” and “for yourself,” and the possibility of “to yourself” sentences with no one earlier in the sentence to refer back to. I also showed something about a “to yourself” word in an inner part of a sentence. It can refer back to either the doer or the receiver of the main sentence.
To say people do something to each other, SK adds an ending with two forms. Like other noun and verb endings, which form you use mostly depends on the rhythm of the word, its beats (linguists call these morae). Usually, -anan goes on bare verbs with an even number of syllables, and -ananan on those with an odd number. Like the “happens by itself” ending, the “to each other” ending takes away the separate receiver. I sorted SK “to each other” sentences by what kind of doer they have. The doers can be two nouns joined by “and.” They can be one plural noun. They can be left out, with the plural ending -kan on the verb, giving a “people (in general)” meaning. They can be one person plus a “with someone” phrase. Or they can be just one person. That last kind is especially interesting. It can only mean that someone acts in return. The person knows their action is, was, or will be returned, even though the other person is not mentioned (I call this a “response reciprocal”). Camargo (to appear) described this same kind of sentence earlier for Kashinawa. Kashinawa is a sister language from the Purus branch of the family. So “response” sentences have now been found in two different branches of Panoan.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
To say people do something to each other's body parts, or each other's things, SK has two ways. One is to put a body-part beginning piece on the verb. The other is to add a second noun in the plain form, with “their” before it. That extra noun can also take a marker meaning “by means of.” In English this would literally come out as ‘They saw each other (by means of) their pictures.’
Chapter 19 looks closely at what I call participant agreement in SK (PA for short). Certain describing words or phrases, ones that are not required in the sentence, get special endings. These endings match the role of the person they describe. That person can be one of the main people in a simple sentence. Or it can be the doer of the main sentence, when other sentence parts are chained to it. As I said at the start of this chapter, one of the main contributions of this book is telling apart two things. One is verbs matching each other in type (“transitivity agreement”). The other is describing words matching a person (“participant agreement”). It also seems right to make one more distinction. Some optional describing words are about the action itself; we can call them “adverbs.” Others are about a person. Only the second kind take the matching endings. You can see this clearly when you compare different ways to talk about stages of life (“as a child”). One way uses the time ending -tian, the other uses matching endings. You also see it when you compare sentence parts with “same-doer / different-doer” markers against sentence parts turned into nouns and used like adverbs. These are sometimes followed by place or time markers.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
I found three basic patterns of matching endings in SK. All three work the same way overall. There is a visible ending when the word describes the person of an intransitive verb, and another visible ending when it describes the doer of a transitive verb. When it describes the receiver, there is no ending (where this applies). I also proposed four basic kinds of describing words, based on which pattern they take. A fifth kind is made up of words that can't take matching endings at all. I have also offered a
possible link between these five kinds and what they mean. The idea is that some are more about the person and some are more about the action. Emphatic words (like “myself”) and stage-of-life words turned out to be the most person-centred. Next come place words, words for “for/against someone,” and ‘altogether.’ Words for how, why and how much can be about either the person or the action. In SK, words for “with someone” and time words can never be about a person.
One especially interesting point is how speakers choose between forms of describing words. This happens mainly in “make someone do it” sentences and in sentences with extra-person endings. Take an intransitive base verb with a “make” ending. A place word can take the receiver ending or the doer ending. This tells you where the person made to act was, or where the person making them was. More surprising still is this. In these same sentences, a place word can take the “intransitive verb” ending, and it then tells you where the receiver or extra person was. Why would that ending point to a receiver? I have offered two possible answers. Maybe the ending matches the meaning: that person is the doer of the base verb. Or maybe the doer of the base verb can still control the ending through grammar. More testing is needed to decide between the two. By looking at these choices, I have shown how SK uses matching endings to show exactly what a word applies to. Most languages don't build such differences into their grammar.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
I have also tried to place participant agreement among the kinds of agreement found in the world's languages. I looked at how it differs from the more typical cases (Corbett 2001, 2002). In SK, the matching endings are not see-through: you can't easily split them into neat pieces. Also,
different kinds of describing words need extra rules. The matching can reach across sentences (from one part of a sentence to another part, with its own verb). It is the only kind of agreement in the language (leaving aside verbs matching each other in type). And the matching depends on grammar, not on the word itself. On top of this, I have found some cases that seem to be matching by meaning. But the key point is this. In PA, a noun decides the form of describing words outside the noun phrase. Yet it doesn't change the form of the words that describe it inside the noun phrase. That's why PA is so unusual. Imagine English making “happily” agree with “she,” while “the tall girl” had no agreement at all. It is agreement “in the wrong place” without agreement “in the right place.” I'll come back to this below.
Finally, Ch. 20 compares PA across the related languages, to better understand this feature. It is unusual in the world's languages, but central to Panoan grammar. This comparison shows that matching endings are found in languages from all the different branches of the Panoan family. They are found both inside one sentence and across sentence parts. And the matching endings are related across these sister languages. So I propose that this feature was part of the grammar of the ancestor language. Also, the matching endings on describing words that are not sentence parts are the same as the same-doer markers. Overall, PA has three ways of marking: one for the person of an intransitive verb, one for the doer, and one for the receiver.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Comparing the languages also shows where the Panoan matching endings came from. They were formed by combining two kinds of markers: markers for things like place and time, plus the markers for doer and receiver. I propose a handful of the place-and-time markers for the ancestor language. (For this I rely on the sound correspondences and rebuilt word pieces given by Shell (1965 / 1975).)
I also show that the ancestor language, Proto-Pano, marked nouns in a three-way system, maybe with some exceptions. It must be stressed that
this Proto-Panoan system is very unusual. It has three different marking patterns. The doer of a transitive verb and the person of an intransitive verb both get a visible marker, but different ones. So the Panoan system is truly three-way. It can't be explained as a mix of the English-type system and the doer-marker type system. If it were such a mix, the person of an intransitive verb would get no marker. (That is the case in some Aboriginal Australian languages; Austin 1981.) (Valenzuela 2002c).
In most Panoan languages, the visible marker for the person of an intransitive verb wore away to nothing. As a result, that person and the receiver came to be marked the same way, with no marker. This gave the doer-marker system, ERG (the doer marker) versus ABS (no marker / the plain form). But the visible intransitive marker and the three-way system survived in the matching endings. This produced an unusual kind of mixed system that had not been reported before (Valenzuela 2002c).

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
Ch. 20 also offers a possible account of how participant agreement came about in Panoan. Here is my proposal. First, place-and-time markers began to be used to mark sentence parts without a full verb form. These parts showed time or logical links between two events. The two events probably shared a main person. Two facts support this idea. The place-and-time markers look the same as, or similar to, the first part of the “same-doer / different-doer” markers. And what the place-and-time markers mean fits very well with the time and logic links those markers show. Next, these place-and-time markers were understood in a new way, as markers showing that the same person was involved. Possibly some of these markers were split up by grammar role, each used in different cases. That would explain why same-doer markers tend to limit which role the person they point to can have.
Then the doer and receiver markers were added to these already-marked sentence parts. They matched the role of the shared person in the main sentence. In some cases these markers may have been unnecessary. But in others they may have helped show whether the doer was the same or different. Then the place-and-time markers and the doer/receiver markers fused into single endings. Each ending now shows three things at once: same or different doer, which event came first, and the role of the person in the main sentence. Some describing parts with their own verb may have been reinterpreted as simple describing words. (Maybe they had a hidden “be” verb or a general-purpose verb.) So sentences with two parts were reinterpreted as one sentence. This is especially clear with words for how, why and how much. After that, PA may have spread to other describing words. Finally, the marker for the person of an intransitive verb was lost in most languages.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
As I said above, Panoan PA started as noun markers matching onto describing words. Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann (to appear) studied, across many languages, describing words that tell you about a person's state during an action (“She came home tired”). Linguists call these depictives. In their view, when such a word outside the noun phrase gets a noun marker matching the noun, that is a clear sign it is a depictive. By this test, Panoan describing words with PA would count as depictives. Schultze-Berndt and Himmelmann (op. cit.) also propose a rule that should hold for every language: “In all languages that allow agreement of depictive constituents, modifiers in a noun phrase also obligatorily agree with their head noun...” This book may give the only known exception to that rule.
Why did Panoan languages develop matching on describing words, but not on words inside the noun phrase? Here's one possible reason. In these languages, a noun marker goes on the whole noun phrase, once. Also, the words of an SK noun phrase do sit together. But sentence parts with “same-doer / different-doer” markers can come before the main sentence, inside it, or after it. They don't have to sit next to it. Also, several such parts can share the same main sentence. So it seems more useful to have a matching system between sentence parts than one inside the noun phrase.

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
I have also compared Panoan with some Aboriginal Australian languages, especially Jiwarli. Today, Panoan PA and Jiwarli “referential double case” (Austin 1995) look very much alike. But I think they probably developed along different paths over time. Still, the reasons behind them were likely about the same. Both help listeners keep track of who is who, and of what a describing word applies to. And both languages lack pronoun pieces on the verb or helper verb. In such languages, you can't always tell which noun a describing word goes with from other clues, such as word order.
Finally, I want to point out that SK has a great many ways of making words match (see for example (170) and (171) in Ch. 7). Matching in verb type or matching to a person can happen between words that are next to each other or far apart. It can work forward or backward. It can happen inside a word or between words, inside one sentence or between sentences. Also, there may be several layers of matching. There is even what we could call “back-feeding” matching. That is, a word that was made to match another word in turn
makes the first word match it back. In (1) below, the main verb bana- ‘sow’ is a transitive verb. So it picks the stage verb peo- ‘begin’, also a transitive verb. In turn, peo- makes the main verb take -kin. This ending means “at the same time, same doer,” in the form for the doer of a transitive verb:

h: Cross-Linguistic Comparison (comparing with languages around the world)
t:
(1) bana-kin peo-ke | ‘began to sow’
In contrast, in (2) the main verb ransa- ‘dance’ is an intransitive verb. So the stage verb peo- must get the “happens by itself” ending, which takes away its receiver. Now it matches the main verb: both are intransitive verbs. In turn, the now intransitive verb peo-koot- makes ransa- take -i. This ending means “at the same time, same doer,” in the form for intransitive verbs:
(2) ransa-i peo-koo-ke | ‘began to dance’
This complexity of SK grammar is one more topic that deserves a detailed study. It can help us compare how agreement works across languages. It can also help us understand the many complex ways languages show whether a verb has a doer and a receiver, and related things.
APPENDIX B:
SHIPIBO-KONIBO TEXTS:
The four texts in this appendix illustrate what can be classified as five different genres: (a) procedural speech and (b) special discourse to make a dog become a good hunter (Text 1), (c) description of a traditional custom (Text 2), (d) narrative of a personal experience (Text 3), and (e) informal conversation (Text 4).
The first two lines provide a transcription of the text with morpheme-by-morpheme glosses, whereas the third and fourth lines provide English and Spanish free translations, respectively. The Spanish versions are included here given that all texts were first translated from Shipibo-Konibo into this language, and only afterwards into English. The Spanish translation includes features of Peruvian Amazonian Spanish and, in Text 4, some instances of bilingual Spanish. The Spanish loans in the Shipibo-Konibo text are given in italics.

h: Grammar Sketch 1 Purpose
t: Here we wish to present the basic features of the Shipibo language (also called Shipibo-Konibo) so that users will have sufficient guidance for the proper use of this dictionary.* We also hope that many Shipibo-speaking students will, through this presentation, have the opportunity to reflect on the grammar of their own language.

h: Grammar Sketch 2 Units of Sound and Writing
t: In this outline we will begin primarily with the letters of Shipibo; we will present the sounds of the language only in their correspondence to those same letters.

h: Grammar Sketch 2.1 Alphabet and Phonology
t:
The Shipibo alphabet, corresponding only to the native sounds of the language, is written, according to the usage adopted in this dictionary, as follows:
a, b, c, ch, e, h, i, j, k, m, n, o, p, r, s, sh, ẍ, t, ts, w, y The letters in this list are classified as consonants, semiconsonants (w and y), and vowels, just as the corresponding letters or digraphs are in Spanish.
A comparison will show that the Shipibo alphabet presented here is the same as the Spanish alphabet, with the addition of sh, ẍ, and ts, and the exclusion of d, f, g, l, ll, ñ, u (except in wa and ke), v, and z. However, note that the letters f, g, y, and l can *Much of the analysis presented on these pages has been adapted from the work of Norma Faust: Lessons for Learning the Shipibo-Konibo Language, Working Document No. 1, 160 pp.
Yarinacocha, Pucallpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics, 1973.
appear with their Spanish values in certain forms borrowed from Spanish. For example, alongside amíco (“friend”) there also exists amígo, the older form in Shipibo. Also note that before the letters e and i, k is used instead of c.  Thus two forms of the same verb ati (“to do”), with the root ak-, are written aká (“done”) and akí (“doing”). In the second form, note the substitution of k for c. The sounds of the letters in Shipibo are similar to those of the corresponding letters in Spanish, with the following exceptions:
o: pronounced between the Spanish o and u.
e: an unrounded,

h: Grammar Sketch 2.1 Alphabet and Phonology
t:
reduced vowel, somewhat like the French eu but with the lips drawn back. However, the letter e may also retain its Spanish value in certain loanwords, for example métro (“meter”), alongside mítoro, the older alternative form.
n: when it appears at the end of a written syllable, it indicates that the preceding vowel is nasalized. This nasalization extends to the vowel of the following syllable if no consonant intervenes. For example, in meran (“inside”), the second syllable is pronounced merã; in awín (“wife”), the nasalized í affects both the preceding vowel and semivowel. When a nasalized vowel is followed by a non-nasalized vowel, the following n is written nh to distinguish it from the consonant n. For example, oínhibake (“saw yesterday”) is written with nh following the nasalized i.
sh: pronounced like the sh in Ankash or Shipibo.
ẍ: pronounced like sh, but with the tip of the tongue curled backward.

h: Grammar Sketch 2.2 The Syllable
t:
A syllable may be open, consisting of a non-nasalized vowel (for example, the a or i of benái, “to find”), or of a consonant followed by a vowel (for example, the syllables ra of rabé, “two”). It may also be closed by a consonant (for example, the sh of yawíx, “armadillo,” or of íshtoti, “to run”) or nasalized (for example, the syllable non of binón, “aguaje palm,” or on of onsá, “fierce,” pronounced õ).
(Note, however, that in certain Spanish loanwords, such as métro (“meter”), syllable division follows the Spanish pattern, including the consonant cluster tr.
The alternative form mítoro of the same word represents a “Shipibo-ization,” with the final orepeated after the t to create a normal three-syllable word in the Shipibo language.)

h: Grammar Sketch 2.3 Stress: Rules and Exceptions
t:
In general, words are stressed on the first syllable. However, when the second syllable is closed, either by a consonant or by a nasalized vowel, the stress falls on the second syllable. Examples of the regular stress pattern include ícha (“much”; second syllable cha is open, so the stress falls on the first syllable í) and waxmén (“cotton”; second syllable men is closed, so the second syllable is stressed).
There are exceptions. Many words, mostly disyllabic, are stressed on the second syllable even though it is open. A class of disyllabic nouns and adjectives (e.g., poró, “stomach”) ends in an open stressed vowel. In addition, many words borrowed from Spanish, especially those of three or four syllables (for example, posícho, “little well”), do not follow the normal Shipibo stress pattern. Other notable exceptions include ochíti (“dog”), píwé (“eat”), joá (“came”), mapéke (“went up”), and an entire class of verb forms whose root ends in a consonant that disappears before another consonant.

h: Grammar Sketch 2.3.1 Clitics
t: There is also a class of words called clitics, which do not bear primary stress but are pronounced as extensions of the immediately preceding or following word. For example, in the sentence Nokon pápa ríki (“He is my father”), the words nokon and riki are clitics and are pronounced as extensions of pápa. Thus the sentence is read as though it were the single six-syllable word nokompápariki, with primary stress on the first syllable pa.

h: Grammar Sketch 2.3.2 Stress Marks in this Dictionary
t: Note that in this dictionary, to highlight the distinction between stressed words and clitics, and to provide pronunciation guidance for readers who are not Shipibo speakers, written accent marks are used, at least in this introductory section. The editor recognizes that normal Shipibo writing does not use written accent marks except in irregular cases. It is hoped that this decision will help students of Shipibo without causing confusion or disappointment among Shipibo users because of accent marks that do not reflect the established orthographic conventions.

h: Grammar Sketch 2.4 Morphophonemic Changes in Words or Parts of Words
t:
There are certain sounds that change or disappear before particular sounds when they occur at the beginning of a word or suffix. Conversely, certain sounds change after particular sounds when those occur at the end of a word or suffix. These changes, together with those described in section 7.1, are called “morphophonemic” changes and are as follows:
1. a: When it occurs in the verbal suffixes -ai and -áx, it commonly disappears after the final a of the preceding verb root or suffix; for example, kái (ka- + -ai) “goes” and káyamáx (ka- + -yama + -áx) “when (someone) went.” 2. k or t: As the final letter of a verb root, k or t disappears before a suffix beginning with a consonant. For example, in mapéati “went up,” the t of the root mapet- disappears. In áti (ik- + -ti) “to be,” the k of the root disappears. The final letters t and k reappear in mápetai “goes up” and iká “has been.” 3. r: This letter disappears after s, sh or x in the same word. In Méraaxa, ea kái (“If I find it, I will go”), the first word consists of méraax plus the suffix -ra, whose initial r disappears.
4. y: This letter, especially in the suffix yama (“not”), disappears after s, sh or x.
For example, pikashámai (pi- + -kas- + -yama + -ai) means “does not want to eat.” 5. y: This letter also disappears when it follows the similar vowel i; for example, piámai (pi- + -yama + -ai) means “does not eat.”

h: Grammar Sketch 3 The Paragraph: Unit of Discourse
t:
The paragraph will be considered here only superficially as a unit of discourse.
Discourse is defined as the entirety of a text—for example, a complete narrative, which is the only type of discourse considered here. A paragraph can be characterized semantically by a central theme or main idea developed in at least two clauses (see section 4). One clause is regarded as the principal clause because it states the paragraph's theme; the remaining clauses are subordinate and develop that theme. Clauses are typically connected by an adverb (see section 7.5) or by an adverbial phrase or clause referring to the preceding clause.
The following last two paragraphs of a traditional tale have been divided into paragraphs according to the judgment of a Shipibo writer:
Játian jóni káa iki, jákiribi jawen xobón. kaxónki jawen awínki yóia iki: —Non bákera yápa aínbo moa kénai. Jára moa enjén aká iki. Jáskara ixónra non méniti iki —aká iki.
Játianki ja bakén nínkata iki. Ja nínkatáxki ja báke jábata iki. Jaskáaxonki ja bakén játo pótaa iki. Játian yápa aínbaon jato nokówetsayamaa iki.
"Then the man returned to his house and told his wife that the mermaid woman wished to marry their son, that he had already accepted, and that they could hand him over," he said.
"The young man, therefore, heard the conversation, and when he heard what had been said, fled from the house, abandoning his parents. From that time on the mermaid never found them again." Two themes may be distinguished here: the father's report to the mother concerning their son, and the son's flight after hearing that report.

h: Grammar Sketch 3 The Paragraph: Unit of Discourse
t:
These two themes are developed through eight clauses connected by adverbs and subordinate clauses typical of a Shipibo narrative. These adverbs include temporal adverbs such as játian (“then”) and moa (“already”); the manner adverb jaskáaxon (“thus”); and the adverbial subordinate clauses kaxónki (“when he had gone”), jáskara ixón (“since this was so”), and ja nínkatáxki(“when he had heard it”), which connect the clauses in logical sekence. In two of the three adverbial clauses, repeated verbs from the preceding clauses appear: kaxón repeats káa(“went”), and nínkatáx repeats nínkata (“heard”). In the third adverbial clause, jáskara ixón, jáskara (“those things”) is a pronominal reference to the preceding clause.
A grammatical characteristic of the narrative paragraph illustrated in the short text above is the absence—except in direct quotation—of the suffix -ra from the indicative clause (see 4.2.1). This suffix may occur in the opening sentence of a narrative but normally does not appear thereafter. On the other hand, note the presence of the suffix -ki (for example, in játianki) as an indicative clause suffix that also appears as the suffix of the interrogative clause (see 4.2.2.1). Thus the narrative paragraph possesses grammatical characteristics that can be identified, although their analysis lies beyond the scope of this introduction.

h: Grammar Sketch 4 The Clause
t: Within the paragraph, classes of clauses are distinguished according to mood and, in addition, according to two types of clause: simple and compound, whether occurring independently or within a paragraph. The clause types and then the clause classes are described below.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.1 Types of Clause: Simple and Compound
t:
A clause is defined as simple if it contains only one main sentence; it is compound if it contains one main sentence together with one or more subordinate sentences.
These subordinate sentences may precede or follow the main sentence. In the two examples below, only the second clause is compound: it contains a subordinate sentence followed by the main sentence.
Enra píti piái.
Ja náshiainra, en pítí piái.
"I am eating meat." "While he is bathing, I am eating meat." The two sentences in the second clause are recognized as subordinate and main by the endings -ain (of the subordinate verb) and -ai (of the main verb) on the verbs náshiain ("while he bathes") and piái ("I am eating").
Although a clause normally does not contain two independent sentences, when they are linked by a “sentence adverb” such as jaínxon or jaínoax, they may be written and punctuated as a single clause, as in the following example:
Moa báriapan sénenketianra, noa jóke báneti; jaínoax noa xéakasa iki.
"Since it was already midday, we returned because we were thirsty." The clause is grammatically marked by a mood suffix, which appears at the end of the first principal element or constituent. In the examples above, the suffix is -ra, the indicative mood, as in the subordinate clause moa báriapan sénenketianra ("since it was already midday") in the last example. The moods indicated by these suffixes are described below.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2 Classes of Clause: Moods
t:
The clause is classified according to three moods: indicative, interrogative, and imperative. According to these moods, the clause, if it is in the indicative mood or interrogative, it is marked by one of the tense endings of the main verb; for example, -ai (“present tense”) in the previously noted indicative verb piái (“I am eating”).
The three principal moods are also marked by mood suffixes. Most suffixes of this class are postposed to the first constituent, or principal element, of the clause. If the clause is simple, this constituent is the first phrase of the sentence (containing at least one word); if the clause is compound, the first principal constituent is the first sentence. In the latter case, the mood suffix appears at the end of the last word of the first sentence. In the two examples already seen:
Enra píti piái.
Ja náshiainra, en pítí piái.
“I am eating meat.” “While he is bathing, I am eating meat.” The mood suffix -ra appears at the end of the first phrase of the simple clause in the first example, and in the second at the end of the first sentence.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.1 The Clause: Indicative Mood
t:
The indicative clause (yóia joi “spoken words”) expresses a direct statement and is marked by the previously mentioned suffix -ra. If it expresses information reported by others, the mood is marked by the “reportative” suffix -ronki (“they say,” “they tell”). The two indicative suffixes, -raand -ronki, are illustrated below:
Eara min jói áxekasai.
Móatianronki Yóashiko Inka rétekana iki.
“I want to learn your language.” “They say that long ago they killed the Inka Mezquino.”

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.2 The Clause: Interrogative Mood
t:
The interrogative clause (yókata joi “question words”), which expresses a question, is marked by one or another of the interrogative suffixes -ki, -rin, -pan, -main, -tsi.
Any of these suffixes may also appear in sentences containing an interrogative word such as jáwe (“what”) to mark the question. The interrogative sentence with each interrogative suffix is described below.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.2.1 Interrogative with -ki
t:
The suffix -ki is attached to the last word of the first element of the clause in a simple question in which the verb is expressed.
¿Miakii jáweranoax joá?    "Where do you come from?" The suffix -ki is the basic marker of the interrogative mood; the other interrogative suffixes are used for more specialized classes of questions.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.2.2 Interrogative with -rin
t:
The suffix -rin is added to the end of the first principal element of the clause, or to the end of the clause itself, to indicate a question of identity or state in the present tense. Although -rin appears as a suffix, it functions as the verb íti ("to be").
Clauses with -rin contain nouns (or pronouns) but no explicit verb, as in the following examples:
¿Tsóarin óa? ¿Jáweranonrin min pápa? "Who is that?" "Where is your father?" Notice that -rin has the double function of a verbal suffix and an interrogative mood suffix.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.2.3 Interrogative with -tsi
t:
The suffix -tsi is added to the end of the first principal element of the clause with the meaning "Is it true that...?" in a question seeking verification, for example:
¿Nímatsi joái? "Is it true that Nima is coming?"

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.2.4 Interrogative with -main
t:
The suffix -main is added to the end of the first principal element of the clause with the meaning "isn't it?" in a question seeking confirmation of an assumption.
¿Nímamain joái? "Nima is coming, isn't he?"

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.2.5 Interrogative with -pan
t:
The suffix -pan unlike the other interrogative suffixes, is added to the verb root to ask whether permission is granted for the indicated action, for example:
¿Jatoribi en bopán? "May I take them?” in which pan replaces the verbal root ending suffix of bo- ("to carry"). The question asks whether permission is granted for the action of bo-; the subject en ("I") indicates the person who would receive that permission.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.3 The Clause: Imperative Mood
t: The imperative clause (yónoti joi, literally "words for commanding") expresses a command or request with a verb whose subject is understood as "you" (singular or plural), although that subject is normally omitted. There are several imperative forms according to differences in their use, described below.

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.3.1 Simple Imperative
t:
The simple imperative is generally used to express a command, request, or permission with the final suffix -we. The following are examples:
¡Oínwe! ¡Oínkanwe! "Look!" "Look! (plural)"

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.3.2 Hortatory Imperative
t:
The imperative suffix -we is also used in two other constructions expressing exhortation—that is, urging one or more people to perform an action together with the speaker.
a. Exhortation to an action without movement If the action does not involve movement, the construction consists of the imperative awé (from áti, "to do") plus the suffix -non added to the root of the encouraged verb. For plural addressees, akánwe is used. Examples:
Yóyoinon awé, Nímá.
Játian Titón jónibo yóia iki —Anón akánwe.
“Let us talk, Nima.” “Then Tito said to the men:
—Let us do it.” In these examples, the actions ("to talk" and "to do") do not involve movement by those being exhorted.
b. Exhortation to an action with movement If the action involves movement (for example káti, ka-, "to go"), the construction uses the imperative kawé, or its plural bokánwe, plus the suffix -nonadded to the root of the verb expressing the encouraged action. The singular (addressing one person) and plural (addressing several people) forms of this hortatory imperative are illustrated below:
¡kanón kawé! Eiba xabuén báchi pinón bokánwe.
"Let the two of us go!" "Let us all go to my house to eat charapa eggs."

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.3.3 Weaker Imperative with -ta
t:
The suffix -ta expresses a less forceful imperative, with the sense of "please" or "let me see," as in:
Ea oímata.  "Come on, show me."

h: Grammar Sketch 4.2.3.4 First- and Third-Person "Imperative"
t:
The suffixes -ba and -non mark a first- or third-person imperative (hortative). The suffix -bafollows the verb root and is followed by -non, as in:
Eapari kabánon.
Ja kabátanon.
"I am leaving, then." "Let him go."

h: Grammar Sketch 5 The Sentence: Classes and Types
t: Two classes of sentences are distinguished according to whether they are principal or subordinate within the clause, and two types according to their transitivity.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.1 Principal or Subordinate Class
t:
A sentence is classified as principal or subordinate according to the suffixes of its respective verb. The two sentence types also differ in their functions within the clause. A principal sentence can stand on its own, whereas a subordinate sentence is always dependent on a principal sentence.
Note, however, that when a sentence represents words quoted or reported from someone who is thinking or speaking, the principal sentence may function as a subordinate clause as the direct object of the verb 'to think' or 'to say.' Thus, in the following example:
Jaínxon Tito —¡Oínwe! —aká iki.
"Then Tito said: ‘Look!’" Epánra játo yóiai moátian jonón néemakato.
"The uncle tells them how, long ago, a sajino made him climb a tree." There are two principal sentences within a single clause. However, the principal sentences ¡Oínwe!("Look!") quoted directly, and moátian... ("long ago...") quoted indirectly, function as subordinate direct-object complements within another sentence.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.2 The Principal Sentence: Word Order
t:
The principal sentence (which may often simply be called the 'sentence') in the indicative mood has a single subject and a single predicate. Its normal order is subject, object or objects (if present), and main verb. This order, however, may vary according to emphasis. In the following examples, the first shows the normal order, whereas the last changes the order to emphasize the word píti("meat").
Enra píti piái.
—¿Jáweki min piái? —Pítira en piái.
"I am eating meat." —"What are you eating?" —"Meat is what I am eating."

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3 The Subordinate Sentence
t:
A subordinate sentence functions as an adverb, adjective, or noun within the principal sentence of the clause in which it occurs. Its internal structure differs from that of the principal sentence in one, and sometimes two, internal features.
Accordingly, there are two classes of subordinate sentences: those marked by adverbial suffixes (-áx and others) and those marked by participial suffixes (-ai and -a). There is also a subordinate class marked by the infinitive suffix -ti, discussed in section 7.4.4.2. The first class functions adverbially; the second, with participial suffixes, functions as an adverb or noun within another sentence of the clause.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1 Subordinate Sentences with Adverbial Suffixes
t: Subordinate sentences with adverbial suffixes are distinguished by their features, meanings, and the classes into which they can be divided. These classes are based on temporal relationships between the subordinate and principal sentence (or sometimes between one subordinate sentence and another).

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.1 Different Subject
t:
The adverbial subordinate sentence is marked by one of the many terminal suffixes characteristic of the adverbial subordinate verb; for example, the suffix -ain in the subordinate sentence of the following clause:
Ja káyamainra, ea káyamaritbai.
"If he does not go, I will not go either." Some of these suffixes indicate the transitivity of the main sentence (this agreement is discussed later in §7.4.3.2). They indicate that the subject refers to a person or thing different from the subject of the main verb. In this outline, the examples use a noun or pronoun as the subject of the subordinate sentence (as in the last example). In narrative texts, however, the subject is often omitted.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.2 Identical Subject
t:
This sentence almost never has an explicit subject, since it refers to the same person or thing that is the subject of the main verb. It is distinguished by its verbal suffix, such as -kin, from kakín, for example:
kakínra, en rétea iki rabé jóno.
"While I was going, I killed two peccaries." Note, however, that where there is a series of subordinate sentences, the subject of one of them may be expressed. The expressed subject of the subordinate verb bikín appears in the following example:
Non bikín, nínkatara, saí íbake.
"When we picked it up, while we were listening, there was a shout."

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.3 Subordinate Sentence Suffix -bi
t:
This sentence may be marked by the emphatic suffix -bi, added after the verbal suffix. It gives either the concessive force of 'although' or the temporal force of 'since.' Ja ói beáinbira, ea kái.
"Although it rains, I am going." kírika manónontianbira, jan bénaraseai.
"Since he lost the book, he keeps looking for it."

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.4 Meanings of Sentences with Adverbial Suffixes
t:
If the previously mentioned suffix -bi ('although', 'since') is absent, the sentence may instead have a temporal ('when'), causal ('because'), or conditional meaning ("if"), or 4) purpose ("in order to, so that"). These meanings are illustrated in the following examples:
Níma oínxonra, Jósekan kénai.
"When he sees Nima, José calls him." (temporal) Nonra bíamaibake, bítikoma íketian.
"We did not achieve it because it was difficult." (causal) Ja jokénra, ea kái.
"If he comes, I will go." (conditional) Eara náshiai, joríbanox.
"I am going to bathe in order to return afterward." (purpose) As can be seen in the last example, the tense suffix following that of the main verb characteristically has the meaning 'in order to' and expresses purpose. The other suffixes—that is, those indicating time prior to or simultaneous with the main verb —may have any of the other three meanings: temporal, causal, or conditional.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.5 Temporal Classes in Sentences with Adverbial Suffixes
t:
The adverbial sentence is divided into three temporal classes according to the relationship between the subordinate sentence and the main sentence. Each class is defined by the tense of the subordinate verb in relation to the tense of the main verb: the first expresses prior time; the second, simultaneous time; and the third, time subsequent to the main verb. The three temporal classes, marked by suffixes on the subordinate verb, are illustrated below:
Méraaxa, ea kái.
"Once I find him, I leave." kakínra, non xawán méraibake.
"When we were going, we saw a macaw." Eara móa kái, joríbanox.
"I am leaving in order to return later." a. Subdivisions of the Temporal Classes: Relationship Between the Subordinate Subject and the Main Subject Each of the three temporal classes is subdivided into two groups: sentences that have the same subject as the main sentence, and those that have a different subject.
An example of the 'same subject' subdivision appears in the following clause:
Níma oínxonra, Jósekan kénai.
"When he sees Nima, José calls him." In this clause, the subordinate sentence, Níma oínxonra ("when he sees Nima"), has the same subject as the main sentence, Jósekan kénai("José calls him").
The unexpressed subject of oínxon is the same as Josékan, the subject of kénai. By contrast, an explicit subject appears as the “different subject” in the first, subordinate clause of the following example:
Ja jokénra, ea kái.    “If he comes, I will leave.” Here ja (“he”) is the subject of jokén (“comes”), and it is different from ea (“I”), the subject of kái, the main verb. The different subject may, however, be

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.5 Temporal Classes in Sentences with Adverbial Suffixes
t:
omitted when it is clear from the context.
b. Another subdivision: Relationship between the subordinate direct object and the main subject The class of adverbial-suffix clauses expressing an action or state prior to the main clause has one additional subdivision. It includes subordinate clauses with a direct object that, although not overtly expressed, is identified with the subject of the main clause. The subordinate verb in this class takes the suffix -a, as in the following clause:
Bakén tsákakara, okhíti káke.    “Because the child struck him, the dog went away.” In this example, ochíti (“the dog”) is both the subject of the main verb káke (“went away”) and the understood object of tsákaa (“struck”).

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.1.6 Adverbial clause at the end of a quotation
t:
A subordinate clause whose verb carries adverbial suffixes may mark the end of a direct quotation, as in the following clause:
Jánra yókata iki: —¿Jáwe késkatax ikárin? —akín.    “He asked him, ‘How did it happen?’ —saying.” In this example, the subordinate verb akín(“saying”) repeats the general meaning of the main verb “to say,” yókata iki, introducing a direct quotation.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.2 Subordinate clauses with participial suffixes
t: Recall that subordinate clauses with the participial suffixes (-ai and -a) function as adverbs or nouns within the clause. Unlike subordinate clauses with adverbial suffixes, however, they are distinguished not only by their different suffixes but also because they do not agree with the verb and bear no relationship to the subject of the main clause. Furthermore, the two kinds of participial-suffix clauses—the adverbial type and the substantive (that is, relative-clause) type—have very different structures, which will be described in the following sections.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.2.1 Adverbial Clause with Participial Suffixes: With a Subordinating
t:
Conjunction This class of subordinate clause differs from adverbial-suffix subordinate clauses not only because of its distinct and reduced variety of suffixes, but also because it ends with one of the temporal conjunctions pekáo (“after”), kamán (“until”), kopí (“because” or “as”), or késka (“as” or “in the same way as”) as the final word of the subordinate clause, as in the following clauses:
Nokón wáí óroa pekáora, ea náshiai.    “After cultivating my garden, I am going to bathe.” Nokón pápa káa pekáora, en átapa réteke.    “After my father left, I killed the hen.” Icha binónra en píke, pórokan chéxai kamán.    “I ate many aguajes, until my stomach hurt” Notice especially in the first two examples that, unlike subordinate clauses with adverbial suffixes, these clauses have neither a subject nor an object related to the subject of the main verb (one is not always the same as nor always different from the other).

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.2.2 Adverbial Clause with the Participial Suffix: With -mabi
t:
There is a reduced type of adverbial clause characterized by the conjunctive suffix -bi, placed after the participial suffix -a plus the negative suffix -ma. Together these three suffixes express the meaning “without” or “without having,” as in the following example:
Jawen pápa nokótamabira, ja níi meran káke.    “Without his father having arrived, he went into the forest.” If the tense suffix -tian appears between the suffixes -maand -bi, the construction takes the meaning “before” or “before having,” together with the past perfect, that is, a time prior to the past tense of the main verb. This temporal expression appears in the following example:
Tántiamatianbira, en nokon wáí óroke.    “Before resting, I cultivated my garden.”

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.2.3 Relative Clause
t:
The relative clause is recognized by the participial suffixes -ai and -a, and it frequently appears with the pronouns ja, jan (“he, she; the one who; that which”) as the initial word. Alternatively, the clause may begin with a noun which functions as the subject or object of the subordinate verb, or simply remain in the participial form.
¿Jáwetianki min jankénhai ja min ákai?    “When are you going to finish what you are doing?” Jan béara nokon kóka iki.    “The one who brought him is my uncle.” Mia riki jan ea átapa cháchiti onánmai.    “You are the one who is teaching me to vaccinate chickens.” It should be noted that the subject of the subordinate clause takes the non-basic form when the subordinate verb is transitive, but the entire subordinate clause functions as a noun in relation to the main verb. This is clearly seen in the following example:
Jan píaitonra mia óinai.    “The one who is eating is looking at you.” The words jan “he” and píaiton “the one who is eating” both have the non-basic ending. The word with the ending -n corresponds to the subordinate verb piai, while the form with the ending -toncorresponds to the main verb óinai “looks.” The participial form may also appear as the only word in this subordinate clause. In that case, the form functions as a simple adjective or noun within the main clause.
For example:
Róno máwatara ochítinin óinai.    “The dog is looking at the dead snake.” Yákata riki nokon pói.    “The one who is seated is my

h: Grammar Sketch 5.3.2.3 Relative Clause
t: sister.” The form máwata “dead” functions as an adjective, while the form yákata “the one who is seated” functions as a noun in the main clause.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.4 Types of Sentences (Main or Subordinate) According to Transitivity
t:
Sentences are divided into two types according to their transitivity; that is, transitive or intransitive. Transitivity is determined by means of the subject of the sentence, if it is expressed, and by means of its predicate. In addition to the transitive and intransitive types, a subtype of stative intransitive may also be distinguished. Transitivity may be indicated structurally through agreement between the subject and the verb of the sentence (see §§7.1.1.1 and 7.1.2.1). There are also other agreements that indicate transitivity; these appear in the suffixes of certain adverbs and subordinate verbs, suffixes that will at times also be called adverbial. We shall arrange these suffixes in pairs whose members alternate according to the transitivity of the main verb. Note that such pairs of suffixes, for example, -ax and -xon, have nothing to do with the transitivity of the subordinate verb to which they are attached.) Examples:
Jáskatax, ea néeíbake.    "Having done so, I went up." Jáskaaxon, en kénake.    "Having done so, I called him."

h: Grammar Sketch 5.4.1 Transitive Sentence Type
t:
The transitive sentence type is recognized first by a verb that is itself classified as transitive, although in most cases the form of the verb does not itself indicate its transitivity. Any transitive verb is capable of taking a direct object, although it is not always expressed; some may also take an indirect object. The presence of an expressed direct object and, in certain verbs, an indirect object, are additional indicators of a transitive sentence.
The transitivity of this type of sentence is evident because an object of the verb is present and because that object appears in the basic form of the noun. In addition, the transitive sentence is defined by a group of suffixes that agree with the transitive verb, especially the subject suffix. This subject ending, in its non-basic form, always contains the letter n, indicating the nasal quality of the preceding vowel.
En námi píai.    "I am eating meat." The verb *píai* 'I eat' is transitive because of its direct object *námi* 'meat' and because its subject 'I' appears in the non-basic form.
¡Ea méniwe!    "Give it to me!" Here *ea* 'me', the indirect object, is in the basic form and indicates a transitive verb.
En píai.    "I eat." Although no direct object is expressed, the non-basic form of the subject still indicates that the verb is transitive.
identification. In many cases of subordinate clauses with adverbial suffixes, the transitivity of the subordinate verb cannot be determined from evidence within the clause. For example, in the clause:
Piáxa, ea kǎí.    “When I have eaten, I am leaving.” it

h: Grammar Sketch 5.4.1 Transitive Sentence Type
t: cannot be concluded from the context that the subordinate clause piáx is transitive, because the subject is not expressed and the possible direct object may also remain unexpressed, as in the example.
