The suffix -ax in the form piáx is useful as a sign that the main verb is intransitive because it agrees with the verb kǎí “I am leaving.”

h: Grammar Sketch 5.4.2 Intransitive-type clause
t:
Both the intransitive-type clause and the transitive-type clause can be recognized in three ways. The first criterion is the most obvious: by means of its intransitive verb (if it can be identified as such). Second, the intransitive clause is identified by any suffix in the clause that agrees with the intransitive verb. This may especially be the basic-form subject suffix or the adverbial suffix of the subordinate verb, as explained in section 5.4. Third, the absence of a direct or indirect object (see 7.1.1.2) is also a good, though not decisive, indication of an intransitive verb. Thus, in the following sentence:
Eara móa kǎí.    “I’m leaving now.” is identified as intransitive by its verb kǎí“go/leave,” recognized as probably intransitive because of its meaning, because it lacks a direct object, and decisively because of its subject ea “I,” the basic form of the pronoun. As with transitive clauses, it is often difficult to determine whether an adverbial subordinate clause is intransitive if one does not already know the transitivity, or at least the meaning, of the subordinate verb. There is also an important exception to the regular structure of the intransitive clause: in the case of kéenti“want,” there may be a direct object, such as the form kírika “book” in the following sentence:
Eara kírika kéenai.    “I want the book.” There is also, however, the regular construction Eara kírikanin kéenai “I want the book,” in which the form kírikanin is not the direct object but rather the instrumental complement, whose presence is normal with an intransitive verb.

h: Grammar Sketch 5.4.3 State Intransitive Clause
t:
Among the clauses recognized as intransitive because they lack a direct object and have a subject in the basic form, there is the special case of stative clauses. In this case the predicate is formed with the verb ití "to be" in the indicative and imperative moods, and by means of the suffix -rin in the interrogative mood. The verb ití is irregular in its present indicative form iki ("I am," "is," etc.). The suffix -rin is added to the end of the first main constituent of the clause. Examples:
Jára kírika iki.
¿Jáweranorín min pápa? “That is the book.” “Where is your father?” The forms iki and -rin, together with the presence in the first example of the subject ja (“that”) matching the complement kírika (“book”), and the basic-form subjects ja and min pápa (“your father”), likewise identify the clause as a stative intransitive clause. If the first sentence is changed to:
kírika riki ja.    “That is the book.” it will be seen that the form riki (“is”) is also irregular. Here the indicative suffix -ra is prefixed to the form iki (“is”) instead of being added normally to the word kírika (“book”) as a suffix, losing its letter a before the first i of iki. The form riki appears as the second constituent of the clause instead of iki.

h: Grammar Sketch 6 Clauses: Classes and Function
t: The main or subordinate clause discussed in section 5 contains four possible constituent phrases, which are combinations of words functioning as units within the clause. These include the noun phrase, the verb phrase, the adjective phrase, and the postpositional phrase.

h: Grammar Sketch 6.1 Noun Phrase: Order and Structure
t:
The noun phrase functions as the subject or object in the clause. A noun phrase consists of a noun or a pronoun as its principal word and adjectives as possible subordinate words. If the principal word is a pronoun, it normally appears without an adjective, as in the following clause:
Náshiäxa, ea kǎí.    “When I have bathed, I will go.” If the phrase contains a noun modified by an adjective, the adjective generally precedes the noun. However, for emphasis, the adjective may follow the noun, as in the second of the following examples:
ícha jóni jóni ícha “many men” “men who are many”

h: Grammar Sketch 6.1.1 The suffix as the final element of the noun phrase
t:
Only the last word of the noun phrase bears the suffix, if there is one. This suffix is most commonly the non-basic form of the noun or adjective, although this also applies to the plural suffix Only the last word of the noun phrase bears the suffix, if there is one. This suffix is most commonly the non-basic form of the noun or adjective, although this also applies to the plural suffix *-bo* and others that may be added to the noun or adjective. For example:
Icha jonínra píkaskanai.
Jóni ichánra píkaskanai.
“Many men want to eat.” “The men, who are many, want to eat.” Here it should be noted that the suffix *-n* falls only on the second word, whether that word is the noun or the adjective within the phrase.

h: Grammar Sketch 6.1.2 The coordinated noun phrase
t:
The noun phrase may consist of a series or list of two or more nouns within a coordinated construction. The conjunction *i*, or one of the pair of 'clause adverbs' *jaínxon, jaínoax* ('and'), may connect the last two elements. One of the conjunctions *itan* and *betan* may connect two noun phrases or adjective phrases. Several coordinated noun phrase constructions are illustrated below:
José i Títora jobékonai.
José betan Títora yóyo ikai.
Jóno bíchi, yáwa bíchi, jaínoax westíora íno bíchi — jábora en béke.
“José and Tito are coming.” “José and Tito are talking.” “A sajino hide, a wangana hide, and a jaguar hide: bring these.” Note in the third example the optional, but very common, use of the pronoun *jábo* ('these') as a word summarizing a list.

h: Grammar Sketch 6.2 The adjective phrase: Function, order, and structure
t:
The adjective phrase includes an adjective as its principal word and an adverb as a possible subordinate word. The most basic phrase consists simply of an simple adjective, modifying the noun in the noun phrase. Thus, the simple adjective ícha appears in the following noun phrase:
ícha jóni    “many men” In the following example, kikín kópiayora riki ja.    “That is very expensive.” the adjective phrase includes not only the main word kópiayora (“very expensive”) but also the subordinate word kikín (“very”). The adjective phrase may also include, as an equivalent of the main word, a series or list of adjectives. These are connected by a conjunction such as itan (“and”), as in the following example:
Nokon pápayosin kéni riki jóxo itan kebóx.    “My grandfather’s beard is white and mottled.” Here the two adjectives jóxo (“white”) and kebóx (“mottled”) function together just as a single adjective such as jóxo would.

h: Grammar Sketch 6.3 The Verb Phrase: Function, Order, and Structure
t:
The verb phrase functions primarily as the predicate of the clause. It generally includes a verb as its main word and an adverb, a postpositional phrase, or the equivalent of one as a possible subordinate element. When present, the subordinate element normally precedes the verb, as in the following examples:
Jákoni áxewe.
Jára Máioshiain kǎí.
Xóbo pekaora en oínke.
Ochítira j́́wi naman yákata iki.
“Learn well.” “He is going to Pucallpa.” “I saw it behind the house.” “The dog is sitting under the tree.” In the third example, notice that the verb phrase is split: the subordinate element *Xóbo pekao* ('behind the house') is not immediately followed by the main word *oínke* ('I saw'). This type of division is common in the verb phrase. Another variation of the basic order occurs when there are two subordinate elements; in that case one normally precedes and the other follows the main word, as in the following example:
Ono riki, j́́wi patax.    “There it is, beside the tree.” In this example the adverb óno (“there”) precedes, and the postpositional phrase jíwi patax (“beside the tree”) follows the verb. Finally, note that the verb phrase may contain a coordinated series of two verbs joined by the conjunction jaínoax or its alternative jaínxon, as in the construction píke jaínxon xéake (“ate and drank”).

h: Grammar Sketch 6.4 The Postpositional Phrase: Function, Structure, and Order
t:
The postpositional phrase, which corresponds to the Spanish prepositional phrase, functions, as seen in section 6.3, within the verb phrase as a modifier of the verb.
For example:
xóbo pekaora en oínke.    “I saw it behind the house.” The phrase xóbo pekao functions as part of the verb phrase, modifying the verb oínke. As noted above, the postpositional phrase consists of a noun phrase (or its equivalent) together with the postposition, optionally bearing a directional suffix.
Thus the postpositional phrase functions adverbially within the verb phrase. In the following example:
Rámara nokon awín betan ea kakónko kǎí.
“Now I am going to kako with my wife.” Notice the postposition betan (“with”), which normally follows the two-word noun phrase nokon awín (“my wife”). In the following examples:
Enra níi meranoa binón béke.
¿Tsóarin mipekao? “I brought aguajes from the forest.” “Who is behind you?” Two variations of the basic structure are illustrated. In the first sentence, note the postposition meran(“inside/from within”) with the directional suffix -oa (“from”), indicating the source of the direct object. In the second sentence, the postposition pekao (“behind”) is attached as a suffix to the prefix form mi- of the personal pronoun mia(“you”).

h: Grammar Sketch 7 Words and Parts of Speech
t: Shipibo words (jóibo) are classified into word classes traditionally called “parts of speech”: noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, adverb, and postposition (corresponding to the Spanish preposition...).

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1 The Noun: Structure and Function
t:
The noun (jáne; lit., “name”) functions as the main word of the noun phrase. Every noun has two forms: one without an ending, called the basic form; the second with a final ending, called the non-basic form. Nouns are divided into five classes according to the ending of the non-basic form.
The suffix -n is added to nouns with an even number of syllables (two or four) ending in an unstressed, non-nasalized vowel. The basic and non-basic forms are illustrated below:
báke, bakén        “child, son” The suffix -kan is added to two-syllable nouns ending in a stressed vowel, as in:
poró, pórokan        “stomach” The suffix -man is added to nouns with an even number of syllables ending in a nasalized vowel, as in:
mekén, mékeman        “hand” In this class, note that the n of mekén disappears before the m of -man.
The suffix -an (or in some cases -en or -in) is added to nouns ending in s, sh or x.
Example:
witáx, witáxan        “leg” The suffix -nin is added to nouns with an odd number of syllables. Example:
téoti, téotinin        “necklace”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.1 Functions of the Basic Form
t: The basic form of the noun is the simple form, that is, without an ending. Note that this form is the preferred one for dictionary citations of nouns, pronouns, and adjectives in the alphabetical vocabulary list. The basic form has several functions, presented below.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.1.1 Basic Form as Subject
t:
In the basic form, the noun or pronoun functions as the main word of the subject of an intransitive verb; for example:
Nokon bákera jóai.        "My son comes."

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.1.2 Basic Form as the Complement of the Verb
t:
The basic form of the noun also functions as any complement of the verb. Some examples are:
Ochítininra jóni natéxke.        “The dog bit the *man*.” Ja ea méniwe.        “Give *that* to me.” Ja jóni riki náwa.        “He is a *mestizo man*.” Here the italicized forms, jóni “man,” ja “that,” and ea “me,” are basic forms. The form jóni functions as the direct object in the first sentence and as the main complement of the predicate in the third. In the second sentence, ja functions as the direct object and ea as the indirect object of the transitive verb méniwe “give.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.1.3 Basic Form as the Complement of a Postposition or Postpositional
t:
Suffix The basic form also functions as the main word of the complement of a postposition or postpositional suffix, except in certain circumstantial complements (see 7.1.2.3). The complement precedes the postposition or suffix. Examples:
Jíwira xóbo patax iki.        “The tree is near the *house*.” Rónora miki jóai.        “A snake is coming toward *you*.” Títara jawen bakeon kéenai.        “The mother loves her *son*.” In these examples, the basic forms xóbo “house,” mi- “you,” and bake “son” function as complements of the postposition patax “near” or the postpositional suffixes -ki “toward” and -on “to.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.1.4 The Vocative Form
t: A slightly modified basic form functions as a vocative, that is, the form used to call a person. This form is identical to the basic form except for the accent, which regularly falls on the last syllable, as in the sentence, ¡Nimá, néri jowé!        "Nima, come here!" in which the vocative form, Nimá, is distinguished from Níma, the basic form.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.2 Functions of the Non-Basic Form
t: The non-basic form functions as the subject of any clause where the basic form is not appropriate. The non-basic form also functions as a possessive word. Third, the non-basic form functions as a circumstantial complement. These functions are presented below.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.2.1 The Non-Basic Form as the Subject of the Clause
t:
The non-basic form functions as the main word of the subject of a transitive verb, for example:
Icha jonínra ákanai.        "Many men are doing it." Here jonín, the main word of the subject, has the non-basic form according to the transitive verb ákanai.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.2.2 The Non-Basic Form as a Possessive Word
t:
The non-basic form can function as the possessive word of an adjective phrase indicating the possessor of something denoted by the following noun. Note the possessive form in the following example:
Nokon epán nóntira metsáira iki.        "My uncle’s canoe is very beautiful." The non-basic form, epán "uncle," is the possessive element of the phrase nokon epán "of my uncle," which functions as a modifier of the noun nónti "canoe" and indicates its possessor.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.2.3 The Non-Basic Form as a Circumstantial Complement
t:
The non-basic form can also be the main element of a noun phrase functioning as a circumstantial complement of means, destination, place, origin, or time, as in the following sentences:
Eara ábionin kái.        “I am going by plane.” Eara Rimán kái.        “I am going to Lima.” Janra íamanxon nónti ákai.        “He makes his canoe in the oxbow lake.” Janra íamamea nónti béke.        “He brought his canoe from the oxbow lake.” Eara kanónshiki nato sábadonin.        “I will leave this Saturday.” In the first sentence the form ábionin "by plane" indicates the means of travel; in the second, Rimán"to Lima" indicates destination; in the third, íaman"in the oxbow lake," together with -xon and the transitive verb, indicates location; in the fourth, the form íaman plus -mea "from," a compound postpositional suffix, indicates place of origin; and in the last, nato sábadonin "this Saturday" indicates the proposed time of the action.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.3 Possessive Form of the Noun with -na
t:
The basic form of the noun plus the possessive suffix -na functions as a possessive noun phrase (see 7.3.4 for the possessive pronoun), unlike the non-basic form which functions as the possessive adjective (see 7.1.2.2 and 7.3.3). The possessed noun does not appear; for example:
Nokon títana riki ja.        “That (that is, that hen) belongs to my mother.” If the possessive noun functions as a relative clause, the suffix -ton or -tonin is added; for example, in the following relative clause (in italics):
Nokon títanaton (títanatonin) piai.        “He is eating the one that belongs to my mother.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.4 The Plural of the Noun
t:
The plural number (ichán jane; literally, “name of many”) of the noun may be indicated with the suffix -bo (non-basic form -baon), which is added to the basic form of the noun. If the context already makes the plural clear, the noun may appear without the suffix. Thus the suffix is needed only in the first of the following two sentences:
Enra átapabo pímakasai.        “I want to feed the hens.” Ja pichika átapara nókona iki.        “Those five hens are mine.” In the second sentence the word píchika "five" indicates that the noun átapa "hens" is plural.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.5 Indication of Sex with the Noun
t:
Although Shipibo nouns do not have grammatical masculine or feminine gender, the sex of certain animals is indicated by the nouns béne "male" and awín "female," which are added to the animal name to form a compound noun, as in the following examples:
átapabene; átapaawín        "rooster, hen" where átapa means "chicken, hen." In at least two compound nouns, aínboapo "queen" and aínbobáke, "girl," the noun aínbo "woman" indicates the female sex of a person.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.6 The Indeterminate Noun
t:
The Shipibo noun is basically indeterminate; that is, there is no definite or indefinite article, nor special forms corresponding to “the,” “a,” or “an.” For example, the form kírika "book" may be translated as either "the book" or "a book," depending on the context. However, the demonstrative ja "that" sometimes functions as a definite article, and the numeral westíora "one" as an indefinite article, as in the following examples:
Ja ói beaínbira, ea kái.        “Although the rain comes, I am leaving.” Moátianronki ípaonike westíora jóni kikínbires kóshi.        “They say that long ago there was a very strong man.” Thus ja ói is better translated as "the rain," and westíora jóni as "a man."

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.7 Derived Nouns
t:
Some nouns are recognized as being derived from a verb root plus one of the suffixes -mis, -yosma, or -ti. The suffixes -mis and -yosma have opposite meanings:
"one who habitually does" and "one who does not do" a specific action, as in the following examples:
onánti (root onan-) “to know”        onánmis “diviner” áxeti (root áxe-) “to learn”        áxeyosma “one who does not want to learn” The suffix -ti added to a root to form a noun has the meaning of “that with which” or “the place where” an action is performed. Thus the second of the identical forms óxati (root oxa-) “to sleep” and óxati “bedroom” is a noun meaning “place where one sleeps.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.1.8 Compound Nouns
t:
There is a large class of compound nouns: two nouns are joined to form one word, generally written without a space between the elements. Although in most cases both nouns appear in their basic form, in some cases the first appears in its non- basic form, as shown by the following examples:
átapa "chicken" + béne "male" = átapabene"rooster" bári, barín "sun" + pói "manure" = barínpoi"moss" In the second example, the first element appears in its non-basic form, and the meaning of the compound noun does not obviously follow from the meanings of its simple components. Finally, in the most typical compound nouns, the meaning of the first element is subordinate and that of the second is primary. For example, joshínbina is a reddish (joshín) species of wasp (bína), the principal element.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2 Pronouns: Structure and Function
t: The pronoun (janén jánetitianbi jáne; literally, "name used in place of the name") replaces the noun to which it refers and functions in place of the noun phrase in the clause, either as subject or complement. As in many languages, there are four classes of pronouns: personal, interrogative, relative, and demonstrative. These are distinguished by their forms and their distribution within the clause. The different classes have non-basic forms formed in a manner similar to nouns.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2.1 Personal Pronouns
t:
Personal pronouns are classified, as in Spanish, into three persons in the singular (westíoran jane; literally, “name of one”) and plural (ichán jane; literally, “name of many”). They are:
The alternation between basic and non-basic forms occurs as it does with nouns.
The pronominal subject of the clause, for example, takes its form according to the transitivity of the verb. The alternating forms ea, en “I” are illustrated in the following clauses:
Eara moa kái.    “I am leaving now.” Enra bími kókoai.    “I am eating fruit.” Min ochítininra ea natéxke.    “Your dog bit me.” Person Intransit ive Transitive Meaning First (sg.) ea en I Second (sg.) mia min you (sg.) Third (sg.) ja jan he, she, it First (pl.) noa non we Second (pl.) máto matón you (pl.) Third (pl.) játo, jábo jatón, jábaon they In the last sentence, the basic form functions as the direct object.
Note that the pronoun ja (“him, her, it”) as a direct object is often omitted but understood, as in the following sentence:
Bakénra béke.    “The child brought him/her.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2.1.1 Prefix Forms of the Personal Pronoun
t:
Personal pronouns that function as complements of a postposition or postpositional suffix appear in prefix form and, in some cases, in a shortened form. The prefix forms e-, mi-, ja-, no-, mato-, jato- are shown in the following postpositional phrases with -iba “to”:
With a postposition such as pekao “behind,” the pronouns take prefixes in the same way; for example, mipekao means “behind you.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2.1.2 Reflexive Forms of the Personal Pronoun
t:
The non-basic forms of the personal pronouns are used with the suffix -bix to express the reflexive meaning “by oneself” or “on one’s own behalf.” Sometimes the variant suffix -binix is added to the forms maton and jaton. These are the reflexive forms:
Person Singular Plural First eiba — “to me” noiba — “to us” Secon d miiba — “to you” matoiba — “to you (pl.)” Third jaiba — “to him/ her” jatoiba, jaboiba — “to them” Singular Meaning First enbíx “by myself” Second minbíx “by yourself” Third janbíx “by himself/ herself” First (pl.) nonbíx “by ourselves” Second (pl.) matónbíx, matónbinix “by yourselves” Third (pl.) jatónbíx, jatónbinix “by themselves” The function of the reflexive form is illustrated in the following sentence:
Bákera janbíx kishpímeeibake.    “The child saved himself.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2.2 Interrogative Pronouns: Forms and Function
t:
The interrogative pronouns tsóa, tsón (“who”) and jáwe, jawén (“what”), together with the interrogative suffix -ki, indicate an interrogative clause. These pronouns function as the subject or object within the sentence. Their use is illustrated below:
¿Tsóaki jóai?    “Who is coming?” ¿Tsónki ráonai?    “Who is healing him/her?” ¿Ochítininki tsóa natéxa?    “Whom did the dog bite?” ¿Minki jáwe óinai?    “What are you looking at?” ¿Jawénki mia tsákaa?    “What hit you?” Notice that the order is subject–object–verb, as in declarative clauses, and that the interrogative suffix is attached to the first constituent of the sentence.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2.3 Relative Pronoun: Forms and Function
t:
The personal pronoun ja, jan functions as a relative pronoun meaning “the one who,” “he/she who,” or “that which.” Ja, jan may function in any person and in either singular or plural, as the subject or object of the relative clause. This is the participial-suffix type of clause (see 5.3.2.3), which functions as a noun within another clause. The form ja in this subordinate clause is called relative because it refers to, or is identified with, an implied (unexpressed) subject or object of the main clause. This relationship is illustrated in the following clauses:
Ja riki jan ea átapa cháchiti onámai.    “He is the one who is teaching me to vaccinate chickens.” Mia riki jan ea onáma.    “You are the one who taught me.” Jábo riki ea jan onáma.    “They are the ones who taught me.” ¿Jáwetianki min jankénhai ja min ákai?    “When are you going to finish what you are doing?” In the third example, where jan (“those who”) follows ea (“me”) within the same subordinate clause, notice that the relative pronoun may be the second word of the relative clause. Normally, however, the relative pronoun is the first word of the relative clause.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.2.4 Demonstrative Pronouns
t:
The forms náto, natón (“this, these”) and óa, oátonin (“that, those”) function as pronouns or adjectives within the noun phrase and express the two degrees of demonstrative meaning in Shipibo, as shown below:
¿Miaki náto kéenyamai?    “Don't you want this one?” ¿Miaki náto téoti kéenyamai?    “Don't you want this necklace?” ¿Tsóarin ja jóai?    “Who is that who is coming?” Oa jónira yómetso iki.    “That man is a thief.” Náto jónira náwa iki.    “This (or that) man is a foreigner.” Notice that the personal pronoun ja, jan (“he”) may also function as a demonstrative meaning “that” or “the one.” Also note in the last example that náto does not indicate location but simply draws attention to someone or something, and may be translated as either “this” or “that.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.3 The Adjective: Form and Function
t:
The adjective also appears in both basic and non-basic forms within the noun phrase. However, it is normal for the noun, as the head word, to occur last and therefore carry the non-basic ending, if there is one. The following examples illustrate this:
Icha jonín píai.    “Many men are eating.” Jóni ichán píai.    “The men (many indeed!) are eating.” The adjective first appears in the form ícha and then in the form ichán according to its position at the end of the phrase.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.3.1 Comparison (Degrees) of the Adjective
t:
An adjective preceded by bebónbires (from bebón'more' + -bires) expresses comparison ('more than'). For negative comparison, namánbires ('less than') may be used instead. The nouns or pronouns being compared precede these forms.
Nokon wétsa riki ea bebónbires xoá.    “My brother is fatter than I am.” Nokon wétsa riki ea namánbires xoá.    “My brother is less fat than I am.” The adjective xoá ('fat') is the point of comparison between nokon wétsa ('my brother') and ea ('I').
The superlative is expressed in the same way, with the adjective preceded by Nokon wétsa riki nénoa jóni bebónbires xoá.    “My brother is the fattest man around here.” This expresses the superlative degree of the adjective.
Another way to express comparison is with the adjective suffix -cha meaning “a little more,” as in:
¿Jáwerátoki nenkécha iki; papán nónti o epána?    “Which canoe is longer: my father’s or my uncle’s?”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.3.2 Adjective Suffixes
t:
Like the verb (see 7.4.1), the adjective may be modified by one or more suffixes called adverbial suffixes. The suffixed adjective appears in the following sentence:
Jakóntanibires siki ea.    “I am more or less well.” The form jakóntanibires consists of the adjective jakón plus the suffixes -tani, -bi, and -res. Their order is not fixed; jakónbirestani has the same meaning.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.3.3 Possessive Adjectives
t:
Possessive adjectives correspond to the personal pronouns and indicate possession.
Icha riki nokon átapa.    “There are many of my chickens.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.3.4 Possessive Adjectives: Conversion to Pronouns Ending in -na
t:
Possessive pronouns are formed by adding the possessive suffix -na:
Person Singular Plural First nokon — my non — our Secon d min — your maton — your (pl.) Third jawen — his/her jaton — their Person Singular Plural First nokona — mine nona — ours Icha riki nókona.    “Many are mine.” Icha riki nokon átapa.    “Many are my chickens.” Notice that nókona in the first sentence and nokon átapa in the second can refer to the same object. The shorter phrase may substitute for the longer one, just as English “mine” may replace “my chickens.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4 The Verb: Classes, Structure, and Function
t:
The verb is classified as transitive or intransitive according to suffix agreement and sentence type. Transitivity is determined primarily by agreement patterns within the clause and secondarily by sentence structure. A clause with a direct object is generally transitive.
The verb is the head of the verb phrase. It contains a simple or compound root, which may include prefixes such as ma-, chosh-, chóshati, machóshti, chókati, wéxati, néxati, ménoti, pékati, sikáti, xókati Compound roots may also be reduplicated. Every verb also has a final suffix indicating tense or mood, for example -ke, oínke, -we, oínwe

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.1 Medial Verb Suffixes
t:
Between the root and the final suffix, a verb may take one or more medial suffixes.
These modify meaning or express grammatical relationships. Some, such as the plural suffix, relate the verb to another word; others are adverbial and modify time or manner.
-kan, -yantan, -beiran, -wan, jowánke Non-adverbial suffixes may add participants to the action and can also change the transitivity of the verb. For example, adding the causative suffix -ma, yakáti, yakámati creates the meaning 'to make someone sit,' producing a transitive verb.
Secon d mina — yours matona — yours (pl.) Third jawena — his/hers jatona — theirs

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.2 Order of the Medial Verb Suffixes
t:
The order of the suffixes that follow the verb root up to the final suffix is more or less fixed. Below is a chart of some of the most common suffixes to provide a guide to their normal order in the structure of the verb.
Comments on the Table 1. Certain suffixes in the first column above affect the meaning of the verb, in many cases by adding the previously mentioned additional participant to the clause. As already noted, the suffix may also change the transitivity of the root.
These suffixes include the reflexive suffix -t (e.g. the -t seen in bénotai “gets lost,” Most closely attached suffixes Modifier suffixes Time suffixes Plural suffix Time suffix -t “reflexive” -yama “negative” -ya, yat “tomorrow” -kan “plural” -ni “very remote past” -ma “causative” -kean “almost” -wan “today” -n “do, transitivizer” -ribi “also” -iba “yesterday” -kin, -kiin “companionsh ip” -yora “much” -yantan “months ago” -n, -(na)an “harm, detriment” -tani “barely” -kati “imperfect past” -xon “benefit” -na “warning” -anan, -ananan “reciprocal” -kas “want” -a “do, transitivizer” -res “only” -i “come, come!” unlike bénoai “is lost”), the causative suffix -ma “cause,” which, when added to a transitive or intransitive root, produces a transitive verb, as for example in oínmati “cause to see, show” (root oin- “see”); and the verbal derivational suffixes -n “make” and -a “make,” which, when added to an intransitive root, produce a transitive verb; for example oxánti “put to sleep” (from the intransitive root oxa- “sleep” plus -n) and áxeati “teach” (from the intransitive root áxe- “learn” plus -a).
All these suffixes form an integral

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.2 Order of the Medial Verb Suffixes
t:
part of the compound root, and all precede any of the remaining suffixes, except occasionally those of the second column.
2. Also in the first column appears -kin“companionship,” one of the suffixes we will call subordinate-action suffixes. The suffix -kin is illustrated in órokinke “helped cultivate,” where the intransitive root oro- “cultivate” becomes the transitive orokin-. Another suffix of the same class is -bo “going,” from oínboai “he sees him while going.” This suffix is added to a transitive root (such as oin- “see”) without changing its transitivity, but adds the subordinate action of “going.” Unlike -n and -a, these suffixes do not add a new participant to the action.
3. The first column also contains suffixes expressing a personal effect on the referent (the person or thing denoted) of the object; for example, harm or damage, as in the suffix -n or -anin the phrase ea tóemaanke “you made me break it.” In the verb tóemaanke, the suffix -anoccupies the position between -ma and -ke after the root toe- “break.” The implication is the harm one person causes another by making that person break something.
4. In the second column, the suffixes -kas “want,” -tani “barely, a little,” -riba “also, again,” and -res“only” follow a simple root, for example in jókaskatiai “wanted to come earlier.” These suffixes may also follow a suffix from the first column, such as -riba after -ma in oímanribake“made (someone) see again.” 5. In the second column, if there had been more space, we would also have added the following modifier suffixes: -tan “go and return”; -kaín, -bain

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.2 Order of the Medial Verb Suffixes
t: “going”; -kiran, -beiran “coming”; -pake“going down”; -ina “going up”; -shin “all night”; -bai “all day”; -yon “completely”; -bekon “between two”; and -men “quickly.” All these suffixes indicate an aspect or direction of the verbal action.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.2 Order of the medial suffixes of the verb (continued)
t:
6. The negative suffix -yama "not," although we place it in the second column, follows the root and any of the other suffixes in the first two columns. Likewise, the suffix -yama precedes the suffixes of the third column, that is, those of definite time; for example in the form oínkinkashamawanake“did not want to help show today.” There the element -kashama is equivalent to -kas “want” + -yama “not.” The negative suffix -yama follows -kas and precedes -wan “today.” 7. In the third column, the definite-time suffixes -ya, -yat “tomorrow,” -wan “today,” and -iba“yesterday” precede the plural suffix -kan, which indicates a plural subject of the verb; for example, nokówankanke “they arrived today.” 8. In the fourth column, the plural suffix -kan follows the definite-time suffixes and all those already presented, and precedes only the aspect/time suffix -ni and the terminal suffixes. The suffix -kan appears in the form oínakinkashamawankanai “they did not want to help show today.” The suffix kan follows -wanand precedes the final suffix -ai.
9. In the fifth and final column are the suffixes -ni, remote past, and -kati, imperfect past; for example, in oímakinkashamakanike “long ago they did not want to help show.” The suffix -ni follows the plural suffix -kan and precedes the final suffix -ke(indefinite past). Note, however, that there is some variability in the order of the suffixes: the second-column suffixes -kas, -tani, -ribi may precede or follow the definite future suffix -yat “tomorrow.” This variation is seen in the forms jótaniyatai and joyátaniai: both mean “will hardly come tomorrow.”

h: Grammar Sketch 10 Besides the normal verb order already described, note the compound verb
t: formed from a non-verbal root plus the verb ati, transitive, or iti, intransitive. The root may be a noun, such as xóbo “house” in xóbo ati “to build a house,” or an onomatopoetic form (imitating or reproducing a non-word sound), such as sai in saíiti “to shout,” or too in tóoati “to bale.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.3 Essential or terminal suffixes of the verb
t:
The terminal suffixes (or endings), which are essential to the verb, take various forms according to whether the clause in which they occur is main or subordinate.
In the main clause, as mentioned above, the forms of the terminal suffixes also vary according to the mood of the clause.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.3.1 Suffixes of the Main Clause
t: 1. Present or indefinite future: -ai, as in Jára jóai, “He comes” or “He will come.” 2. Definite present: -í plus the form itai of the verb ití, as in Eara kaí itai “I am in the act of going.” 3. Indefinite future: the infinitive suffix -ti plus the form iki of the verb ití, as in ¿Jáwetianki noa nokóti iki? “When are we going to arrive?” 4. Indefinite future: the suffix -nonxiki, as in Rámatanibira ea kanónxiki “I will go soon.” 5. Indefinite past (indicative only): -ke, as in Pítira en béke “I have brought food.” 6. Indefinite past: another suffix, -a. It is always used in the interrogative and sometimes in the indicative. The past participle suffix -a may optionally be followed by iki. Compare ¿Jaki máwuata? “Did he die?” and Jara máwuata iki“He has died.” 7. Past from several years ago: -kato, as in Ea máxkotianra en oínkato “When I was a child, I saw it.” 8. Very remote past: -ni + -ke, as in Jonínra íno rétenike “In ancient times, a man killed a tiger.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.3.2 Suffixes of Subordinate Clauses
t:
The verb suffixes used in subordinate clauses fall into two groups. Participial subordinate clauses use the participial suffixes -ai for the present and -a for the past.
Ja jóáira nokon épa íki.    “The one who is coming is my uncle.” Ja nokon epán bóáira nokon báke íki.    “The one carrying my uncle is my son.” Nokon wái óroa pekáora, ea náshiai.    “After I have cultivated my chacra, I will go bathe.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.3.2 Adverbial-Clause Suffixes (continued)
t:
The adverbial-suffix clauses, on the other hand, have their verbs marked with various suffixes according to the temporal relationship with the main verb. These suffixes are summarized in the following table:
Subordinate verb Main verb When the subordinate action is before the main action When the actions are simultaneous When the subordinate action is after the main action Same subject as main verb Intransitive -ax -i -nox Transitive -xon -kin -noxon This table is useful as a reference for visualizing three key features of these subordinate suffixes: 1) whether or not certain suffixes agree with the main verb (that is, whether they indicate the transitivity of the main verb in the clause); 2) the temporal relationship of each suffix to the main verb; and 3) whether the subject of the subordinate verb is identical to, or different from, the subject of the main verb —or, in the unique case of the suffix -a, whether the subject of the main verb is identical to the direct object (expressed or not) of the subordinate verb. The following clauses illustrate several subordinate suffixes and these three grammatical features.
Níma oínxonra, Jósekan kénake.
“When he saw Nima, José called him.” Ja ói beaínbira, ea kái.
“Although it is raining, I am leaving.” kírika áananra, nokon wétsa téetai.
“My brother studies and at the same time works.” Ochítinin natéxara, báke saí ike.
“When the dog bit him, the boy cried.” In the first example, the suffix -xon indicates that the subordinate verb oínxon "(when) saw" refers to an action that occurred earlier than the principal verb kénake"called"; the principal verb, kénake,

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.3.2 Adverbial-Clause Suffixes (continued)
t:
is transitive and has the same subject, Jósekan "José".
In the second example, the suffix -ain indicates simultaneous time between the subordinate verb beaín and the principal verb kái "I am leaving." The two verbs No agreement with main verb -taanan -anan Different subject No agreement -ken (indefinite time) -ain -non No agreement -ketian (definite time) -aitian, -nontian Direct object identical to subject of main verb No agreement -a have different subjects. Notice also that the subordinate-clause suffix -bi "although" follows -ain without becoming part of the verb. Likewise, -ra is an indicative suffix belonging to the entire clause rather than to the verb or subordinate clause.
In the third example, the suffix -anan indicates that the actions "to study" and "to work," performed by the same subject, are simultaneous.
In the fourth example, the suffix -a indicates that the action “to bite” precedes “to cry,” and that the understood object of natéxa "(when) bit" is báke "the boy," who is also the subject of saí ike "cried." According to the diagram, the subordinate suffixes -ain, -anan, and -a do not indicate whether the principal verb is transitive or intransitive.
Finally, note the special function of the suffixes -i and -kin. These mark verbal complements. káti "to go" typically takes -i to express the subject's purpose, whereas péoti "to begin" typically takes -kin.
Eara pásiani jóke.
“I came to take a walk.” Enra pikín péoke.
“I began to eat.” In the first example, pásiani "to take a walk" expresses the purpose of the subject ea "I" of the principal verb jóke"came." Finally, the last sentence can also

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.3.2 Adverbial-Clause Suffixes (continued)
t:
be expressed by reversing the verbal suffixes.
Enra péokin píke.
“I began to eat.” There is another type of verbal complement that serves as the complement of certain specific verbs and ends in -ti; this will be presented in section 7.4.4.2.a.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.4 Subordinate verb forms with a special function
t: There are verb forms that function as participles or infinitives and therefore share some of the characteristics of adjectives or nouns. These forms are classified as participles or infinitives and are recognized by their suffixes and by the way they function in the sentence.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.4.1 Participial verbs: Form and function
t:
The participial suffixes mentioned above are -ai for present time and -a for past time relative to the main verb. These participles function as verbs in relative clauses (see 5.3.2.3). At the same time, they have an adjectival character because they describe a noun within the clause. The following examples illustrate participial verbs:
Ochítininra róno máwata oínai.
“The dog is looking at the snake dead.” Jóni jóaira nokon pápa iki.
“The man who is coming is my father.” Jatíbi aínbora yákata iki.
“All the women are seated.” The words máwata "dead," jóaira "coming," and yákata"seated," function as adjectives by providing secondary descriptive information about a person or thing and, as verbs, describe an action or event.
Remember that these same subordinate forms ending in -aiand -a also function as main verbs: -ai marks the present or indefinite future, while -a marks the indefinite past.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.4.2 The infinitive: Form and function
t:
The Shipibo infinitive ends in -ti and has a variety of functions; among them, it may function as a verbal complement or as a subordinate verb.
a. The infinitive as a verbal complement In its function as the complement of the verbal phrase, the infinitive most commonly precedes certain verbs including átipanti "to be able," játi "to have to," áxeti "to learn," onánti "to know," all of which involve some type of mental operation. The use of the infinitive as a complement is illustrated in the following sentences:
Enra mia akínti átipanyamake.
“No te puedo ayudar” → “I cannot help you.” Rámabira en jankénhati shínanai.
“Ahora pienso terminar.” → “Now I am thinking of finishing.” b. The infinitive as a verb of purpose The infinitive also functions (somewhat like the participles mentioned above) as the verb of a subordinate clause expressing the purpose of the action of the main verb. In such a subordinate clause of purpose, the infinitive suffix has the force of “in order to” or “so that.” This use of the infinitive is illustrated in the following sentence:
Játian nokon papán, jíwi bóchiki, tápoa iki; jaín noa óxati.
“From there my father, up in a tree, built a platform for us to sleep there.” It is useful to recall the adverbial clauses mentioned above, with the pair of suffixes -nośh, -nośhon (“for”), and the suffix -non (“so that”), which indicate time subsequent to the main verb and, like the infinitive, express the subject’s purpose.
Likewise, the verbal complements ending in -i or -kin also imply the subject’s purpose (see 7.4.3.2).
c. The infinitive in indirect

h: Grammar Sketch 7.4.4.2 The infinitive: Form and function
t:
quotation After the verb yóiti “to say,” the infinitive functions as the verb of an indirect quotation—for example, of a command—as in the following sentence:
Enra ja yóia iki moa káti.
“I told him to go away now.” where the direct command would be: “¡Go away now!” d. The infinitive as the main element of the principal verb Recall that the infinitive form of the verb followed by a form of the auxiliary verb ití functions as the principal verb of the indefinite future: káti iki “is going to come.” e. The infinitive with inflection In Shipibo, the infinitive can take the nominal ending -n or -nin of the non-basic noun form (when the verbal root has two or three syllables, respectively). This “non-basic” infinitive functions as a complement of destination or means; for example, in the following sentences:
Eara kéenai Rimán katín. — “I want to go to Lima.” Eara yokátinin rábinai. — “I am ashamed of asking him.” Note that the infinitive form without any suffix is the citation form used for Shipibo verb entries in the dictionary. That is, verbs are always listed in their simple infinitive form, without inflection and without preceding suffixes, in the alphabetical list of Shipibo words. Thus, for example, the dictionary lists the verb oínti “to see.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.5 The Adverb: Form and Function
t:
The adverb functions within the verb phrase as a subordinate element modifying the verb, as moa “already” in the verb phrase móa kái of the sentence Eara móa kái “I am already leaving.” Although adverbs cannot always be classified by suffixes or prefixes as verbs, nouns, or adjectives can, some adverbs do contain suffixes. These correspond to certain verbal or nominal suffixes. Suffixed adverbs are classified into groups of two or three forms sharing the same root. These groups are described below.
For example, pairs of adverbial forms may share the same adjectival root and the same meaning as an adverb of manner. These adverbs end in -i, used with intransitive verbs, and -akin, used with transitive verbs. The verb determines which adverbial form is used. Thus the pair jákoni, jakónhakin means “well,” derived from the adjective jakón “good.” These alternate forms appear in the following sentences:
Jákoni jaín niwé. — “Stand well.” Nokon báke jakónhakin koíranwe. — “Take good care of my little son.” Other analogous adverb pairs related to intransitive and transitive verbs are ikáma, akáina (“no,” in answer to a question with an intransitive or transitive verb), and the sentence adverbs jaínoaśh (with an intransitive verb) and jaínśhon (with a transitive verb), meaning “then.” Some basic groups of adverbs of place are related through a series of orientation suffixes. The opposite adverbs néno“here” and óno “there” are related by the locative suffix -no; the adverb stems o- and ne- require this suffix to complete the word. If the suffix -no were changed to -ke, the adverbs néke “this way”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.5 The Adverb: Form and Function
t: and óke “that way” are formed. All of these adverbs may in turn acquire a directional meaning by means of a second directional suffix following the first. The source suffix -a, for example, or -aśh “from,” forms the orientation adverbs nénoa “from here,” nénoaśh (nénoa + -aśh) “from here,” nékea “from this side,” nékeaśh “from this side,” and a corresponding series with óno and óke (ónoa, ókea, etc.).

h: Grammar Sketch 7.6 The Postposition: Order and Function
t:
Orientation adverbs that also function as postpositions take orientation suffixes in the same way. The adverb—and, for example, the postposition—bebón “in front of” may take the double suffix -meaśh (-mea + -aśh) with the meaning “from,” or the suffix -śhon, indicating the location of an action (with a transitive verb). These distinctions are illustrated below:
wíntira bebón iki. — “The paddle is over there in front.” Jára śhobo bebómeaśh jóke. — “He has come from in front of the house.” Bakénra bebónśhon píai. — “The child is eating it there in the front row.” Time adverbs such as bási “for a long time,” ráma “now,” and bakísh “tomorrow” function without the transitivity or orientation agreement suffixes. However, some of these adverbs may take other kinds of suffixes, such as -yora in basiora “for a very long time,” or -tian “when” in rámatian“at this time.” The postposition is identified by a form that, as noted, may also function as a locative adverb. As a postposition it follows its complement, unlike Spanish prepositions. That complement is, as noted earlier, a noun phrase. If the noun phrase consists only of a personal pronoun, the shortened prefixed form is attached to the postposition. Like the adverb, the postposition normally precedes the verb and may appear before or after the object, if there is one. The following illustrate postpositional and adverbial use:
Ochítira bebón kái. — “The dog goes ahead.” Ochítira ebebon kái. — “The dog goes ahead of me.” Ochítira Níma bebón kái. — “The dog goes ahead of Nima.” First the form bebón is seen

h: Grammar Sketch 7.6 The Postposition: Order and Function
t:
functioning as an adverb, then in postpositional phrases with the prefixed pronoun e-“my,” and finally, in the last example, with the noun Nímaas its complement.
Whether functioning as an adverb or as a postposition, the form may take certain orientation suffixes discussed in the preceding section on adverbs. The postpositional use of the suffixed form is illustrated in the second of the following sentences:
Enra bebómea wínti béke. — “I have brought the paddle from the front.” Enra nónti bebómea wínti béke. — “I brought the paddle from the bow of the canoe.” Note the loss of the letter n in bebón before the initial m of -mea. This is the morphophonemic phenomenon previously mentioned in §7.1 concerning noun forms.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.7 The Conjunction: Forms and Function
t: Traditionally, Shipibo has not had a class of words corresponding directly to Spanish pero, o, aunque, porque, para que, or cuando, etc., that connect words, phrases, or clauses in the same way. Instead, subordinate-clause suffixes generally fulfill this function. Nevertheless, a small number of traditional Shipibo words, although they are formally adverbs or postpositions, function as coordinating or subordinating conjunctions. In addition, there are a few coordinating conjunctions borrowed from Spanish that function in the same way in Shipibo.

h: Grammar Sketch 7.7.1 The Coordinating Conjunction
t:
The coordinating conjunction with the meaning "and" joins phrases of the same class. It links two verbal, nominal, or adjectival phrases that are the only members or the final members of a series. The words functioning as coordinating conjunctions meaning "and" are described below.
1. The forms jaínoax and jaínxon, which also function as sentence or paragraph adverbs meaning "then," are used as conjunctions linking the last two nouns in a coordinated series, as in the following sentence:
Jóno bichi, yáwa bichi, jaínoax westíora íno bichi, jabo boí, ea iká riki. — “When I was carrying peccary hides, wangana hides, and tiger hides, that happened to me.” Notice that when these forms function as conjunctions, just as when they function as “sentence adverbs,” they indicate the transitivity of the main verb by means of the suffix -xon or -ax. Thus, in the example, the form jaínoax is associated with the intransitive verb iká riki “it happened.” 2. The form itan may likewise connect coordinated words without regard to the transitivity of the verb, as in the coordinated phrase jóxo itan kebóx “white and speckled.” Some speakers also use the borrowed form i.
3. Another form borrowed from Spanish is o. This conjunction functions just as it does in Spanish to relate two alternative words, as in the phrase José o Tito (“José or Tito”).

h: Grammar Sketch 7.7.2 The Subordinating Conjunction
t:
The subordinating conjunction normally appears as the final word of the previously described adverbial subordinate clause with participial suffixes. This group includes kaman “until,” pekao “after,” kopí “because,” and keska “so that.” Their use is illustrated below:
Icha binónra en píke, pórokan chéxai kaman. — “I ate many aguaje fruits, until my stomach hurt.” Oroa pekáora, ea náshiai. — “After cultivating, I bathe.”

h: Grammar Sketch 7.8 The Interjection
t:
The interjection appears as an emotional expression without a grammatical relationship to any other class of word; that is, it functions as a complete utterance.
A clause following the interjection may explain its cause. In the following example, the interjection éeri means “ouch!” and is followed by an explanatory sentence:
¡Eeri! Móara min ea tóenaanmaake. — “Ouch! You already made me break it.”

h: Grammar Sketch 8 Prefixes and Suffixes: Function and Syntax
t:
Prefixes and suffixes, like words, phrases, sentences, and clauses, will be considered in classes according to their syntax; that is, according to their place in the ordering of linguistic elements within an expression.
Prefixes and suffixes are generally added to words or word roots in an ordered sequence.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.1 The Prefix: A Single Form in the Word
t: By definition, a prefix occurs before the word or word root. Generally it is attached directly to a shortened root, together forming a compound root. In the verb machóshti, for example, the prefix ma- “on the head” and chosh- (the shortened form of chosha- “to strike”) combine to form the compound root machosh- “to strike on the head.” A word does not take more than one prefix.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.2 The Suffix: Two Classifications
t:
A word, however, may contain not just one but several suffixes. Especially in verbs, these are classified as medial and final suffixes: a medial suffix never follows a suffix classified as final.
In another classification, suffixes are generally divided into inflectional, modifying, and derivational suffixes. These categories are described below.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.2.1 The Inflectional Suffix
t: An inflectional suffix—for example the plural suffix -bo in jónibo “men”—marks a grammatical relationship between two or more words in the clause. In the sentence Jónibora békanai “The men are coming,” the plural suffix -bo on jónibo agrees with the plural form of the verb békanai “are coming.”

h: Grammar Sketch 8.2.2 The Modifying Suffix
t: A modifying suffix, on the other hand, such as the tense suffix -iba “yesterday” in joíbake “came yesterday,” or the suffix -yora “very, much” in keényorai “loves very much,” simply modifies the meaning of the word in which it appears. Some, such as -iba, occur only with verbs; others, such as -yora, can modify non-verbs as well, as in the adjective jakónyora “very good.”

h: Grammar Sketch 8.2.3 The Derivational Suffix
t:
A derivational suffix, when added to a word or root, creates a new word with a different meaning and different grammatical relationships. For example, adding the derivational suffix -n to the intransitive root oxa- from oxati “to sleep” produces the transitive verb oxánti “to put to sleep” or “to lull.” There is a special phenomenon involving certain suffixes, for example the diminutive suffix -shoko: it is generally classified as a modifying suffix, but in some cases it functions as a derivational suffix. In those special cases, the suffix forms the final element of a compound word. Compare bákeshoko “little child” and pápashoko“grandfather.” The form bákeshoko is clearly the diminutive of báke.
The form pápashoko derives from pápa “father,” but is not its diminutive; rather, it is a separate word with a distinct though related meaning.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3 Orientation to Certain Prefixes and Suffixes
t: The following sections present prefixes and suffixes, some of which have not yet been discussed. They are organized according to the part or parts of speech with which they are associated.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.1 Prefixes Indicating Parts of the Body
t:
In general, Shipibo prefixes are shortened forms of body-part names and function mainly as the first elements of compound verbs, though they also occur in compound nouns and adjectives. The prefix ma- derives from mápo“head,” appearing in machóshti “strike on the head” and mabéx “covered with sores on the head.” Other prefixes are: me- (mekén, hand); pon- (ponyán, arm); ke- (kešá, lip/ mouth); be- (béro, eye/face); bo- (bóo, hair); ta- (táe, foot); wi- (witáx, leg); re- (rekín, nose); pa- (pabíki, ear); jan- (jána, tongue); šo-, chest; pe- (peká, back); ra- (yóra, body); xan- (cf. xáni, female pubic hair), groin; še-(šéta, teeth); te- (téšo, neck); and tsi-, buttocks.
Examples: béxati → mabéx; chókati → mechóti; xókati→ pónxoti; néxati → tanéxti; pékati → kepéti; ménoti→ raménoti; wéxati → ponwéxti; šíkati → béškiti.
Note that mabéx is an adjective, not a verb. The corresponding verbal form continues on the next page.
(The corresponding verb for mabéxti “to become covered with sores on the head,” just as the adjective béxa“covered with sores” corresponds to the verb béxati “to become covered with sores.”)

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.2 Postpositional Suffixes
t:
There is a group of suffixes, called postpositional suffixes, which, when added to a noun, to the shortened forms of the personal pronoun, or to certain adverbs of place, indicate the orientation of the complement. These suffixes express origin, source, or the direction of the subject’s movement. In this way the postpositional suffix functions like a postposition, following its complement. Unlike an independent postposition, however, the suffix cannot function independently as an adverb. The principal postpositional suffixes are the following:
1. The suffix -iba (“to,” “toward,” or “to the home of”) indicates destination when referring to a person or an animal, as in the following examples:
Eara Títóiba kái. — “I am going to Tito’s house.” Jára noiba jóai. — “He is coming to our house.” 2. The suffixes -ki (“to,” “toward,” “on,” “against”) and -on (“to,” “for”) both indicate a referential complement; that is, the action of the verb is carried out with reference to the complement. The suffix -ki implies hostility or an unfavorable attitude, whereas -on implies interest or a favorable attitude. They are illustrated below:
Rónora miki jóai. — “A snake is coming toward you.” Eara rónoki rakéyamai. — “I am not afraid of the snake.” Eara mion rakéke. — “I was afraid for you.” Títara jawen bákeon kéenai. — “The mother loves her son.” 3. The suffixes -nko and -ain mean “to” and indicate the subject’s destination. The suffix -nko is added to nouns with an even number of syllables ending in a non- nasalized, unstressed vowel, while -ain is added to nouns ending in a stressed nasalized

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.2 Postpositional Suffixes
t:
vowel, a consonant, or having an odd number of syllables. They are alternate forms with the same meaning, as shown below:
Eara kakónko kái. — “I am going to kako.” Eara Ikitóain kái. — “I am going to Iquitos.” Eara iáin kái. — “I am going to the lake.” Note that the word iaín “to the lake” in the last example is a combination of the suffix -ain with ián “lake.” The word ián loses its final n when -ain is added, since the final n of the suffix already marks nasalization for the entire word. The a before the n of ián likewise disappears before the initial vowel of -ain.

h: Grammar Sketch 4 Suffixes Indicating Place of Origin
t:
The suffixes -a, -nia, -oa, -mea, -kea indicate that the complement is the place of origin of the subject or direct object. The place of origin may be expressed by either an adverb or a locative noun. The suffix -a is attached to an adverb, as in:
Eara nénoa iki. — “I am from here.” Eara kakónkonia iki. — “I am from kako.” The locative noun káko first takes the suffixed form kakónko before receiving the suffix -nia.
The suffix -oa is added after -ain, as in:
Eara Ikitoainoa iki. — “I am from Iquitos.” The suffix -mea is added after a nasalized vowel (the nasalizing n disappears before the suffix), as in:
Jánra jemámea báke béke. — “He brought his son from the village.” The suffix -kea is added after the consonant š or after a non-nasalized vowel, as in:
Enra xóbo chichókea binón béke. — “I brought aguajes from inside the house.” Regarding the suffixes -mea and -kea, note first that they may also be attached to a postposition itself (for example meran “inside,” with the final n deleted), as in:
Enra níi meramea binón béke. — “I brought aguajes from the forest.” 2) When these suffixes are added directly to the noun, the noun appears in its non- basic form (with the final nremoved), as in the following sentence:
Náto íamamea yápa riki. — “This is a fish from the lake.” 5. The final suffix -ax is added to the complement of origin; that is, to a noun that already carries one of the suffixes -a, -nia, -oa, -mea or -kea. This combination indicates

h: Grammar Sketch 4 Suffixes Indicating Place of Origin
t:
that the complement is the place from which the subject comes, as in:
Jara íamameax jóke. — “He came from the lake.” Notice that the final a of -mea disappears before the initial a of -ax (that is, -mea + -ax is reduced to -meax).
6. Two other important suffixes are -ya, -yaton (“with” or “having,” expressing possession) and -oma, -omatonin(“without,” expressing absence). Although -ya and -omaare properly classified as adjectival suffixes, they may also be considered here. Their contrast is illustrated below:
Bákeya riki ea. — “I am with my children,” or “I have children.” Bákeoma riki ea. — “I am without my children,” or “I do not have children.” Notice that when the suffix -ya has a descriptive meaning, it may optionally be omitted. Thus one may say Náto bakén yorá tsišaya iki or Náto bakén yorá tsiša ikiwith the same meaning: “The body of this child has (is covered with) freckles.”

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.3 Reflexive verb suffixes
t:
The suffixes used to convert a transitive verb into a reflexive intransitive verb, mentioned earlier in §7.4.1, are added directly to the verb root. They include:
1. -kaaadded to roots ending in a with two or three syllables, as in nátaakaati“to empty oneself” (from nataa“to empty”).
2. -kooadded to two-syllable roots ending in o or ot, as in réokooti“to turn oneself over” (from reo-“to turn”).
3. -eeadded to two-syllable roots ending in es, esh, or ex, as in ménexeeti“to tie one's hand” (from menex-“to tie the hand”).
4. The suffix -ii is added to three-syllable roots whose final vowel is i or to roots ending in is, iš, ix, os, osh, or ox, as in máchošiitii “to hit oneself on the head” (from the root machosh- “to hit on the head”).
5. The suffix -mee is added to roots ending in the nasal consonant n and to three- syllable roots, as in tarameeti “to roll oneself around” (from taran- “to roll”), and ménatexmeeti “to bite one's own hand” (from menatex-“to bite the hand”).
6. The suffix -oo is added to three-syllable roots ending in o, as in máxkorooti “to cut one's own hair” (from maxkoro- “to cut the hair”).
7. The suffix -kee is added to two-syllable roots ending in e or et, as in pápekeeti “to make a hole in one's own ear” (from papet- “to make a hole in the ear of”).
8. The suffix -kii is added to two-syllable roots ending in i, it, or -ot, as in méchokiitii “to wash one's hands” (from mechot- “to wash the hands”).
9. The suffix -t is added to

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.3 Reflexive verb suffixes
t:
certain roots that shift the stress from the first to the second syllable and sometimes change the final vowel, as shown below:
• nókoti → nokóti — “to find; to arrive” • síkati → sikíti — “to paint; to paint oneself” Notice that the suffix -t does not always create a reflexive verb. In some cases (for example, nokóti “to arrive”), the derived verb is simply intransitive rather than reflexive.
Each reflexive suffix also has a pre-vocalic form ending in t. Thus, -kaa becomes -kaat before a following vowel-initial suffix. For example, nátaakaatai “it empties itself” contains the pre-vocalic form -kaat before the final suffix -ai. Compare this with nátaakaake “it emptied itself,” where the ordinary form -kaa appears.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.4 The Negative Suffix
t: The negative suffix has two forms, -ma and -yama. Both mean “not,” but each functions in different types of constructions.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.4.1 The Form -ma: Function and Syntax
t:
The form -ma is added to nouns, adjectives, infinitives and participles of verbs, adverbs, and postpositions. Examples of this negative suffix follow on the next page.
Jaíma riki. — “It is not there.” Nokon wétsama riki. — “He is not my brother.” In some cases, when the suffix is attached to an already suffixed word, the two elements form a compound word. These combinations can be seen in words such as jakóma“bad” (“not good”), ánima “small” (“not large”), and yóitima “disobedient” (“not obedient”). Some of these forms appear as dictionary headwords.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.4.2 The Form -yama: Verbal Suffix
t:
The form -yama functions exclusively as the negative suffix of the verb within the verbal phrase, as in:
¡káyamawe! — “Don't go!”

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.5 The suffix -painon (“hopefully”)
t:
The suffix -painon forms part of a construction similar to the compound noun but carries the meaning of “hopefully” or “may it be so.” When added to a verbal root, the two elements form a compound noun. This noun serves as the subject of the verb riki (“to be”) in an indicative sentence. The construction states that the action expressed by the verbal root plus -painon represents a wish.
Bénxopainon riki. — “Hopefully he gets better.” A person is said to be a bénxopainon, that is, someone who, according to the wish being expressed, should come to be bénxo (“getting better”). The suffix -painon contributes the sense of desire conveyed in English by “hopefully” or “may...”.

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.6 Suffixes Added to More Than One Part of Speech
t:
Some suffixes function as modifiers for more than one part of speech. They express a wide variety of meanings adaptable to different grammatical functions.
1. -bicho means “only, just” and is added to nouns, pronouns, and verbs, as in eabicho, nokon wétsabicho, yóibichoai (“only me,” “only my brother,” and “he only speaks”).
2. -kaya has several meanings. When added to a verb, noun, or pronoun, it can mean “actually” or “in fact,” as illustrated on the following page.
Enra ja bíkayake. — “I actually received it.” Jakayara nokóke. — “He actually is the one who arrived.” 3. -koma When added to a verb infinitive, this suffix forms an adjective meaning “difficult” or “impossible,” as in bítikoma “impossible to obtain” and onántikoma “difficult to know.” When added to a noun, it can mean “bad,” as in jónikoma “bad man.” 4. -res The suffix means “no more.” It may be added to adjectives, nouns, pronouns, and verbs, often together with other suffixes, as in jakóntanibires or jakónbirestani “only a little better,” eares “no longer I,” and káresai “he goes away no more.” 5. -ribi, -riba These alternate forms (used according to whether the word has an even or odd number of syllables) mean “again” or “also.” They attach to verbs, nouns, pronouns, and adjectives, as in oínribike “looked again,” biríbake “also received,” earibi “me too,” and jaskáribi “that way too.” 6. -shaman / -yora These intensive superlative suffixes (with variant -ira) mean “very,” “much,” or “well.” They attach to adjectives and verb roots. Examples include jakónyora or jakónshaman “very good,” chéxayorake “hurt a lot,” and

h: Grammar Sketch 8.3.6 Suffixes Added to More Than One Part of Speech
t:
áxeshamanai “learns well.” In addition, -shaman appears in compounds such as jáwekeskashaman “exactly like,” and xóboshaman “large, fine house,” expressing superlative intensity.
7. -shoko The diminutive suffix (“-ito/-little”) is added to adjectives and nouns. In some cases it changes the meaning enough to create a new compound word.
Compare báke “child” / bákeshoko “little child,” jakón “good” / jakónshoko “pretty,” kírika “book” / kírikashoko “little book,” and pápa “father” / pápashoko “grandfather.” The final pair especially illustrates the semantic shift.
8. -tani This suffix means “a little” or “barely.” It is added to adjectives and verbs, as in jakóntani “a little better,” and in the following sentence:
Eara kéentanike. — “I liked it a little,” or “I barely liked it.” 9. -tian is a suffix that carries the force of “when” in certain subordinate verbs. It is also added to some adjectives, nouns, pronouns, and adverbs. In these cases, the word together with the suffix -tian forms a temporal adverb. As with subordinate verbs, the suffix has the meaning of “when.” This can be seen in the following pairs:
• máxko "boy"; máxkotian "during boyhood" • báke "child"; báketian "during childhood" • bári "sun"; báritian "during the summer" • moa "already"; moátian "formerly" • ja "that"; játian "then" • jáwe "what"; jáwetian "when" Because the suffix -tian changes the part of speech—and, to some extent, the meaning of the word as shown in the last examples—it is classified here as a derivational suffix.

h: Dictionary: Guidelines For The Use Of The Shipibo
t: DICTIONARY

h: Grammar Sketch 1 The introductory term and the lexical form of the dictionary entry
t:
Each entry in the Dictionary, arranged alphabetically, has as its subject a single “term” (word, prefix, or suffix), and it is treated in the traditional manner explained in this brief introduction. The introductory term (also called the “entry term” or “headword”) appears in the form considered the most basic, in boldface, at the beginning of the entry. This form, which appears at the beginning of each dictionary entry, is called the “lexical form” or “citation form” because it is used for reference. Among introductory terms, prefixes and suffixes appear without an accent, just as certain words that are pronounced without stress. For example, the following terms would appear in separate parts of the Dictionary in the following order:
• ábion… • nokon… • -ke… • ra-… Suffixes and prefixes are identified by the hyphen placed at the beginning or the end, as appropriate. If a suffix and a prefix are spelled the same way, the prefix is listed first. If two words are spelled the same, the word whose accent occurs earlier is written first:
• ma-… • -ma… • máwati… • mawáti… The lexical or introductory form of a verb, which serves as the headword, is the infinitive ending in -ti (mawáti, as in the example). The introductory form for nouns, pronouns, and adjectives is the so-called basic form, which is the shortest form (for example, poró rather than pórokan). The introductory or citation form of an adverb that has two alternative forms is the one that agrees with the intransitive verb (for example, jaínoax rather than jaínxon). Likewise, the introductory

h: Grammar Sketch 1 The introductory term and the lexical form of the dictionary entry
t:
form of a suffix that has two alternative forms is the shorter one (for example, -bix rather than -binix).
The Variant or Irregular Form of the Introductory Term When an introductory term has a variant (a form with the same meaning but somewhat different in pronunciation or spelling from the introductory form) or an irregular form, it is placed immediately after the introductory term. A regional variant is preceded by one of the abbreviations koni. (konibo), pish. (Pishuibo), or xet. (xetebo) if the variation corresponds to one of these regional varieties:
jabón koni. janbón...
If the variant is not regional but belongs to the common speech of all regions, it is preceded by tb. (“also”):
pítsokori tb. kopítsori...
An irregular form is preceded by its corresponding abbreviation (pl. or another):
káti pl. bóti...

h: Grammar Sketch 2 Part of Speech (Word Class)
t:
Following the introductory term and its variants, the part of speech (word class) always appears as an abbreviation in italics: s. (noun), pron. (pronoun), adj.
(adjective), v. i.(intransitive verb), v. t. (transitive verb), adv. (adverb), posp.
(postposition), conj. (conjunction), interj.(interjection). If the introductory term is a prefix or suffix, the abbreviation is sf. or pf. as appropriate, followed by the remaining words and abbreviations that classify the prefix or suffix:
ábion s.
-ke sf. vbl.
ra- pf. modif.
The abbreviations vbl. and modif. stand for “verbal” and “modifier.” If a word has two grammatical functions, it appears as a single dictionary entry with two part-of- speech abbreviations:
rastón s. y adj....
Then, in the normal format, each part-of-speech abbreviation appears a second time, immediately before the meaning or meanings that correspond to it:
rastón s. y adj. s.: thickness… adj. 1: thick…

h: Grammar Sketch 3 The Principal Form
t:
If the dictionary word is a noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, or, in some cases, an adverb or suffix, it will be presented not only in its basic form but also in a second form called the “principal form.” This second form shows an ending or principal suffix added to the root or basic form of the word. In addition, entries for certain adverbs and suffixes that have a second form longer than the basic form include this alternative as the principal form. Principal forms provide a fuller description of the word (or suffix) in the entry. Nouns, pronouns, and adjectives are presented with their non-basic form as the principal form; verbs with their past participle; adverbs with their transitive agreement form; and suffixes with their longest written form as the principal form. For an entire class of suffixes, the principal form is the one added to a root having an even number of syllables. When present, the principal form follows the part-of-speech label and, like the introductory form, appears in bold.
ábion s. ábionin… mawáti v. i. máwata… -anan sf. vbl. -ananan… Variant of the Principal Form Like the introductory form, the principal form may also have a variant or an irregular form following it. A variant is preceded by the same abbreviations used with the introductory form:
awápa s. awápan koni. awápanin… If the introductory term has a variant or an irregular form, the principal form normally has the corresponding one as well:
jabón koni. janbón s. jáboman koni. jánboman… káti pl. bóti v. i. káa pl. boá…

h: Grammar Sketch 4 Etymology
t:
The information that appears, where appropriate, in brackets and before the definition of the word is called the “etymology.” The etymology of this Dictionary will present a morphological analysis (of the form) of the word, or it will indicate the Spanish or Quechua origin of the entry term or one of its subentries (see section 8, which discusses subentries).
If the information begins with the formula “from Ship.” (Shipibo), the data that follow identify the constituent elements of the entry word. Whenever possible, these elements are identified in Shipibo. When this is not possible, a suggestive comparison is provided—for example, with a word that is probably related in both form and meaning. If, on the other hand, the information includes the formula “from Span.” (Spanish) or “from Quech.” (Quechua), it means that the entry word was borrowed into Shipibo from the language indicated. The source word or element, whether Shipibo, Spanish, or Quechua, is written in italics and followed by a brief Spanish gloss. The following examples illustrate the etymology of one native term and two borrowed terms:
awájora s. awájoran [from Ship. awá "sachavaca" + jóra "seed"] : species of tree… sánto s. santón [from Span. santo]… átipanti v. i. y v. t. [from Quech. atipay, atipan "power"] : power If the etymology simply says "from Span." without a gloss, it indicates that the original Spanish form is the one appearing in the following definition, identical or very similar to the introductory term:
ábion s. ábionin [from Span.]… : airplane… The etymology is not part of the definition of the dictionary entry;

h: Grammar Sketch 4 Etymology
t: that is, the glosses in brackets are not used to define the entry itself. It is common, however, for the meaning of the source term to be the same as that of the entry word, as in the last example.

h: Grammar Sketch 5 The Definition
t:
The definition, or equivalent meaning in Spanish, follows the etymology and then the principal form with its variant; or, if these are absent, it follows the part of speech. A definition of a Shipibo word consists of at least one Spanish equivalent, which may be: (1) a single-word substitution in Spanish, or (2) an explanation of the meaning with a phrase in Spanish, always preceded by a bold colon, as in the following two examples:
bína s. binán : wasp astó adj. ástokan : full of thread If the definition includes more than one equivalent meaning, all equivalents are separated by bold colons and are treated as synonyms:
kanóti s. canótinin : crossbowman : bow...
There are two ways to indicate that a dictionary entry has more than one meaning.
The most common is to include at least two numbered definitions:
béne s. benén 1: male... 2: husband : spouse The other method is to indicate a meaning closely associated with the previous one by means of the "sense separators" específ. (“specifically”) or tb. (“also”). The separator específ. marks a more restricted use and, in many cases, the principal use of the preceding meaning; tb. marks a distinct but closely related meaning.
mesó s. ... : portion; específ. : handful : bundle masén s. ...1: squash; tb. : squash fruit 2: *huingo; tb. : inedible fruit of the *huingo

h: Grammar Sketch 6 Usage Note
t:
Whenever a usage note accompanies a word definition, it is placed immediately after that definition. It is introduced by a dash followed by the word “Use.” The note may provide guidance about grammar, regional or cultural usage, co- occurrence with other words, or restrictions on current usage of that meaning, as in the following examples:
astó adj. ... : full of thread —Use: Use when referring, for example, to a spindle or bobbin.
ashón adv. ... : very : more —Use: Used mainly among xetebo speakers.
áti v. t. ... 3: say —Use: Use with a direct quotation as the direct object.
poínkoskon kencha s. ... : kneecap —Use: Rarely used today.
If a second usage note follows the first, it has the same format:
jáwetio adv. : how much (size or distance)? —Use as an interrogative word. —Use with an adjective or adverb indicating size or distance.
Sometimes the usage note is used instead of a word definition:
-a sf. vbl.
—Use attached to the end of the verb...
Níma s. Nimán ...
—Use as a masculine personal name.
A usage note may also appear in place of the definition among the numbered senses of an entry:
pápa s. papán 1: father : dad...
—Use the vocative form “papá” when addressing one's father...
2: male relatives...
In some cases, a second usage note is added to a usage note that substitutes for the definition in order to provide additional guidance:
-pan sf. vbl.
—Use attached to the end of the verb with the meaning “to be able to” or “to have permission.” —Use in the sentence as a marker of the interrogative mood.

h: Grammar Sketch 7 Verbal Illustration of the Definition
t:
If the definition of a word, or its substitute, includes a verbal illustration, consisting of a word, phrase, or sentence offered as an example, it is placed immediately after the definition or after the last usage note. The verbal illustration appears inside angle brackets (<...>) and includes the illustrative Shipibo text in bold, followed by its Spanish translation:
ábion s. ábionin [from Span.] : airplane ⟨Rimámea ápo ábionin jóketianra noa rárorke. When the President came from Lima by airplane, we were happy.⟩ If there is more than one verbal illustration, they are presented consecutively:
ke- pf. modif. ...6: in the mouth : on both lips ⟨kempís of foul breath⟩ ⟨kekóx of a strong blow⟩ ⟨kewínti to answer energetically⟩ Note that the translations of the examples are not intended to be literal (as a learning aid), but rather free translations that express the Shipibo text in natural Spanish with the correct and clear meaning, without following Shipibo grammatical structure. Certain Shipibo words remain untranslated, and in a few cases words may be added in translation that are not present in the Shipibo text but help the reader understand the meaning of the example. For example:
