aménwaka s. ... : Amawaca ⟨Aménwaka jónibora ráomis iki. The Amahuaca have the custom of practicing sorcery with plant poisons.⟩ The translation provides broader information than the words of the Shipibo example. It could simply be translated as “The Amahuaca are vegetarians,” but in this case the meaning of the translation would be less specific.

h: Grammar Sketch 8 The Subentry
t:
If there are subentries, they will consist of phrases or compound words that follow the final verbal illustration of the headword and will appear in bold. Both the subentry and the headword have their own definition and, in many cases, a verbal illustration that follows it. Normally an etymology is placed between the compound word or subentry phrase and its definition.
There are two classes of subentries: the first consists of compound nouns, and the second of phrases that typically include the headword together with another word.
Subentries of the first class are generally defined as species or kinds of the headword:
bína s. binán : wasp ⟨Bína méeyamawe; miara tékanake. Do not disturb the wasps; they may sting you.⟩ boshibína [from Ship. …] : species of long-bodied wasp kóyobína [from Ship. …] : species of wasp resembling the ant called kóyo in color and size chánabína [from Ship. …] : species of wasp choríshbína [from Ship. chorísh 'hard' + bína …] : species of wasp The second class consists of phrases that typically include the headword together with another word, in a verb + noun combination:
mátsi s. matsín 1: cold; cold weather; specif.: winter ⟨Nato oxénra mátsi pakénoxiki; jáskara kopíra non károai. This month will be cold; therefore we will prepare firewood.⟩ matsín áti [from Ship. mátsi, matsín 'cold' + áti 'do'] : to feel cold.
—Use with the subject meaning “cold” and the complement indicating the one who feels the cold.
⟨Enra yonáke. Eara matsín ákai. Since I have a fever, I feel cold.⟩ mátsi íti … : to become cold.
mátsi jíkiti [from

h: Grammar Sketch 8 The Subentry
t:
Ship. mátsi 'cold' + jíkiti 'enter'] : for rheumatism to appear or begin.
kírika s. kírikanin … : paper kírika yóyoati [from Ship. kírika 'paper' + yóyoati 'make speak'] : to read.
Note that the normal placement of a subentry is under the article of its first word.
kírika… kírika yóyoati… Note also that some phrases that could be placed as subentries are instead entered as separate dictionary articles:
wishtín s. wíshtiman : star wishtín mexoai s. … : artificial satellite

h: Grammar Sketch 9 References
t: The references presented in the Dictionary are of four types: basic, subentry, synonym, and grammatical. Basic and subentry references present word variants that appear in bold in the alphabetical list, but instead of the information of a full entry, only a note reading “See” (followed by a headword in bold) is given. This note directs the reader to the introductory form of the entry containing the corresponding information for the referenced form.

h: Grammar Sketch 9.1 Basic reference
t:
The reference called the basic or simple reference presents the variant form of a dictionary word in alphabetical order. This form, as the introductory term of the reference, is followed by the word “See” and the corresponding headword.
Information about the variant will be included under that headword:
kopítsori See pítsokori pítsokori tb. copítsori… : matamata…

h: Grammar Sketch 9.2 Subentry reference for compound nouns
t:
Subentries whose introductory form is a compound noun will have corresponding subentry references placed in the alphabetical position of the compound noun. This reference simply directs the reader to the dictionary entry under which the subentry will be found. The following examples illustrate this type of reference:
ániparanta See under paránta paránta s. … : plantain ániparanta [from Ship. …] : cooking plantain

h: Grammar Sketch 9.3 Paragraph or Synonym List Reference
t:
Most terms, except the introductory term, which appears in a synonym paragraph (see section 10), also have reference entries at the end of the corresponding dictionary article. The reference begins on a new line with the abbreviation sinón.
followed by the words “See under” and the introductory term of the synonym paragraph in bold:
áyahuasca s. … : *ayahuasca… sinón. AYAHUASCA, NISHI, ONI may denote ayahuasca… óni s. onín : *ayahuasca… sinón. See under áyahuasca Many simple lists of synonyms are also presented. The reference begins on a new line with the abbreviation sinón.followed by the synonyms. However, the complete list is not always repeated in every related entry.
In some cases an entry with more than one meaning includes both a synonym paragraph and a synonym list.
áko adj. … 1: thin : slender… 2: dried out… 3: empty… sinón. AKO, WIRISH, OSHI, SHEPA all… sinón. jáwebioma wirísh adj. … thin… sinón. See under áko jáwebioma adj. … 2: empty sinón. áko

h: Grammar Sketch 9.4 Grammatical Reference
t:
The reference “See Grammatical Outline” followed by a section number at the end of an entry directs the user to the corresponding section of the grammatical outline for further grammatical information.
-we sf. imperat. … See Grammatical Outline4.2.3.1; 4.2.3.2

h: Grammar Sketch 9.5 The Asterisk (*) or Obelisk (†) as a Reference
t:
The asterisk is placed before a term as a reference device in the definition, etymology, or translation of a verbal illustration. It identifies a word typical of Peruvian Spanish and directs the reader to the glossary of regional vocabulary in Appendix A of the second part of this volume. The obelisk (†) identifies a geographical place in the region and directs the reader to the list of regional geographical locations in Appendix B for brief information.
ábion s. ábionin... : avioneta ⟨Kashíboainoa ábionbora... Todas las avionetas en †Kashibokocha...⟩ bokón s. bókoman : *cetico...

h: Grammar Sketch 10 The Synonym Paragraph
t:
If a synonym paragraph is present, it appears as the final part of the article. It begins with the abbreviation sinón.followed by a list of synonyms written in capital letters. The brief explanation that follows indicates the meaning shared by the synonyms and any differences in meaning or usage.
áyahuasca s. áyahuascan ... : *ayahuasca...
sinón. AYAHUASCA, NISHI, ONI may all denote ayahuasca. AYAHUASCA and NISHI are used in Shipibo speech to refer both to the drink and the plant; ONI, however, is little used. In Konibo speech NISHI refers to the vine, ONI to the derived substance, and AYAHUASCA is infrequent.
It is important to note that in this bilingual dictionary the concept of synonym is special and innovative. In the example above, the three Shipibo words can all be translated into Spanish the same way; therefore they are 'translation synonyms.' A Shipibo speaker, however, will not necessarily recognize them as synonyms. For example, JENE and OMPÁX can both be translated as 'water', but for the Shipibo speaker they refer to different kinds of water. The purpose is therefore to present groups of Shipibo words that may be translated the same way into Spanish without implying they are interchangeable in Shipibo.

h: Grammar Sketch 11 Example of a Dictionary Entry with Explanations
t:
Finally, two fully annotated dictionary articles are presented as more complete examples:
káti pl. bóti v. i. káa pl. boá 1: go; tb. go away; depart —Use the plural bóti when the subject refers to 'several', 'many', or 'a mass entity.' ⟨Pápara yómerai kawánke. Father went fishing. ⟨Níwe béketianra naikóin boá iki.
When the wind came, the clouds went away. ⟨Píshta nete sénenamabira boí íkanai, korákanin jato párana. Still not all visible on this page… ...the day of the festival, but now they are leaving because the chief deceived them.) 2: to fall (e.g. into the water) ⟨Min átapara jéne meran kánake. Careful! Your hen is going to fall into the water.⟩ —Use the form katánwe instead of kawé as the imperative.
⟨Jákiribi min xobón katánwe. Go back to your house again.⟩ See Grammar Outline 4.2.3.2.b moara ea kái also moara kái also eara moa kái [from Shipibo; lit. “I am leaving now”; from moa 'already' + -ra indicative mode suffix + ea 'I' + kái 'go', from káti 'to go'].
—Used as a farewell by the person who is leaving; the usual reply is kawé, literally “go” or “be on your way.” 1. introductory term: káti 2. variant or irregular form of the introductory term: pl. bóti 3. part-of-speech abbreviation: v. i.
4. principal form: káa 5. variant of the principal form: pl. boá 6. etymology: not present in this article 7. definition 1: to go; also: to leave; to depart 8. verbal illustration of definition 1: ⟨Father ... to fish.⟩ 9. definition 2: to fall (e.g. into the water) 10. usage note: Use

t:

11. subentry: moara ea kái 12. etymology of the subentry: [from Shipibo ... moa...] 13. usage note instead of a definition for the subentry: Used as a farewell...
14. references: none in this article 15. synonym paragraph: none in this article kawánti also kawánwanti v. i. káwana also kawáwana [from Shipibo ka- 'on the back' + -wan 'recently' + -ti inflectional suffix] 1: to pass ⟨Néno ábion kawánhibake, kikínbires íshto. Yesterday a very fast airplane passed by here.⟩ 2: to move from one side to another; to go around.
—Use with a reduplicated root.
